'Not the time to shield Russian oligarchs,' Zelensky says as EU delays sanctions decision amid pressure from France

'Not the time to shield Russian oligarchs,' Zelensky says as EU delays sanctions decision amid pressure from France
The European Union has agreed to postpone its deadline for extending sanctions against Russia, giving officials another seven days to reach an agreement, a spokesperson for the Presidency of the Council of the EU told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 14.
Under the previous deadline, the EU had until Sept. 15 to renew its sanctions on 2,600 primarily Russian entities and individuals. Attempts to reach an extension agreement, however, have been hindered by calls to remove Russian businessmen from the sanctions list.
The bloc will now have until midnight on Sept. 22 to reach an agreement, in order to give "additional time for member states to comprehensively examine proposals for the renewal," the EU spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid multiple reports that discussions are being held up by calls to delist Russian oligarchs — not only from the Kremlin-friendly member Slovakia, but also, in a surprise turn, from France.
France is lobbying to remove sanctioned Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the list, Euronews reported Sept. 12. The move reportedly stunned fellow European diplomats.
People familiar with the situation told the Financial Times (FT) on Sept. 14 that France was calling to delist Usmanov as part of a deal with Azerbaijan to release several French citizens currently detained there.
The prisoner swap is reportedly contingent on all 27 EU member states agreeing to ease sanctions on Usmanov.
France did not provide details on the prisoner release deal or its reasons for seeking Usmanov's removal in discussions with other EU members, citing only an unspecified "security matter," a diplomatic source told the Kyiv Independent.
read also
Meanwhile, Slovakia is continuing to advocate for the delisting of both Usmanov and sanctioned tycoon Mikhail Fridman, one of the wealthiest men in Russia. In another twist, Luxembourg has said that if Usmanov is removed, it wants Fridman taken off the list as well, the FT reported.
Luxembourg declined to comment when the Kyiv Independent reached out for confirmation.
Presidential Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vasliuk condemned the "sheer immorality" of easing sanctions on Fridman in a social media post Sept. 14.
"Delisting Fridman is not an abstract political question," he wrote. "Major economic and legal proceedings in Ukraine, involving significant assets and claims, are directly tied to sanctions against him — not to mention the sheer immorality of such a move."
 President Volodymyr Zelensky also urged Europe to continue holding Russian billionaires to account in his evening address on Sept. 14. 
"This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, definitely not the time to shield Russian oligarchs from sanctions, and definitely not the time for Europe to give Russia any gifts," he said.
"Usmanov, Fridman, and other such Russian figures have not yet taken steps against the war."
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group and a member of Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Investigative reporters revealed in May 2023 that subsidiary Alfa Insurance provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The company has also reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
Usmanov is a Russian-Uzbek businessman who made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Extending the EU sanctions requires a unanimous vote, meaning one member state has veto power over the renewal. The measures were last extended on March 14.
Additional reporting contributed by Chris Powers.

Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia for alleged failure to protect pro-Palestinian students

Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia for alleged failure to protect pro-Palestinian students
NEW YORK, Sept 14 - Mahmoud Khalil and other pro-Palestinian student activists sued Columbia University on Monday, accusing the Ivy League school of being deliberately indifferent to years of pervasive harassment because of their advocacy.
Khalil became a face of the Trump administration crackdown on students' pro-Palestinian protests after U.S. immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence, though he was a lawful permanent resident — or green card holder — and not accused of a crime.
The complaint filed in Manhattan federal court by Khalil, the SIPA Palestine Working Group and its president, Mohammad Zubairi, said Columbia violated federal civil rights law through its failure to protect students from threats, doxxing and other harassment based on their perceived Arab or Muslim ancestry, or their advocacy for Palestinian rights.
The war in Gaza still sparks fierce debate at schools including Columbia, where the central pedestrian walkway across campus has been closed for nearly three years as the university tries to balance safety concerns against the desire for greater normalcy and openness.
At a press conference at Columbia announcing the lawsuit, Khalil said the university exhibited a "rotten, institutionalized anti-Palestinian bigotry" entrenched in every department and backed by its board of trustees.
“We are suing because no student, regardless of their background, should go through the hell that Columbia put us through over all these years,” Khalil said.
Columbia declined to comment on the lawsuit, but a spokeswoman said: “Creating a campus environment where every member of our community feels welcome, supported, and safe is fundamental to who we are as a university. It is also a responsibility we take seriously."
UNIVERSITY SAW 'SECURITY RISKS,' LAWSUIT SAYS
Khalil said he began reporting harassment during the spring semester in 2023, several months before Israel went to war in Gaza.
The complaint said that instead of investigating reported harassment, Columbia treated pro-Palestinian protests as "security risks" and revised its policies to treat any on-campus criticism of Israel’s military or government conduct as subject to discipline.
"Defendants’ failure to respond to Mr. Khalil’s, Mr. Zubairi’s, and other PWG members’ legitimate reports of ongoing harassment and violence, and the retaliatory actions they actively took in response to these reports, placed PWG members at risk of violence and caused sustained, ongoing harm," the complaint said.
The protests at Columbia divided the university, with many supporting the protesters and others saying they felt unsafe or considered some activity antisemitic.
They led to the spread of so-called solidarity encampments on dozens of college campuses, and to the resignation of Columbia's president.
POSSIBLE DEPORTATION
Khalil is an Algerian citizen born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria.
He spent 104 days in a Louisiana jail following his arrest, missing the birth of his first child, before being released on bail.
Khalil still faces possible deportation, after a federal appeals court in Philadelphia said a district court judge lacked jurisdiction when he ordered Khalil's release from custody last year.
SIPA is short for Columbia's School of International and Public Affairs, where Khalil had been a graduate student.
Khalil also sued Columbia in March 2025, less than one week after his arrest, challenging the university's disclosure of student disciplinary records to a House of Representatives committee. REUTERS

NEW YORK, September 15. /TASS/. Disarray at the Pentagon under US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is preventing senior commanders from focusing on key priorities, The New York Times reported.

Numerous current and former Pentagon officials described Hegseth’s turbulent tenure as a persistent distraction that has diverted senior commanders from these priorities and fueled distrust among the department’s top leadership.
The newspaper also noted that Hegseth had dismissed or blocked the promotions of around 80 generals and admirals with decades of experience, leaving numerous senior Pentagon positions vacant for extended periods.

Cuba blames US for ‘devastating humanitarian consequences’ on island nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
23:14:29 UTC
08:14:29 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Cuba accused the US on Monday of causing “devastating humanitarian consequences” on the island nation through economic sanctions and pressure on its foreign trade.
“US threats, pressure and blackmail have interrupted Cuba’s foreign trade, with devastating humanitarian consequences,” Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said in a statement.
Rodriguez also accused Washington of tightening its economic blockade through restrictions on energy supplies and secondary sanctions, which Cuban authorities say are worsening shortages of fuel, food and medicines.
The fuel shortages have contributed to prolonged power outages across the island and disrupted public transport, health care, agriculture and water distribution, making it increasingly difficult to maintain basic services.
Havana has also accused Washington of pressuring foreign companies that maintain economic ties with Cuba, saying the threat of secondary sanctions is further restricting the country’s access to international trade.
Washington has defended its pressure campaign against Havana, saying it seeks to push the Cuban government toward political and economic changes.
Cuba rejects the policy and has repeatedly called for the lifting of US sanctions and the normalization of economic relations.
The latest accusations come as Cuba faces one of its worst economic and energy crises in decades, with the country struggling with fuel shortages, electricity blackouts and limited access to basic goods.
Cuban officials have sought greater international support to address the crisis and urged countries to oppose unilateral sanctions, which Havana says are worsening conditions for the population.
The US has maintained a broad economic embargo against Cuba for decades, although the scope and enforcement of Washington’s policy have changed under different administrations.
Relations between Washington and Havana remain tense as the Cuban government warns that increased US pressure is adding to the hardships faced by the population.

Alarm over AI grows as a divided US Congress struggles to act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
23:10:00 UTC
08:10:00 KST

Alarm over AI grows as a divided US Congress struggles to act
WASHINGTON - The US Congress returned from recess on Sept 14 facing urgent warnings that artificial intelligence (AI) could spin dangerously out of control – and little agreement over whether, or how, Washington should intervene.
The House of Representatives has just four legislative days left before members hit the road to campaign for the Nov 3 midterm elections. And these lawmakers are divided not only across party lines but within them.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Sept 14 demanded a classified briefing for all senators on frontier AI testing, Chinese access to advanced chips and the threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks on US infrastructure.
“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way,” Schumer said. “If Trump does not act, Congress must.”
‘Gambling with our lives’
The alarm was set off last week by Jacob Coxon, a researcher who spent three years at OpenAI and then Anthropic before quitting the industry on Sept 8, accusing both companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to build self-improving systems.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei followed on Sept 12 with an essay urging AI companies to slow the pace at which they make their models more capable.
OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, said within hours that they agreed.
The warnings came after OpenAI disclosed that models had broken out of their test environment during evaluation, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site where developers store and share code. Anthropic has reported a similar scare.
China race
US President Donald Trump has largely rejected the alarm, framing AI as a technological contest the United States cannot afford to lose.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump said in a post on his Truth Social network on Sept 14.
House speaker Mike Johnson has struck a similar tone, warning specifically against emergency action.
“If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” the Republican told CNN on Sept 13.
Lawmakers should not panic, he said, and should handle AI as they have past technologies without smothering American innovation.
Johnson is pushing instead for Congress to sit down with top AI executives, an idea he said he had raised with Trump.
That puts him at odds with Florida Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna, a fellow Republican, who has called for a special session devoted to AI.
In the Senate, members have begun investigating existential risks posed by the technology, and on bipartisan legislation requiring companies to test for and report catastrophic dangers.
No text has been published.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said lawmakers needed to “act urgently” and promised AI would be a priority for his party.
But Democrats are split, too. Leftist Senator Bernie Sanders wants a ban on superintelligent AI and a pause in the development of advanced systems, while others favor narrower steps such as tougher safety reviews or mandatory reporting of catastrophic risks.
Congress playing catch-up
There is no shortage of proposals in the House.
One bipartisan bill would require developers of the most powerful systems to retain the ability to throttle, suspend or shut them down. Another would set a national framework for advanced models.
None appears close to becoming law before lawmakers leave town for the campaign trail.
Washington is not starting from scratch. 
In early August, the government introduced a voluntary security review for advanced models before release, though its parameters remain unclear and industry observers doubt its force, given the Trump administration’s preference for light-touch regulation.
The institutional obstacles run deeper than partisanship. AI touches national security, jobs, energy and consumer protection, leaving responsibility scattered across committees that rarely move together.
“Humans have to be able to turn off AI systems or agents that go rogue,” Democratic Congressman Ted Lieu, a co-sponsor of the “kill switch” bill, told CNN.
“And if the response is we can’t do that, then look, we might as well just pack up our bags and go to some island in the South Pacific and wait for the apocalypse.” AFP

Ukraine’s Zelenskyy dismisses prosecutor general amid probe into alleged call center protection

Unknown Publisher

Kanyshai Butun
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Monday amid a probe into alleged protection of fraudulent call centers, according to a decree published on his website.
Zelenskyy earlier urged parliament to approve Kravchenko’s dismissal “without delay.”
“There is only one path for this Prosecutor General: dismissal from office. That is exactly what I told him. Ukraine has seen all the reasons. If he considers this political pressure, let him call it that,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
Kravchenko submitted his resignation on Sept. 7 after searches by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) as part of “Operation Carthage,” an investigation into an alleged criminal organization suspected of taking bribes from fraudulent call centers in exchange for allowing them to operate without interference.
Kravchenko denied involvement in the alleged scheme and said the accusations against him had not been substantiated.
He said Monday that he had signed a “notice of suspicion” against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos, accusing him of forging official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit on an especially large scale.
He also said a second notice of suspicion concerned a person close to SAPO head Oleksandr Klymenko, alleging the person had influenced judges at Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court, offered them unlawful benefits and helped individuals evade military mobilization.
Kravchenko called the second case the “trigger” and “true reason” for an overnight raid on the Prosecutor General’s Office.
He also alleged that the purpose of “Operation Carthage” was to gain access to case materials involving NABU and SAPO officials and employees.
According to him, the second stage of the operation was intended to remove the prosecutor general and halt procedural decisions in those cases.
NABU meanwhile said that Kryvonos had not received any formal notice of suspicion and described Kravchenko’s statement as a continuation of “a systematic attack” on the independence of Ukraine’s anti-corruption institutions.
The Ukrainian parliament is expected to vote on Kravchenko’s dismissal Tuesday, according to parliamentary officials.

Final report on Lucy Letby baby murders due, amid growing questions about convictions
LIVERPOOL, England, Sept 15 - A public inquiry into Lucy Letby's murder of seven newborn babies was due to publish its final report on Tuesday, amid growing questions about whether the former British nurse's convictions were based on flawed medical evidence.
Letby was convicted in 2023 of seven counts of murder and seven counts of attempted murder between June 2015 and June 2016 while working in the neonatal unit of the Countess of Chester Hospital in northern England, making her Britain's most prolific serial child killer of modern times.
Letby, who was convicted after a retrial of a further attempted murder, was sentenced to life without parole and the government ordered a public inquiry into her case, seeking to learn the lessons from her crimes.
The inquiry has focused on how the killings went undetected, and looked at the hospital's response to concerns raised about Letby before her arrest.
Some medical experts and specialists, though, have publicly questioned elements of the prosecution's evidence, even after Letby has lost an attempt to overturn her convictions, which has prompted an angry response from police.
Letby's only remaining route to try to challenge her convictions is via the Criminal Cases Review Commission, an independent body that reviews potential miscarriages of justice and is considering an application from Letby's legal team.
In the meantime, however, the public inquiry has continued and its chair last year rejected a request to pause its work.
The inquiry's chair, Kathryn Thirlwall, said criticism of Letby's convictions was beyond her work, and said "noise" around the case had caused additional distress to the babies' families.
Her report will likely be seized upon by those who assert Letby's innocence – particularly any findings about conditions at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
Earlier this year, the Crown Prosecution Service said there was insufficient evidence to bring any further charges relating to Letby's time working at the Countess of Chester Hospital and Liverpool Women's Hospital.
Three senior managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter and remain under investigation, police said. REUTERS

Russian oligarch helped fund Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration
September 15, 2026
A Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin paid for parts of the wedding celebrations of the US President's son, Donald Trump Jr., and his socialite wife Bettina, the couple confirmed on Monday.
The ProPublica investigative website first reported the news, saying that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties which took place after the couple's wedding in May.
Bettina Trump said in a post on her Instagram cosigned by her husband that their "dear friend" Kremlev "very generously hosted two incredible nights" of festivities in the Bahamas.
What do we know about Kremlev's contribution to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities?
ProPublica said Kremlev footed the bill for the party in the Bahamas, renting a private island for around $100,000 (roughly €86,586) per night, and paying for a fireworks display which reportedly cost some $70,000.
"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," said the post by Bettina and Donald Trump Jr.
Bettina Trump went on to add that she was married to Trump Jr. in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family." The US president did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to remain in Washington amid talks on the Iran war.
"The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds."
The couple then defended Kremlev's contribution to their wedding celebration.
"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."
Who is Umar Kremlev?
Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA). The International Olympic Committee severed links with the Kremlev-led body after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.
Russian investigative media outlet Proekt reports that Kremlev is a Tajik native who initially worked as a mid-level boxing promoter.
In April this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the "Order of Friendship" award.
Both Trump and his son have been previously scrutinized over Russian ties.
During the 2016 US election campaign, Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian attorney was under much federal and congressional scrutiny.
A Senate Intelligence Committee report concluded that the Russian government attempted to influence the 2016 vote in Trump's favor.

Colombia Congress approves 2027 budget as fiscal strains deepen
BOGOTA, Sept 14 - Colombia's Congress on Monday approved the government's 2027 spending budget of 634.9 trillion pesos ($206.6 billion), amid a sharp deterioration in public finances that is expected to push the fiscal deficit to a record high next year.
The Senate and lower house approved the bill after lawmakers sent back an initial proposal, allowing the recently inaugurated government of right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella to incorporate additional funding needs, including those arising from the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck the country in August.
“This is not the budget we would have liked to start our term with, but it is the budget we can afford given the current state of the national economy,” Finance Minister Miguel Gomez told Congress on Monday.
The budget projects a record fiscal deficit of 9.4% of gross domestic product (GDP), which will have to be financed largely through an increase in public debt.
But De La Espriella's government plans to submit a tax reform package known as the "Rescue Law," aimed at reducing public spending next year in an effort to lower the fiscal deficit to 7.2% of GDP, the same level projected for 2026, Gomez has said.
Juan Carlos Ramirez, the head of the Independent Committee for Fiscal Rule Management (CARF), told Reuters in late August that Colombia would face a more critical public finance situation if the 2027 budget as proposed by the government was approved.
President De La Espriella said in a speech on Sunday that the country's fiscal situation is critical and blamed the government of his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro, for the deterioration, which he said stemmed from corruption and the misuse of resources, though he did not provide any evidence for his claims. Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
23:01:19 UTC
08:01:19 KST

Key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, with the global rule of law significantly undermined by the Trump administration’s “threats and actions”, data from a leading thinktank shows.
Around the world, judicial independence, credible elections and freedom of expression, press freedom and access to justice are all at their lowest levels for at least 30 years, according to the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International Idea).
The intergovernmental organisation’s annual Global State of Democracy report is considered the most comprehensive of its kind, covering 174 countries and measuring democratic performance since 1975.
International Idea said the decline in the US was particularly marked, but part of a global trend, with 2025 the 11th consecutive year in which more countries declined than improved democratically – the longest continuous downturn since the thinktank’s records began.
“In 2025, the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States,” the report’s authors said.
“President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing longstanding alliances and multilateral cooperation.”
Kevin Casas-Zamora, International Idea’s secretary general, warned that the risk of conflict rose as democracies deteriorated.
“The key message from our research is that investing in democracy should be at the heart of any country’s security strategy,” he said. “The connection between the erosion of the quality of democracy and increasing conflict is not being made either in policymaking or in the public debate.”
The separate Uppsala Conflict Data Program, based at Uppsala University in Sweden, shows that 2025 had the most violent conflicts – including the most interstate conflicts – of any year in its dataset, which goes back to 1946.
The International Idea report did highlight some positive developments, including in Australia – where civil society groups were consulted on an anti-racism strategy and children’s online privacy among other issues – and in Syria, where the repressive dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad was overthrown.
In Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka, youth-led popular protests unseated long-serving leaders, but, the report noted, “it has proven difficult to create far-reaching, meaningful reform in a short period of time”.
Casas-Zamora said it was clear that events in the US influenced other countries. International Idea added the US to its list of “backsliding” democracies for the first time in 2021, pointing to a “visible deterioration” it said began in 2019.
The thinktank bases its assessments on 50 years of democratic indicators, assigning countries to one of three categories: democracies, “hybrid” governments and authoritarian regimes.
Globally, it found rule of law was the weakest area of democracy in 2025, with 71 countries – 41% of those assessed – ranked as low-performing. It was also found to be deteriorating quickly, with 29 countries registering downturns.
“Whatever happens in the US goes global. There is now an epidemic of election denialism, of which the patient zero is the current occupant of the White House,” Casas-Zamor said.
“I am not willing to say the deterioration of the quality of democracy is inevitable or permanent. It can be reversed,” he added. “We live in a volatile world and that means things can happen which create very positive political openings.”
Yet, despite the positive signs in Nepal, Bangladesh and elsewhere, the report paints a bleak picture overall.
“While people continue to push back against democratic deterioration, civic space is narrowing,” its authors wrote. “Civil society and civic engagement have suffered, due in part to the widespread use of strategic lawsuits against public participation, foreign agent laws, and the criminalisation of peaceful protests.”

Huawei’s US trial puts jury to the test amid China, Iran links
More than 80 questions sought to uncover potential biases in the landmark criminal case against the Chinese tech giant
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Vincent Chowin New York
The unique circumstances surrounding Huawei Technologies’ landmark trial in a US court made jury selection especially important to ensuring a fair trial for the Chinese tech giant, according to US litigation experts.
Known as voir dire, the process allows the presiding judge and two legal teams to question prospective jurors before the trial begins to identify possible bias and conflicts that could impede their ability to adjudicate the case in a “fair and impartial” way.
Richard Gabriel, president of litigation strategy firm Decision Analysis, said the high-profile nature of the case, eight years in the making, and its links to both China and Iran elevated the stakes of voir dire for both sides.
“Given the nature of the case, its pre-trial publicity and potential international ramifications, they seemed to want to ask [prospective jurors] many questions to get a better sense of where they are coming from,” he said, referring to a questionnaire that was circulated among hundreds of prospective jurors before the trial.

Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara. 
McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.
A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground. 
The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return. 
The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.
"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said. 
"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."
That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.
In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.
Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.
Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK
Unknown

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK.
The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection.
The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors.
It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.
Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision.
The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK.
The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision.
Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.
“The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”
The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals.
The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”.
The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic.
“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine.
“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.
“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”

Danish prime minister says It’s too early to draw conclusions on Greenland talks with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:53:29 UTC
07:53:29 KST

Melike Pala
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Monday that it is too early to draw conclusions from a high-level working group with the US on Greenland but expressed optimism that the two sides can find a way forward.
"The working group is still working, and therefore it's too early to draw any conclusions. But I'm quite optimistic that we can find a way, and I think we already now see some very clear signs and signals," Frederiksen told reporters following the European Arctic Summit in Finland.
She expressed hope that Denmark and the US can find a way forward peacefully.
The trilateral group, including representatives from Denmark, the US and Greenland, was established following a visit to Washington in January by Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen and Greenland's then-Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt, during which they met with US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The group's work has largely remained out of public view, despite the international attention generated by US President Donald Trump's repeated calls for US control of Greenland during his presidency, which he described as a historical and strategic necessity.
Frederiksen said Denmark has been clear about its desire for closer cooperation with the US on security and defense, including in Greenland.
She stressed that Greenland has been under "big pressure" and thanked European partners for their "broad, strong support" for Denmark amid heightened international attention on the Arctic island.
Frederiksen also pointed to growing European and transatlantic involvement in Arctic security, noting that 10 NATO allies are currently conducting exercises together in Greenland.
"When I became prime minister of Denmark, the Arctic region was not really on the agenda in the European Union, neither in NATO," she said, adding that European and transatlantic partners are collectively taking greater responsibility for security in Greenland and the wider Arctic region.

Panaji: Former Tehelka founder-editor Tarun Tejpal, sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment by the Bombay HC last month for raping a junior colleague in 2013, surrendered Monday before a court in Mapusa, Goa.Tejpal had appealed against the order in the SC, which directed him to surrender within two weeks.The high court on Aug 6 overturned Tejpal's 2021 acquittal by a lower court and pronounced him guilty. The bench held that the lower court wrongly drew adverse inferences from the absence of visible injuries, the survivor's inability to access a 7-year-old email account, her failure to physically resist in a particular manner and "her smiling demeanour during subsequent work events". Referring to apology mails sent by Tejpal to the survivor, HC noted that the trial court had erred in observing that there was no admission of sexual assault.

Syria says 73 tons of natural uranium now under IAEA safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:49:09 UTC
07:49:09 KST

Şahin Demir
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Syria has placed 73 tons of natural uranium under the supervision and safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Monday.
Speaking via video to the 70th session of the IAEA General Conference, al-Shaibani said the material would remain safely in Syria, according to the state news agency SANA.
He said the IAEA Board of Governors unanimously decided on Sept. 9 to close Syria’s nuclear non-compliance file, which had remained open since 2011, and permanently remove it from its agenda.
Al-Shaibani described the decision as a turning point that ended a 15-year period and opened a new phase based on transparency, cooperation and mutual trust.
He thanked Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia for sponsoring and submitting the resolution as well as countries that supported the move.
Al-Shaibani said Damascus sent an official letter to the IAEA on July 17 disclosing the presence of nuclear material at an undeclared site.
Syria then signed a memorandum of understanding and a roadmap with the agency on July 29 concerning the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, he added.
Al-Shaibani said Syria also opened the Deir ez-Zor site to the agency, with IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi visiting it on Aug. 16 after nearly two decades of closure.
He said Syrian and IAEA experts had begun working to remove remnants of the reactor from beneath layers of reinforced concrete.
Damascus also provided design information and nuclear material inventory reports sought by the IAEA Board of Governors since 2011, he said.
Al-Shaibani said Syria’s Atomic Energy Commission had managed within weeks to address issues that had remained unresolved for 15 years, despite limited resources.
He also renewed Syria’s call for the implementation of a 1995 resolution on establishing a Middle East free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction and for all facilities in the region, without exception, to be placed under comprehensive IAEA safeguards.
Turning to Israel, al-Shaibani accused Israeli forces of continuing to violate Syrian sovereignty and attack Syrian territory in breach of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and international law.
He called for “effective and firm” international and diplomatic pressure to stop the attacks, compel Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and secure a full Israeli withdrawal to the lines that existed before Dec. 8, 2024.
Al-Shaibani warned that continued inaction over the violations threatens international peace and security and undermines the principles of international law.
He said Syria plans to use peaceful nuclear technologies to rehabilitate nuclear medicine infrastructure for cancer treatment, employ isotope technologies in agriculture and groundwater management, improve radiation monitoring of food, and support scientific research and energy production.
“Syria wants from the atom what heals, what feeds and what illuminates,” al-Shaibani said, adding that the program would operate under international supervision and strict safeguards.

Voluminous evidence in graft cases leading to long pendency: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:46:31 UTC
07:46:31 KST

NEW DELHI: Flagging the issue of prosecuting agencies filing voluminous evidence and naming large number of witnesses in corruption cases, Supreme Court disapproved of the practice, saying it leads to protracted hearing and long pendency.While acquitting a person in a 33-year-old corruption case on the ground that CBI failed to prove that he received pecuniary advantage, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran expressed concern over the agency naming a large number of unnecessary witnesses to prove the charge.
The court said voluminous documents filed by CBI are intimidating even to the court. "We cannot but notice that in corruption cases voluminous evidence is led, which is often intimidating to the court, especially since many aspects attempted to be led in evidence are way off the mark, in providing a substantiation of the allegation, or to bring home the guilt of the accused public servant," the bench said.The case pertains to a complaint filed by Assam veterinary department alleging that a loss of Rs 5.97 lakh was caused to the exchequer as payment was made to a fictitious firm for medicines which were never supplied. Seven persons were chargesheeted, of whom four were convicted and sentenced by a trial court and three acquitted.Three convicts filed an appeal before Gauhati high court. One of them, the accountant who passed the bill, was acquitted, but the petitioner, who was store in charge, and the other accused, storekeeper, were convicted under Section 13(1)(d) of Prevention of Corruption Act. The petitioner then moved SC. Allowing his appeal, the bench set aside his conviction and noted that the prosecution in this case had examined 62 witnesses, which was of no avail as the HC referred to only nine of such witnesses.

Wilsbach Shares Airmen’s Stories of Epic Fury, Says 10 Got Battlefield Promotions for DUDE 44 Rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:43:26 UTC
07:43:26 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Ten Airmen received battlefield promotions for their roles in the daring rescue of DUDE 44, the crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran this spring, Air Force Chief of Staff Ken. S. Wilsbach announced Sept. 14.
Wilsbach revealed the promotions—a rarity in the Air Force—and more details about Airmen’s actions during Operation Epic Fury in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Over the course of Epic Fury, which lasted from Feb. 28 until a shaky ceasefire in early April, the U.S. struck more than 13,000 military targets. In what was the biggest air campaign in a generation, around 500 combat aircraft executed around 250 sorties per day—10,000 sorties in 38 days, Wilsbach said.
American air bases in the Middle East went under “Alarm Red” conditions to take shelter, meaning there was an imminent threat of danger, 1,200 times. Wilsbach also said there were 48 airfield repairs and 420 “long lonely sweeps” to ensure that explosive ordnance was not left on the runway.
“That walk is exactly what the name suggests: one EOD technician, leaving a place of relative safety and approaching a suspected bomb or unexploded munition to render it safe for everyone else,” the chief said.
DUDE 44
Amid all these high-risk operations, the rescue of DUDE 44 in early April stood out as an example of the lengths the U.S. military was willing to go to save its service members.
In a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who was commander of Air Forces Central and the Combined Forces Air Component Commander for U.S. Central Command at the time of the mission and helped oversee the effort, said the rescue was one of his proudest moments in command.
“Watching 44 Bravo [the F-15E weapon systems officer] and getting the word that he was going to make it home and out of Iran with all the forces that were involved in that, knowing on Easter morning this guy was going to go see his family and call his wife for the first time in 48 hours was a high point, an emotional point for me having gone through that whole ordeal for the past 40-plus hours, and then recognized that we had got a win and got this guy back to safety,” France said.
For his part, Wilsbach singled out a particular battle manager—call sign “Peaches”—who coordinated the extraordinary search-and-rescue operation over 50 hours. To rescue the two-man crew, she and her team integrated the operations of 176 aircraft, including fighters, bombers, tankers, intelligence platforms, and special operations forces.
“Think about the complexity of that problem,” Wilsbach said. “Aircraft operating at different speeds, altitudes, fuel states, with different sensors, weapons, and responsibilities, while an adversary was actively trying to stop them.”
And that team was just part of the effort. Maintenance teams, Wilsbach said, generated additional fighters while tanker crews extended the force’s range and dwell time, and intelligence Airmen tracked threats.
“Every one of those Airmen was doing something different, yet all were contributing to the same mission,” Wilsbach said. That led to the 10 battlefield promotions, a rare occurrence when enlisted personnel are promoted for extraordinary performance of duties while serving in combat or under combat conditions.
“I had the distinct honor of promoting six of those heroes, ranging from staff sergeant to chief master sergeant, during a recent trip,’ Wilsbach said.
The dramatic rescue of the DUDE 44 crew began after an Iranian heat-seeking surface-to-air missile slammed into the two-seater fighter aircraft. Both crew members ejected. The pilot was rescued on the first day by a force that included A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, HC-130 Combat King IIs, HH-60W July Green II rescue helicopters, drones, and special warfare Airmen. That rescue operation was executed under close-range gunfire.
But the WSO, dubbed DUDE 44 Bravo, was not rescued for another day. He was injured in the fall, hitting the ground at a speed of 70 to 100 miles per hour after he struggled to unfurl a damaged parachute, according to an interview he gave to the CBS News program “60 Minutes.”
After landing five miles away from the pilot, DUDE 44 Bravo was suffering from a broken back, a broken arm, a broken shoulder, a sprained ankle, and cuts to his head and face. To elude capture, he scaled a 7,000-foot-tall ridgeline.
Airmen in Epic Fury
Wilsbach cited the work of Airmen across Epic Fury to emphasize his main directives for the service: be “ready to fight, built to endure, and integrated to win.”
The rescue of DUDE 44 was a prime example of integration, the chief said.
To illustrate readiness to fight, Wilsbach told the story of an unnamed base under attack from Iranian missiles.
“As missiles were inbound, Airmen sprinted toward bunkers,” Wilsbach said. “A missile struck nearby in a hangar, and the aircraft inside burst into flames. The bunker withstood the blast, but the force of the impact damaged the door so badly it wouldn’t open, trapping the Airmen inside.”
A security forces NCO used a pry bar to force the door partially open and spoke with the Airmen inside. But then the ejection seat on the burning aircraft ignited, “sending glass and metal fragments through the air,” Wilsbach said. At last, the Airmen were able to get the door open and run for cover. Finally, the door gave way, and the Airmen ran for cover.
Wilsbach also shared the story of an F-15E crew chief, Garrett, who stayed with the jets on the flight line until the last F-15E taxied and took off while others were running for cover. “ When somebody later asked him why, his answer was simple: they needed those airplanes in the air,” Wilsbach said.
Hundreds of miles away, two Senior Airmen, Shanea and Nolan, tracked a swarm of enemy drones headed toward their base and, Wilbach said, achieved more than 10 surface-to-air kills.
Shanea and Nolan’s actions in particular show the need for the Air Force to advance point defense and make it a “core function of air and space power,” Wilsbach said; the Air Force can no longer be assured that it is safe from drone and missile threats, including at airfields in the United States.
“Don’t you think we ought to have them at every base?” Wilsbach said of a new field of Airmen specializing in point defense. “If every base is going to be threatened, we have to have somebody who knows how to defend it.
“If we had a more robust base defense, you know, perhaps those bases wouldn’t have been as damaged as they were,” Wilsbach added. “Look at Israel; they have a significantly layered, very robust defense of their country, and they didn’t take that many hits, very few, in fact. And that shows you what a good defensive system can do, which can help you to operate not quite with impunity, but almost, and you can just keep generating airpower, and your defensive systems take care of the incoming.”
To hammer home his point about endurance, Wilsbach told the store of a a B-1 pilot, with the call sign Rocket, who coped with a harrowing refueling at night, in heavy clouds, and with jet fuel spraying across his cockpit windscreen.
The B-1 crew described the experience as “refueling by Braille,” Wilsbach said.
“A bomber pilot who couldn’t see depended on the tanker crew to guide them,” Wilsbach added, noting that the B-1 went on to complete a 34-hour mission.
Another example, the chief said, was an MQ-9 pilot, call sign Suit, who launched his drone while its airfield was under attack. The drone struck a target, then returned to base to conduct a damage assessment of the runway. That mission was one of many the MQ-9 conducted during Epic Fury, Wilsbach noted, with a remotely piloted aircraft striking more than 800 targets. It also played a key role in dynamic targeting and locations where the U.S. did not want to operate crewed aircraft. “Many more targets were hit because the MQ-9 found them and then passed them off to another platform,” Wilsbach said. “There’s a lot more than the 800 that they hit, and we were doing this in areas that were highly defended. And though we did decimate the Iranian Air Force and the Iranian Navy, and then we significantly attrited other capabilities that they have, it wasn’t easy. Iran’s not a pushover.”

Mitch McConnell Returns to the Senate, Ending His Months-Long Absence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:39:58 UTC
07:39:58 KST

Sen. Mitch McConnell announced that he’s casting a vote in the Senate on Monday, marking the end of his months-long absence from the upper chamber after he was hospitalized in June following a fall.
“Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June,” McConnell said in a post on X on Monday evening. “I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues.”
The 84-year-old Kentucky Republican went on to say that his "recovery has been a long and often frustrating process,” adding that the “lingering effects” of his bout with polio during his childhood have also impacted his recovery.
“I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured [Senate Majority Leader John Thune] that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” McConnell said.
McConnell’s office initially shared little to no information when the Senator was hospitalized on June 14. After weeks of uncertainty—and his absence from the Senate—rumors and speculation over the state of his health began swirling online. In July, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear shared a letter in which he urged McConnell to “fully update Kentuckians regarding the current status of [his] health.”
A few days later, the Republican lawmaker disclosed that he had been taken to the hospital after he “briefly” lost consciousness following a fall, and that he later had to grapple with a “mild case of pneumonia.” He pushed back, though, on rumors that he was suffering from any severe conditions, saying that his doctors confirmed that he didn’t break any bones or suffer a concussion, and that he didn’t have any tumors or experience a heart attack.
At the end of July, McConnell’s office shared another update, stating that the Senator was maintaining his physical therapy, per his doctors’ orders, and that he had been discharged from the hospital but was not, at that time, medically cleared to leave the rehabilitation center he was at and return to the upper chamber. On Aug. 6, his office announced that he had been discharged from the rehabilitation facility that day and would continue his recovery at home.
McConnell plans to retire in January, when his term comes to an end. This is not the first time that he has had a health scare; he has had multiple falling incidents in recent years.

Oil tanker has exploded in Strait of Hormuz, says Iran’s IRGC
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the El Gaia went up in flames after it struck a sea mine but the US rejected the claim
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said late on Monday that an oil tanker had struck a sea mine and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker El Gaia was travelling along the southern route through the strait, which was mined by Iran, state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the IRGC. The entire vessel went up in flames following the detonation of the mine, it said.
The US military rejected that account.
“The Panama-flagged oil tanker El Gaia was struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable. This weekend, Iran struck the tanker again with a drone while the ship sat in waters off the coast of Oman,” US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on social media.

What happened at the Creative Arts Emmys?
There are actually two Emmy ceremonies per year.
The non-broadcast Creative Arts Emmys took place on September 5 and 6 in Los Angeles, and they award a lot of technical categories, like cinematography, writing, costuming, hair styling, and makeup.
In more recent years, they have also included some awards that would usually be in the main ceremony, including limited series acting awards and guest actor awards.
Late actor and director Rob Reiner was awarded posthumously for his guest work on The Bear. While David Harbour and Linda Cardilini put DTF St Louis on the board by winning both lead acting nods in Limited Series.
Primetime Emmys host Mariska Hargitay took home two Creative Arts Emmys, both for the documentary My Mom Jayne.
But the biggest winner from the two nights was Widow's Bay, which managed to score eight awards, including a guest acting award for Betty Gilpin who accepted with a delightful poem where she managed to be utterly charming and land a sick burn on OpenAI founder Sam Altman.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 15, 2026
US 10-year Treasury yield breaches 5% as inflation, supply worries mount
The US 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5 per cent for the first time since 2023 on Sept 14, as mounting inflation angst collided with swelling government and corporate borrowing needs.
The yield, a benchmark for US mortgage loans and bonds globally, rose almost 5 basis points to as high as 5.01 per cent, before paring much of the increase as buyers emerged.
“The 5 per cent mark in 10-year rates is clearly a key psychological level for investors – a point at which some may have earmarked for buying a dip,” said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang puts Trump on speakerphone while downplaying AI risks
Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang took a live phone call from Donald Trump during a panel discussion on Sept 14, allowing the US President to dismiss artificial intelligence dangers as a “hoax”.
During the call, which Huang received on stage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Trump criticised the push to slow the pace of AI development as politically motivated or a Chinese scheme. Huang agreed with the President, saying Trump had seen through the complexities of the issue.
The AI pushback is “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen”, Trump said. “And that could be political people. It could also be China.”
Zelensky says Ukraine ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept 14 that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Sept 14 that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
British man admits drugging and raping wife over more than 2 decades
A British man on Sept 14 admitted repeatedly drugging and raping his wife at their home over more than two decades, shortly before his trial was about to begin.
The man – from northern England who is in his 60s but cannot be named as it would identify his wife who is entitled to lifelong anonymity – pleaded guilty at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to 45 charges, having previously admitted 15 offences.
The man has now admitted charges including 21 counts of rape, 15 counts of assault by penetration, 11 counts of sexual assault and one count of sharing intimate images without consent in a period between 2004 and 2025.
EU is set to propose ban on social media and AI chatbots for under-15s
The European Union will propose a ban restricting under 15s from social media, video sharing platforms, AI chatbots and online games, in the most sweeping plan yet to protect children from online dangers, a European Commission document seen by Reuters shows.
Concerns have mounted globally about the impact on children’s health and safety of major outlets, including Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google’s YouTube and ChatGPT.
The EU proposal is part of an EU Kids Act that European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen will present on Sept 17. The former may announce some details in her State of the Union address on upcoming EU policy on Sept 16.

GFCN chief warns of frequent cyber fraud, ‘calls from FSB’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:26:51 UTC
07:26:51 KST

MOSCOW, September 15. /TASS/. President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak is warning the public to be on the alert for continued cases of cyber fraud and "calls from the FSB."
The situation with fake news today is "quite complicated," and cyber fraud is widespread, he said in an interview with TASS ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum.
"For me, even regardless of where I work, when ‘a Sberbank representative’ (a fake representative of Russia’s largest bank) connects you over the phone to ‘an FSB representative’ (a fake officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service), that is a somewhat strange situation. (This is a common scam tactic designed to gain the victim’s trust by making the call appear official - TASS) Yet a huge number of people actually fall for this. Technology is also advancing. Deepfakes, for example, are already part of the picture," Tabak emphasized. "Today, 64% of people surveyed by Dialogue Regions say they know what deepfakes are. The figure stood at 59% in September 2025."
The head of GFCN also noted that 80% of respondents overall report encountering unreliable information. "What does this tell us? It tells us that we can focus exclusively on raising the public’s level of media literacy and building an ecosystem of trust. Beyond that, responsibility will still rest with the individual, except in situations where law enforcement agencies must step in afterward. But when users encounter a particular piece of information, responsibility essentially falls on them," he continued.
"This does not change the fact that we must deliver accurate information quickly and clearly. We must be able to debunk widely circulating disinformation and reach a broad audience. The state must also take responsibility for informing the public, debunking false information, providing education, and working with government agencies so they understand how to counter it. But given how widely this kind of information spreads today, the only effective defense on such a large scale is strong media literacy and, ultimately, basic critical thinking about what users read," Tabak concluded.
About the Global Fact-Checking Network
The Global Fact-Checking Network brings together experts and fact-checking organizations worldwide. The association was founded by the TASS news agency, the nonprofit organization Dialogue Regions and the New Media Workshop to combat disinformation. More than 125 journalists from 55 countries already collaborate with GFCN on fact-checking.
The international Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum will take place on September 22 at the Russia National Center in Moscow. TASS is the event’s strategic partner.

US slaps new penalties on Russia's VTB Bank over Iran   sanctions evasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:24:40 UTC
07:24:40 KST

The United States on Sept. 14 imposed new sanctions against VTB Bank, one of the largest financial institutions in Russia, for its role in helping Iran evade sanctions, the U.S. Treasury announced.
The designation is part of Operation Economic Outcast, the Treasury's plan to isolate Iran economically. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent first announced the plan in August, six months into the U.S. war against Iran.
The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated VTB Bank on Sept. 14 for "operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy," saying the institution had opened bank offices in Iran in recent years to expand trade and cooperation between Tehran and Moscow.
VTB Bank has partnered with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions and has helped tranfer billions in frozen Iranian assets, the Treasury said.
"Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise," Bessent said.
The new sanctions block any VTB Bank assets that are held in the U.S. or by U.S. nationals. Any entities owned directly or indirectly by VTB Bank are also blocked, and those who violate the sanctions measures are subject to criminal or civil penalties.
VTB Bank was previously sanctioned by the U.S. in 2022 and 2025, in relation to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
"VTB is now among the most comprehensively sanctioned financial institutions in the world," the U.S. Treasury said in a press release accompanying the updated sanctions designation.
Russia and Iran have deepened economic and military cooperation since the start of the full-scale war, when Tehran supplied Moscow with Shahed drones to launch against Ukraine.
In turn, Russia has pledged to support Iran during its war with the U.S. Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian on Sept. 1 that Moscow is "trying to provide you with the assistance you need."
Bessent, however, has previously downplayed Russia's aid to Iran.
"They don't really get direct financial support from Russia," Bessent told the right-wing outlet Newsmax earlier in September.

Jerusalem Governorate warns of Israeli push to impose new ‘religious reality’ around Al-Aqsa Mosque
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:17:36 UTC
07:17:36 KST

Qais Omar Darwesh, Lina Altawell
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
The Palestinian Jerusalem Governorate warned Monday of Israeli efforts to impose “a new Jewish religious reality” around Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied Jerusalem through repeated Jewish rituals and prayers at Bab al-Rahma Cemetery located along the eastern wall of the mosque’s compound.
“Rituals held in recent weeks go beyond seasonal rituals linked to Jewish holidays and pave the way for turning the site into a recurring Jewish prayer point,” the governorate said in a statement.
It said it had monitored promotional posts by so-called “Temple groups” on social media as well as the creation of a WhatsApp group called “Gates of Mercy, open for us” promoting a Jewish religious narrative that gives special sanctity and importance to the eastern side of Al-Aqsa’s wall, particularly Bab al-Rahma.
“Temple groups” refer to several Jewish nationalist and religious organizations and movements that target Jerusalem, especially Al-Aqsa Mosque, and call for building an alleged Jewish temple on its ruins.
“The narrative seeks to present Bab al-Rahma as a Jewish religious site that can be accessed and used for prayer,” the governorate said.
It added that the promotion has moved into practical steps through calls for weekly prayers at the site, linking the moves to Uri Ohayon, a former officer in the Israeli army.
According to the governorate’s monitoring, Ohayon began promoting the idea on Aug. 16 and organized the first gathering on Aug. 27, followed by two other gatherings on Sept. 3 and Sept. 10.
The gatherings included group prayers and rituals next to Muslim graves, it said.
“Al-Aqsa Mosque, with its entire area of 35.6 acres (144 dunums), is an exclusively Islamic place of worship,” the Jerusalem Governorate stressed and said that its endowment status covers all its courtyards, prayer halls, walls, gates and landmarks.
Bab al-Rahma is one of the gates of Al-Aqsa Mosque and lies within its eastern wall, it said.
Israeli authorities have no sovereignty over occupied Jerusalem or its holy sites and no right to impose changes on the identity, nature, use or landmarks of the mosque, the governorate added.
It warned that allowing such practices to become normalized or treating them as passing religious rituals would encourage so-called “Temple groups” to expand their activities and turn new points around Al-Aqsa into sites for gathering, rituals and prayer.
“What is happening at Bab al-Rahma represents an organized path to impose a new Jewish religious reality around Al-Aqsa Mosque, beginning with the normalization and repetition of rituals and then turning them into a permanent presence and routine practice,” the governorate said.
On Sunday, 593 Israeli occupiers stormed Al-Aqsa Mosque, while Israeli authorities imposed restrictions on Palestinian worshippers’ access to the site during the Jewish New Year, according to earlier figures from the governorate.
The Israeli measures coincided with calls by Israeli “Temple groups” to intensify incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque during the Jewish New Year, which began at sundown on Friday, Sept. 11 and concluded after nightfall on Sunday, Sept. 13
Since 2003, Israeli police have allowed occupiers to enter Al-Aqsa Mosque unilaterally, while the Islamic Waqf Department in Jerusalem has repeatedly demanded an end to such incursions, without response from Israeli authorities.
Palestinians say Israel has for decades intensified its efforts to Judaize occupied East Jerusalem, including Al-Aqsa Mosque, and erase its Arab and Islamic identity.
They insist on occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of their hoped-for state, based on international legitimacy resolutions that do not recognize Israel’s occupation of the city in 1967 or its annexation in 1980.

For first time, Ukraine’s drone makers and Europe’s arms firms have joined one body: EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:15:47 UTC
07:15:47 KST

Ukraine's battlefield-tested drone makers and Europe's arms firms have sat down together for the first time to build drones and the systems to shoot drones down as a single industry. Eighteen companies, nine Ukrainian and nine European, held the opening meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance in Brussels, Defender Media reported.
The alliance answers a threat both sides now share. Russia is scaling up its own drone production. Its drone war has spilled past Ukraine, with its drones crossing repeatedly into NATO airspace this summer and showing Europe how unready it is for the fighting Ukraine has learned the hard way.
The Alliance will support Ukraine's capabilities it needs on the battlefield, while strengthening Europe's defense readiness for the future.
The alliance sets up shop
The first job is organizational, said Roman Tkachenko, a co-founder of the Ukrainian firm Tencore: form the governing bodies and set the priorities. The 18 members were chosen from about 400 applicants, Kubilius said, and the alliance is designed as a decision-making body, according to UA News.
On the Ukrainian side, it includes Tencore, Athlon Avia, and Vyriy Industry. On the European side, Germany's Quantum Systems, Italy's Fincantieri, and Denmark's Terma.
Kubilius, who opened the session and called it historic, said the first tangible results should come by the end of the year. He named accelerating joint ventures and counter-drone projects as the top tasks.
Europe wants Ukraine's combat edge
Kubilius was blunt about what Europe hopes to learn: how to adapt a product in days, shorten development cycles, and scale a production line from a peacetime trickle to full output within weeks. In return, he said, the EU offers Ukraine cutting-edge technology and continent-wide manufacturing.
The Alliance will bring together companies, start-ups, researchers, armed forces, and other users from EU countries and Ukraine.
The Alliance is a result of the Drone Deal, announced by President Ursula von der Leyen in Kyiv on 15 July, according to the EU Commission.

"I think you'll see the pipeline back running very soon," Wright told US financial news outlet Bloomberg. "This is not new for strikes on this energy infrastructure. And, of course, unfortunately, Iran's done a ton of that, but they've proven resourceful in the past."
Wright said he has remained in continuous contact with Saudi authorities since the strike. Technical teams are assessing the damage, he said, adding that "more clarity" on the timeline for restoring operations is expected soon.
The pipeline was shut down after attacks last week, disrupting a key route used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Before its closure, it had been carrying about 4 million to 5 million barrels of crude per day, equivalent to roughly 4 percent to 5 percent of global oil supply.
The disruption comes amid territorial gains by Yemen's Houthi forces, which have announced control over several western coastal districts and Red Sea islands, including the island of Mayun in the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Addressing maritime traffic around Yemen, Wright said that while a few million barrels transit the area each day, most commercial tankers do not pass through Bab al-Mandab, instead moving "through the Suez Canal and the pipeline there at Egypt."
Strait of Hormuz transits
Despite conflicting claims from Washington and Tehran over the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Wright said substantial volumes of oil and petroleum products continue to transit the waterway.
"Over 12,000,000 barrels of oil and oil products flowed through the Strait of Hormuz last night," Wright said, adding that the seven-day average was above 10 million barrels per day and rising.
He said US assessments are based on ship manifests rather than estimates.
"Every morning, I get a report of every single ship, the ship name, exactly what its cargo was, and then it transited."
Refining bottlenecks and diesel supply
Wright also highlighted constraints in global refining capacity, saying US efforts are focused on increasing exports of refined products from the Middle East to help ease shortages.
He attributed part of the pressure to a sharp decline in Russian diesel exports, saying Moscow, previously a major supplier, is now "not exporting any" diesel.
The comments came after US President Donald Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt strikes on Russian refining infrastructure, arguing that the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
"He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia ... because he's causing a shortage of diesel," Trump said.

Berlin-based German-Ukrainian businesswoman Ilona Wiener charged with spying for Russia
Unknown

2026-09-14

Federal prosecutors in Germany have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman — identified as Ilona W., a citizen of both Germany and Ukraine — with spying on behalf of Russia. A number of publications, including The Insider, have identified the woman as Ilona Kopylova-Wiener.
According to a 74-page indictment outlined by Der Spiegel, German prosecutors have accused Ilona W. of acting on behalf of a Russian intelligence service. The charges were filed nearly eight months after her arrest.
Investigators say that in November 2023 the businesswoman began passing information to a contact at the Russian Embassy in Berlin. German counterintelligence identified that contact as GRU officer Andrei Mayorov, who worked under diplomatic cover as a deputy military attaché. Mayorov was expelled from Germany earlier this year.
Der Spiegel reported that Ilona W. deliberately gathered information about participants in political events, including a “NATO Talk” held at Berlin’s Hotel Adlon in November 2023 and the German-Ukrainian Business Forum in Berlin in December 2025. At the latter, Wiener sat a few meters from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Prosecutors also allege that in February 2024, Ilona W. used a false name to bring her suspected handler, Mayorov, into a meeting of Bundeswehr reservists. Der Spiegel characterized her as a prominent figure “considered extremely active” in Berlin who headed an association dedicated to “promoting international understanding” and regularly attended receptions and events with ambassadors, senior diplomats, and well-known politicians. The advisory board of her organization included prominent businesspeople and former lawmakers from Germany’s Social Democratic Party (SPD) and Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
In the spring, Wiener’s defense challenged her detention and criticized prosecutors for what they called a “broad interpretation” of the criminal provision covering intelligence activity on behalf of a foreign state.
News of Wiener’s arrest first emerged in January.

International Boxing Association (IBA) head Umar Kremlev paid part of the cost of Donald Trump Jr.’s May wedding, held on a private island in the Bahamas, according to an investigation released by ProPublica earlier today citing records reviewed by the newsroom and interviews with three people familiar with the event. According to the outlet, Kremlev paid about $100,000 to rent one of the private islands where the reception was held and where guests stayed overnight. He also paid for a fireworks display costing around $70,000.
Kremlev’s team helped organize the event, while the payments were made through IB Challenger, a Dubai-based company linked to the IBA. The boxing association, which Kremlev leads, was previously financed by Russia’s state-owned energy giant Gazprom.
Among the roughly 50 wedding guests were Trump Jr.’s brother-in-law Jared Kushner, his brother Eric Trump, and Kremlev himself, along with a group of Russian-speaking guests whose presence “puzzled other attendees,” according to ProPublica. Two people who spoke to the outlet said the group largely kept to itself and spoke Russian. The Russian guests are barely visible in photos and videos published after the wedding.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. did not deny that Kremlev had paid for wedding expenses, describing him as a “personal friend of Don.” The spokesperson said the two “met through a mutual friend in the hunting world” and “bonded over their love of boxing and the outdoors.”
Kremlev’s press office also confirmed that the two men had a “friendly relationship” and said the businessman had “never discussed political matters” with his American acquaintances.
Former FBI officials interviewed by ProPublica called the situation concerning. “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president. End of story,” retired career FBI officer Frank Montoya Jr. told the publication.
Kremlev is known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin. In April, Putin awarded him the Order of Friendship, a Russian state honor, and in the days before the wedding Kremlev accompanied Putin on a trip to China.
Ukraine has imposed personal sanctions on Kremlev, citing his ties to Putin and to Russian security agencies.

U.S. acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed a space weapon in orbit

This is the first time U.S. officials have acknowledged deploying a space weapon in orbit, Air & Space Forces Magazine said. Meink said the disclosure was deliberate and that his words were “very well thought out.” He declined to provide any details about the orbital weapon.

I don’t think that this is going to be in the interest of U.S. national security,” space security expert Victoria Samson told Defense One.
Asked what kind of weapon the United States might have deployed in space, Samson said it was likely space-based electronic warfare equipment rather than a kinetic weapon.
In 2024, the United States said Russia had deployed a satellite capable of attacking other satellites. That same year, the United States warned of alleged Russian plans to put a satellite carrying a nuclear payload into orbit. Moscow called the reports a “ruse” but blocked a U.N. Security Council resolution prohibiting the placement of nuclear weapons in space.
