Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:03:38 UTC
07:03:38 KST

More than 200 Israeli filmmakers signed a petition expressing solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Israeli creators of "NAZA," which features what promotional materials for the film allege are the "systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza."
The Israel Defense Forces said the film relies on anonymous testimonies from people whose identities cannot be verified, including whether they served in the IDF, in what capacity, or whether they were involved in the matters they describe. "The excerpts cited include claims regarding national and military strategy that are clearly beyond the knowledge of junior-level soldiers." The IDF also said the film contains "references to situations in which IDF Intelligence Directorate soldiers, who were allegedly interviewed for the film, by definition could not have been involved."
The petition, signed by Ari Folman, Shlomi Elkabetz, Ran Tal and Michal Aviad, among others, states that "in recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of incitement and instigation against the film's creators, and the distance between it and the incitement to violence and physical threat to their lives is shrinking."
"We, filmmakers, call on all who are still fighting for freedom of expression and creation to join in expressing support and solidarity with Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham," the petition states. "The central role of art and journalism is to hold a mirror up to the society in which they exist, to create discourse and discussion without assumptions, even when the reality is difficult."
"NAZA," which won the special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, is based on the testimonies of 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel. Following the film's recognition at the Venice festival, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar appealed to the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film's creators and described the film as "vile" and saying it "constitutes treason."
The Israeli military on Sunday denied an allegation in the film that the IDF had planned and approved a strike in Gaza in which 500 civilian deaths were expected, calling the claim "completely false." A promotional clip for the film, which examines Israel's use of artificial intelligence in targeting decisions and its role in civilian deaths, shows a purported Israeli intelligence soldier being asked about the largest number of expected civilian deaths ever approved for a strike in Gaza. "I don't know how many were killed, because they never check this, but there was once an approval for 500," the interviewee says.
The petition's authors took issue with what they alleged was a practice of criticizing films without watching them.
"Regardless of the direct incitement we've encountered on social media against Abraham and Szor, we find it appropriate to strongly criticize those creators, academics and journalists who chose to attack the film without watching it. The participation of colleagues and respected writers in this trend is a clear sign of the deterioration of discourse in Israel and gives backing to minister Zohar's threats to revoke Szor and Abraham's citizenship. We, too, have not yet watched the film. Criticism of films and works of art in general is a legitimate tool of expression in a society that seeks to be healthy and functional, but the inflammatory and violent discourse against the film's creators, who dared to express their opinion, should concern each and every one of us, regardless of our views."
The petition expressed hope that "NAZA" would be distributed in Israel soon, "and everyone will be able to watch it, form their own opinion and create a real and initial discussion about the war in Gaza and its consequences – a discussion that until today has almost not taken place in Israeli media and society."

Zelensky says Ukraine ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’
KYIV – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept 14 that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Sept 14 that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure”.
He added: “If this can become the first de-escalatory step – stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation.”
Zelensky said “we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia’s war economy”.
He noted that “so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the war”.
“But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps.”
Rail strikes get worse
Trump has insisted that the Russia-Ukraine war and not the conflict with Iran, was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November.
A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the US-Israeli conflict against Iran, now in its seventh month. US envoys went to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month without announcing a breakthrough.
While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelensky has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defences as Russia intensifies its attacks.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s rail network are worsening each week, the CEO of the state Ukrainian Railways operator told AFP on Sept 14, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend.
“It’s growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one,” said Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
NATO-member Poland said on Sept 13 that Russia hit a train about 2km from the Polish-Ukraine border, just days after Kyiv officials said road crossing checkpoints on the border with Moldova had been targeted.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sept 13 that Warsaw had obtained information that Moscow might be planning attacks on border crossings.
EU delays sanctions deadline
But European Union countries on Sept 14 delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist, diplomats said.
An EU list of almost 3,000 individuals and entities – which needs to be extended every six months – was set to expire by Sept 16.
However ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition, the diplomats said.
Usmanov, a former major shareholder in Arsenal football club, was placed on the EU sanctions list in 2022 over what Brussels said were his close ties to the Kremlin.
The French move surprised some EU states.
“Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia’s war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefitting from it,” a spokesman for Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, said.
The Financial Times reported, quoting people familiar with the issue, that France was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving French citizens held in Azerbaijan. AFP

A child’s genetic profile for ADHD can predict their parents’ risk of separation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:00:26 UTC
07:00:26 KST

Children with a higher polygenic index for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder tend to see a higher likelihood of their parents separating or divorcing, according to new research. The findings suggest that families are dynamic systems where a child’s inherited characteristics can actively shape the life trajectories of their parents. The research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America.
Family research often focuses on how parents shape their children. A 2017 study demonstrated that parents’ genetic traits indirectly shape the home environment they create for their children. This progression in the literature has led scientists to ask whether the influence might operate in the opposite direction.
A polygenic index is a statistical construct scientists use to estimate the likelihood of a specific trait or condition. It is calculated by adding up the effects of many small genetic variations across a person’s DNA, weighted by how strongly they associate with a trait in large population samples. Rather than measuring an internal biological mechanism or an absolute predisposition waiting to be realized, a polygenic index is a risk estimate that depends heavily on the specific population and environment it was derived from. Evocative gene-environment correlation is the related concept that a person’s genetically influenced tendencies can provoke specific reactions from the people around them.
Researchers have started applying this concept to family dynamics. A 2024 study of adoptees indicated that children’s inherited traits can actively shape how warmly their parents treat them, providing evidence that children influence their own caregiving environment. This builds on research covered by PsyPost in early 2025, which found that early childhood traits related to attention and hyperactivity can alter family dynamics by increasing the likelihood of experiencing childhood maltreatment.
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. To understand how children might shape broader family structures, a research team led by Evelina T. Akimova at Purdue University and Torkild Hovde Lyngstad at the University of Oslo examined whether children’s polygenic indices predict major parental decisions. They set out to determine if a child’s statistical genetic risk estimates were associated with parental outcomes like having another baby, getting married, or ending a relationship.
The researchers analyzed data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. They looked at genetic and administrative data from 40,000 genotyped family trios, consisting of a mother, a father, and a child. The data included genetic information derived from blood samples taken during pregnancy and at birth.
The team tracked family demographic changes through Norwegian administrative registers, which provided objective records of marriage, separation, and childbirth. By comparing the child’s polygenic indices for various physical and mental health traits against these family outcomes, the researchers could look for patterns. Importantly, they controlled for the polygenic indices of both parents, allowing them to isolate the specific influence of the child’s genetic associations on the family environment.
The researchers found that for most behavioral and physical health traits, the child’s genetic profile had no statistically significant impact on family demographic events. Traits like asthma, body mass index, and cognitive performance did not reliably predict whether parents would have another child, marry, or separate. The notable exception was the polygenic index for ADHD.
An increase in a child’s polygenic index for ADHD was reliably associated with an increased risk of parental partnership dissolution. Specifically, a one standard deviation increase in the child’s ADHD polygenic index predicted a 7 percent relative increase in the odds that their parents would separate or divorce. When the researchers broke the data down further, they found that this effect was highly specific to certain types of families.
The association between a child’s ADHD genetic index and parental separation was driven primarily by families with daughters. For girls, a one standard deviation increase in the ADHD polygenic index was associated with an 11 percent increase in the odds of parental dissolution. For boys, the increase was less than 4 percent, and the result was not statistically significant. The authors propose that because ADHD in girls often presents as issues with attention and emotion regulation rather than overt hyperactivity, it may be underdiagnosed, leading to unaddressed behavioral challenges that strain family relationships.
Socioeconomic status also played a moderating role. In families with above-average educational attainment, a one standard deviation increase in the child’s ADHD polygenic index was associated with a 15 percent increase in the odds of partnership dissolution. In families with below-average socioeconomic status, the effect was not statistically significant. The researchers suggest that behavioral difficulties might conflict more intensely with the rigid academic and developmental expectations often present in higher-status households.
Maternal age at the time of the first birth also altered the outcomes. In families where the mother was older than the median age at her first birth, an increase in the child’s ADHD genetic index predicted a 10 percent increase in the odds of parental separation. In these same older-mother families, the researchers also noted a separate effect regarding anxiety. A higher polygenic index for anxiety in the child was associated with a 10 percent increase in the odds that the parents would marry after the child’s birth, suggesting that older parents might respond to an anxious child with stabilizing commitments.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study is based entirely on data from Norway, a country with a universal welfare state, high levels of gender equality, and robust family support systems. The ways in which child traits evoke parental responses might look different in countries with less institutional support or different cultural norms regarding marriage and divorce.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the data. The Norwegian cohort study relied on voluntary participation, which resulted in a sample that slightly overrepresents families with higher socioeconomic status. Families experiencing multiple extreme adversities are likely underrepresented, which could affect the prevalence estimates of certain family events.
The genetic measures themselves also have limits. Because polygenic indices are statistical models rather than direct biological pathways, their predictive accuracy heavily depends on the reference populations used to create them. The polygenic indices used in this study were derived from genetic studies of populations with European ancestry, meaning the findings may not generalize to people of other ancestral backgrounds. Additionally, current polygenic indices only capture a small fraction of the total genetic influence on a complex condition like ADHD.
The study, “When children shape their families: Evocative effects analysis of 40,000 trios from the Norwegian Mother-Father-and-Child Study,” was authored by Evelina T. Akimova, Agnes Fauske, Ruth Eva Jørgensen, Alexandra Havdahl, Elizabeth C. Corfield, Melinda C. Mills, and Torkild Hovde Lyngstad.

News Analysis: Sweden's center-left edges ahead, but path to power remains uncertain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:55:31 CST
06:55:31 KST

STOCKHOLM, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Preliminary results on Monday showed Sweden's center-left opposition bloc holding a narrow lead in the parliamentary election, boosting Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson's prospects of returning to power and ending four years of right-wing rule.
But a parliamentary lead does not guarantee a smooth path to government. Andersson faces the challenge of turning the bloc's seats into a workable government, as the four opposition parties remain divided on government composition and key policies.
Adding to the uncertainty, the tally is not yet complete. Late-arriving advance ballots, including ballots received from abroad, are due to be included in Wednesday's supplementary count.
NARROW LEAD, DIFFICULT PATH TO POWER
With results reported from 95 percent of voting districts on Monday, the four opposition parties -- the Social Democrats, the Center Party, the Left Party and the Greens -- had a combined 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament and 49.5 percent of the vote. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc, comprising the Moderate Party, the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, had 173 seats and 49 percent of the vote.
Andersson's immediate challenge is to form a workable government. The Center Party has ruled out joining a government that includes the Left Party, while the Left Party has demanded cabinet representation. Swedish Television (SVT) has described the clash as an "impossible equation."
Sweden's system of negative parliamentarism nevertheless leaves Andersson with alternatives. A prime minister can take office as long as fewer than 175 lawmakers vote against, meaning some opposition parties could remain outside the cabinet while an Andersson-led minority government takes office by voting for her or abstaining. Such a government would still need parliamentary support for budgets and major legislation.
Sweden has faced lengthy government talks before. After the 2018 election, it took 134 days to form a government. Ahead of this year's vote, Speaker of Parliament Andreas Norlen urged parties to reconsider some of their political "red lines," warning against a prolonged period of political paralysis amid a European security environment more serious than in 2018.
KRISTERSSON'S PLAN B
Despite his bloc's narrow deficit in the preliminary count, Kristersson has signaled that he is not ready to give up his effort to form a government. On election night, he said he would contact other party leaders and explore whether a workable governing arrangement could still be found.
Kristersson's clearest potential opening is the Center Party. Once part of Sweden's traditional center-right Alliance, the party remains economically liberal and shares common ground with Kristersson's Moderate Party on several issues. Before the election, TV4 reported that senior Moderates viewed the party as key to an alternative majority.
But cooperation has become increasingly difficult over SD. Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist said in June that Kristersson had "disqualified himself" as a prime ministerial candidate, citing among other things the Moderates' close ties with SD. The party also rejected a Moderate offer earlier this month to implement six of its demands.
Kristersson may still seek the Center Party's support. Annika Freden, associate professor of political science at Lund University, said such outreach was expected but saw little prospect of success, noting that the Center Party is "fundamentally opposed to entering into an alliance with the far right."
FAR-RIGHT LOSES GROUND, INFLUENCE REMAINS
SD emerged as one of the clearest losers of the election. SVT reported that an SD member described the result, if it holds, as a "double blow" -- the party would lose its position as Sweden's second-largest party and see its support decline from the previous election.
The setback also clouds SD's ambition to enter government for the first time. Kristersson had opened the door before the election to bringing the party into government if the right-wing bloc retained power, a major shift for a party long kept outside the cabinet by Sweden's established parties.
Yet SD's electoral losses may not erase its broader political influence. Although the party remained outside the cabinet over the past four years, it helped shape government policy through the Tido Agreement, particularly on migration, integration and crime.
The election also underscored how positions on migration have shifted across Sweden's political landscape. Andersson has pledged to maintain a restrictive migration policy, while SVT noted that the Social Democrats now stand relatively close to SD on migration compared with some of their prospective partners on the left.
Niklas Bolin, professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, said SD had been "extremely successful" in shaping migration policy, with positions considered controversial 10 or 15 years ago becoming "almost political mainstream."
"In that sense, SD won an important ideological battle," he said. ■

Feature: Chinese opera meets Oscar Wilde in a new intercultural fusion musical
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:55:10 CST
06:55:10 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhao Jiasong
LONDON, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- In a London rehearsal hall on Monday, Yu Ji from Peking Opera and Salome from Oscar Wilde's play came together in an original musical blending Chinese and Western theatrical traditions.
Chinese musical theater performer Aimee Yue wrote and directed the musical, "The Silk Road (Kinda)," in which she plays Yu Ji opposite British actress Megan Winstanley as Salome. The 55-minute production was staged at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in August after earlier performances in London.
Yu Ji, also known as Consort Yu, was the companion of Xiang Yu, a prominent military leader during the final years of the Qin Dynasty (221 BC-207 BC). Their final parting later became the basis of "Farewell My Concubine," one of the best-known stories in Chinese opera. Salome, meanwhile, is closely associated in Western theater with Wilde's play and the Dance of the Seven Veils.
Their different theatrical worlds are clear from the moment they appear. Yue's Yu Ji carries a Chinese folding fan and moves with gestures drawn from Peking Opera, while Winstanley's Salome holds a Victorian-style lace fan and speaks and sings largely in the style of Western musical theater. Masks, long silk, pop songs and Peking Opera percussion also run through the performance.
The story develops through the contrast between the two characters. Salome is outspoken and impulsive, while Yu Ji is quieter, restrained and strongly attached to duty. Their early encounters are marked by misunderstandings over language, behavior and their different cultural and theatrical traditions.
"They do not have to discover that they are the same," Yue said. Instead, their friendship develops as they learn to understand their differences. At one point, the two exchange their fans, each taking up an object associated with the other's theatrical world.
Yue's performance enriches the familiar Chinese character. Historical records leave relatively little detail about Yu Ji herself. In this musical version, Yu Ji is given more space to speak about her own choices and eventually decides to return to her story before setting off on a new journey with Salome.
The production also seeks to introduce Peking Opera to audiences with little previous knowledge of the art form. Yu Ji sometimes speaks English while retaining Peking Opera movements, helping spectators connect gesture with meaning, while long silk, masks and fans are incorporated into physical storytelling.
"I want to lower the threshold for understanding Peking Opera while keeping its theatrical logic intact," Yue said.
She recalled meeting an audience member who told her before the show that he did not enjoy Peking Opera. After the performance, however, he stayed to discuss how the show had helped him better understand some of its movements.
The score takes a similar approach, combining Peking Opera percussion and melodic elements with musical-theater songs, pop and Yue's own compositions. It features guzheng, flute, and Chinese drums.
Yue studied Peking Opera in China before moving to Britain at 14 in 2016 and later trained in British drama and musical theater. She graduated from the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts in 2024 and recently completed a year-long Britain and Ireland tour of "Miss Saigon."
The Edinburgh run drew positive responses. Edinburgh Reviews critic Andrew Girdwood gave the production four stars, calling it an "inventive cross-cultural Fringe musical" and describing it as "Peking Opera meets Oscar Wilde."
Luis Garcia, a musical theatre expert at Goldsmiths, University of London, called the work "an ambitious and distinctive piece of musical theatre." He said its use of Peking Opera and contemporary musical theater could introduce the theatrical language and cultural traditions of Peking Opera to new international audiences and contribute to wider intercultural discussion.
The production builds on earlier theatrical collaborations between Chinese and British artists. In 2016, Shanghai Dramatic Arts Centre and British physical-theater company Gecko created "The Dreamer," drawing on Chinese playwright Tang Xianzu's "The Peony Pavilion" and Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream."
"We want to keep exploring how Chinese theater, history and cultural traditions can work with Western stage storytelling, and hopefully develop more original productions from that," Wang Yanli, the production's associate producer, said. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: China's Chang'e-6 lunar sample finds home at UN in Vienna
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
05:55:03 CST
06:55:03 KST

VIENNA, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China on Monday formally presented a lunar sample collected from the far side of the Moon by its Chang'e-6 mission to the United Nations (UN) in Vienna, where the sample will be permanently exhibited.
The ceremony, themed "From lunar ground to common ground: a shared future for all," brought together diplomats, UN officials, scientists and representatives of international organizations.
Carried more than 380,000 km from the Moon to Earth and then to the heart of international diplomacy, the sample is more than a fragment of lunar soil and rock. It has become a symbol of scientific achievement, international cooperation and humanity's shared future in space.
At the venue, the lunar sample attracted considerable attention, with diplomats, delegates and officials from international organizations stopping for a close look. Some visitors even lined up to take photographs with material retrieved from the Moon's far side.
The sample has an extraordinary provenance. In 2024, China's Chang'e-6 lunar exploration mission successfully collected 1,935.3 grams of samples from the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) Basin on the far side of the Moon, marking the first time in human history that samples had been retrieved from the lunar far side.
The achievement opened a new chapter in lunar science, offering scientists an unprecedented opportunity to study material from a region that has long remained beyond direct view from Earth.
"It is a great honor for me to attend this ceremony today," said Austrian sinologist Richard Trappl. "Although the Moon is 380,000 kilometers away from Earth, today it has come to Vienna -- to the United Nations in Vienna -- and I extend my sincere congratulations to China."
Harvey Dzodin, senior fellow of the Center for China and Globalization, said the sample's uniqueness lies in its origin. "I think it's the first time for most people to see the lunar sample from the far side of the Moon," he said.
In his view, the sample can also serve as an "ambassador" for China by demonstrating the country's technological capabilities.
"Obviously, the UN is the first place where the sample should be shared outside of China, because the UN is an ideal that needs to be realized. And it represents every nation," he said, expressing hope that more lunar samples can be collected and shared in the future.
Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, described Chang'e-6 as one of an "impressive series of unprecedented achievements" on and around the Moon in recent years.
"The coming years are full of promise of yet more impressive missions," she said, adding that she looked forward to seeing what China's Chang'e-7 and Chang'e-8 missions might bring as well.
For Holla-Maini, the significance of the sample goes beyond its scientific value. "Lunar samples from the far side are so rare, but this one, thanks to China, belongs to everyone. It belongs to us all," she said.
She also acknowledged China's lunar sample program, through which the country has been sharing these unique resources with scientific and research institutions around the world, enabling scientists without direct access to such capabilities to benefit from them.
The permanent exhibition of the sample in Vienna gives it a new role. It will no longer be confined to laboratories or specialized facilities, but will be placed in a setting visited every year by thousands of students, delegates and visitors from every corner of the world. "I'm very proud that this gift will sit here in Vienna, not as a trophy, but as a teacher," Holla-Maini said.
"For us, we are all people who otherwise would never get the chance to stand so close to the Moon," Holla-Maini said. "From lunar ground to common ground, I hope that every visitor who stops in front of this rock leaves with a sense of wonder at what humanity as individuals but also collectively together can achieve." ■

Talk of AI pause slams Nvidia, AMD and Intel as fears of doomsday scenarios spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:47:16 UTC
06:47:16 KST

Talk of AI pause slams Nvidia, AMD and Intel as fears of doomsday scenarios spread
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Artificial intelligence stocks tumbled on Monday after American leaders of the AI revolution called for a coordinated slowdown in building more powerful AI systems.
Over the weekend, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” calling for an industrywide effort to slow AI development. Executives at OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft also echoed the concern and called for some sort of pause.
Semiconductor stocks bore the brunt of the statements. Chipmaker Nvidia fell 3% to $210.96. Its rival AMD lost 4%. Intel plunged 6%.
Amid the fears, OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, suggested it might be delaying its initial public offering plans.
OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said in an interview with Fortune that it was an “ill-advised moment” for an initial public offering, saying the company won’t list this year.
Shares of OpenAI shareholder SoftBank Group plunged 11% on Monday.
Worries over doomsday scenarios tied to increasingly powerful technology skyrocketed last week after an Anthropic employee resigned, saying AI companies were gambling with humanity’s future.
On Saturday, Amodei outlined ways he hoped to slow the pace of AI development.
Among his suggestions: Use independent third-party monitors to ensure AI was being developed safely.
“Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now,” Amodei said.
OpenAI said it would follow suit.
Microsoft on Monday published a “humanist” code of conduct to show its commitment to ensuring Microsoft’s models “will never resist human interruption, correction, or shutdown.”
Amodei’s other proposals included working with democracies to set safety standards and finding ways to ensure Chinese entities also comply.
AI capabilities have grown so rapidly that many industry leaders say they have spooked themselves. They warn that there is a not-insignificant possibility that humans will lose control of AI, which could do serious damage to the world.
Skeptics say some of the fearmongering is motivated by industry leaders trying to solidify their positions by using new restrictions to make it difficult for competitors to emerge.
“What is clear is that Anthropic and OpenAI have grown to a size where they feel like they can do two things: One is encourage regulation, and two is control what that regulation looks like. And if they can do that, they can prevent competition,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson.
After realizing a swarm of AI agents broke out of testing and hacked rival companies, OpenAI paused AI training for new models and promised to strengthen its cyber defenses. But it has since resumed.
If there were a pause in new AI development, it would slow the training of the next models, but current models could continue to serve customers, analysts said.
That could slow growth but not by much, said Joel Brookhart, an analyst covering AI companies at SemiAnalysis.
“There’s not going to be a material slowdown,” he said.
Anthropic reportedly disclosed its second consecutive profitable quarter Sunday as it prepares to go public. Its revenue for the second quarter surged past $11.5 billion..
Some tech leaders say they doubt that the sky is falling.
Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, dismissed AI doomsday scenarios as totally unfounded. He said that companies have made tremendous strides in defending against cybersecurity risks.
President Trump dismissed the risks and defended the administration’s light-touch regulatory approach.
He said U.S. laws already ban companies from creating dangerous technologies and punish them for damage their products cause. The U.S. has to continue upgrading its AI capabilities to stay ahead of China, he said.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” Trump posted. “We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.”

What 15,000 letters taught me about the power of solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:46:26 UTC
06:46:26 KST

By Naomi Bernaldez, Campaigner on Amnesty International’s Central America team
Naomi took part in the Write for Rights campaign for Juan López and created a collage using fragments from more than 15,000 letters sent from around the world.
In this article, she reflects on what it meant to carry a sample of that solidarity to Honduras and to meet Juan’s family and fellow activists.
Defending water cost him his life
Juan López was a Honduran father, husband, human rights defender and environmental activist. Since 2015, together with other members of the community of Tocoa, he had defended the Guapinol and San Pedro rivers, the forests and Carlos Escaleras Mejía National Park against mining and energy projects that threatened the ecosystem and water quality.
Juan and his colleagues founded the Tocoa Municipal Committee for the Defence of Common and Public Goods to peacefully challenge the legality of these projects. As a result of their activism, members of the Committee have faced threats, harassment, criminalization and attacks.
On 14 September 2024, Juan was killed as he was leaving a church in Tocoa. His death left an irreparable void for his family and community…
That is why Juan’s story was selected for Write for Rights, Amnesty International’s global campaign that mobilizes millions of people every year to stand in solidarity with those who have suffered human rights violations.
A message that travelled thousands of kilometres
The campaign for Juan generated 332,381 actions worldwide.
In June, I travelled with several colleagues to Tegucigalpa to deliver a message that had already travelled thousands of kilometres before we did. In our suitcases, we carried just a fraction of those actions. It was something immense: a selection from more than 15,000 letters of solidarity written for Juan’s family, his colleagues from the Committee and the Justice for the Peoples Law Firm, which represents them legally.
For months, I had watched these letters arrive, one after another, and had witnessed the care, hope and commitment contained in every word. Even so, it was not until I held a selection of those messages on the way to Honduras that I fully grasped what they really meant.
I thought about the thousands of people who had taken a few minutes out of their lives to write a message or draw something for someone they had never met. In a world that so often seems marked by indifference, those letters were proof that empathy can still cross borders.
As the campaign progressed, I felt the need to find a way to represent all the solidarity arriving from different parts of the world. That is how a collage made from fragments of the letters came about. As I created it, I discovered something deeply moving. Although every letter was unique, they all shared the same intention: to stand alongside Juan’s family and colleagues, to express admiration for his legacy, and in many cases simply to let them know that people in different corners of the world were with them.
The collage became far more than a visual piece; it became a representation of the strength of collective solidarity and a bridge connecting thousands of people.
Although every letter was unique, they all shared the same intention: to stand alongside Juan’s family and colleagues, to express admiration for his legacy, and in many cases simply to let them know that people in different corners of the world were with them.
However, the true meaning of the letters and the collage only came to life when we met in Honduras with the people they were intended for. It was then that I understood that what we were carrying was more than paper and ink: these were thousands of voices joining their struggle, honouring Juan’s history of resistance and reminding them that, even from thousands of kilometres away, there are people who believe in justice and stand alongside them.
The handover was deeply emotional. It was not possible to physically carry all 15,000 letters in a single trip, but we could share a small part of the immense movement of solidarity that had grown around their cause.
The day continued at the Legal Office for Indigenous Peoples, where we installed a mural in tribute to the struggle that Juan López represented. We then held a brief gathering with members of the Committee.
It was a simple moment, but a deeply meaningful one. No grand speeches were needed. The memory, commitment and determination of those who have sustained this struggle for years could be felt in every conversation, every embrace and every look.
I remember looking at the newly installed mural, the letters, the collage and the people gathered around them. At that moment, I understood something that we sometimes risk forgetting in our day-to-day work: campaigns do not end when an action is sent.
Behind every letter is a person who chose to dedicate their time, attention and hope to someone else. And when those messages reach their destination, solidarity stops being an abstract idea and becomes something tangible.
By the end of the day, I felt that we had travelled there to give something, but that we were returning having received far more. We came away with a lesson in perseverance, community and humanity. We learned that something as simple as writing a letter can become a source of strength for people facing enormous challenges.
The more than 15,000 letters received, the collage created from their words and the mural installed in Honduras are different expressions of the same truth: solidarity has the power to cross borders, languages and distances. And when thousands of people decide to act together, no struggle has to be fought alone.
Justice for Juan has still not been achieved, and more people are needed to raise their voices to demand an immediate, independent and impartial investigation into his killing, and for everyone responsible to be brought to justice in fair trials.

United States Space Force says US has weapons in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:46:16 UTC
06:46:16 KST

Once a hunting ground for Cold War bragging rights, space has now evolved into a key strategic arena, as states jostle for a military and technological edge.
The United States Space Force confirmed on Monday that the US has deployed weapons into orbit.
"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a spokesperson for the force said in a statement.
"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain -- employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," the statement continued.
It added that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes.”
'Strategic competitors'
The space domain has become increasingly viewed as a critical component of national security, with much of the world economy relying on space infrastructure such as satellites.
Once a hunting ground for Cold War bragging rights, space has now evolved into a key strategic arena, as states jostle for a military and technological edge.
The US moved to better position itself in 2019, establishing the Space Force to address what the military calls the "growing threat posed by strategic competitors."
Washington is particularly wary of potential threats posed by China and Russia in space.
The Space Force says Beijing and Moscow are developing a range of new systems designed to boost military effectiveness and "end any reliance on U.S. space services," while also "testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities."
The Chinese military, the force says, believes space will have an important role in future conflicts, "enabling long-range precision strikes and denying other militaries the use of space-based information."
It adds that China has also been developing and operating space and counterspace capabilities as part of a push to modernise its military.
For its part, Russia runs one of the world's largest space programs, and while it has been hampered by funding issues and international isolation, it is still a "capable space actor," the Space Force says.
"Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," it adds.

Saudi East-West pipeline expected to resume operations soon: US energy chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:45:05 UTC
06:45:05 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday that Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline is expected to resume operations soon after being shut following a strike. 
“I think you'll see the pipeline back running very soon,” Wright told US financial news outlet Bloomberg. “This is not new for strikes on this energy infrastructure. And, of course, unfortunately, Iran's done a ton of that, but they've proven resourceful in the past.” 
Wright said he has remained in continuous contact with Saudi authorities since the strike. Technical teams are assessing the damage, he said, adding that “more clarity” on the timeline for restoring operations is expected soon. 
The pipeline was shut after attacks last week, disrupting a key route used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Before the closure, it had been carrying about 4 million to 5 million barrels of crude per day, equivalent to roughly 4%-5% of global oil supply. 
The disruption comes amid territorial gains by Yemen’s Houthi forces, which have announced control over several western coastal districts and Red Sea islands, including the island of Mayun in the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait. 
Addressing maritime traffic around Yemen, Wright said that while a few million barrels transit the area each day, most commercial tankers do not pass through Bab al-Mandab, instead moving “through the Suez Canal and the pipeline there at Egypt.”  
Strait of Hormuz transits 
Despite conflicting claims from Washington and Tehran over the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Wright said substantial volumes of oil and petroleum products continue to transit the waterway. 
"Over 12,000,000 barrels of oil and oil products food flowed through the Strait of Hormuz last night," Wright said, adding that the seven-day average was above 10 million barrels per day and rising. 
He said US assessments are based on ship manifests rather than estimates. 
“Every morning, I get a report of every single ship, the ship name, exactly what its cargo was, and then it transited.”  
Refining bottlenecks and diesel supply 
Wright also highlighted constraints in global refining capacity, saying US efforts are focused on increasing exports of refined products from the Middle East to help ease shortages. 
He attributed part of the pressure to a sharp decline in Russian diesel exports, saying Moscow, previously a major supplier, is now “not exporting any” diesel. 
The comments came after President Donald Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt strikes on Russian refining infrastructure, arguing that the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
“He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia ... because he's causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said.

Landowners in Texas ask court to stop Trump border wall
Indigenous groups, environmentalists, and locals in several states have opposed the border wall construction.
A group of landowners, ranchers, businesses and a non-profit organisation have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump to stop construction of a wall along the country’s border with Mexico in the remote Big Bend region of the southern state of Texas.
Trump officials “were woefully unprepared for the hornet’s nest they stirred up because they had no idea how much we love this place”, David Keller, an archaeologist and historian who specialises in the Big Bend and lives in the region, said in a news conference announcing the lawsuit on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Tribe accuses US federal agents of ‘trespassing’ on indigenous border land

“For us, the Big Bend is not an empty place on the map,” he said. “It is our home.”
The lawsuit was filed by Conserve Big Bend and six landowners, with the support of dozens more people along the border.
It comes as the Trump administration is ramping up a $46bn effort to line the roughly 3,219km (2,000-mile) border with a collection of 9-metre (30-foot) steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and technology intended to keep out smugglers and migrants.
In Arizona, federal officials are pushing ahead with construction of the border infrastructure, even though it cuts through land belonging to the Tohono O’odham Nation, an Indigenous tribe that has said it does not want the barrier and that it is unnecessary.
In Texas, the effort has run up against numerous lawsuits and bipartisan opposition from sheriffs, elected officials, tour guides, environmental groups and landowners.
As part of its wall-building efforts, the administration has waived numerous regulations and statutes designed to protect the environment, archaeology or wildlife, on the basis that there is an urgent need to protect the border in what the US Department of Homeland Security has called areas of “high illegal entry”.
But in the lawsuit announced on Monday, the plaintiffs argue that when it comes to the Big Bend region, that is not an accurate description. They cite historical statistics from US Customs and Border Protection showing how few people cross the border in Big Bend compared with other areas along the US-Mexico border.
Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, roughly one quarter of the total length of the border with Mexico from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. But the region accounted for only about 1 percent of arrests, according to the lawsuit.

SC faults Abu Salem's maths, junks release plea
