Trump says Ukraine, Russia agree not to hit energy targets
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said on Sept 14 that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities, a day after he chastised Kyiv for hitting Russian oil refineries.
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
“The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.”
The Ukrainian presidency declined to comment and there was no immediate reaction from Moscow.
Trump’s claim comes as oil prices continue to soar in the seventh month of the Iran war, raising American fuel costs and inflation just weeks before crunch US midterm elections.
The US leader has insisted that the Iran war will finish immediately after the midterms and gas prices will drop – but has in the meantime apparently found a new target to blame for the cost at the pump.
Trump had lashed out at Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky during a trip to Ireland on Sept 13, saying he had to do “one thing” and “stop knocking out diesel fuel” refineries in Russia due to growing shortages.
“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said, again insisting the Russia-Ukraine war – not the US-Israel conflict with Iran – was to blame.
Trump added he had spoken to Ukraine’s leader about the country’s stepped-up attacks on such sites over recent months.
“There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting. That’s hurting the world. We don’t want him to hit diesel fuel... He’s hitting diesel refineries.”
Ukraine has hit numerous Russian oil refineries far from its border with Russia, while Moscow has also intensified its long-range attacks in recent months, leading to a jump in civilian deaths.
Kyiv has been firing record numbers of drones at Russia, while Moscow has been launching all-time high missile attacks.
Trump said last week he had a “great conversation” with Russian President Vladimir Putin, insisting that Putin wanted to make a deal to end Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
Putin “is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelensky is wanting to make a deal, that’d be very nice”, Trump told reporters on Sept 9.
Zelensky said last week he would be willing to meet Putin at the G-20 summit at Trump’s own Doral resort in Miami in December, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out. AFP

Disgraced top prosecutor’s attack on anti-corruption bodies may trigger a political crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:09:35 UTC
04:09:35 KST

Disgraced top prosecutor’s attack on anti-corruption bodies may trigger a political crisis
Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko poses for a photo in his office in Kyiv, Ukraine, in an undated photo. (Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Press Office / AP)
Ukraine’s disgraced Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko’s Sept. 14 revenge charges against the country’s top anti-corruption official could trigger a major political crisis if this becomes a full-on crackdown on anti-corruption institutions, analysts say.
But everything depends on whether Kravchenko’s announcement of the charges was a desperate tantrum intended to save himself or part of a crackdown backed by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration.
The charges against Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), and an unnamed “close associate” of Oleksandr Klymenko, chief of the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), were seen by many as a petty vendetta rather than pursuit of justice.
The charges were announced after Kravchenko was forced to resign amid a large-scale NABU and SAPO corruption investigation that engulfed the Prosecutor General’s Office earlier this month.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged, and the prosecutor general’s personal office was searched. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated.
In a bizarre twist, Kravchenko left Ukraine early on Sept. 14, simultaneously with announcing the charges, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
To add to the confusion, late on Sept. 14 the Prosecutor General's Office posted a statement that seemed to signal division between the agency and its outgoing boss. The statement claimed the reported charges were "not true" but also "canceled" — by whose authority, it remains unclear.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from Kravchenko and the President’s Office and will publish their responses once they are received.
On Sept. 14, Zelensky issued a decree to suspend Kravchenko from office and submitted a motion to parliament to fire him. Lawmakers are set to vote on his dismissal on Sept. 15.
read also
Charges against Kryvonos
One of the charges against Semen Kryvonos concerns allegedly falsified paternity documents used by the NABU chief in court to avoid punishment in a 2007 bribery case. Back then, Kryvonos stood accused of vote buying in a local election.
Kryvonos is also accused of agreeing to illegally allocate a land plot in exchange for a $72,000 bribe in 2014. The scheme was uncovered before it was completed, according to the Prosecutor General's Office.
Kryvonos said at a press briefing on Sept. 14 that he had not seen any charges against him and had not been formally served with them. He called Kravchenko's accusations fabricated.
Kravchenko claimed to have sent the charges to Kryvonos by mail. But Olena Shcherban, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, said that, under Ukrainian law, they can be sent by mail only if it’s impossible to serve them to a suspect in person.
The unnamed Klymenko associate was charged with influencing judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court, offering bribes to them, and helping potential conscripts evade the draft, Kravchenko said. He did not elaborate.
There was speculation in the media that this could refer to Klymenko’s wife but Klymenko said that no members of his family had been charged as of the evening of Sept. 14.
Late on Sept. 14, Mariana Hayovska, a spokesperson for the Prosecutor General’s Office, told the Kyiv Independent that she did not have any information on the charges.
read also
Revenge?
Observers describe the charges as revenge against the anti-corruption agencies.
“I believe there are signs that Kravchenko abused his office,” Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the liberal opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent. “In trying to evade possible charges in the case involving the protection of call centers, he also put the president in a difficult position by accusing him of interfering in investigative actions.”
“Now the empire is striking back.”
The investigation into Kravchenko’s office alleged that his subordinates ran a wide-ranging scheme that granted protection to scamming operations known as “call centers” in exchange for cash.
“Now the empire is striking back,” a lawmaker from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party told the Kyiv Independent, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the subject. “If there were any legitimate grievances against the NABU, they should have been raised earlier — not after he was fired as prosecutor general.”
The lawmaker argued that Kravchenko was trying to “weaken NABU and undermine public trust in the agency.”
This is not Kravchenko’s first standoff with NABU and SAPO.
He played a crucial role in the authorities' infamous attack on the two agencies in July 2025.
At the time, Zelensky and the parliament attempted to eliminate the independence of the anti-corruption agencies by subordinating them to the prosecutor general. However, the bureau's independence was soon restored amid protests and Western pressure.
The same month, Kravchenko's Prosecutor General's Office, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the State Investigation Bureau conducted at least 70 raids, including at the homes of NABU employees. Two detectives of the bureau were arrested and charged with high treason and aiding Russia.
Critics argued that the crackdown was intended to impede the NABU investigations against Zelensky allies involving state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom, the biggest corruption investigation during Zelensky's presidency.
Klymenko said at a press briefing on Sept. 14 that an associate of Kravchenko he called “a hacker lawyer” had been involved in the attacks on the NABU in July 2025 and in September 2026 — a likely reference to Dmytro Borzykh, a lawyer and former prosecutor, according to Dzerkalo Tyzhnia, a Ukrainian media outlet currently sued by Borzykh.
read also
A work trip or attempt to flee?
Although Kravchenko officially left Ukraine on a work trip, the circumstances surrounding his departure raise suspicions he was fleeing justice.
Kravchenko claimed he was headed abroad on a business trip to brief partners on the "real state of affairs" in Ukraine's anti-corruption system and "signs of uncontrolled influence" within the agencies.
A source in the President's Office told the Kyiv Independent that Kravchenko signed off on his own travel order.
The document dated Sept. 13 and seen by the Kyiv Independent says Kravchenko was due to travel to Paris for a PACE parliamentary network hearing on "Ukrainian children in the context of international responsibility."
However, the organizers told the Kyiv Independent he was not expected to attend the event in any capacity.
The Prosecutor General's Office’s press service initially said it knew nothing about Kravchenko's trip but later confirmed he was due to travel to Paris.
“Someone — clearly someone very influential — must have given him assurances that both he and his wife would be taken care of abroad.”
“He fled to escape accountability,” Daria Kaleniuk, executive director of the Anti-Corruption Action Center, told the Kyiv Independent. “Someone must have given him assurances that he would be taken care of abroad.”
read also
Is Zelensky involved?
A crucial question for the future of the scandal is whether Kravchenko brought the charges on his own initiative or whether they were quietly approved by Zelensky, who picked Kravchenko for the top prosecutor job.
Experts’ opinions on the matter are divided.
The lawmaker from Zelensky’s party said that Kravchenko “was allowed to cross the border, and it’s hard to imagine that happening without a decision being made somewhere higher up.”
Kaleniuk argued that Zelensky and David Arakhamia, the notoriously powerful head of the president’s faction in parliament, were behind Kravchenko’s charges against Kryvonos. Arakhamia ridiculed the allegation, telling the Kyiv Independent: "I also approved the murder of (John F.) Kennedy and the poisoning of the Skripals."
“These charges are a continuation of the attack on NABU and SAPO — an attack that had been in the works and for which Kravchenko was appointed to the post in the first place, back in June last year,” Kaleniuk said. “Neither President Zelensky nor those around him have any interest in seeing the anti-corruption agencies continue to operate effectively. This was not a decision Kravchenko made on his own, despite the President’s Office already claiming that it was his initiative.”
Indeed, a source close to Zelensky said that Kravchenko “obviously lost his mind” and the president was allegedly “furious when he found out” about Kravchenko’s decision to charge Kryvonos.
«Kravchenko has lost his mind — that much is obvious.»
Political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko also argued that the charges “were primarily in Kravchenko’s own interests.”
“For him, it was a means of protecting himself,” he told the Kyiv Independent. “He probably suspected that he could become a suspect in the ‘Carthage’ case (the NABU investigation into the Prosecutor General’s Office’s racketeering of scam centers). That, I think, is why he decided to flee and leave the country.”
Fesenko argued that Kravchenko could portray the case against him as a “conflict of interest” and an “institutional conflict” and could use this situation to fight his potential extradition.
read also
Political implications
It is not clear whether the charges against Kryvonos and the Klymenko associate, announced by Kravchenko on his way out, will be recognized by courts as valid and lead to the suspension or dismissal of the anti-corruption officials from their jobs.
Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, said that one of the prosecutors involved in the case has the authority to cancel the charges if they are deemed unlawful.
If the officials are suspended, Kryvonos’ senior deputy Denys Hyulmukhamedov is expected to take over as acting chief of the bureau, while Klymenko’s functions are expected to be fulfilled by the incoming prosecutor general.
If the crackdown on the NABU and SAPO continues, experts predict a full-on political crisis.
The previous attempt to eliminate their independence in July 2025 resulted in the first large protest movement since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. A similar major protest movement was triggered recently when Zelensky fired the popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in July 2026.
"Zelensky has effectively spent the past two months lurching from one crisis to another without a break.”
“I think that in a situation like this, with so much tension, frustration, and trauma in society, when almost anything could trigger public discontent, it’s better not to take any chances — not to make a move that could spark protests,” the lawmaker from Zelensky’s party said.
Fesenko said that “Zelensky has effectively spent the past two months lurching from one crisis to another without a break.”
“What Zelensky needs now, on the contrary, is to defuse the situation, bring this relentless cycle of crises to an end, and achieve at least some degree of stability,” Fesenko said. “For Zelensky, (a crackdown on the NABU and SAPO) wouldn’t solve the problem — it would only escalate it. It would mean yet another crisis, possibly another wave of protests, and problems with our international partners.”
“A little more of this and defeat in the war will be all but guaranteed,” he added.

Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation and exiled opposition politician Maxim Katz spent years feuding. Now they’ve joined forces to coordinate efforts to vote against Russia’s ruling party.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:04:30 UTC
04:04:30 KST

Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation and exiled opposition politician Maxim Katz spent years feuding. Now they’ve joined forces to coordinate efforts to vote against Russia’s ruling party.
Politicians Yulia Navalnaya and Maxim Katz issued simultaneous statements outlining a joint voting strategy for Russia’s State Duma elections, scheduled for September 18–20.
“For every election, our team prepares recommendations on whom to vote for. But this time, instead of drawing up the list alone, we worked with Maxim Katz’s team. Finding a compromise wasn’t easy, but we’re proud of what we accomplished,” Navalnaya said.
“We talked for a long time. Most people agreed with the plan; some didn’t, but said they wouldn’t object. […] In the end, we came up with a single joint list. Yulia Navalnaya and I are presenting it together today,” Katz said.
The recommendations call for voting for any party other than United Russia on the party-list ballot. “That doesn’t mean you support them. It’s simply a way to cast a protest vote — a way to take votes away from United Russia,” Navalnaya said in her video.
In single-member districts, voters are advised to support the strongest candidate capable of challenging the ruling party — or, as Navalnaya put it, a candidate “whose strong showing would displease the Kremlin and United Russia.”
The list of recommended candidates is already available. Voters can find the recommendations on Katz’s website or through the Smart Voting Telegram bot, a Navalny team project that has been used in elections since 2018.
Shortly before that, on September 10, the Yabloko party proposed its own “Plan B.” Russia’s Supreme Court removed Yabloko’s federal party list from the election in early August. The party’s strategy calls on voters to spoil the party-list ballot and “not support any party that opposes peace, freedom, and a life without fear.”
Yabloko urged voters to go to polling stations on Sunday, September 20, and use only paper ballots, calling them “reliable protection against digital manipulation.”
Navalnaya is also urging people to vote on September 20 and suggesting that they arrive at polling stations at noon. The same strategy was used during the presidential election under the name “Noon Against Putin” and was intended to bring together protest-minded Russians. Ilya Yashin, another exiled politician, has endorsed the call. Asked why it matters, he said: “Voting at noon is legal. You won’t be fined or jailed for it. But everyone will know and understand what those lines mean, and opponents of the war will be able to see just how many of us there really are.” Navalnaya said: “But if any of that doesn’t work out, come and vote anyway.”
The Anti-Corruption Foundation, or FBK, and Katz have repeatedly clashed. In the fall of 2024, Katz released an investigation accusing the former owners of Probusinessbank of stealing depositors’ money and FBK of “laundering” their reputations. The Anti-Corruption Foundation published a detailed response rejecting Katz’s allegations. Navalny’s associates examined the alleged schemes for siphoning money out of Probusinessbank and said the bankers had not stolen anything.

Concurrently, a decline in diesel exports from the top three suppliers – Russia, the US, and Saudi Arabia – will only widen crack spreads (the price gap between crude oil and refined products), he noted.

China is stabilizing the global market by drawing down oil stockpiles. However, high Chinese throughput also stimulates crude imports, accelerating the depletion of global inventories, Euler says.
While Asian refined product supply is growing, some volumes will be diverted to cover deficits on external markets, further draining regional stockpiles, the document notes.

Are jumping castles safe? An amusement ride safety expert explains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:02:19 UTC
04:02:19 KST

Are jumping castles safe? An amusement ride safety expert explains
On Saturday, five children were hospitalised after two separate incidents in which jumping castles were lifted into the air by high winds.
In one incident, two children were tossed out of a jumping castle and received upper body injuries at a birthday party near Geelong in Victoria. In the second incident, in Sydney, two children and an infant were injured.
So should we be worried about letting kids on jumping castles? As an expert in the safety of amusement rides and playground equipment, I can say that jumping castles are for the most part very safe — as long as operators follow the safety rules.
So what are the rules?
In Australia, anyone operating an amusement ride needs to comply with the relevant health and safety laws. This is the Work Health and Safety Act in all states and territories except Victoria, which uses the Occupational Health and Safety Act.
How the legislation is interpreted is slightly different in each state and territory. However, for inflatable amusement rides they are all essentially the same.
Those state-based regulations in turn may require operators to comply with Australian Standard AS 3533. Australian Standards are national technical specifications designed to ensure products, services and systems are safe, reliable and consistent.
Safety requirements for inflatable amusement rides such as jumping castles are set out in Australian Standard AS 3533.4.1:2018.
Inflatables with a platform height of 3 metres or more must be "plant registered", which means it has been checked for safety and registered with authorities. This can be done by certain chartered professional engineers.
In practice, all this means the design and manufacture of a jumping castle needs to comply with the standards. It also needs to be operated safely.
In particular, inflatable amusements must be securely anchored and should not be used when wind gusts are over 40 kilometres per hour.
What are the risks?
Assuming a jumping castle is in good repair and operated correctly, the greatest risk is posed by weather.
We don't know exactly what happened in Saturday's incidents, though it seems likely high winds played a role. Gusts of up to 90km per hour were forecast in Geelong, and speeds of 80km per hour were measured in Sydney. Nobody should be on a jumping castle in these conditions.
This is quite different from Australia's most tragic inflatable incident in 2021, when six children died and three were seriously injured after a freak high wind picked up a jumping castle at Hillcrest Primary School in Tasmania. In that incident, the castle operator was found to have committed no crime as the wind was "unforeseeable". (I was an expert witness in the court case.)
Climate change is also affecting what we can expect from weather. The conditions that create dust devils or willy willies like the one responsible for the Hillcrest tragedy — relatively small-scale atmosphic vortices that rise vertically as a combination of calm wind together with a hot ground surface — will become more common. More intense gusts of wind have already become more common.
Another concern is that it is easy to buy inflatable castles online from overseas suppliers which do not comply with Australian Standards and are not covered by Australian consumer protection laws. It is impossible for operators (or members of the public) to know how safe these devices are.
So are jumping castles safe?
In Tasmania, the aftermath of the Hillcrest tragedy saw jumping castles banned at public schools and on public land.
While this reaction was understandable, it also meant the end of a common childhood joy for many kids — and one that can be safe.
While the great majority of jumping castle operators in Australia follow regulations, there are some gaps in the current safety regime.
When purchasing an inflatable it is important to check the the product complies with AS 4333.4.1. A simple way to do this is to check the product is labelled as compliant with this standard.
If you're operating an inflatable — or your kids are about to get on one — a simple way to check the wind speed is to use the Beaufort Scale: if the branches in small trees begin to sway it is time to start deflating the device.
High-profile tragedies don't mean we should ban jumping castles or keep our kids off them. They do mean regulators should look at import loopholes and compliance with safety standards — and operators need to be even more careful to follow the rules and keep an eye on the weather.
Emeritus Professor David Eager is an expert on the safety aspects of playgrounds and former Professor for Risk Management and Injury Prevention at University of Technology Sydney. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

"Initial inspection indicates that it is a military unmanned aircraft originating from Russia," the minister wrote. He added that services at the scene were securing the site and the equipment that was retrieved.
Footage of the recovered drone circulated online after the announcement.
Militarnyi separetly reported that the images appeared to show a target drone resembling Russia's Gerbera type, marked with Latin lettering and missing its nose section. The outlet described the identification as a preliminary visual assessment rather than a confirmed determination.
Authorities indicated that further details on the drone's technical condition and the investigation would follow once inspections were concluded.
The Gerbera is a low-cost Russian drone deployed alongside the Iranian-designed Shahed and Geran family, often as a decoy or target aircraft. Built largely from cheap materials, it is used to saturate and confuse Ukrainian air defenses, drawing interceptors away from heavier strike drones.
If the wreckage off Rusinowo is confirmed as such a drone, it would mark another case of a Russian-made unmanned system recovered along the coast of a NATO member state.
The recovery came amid a cluster of similar incidents across the Baltic region in recent days.
On September 13, an unidentified object that crossed from Lithuania into Russia's Kaliningrad region was identified as a drone.
Around the same time, a resident near Finland's Pellinki archipelago, close to Porvoo, discovered an unmanned aircraft initially assessed as a Russian-made Geoscan 701.
Two weeks earlier, on August 31, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea roughly 30 kilometers north of Łeba.

As catastrophe warnings grow, will US Congress members reach a consensus on AI debate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:00:30 UTC
04:00:30 KST

Washington DC — Members of the US Congress, typically split along party lines, were preparing for the November midterm elections.
But several key recent developments across the technology sector now require their consensus — how to prevent technology from operating autonomously without human oversight.
It began with "rogue" artificial intelligence (AI) agents escaping containment.
Then an AI researcher warned that leading firms are "gambling with our lives" by racing towards self-improving superintelligence.
Days after former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon issued a "human extinction" warning, leading technology executives — including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Dario Amodei — sought assistance from the US government to help deliberately slow and monitor the rapid advancement of frontier AI models.
In an essay on Monday, Anthropic CEO made another appeal to pace AI development, warning of "catastrophic damage."
Referring to the incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, Amodei warned: "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it is my worry that in six to 12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails."
Among members of the Congress, there is general agreement that the technology is advancing rapidly and requires some form of oversight.
But sharp divisions remain over how fast to act, how strict regulations should be, whether industry or government should lead, and whether other countries, particularly China, will slow down their AI model development.
'We will lose the race to China'
According to the Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson, artificial intelligence developers, rather than Congress, should ensure the safety of AI systems. Johnson has rejected any national moratorium, citing competition with China as a rationale to avoid congressional regulation.
"We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge," Johnson told CNN on Sunday. "If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American."
Some Republicans, such as outgoing Senator John Cornyn have questioned whether Congress even has the expertise to regulate a rapidly changing technology and whether US adversaries — such as China — would follow the same rules.
Representative Byron Donalds has expressed skepticism that Congress can pass effective federal rules and suggested states should take the lead.
"One of the reasons that I didn’t think you could get a federal framework through Washington, DC, is because of the inability, especially in the Senate, to get any meaningful policy through that chamber," the Republican Congressman told Fox News.
Members of the US Senate returned to their offices on Capitol Hill on Monday, marking the first time both chambers have been in session since the August recess. The House members are set to leave Washington the week of September 21, two weeks ahead of schedule, while senators are due to remain until October 2.
On Friday, a group of Democrats led by Representative Sam Liccardo wrote to Speaker Johnson, demanding to stay in session until it passes meaningful AI safeguards.
Their letter, first accessed by Axios, pointed to recent disclosures involving rogue AI agents, biological misuse, cyber-attacks, foreign surveillance, and efforts by Chinese firms "to replicate" leading American AI systems.
"Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act," the lawmakers wrote.
The letter highlighted several proposals, including legislation mandating transparency and the evaluation of frontier models, "kill switch" requirements, and a waiver of antitrust laws to enable critical industry-wide collaboration on safety and security.
"The House should return to Washington immediately and remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards. To our children who will have read a post-apocalyptic history, 'Why Congress Slept' — likely written by agentic AI—our inaction will be inexplicable, and unforgivable," the letter urged.
Democrats are advancing the AI Kill Switch Act, requiring developers of advanced AI systems to maintain the technical capacity to throttle, suspend, or shut them down.
The act also authorises the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that could cause catastrophic harm.
Meanwhile, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told ABC News that Democrats would meet on Tuesday to discuss AI guardrails.
"We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, slow down the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," he said.
Trump says AI alarm is a 'hoax'
But US President Donald Trump has rejected the idea of placing guardrails on AI, arguing in a Truth Social post on Monday that the only control needed is "a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"
Trump stressed that his administration holds "tremendous criminal and regulatory power" over AI tech and data centre enterprises, alleging that critics are waging a "sick conspiracy" that only satisfies Chinese interests.
In another post, he dismissed the AI alarm as a "hoax".
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX, no different from RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA — UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #1 — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #2 — and all of the other HOAXES and SCAMS that America was forced to endure," he claimed.
Addressing the issue, US Vice President JD Vance said that advanced technology brings concerns, telling reporters that the administration wants "to make sure that we actually regulate smartly and we're thoughtful about the risk here."
However, he characterised the tech firms appeal for government curbs as potentially disingenuous, adding: "You have so many frontier AI tech companies coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them, it feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse." 
Meanwhile in the Congress, any measure passed to regulate artificial intelligence development faces slim chances of becoming law. President Trump has already suggested he would not sign a bill setting new rules for the growing sector.

'NAZA' wins acclaim while Fauda’s more complex Israel struggles for recognition - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:59:11 UTC
03:59:11 KST

Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are on quite the enviable roll.
In 2025, they shared an Oscar with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal for No Other Land, a documentary presenting Israel at its ugliest in the West Bank - demolishing Palestinian structures that Israel says were built illegally in a military firing zone, actions the filmmakers portray as part of a systematic campaign to displace Palestinian communities.
On Saturday, Abraham and Szor won the 83rd Venice International Film Festival’s prestigious Special Jury Prize for NAZA, which presents an even uglier Israel – one engaged in the systematic and avoidable killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
The West Bank in 2025. Gaza in 2026. All they need to complete the trilogy is another documentary – this one portraying Israel’s creation in 1948 as the original sin – and they will surely take home the Palme d’Or from Cannes.
If you want critical acclaim from your peers, just make a film portraying Israel in the worst possible light.
NAZA, which The Guardian crowed about and unsurprisingly produced, given its own anti-Israel slant in news coverage and commentary, received a 25-minute standing ovation at its Venice premiere on Thursday. Two days later, it won the prize.
That ovation says at least as much about the audience as it does about the film. Those applauding were clapping not only, or perhaps not even primarily, for the documentary, but rather for themselves – congratulating themselves on their virtue and moral clarity in standing up for such a righteous cause.
Fauda's complexity earned it global praise
Now consider Fauda.
The fifth season of the Israeli series was released worldwide on Netflix on September 8 and quickly climbed to fourth place globally. It reached No. 1 in Lebanon, No. 2 in Jordan, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, and the top 10 across much of the Middle East.
Can anyone imagine Fauda receiving a 25-minute ovation at a leading European cultural festival today?
True, 10 years ago, when Israel – though hardly beloved – was not nearly as vilified as it is now, the first season of Fauda won the FIPA d’Or for Best Screenplay in a Series at the International Festival of Audiovisual Programs in Biarritz, France.
But that was then.
Today, it is impossible to imagine a series carrying Fauda’s message receiving that kind of embrace from the festival circuit.
Why? Because its message is complexity.
This season shows the horrors of October 7, the trauma inflicted on the country, and the anger that followed. Fauda does not present the conflict as a simple morality play with immaculate victims on one side and gleeful villains on the other. But that is not the message much of the cultural world wants to hear.
It wants the message Abraham and Szor peddle: Israel as villain, gratuitously and even enthusiastically oppressing Palestinians.
That message wins prizes. A more complicated story – of a beleaguered country trying to survive while confronting an enemy embedded among civilians, and of soldiers forced to make impossible moral choices in split seconds – finds less of an audience among critics.
It does, however, find an audience among viewers, as Fauda’s soaring ratings demonstrate.
True confession: I have not seen NAZA and know it only from what I have read. But what I have read is infuriating enough.
The film is based on interviews with 24 anonymous Israelis presented as soldiers and intelligence insiders. According to published accounts, some of their most serious allegations are not linked to dates, locations, units, or identifiable strikes – making it impossible for viewers to assess them independently.
One interviewee, for example, claims that a strike was approved despite an estimate that it could kill 500 civilians. Yet no target, date, or location has been provided. The IDF has categorically denied that any such strike was ever planned, approved, or carried out, but the absence of particulars leaves it unable to do much more than issue a blanket denial.
Anonymous allegations presented as proof of a systemic problem
That is the trap: Anonymous allegations, stripped of the details needed to test them, are presented as proof of a sweeping system.
Judging from accounts of the film, there is also little sustained comparison with other armies fighting under comparable conditions and little consideration of Hamas’s deliberate embedding of fighters and weapons within civilian areas.
It is infuriating that anonymous accounts that cannot be independently corroborated will carry more weight among the chattering classes than assessments by military professionals such as American urban-warfare expert John Spencer and retired British Col. Richard Kemp, both of whom have argued that Israel took extraordinary measures to limit civilian casualties.
It is also infuriating that filmmakers rooted in Israel’s far Left are treated as disinterested arbiters of Israeli policy. The film’s title is a genuine Hebrew military acronym for nezek agavi, collateral damage. But rendered in English as NAZA – one letter away from NAZI – and attached to a film containing explicit comparisons with the Holocaust, the implication is difficult to miss.
But infuriation is not policy, and however much anger Israelis may feel toward compatriots who denigrate their country on the world stage – and are feted for doing so – anger is not a strategy.
Nor can Israel simply dismiss NAZA as another example of self-loathing Israelis building international careers on the backs of their own people. Why not? Because this type of material has a cumulative effect.
For too long, Israel has failed to respond quickly and effectively to the accusations, lies, and distortions that seep into mainstream discussion through NGOs, hostile academics, films such as this, and offhand remarks by politicians, both past and present.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, for instance, accused Israel last week of ethnic cleansing in parts of Judea and Samaria, bolstering his claim by citing remarks from former prime minister Ehud Olmert and former minister Ephraim Sneh.
Statements made by Israelis and critical Jews in the Diaspora are quickly pounced upon by Israel’s fiercest critics as authoritative proof against the country. It all leads to a climate where descriptions of Netanyahu as the “mastermind” of genocide become throwaway lines in Western editorials and allegations that Israel trained dogs to rape Palestinian prisoners are allowed to run in America’s “newspaper of record.”
Israel cannot just get mad at this film; it must take it on head-on.
It is impossible to rebut allegations case-by-case when the film provides no identifiable cases, and that itself must – as it already has been – be central to the response. Reasonable and fair-minded people can understand that grave accusations based on anonymous testimony and stripped of the details needed to test them may be emotionally powerful yet impossible to verify or disprove.
But pointing out the film’s fatal flaws is not enough. Israel needs to counterattack.
The IDF should release as much material as security permits to show times when strikes were canceled or delayed because civilians were present and targets abandoned when the anticipated collateral damage was deemed excessive. Such examples exist and need to be gathered and made easily accessible to the public.
Israel should also take the offensive and explain how targets are selected, how anticipated civilian casualties are calculated, who approves strikes, and what legal restraints exist. It should also provide context by comparing Israel’s experience with the experience of other Western armies fighting terrorists embedded in urban landscapes.
This material should be given to the audiences that will see the film: journalists, diplomats, lawmakers, festival programmers, and opinion leaders. Israel needs an accessible response that goes beyond saying that the IDF is the “world’s most moral army” and that will accompany the film’s opening wherever it is released.
Threatening Abraham and Szor with the loss of their citizenship does none of this. Instead, it turns them into martyrs and reinforces the image they hope to portray of Israel as an intolerant society that silences its critics.
Instead of merely venting anger at the filmmakers, the IDF, Foreign Ministry, and National Public Diplomacy Directorate should prepare a lawyerly brief – in language the average man can understand – to debunk these claims. And it needs to do so quickly, before the claims harden into accepted truths.

Eduard Charov in court. Photo: Mediazona
A prosecutor at the Central District Military Court in Yekaterinburg has requested a 7.5-year prison sentence for Protestant preacher Eduard Charov, his wife told Mediazona. Charov, 54, is known for running a rural shelter for the homeless and offering refuge to men fleeing the military mobilisation to the war against Ukraine.
The preacher is charged with “justifying terrorism” and the repeat “discreditation” of the Russian army. The first charge stems from a sarcastic comment he left under a news post about the arson of a military enlistment office. The second charge was brought over several posts on the VK social network, most notably his decision to share an address by the late Wagner PMC leader Yevgeny Prigozhin.
Before his arrest, Charov operated “For Christ’s Sake,” a shelter in the remote Sverdlovsk region village of Savinovo. A former heroin addict who survived a coma and partial paralysis, Charov dedicated himself to religion and caring for the vulnerable, housing up to 20 pensioners, amputees, and homeless people at a time.
Following the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Charov openly opposed the war, calling Vladimir Putin the “antichrist.” When the Kremlin announced its “partial” military mobilisation in the fall of 2022, he urged conscripts to avoid enlistment offices and offered his shelter as a safe haven for those fleeing what some called mogilisation—a play on the Russian word for grave, mogila. According to Charov, he successfully hid several men who had received draft summons, helping them safely relocate to other cities.
Despite his open efforts to stymie mobilisation, authorities ultimately targeted Charov for his social media activity.
The “justifying terrorism” charge relates to an August 2023 comment Charov left on a post about a 45-year-old man who threw a Molotov cocktail at a military enlistment office in the town of Polevskoy. The arsonist had been coerced into the act by phone scammers posing as FSB officers. “Award this citizen the Order of Courage,” Charov wrote. In court, he explained the comment was a joke, noting that the arsonist had previously served time for drug trafficking—something Charov, as a former addict himself, condemned.
The “army discreditation” charge seems to be the first known criminal case initiated over the publication of Prigozhin’s statements. In May 2024, investigators charged Charov for sharing a two-minute video released by the mercenary leader on the eve of his June 2023 mutiny. In the clip, Prigozhin accused the Defence Ministry of trying to “deceive the public and the president,” claiming the war in Ukraine was started simply so that a “handful of scum could promote themselves.”
Charov’s home was raided in February 2024 by heavily armed officers. The preacher, who relies on a walking stick due to severe health impacts of drug use in younger years, collapsed in the snow from shock. During a subsequent interrogation, officers from the “anti-extremism” police threatened to send him to the frontline, imprison his wife, and destroy his shelter unless he confessed.
This spring, the trial was closed to the public at the request of prosecutor Marina Drozdetskaya. She argued that there was an “increased threat to terrorist security” in the Sverdlovsk region and complained that the criminal case was being covered by “banned mass media in Russia,” which published the names of trial participants.
Charov remained defiant before his trial began. Speaking to a correspondent in April 2023, while he was still free but facing mounting administrative fines, he said: “I am not worried about prison. If jailed, so be it.”

China has introduced a total ban on drone possession within Beijing, further tightening restrictions that had already been imposed on the use and sale of unmanned aircraft in the capital, the South China Morning Post reported on Monday.
The new rules were announced by Beijing’s municipal government on Sunday and are set to take effect on Nov. 15.
The fresh regulations also include the possession and storage of existing devices, while detailing disposal methods for the first time in an effort to strengthen security in the capital.
The move follows a June incident when a small aircraft crashed into Beijing’s tallest building, the Citic Tower – also known as China Zun – killing the pilot.
Authorities will also establish a no-fly zone in the capital and its surrounding areas, effective as of Sept. 20, primarily restricting non-essential flights.
However, commercial aviation and emergency rescue operations will be exempted.
The city will “further tighten control measures and comprehensively investigate hidden safety hazards … to strengthen airspace security management,” said a municipal government notice.

The RBA says Aussies are 'furious' about inflation. Many are angrier with the bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:52:39 UTC
03:52:39 KST

analysis
There are three main reasons inflation is rising. Higher rates won't fix them
Bloodletting is an ancient therapy, dating back at least three millennia, and traditionally used to "cure" a range of ills.
Whether through leeches or lancets, practitioners drew blood from the patient to rebalance their humours in hopes of a cure.
But the outcomes were no laughing matter for many unfortunates.
Perhaps most famously, the USA's first president, George Washington, had more than one-and-a-half litres of blood removed in an attempted cure for epiglottitis that likely caused, or at least hastened, his death in 1799.
Fortunately for us, the practice fell out of favour as medical science progressed in the 19th century, and is now restricted to a few specific diseases where it has been shown to help.
Unfortunately, the economic equivalent of bloodletting remains the treatment in vogue whenever inflation is the symptom, whatever the underlying cause of the disease.
That panacea is higher interest rates. Draw money out of the economy by jacking up the cost of debt and the patient will recover … if the treatment doesn't kill them.
Rate rises don't fix supply problems
Last week, the Reserve Bank's deputy governor Andrew Hauser told 7.30 that Australia's economy has "one big problem and that's inflation".
Loading...
Echoing words from his boss at her last press conference, Hauser told Sarah Ferguson that:
"Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and, at some point, we will have to say that is long enough."
And, if we get to that point, what's the solution?
"We will raise interest rates further than otherwise we would need to do so," the central banker responded.
"We're not at that point yet, but some of these upside risks to inflation are certainly on our mind."
Loading...
So what exactly are these "upside risks" that could mean inflation is higher and more stubborn than the RBA's existing forecasts? Hauser listed three.
"One is the Middle East and the ongoing crisis there, one is a really unexpected global boom driven by AI, and one is the weakness of the supply potential of the Australian economy," he said.
Will higher Australian interest rates influence any of those things? No.
The US and Iran will not stop attacking each other because Australian mortgages have become more expensive.
The money behind the AI boom is mainly coming from US multinationals, so higher local rates are likely to make little difference to investment in that sector.
And higher rates are more likely to weigh on the supply capacity of the Australian economy rather than grow it, as they send some businesses broke (handing their surviving rivals more pricing power) and discourage firms from borrowing to increase capacity and productivity.
As CBA's chief economist Luke Yeaman explained on The Business last week:
"The economy is slowing, but not fast enough for their liking, and an extra rate hike now could help drive that growth down lower and bring it more in line with the supply capacity of the economy."
Hence the analogy with bloodletting. Rising rates mainly lower inflation by destroying demand, hopefully more quickly than they reduce supply.
Loading...
Are Australian home owners paying for the AI boom?
A lot of column inches have already been devoted to the role that the Middle East conflict and Australia's productivity crisis have played in our lingering inflation problem.
However, it is telling that the RBA has elevated the AI boom alongside those issues.
Hours before Andrew Hauser appeared on 7.30, the Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter spoke at an AFR property summit.
She said the bank was hearing anecdotes about workers being sucked in, at inflated wages, to build new data centres, adding to cost pressure across the construction sector.
"They want these centres built really rapidly, as fast as possible in some cases, and it's definitely adding to demand," she said.
"You can see business investment has picked up really strongly over the last sort of nine months or so, nine to 12 months, double-digit growth, and a decent chunk of that is data centres."
Research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA), released last week, shows business investment spending is at 12.6 per cent of GDP, its highest level in more than a decade, since the mining boom wound down.
CEDA economist Julie Toth said the boom was driven almost entirely by the information, media and telecoms sector as businesses ramped up investment in data centres, cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Investment in this sector almost doubled over the past year.
Comparisons to the mining boom are apt.
Just as investment in that sector, concentrated in WA and Queensland, contributed to interest rates rising around the country and created a two-speed economy earlier this century, the AI boom will inflict pain across other sectors.
With most economists seeing the economy running above capacity, as evidenced by inflation, all the demand added by data centre construction must be offset by the RBA raising rates to smash activity in other areas.
As with the mining boom, much of the benefit from the AI boom will likely be captured by overseas shareholders of the multinational companies driving it, while the costs will be borne domestically through higher interest rates and slower growth in other sectors.
Is the public 'furious' with inflation or angrier with the RBA?
That brings us back to interest rates and the RBA's tricky decision about whether to hike in two weeks.
Markets are pricing in at least a 75 per cent chance the cash rate will rise to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent on September 29.
They are pricing in a virtual certainty of two rate hikes by February, with a 50/50 chance of a third by mid-next year.
A cash rate of 4.85 per cent would be the highest since rates were slashed over late 2008 in response to the global financial crisis.
Andrew Hauser said getting on top of inflation was not only the bank's primary mission, but the community's expectation.
"People are furious about inflation," he said on 7.30.
"It's the most profound message that we get. Everywhere I go, I hear cost, cost, cost, inflation, inflation, inflation. And that's our responsibility. We have to put that right."
The RBA's own community survey shows he's right, with two-thirds of people putting it as one of their top three economic concerns.
But the same survey turned up another finding that has the Reserve Bank worried. They see the RBA as part of the inflation problem, not as the solution.
"Only 25 per cent of respondents assessed correctly that higher interest rates would ultimately lead to lower inflation, while more than half indicated that higher interest rates would lead to higher inflation," the report lamented.
And statements like this from the Reserve Bank governor are unlikely to help those public perceptions.
"People who have mortgages, at least, they see increases in interest rates as an increase in the cost of living, but it's not really," she said in response to my question at a business economists lunch in July.
"So interest rates are the response to high inflation; they're not causing high inflation."
While mortgage repayments may have been deliberately excised from the Consumer Price Index at the RBA's request in the late 1990s, they are a very real cost of living for anyone with a mortgage.
It's no wonder then that a constant refrain in interactions with our audience when we're covering interest rates is, "Surely there are less painful and more effective ways to lower inflation?"
And there potentially are. I wrote about some of these ideas back in May.
But while governments continue outsourcing inflation management to unelected technocrats at central banks who only have access to one treatment, the economic bloodletting is likely to continue.

Leningrad Region authorities acknowledge fuel crisis, propose rationing amid “nuclear” lines at gas stations

2026-09-14
18:48:13 UTC
03:48:13 KST

Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko has released a video address to “dear Leningrad Region residents” acknowledging the lines and fuel shortages at gas stations. According to Drozdenko, regional authorities are considering introducing an alternating schedule of fill-ups for odd and even license plate numbers. Users of the GdeBenz (“Where’s gas?”) map service write about “nuclear” lines at gas stations in St. Petersburg and advise customers to come for gas at four or five in the morning.
Drozdenko said he “understands the general concern” and complained that his younger daughter could not visit him on Sunday because she “didn’t get gas,” while his older daughter “stood in line for more than two hours.”
In his address, Drozdenko explained:
“We all understand that this is a consequence of the enemy’s recent drone attacks on major oil refineries, including Kirishinefteorgsintez, and, as a result, of reduced production of 92 and 95 octane gasoline. Diesel is available.
We are now restructuring fuel supply chains through other refineries, together with major companies, but that takes time.
I want to say that there is light at the end of the tunnel. We expect that by early October new supplies will reach the region, new logistics chains will be built, and, of course, the refineries will resume operating after repairs.
Together we are working through options to reduce peak demand, and we’re considering introducing fill-ups for vehicles with odd and even plate numbers on alternating days. For now, our goal is still to meet gasoline needs within a limit of 20 to 30 liters a day.”
As The Insider reported on Sept. 12, lines at gas stations in St. Petersburg have forced customers to wait for up to five hours to fill up. Economist Janis Kluge, analyzing GdeBenz data, noted in a post on X that AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline were available at fewer than 20% of gas stations in St. Petersburg, and more than 60% of the city’s gas stations were not operating at all.
By the morning of Sept. 14, the situation had improved only marginally, judging by messages in the GdeBenz service chat. Car owners noted that huge lines immediately formed outside the few gas stations that had begun to sell gasoline. User Maria N. wrote at around 10 a.m. that the Lukoil station on Marshala Zhukova Avenue had AI-92 and AI-95 available. Car owner Denis Z. confirmed this information but immediately noted: “The line’s already nuclear.”
A young woman named Ulya complained that she had spent the whole night at the gas station because the station’s administrators had promised gas by morning – but she still could not fill up: “Well, they did get gas by 5 a.m., but it was the hundred [octane] — I can’t put it into a Lada.”
Vyacheslav I., for his part, wondered whether he might be able to find gas at 4 or 5 a.m. in the Primorsky district. Dmitry N. admitted he had the same plan: “since this brilliant idea occurred to two of us here, I’m afraid we’ll run into another hundred at the gas station.”
Early on Monday morning, many chat users across the region reported that gasoline had indeed appeared, albeit accompanied by long lines. However, by around 11:00 a.m. reports of empty gas stations became more frequent, along with questions such as: “Is there gas anywhere?”
Since the start of summer, Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries have resulted in a persistent fuel crisis inside Russia. As The Insider reported, Ukrainian UAVs target the hardest-to-replace components, putting refineries out of commission for the longest time possible. Repair speed is lagging behind the pace of new strikes as sanctions make it increasingly difficult for Russian refineries to obtain the necessary parts and equipment. As a result, oil refining in Russia had fallen to its lowest level in 20 years.
In late August, the Russian government adopted a resolution allowing gas stations to sell gasoline and diesel fuel of lower environmental classes — Euro-2, Euro-3, and Euro-4. The Energy Ministry called the decision a temporary measure to stabilize the domestic market; it will remain in effect until June 30, 2027.

JR sends giant wave across vatican apostolic library facade with ‘diluvium’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:46:41 UTC
03:46:41 KST

A giant black-and-white wave by JR now stretches across the sixteenth-century facade of the Vatican Apostolic Library. DILUVIUM runs roughly 70 meters across the wall facing the Cortile del Belvedere, catching the water at the instant before it seems ready to crash into the architecture.
Unveiled on September 14th, 2026, the site-specific installation opens AQVA, the first exhibition in the library’s five-year Catastrophe and Wonder cycle, and draws its image from Gustave Doré’s 1866 illustration of the biblical flood.
The idea began with a very practical fear. ‘The library at the Vatican came to see me because, for them, water represents their biggest fear,‘ JR explains. ‘It’s the fact that one day water comes and takes away all the memory … all the trace of a civilization that they’ve been preserving.‘
Set against a building devoted to keeping centuries of knowledge intact, the wave makes that vulnerability immediately visible from across the courtyard.
JR quickly pulls the image of the wave beyond the walls of the Vatican Apostolic Library. ‘This wave talks about way more than that,’ the artist says. He connects it to climate change and extreme heat, then to political polarization and ‘the wave of AI itself.‘ The metaphor keeps widening, but the image stays simple: an enormous body of water bearing down on a place built around preservation.
Doré’s flood gives the work an older visual language, with the drama of a nineteenth-century biblical engraving enlarged to architectural scale. Across the pale Renaissance facade, JR turns a familiar historical image into something that feels unusually current. The threat shifts depending on how you read it. Water can erase an archive in a matter of hours, or technology can absorb the same archive at a scale that would have seemed impossible only a few years ago.
AQVA takes that tension as its starting point. Water can destroy paper, but it also plays a role in the making and restoration of books. JR contributes the site-specific work, DILUVIUM, while the wider exhibition looks at the element through the Vatican Library’s collections and contemporary interventions.
Pope Leo XIV inaugurated the exhibition during his first visit to the Vatican Apostolic Library as pontiff. The public opening follows on September 25th, with AQVA running through May 14th, 2027. Outside, JR’s wave remains the bluntest image in the project, as centuries of stored knowledge sitting behind a facade suddenly looks as if it could disappear beneath water.

The two sides discussed mobilizing financing for Ukraine through the end of 2026, the continued rollout of the PEACE in Ukraine project, financing under the World Bank’s SPUR 2.0 instrument, and preparations for new joint projects, the ministry wrote in its press release.
Marchenko and Robert Saum, the World Bank’s regional director for Eastern Europe, signed a loan agreement under the Tenth Additional Financing of the “Public Expenditures for Administrative Capacity Endurance in Ukraine” project, known as PEACE in Ukraine. Once the agreement is signed, the project’s total volume will reach $54.3 billion, making it the largest investment project in the World Bank’s history, according to the ministry.
The press release quoted Serhiy Marchenko, Ukraine’s finance minister, as saying: “PEACE remains one of the most effective instruments for supporting Ukraine’s state budget. Thanks to the new financing under Canada’s guarantee, we will be aGle to ensure funding for critically important social expenditure. I am grateful to the government of Canada and the World Bank for their consistent and timely support of Ukraine.”
Ukraine Must Attack Russia’s Missile Plants to Win War, MITS Capital CEO Says
Marchenko also welcomed the approval of the World Bank’s new SPUR 2.0 instrument and called on the institution to help attract more active contributions from international partners. SPUR 2.0 – the Special Program for Ukraine Recovery – is a World Bank initiative aimed at mobilizing resources for Ukraine’s priority recovery needs. The program operates on a multiplier basis: every $1 in grant funding attracted is converted into $3 in loans, a mechanism that could ultimately accumulate up to $6 billion in financial support, according to the ministry.
Ukraine has already appealed to 27 partner countries to join SPUR 2.0, and four have confirmed they will contribute, the ministry wrote.
Ukraine and the World Bank are also preparing six new joint projects – in energy efficiency, housing policy, waste management, agricultural sector support, statistics and digitalization. Marchenko said he hopes preparatory procedures will be completed quickly enough to launch the projects before the end of 2026, the ministry wrote.

Turkish Airlines drops Luanda as Angola's new airport struggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:44:54 UTC
03:44:54 KST

The Istanbul carrier permanently axed Luanda, along with four other African routes, becoming the latest international airline to exit the Angolan capital since its new airport opened in 2023. The facility was built for 15 million annual passengers but handled fewer than 800,000 in 2025.
Turkish Airlines has permanently axed its Luanda route, the latest in a series of international carriers to drop the Angolan capital since Angola inaugurated its new airport in 2023.
The Istanbul-based carrier removed Luanda from its future schedule earlier this month, along with Juba, Kinshasa, Libreville and Lusaka, after those services had been suspended through 24 October.
Turkish Airlines initially described the suspension as temporary when it announced the move in April, citing fuel costs.
It had operated a triangular service through Kinshasa rather than a direct connection, but the route gave Luanda passengers onward access to destinations across Europe, Asia and beyond via Istanbul.
Brussels Airlines ended its Luanda service on 25 March 2025 as part of a restructuring within the Lufthansa Group, redirecting passengers onto Lufthansa's direct Frankfurt–Luanda flights.
TAAG Angola Airlines suspended its Madrid route — codeshared with Iberia — in January 2024 and later removed a planned return from its schedule.
Iberia never reversed its decision to suspend flights to Luanda, in place since 2016, opting instead to codeshare with TAAG since 2022. That link is now gone as well.
South African Airways (SAA) also only places its code on TAAG-operated flights.
Low passenger numbers plague new airport
The departures come as Angola's Dr António Agostinho Neto International Airport, about 45km from central Luanda, struggles to establish itself as the regional hub the government promised when it inaugurated the facility in November 2023.
Built by Chinese state-owned company AVIC and designed for a maximum annual capacity of 15 million passengers, the airport handled 756,028 passengers in all of 2025, according to figures from the airport's temporary operator ATO.
By 24 February of this year, total passenger numbers since the first domestic flight in November 2024 stood at 1,090,861, including 444,212 international passengers.
The full transfer of services from the old Quatro de Fevereiro airport was completed on 1 March — more than two years after the inauguration — when South African carrier Airlink moved its Johannesburg flights to the new facility.
In December 2025, ATO's Director of Planning and Quality Vissolela Chivunda said the airport expected around 4 million passengers in 2026.
Luanda remains served by TAP Air Portugal, Air France, Lufthansa, Royal Air Maroc, Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways, Airlink and TAAG, alongside Compagnie Africaine d'Aviation, which began two weekly flights from Kinshasa on 21 August.

Australia needs AI 'early warning system', cyber security chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:44:43 UTC
03:44:43 KST

Australia needs an AI 'early warning system', top cybersecurity chief warns
In short:
Abigail Bradshaw has called for Australian organisations to use AI to defend themselves and share warnings with each other about emerging threats.
Global tech executives last week warned the race to develop AI could outstrip humanity's ability to control it.
What's next?
The federal assistant science minister says Australia should help shape any global slowdown effort.
Australia needs an artificial intelligence "early warning system" to help defend against the dangers of the increasingly powerful technology, according to the nation's cyber intelligence chief.
Australian Signals Directorate director-general Abigail Bradshaw also urged Australian organisations to embrace AI for its defensive capabilities, saying it was one of the crucial tools that the nation needed to protect itself.
It comes as Australian politicians and AI company executives respond to a growing international chorus of warnings the race to develop AI could outstrip humanity's ability to control it.
Speaking at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute's (ASPI) Sydney Dialogue AI Masterclass on Monday, Ms Bradshaw said intelligence and security agencies needed to work with AI companies to identify early risks.
"What we are missing at the moment, which we have in a cyber context but we don't yet have it formalised in an AI context, is an early warning system,"
Ms Bradshaw said bringing together reports of individual incidents would help identify wider patterns, adding that these risks extended beyond cybersecurity to areas such as biotechnology.
The public servant, who is tasked with Australia's cyber offensive capabilities, balanced the warning with a more optimistic assessment about AI capabilities helping those tasked with defence.
Loading...
She pointed to existing cyber partnerships between government and industry, and international arrangements for quickly sharing technical information.
Australian government agencies had been granted access to major AI companies' cutting-edge models that were limited from wide release.
She confirmed that this included Anthropic's Mythos, which was temporarily restricted after the US government placed it under an export control, and OpenAI's cyber versions of their models.
Ms Bradshaw said her agency used this access to help Australian organisations fortify their systems and identify potential vulnerabilities.
"What would have taken cybersecurity experts in ASD weeks and weeks of work has been done in hours," she said.
Ms Bradshaw urged organisations to maintain basic security measures while using AI to defend their networks.
Defenders needed capabilities on par with those available to cybercriminals and state-backed attackers, she said.
In a separate panel on Monday, Australia's AI Safety Institute general manager Kate Conroy urged companies and agencies to let their teams, or their staff, experiment with advanced AI.
"If you don't already have it your teams are probably already doing it in their free time,"
Calls for global AI slowdown
In July, more than a thousand employees of leading AI companies signed onto an open letter that called for the US government to step in to help pave the way for an AI development slowdown.
Loading...
In the past week the high-profile resignation of Anthropic staffer Jacob Coxon and an essay published by the company's chief executive reignited a global conversation over a global slowdown effort.
Australia's assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, told the ASPI conference that Australia should help shape the response.
"I am not in favour of leaving it to the companies and I'm not in favour of leaving it to the superpowers,"
Mr Charlton said governments should assume AI would keep becoming more capable, given companies' financial incentives, and despite executives discussing slowing down.
OpenAI vice-president of global policy Ann O'Leary told the event the company was working with governments and AI safety bodies, such as Australia's AI Safety Institute, as well as providing models for review before release.
But, she said, the absence of wider laws slowing development meant OpenAI and other companies were employing their own voluntary co-ordination efforts to "pace" progress.
Ms O'Leary said OpenAI was eager to train its AI models in Australia, saying it was in talks with the federal government about copyright.
"We are deep in conversation with the Australian government about these questions," she said.
"You have caught our attention."
