Rumors of another mobilization have pushed some Russians from contingency plans to packed bags. Readers tell Meduza where they’ve fled.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:44:27 UTC
03:44:27 KST

Rumors of another mobilization have pushed some Russians from contingency plans to packed bags. Readers tell Meduza where they’ve fled.
Meduza recently asked readers who had decided to leave Russia in recent months to tell us how they found the courage to take such a difficult step. We wanted to know more than why people were leaving the country in 2026. The reasons clearly include the economic crisis, Internet restrictions, Ukrainian drone attacks, and rumors of possible mobilization. Above all, we wanted to know whether Russia was experiencing a genuine new wave of emigration. Judging by the number of letters our newsroom received, the answer is yes. Here are some of the most compelling stories you sent us.
Warning: This article contains adult language.
Alexey
Fryazino, Moscow region
I consider the mobilization rumors entirely credible, so I’m urging friends who are staying in Russia to gather medical records documenting their health problems — whether it’s a knee wrecked playing soccer or a patched-up skull from being hit by a flying board.
I had been thinking about moving abroad for a long time, but I couldn’t get a Czech work visa during the COVID restrictions. I have a friend there who would have hired me. Then the war began, and the Czech Republic stopped issuing work visas altogether. I didn’t have enough money to leave without a destination or a plan, and I became depressed.
Then a distant relative died, and I learned that I was the heir. I sold the apartment I inherited, so now I can afford to leave.
I’ve been preparing for the move for almost a year. At first, I considered Germany because my grandfather had German roots. But that didn’t work out. It turned out my crafty grandfather had forged some documents in 1940 and had himself registered as Jewish, though his old photos suggest he would have looked right at home on a poster for some German political party. As a young man, he was a blond, athletic guy who stood nearly 6 feet 3 inches tall. How he managed to make a deal with the women at the passport office is a mystery.
In short, there’s no way to prove that I have German roots, so my wife and I decided to go to Paraguay. I think South America may be even better: taxes are lower than in Germany, and the culture makes more sense to me. We’ll fly to Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil because more tickets are available and they’re cheaper, then take a bus to Paraguay. This route takes us not to the capital, Asunción, but to the industrial area around Hohenau, where it’s easier to find affordable housing and work in my field.
We’re in the home stretch now. I’m waiting for apostilles for my documents and struggling to learn Spanish, which isn’t easy at my age. I’ve already sold or given away everything I’m not taking with me.
For me, staying or leaving isn’t really a choice, because I don’t want to take part in war crimes. I have no reason to return to Russia from Paraguay — even at the coldest time of year, nighttime temperatures there only occasionally fall to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. And there are no Internet restrictions.
Ksenia
Moscow
I’m panicking — sheer panic. The last time I was under this much stress, my hands started trembling, and I experienced my first symptoms of borderline personality disorder. I spent a year and a half taking antidepressants and going to therapy to learn how to manage my mental health. Now overwhelming feelings of hopelessness and helplessness keep washing over me in waves. My partner and I are both medical professionals, which means we’re automatically liable for military service.
My instinct is to run and never look back. Every day, I’m afraid, I cry, and I track price changes and political developments. I can think of only one thing: “I just hope we make it out in time.” But getting our degrees recognized so we can work abroad and transporting our pets will make leaving more complicated.
I was already thinking about moving four years ago, but circumstances made it impossible at the time.
The last straw for me — ridiculous as it may sound — was an advertisement for the notorious Alabuga Polytechnic. I saw the children and heard what they were saying, and the hair on my arms literally stood on end. I’m afraid to live in a country where a generation with such ideas is growing up. I’m terrified that my children will have classmates, fellow university students, colleagues, and neighbors like that.
My husband and I decided that we want to move to Germany. It came out ahead on every criterion that matters to me, including how difficult it would be to achieve certain life goals there. I’ve never lived anywhere but Russia, though my sister emigrated in 2023. I’ve also traveled a lot, so I have some idea of what to expect. It’s going to be fucking hard. But hard is better than impossible.
We’re now learning German, getting our pets microchipped and vaccinated, and obtaining apostilles for our documents. I applied for a second passport and withdrew all the money from my savings accounts. I still haven’t exchanged my rubles or figured out how and where to flee if mobilization begins before we can complete all the necessary preparations.
I don’t plan to return to Russia. No matter what happens or who is in power, I no longer believe in this country. I don’t believe it is my homeland, and I don’t want it to be my future children’s homeland.
Stanislav
Kirov region
When I think about the possibility of mobilization, I’m horrified and afraid for my life. I know I don’t want to become a killer or a war criminal. That was how I felt in 2022, and my reaction hasn’t changed since.
I’ve never emigrated, but I’ve traveled extensively: I’ve visited 20 countries, including some in Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia. In May, after returning from Morocco, I finally realized that Russia would not improve as long as Putin remained in power. The deciding factors were the drones, burning oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, communications restrictions, and idiotic, barbaric laws.
I sold my most valuable possession — my computer — and left for South Korea with 1,000 euros in my pocket. I’ve been here for a month. I may be undocumented now, but I’ll obtain refugee status later and try to stay for the long term. It’s safe here, and even ordinary factory workers earn good wages.
Dmitry
Moscow
I first heard rumors of mobilization in May or June and didn’t take them seriously. But that changed over time.
My employer was considerate enough to hire a military lawyer to advise my colleagues and me. His conclusion was that no one is safe from mobilization. I, for example, never served in the military, am not registered with a military enlistment office, and am over 30, but I’m still at risk. Afterward, my employer drew up guidelines on how we could protect ourselves from possible mobilization. Moving to another country is just one option.
I’m still not completely sure whether I’ll go. For now, it’s my Plan B. I only recently bought an apartment, and I’m still paying it off. That makes leaving more difficult, but if necessary, I’ll transfer it to my mother and go. Plan A is to enroll in a part-time master’s program. I’m studying for the entrance exams now, and I’ll find out by mid-September whether I’ve been accepted. This option guarantees me nothing — military enlistment officers could simply stop me in the subway, restrain me, and take me away. But enrollment in a master’s program would give a lawyer grounds to demand my release.
If the master’s program doesn’t work out, I’ll go to Armenia. Renting a place in Yerevan would be a little expensive for me, so I’ll head to a smaller city. All I need to be happy is Wi-Fi and a grocery store. I’ll live there for a month or two at first, then see how events unfold. If things go badly — multiple draft notices and criminal charges for evasion — I’ll apply for a digital nomad visa in Spain and move there. I’ve already arranged this with my employer.
I’ve prepared the essential documents: I had my degree apostilled and translated, and I obtained a second passport. I also have a foreign bank card. If I decide to leave, I won’t have much time. I’ll urgently need to transfer my apartment, draw up a general power of attorney, buy tickets, and book accommodations.
Ivan D.
St. Petersburg
I started thinking about moving abroad in February or March 2026, as the number of repressive laws kept growing. You would think that in an election year, the authorities would be trying to make themselves look good. I first heard what sounded like rumors of post-election mobilization in early spring, and I was somewhat skeptical. But I have even less trust in the current government. Perhaps the mobilization will be covert.
Whatever happens, I definitely don’t want to be in Russia watching it unfold. Over time, my friends and I became increasingly certain that we would emigrate. None of us had ever emigrated before.
We’ll go to Georgia first because we can stay there for a long time without dealing with much paperwork. From there, we plan to apply for the United Kingdom’s Global Talent visa, since all of us have accomplishments that could qualify us. Those whose applications are rejected will decide what to do next, but we already have several backup options in mind.
I have almost everything ready for departure. My belongings are packed, my apartment is ready to rent out, my documents have been apostilled, and powers of attorney have been drawn up. The tickets and accommodations are booked. I’m gradually converting my rubles into cash and dollar-pegged cryptocurrency.
Leonid
Moscow
As a reserve officer, I have feared mobilization since the war began. At times, that fear has intensified or subsided. By this spring, after assessing the situation, I realized that I probably couldn’t put off deciding whether to emigrate any longer. And mobilization aside, other reasons to move have accumulated — the worsening socioeconomic situation, for example.
I moved to a Central Asian country that I had visited many times for work and vacations. My family hasn’t joined me yet; I’m here with my business partner. We’re developing a platform. My older child will arrive a little later. My wife and I decided that our younger child would finish ninth grade in Russia, after which the two of them would move here as well.
Alexey (name changed)
St. Petersburg
At first, the rumors of possible mobilization seemed baseless. Now I think there’s a fairly high chance that mobilization will happen in some form.
I’ve been thinking about emigrating for a long time, and now everything has come together — both my personal resources and the external threats. I’m turning 30 soon. I’ve only just begun building a family, and I need stability if I’m going to think about having children, for example. I don’t feel that stability in Russia, with its “horror without end.” One reason I’m determined to leave is the simple realization that, if I put in a great deal of effort, emigration offers me a chance to build a normal future. Russia offers no such chance and is unlikely to do so in the future.
I hadn’t emigrated before because I lacked the necessary resources, both financial and emotional.
I left for Serbia in late August, and I see it as a base for the next one to three years. I’m now applying for a residence permit. After that, I’ll see what happens in the world. I don’t plan to settle in Serbia for the rest of my life.
Georgy
Domodedovo, Moscow region
I’m 27 years old. I was born in Domodedovo and have lived here all my life.
Like many people, I think, I gradually began to feel that something bad — a new wave of mobilization — was coming. That feeling probably began in the fall of 2025, when advances on the front began slowing down and the economy noticeably deteriorated. News channels, political bloggers, and experts all began voicing the same concern.
That same fall, I began mentally preparing for the possibility of leaving, just in case. I made the final decision when drones began regularly attacking Moscow and the surrounding region. I saw them above my house. One morning, after explosions had kept me awake all night, I was on my way to work when I looked out from an overpass and saw thick columns of black smoke on the horizon. Wildberries warehouses were burning. That was when I decided I’d had enough and began making concrete preparations to leave. Before that, I had only traveled abroad.
I did everything I could. I built up an emergency fund, bought a powerful laptop, persuaded my employer to let me work remotely, obtained a second passport and apostilles for my documents, and renewed documents that were about to expire.
I’m in Yerevan now. I have friends here, so I’m not alone. I don’t have any firm plans. Preparing to leave and the move itself took an enormous amount out of me. First, I want to get settled here, regain some stability, improve my English, and either find a job abroad or try to start my own business.
Anton
Rostov-on-Don
I wanted to leave even before the war, but something always held me back: prices, a well-paid job with a European company, taxes, my parents, and other relatives.
For a very long time, I told myself that the war would end and then we would start living normally again. At the same time, I couldn’t believe that the country I remembered from before the war had really sunk this low. Russia was never perfect, but it felt as though it was developing, as though you could build something and move forward with the rest of the world.
My wife and I used to travel three or four times a year, and even in 2024 and 2025, returning to Russia felt normal. But after two trips in 2026, coming back became enormously stressful. It felt as though the rest of the world was simply getting on with life. Yes, there are crises, high prices, corruption, and employment problems everywhere, but at least those are ordinary problems people face in life.
The country isn’t merely developing more slowly than the rest of the world — it’s actually moving backward. Instead of wondering what new opportunities will appear in a few years, you wonder which of the things you’re used to will stop working next. For people in IT, this is a particular problem. I don’t even want to complain about VPNs anymore — everyone already knows what’s happening to them. And I don’t need a VPN to look at cat pictures; I need it to do my job properly.
It used to seem as though propaganda existed in a separate sphere and that the people around you understood what was really happening. It doesn’t feel that way anymore.
I have friends from Moscow who work in IT. Some used to work for American companies and were very close to Western culture. Now some of them say, “If you’re not with us, you’re against us. If you don’t like something, leave. If you voice criticism, you’re helping the enemy.” Some now seriously argue that it’s long past time to nuke Kyiv. But overall, the war doesn’t bother them. They go to bars and fly to Turkey and Thailand. One of them came to Taganrog, spent some time living with air-raid sirens and explosions, and decided that Ukraine needed to be bombed even harder.
For the first time, I now realize that even if the war ends tomorrow, almost nothing will return to how it was. The Internet restrictions will remain, international companies are unlikely to resume operations en masse, and militarization isn’t going anywhere — it will probably only intensify. People will return from the war after living for a long time in a completely different reality, accustomed to violence and large payments. I have no idea how they’ll return to ordinary life or where they’ll be able to earn that kind of money.
That is probably the main turning point for me: I used to be afraid that I would leave and then regret it, but now my greatest fear is that I won’t get out in time. The worst part isn’t even mobilization, the crisis, or any specific threat. It’s the feeling that you have become a stranger in your own country and that it’s moving in a completely different direction from where you want to go.
That’s why my wife and I are gathering the documents we need to move to Spain. Applying for residence permits and completing the other formalities will take quite a while, so we expect to move after New Year’s. I hope nothing happens this fall.
Pavel
St. Petersburg
The rumors of possible mobilization don’t surprise me at all. I feel only the grim certainty that people in this country are treated as worthless: when the authorities need cannon fodder, they get it. Human life is the highest value to me, so the authorities and I are going our separate ways. I don’t want to kill people. When did we incur such a debt to this country, and what for?
I have emigrated before, but only for four months, when I lived in Turkey. I don’t want to move until I have all my documents. But if the situation begins changing quickly, I’ll try to get a five-year passport on short notice, just so I can leave and sort everything out once I’m abroad.
I’ve already had my degrees apostilled, applied for a new passport and driver’s license after mine unexpectedly went “missing under unknown circumstances,” drawn up a general power of attorney for people close to me, and requested a criminal record certificate.
I’m not even considering any CIS country. I’m thinking more about Vietnam as an initial destination. After that, I may move to Indonesia, where Russian banks’ UnionPay cards work perfectly, and it is easier to obtain legal residency than in many other countries. Then I’ll consider a permanent move to Australia. But everything will depend on the situation in Russia — I may return.
Fyodor (name changed)
Kazan
I’m not seriously considering moving to another country right now, barring extreme scenarios such as a hybrid or full-scale civil war in Russia, a revolution involving mass violence, famine, or the complete collapse of the ruble.
I have emigrated before — I lived in Israel for almost two years. I didn’t like it at all, though not because it was expensive. My wife and I had money then and still do. There were other reasons.
Even so, I’m prepared. My new passport is almost ready, and I have the necessary money, apostilled documents, packed suitcases, and a clear plan of action.
One thing I know for certain is that I’m unhappy with the way European Union authorities treat Russians. For example, I was outraged by the European Court of Human Rights’ recent refusal to consider complaints from Russians.
I do, however, like the Armenian government’s approach: it is guided by practical considerations, not ideologically charged narratives. [If we move there,] my wife will be able to find a skilled job in Armenia, while I plan to work remotely.
But the move wouldn’t be long-term. I love Russia very much, value the history of Russia’s democratic movements, and remember times and events when it seemed that our beautiful future Russia was just around the corner — if only we pushed a little harder.
I’m not going to give up. Nor do I believe that my generation, born in the 1990s, has lost or that we will never again have a historic opportunity to fix Russia.

IDF targeting decision made by highly trained human operatives, not AI, IDF tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:43:03 UTC
03:43:03 KST

There are highly trained air force operations and legal military officials involved in IDF targeting decisions, despite claims by the NAZA film that the military has given over its discretion to artificial intelligence (AI), The Jerusalem Post has learned.
There is significant frustration from the high levels of the IDF, some of which was made public in a speech by IDF Spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Effie Defrin, that the NAZA movie was not shared with the military – in parallel to its being shown and reported on to the world – in order to give the IDF a fair chance to respond to specific allegations.
It is not that top IDF officials do not know about collateral harm to Gazan civilians. They do, and they view it as a tragic aspect of war, worsened by Hamas trapping much of its population into being used as human shields, the Post understands.
The IDF argues that the messages that have emerged from media reports about NAZA are that it is a film that ignores Hamas and all of the massive efforts it took during the war to evacuate civilians and to call off legally valid attacks because the IDF wanted to avoid harming civilians, valid or not.
It is critical to remember in this debate that the laws of war do not require a ratio of zero dead civilians, or of fewer dead civilians than combatants.
Rather, what is known as the proportionality calculation is highly elastic and connected to the specific circumstances, the value of the concrete military goal in question, the harm to civilians, and how viable it is to warn civilians to leave beforehand.
The Post has learned that, in some cases, the air force even redirected missiles away from hitting Hamas terrorists after firing them, when civilians unexpectedly appeared close to the strike zone.
IDF acknowledges mistakes possible in complex operations
On the other hand, the Post has heard acknowledgments from the IDF that in complex operations, such as the chaotic rescue of hostage Noa Argamani in June 2024, more mistakes can happen because there is even less time for the human beings involved to fully comprehend the entire battlefield.
In that particular case, the IDF rescue vehicle carrying Argamani, other hostages, and IDF soldiers out of a Hamas-controlled area got stuck and could not continue the escape.
The IDF had minutes to save the rescuers lest all of the hostages and rescue soldiers be quickly surrounded and killed.
Previously, IDF sources at the time had told the Post and other media that more mistakes were made in that operation regarding nearby civilians than would have been made had the operation continued as planned.
But the Post has also now learned that despite a chaotic situation, those air force and other officials involved were still able to exercise a large degree of discretion to enable them to avoid hitting civilians beyond a certain volume.
The IDF believes the NAZA filmmakers are manipulating the public by the use of the acronym NAZA – which stands for “collateral damage” – making it appear to be a dehumanizing term. Rather, the whole point of injecting that term into every attack is that – unlike Hamas – the IDF is always trying to reduce harm to civilians as a basic tenet of its “formula.”
Previously, the Post has also reported that when the IDF sets some kind of minimal formula for how many civilians killed per Hamas official are “acceptable collateral damage,” this is never meant to lead to an automatic approval, but to be a minimum standard, though IDF officials will try to improve the odds, subjecting civilians to as little danger as possible, even indirectly.
IDF views ratios of 100 or 500 civilians per Hamas terrorists as nowhere near reality
Moreover, the Post has learned that the IDF view is that the astronomical ratios of 100 or 500 civilians per Hamas terrorists is nowhere near the reality; the ratios are much lower.
That is not to say that there have not been examples in which the ratio has been considerably higher, but that has tended to happen when mistakes were made – such as in a case where one house was targeted to kill a Hamas official, but it turned out that under the house was a tunnel that the IDF was unaware of, and the collapse of the targeted house and the portion of the tunnel beneath it resulted in the unintentional collapse of a block of houses.
Previously, the Post and various other media have reported on some intense disagreements after March 2025 specifically, when certain air force officers believed that certain Southern Command officers were being too aggressive about calling in some airstrikes.
While this is not something that all IDF officials would deny, the Post understands that they would not place such disagreements in the context of the NAZA movie.
Rather, these IDF officials would say that such disagreements are a natural result of professional differences, sometimes within a particular arm of the military and sometimes between different arms of the military, whose missions and contributions to the war effort may lead to different perspectives – but not relating to debates about genocide.
Most frustratingly for the IDF, the Post understands that the 24 presumed IDF soldiers who were interviewed for the NAZA movie did not – allegedly, as the IDF says it does not know who they are – speak to higher IDF levels who might have been able to better contextualize for them the confusing and heart-wrenching issues that, according to NAZA, they were confronting as part of their role in war-fighting.

Blood test found to detect lung cancer with nearly 93% accuracy for average cost of $60 - study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:42:57 UTC
03:42:57 KST

A clinical study found that a new test designed to detect lung cancer had an accuracy rate of nearly 93% in patients, potentially replacing the need for costly and complex genetic sequencing for diagnosis with a $60 blood test.
The study, led by Dr. Abd Agbaria, head of Oncology at the Bnai Zion Medical Center, in collaboration with researchers at Tel Aviv University, included 103 participants and was published in npj Precision Oncology.
The test uses a dedicated chip and fluorescence analysis to examine fragments of cell-free DNA in the blood for distinct methylation patterns.
Methylation, a process in which a cluster of hydrogen and carbon atoms is added to DNA, often inhibiting gene expression, can inhibit sections vital for tumor prevention. Identifying methylation patterns enables researchers and healthcare professionals to identify cancerous cells and determine the type of cancer.
In Agbaria's study, the blood test demonstrated a sensitivity of 93.1% and a specificity of 90.3% among patients with stage 2 to stage 4 cancer. The test also distinguished between adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
Agbaria emphasizes advantage of early diagnosis
"Lung cancer is a disease in which the timing of diagnosis is enormously important. The earlier we are able to detect the disease, the greater the possibilities for treatment and cure. Our goal is to develop a tool that is simple, accessible, and readily available, which can help us detect the disease at a stage when meaningful intervention is still possible," Agbaria said.
Agbaria also warned that before the test can be incorporated into regular use, broader testing will be required. A larger trial is ongoing at several medical centers in Israel and Europe.
The study is the result of a collaboration between researchers from Tel Aviv University, JaxBio Technologies, Bnai Zion Medical Center, and Sheba Medical Center.

Jerusalem Deputy Mayor Arieh King calls to immediately end municipal services to British Consulate

Jerusalem Deputy Mayor Arieh King called on the Israeli government to immediately cut water, internet, and other services to the British Consulate in Jerusalem on Monday, questioning why, if the British government views the mission as being on territory occupied by Israel, it continues to use services provided by Israel.
King’s comments came as he led a handful of protesters demonstrating outside of the consulate, less than a month before the deadline Israel set for the mission to close. The turnout fell far short of King’s expectations, with the few protesters in attendance planting flags in support of Otzma Yehudit, the far-right party of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the consulate closed after the UK announced sweeping measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, including a planned ban on settlement imports to Britain.
“If you are looking at Jerusalem as the occupied territory, and if you are not considering us, the municipality of Jerusalem and the government of Israel, as the sovereign of this place, why are you getting all of these services from us?” King asked. “I’m calling the Israeli government to disconnect the electricity, the water, the telephone services.”
King said the consulate receives water supplied by Hagihon and telephone and internet services from Bezeq. He also said part of the road next to the mission had been closed for the consulate’s security, with the Jerusalem Municipality authorizing the arrangement.
“If you are serious and not just a pure hypocrite,” King said, the British government should disconnect those services itself rather than waiting for Israel to act, instead of announcing measures he described as being done “for propaganda.”
What are the UK's sanctions?
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the measures last week, saying they were intended to preserve the viability of a two-state solution and combat settlement expansion and settler violence.
As part of the sanctions regime, he announced, the UK “will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.”
In his remarks, he also said it is now officially the view of the British government that Israel’s continued occupation of the Palestinian territories is unlawful and that “settler terrorists” were perpetrating ethnic cleansing against Palestinians in parts of the West Bank.
That day, the UK published a joint statement signed by Miliband and the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden.
The aforementioned countries said that they intended to introduce national restrictions, support European restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, or were actively considering such measures, asserting that the settlements are illegal under international law.
What was Israel's response?
Israel’s response came shortly after, with Sa’ar accusing Britain of hostility toward Israel. Sa’ar and other Israeli officials, including President Isaac Herzog, also accused the UK of trying to interfere with Israel’s upcoming elections.
The foreign minister also argued that Jews have a historic right to live in the West Bank, where Jewish presence dates back thousands of years, saying, “The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel.”
Sa’ar also argued that the UK’s measures would push a negotiated solution further away rather than bring it closer.
Israel’s subsequent countermeasures against Britain included ordering the British Consulate closed, expelling British representatives from the Civil-Military Coordination Center in Kiryat Gat, and ending British training of Palestinian Authority security forces.
Separately, King has pushed for a symbolic municipal response to the dispute. Last week, he called for Jerusalem’s King George Street to be renamed “Tabur Haaretz.”
When asked by The Jerusalem Post how Israel could maintain its diplomatic standing while asserting sovereignty over east Jerusalem as other countries consider similar measures, King said Monday’s protest was focused specifically on governments with a diplomatic presence in Jerusalem.
“We are here in front of the British Consulate, like we were seven months ago in front of the French Consulate,” King said. “We are not demonstrating against governments of countries that don’t have a presence in Jerusalem.”
King clarified that his remarks were directed at the UK’s Labor government, and not “the people of Britain.”
During his remarks to reporters, King also rejected the British government’s characterization of the territory as occupied, arguing that Israel had not taken it from a Palestinian state.
“There was not a Palestinian state, not in 1948 and not 1967,” he said. “So, who did we occupy it from?”
King further rejected a distinction between Jewish communities in east Jerusalem, the West Bank, and places within the pre-1967 lines, such as Tel Aviv.
“There is no difference between east Jerusalem and Judea and Samaria or Binyamin,” he told the Post. “There is no difference between Tel Aviv and Jericho and Jerusalem.”

Bob Mackie, costume designer to stars daring to be noticed, dies aged 87
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:39:17 UTC
03:39:17 KST

Bob Mackie, the costume designer behind some of the most sexy and glamorous outfits worn by celebrities in the past 50 years, has died at the age of 87.
“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement posted on his Instagram account. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”
Mackie’s work can be seen in the wardrobes of stars ranging from Marilyn Monroe to Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli, Elton John, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner and – perhaps most memorably – Cher. He designed the ‘naked’ dress the singer wore to attend the Met Gala in 1975, the midriff-baring outfit with an oversized Mohawk headdress she wore to the Oscars in 1986 and the transparent body stocking she wore for the If I Could Turn Back Time video in 1989.
The Met Gala outfit has since become a reference for a younger generation. Kim Kardashian wore a dress modelled on it for the same event in 2015.
More recently, Taylor Swift wore one of Mackie’s original Jubilee! cabaret costumes on the cover of her 12th studio album, The Life of a Showgirl, while Sabrina Carpenter and Zendaya have also worn archival looks by the designer. In 2024, the singer Miley Cyrus paid an undisclosed sum to buy the Mackie tasseled mini dress she had worn to perform at the Grammys.
Last year at an auction, Cher’s “naked” bodysuit fetched $57,600 (£42,600), seven times its estimated price, while a silver and gold fringed bodysuit with lamé wings that Mackie designed for Tina Turner for a 1977 performance sold for $19,200 (£14,200).
The designer first began working with Cher for The Sonny and Cher show in the 1960s and remained a collaborator for decades. Cher has paid tribute to his contribution to her career, saying that without Mackie “I would have been a peacock without feathers”.
Mackie’s first notable design has another connection to Kardashian – as assistant to designer Jean Louis, he sketched the dress Marilyn Monroe wore to sing Happy Birthday to president John F Kennedy in 1962. Kardashian wore the original dress to the Met Gala in 2022 – to the disapproval of much of the fashion world, who thought it should be preserved. Mackie was one of the people who spoke out. “I thought it was a big mistake,” he said to Entertainment Weekly. “It was designed for [Monroe]. Nobody else should be seen in that dress.”
In 1963, he began to work on The Judy Garland Show, and met his collaborator and partner Ray Aghayan. Work for the Supremes, and then Diana Ross, followed. The duo were nominated for an Oscar for the costumes Ross wore in the 1973 Billie Holliday biopic Lady Sings the Blues.
Mackie’s motto was “dare to be noticed” and his costumes certainly gained attention for the people wearing them. Elton John’s duck costume, worn in 1980, has become notorious. But the designs also sometimes made points. Cher’s outfit for the Oscars in 1986 was so flamboyant because the star felt she was snubbed for her performance in Mask and wanted to take revenge when she was presenting an award.
Speaking to the New York Times a year later she said: “OK, you can go in a simple black dress and be just like everyone else. But then I decided, I’m going to remind them of what they don’t like about me.” Mackie obliged with his creation.
Turner’s “flame” dress, worn in 1977 after her split from her abusive partner and musical collaborator, Ike, turned the star into a gloriously unsubtle phoenix rising from the ashes.
The designer hasn’t always been harmonious with his clients. His work with Cher had tensions. In 2018, talking to the Guardian about the raunchy Turn Back Time outfit, he said he thought it was “vulgar and horrid”. “I told her: please, I don’t want any credit for this,” he said. In 2019, he described Garland as “a big handful” and said he refused to design costumes for a recent Cher tour. “I’m in touch with clients only when they need clothes,” he said. “I never want to be their best friend.”
Mackie diversified beyond costume design. He launched a clothing line in 1982 and made Bob Mackie collectible Barbies. Working with QVC from 1999, Mackie’s aesthetic has been utilised on everything from fragrance to luggage to high-end jewellery – and in 2009 he appeared as a guest judge on RuPaul’s Drag Race.
Mackie gained plaudits for his unique take on glamour in recent years. The Fashion Institute of Technology staged the Unmistakably Bob exhibition in 1999, and he received the prestigious Geoffrey Beene CFDA Lifetime Achievement award in 2019. He was front and centre of the Diva exhibition at London’s V&A in 2023, with Turner’s flame dress a highlight. The exhibition showed how Mackie’s design accentuated Turner’s showmanship and made her performance even more memorable. This was, ultimately, Mackie’s talent. “I’m very serious about this,” he said in 2018. “It’s not just flamboyant, crazy stuff. It’s all very worked out.”
Several celebrities paid tribute to the designer on social media.
Carpenter wrote on Instagram that she felt “so lucky to have met Bob.
“His one of a kind creations have inspired and brought so much happiness and confidence to my world and they will continue to always x Mackie girl forever.”
Kathy Lennon, a member of the vocal group The Lennon Sisters, described Mackie as “always so welcoming and complimentary when we went to his amazing costume showroom.”
“In a sea of ego, he seemed to have none,” Elton John wrote on Instagram. “One of the most courteous, incredible people I ever had the pleasure of working with.”
The Canadian model Coco Rocha said it was an “enormous privilege” to work with Mackie and wear his designs.
“There are designers whose work defines a moment, and then there are those rare few whose imagination teaches fashion something for generations,” Rocha said on Instagram. “Bob was one of them. His clothes had wit, drama, fantasy and joy.”

Yohanan Elishov, last survivor of Israel’s iconic Ink Flag raising in Eilat, dies at 95
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:32:52 UTC
03:32:52 KST

Yohanan Elishov, a Palmach fighter and one of the last surviving combatants of Israel’s 1948 generation, died Monday at the age of 95.
Elishov was the last living person who had been present at the historic raising of the Ink Flag following the capture of Eilat during the War of Independence, an image that became one of the most recognizable symbols of Israel’s founding.
Born in Petah Tikva, Elishov was among the prominent Palmach fighters who took part in the establishment of the state. After enlisting in late 1947, he trained under the command of Rafael Eitan and was later sent to Jerusalem to reinforce the Harel Brigade, where he served as the personal runner of commander Haim Poznansky, known as “Poza,” in the 4th Battalion.
During the Battle of Nabi Samuel, Elishov helped evacuate wounded soldiers and equipment. He later took part in key battles along the road to Jerusalem, including the capture of Beit Mahsir and the attempt to break into the Old City.
During the first ceasefire, he was transferred to the southern front and fought in major operations in the Negev and Sinai. He was present at the historic raising of the Ink Flag in Eilat and later served as Yigal Allon’s driver.
Elishov went on to serve for many years in the reserves with the Artillery Corps, taking part in every Israeli war from the 1956 Sinai Campaign through the First Lebanon War.
In civilian life, he spent decades helping build the country and develop its national infrastructure. For years, he worked as a heavy-vehicle driver for the Solel Boneh construction company and took an active role in paving roads and building development projects in southern Israel, the Negev, the Dead Sea area and the Makhteshim region. He later worked as a purchasing agent in the company’s industrial division.
Even after retiring, Elishov continued volunteering for years with the Israel Diabetes Association.
His son Yoav recalled that his father’s unusual path began long before his military service.
“My father started out as someone who was severely dyslexic,” he told Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. “He didn’t want to study, and he started working in a garage at age 13. At 16, he joined the Palmach, and that’s where his very special journey began.”
“When my father raised the Ink Flag, he didn’t understand the magnitude of the event,” Yoav said. “They didn’t have a flag, so their clerk took a sheet and drew on it. Only later did it become a historic icon.”
Another son, Yuval, described Elishov as a devoted family man whose values remained rooted in the ideals of the generation in which he grew up.
“My father wasn’t an educated man,” he said. “He said he didn’t want to learn English and that first the English should learn Hebrew. He was a wonderful father, a family man, and he was involved in our lives and pushed us toward values of love of the country. Until a very old age, we didn’t travel abroad.”
“People like my father were people with straightforward values,” Yuval added. “They had simplicity, wisdom and modesty. Even after the injuries he suffered from a mine, he didn’t rush to seek the disability benefits he might have been entitled to. He always said that anyone who is healthy should go serve the country.”
According to Yuval, his father remained lucid until his final day and continued to closely follow developments in Israel.
“Years ago, he said they were lying to us and that we didn’t have enough soldiers in the army,” he said. “He said it a decade ago, and I remember we got annoyed with him. After October 7, we told him he had been right. He saw what was coming.”
“He was one of the people who built the country, and from his perspective they were destroying the country he had built when accusations were directed at things he saw as part of the consensus, like the courts, the army and the Mossad,” Yuval said. “He was very angry about that.”

Canada Seeks 'Unique Alliance' With E.U. Amid U.S. Trade War. Here's What It Could Look Like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:32:01 UTC
03:32:01 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is seeking a “unique alliance” with the European Union as he aims to strengthen international ties amid a deepening trade war with the U.S.
“What we are looking, and will begin discussions for, [is] a unique alliance with the European Union,” Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday. “We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths.”
Canada’s European pivot has been months in the making, following growing tensions between Carney’s government and the Trump Administration. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Carney has encouraged Canadians to take back economic power at the kitchen table, and many have embraced a boycott of U.S. products. Trump has also repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty, speaking openly of his desire to annex the country and make it the “51st state.”
The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country's annual trade report, making it Canada’s largest trading partner. But Carney is keen to build an international support network that isn’t reliant on the U.S.
At the E.U.-Canada summit in June 2025, Canada established a new Security and Defense Partnership with the bloc. “Our partnership is grounded in the core values we share: democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and open, rules-based markets," read a joint statement marking the occasion.
In January, Carney notably met with China’s President Xi Jinping to forge what he referred to as a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market. Carney agreed to cut his country’s 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
Continuing with these efforts, Carney on Monday brought together executives and senior leaders from global investment firms to encourage them to invest in the country at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto.
He’s heading for a three-day trip to Europe on Tuesday, where he’ll meet with various European leaders including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He’s also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, in what could symbolize the mark of a new era between Canada and Europe.
Here’s a look at the alliance options on the table between Canada and the bloc, and what that could mean for U.S.-Canada relations.
Is Canada trying to join the E.U.?
Canada is not looking to join the E.U. as a member, Carney clarified amid questions over what a firmer relationship between his country and the 27-member bloc might look like.
“We’re not looking to become a member,” Carney said, emphasizing he’s instead keen to form an alliance. “We’re stronger together, and this is at a time where the world’s more dangerous and divided, and friends need to stick together in these times.”
Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union explicitly states that any “European State” can apply for membership, making Canada ineligible.
However, a report in the Wall Street Journal, quoting officials from both sides, said Carney is keen for Canada to become an “associate member” of the E.U.
When approached for comment, the European Commission directed TIME to remarks made during a Monday press briefing in Brussels.
“Canada is a strategically important partner for the European Union, and indeed a close friend,” the European Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters. “We deeply value this co-operation. You will recall that at our E.U.-Canada summit last year, we set a very high level of ambition for cooperation across the board, this year our ambition is even higher.”
When asked directly what discussions had taken place between Canadian and European officials, or what this “unique alliance” could look like, Gill declined to answer.
TIME has reached out to the Canadian Prime Minister’s office for comment.
Frank Schimmelfennig, a professor of European politics at ETH Zurich, predicts that Canada may wish to pursue deeper cooperation through additional trade agreements, or take inspiration from countries that have close relationships with the bloc without being E.U. members.
“Canada is already one of the most integrated non-European countries. It has the densest network of institutional relationships with the E.U.,” he tells TIME, referencing the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), a major free-trade deal between the E.U. and Canada, signed in 2016, and Horizon Europe, an initiative on collaborative research launched by the European Union in 2021 and joined by Canada in 2024.
“Canada could have more of the same, which means additional sectoral agreements for sectors that haven't been covered yet,” he says. “That would basically be a lateral extension of the current relationship. Anything more, would mean access to the internal market which would require an arrangement like the EEA.”
The European Economic Area (EEA) includes countries such as Iceland and Norway, which are not members of the E.U., and provides for the free movement of goods, services, and people within the E.U.’s member states, while enabling cooperation across multiple industries.
“The EEA countries have access to the E.U. internal market in return for adopting the relevant E.U. regulations and directives, so that would be a much denser legal integration than what Canada has now,” says Schimmelfennig.
Burgeoning E.U. relationship comes amid deepening U.S.-Canada trade rift
At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney declared a "rupture" in the international rules-based order. He said "great powers" were using tariffs and financial systems as instruments of coercion. He did not directly name Trump or the U.S.
The speech came at a moment of acute transatlantic tension over Trump’s push to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland and his short-lived threats to tariff European allies until Denmark relented.
Patrick Leblond, an associate professor at the University of Ottawa, says Carney’s movements now are in response to the world “seeing a United States that is becoming more protectionist, nationalist, and willing to use its leverage points to gain concessions, including on very close allies like Canada and Europeans.”
“For Canada, [the consensus is] we need to do more with partners who share our values based on liberal democracy, open markets, rule of law, international agreements, and the first port of call for Carney is the European Union,” Leblond tells TIME.
These trade efforts, he continues, may allow Carney to “build momentum, and hopefully bring other countries” into a broader coalition of what the Canadian leader has often called “middle powers."
In July, Carney, in a joint op-ed with Finland’s President Alexander Stubb, urged the “middle powers of the world” to “unite.”
Championing middle power countries that possess significant economic power and diplomatic influence, but lack market or military power, the leaders implored: “In a rapidly changing world, we have the grit and the sisu to chart the path ahead—and we know that so have many others whom we invite to join us on this quest.”
Leblod explains that “ultimately trust has been eroded” with the U.S. and Canada must re-think its place in the wider global economy in the long-term.
“The first time we thought Trump was a blimp, but he's not, and we're looking at what's happening in terms of democracy and political polarization, and a lot of Canadians think we can't rely on the U.S.,” he says.
According to a poll by Nanos Research, conducted between Aug. 30 and Sept. 2, 74% of Canadians disagreed that “the U.S. is a trustworthy ally of Canada.” An earlier poll by Angus Reid Institute, conducted between July 10-14, found that 42% of respondents said they think the Canadian government should approach the U.S. as an enemy/potential threat.
The E.U. has also clashed with Trump over tariffs, his Greenland annexation threats, and the wider split between the U.S. President and several European leaders.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in February warned of “a deep rift” between Europe and the United States, arguing that the latter “will not be powerful enough to go it alone.” But relations have since soured further amid the fallout of the Iran war, particularly between Merz and Trump.
Meanwhile, Canada has also embraced Europe in the cultural space. It was announced earlier this year that Canada will join the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027, becoming the first new participant since Australia in 2015.
Carney to address European Parliament
Carney’s highly-anticipated speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg this week stems from an invitation extended by European Parliament president Roberta Metsola.
Leblond predicts Carney will use the speech “to reiterate a lot of the things he mentioned at Davos,” but with a strong, intentional focus on the E.U.
“I would expect that he will use that address to call on the E.U. to work with Canada to push this idea of co-operation beyond the North Atlantic and include partners and allies in the Indo-Pacific,” he says.
The Canadian leader is also expected to be a guest at the State of the European Union debate, where European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is due to deliver a speech outlining the Commission's work and plans for the future.
Von der Leyen called E.U.–Canada ties “one of the closest partnerships in the world” when she celebrated 50 years of E.U. diplomatic presence in Canada in May. She declared the two sides were “closer than ever” as they confronted wars, an energy crisis and “new fractures in old alliances.”
Schimmelfennig says Canada inching closer to the E.U. is a strong display of “how both partners are affected by the deteriorating transatlantic relationship” with the U.S. “They feel that they need to move together because the world is getting more dangerous, and more difficult for both [parties],” he says.

Argentina's Milei plans bill to toughen sanctions against firms operating in Falklands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:31:42 UTC
03:31:42 KST

Argentina's Milei plans bill to toughen sanctions against firms operating in Falklands
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 14 - Argentine President Javier Milei is preparing legislation this week to toughen sanctions against companies operating in the Falkland Islands, a move analysts say raises uncertainty over whether he may escalate tensions with Britain by targeting other sectors of the disputed islands' economy.
The proposed bill will build on sanctions proceedings that Argentina's government says it has opened against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and claims as its own even though Britain controls them. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 and fought a 10-week war over them before surrendering to Britain.
Congress is set to receive Milei's 2027 budget proposal by Tuesday. It is expected to boost defense spending to address a sharper focus on sovereignty issues.
This month, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Washington could reconsider its traditionally neutral position on the Falklands dispute. Since then, Argentina has accelerated efforts to target companies involved in oil drilling activities around the islands.
Milei's proposed legislation includes tougher penalties for unauthorized operations around the islands, congressional aide Marcelo Seghini told Reuters. He said it would extend sanctions to affiliates and cover other activities affecting Argentina's natural resources.
It follows a criminal complaint filed last week against companies linked to the Sea Lion offshore project in the Falklands.
Argentina's government has not responded to Reuters requests for comment or provided a list of companies facing sanctions proceedings, though names have been reported by local media.
Analysts said they were uncertain about the scope of Milei's proposed "national sovereignty defense" bill but called his sanctions an aggressive effort to translate Argentina's sovereignty claims into legal and commercial pressure.
"It was not a project developed over time or meticulously prepared," said Marcelo Elizondo, Argentina's representative to the International Chamber of Commerce. Trump's comments, he said, "created a climate that the government sought to exploit quickly."
Companies and investors are weighing whether sanctions could ultimately affect firms with operations in Argentina, including those involved in the country's vast Vaca Muerta shale oil formation.
The government has already faced pushback over the reported sanctions. Dutch geodata specialist Fugro published a statement saying it had been incorrectly identified by local media as collaborating with the Sea Lion project, adding that its activities in the area were limited to work on a sub-sea telecommunications cable.
BROAD SANCTIONS
Experts said the measures could complicate development of the Sea Lion project by creating a chilling effect around companies working with project owners Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration.
Both companies have said the oilfield project holds valid licenses from the Falkland Islands government and have indicated they do not expect Milei's actions to derail development.
A government document reviewed by Reuters included a range of shareholders and financial intermediaries among companies marked for possible sanctions. They included Vanguard, First Eagle, Canaccord, Aberdeen-owned Interactive Investor and Hargreaves Lansdown.
Oil majors SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton have said in recent days they would not participate in activities on the islands.
“Without major service companies, one would have to turn to mid-sized firms with less established technical capabilities—companies that might be more expensive or slower to mobilize,” Juan Jose Carbajales, a former undersecretary of hydrocarbons in the former center-left government of President Alberto Fernández.
Seghini, the congressional aide, told Reuters the Milei government was considering expanding sanctions to the fishing industry in the expected legislation, potentially targeting a sector that underpins much of the Falkland Islands economy.
"The more you widen the supply chain, the more risk you run that these sanctions will be costly to you," said Federico Merke, a political scientist at the University of San Andres in Buenos Aires.
OPPOSITION PRESSURE
The sovereignty package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress and has struggled to secure support for some economic reforms.
Center and left-wing opponents have long accused libertarian Milei of not doing enough to defend Argentina's claim on the Malvinas, and they now say he is acting for political reasons ahead of a likely 2027 reelection bid.
"He is clearly using the Malvinas for political opportunism," said Aldo Leiva, an opposition lawmaker. "If he wanted to defend the sovereignty of the Malvinas in these two years of government, he had the tools to do it."
Marcelo Garcia, a Buenos Aires analyst at the consultancy Horizon Engage, said Milei’s legislation makes investors uneasy because it may help the opposition force him to escalate measures against the United Kingdom.
“There was already concern about the elections next year, what if there’s a populist backlash in Argentina?” said Garcia.
Francisco Cafiero, a former secretary for international relations at the defense ministry, said the episode reflected a broader lack of strategic clarity.
"Here, we navigate amidst uncertainty and improvisation," he said. REUTERS

Russia using Belarusian LTE networks, relay stations for mass drone attacks on Ukraine, Kyiv says
Russia is likely using Belarusian Long Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of the petrol-powered drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12.
Speaking on a Radio NV livestream, Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov said the flight path of the drones used in the attack suggested the use of domestic mobile networks for the cross-border attacks.
"If we look at the movement of jet-powered and conventional 'Shaheds,' they stay close to the border with Belarus," he said.
"I came to the conclusion that the 'Shaheds' probably have connectivity to Belarusian commercial LTE networks."
Separately, on the same day, State Border Guard Service Spokesperson Andrii Demchenko told Ukrainian television that Russia was also using radio repeater stations in the attacks.
"The air strikes that targeted Rivne, Volyn, and Lviv oblasts were also actually carried out from the territory of Belarus," Demchenko said.
"The air assets launched by Russia were fed with a signal through repeaters that were also located precisely on the territory of this country."
The placement of such relay stations in Belarusian territory has been a cause of tension between Kyiv and Minsk, with President Volodymyr Zelensky in the summer issuing a formal ultimatum for the equipment to be taken down.
At the time, Zelensky claimed that counterpart Alexander Lukashenko had agreed to take down the repeaters.
Lacking access to technology like SpaceX's Starlink, Russia consistently uses a mix of innovative radio technology to maintain connection with Shahed-type drones during mass attacks on Ukraine.

Air Force Leaders Eye Point Defense Acquisition Czar, Say It’s No Longer a ‘Side Hustle’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:23:59 UTC
03:23:59 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force officials are exploring the idea of creating a new acquisition office to oversee the point defense mission, in the service’s latest move to intensify its focus on defending airbases from drone and missile attacks, Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said Sept. 14, during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Since late 2023, the Air Force has been racing to get ahead of rapidly growing drone threat after unidentified drones hovered unchecked over Langley Air Force Base, Va., catching base commanders off guard. Since then, the service has been on a steady march to bolster airbase defense against drones and other new missile threats with everything from new doctrine on the “Point Defense of Air Bases” to plans for creating a point defense career field to ensure personnel are trained and equipped to defend bases from aerial attack.
Meink and Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach both devoted significant portions of their keynote addresses at the conference to point defense—reflecting the growing focus and urgency from senior leadership to tackle the issue.
“We can no longer treat point defense as a side hustle,” Wilsbach declared. “We must make it a core function of air and space power.”
On the personnel side, the new point defense career field will be operational in two years, Wilsbach said. Already, the Air Force has selected its first two career field managers—Wilsbach recognized one of them during his keynote.
On the acquisition side, the Air Force is now considering standing up a new portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to focus on “the kit side” of point defense “to further increase security for our Airmen and Guardians,” Meink said.
“How do you make sure that they have the kit they need to do the job?” Meink said, adding that the explosion of counter-drone innovations from industry “is a rapidly changing environment.”
PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to replace program executive offices. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.
“We are delegating almost every authority we legally have to our PAEs for most programs,” Meink said. “That now includes milestone decision authority, a big first on our acquisition community.”
Meink cautioned that the creation of a point defense PAE is “not going to be tomorrow.” But he sounded confident that it is a matter of when, not if, the new organization is created: “We’re already walking down the road, and eventually we’ll evolve into PAE for it.”
The need, he added, is clear.
“There definitely has to be continually increasing focus on making sure we can defend our Airmen and Guardians wherever they are in the world,” Meink said.
Wilsbach teased one acquisition program that may one day fall under the future point defense PAE, saying the Air Force will create a “point defense weapon system,” an umbrella effort that will bring together kinetic and nonkinetic counter-drone capabilities. He offered no further details about the new program.

A boat carrying migrants sank off Crete: one dead, 20 missing
Kyiv • UNN
51 migrants were rescued off Crete after a boat from Libya sank. One person died, and 20 others are still missing.
A boat carrying migrants from Libya to the island of Crete began taking on water and lost power. As a result of the incident, at least one person died and another 20 are considered missing, UNN reports, citing AP.
The Greek Coast Guard said that early Monday morning, 51 people were rescued at the scene — approximately 75 kilometers south of Crete. Patrol boats, a helicopter, a drone and commercial vessels were involved in the search operation; the European Union border protection agency Frontex also provided assistance.
The dangerous route across the Mediterranean from eastern Libya to Crete has become one of the busiest routes for irregular migration to Europe, while the number of migrants has generally declined on other routes.

Destroying Ukraine has ‘totemic’ role for Russia, British expert says

Unknown Publisher

Destroying Ukraine has ‘totemic’ role for Russia, British expert says
British expert Jade McGlynn, Head of the Ukraine and Russia Program with the Centre for Statecraft and National Security at King’s College London, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Their entire ideology revolves around claiming that the Ukrainians are just Russians who've been brainwashed or being used by the West as their proxy element,” the expert said.
In this regard, she believes the only thing that will change the calculus in the Kremlin would be if Moscow “has to choose between the stability at home and continuing to prosecute the war.”
“Destroying Ukraine has taken on this totemic role within the Kremlin's vision of Russia and its role in the world so the only thing that would force a reconsideration or recalculation would be if there begins to be a lot of trouble at home. I think the focus should be on the home front, the deep strikes on various elements, exerting much more pressure on the economy,” McGlynn said.
She believes the Russian people will not necessarily rise up against the regime, but such social tensions “always find a way, sometimes in quite unexpected ways.”
According to the researcher, many Russians are still “very happy to go along with the war, provided it doesn't affect them.”
“So, I think it's reasonable to show, including through petrol prices, the millions that make this war possible, whether because they work in the propaganda studios or in military production factories, or simply paying taxes, that there are consequences and that you can no longer ignore the war. It can no longer remain just some special military operation somewhere far away that you don't need to know about,” the expert said.
Therefore, she believes, any measures that increase this pressure would be helpful.
At the same time, she stressed that the West needs to do more to support Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, including by providing more interceptor missiles.
“We’ve seen some very positive moves from European countries in the last few days in terms of procuring them. But it’s also about ensuring that Ukrainians have generators in order to have access to heat over this winter, because if this is going to end up being a race to exhaustion, then we need to be doing a lot more to ensure that it's not Ukraine that’s exhausted first,” the expert stressed.
As reported, on Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump called on Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries amid a sharp rise in diesel fuel prices worldwide.
Earlier, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he believed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had affected diesel fuel prices in the United States.

Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding

03:17:43 KST

Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed on Monday that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events.
Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest child, married the Palm Beach socialite in a lavish three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands in May.
Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show.
In a statement signed by the couple and shared on Bettina Trump’s Instagram after ProPublica’s report was published, they confirmed Kremlev’s contributions to the celebrations and characterized them as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful”.
A top Democrat demanded answers on the Trumps’ ties to Kremlev.
“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” posted Robert Garcia, the ranking member and lead Democrat on the House oversight committee, on social media. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”
Kremlev has a longstanding relationship with Putin. He is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a sporting body that has been backed by the state-owned Russian energy company Gazprom. According to ProPublica, the wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions.
In the days before the wedding party, he reportedly went to China as part of a delegation accompanying Putin, and the month prior the Russian president had bestowed him with a state honor, the Order of Friendship. The Ukrainian government has imposed sanctions on Kremlev, citing his closeness to Putin and Russian security services.
Alexander Lagutin, a businessperson who has held senior roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company, had been with Kremlev on the China trip. Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA, Elena Sobol, attended the wedding, too.
While the event was extravagant, the guest list was intimate, with only about 50 people attending, most of whom were immediate family, close friends and business partners of the couple. Then there was Kremlev, who reportedly didn’t attend the ceremony itself, which was limited to just 18 guests, but was present with a large contingent of Russians at the party, much to the confusion of the other guests. The group reportedly sometimes stood off by themselves speaking Russian, according to ProPublica.
The affair has raised questions about the implications of a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting and gaining such intimate access to the US president’s family. In recent years Trump Jr has emerged as a leading campaign surrogate for Trump and has even been touted as a potential political heir.
Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew), said it is in the public interest for Congress to strongly consider requiring financial disclosure statements of a president’s adult children, in addition to the president themselves.
The crux of the issue is the nature of the friendship, and whether the giving of gifts is genuine or designed to influence, Sherman said. “We know that private companies and foreign governments have been seeking to gain Don Jr’s favor in order to serve their own financial interests. And so, it’s important that there is a measure of transparency when folks tied to the Russian government are lavishing the president’s rich adult son with expensive gifts.”
He added: “Most of us learn as children that ‘there’s no such thing as a free lunch’. It’s one thing if, in the nature of this friendship, there’s a mutual exchange of lavish gifts. It’s another if someone’s daddy becomes president and then all of a sudden this new friend starts giving gifts – that context very much matters.”
In similar vein, retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr told ProPublica: “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president.”
It remains unclear why Kremlev helped pay for the wedding and why he was there, when he appears to have only met Trump Jr – the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, who has a personal net worth somewhere in the ballpark of $300m – quite recently.
Donald Trump famously didn’t attend the wedding. “He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair,” the US president told reporters a few days before the nuptials. “I said, you know, this is not good timing for me. I have a thing called Iran and other things.”
In response to detailed questions from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had helped fund the wedding. “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” the spokesperson said, adding Kremlev is “not someone he has a business relationship with” and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world.
In their joint Instagram statement, Trump Jr and Bettina Trump thanked “our dear friend Umar” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”.
They said they “got married privately” on 22 May “surrounded ONLY by our family”, and said the Russian businessman had simply given them a gift.
“Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” they said.
