Is the United Kingdom breaking apart? Separatist leaders join forces in historic push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:16:41 UTC
03:16:41 KST

The leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland — the three semi-autonomous nations that, together with England, make up the United Kingdom — signed a declaration of intent Monday calling for referenda that could lead to independence from Britain and, in effect, the breakup of the United Kingdom.
The meeting in Cardiff, the Welsh capital, was dubbed the “separatists’ summit” by local media. It brought together Scottish National Party leader John Swinney, Welsh Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth and Sinn Féin Vice President Michelle O’Neill.
All three also head their respective devolved governments, an unprecedented situation that emerged after local elections in Wales in May brought the pro-independence Plaid Cymru to power for the first time. Ap Iorwerth hosted Monday’s summit.
Although the gathering reflects renewed hopes among independence movements in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland of securing referenda on their constitutional futures, the authority to approve such votes ultimately rests with the central government in London, which strongly opposes them.
As a result, an actual breakup of the United Kingdom still appears a distant prospect. The declaration signed Monday did not set out a clear timetable and appeared primarily intended to increase pressure on Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham.
The United Kingdom consists of four constituent nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have substantial autonomy over many domestic affairs through their devolved governments and legislatures, but they remain subject to the authority of the British government and Parliament in London, which also governs England directly in areas covered by devolution elsewhere.
The pro-independence Scottish National Party, or SNP, has governed Scotland since 2007. Under pressure from the party, the British government agreed to allow an independence referendum in 2014. The independence movement lost that vote, with 55% of Scottish voters choosing to remain in the United Kingdom.
In Wales, on the western side of Britain, polls have historically shown that most residents oppose breaking away from the United Kingdom. But the political landscape shifted in May when the pro-independence Plaid Cymru came to power for the first time.
The situation in Northern Ireland is more complicated because of the violent history surrounding the question of its constitutional status. Irish nationalists favor reunification with the Republic of Ireland, the independent country covering most of the island, while unionists favor remaining part of the United Kingdom.
From the late 1960s until the end of the 1990s, Northern Ireland was gripped by a period of sectarian and political violence known as the Troubles. The conflict largely pitted predominantly Protestant unionists against predominantly Catholic nationalists seeking a united Ireland. About 3,500 people were killed.
The conflict largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Northern Ireland has remained mostly peaceful since then, although sporadic unrest has continued and the question of Irish reunification remains politically sensitive.
Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum on Irish unity can be held if the British government determines that it appears likely that a majority of voters in Northern Ireland would support reunification.
The independence movements in the three nations received a boost last week following remarks by Burnham during a debate in the House of Commons.
Asked by an SNP lawmaker about the difference between Scotland and Northern Ireland when it comes to the ability to hold a referendum on their constitutional status, Burnham replied that they were the “same situation.”
The remark was interpreted as potentially opening the door to another Scottish independence referendum after the independence movement’s defeat in 2014. Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, said Burnham’s comments meant that if sufficient public support emerged for another referendum, the government in London would not be able to prevent one.
Burnham quickly sought to walk back his remarks. In a letter to Swinney, he stressed: “Independence and a referendum are off limits as it would take our focus away from growing the economy and helping families with the cost of living.”
Separatist aspirations received another boost shortly before Monday’s Cardiff summit from unusual comments by U.S. President Donald Trump during a weekend visit to Ireland.
Trump voiced support for the reunification of Ireland and Northern Ireland, saying it would be “a fantastic thing.”
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters, adding: “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
Trump’s comments marked a departure from Washington’s longstanding neutrality on the question of Irish reunification and came at a sensitive moment in relations between the United States and Britain.
London has been concerned about possible retaliation from the Trump administration amid a sharp dispute between the longtime allies, fueled in part by Britain’s refusal to side with the United States in its war with Iran.
Against that backdrop, Trump has also recently said his administration is reconsidering the longstanding U.S. neutral position on the sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina over the British-controlled Falkland Islands.
Declaration of intent, but no clear targets: ‘Westminster’s days are coming to an end’
The document signed Monday in Cardiff was worded in relatively broad terms and set no clear targets for their demands for future referendums.
The three signed it not in their official capacities as heads of their respective devolved governments but as leaders of pro-independence parties. That means the document is not an official government agreement but rather a declaration of intent outlining their aspirations for future cooperation.
“For the first time ever, people across these islands have first ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom,” the document said.
“For people watching across these islands — for people watching around the world — there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end,” it said. Westminster is commonly used as shorthand for Britain’s Parliament and central government.
The leaders pledged to strengthen cooperation among their parties and identify practical areas where working together could produce tangible change.
The document also outlined plans to “reject Whitehall’s broken economic model,” using another common shorthand for the British government, derived from the London street where many government departments are based.
It also declared that “the future of our nations belong in the European Union,” reflecting opposition among many voters in Scotland and Northern Ireland to Britain’s departure from the EU, known as Brexit. Wales, however, voted by a narrow majority to leave the bloc in the 2016 referendum.
The three leaders declared that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have a “right to determine its own future,” but again stopped short of setting clear targets or timetables for exercising that right.
“No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future,” the declaration said. “We recognize that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time.”
Michelle O’Neill, vice president of Sinn Féin and first minister of Northern Ireland, said during Monday’s meeting that no British prime minister would be able to prevent the eventual breakup of the United Kingdom.
“Our common cause here is that Westminster does not and will never serve our people well,” she said.
Sinn Féin is calling for a referendum on Irish reunification in Northern Ireland by 2030. O’Neill said Trump’s comments over the weekend showed that “the unity debate is very much alive. Our nations have the right to self-determination.”
Mary Lou McDonald, president of Sinn Féin in Ireland and Northern Ireland, also attended the signing ceremony. She described the agreement as “historic.”
“We have the right to referendum. We have the right to decide our future. We will not accept or tolerate any prime minister telling us that right is off the table,” McDonald said.
Scottish First Minister John Swinney, who leads the pro-independence SNP, said he hoped Scotland would hold another independence referendum within five years. He stressed, however, that he would rather leave the question of timing to the Welsh people when it came to Wales.
Swinney described Prime Minister Andy Burnham as the “last prime minister of the United Kingdom.”
Alongside the Welsh and Northern Irish leaders, Swinney stressed that each independence movement would follow its own path.
“We will each individually be responsible for our own journeys,” he said, “but we are absolutely united by that principle of self-determination.”
Union supporters furious: ‘They want to destroy the United Kingdom’
The significance of the declaration is largely symbolic. Although its signing increases pressure on the government in London, the final say over whether future referenda can be held ultimately rests with the British government.
Burnham’s spokesperson reiterated the government’s opposition Monday and called instead for a focus on improving the economic situation of people across Britain.
“The Prime Minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the Union,” the spokesperson said. “The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around our shared values and problem-solving rather than division.”
“The UK Government is focused on addressing the issues that matter most to families, including easing pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums,” the spokesperson added.
The separatist declaration also drew criticism from supporters of the union in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales.
“Many people across Scotland will recoil at the sight of John Swinney joining forces with Sinn Fein in their shared desire to destroy the United Kingdom,” said Russell Findlay, leader of the Scottish Conservatives.
“They will also be appalled by the SNP's continued disrespect towards the majority of Scots who reject separation and want the devolved government in Edinburgh to get on with its job,” he said.
Emma Little-Pengelly of Northern Ireland’s Democratic Unionist Party, or DUP, which supports remaining part of the United Kingdom, also criticized O’Neill over her participation in the Cardiff summit.
Little-Pengelly serves as deputy first minister alongside O’Neill under Northern Ireland’s power-sharing system, a central feature of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. She accused O’Neill of attempting to use the office of first minister for political purposes.
“We need to be very clear. It is not a summit of first ministers. She may be first minister, which is of course a joint role along with myself, but she is there absolutely in a Sinn Féin capacity,” Little-Pengelly said. Meanwhile, Burnham’s office announced Monday evening that his father, Roy, had died at age 86.
His father had Alzheimer’s disease, and Burnham said in July, shortly before succeeding Keir Starmer as prime minister, that his condition had deteriorated to the point that he was unaware his son was about to become prime minister.
Burnham said at the time that alongside his sadness, he also felt a sense of pride.
“The way I see it, it’s his achievement too,” Burnham said. “An achievement for the whole family, even though he is not aware of it.”
Following his father’s death, Burnham’s office said all of the prime minister’s engagements Monday and Tuesday had been canceled, including a meeting Monday evening with senior business leaders.

The Saudi energy minister has said that its national nuclear energy project is proceeding according to plan, stressing that nuclear power has become an essential part of the country’s energy mix.
Speaking at the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna on Monday, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the world is witnessing rapid growth in energy demand, driven by economic, technological, and industrial expansion.
“Diversifying energy sources and ensuring their reliability and sustainability have become necessary to support economic growth and energy security,” he said.
“Saudi Arabia has consolidated its position as a reliable source of energy and an active partner in global energy markets, while continuing to invest its various resources in the energy and minerals sectors,” he said.
“The Kingdom is moving ahead with building a comprehensive national energy mix, including nuclear energy, to benefit from available resources,” he added.
Prince Abdulaziz stressed that Saudi Arabia is not developing its nuclear program “in isolation from the international community,” but continues to strengthen its national and regulatory nuclear energy systems and work transparently with partners in the energy and minerals fields.
“The inclusion of nuclear energy in the national energy mix is being carried out under a solid regulatory framework in line with the Kingdom’s international obligations,” the minister added.
“The Saudi nuclear program is peaceful and clear, and not deep in mountains or bunkers,” he said, adding that it is based on transparency and commitment to international standards.
He said Saudi Arabia works transparently and will continue to do so in cooperation with partners and the IAEA.
Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia has vast mineral wealth and is committed to securing mineral supply chains, developing rare earth discoveries, and turning resources into sustainable economic value.
He said the kingdom is moving ahead with uranium exploration and working to extract associated uranium as part of fertiliser production.
“Saudi Arabia has discovered 110 million tons of raw materials containing uranium concentrations in the Medina region,” he added.
Prince Abdulaziz also said Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest exporter of phosphate fertilisers.

The Guardian view on Reform UK: crypto billionaires must be stopped from undermining democracy | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:13:14 UTC
03:13:14 KST

The staggering sums gifted to Reform UK over the weekend have transformed the context for the representation of the people bill making its way through parliament. The announcement of two £36m donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, both crypto billionaires who have lived abroad, makes Andy Burnham’s decision not to impose a limit on political donations – a move he supported before becoming prime minister – look even more misguided. Fortunately the House of Lords still has the chance to amend the bill. It should take it by imposing meaningful limits on both political donations and party spending.
It is unclear whether either man meets the criteria set out in the Rycroft review into foreign influence in politics. It set a maximum of £100,000 per annum for people who have not been in the UK for at least a year. Mr Delo previously lived in Hong Kong while Mr Harborne is based partly in Thailand; Nigel Farage said on Monday that he does not know the details of their movements. While ministers will view the prospect of a legal fight over eligibility with trepidation, they must do what it takes to ensure rules are met.
Reform UK’s support has fallen since a year ago, when polls showed it ahead of Labour, and again since May when it won more than 1,400 seats in local elections. After a summer dominated by investigations of its finances, and with the police widening their inquiries to include footage, aired on Channel 4, of officials apparently discussing ways to get around electoral law, Nigel Farage’s unfavourability rating has hit a 10-year high. But while this reversal of fortune has brought relief to opponents, there is no room for complacency. In 2024, 34% of votes secured a huge majority for Labour. The danger of a Farage premiership and all that it could mean for UK politics and civil society remains real.
Mr Farage no longer advertises his closeness to Donald Trump in the way he once did. But he shares the US president’s enthusiasm for crypto currencies, which is part of a wider agenda of aggressive financial deregulation. Last year he told a conference that he wants to turn the UK into “the world’s premier hub for cryptocurrency”. No wonder that Mr Harborne appears to be competing to be the party’s top supporter with Mr Delo – who was pardoned by Mr Trump following a 2022 conviction for failing to implement adequate anti‑money laundering controls.
The Rycroft review focused on foreign influence for good reason; it is for UK voters to choose their government. But ministers must look beyond the narrow question of outside interference. As well as donation and campaign spending caps, they should regulate party expenditure across the electoral cycle. Otherwise mega-rich donors can pay for years of polling, advertising, data and staff, before election-period limits apply.
A statement from unions is expected to signal a change of heart and support for a cap on donations. Ministers will need to find a carve-out protecting contributions from their members. A mechanism to prevent charities becoming a back door for rich individuals to fund parties is also needed. Democracy is undermined when the vastly wealthy make politics look like an auction, upending norms built up over decades. It is entirely wrong that two wealthy individuals should be able to spend their way to such an influential role in Britain’s political life.

2026-09-14
18:11:38 UTC
03:11:38 KST

Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the 92N6 multifunction radar of a Russian S-400 Triumf air defense system in Sochi, the General Staff said on 14 September. The S-400 is Russia's longest-range air defense system. The radar tracks aerial targets and guides the system's missiles onto them, which makes it the part of an S-400 that decides whether the launchers can fire at anything. The strike came on 13 September and overnight into 14 September, alongside hits on drone launch sites, radars, and relays elsewhere in Russia and occupied Crimea, according to the military.
What was hit in Sochi
Ukrainian monitoring channels reported the explosions hours before the military did. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published night footage from Sochi at 3:29 with the sound of small arms fire, drone engines, and an explosion in the air, then a second clip in which the blast came on the ground. At 4:25 the channel posted a clip of distant explosions in Dagomys, a suburb of Sochi.
Sochi's regional operational headquarters claimed that falling drone debris injured five people in the city, including a child, and that one adult went to hospital and three private houses took damage. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight.
By 11:34, Exilenova+ reported that a new-generation medium-range air defense system and the infrastructure of a military unit near Dagomys had preliminarily been hit overnight.
Sochi is a Russian resort city on the eastern Black Sea coast, about 600 km from the front line in southern Ukraine. Drones hit two fuel depots there and an air defense position near the Abkhazia border on 4 September, and satellite imagery later showed nine destroyed storage tanks and impact marks at the air defense position, which Russian officials had never acknowledged.
The rest of the target list
Near Kursk and the occupied city of Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit sites where Russia stores, prepares, and launches attack drones, the General Staff said. A drone control point of a Russian unit was struck in Novohrodivka, Donetsk Oblast.
Radar stations were hit in Litizh, Trostenchik, and Lipovka in Bryansk Oblast, and three signal relays in Rokhmanovo, Krasny Styag, and Kamen in the same oblast. At Saky airfield in occupied Crimea, Ukrainian forces struck a short-range radio navigation system.
The extent of the damage is being assessed, the General Staff said, adding that work against key Russian military targets continues.

The Guardian view on the united Ireland debate: shifting dynamics need to be treated with caution | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:11:31 UTC
03:11:31 KST

A decade ago, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) viewed Brexit as a potential gamechanger in the struggle to resist future pressure for a united Ireland. As the author and journalist Fintan O’Toole wrote in an essay published last year, the DUP hoped that the 2016 referendum would deliver “a double exit. Brexit would not simply mean the UK’s departure from the EU. It would also be an act of separation from the Republic. It would reverse the slow drift towards integration.” That proved to be, to put it mildly, a deeply flawed judgment.
The direction of travel since 2016 has instead been the opposite. Rather than leading to a hard border between Northern Ireland and Ireland, which would have disastrously undermined the Good Friday agreement, the UK’s divorce agreement from Brussels eventually placed one in the Irish Sea. The logic of further economic integration between north and south within the EU’s single market was reinforced.
At the same time, demographic change has meant that people with a Catholic background now outnumber those with a Protestant one in Northern Ireland, changing the political calculus. In 2022, Sinn Féin won a historic victory in Stormont elections, leading to Michelle O’Neill’s appointment as the first nationalist first minister. On Monday, during a meeting with the heads of the UK’s other devolved nations, Ms O’Neill welcomed off-the-cuff remarks by Donald Trump during an unofficial visit to Ireland, in which he said he would “love” to see unification. The US president’s comments, she claimed, reflected the fact “that there is a growing conversation around constitutional change”.
That is undoubtedly the case. But it is a debate that has barely begun, and one which needs to be conducted with care and caution. The 1998 Good Friday agreement was intentionally vague about the criteria for holding a border poll. Successive governments in London and Dublin have since preferred to concentrate on promoting and developing cross-border co-operation.
Given the history, and the level of political risk involved, that was a sensible strategy. But the dynamics of the debate have shifted. Mr Trump’s blithe remarks followed hard on the heels of an early spat between Ms O’Neill and Andy Burnham, after the prime minister said during a visit to Belfast that a poll on a united Ireland was “off the table”.
In the short and medium term, Mr Burnham’s position makes sense. Sinn Féin’s commitment to a referendum on Irish unity by 2030 is wildly unrealistic. But for all sides, sleepwalking into a vote without adequate preparation is equally unpalatable. In the absence of a proper debate, commitment to unity in the Irish republic is broadbased but shallow. In Northern Ireland a disturbing revival of tensions over Orange Order marches in Catholic areas suggests deepening polarisation, fuelled by ongoing political dysfunction at Stormont.
A sober, lengthy and detailed public conversation is required over what form unification might take, and the possible trade-offs involved. In an interview with the Guardian last month, the former prime minister Gordon Brown suggested that “of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united”. Unlike Mr Trump, though, he added a significant rider. Reaching that outcome would be “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.” Leaders on all sides of the debate should heed that caveat.

three centuries-old japanese craft traditions converge in loudspeaker collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:10:39 UTC
03:10:39 KST

Animism Objects brings japan’s craft traditions into audio design
Tokyo-based VOID Inc. launches Animism Objects, a loudspeaker label that brings traditional Japanese materials and artisanal techniques into contemporary audio objects. The project is set to be presented during London Design Festival 2026. Animism Objects draws from San’in, a region where Japan’s creation myths have been passed down for more than a millennium. In this landscape, nature is understood not simply as a resource, but as part of everyday life, memory, and ritual. The region is also associated with materials and techniques developed over centuries, including Washi, made by hand from natural plant fibres; Aizome, the traditional Japanese practice of indigo dyeing; and Yakisugi, a woodworking technique that chars the surface of cedar boards to increase durability and fire resistance. These processes bring distinct material qualities to the speakers while retaining visible traces of their making. The surfaces reflect variations in the natural materials and the work of the craftspeople who produce them, connecting the finished objects to accumulated knowledge, care, and ritual practice. Each technique gives the speaker a different tactile and visual character.
Traditional craft and technology converge in three speakers
The first Animism Objects collection comprises three editions: Washi, Aizome, and Yakisugi, with each limited to 10 sets. The three finishes establish different relationships between the speaker’s contemporary form and the traditional processes used to construct its surface. The project takes its conceptual starting point from Animism, understood here as an approach in which people, nature, and objects exist in relationship with one another. For the London exhibition, this idea is considered through the combination of traditional Japanese craftsmanship, technology, and contemporary design. By incorporating established materials and techniques into audio products, Animism Objects examines how inherited knowledge can continue to operate within contemporary design. The project positions craftsmanship not only as a form of preservation, but as a material and cultural practice that can inform new objects and their relationship to everyday life.

EU Fails to Renew Russia Sanctions as Slovakia Seeks to Protect Russian Oligarchs
European Union ambassadors meeting in Brussels failed on September 14 to renew one of the bloc's core Russia sanctions schemes, leaving the measure a single day from expiry.
Five EU diplomats told POLITICO about the deadlock, and three noted that ambassadors would reconvene later that same day for further discussion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Unanimous agreement was required on Monday because the regime—which governs asset freezes on roughly 3,000 individuals and companies— expires Tuesday, according to POLITICO.
Slovakia has demanded that the bloc strike two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the sanctions list, the diplomats told POLITICO. France has reportedly sought to broker a compromise by proposing that only Usmanov be delisted.
France reportedly attempted to reach a compromise by suggesting that only Usmanov be delisted.
Most other capitals were unwilling to consider removing anyone while Russia fires record numbers of missiles at Ukrainian civilian targets, the report noted.
One of the diplomats stated that "against the backdrop of rising hybrid threats and Russian drone attacks only 1 kilometer from the Polish border, it's hard to believe that France is actually asking for this."
A further dispute centers on the length of any extension. Since 2014 the measures have customarily been renewed for six months, though some capitals now favor a 12-month rollover. Slovakia is understood to be unwilling to back the longer period, POLITICO reported.
The standoff comes after months of steadily expanding EU measures against Moscow.
In mid-August the bloc was preparing its largest sanctions effort to date, aiming to enlarge the blacklist by roughly a third and push the total number of listed individuals, companies, and organizations close to 3,000.

Are gender differences really power differences? Large-scale analysis finds strong behavioral parallels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:00:57 UTC
03:00:57 KST

New research suggests that many psychological and behavioral differences between men and women might actually stem from differences in social power. The findings indicate that holding a high-power role produces behavioral effects strikingly similar to traits often associated with men, while low-power roles produce effects resembling traits often associated with women. This research was published in PNAS Nexus.
The origins of behavioral differences between men and women remain a topic of intense debate in the social sciences. Evolutionary theorists tend to trace these differences back to natural selection and biology. In this view, men and women developed distinct psychological attributes to adapt to different reproductive and survival roles in early human history.
Sociocultural theorists approach the issue differently, emphasizing how societal roles and social power shape behavior. They argue that hierarchical structures and unequal resource allocation reinforce gendered behaviors beyond any biological roots. A 2019 review indicated that human brains and hormonal systems are not strictly divided into two distinct categories, which supports the idea that many gender differences are shaped by culture rather than rigid biology.
At the center of this debate is the concept of social power, defined as the actual or perceived control over valuable resources. Across many areas of society, men tend to hold more power than women, occupying more leadership roles and controlling more financial assets. Because power differences are so frequently tied to gender, some researchers suspect that power dynamics might be the true source of many presumed gender differences.
Adam D. Galinsky of Columbia University and his colleagues set out to systematically test this idea. They wanted to see if the behaviors resulting from experimental manipulations of power would match up with known differences between men and women. By comparing these two separate areas of research, the team aimed to determine if power imbalances could provide a useful explanation for gender differences.
To conduct the analysis, the researchers first collected data from experiments that randomly assigned people to high-power or low-power roles. They performed a statistical check on 270 of these experiments to ensure the existing literature on power was reliable. From there, they identified 59 distinct psychological and behavioral outcomes that are genuinely affected by having or lacking power.
Next, the research team gathered 102 outcomes from meta-analyses of sex and gender differences. Meta-analyses are large-scale statistical reviews that combine data from many individual studies to find overall trends. The researchers then grouped the findings from both the power experiments and the gender meta-analyses into four broad categories for comparison.
These four categories included agency, communion, self-evaluation, and cognitive processes. Agency involves striving for independence, assertiveness, and control over one’s environment. Communion relates to social connection, empathy, and cooperating with others. Self-evaluation involves how people view their own abilities, and cognitive processes include attention, problem-solving, and spatial reasoning.
The comparison yielded a massive overlap. The researchers found that about 71 percent of the recorded gender differences were entirely consistent with the effects of power differences. In contrast, only about 8 percent of the gender differences showed the opposite pattern.
Sonya Xinyue Xiao, a developmental psychologist who directs the IBAY Lab and was not involved in the study, told PsyPost that her confidence in the results is “pretty high.”
“The method they used is very rigorous in testing their hypotheses that focus on whether power effects are aligned with sex/gender differences when there is a significant power effect,” she said.
Specifically, high-power individuals and men both tend to display higher agency, including traits like dominance and a willingness to take risks. They also both show more positive self-evaluations and display similar cognitive processing styles. On the other hand, low-power individuals and women both tend to display higher communion, exhibiting more interpersonal sensitivity and social cooperation.
To check if this alignment was unique to power, the researchers ran a similar comparison using the personality trait of extraversion. Extraversion is known to correlate with having power and influence, so the team wanted to see if it would also perfectly mirror gender differences. The results showed that it did not.
While extraverts and high-power individuals share some traits, they diverge in the area of communion. Extraverts tend to be highly communal and social, whereas high-power individuals and men tend to score lower on communion. This divergence provides evidence that social power has a specific and uniquely strong relationship with gender differences.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on comparing two separate bodies of literature, meaning the link between power and gender is observational in this context. The researchers did not conduct a new experiment to see if giving women high-power roles would immediately erase the observed gender gaps in these specific traits.
“The gender differences in many constructs are very small, but power differences may be large; it is important to keep in mind that the findings are pointing at similarity in directions rather than magnitudes,” Xiao noted. “As the authors mentioned in their discussions, their findings do not actually prove causal relations between social power and sex/gender differences.”
Additionally, grouping dozens of distinct psychological concepts into broad categories requires subjective judgment. Although the researchers used independent experts to classify the traits, personal biases or cultural perspectives could have subtly influenced how the categories were organized. The authors note that their results do not mean power explains all behavioral differences between men and women, but rather that it is likely a major contributing factor.
Future studies could directly test these ideas by assigning men and women to high- and low-power roles in the same experiment. This would help clarify exactly how power shapes behavior across different genders in real time.
“As a developmental psychologist, I am curious to see research examining how the potential causal relation between social power and gender difference changes over time — perhaps the role of social power increases as we age,” Xiao said. “Because gender is highly salient during childhood, whereas one’s gendered experiences of social power may come later.”
The study, “Are many sex/gender differences really power differences?,” was authored by Adam D. Galinsky, Aurora Turek, Grusha Agarwal, Eric M. Anicich, Derek D. Rucker, Hannah R. Bowles, Nira Liberman, Chloe Levin, and Joe C. Magee.

The FSB, SVR and GRU are corrupt, often sloppy and still capable of penetrations, sabotage and assassinations abroad.
 “They remain formidable precisely because there’s no accountability,” he tells Kyiv Post special correspondent Jason Jay Smart.

Wiswesser traces that culture through the poisoning of Sergei Skripal, the assassination of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin and Vladimir Putin’s successful effort to bring convicted assassin Vadim Krasikov back to Russia.

Trump seeks halt to energy attacks by both Russia, Ukraine
September 14, 2026
US President Donald Trump claimed a breakthrough on Monday in diplomacy between Ukraine and Russia, although his unsubstantiated declaration only elicited a very reserved comment from Ukraine and no immediate word from the Kremlin.
The assertion comes amid indications from both Russia and Ukraine that they would be willing to continue with US-brokered negotiations, which have been largely stagnant throughout Trump's second term.
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week told DW that he would be willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December if rumors of Putin being invited materialized.
What did Trump say?
Trump appeared to claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other's energy targets.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" Trump or his team wrote.
"The World's Diesel price is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War [sic], not Iran," the Truth Social comment continued, demonstrating — as a quickfire series of agitated follow-up posts would reinforce — a desire to downplay rising US oil prices, the role of Trump's war in Iran in pushing them skywards, and economic pressures closer to home.
What, if anything, did Ukraine and Russia say?
There was no immediate comment on the matter from Moscow.
Ukraine's presidency declined to comment but President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a more guarded statement online.
He did, however, say that he had recommended seeking such an accord, as winter approaches — if Russia's cooperation could be ensured after years of it targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
"Ukraine has proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote online. "Food, energy, and other basics that sustain life must be protected, and Russian strikes are directed primarily against them."
But Zelenskyy cautioned that Kyiv "is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by an agreement," if one could be reached.
"If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes."
He said Kyiv would need assurance that this was a lasting deal and not just a bid to secure temporary relief in fuel prices in Russia ahead of elections at the end of the week.
"We expect specifics from our partners," Zelenskyy concluded, without naming names.
Ukraine has been targeting Russian warehouses, refineries amid Iran war
As Trump's war in Iran pushed oil prices to highs not seen since the immediate aftermath of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv has started using long-range drone strikes to target Russia's refinery and petroleum supply infrastructure.
This has caused isolated shortages and price increases, even in oil-rich Russia.
Ukraine has also launched a series of high-profile strikes on Russia's best-known online retailer Wildberries, accusing it of providing logistical support to the military.
The US miltiary action of the last six months in the Gulf has also left Ukraine poorly placed to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles, because of US Patriot missile supplies being depleted in the Middle East.
In recent winters, Russia has frequently targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure to try to exacerbate difficulties of dealing with the cold. Last winter, as a particularly fierce cold snap hit Kyiv and other parts of the country, Trump announced a brief halt to strikes on Kyiv which only held for a few days.

Russia’s new jet drones are better at evading Ukrainian air defenses, but experts say Moscow’s drone program is ‘critically dependent’ on Chinese components
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:58:03 UTC
02:58:03 KST

Russia’s new jet drones are better at evading Ukrainian air defenses, but experts say Moscow’s drone program is ‘critically dependent’ on Chinese components
Russia has made a “leap forward” in the mass production of long-range drones and cruise missiles that are far better at evading interception, The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times report.
These weapons include jet-powered variants of the Geran drone and small Banderol cruise missiles. The original Gerans were copies of the slow Iranian Shahed drones, which Ukraine learned to shoot down effectively, according to the WSJ. Russian engineers, however, equipped the drones with turbojet engines, increasing their speed and survivability and making them harder for Ukrainian defenses to intercept.
The FT provides technical specifications for the drones. The first-generation Geran-1, powered by a piston internal combustion engine, could carry a warhead weighing up to 20 kilograms and reach a top speed of 185 kilometers per hour. The new jet-powered Geran-5 can fly at up to 600 kilometers per hour and carry a warhead weighing several dozen kilograms. The Geran-5 now resembles a missile more closely than it does the original Shahed.
According to the FT, Russia first used the Geran-5 in January 2026. In recent weeks, the newspaper says, the new Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones Russia has launched at Ukrainian cities have evaded air defenses far more effectively than their predecessors. Ukraine’s Air Force says Russia launched 2,800 jet-powered drones in August. Since August 27, the launches have been nearly continuous.
Ukrainian experts who examined the weapons’ wreckage believe components sourced from China in violation of international sanctions largely enabled the breakthrough in drone production. Analysts at DroneSec agree, saying Russia relies on Chinese parts, including jet engines, onboard computers, and other electronics. DroneSec CEO Mike Monnik says Russia is “critically dependent” on Chinese components for its drone program. Most of these Chinese-made parts are commercially available dual-use components.
Russia developed and deployed the new Geran variants in just a couple of years, upgrading earlier models, testing them in combat, and quickly beginning mass production, the WSJ reports. According to the FT’s sources, including some close to the Kremlin, Russia’s drone capabilities have grown so much that Tehran asked Moscow for the latest Gerans for its war against Israel and the United States.
Moscow has outpaced its adversaries, according to the WSJ. Ukraine developed one of the first jet-powered drones two years ago but lacks the resources and capacity to mass-produce them.
“In the West, we tend to underestimate Russia, but it can move very quickly from ideas and experiments to mass production. Western militaries should learn from Russia’s ability to complete that cycle,” said Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The FT says the new drones fly at speeds and altitudes that blur the line between drones and cruise missiles. “Soon we’ll probably see these drones having stealth capabilities, and that means it will become even more expensive to manufacture, procure and use them, but also more expensive to destroy them,” said military analyst Konrad Muzyka, head of the Polish consultancy Rochan Consulting.

NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) leader Supriya Sule on Monday questioned the registration of a CBI FIR into the death of Disha Salian, saying she was surprised because the case had earlier been treated as closed by the same government.Salian, a former manager of late actor Sushant Singh Rajput, died after falling from the 12th floor of a building in Mumbai’s Malad area on June 8, 2020. The CBI registered an FIR on September 13 following a direction from the Bombay High Court for a fresh probe into the circumstances surrounding her death.“I was surprised to hear how this (registration of an FIR by CBI) happened because it is the same government that had closed the case. I do not understand what is happening,” Sule told reporters in Pune.She said she would speak to Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut to understand the latest developments.
What is in the CBI FIR?
According to CBI officials cited by news agency PTI, the FIR does not name any individual as an accused, in line with the Bombay High Court’s directions. It invokes IPC provisions relating to criminal conspiracy, gang rape, murder, disappearance of evidence and public servants allegedly framing incorrect records.
The FIR followed a September 2 order by the Bombay High Court on a petition filed by Salian’s father, Satish Salian. The CBI began recording statements after the court directed it to conduct a thorough investigation.The court had criticised the Mumbai Police investigation, noting “glaring discrepancies” and observing that the probe “raises more questions than answers”.It had also directed that nobody should be treated as an accused unless investigators found sufficient grounds for reasonable suspicion based on the material collected during the probe.
Advocate claims names are in FIR
Advocate Nilesh Ojha, who represents Satish Salian, claimed on Monday that the FIR contains the names of several individuals, including Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray, Rohan Roy, Rhea Chakraborty, Param Bir Singh, Dino Morea and Sooraj Pancholi, among others.
However, the CBI has not publicly confirmed the names claimed by the advocate, according to PTI.Ojha said the FIR was registered after the CBI conducted preliminary verification of Satish Salian’s complaint and recorded his statement. He said the case covers allegations of gang rape, murder and an alleged cover-up, invoking IPC Sections 376D, 302, 201, 217, 218 and 120B.Satish Salian had earlier approached the court alleging that his daughter was murdered.Speaking to news agency ANI on Friday, he said he had provided investigators with the names of people whom he wanted examined.“I stated the facts exactly as they were; I told them everything that happened to my daughter. I listed all the names: Aditya, Sooraj Pancholi, Dino Morea, and the bodyguards. They noted everything down,” he said.
Sule raises political conspiracy claim
Asked whether she saw a possible political conspiracy behind the development, Sule did not give a direct answer.“Anything is possible,” she said, while referring to what she called “ICE” — Income Tax, CBI and Enforcement Directorate — and alleging that central agencies had previously been used against political figures who later joined the ruling party.
AIMIM leader Waris Pathan, meanwhile, said the case should not be politicised and should be left to the courts.“There is no need to give the Disha Salian case a political colour. There is no need to politicise it,” Pathan said, adding that the matter was sub judice and that “it is best to let the court decide”.
Salian’s death had earlier been recorded as an Accidental Death Report. The Bombay High Court had raised concerns over the fact that no FIR was registered despite allegations by her family that she had been murdered.The court also noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to her family for years.Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence six days after Salian’s death.The CBI later submitted a closure report in Rajput’s case, concluding that he died by suicide; that report remains pending before the competent court.The Bombay High Court has directed the CBI to investigate the Salian case and has left it to the agency to determine whether a criminal case is made out based on the evidence collected.

India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
India to provide Nepal with 654 megawatts of electricity daily to meet urgent needs after devastating glacial floods.
India has approved the expedited export of electricity to neighbouring Nepal to help it overcome shortages caused by extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure from devastating floods last month.
In a statement on Monday, India’s Ministry of Power said up to 654 megawatts of electricity would be transmitted for 18 hours per day until December 31.
“The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal,” it said.
It added that in December it would also review the amount of power to be exported from January.
The flooding, triggered on August 26 by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.
At least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal were hit, with at least 900 power station workers among the more than 5,500 people still missing in the country.
Almost 100 percent of the country’s energy needs were met by hydropower before the floods hit. Since then, Nepal has been forced to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.
Thousands of displaced people are sheltering in aid centres, with little hope of returning home soon. The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors.
Nepali officials say at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, adding that the disaster shows how climate change has hit poor countries that did little to cause it.
The Himalayas, where Nepal is nestled, are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening water security as the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study released this month.

In Gen Z Romance Shows Like Crew Girl, Sports Are the New Sex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:52:09 UTC
02:52:09 KST

In the Netflix teen drama Crew Girl, 16-year-old solo rowing champ Teagan Tao has her life uprooted when her hotel-magnate dad gets a tip that he’s about to be arrested for financial crimes and disappears. Suddenly, Teagan (Miku Martineau) and her flighty mom, Ella (Jessica Paré), are broke and moving across the country to the crumbling New England house where Ella grew up. The town is all clam shacks and marinas—and the prestigious Easton Prep, where Teagan matriculates thanks to an education trust that was somehow spared from the seizure of the Taos’ assets. The only problem, besides the rampant snobbery, is that Eaton has no girls’ crew team. Forced to coxswain for the boys, Teagan starts falling for two of her teammates: kind, working-class townie Cam Dillinger (Kyle Clark) and bratty airline scion Josh Regis (Sam Braun), who’s locked in a premature succession battle with his cousin Ryder (Connor Paton). Meanwhile, a gay rower, Baloo (Jude Wilson), is secretly hooking up with a guy on a rival team.
All of which is to say that Crew Girl, whose first season is now the no. 1 show on Netflix, plays like a greatest-hits compilation of teen romance tropes. First among the classics is a love triangle (see: Twilight, Riverdale, The Vampire Diaries, My So-Called Life). As is often the case, this one is enhanced by the quaintness of its small-town setting (Dawson’s Creek, One Tree Hill) and complicated by both wealth disparities (Gossip Girl, Pretty in Pink) and one character’s fish-out-of-water, new-kid-in-school status (The O.C., Beverly Hills, 90210). There’s also a youthful mom (you might remember Paré as Mad Men’s Megan) doing a painfully slow will-they-won’t-they dance with an old friend (Thomas Cadrot), à la Gilmore Girls’ Lorelai and Luke.
But what’s remarkable about Crew Girl—which is, despite an effervescent lead and a few fun storylines built around eccentric minor crew-boy characters, otherwise decidedly mid—is how comprehensively it showcases the conventions unique to the genre’s newest generation. TV has, in the last few years, capitalized on publishing’s pandemic-era romance boom, churning out love stories tailored to the young, female audience driving authors like Emily Henry and Ali Hazelwood up best-seller lists. Often, that means adapting popular YA or New Adult novels; Prime Video’s success with Jenny Han’s coming-of-age, beach-town love triangle The Summer I Turned Pretty paved the way for Netflix’s take on Ali Novak’s My Life with the Walter Boys as well as XO, Kitty, Han’s spinoff of her book-to-film franchise To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before. Queer romance, mainly of the gay male variety, from Netflix’s tender and chaste Heartstopper to the spicy Canadian phenomenon Heated Rivalry, which streams on HBO Max in the U.S., has also jumped from page to screen. (Crew Girl isn’t an adaptation, but a novelization released in tandem with the show suggests it’s meant to feel like one.) This year has seen a particular glut of new titles, from Netflix’s figure-skating drama Finding Her Edge to Prime’s Off Campus and Every Year After. The latter platform even scored a hit in August with an exceptional original teen romance, Sterling Point, proving the niche isn’t entirely dependent on preexisting IP.
These shows have all the love triangles and class struggles and outsider angst that have defined youthful romance tales since Jane Austen was writing them, capturing eternal adolescent fantasies (being desirable enough to have two people fighting over you) and fears (not measuring up to the rich kids) alike. Pretty appears to have sparked a mini-trend of siblings competing for the same crush, a trope that also pops up in Every Year After, Walter Boys, and Finding Her Edge. The fraught post-DEI-backlash politics of representation, especially for the most racially and ethnically diverse generation on record, are evident in the shows’ leads. Like Crew Girl’s Martineau, many are multiracial but play characters with vaguely defined backgrounds who live with either a single white parent or a white surrogate family. (New York magazine just spotlighted the "Wasian generation," a long list of up-and-coming white and Asian stars, citing Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams, Pretty’s Lola Tung, and XO, Kitty’s Anna Cathcart among other white and Asian stars.) Liberal and minority viewers get to see mixed-race families and romances, and a TV landscape that isn’t all white. The anti-”woke” crowd is spared identity politics, non-English dialogue, and often all other forms of cultural specificity. Savvy streamers avoid backlash from both sides.
What’s most striking about these series, though, are the novel ways in which they embrace physicality. With the steamy exceptions of Heated Rivalry and Off Campus (both geared toward a slightly older age range), the sexual content is pretty PG-13. Objectification is kept to a minimum, at least by characters we’re supposed to like. Yet bodies are conspicuously activated, in what feel like pointed responses to—and, for young viewers, escape hatches from—digital disembodiment.
Summer romances, and specifically those that bring together wealthy vacationers and the locals who work for them, aren’t new to fiction. It’s the prominence of nature in the recent crop of teen romances (and teen hits in other genres, like Netflix’s Outer Banks) that makes an impression. As it toggles between protagonist Percy’s (Sadie Soverall) life in her late 20s and a sequence of idyllic teenage lake-house summers glimpsed in flashbacks, Every Year After uses its setting to visualize two brothers’ rivalry for her affection. In one recurring image, Percy sits at the edge of her house’s dock, looking on as sensitive Sam (Matt Cornett) and arrogant Charlie (Michael Bradway) shove each other off a slippery wooden raft. Sterling Point brings a high-strung New York City girl (Ella Rubin) to an island in Canada’s Muskoka region, a paradise of lush, lakefront forests. Her rich-vs.-poor-boy love triangle plays out over lazy days spent boating, swimming, and sunbathing on rocky beaches. Cellphone service is conveniently spotty.
An abundance of sports romances make such physicality even more explicit. In Off Campus and Heated Rivalry, the boys who serve as eye candy for any viewer attracted to men are always slamming into each other on the ice and changing together in the locker room. In Finding Her Edge, a show about young Olympics hopefuls at a residential training center, an ice-dancing duo is bound to become a love affair (as long as the guy is into girls). Even the neurotic hero of Heartstopper (Joe Locke) finds first love on the rugby field. Crew Girl casts many thirsty gazes on the musclebound upper bodies of Teagan’s teammates. These stories aren’t just about the sweaty sensuality of athletes in motion, though. They’re about ambition and passion and the competitive spirit as romantic accelerants—about how the shared commitment to spend hours every day striving for excellence while one’s peers are screwing around online can bond people.
Why use athletics as a fig leaf for sex in the uncensored age of streaming, years after shows like Euphoria and Skins obliterated the notion that TV for teens should be wholesome? Maybe because modesty is in. Gen Z’s squeamishness about sex on screen has fueled successive waves of hand-wringing among their elders. The so-called sex recession plaguing this cohort in real life has been duly noted, with suggested explanations ranging from extreme onlineness in general to poor socialization during the COVID years of Zoom school and virtual prom in particular. The thing is, biologically speaking, teens are the same jumble of hormones in 2026 that they were during the Summer of Love. “Many of them are very horny,” Carter Sherman, the author of The Second Coming: Sex and the Next Generation's Fight Over Its Future, assured WIRED last year. “They would like to be having sex, and in fact they feel a lot of shame over the fact that they haven't had sex yet or that they’re not having sex enough.” As transitional objects to ease anxieties around physical intimacy, swimsuits and erg machines make a lot of sense.
The most salient takeaway from Crew Girl and its ilk might be buried in a less eye-catching finding of 2025’s Teens and Screens, the annual UCLA report on young people’s attitudes toward entertainment media that reliably stokes the “Gen Z hates sex scenes” panic. Relatability is the new watchword. Whereas millennials wallowed in wealth porn, took vicarious flight with superheroes, and sucked the life out of vampire content, today’s adolescents ranked “people with lives like mine” as the No. 1 element they’re looking for in TV shows and movies. Although they’re aspirational enough to feel escapist, with their summer houses and prep-school popularity contests, this season’s teen romances reflect that shift. For a generation raised in the sensory deprivation tank of the internet, whose fears of infinite digital liminality just gave us the horror movies Backrooms and It Ends, the fantasy is humbler than superpowers. It’s being grounded in physical space, a human body capable of sharing tactile experiences with other embodied people. Sex is one way to make those connections. Crew is another.

Hezbollah terrorists are attempting to establish a presence within the boundaries of the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, IDF Northern Command sources revealed on Tuesday.

The IDF said on Friday morning that what remains of the Ali al-Taher ridge, beneath which Iran spent two decades building Hezbollah’s last and most significant line of defense in southern Lebanon, is “nothing more than a sandbox.” Hezbollah and Iran suffered a major blow overnight. The operation to capture the ridge lasted months, as dozens of terrorists, estimated to number around 50, were entrenched inside the tunnels.

02:51:35 KST

A new international song featuring voices representing 17 countries was released ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, with organizers calling on people around the world to sing it together on the anniversary.
“The Whole World Sings Together,” created and produced by Friends of Zion Heritage Center founder Dr. Mike Evans, was designed as a message of solidarity with Israel and the Jewish people and of remembrance for the victims of October 7.
The music video brings together voices representing the United States, Israel, China, India, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Hungary, Iran, Yemen, Germany, Argentina, South Korea, Great Britain, Italy, Russia and Mexico.
Friends of Zion said the project sought to bring together people from different languages and cultures around a message that “the Jewish people are not alone.”
Organizers are inviting people around the world to watch and share the video and sing along on October 7, the third anniversary of Hamas’s 2023 attack on southern Israel.
Inspired by ‘We Are the World’
Evans said the idea was partly inspired by “We Are the World,” the 1985 charity single written by Lionel Richie and Michael Jackson and produced by Quincy Jones. The recording brought together dozens of prominent American musicians as USA for Africa and raised money for famine relief in Africa.
“In 1985, the world sang together for Africa. Now, the world must sing together for the Jewish people,” Evans said.
“October 7 cannot become another date that fades from memory,” he added. “We will remember the lives that were taken, the families that were shattered, the hostages who suffered, and the people who continue to carry wounds the world cannot see.”
The new song centers on themes of remembrance, solidarity and recovery, with its recurring line declaring: “The whole world sings together.”
According to Friends of Zion, the October 7 initiative aims to create a shared international moment in which supporters of Israel and Jewish communities can participate, regardless of where they live.
The official music video for “The Whole World Sings Together” has been released on YouTube ahead of the anniversary.

The end of the SDF: What the dissolution means for the Kurds and Sharaa's state - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:51:19 UTC
02:51:19 KST

The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) was formed back in 2015.
A year earlier, ISIS had proclaimed itself to be a worldwide caliphate, claiming religious and political authority over all Muslims.
It then proceeded to conquer and absorb great swathes of Syria and Iraq, and it was designated a terrorist organization by the UN, the US, and many other countries, including Muslim-majority states.
Opposing ISIS in northern Syria were the Kurdish-led YPG (People’s Protection Units). Together with the closely linked YPJ (Women’s Protection Units), they joined with Arab, Assyrian, and other local armed groups to create a broader coalition – and this became the SDF.
The US had already begun supporting the YPG, particularly during the battle for Kobani in 2014-15. After the SDF was formed, Washington began arming, advising, and providing air support to it as its principal ground partner against ISIS.
Backed by Washington, the SDF proved remarkably successful in combating ISIS. It conquered stronghold after stronghold, and finally, with the capture of Baghouz in 2019, ended the ISIS caliphate in Syria.
In the years that followed, the SDF developed its own security forces and civilian administration, and became the military and governing authority across much of north-eastern Syria.
Because the SDF was Kurdish-led and YPG-dominated, its powerful presence was opposed by Turkey.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan regards the YPG as closely linked to the PKK, a political and militant element within the Kurdish autonomy movement that Turkey and the US designate as a terrorist organization.
He was doubtless delighted with the announcement on August 25 by Mazloum Abdi, commander-in-chief of the SDF.
Speaking in a televised press conference in Damascus, he declared that, following an agreement with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the SDF’s mission had ended and that it was being dissolved “as an independent military force” and was being integrated as brigades into the Syrian army.
His announcement covered not only the SDF’s military functions, but also the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria and its affiliated military and civilian institutions.
Abdi said these structures had likewise been integrated into Syrian state institutions.
As president of the post-Assad government in Syria, Sharaa is attempting to bring the disparate political, military, and social forces that have been operating independently under the authority of a unified Syrian state.
A transitional administration
On March 10, 2025, Sharaa and Abdi hammered out a deal. The SDF’s civilian and military institutions, including border crossings, oil and gas facilities, and airports, would come under state control.
In return, the Kurds would be recognized as an integral part of Syria, be granted citizenship, political participation, and other rights.
The deal lacked detail and was too fragile to hold. In January 2026, government forces launched a lightning offensive against the SDF, rapidly capturing substantial SDF-held territory.
The SDF’s hopes of US protection, as in the past, were dashed, but a generous ceasefire deal saw SDF personnel entering Syria’s defense and interior ministries, while the government took over the border crossings, oil and gas fields, and civilian institutions.
The integration process continued over the next few months, eventually leading to Abdi’s dissolution announcement, which was not, of course, simply a voluntary decision by the SDF to disband.
It was the end-point of a negotiated political settlement whose terms were progressively reshaped by the dramatic change in the military balance.
The SDF leadership ultimately calculated that incorporation into the new Syrian state offered a better prospect for preserving Kurdish interests than trying to maintain an autonomous armed enclave against Damascus, Turkey, and a less dependable US patron.
A few days after the SDF’s dissolution, Sharaa appointed Abdi as a presidential adviser. The appointment was widely read as a sign that Sharaa, far from trying to destroy the Kurdish leadership, was intent on integrating it into the nation’s governance.
The SDF’s disappearance is a major piece of Sharaa’s state-consolidation project, but it is not the last, or necessarily the hardest, piece. Major steps are still required.
He has to complete the acquisition of a state monopoly on armed force.
The SDF was the biggest remaining autonomous military structure, making its dissolution a major breakthrough, but a fair number of former rebel and militia formations still need to be subordinated to the state.
He has to resolve the problem of the semi-autonomous Druze community in Sweida, which remains largely outside effective central government control. His challenge is negotiating a restoration of state authority without provoking another major sectarian conflict.
Then there is the problem of building a genuinely national political settlement. Ideally he would like Syria’s Kurds, Druze, Alawites, Christians, and other minorities to accept that their future security lies within a central Syrian state.
The Kurdish settlement illustrates the model Sharaa appears to favor – recognizing communal rights, but eliminating autonomous armed and quasi-state institutions.
Sharaa needs, within a reasonable period of time, to complete the transition from revolutionary government to a fully functioning state – national ministries, judiciary, police, taxation, public services, and a unified economic administration.
It is currently a fragile transitional administration dependent on concentrated presidential power.
Steps toward a functional Syria
Finally, there is his declared objective to establish a permanent constitution and elected government.
On March 13, 2025, Sharaa signed a Constitutional Declaration establishing the legal framework for a five-year transitional period leading to a permanent constitutional settlement and democratic elections.
The People’s Assembly, which first convened in Damascus in July 2026, is a transitional legislature rather than a fully elected parliament.
Two-thirds of its 210 members were selected by regional electoral colleges, while Sharaa appointed the remaining 70.
The roadmap is to move from this interim framework to a permanent constitution, followed by parliamentary elections.
The Constitutional Declaration provides for a five-year transition from March 2025, ending only when both the permanent constitution has been adopted and elections held under it.
March 2030 is currently the outer horizon. The immediate next step is to establish the body to be charged with drafting the new constitution.
The absorption of the SDF’s military and administrative functions into the state was a vital step toward the eventual achievement of a fully functioning, democratic, constitutional Syria.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com.

Beyond the Headlines: 'But I already heard the shofar at Selichot' - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:51:11 UTC
02:51:11 KST

After a talk I gave recently ahead of Rosh Hashanah, a teenage girl came up to me and asked, “What is the most important thing my family and I should actually do on Rosh Hashanah?”
“Hear the shofar,” I told her. “That’s the central mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah.”
“Oh, then we’re fine,” she said. “We already heard the shofar during the Selichot prayers at the Western Wall.”
That was when I realized I had gotten something wrong.
I had just given an entire talk filled with ideas for Rosh Hashanah—about the media, social networks, self-improvement—and somehow I had failed to explain the most basic thing of all.
I told her that hearing the shofar during Selichot is a meaningful custom, but hearing it on Rosh Hashanah is different: it is a Torah commandment. A special blessing is recited before the shofar is sounded, and while it is being blown, we remain silent and simply listen.
This year, since the first day of Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, when we do not blow the shofar, we will only hear it on Sunday, the second day of Rosh Hashanah. The shofar is usually blown between the morning and early afternoon, in synagogues throughout the Jewish world. Many communities publish the times in advance, so it is worth checking. Or you can simply come to synagogue for the service.
The girl thanked me and said she would tell her parents. Then she added that until now, she had thought apples and honey were the main thing about Rosh Hashanah.
We are living at a time when there is such a deep desire to connect, to learn, to do more. But at the same time, many people are missing even the most basic practical Jewish knowledge.
So, with all due respect to the short ideas and inspiring messages I post every morning, sometimes, before explaining that the word shofar is connected to shipur, “improvement,” we need to start with something much more basic: What are we supposed to do? Where do we do it? When? And how?
Don’t be embarrassed to ask. And don’t hesitate to explain it to someone else.
Thank you to the teenage girl from Or Akiva, who taught me an important lesson last night.
No matter how far you stray
If I had not heard this story with the names of actual people, I would never have believed it. But Franny Weissman shared with me the following tale which, in fact, began more than 100 years ago:
"I came on aliyah from the United States and got married to Evyatar, a native Israeli whose grandmother's parents, along with two of her siblings, were murdered in Auschwitz. Ten of her siblings survived and nine of them decided to make aliyah together, but one sister settled in the United States, never revealing to anyone that she was Jewish. She announced that after the Holocaust she would not bring children into the world, and eventually she married a non-Jew. She did not reveal her identity even to him.
“When her family tried to connect with her, she ignored them. Over and over again I heard the story of Aunt Adelle. There are more than 350 family members now in Israel, four generations, but she has always been the one piece missing from the puzzle.
'Hitler is gone. The war is over.'
“Two years ago, I was asked to travel to the United States to recruit girls for an educational program in Israel. My husband encouraged me to agree to the mission and said, ‘Even if you bring just one soul to Israel, it will be a great success.' They scheduled a lecture tour for me across the United States, and one of the lectures was in Florida. As it turned out, I was just five minutes from the home of Aunt Adelle. I couldn’t believe it. I knocked on the door, and asked for Adelle Schwartz. The housekeeper said that there was no one there by that name, but I realized that she had changed her name. I entered and saw someone who looked a lot like her siblings. I connected them through a video chat and they began to converse in Hungarian. Soon they were crying and sobbing. Even the housekeeper cried.
“Before we parted, I took her hand and said, ‘Adelle, Hitler is gone. The war is over. You have a large family now. You are not alone. No matter how far away you may be, you can always come back. Don’t let Hitler win. At the very least, come to Israel to be buried.’
“We parted with great emotion and stayed in touch. Recently, we received word from an American attorney that Adelle had passed away at the age of 102. We then learned that she had changed her mind: instead of being cremated, she wanted a Jewish funeral.
“We did everything we could to bring her to Israel — the country she had kept at a distance for most of her life. Her funeral was held at Moshav Nir Etzion, and she was buried in the family plot. We were all there, and it was one of the most moving experiences of my life.
“We saw with our own eyes the meaning of the verse: ‘Even if your exiles are at the end of the heavens, the Lord, your God, will gather you from there, and He will take you from there’ (Deuteronomy 30:4).
“As my husband had told me, ‘If you bring even one soul to Israel, it will have been a great success.’”
Translated by Yehoshua Siskin and Janine Muller Sherr
