EXPLAINER - Historic Cardiff declaration: How Britain enters new era of self-determination talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:50:40 UTC
02:50:40 KST

- In joint declaration, leaders of Scottish National Party, Sinn Fein, and Plaid Cymru call on UK government to prepare for, plan, and facilitate constitutional change
- In response, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he 'believes strongly in the union'
Monday's meeting in Wales’ capital Cardiff between the first ministers of three devolved UK nations marks the latest step in a long-running debate over the future of the union, with a joint declaration signed by nationalist party leaders stressing the right to determine their own future and also calling on the UK government to “prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change.”
Landmark self-determination declaration
The joint declaration signed in Cardiff by Rhun ap Iorwerth, first minister of Wales and leader of Plaid Cymru; John Swinney, first minister of Scotland and leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP); and Michelle O'Neill, first minister of Northern Ireland and vice-president of Sinn Fein, said the political landscape "is changing."
The Celtic Alliance leaders said they believe the "future of our nations belongs in the European Union," adding that, for the first time ever, there are first ministers in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland "who are all committed to independence from the UK."
The move came after US President Donald Trump said Sunday that integrating Ireland and Northern Ireland represents "one of the naturals of all time," suggesting historical partitions should be resolved.
On Saturday, visiting Ireland, he also said he would "love" to see a united Ireland.
The new declaration, however, is only the latest step in a long-running debate over the future of the union since 1997.
Good Friday Agreement and beginning of devolution era
The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a landmark peace deal signed in 1998 to end decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as the Troubles.
It states that Northern Ireland's constitutional status can only change through a majority vote, known as the "principle of consent," an important point which has loudly been raised by Irish nationalist party Sinn Fein.
Scotland and Wales’ devolution processes began with public referendums in 1997 which led to the passing of the Scotland Act 1998 and the Government of Wales Act 1998, and the official opening of both the Scottish Parliament and the National Assembly for Wales (Senedd) in 1999.
Northern Ireland’s devolved institutions also began operating under the Good Friday Agreement framework the same year.
SNP victory and Scottish independence referendum
In 2007, the Scottish National Party (SNP) led by Alex Salmond managed to enter government with 45% of the vote, forming a minority government.
But in the 2011 elections, the SNP was able to win a landslide of 69 seats to form a majority government in Holyrood, the first majority government since the opening of the Scottish Parliament.
In 2013, the pro-independence SNP reached a deal with the UK on the Scottish Independence Referendum Act 2013 setting out an independence proposal requiring a simple majority to pass.
The referendum asking voters "Should Scotland be an independent country?" was held in Scotland on Sept. 18, 2014.
The “no” side won with just over 2 million (55.3%) votes against independence and some 1.62 million (44.7%) votes in favor with 84.6% turnout, the highest recorded for an election or referendum in the UK since the January 1910 general election.
Brexit, UK Supreme Court ruling
The idea of holding another independence referendum flared up in Scotland once again with the UK’s 2016 Brexit referendum. Although an overall majority in the UK voted in favor of leaving the EU, most people in Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain in the bloc.
In 2019, when Boris Johnson became British prime minister, he stressed that he would reject any request to hold a second vote on Scotland's future in the UK.
In 2021, the SNP, led by Nicola Sturgeon, won another election in Scotland, paving the way for a possible second independence referendum returning to the center of Scottish politics.
However in 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the Scottish Parliament lacks the legislative competence to hold a second independence referendum without consent from the UK government
Changes in Wales, Northern Ireland leadership
After capturing the largest number of seats in the Northern Ireland Assembly for the first time in 2022, the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein Party won the 2024 elections and its leader Michelle O'Neill was appointed Northern Ireland's first-ever nationalist first minister.
In Wales this May, Plaid Cymru made history in the Welsh Senedd elections, ending 100 years of Labour control and making Rhun ap Iorwerth the first minister of Wales.
In the 2021 Senedd election, Plaid Cymru had committed to holding a referendum on Welsh independence by 2026 if the party won a majority in the Senedd.
Thus this May saw, for the first time in history, the three devolved governments of the UK—Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland—all led by pro-independence first ministers who have pledged to leave the UK.
In response to Monday’s declaration, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he “believes strongly in the union.”

5,000-year-old drainage network, workshop-houses unearthed in W. Türkiye
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
01:46:40 CST
02:46:40 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists in Türkiye's western Izmir province have unearthed a 5,000-year-old stone drainage network and ancient "workshop-houses," shedding new light on prehistoric urban planning, authorities said Monday.
The findings were uncovered at Liman Tepe in Urla, a 5,300-year-old Bronze Age port city known for hosting both land settlements and Türkiye's first underwater harbor excavations, according to Vasif Sahoglu, head of the excavation team and director of Ankara University's Research Center for Maritime Archaeology.
The 5,000-year-old settlement dates back to the Early Bronze Age, a pivotal era when early Anatolian cultures established fortified coastal cities and extensive trade networks across the Aegean Sea.
Detailing the discoveries, Sahoglu noted that the stone channels were built between terraced levels to divert rainwater away from the settlement. He described the water management network as a rare engineering feature, with very few examples found in Western Anatolia and the broader Aegean region from that era.
The excavations also revealed "long houses" -- measuring over 25 meters in length and about 5 meters in width -- featuring large storage jars embedded into the floors at their entrances, likely used to hold water or grain.
Sahoglu described these buildings as "workshop-houses," as archaeological findings, including weaving weights and metallurgical remains, indicate they were used for both daily living and manufacturing.
The comprehensive research at Liman Tepe, which began in 1992, involves both terrestrial and maritime archaeology. Underwater excavations at the site began in 2000, with this year's work focusing on determining when the ancient harbor's stone breakwater was built and how long it was used.
During these underwater operations, marine teams also recovered organic materials such as olive pits and grape seeds, which Sahoglu noted provide crucial insights into the ancient settlement's maritime trade. ■

Alligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog says
Unknown

Before the facility was shuttered, detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”.
The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were published on its website – and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies.
The report also provides the first official confirmation that guards repeatedly used the highly restrictive cages on detainees in direct contravention of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rules.
In December, the Guardian was the first to report an Amnesty International dossier detailing multiple alleged human rights abuses at the controversial camp in the remote Florida Everglades, including how people were regularly shackled outside in metal cages for hours as well as exposed to brutal heat, sunshine and swarms of mosquitoes.
At the time, a spokesperson for Ron DeSantis, the Republican Florida governor whose administration ran Alligator Alcatraz on behalf of the federal government, dismissed the claims now confirmed by the DHS report as “fabrications” – and the Amnesty report as “a politically motivated attack”.
On Monday, his office declined to answer why it falsely denied using the cages and instead attempted to portray the detainees – with no evidence – as “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful while awaiting deportation”.
In a statement, Alex Lanfranconi, DeSantis’s communications manager, contended that “the leftwing media wants to focus on a confinement area” which “adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement”.
His statement added: “We’d make it even smaller if we could.”
Amy Fischer, Amnesty International USA’s director for refugee and migrant rights, said in a statement: “The findings confirm what we documented months ago: the horrific treatment of people detained at Alligator Alcatraz was real, not a hoax, as Trump administration officials were on the record saying.
“This report should serve as a reminder that the public must never simply take the government’s word when officials deny that human rights violations are occurring.”
The notorious immigration jail closed in June after a year of operation during which DeSantis boasted of detaining and deporting more than 21,000 immigrants. Officials cited the risk of holding detainees in tents during hurricane season for the closure.
Critics, however, said the $1.2m of taxpayers’ money that DeSantis was spending on the camp daily was fast becoming a political millstone – while separate lawsuits swirled over the jail’s impact on the environmentally fragile Florida wetlands, and the harsh mental and physical treatment of detainees that several Democratic lawmakers decried as akin to “torture”.
The inspector general’s office report exposed numerous failings found during an unannounced January 2026 visit by DHS inspectors to Alligator Alcatraz, which they refer to as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF). Many of the shortcomings, they said, posed “significant risks to detainee health and safety”.
“FSSF did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health,” the report said.
Additionally, it studied records that revealed 79 instances between July 2025 and January 2026 in which guards placed detainees in the metal cages for up to two hours at a time.
Each cage, the report noted, offered only about 18 sq ft of floor space, less than half the minimum 37 sq ft required for single-person spaces by ICE’s own published national detention standards. The inspector general’s discovery of cases in January means detainees were still being confined in the cramped cages more than a month after Amnesty International exposed the practice and DeSantis’s office denied it was taking place.
The report acknowledged concerns raised by the Democratic US senators Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Dick Durbin of Illinois in March over the use of the cages known to detainees as “The Box”. But the report said facility staff insisted they were used as “calming areas” for detainees “to deescalate and have time alone”.
“Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time” in them, the report said.
However, inspectors found at least one time in which a cage was documented to have been used as a disciplinary tool: for a detainee who “failed to comply with a lawful command”. Inspectors noted that there were locking mechanisms on the cages.
“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG,” the report said. “Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and wellbeing.”
Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and chief executive of the immigration advocacy group Global Refuge, said in a statement: “There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike.
“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food and basic hygiene. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty.”
Other failures noted by the DHS inspectors during their tour of detention spaces, and kitchen and bathroom areas, included overcrowding, a lack of sufficient recreation time for detainees, and inoperable telephones preventing detainees from contacting their attorneys or families, and poor food hygiene standards leading to the risk of contamination and illness.
Multiple detainees told the inspectors in January they had limited or no access to clean drinking water. The Guardian reported in June that the practice appeared to be continuing, with detainees complaining that guards were withholding clean water and food as punishment – or until they signed documents in English that they did not understand.
The Florida department of emergency management, which oversaw the operation of the facility using private guards, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid US trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:42:33 UTC
02:42:33 KST

Mark Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid US trade war
Hundreds of investors overseeing nearly $120 trillion in assets will gather in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit.
For decades, one of Canada’s biggest selling points to foreign investors was its access to the world’s largest economy next door.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is now trying to sell something bigger — to bet on Canada itself.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Canadian economy recovers sharply in Q2 but shadow of US tariffs in future
- list 2 of 4With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
- list 3 of 4The losers of the US-Canada trade war
- list 4 of 4Bombardier looks to hire 500 new workers in US, despite Trump threat
On Monday and Tuesday, hundreds of global investors will gather in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit. The invitation-only meeting will bring some of the world’s largest pension and sovereign wealth funds and asset managers together with corporate executives, Canadian premiers and federal officials.
Carney, a former central banker with deep ties to the global investment world, wants them to put money into everything from mines and pipelines to ports, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing. It is part of a much bigger push to catalyse $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years, with about $280bn in public investment and government incentives to help draw in private and institutional capital.
The summit comes just days after another escalation in Canada’s trade war with the United States which has been ongoing since President Donald Trump started his second term and unleashed a wave of tariffs across the world, including on Canada, one of its historically closest allies.
Relations have ruptured as Trump has repeatedly referred to Canada as the 51st state of the US and Carney as its “governor”. The threats are particularly damaging to Canada which, pre-tariff, sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to its southern neighbour.
After talks collapsed last month, Washington imposed levies of 50 percent on about US$20bn worth of Canadian goods, prompting Ottawa to impose retaliatory tariffs of 15 to 50 percent on a similar value of US imports.
While the two sides have been negotiating, Carney has also been travelling the world to shore up relations and re-start or beef up trade ties, efforts that are bearing some fruit in Toronto with the summit.
“Carney is trying to turn a period of external pressure and uncertainty caused by the Trump trade war into an affirmative agenda,” said Vina Nadjibulla, cofounder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a non-partisan policy think tank in Canada. “Build more at home, diversify Canada’s economic relationships abroad and attract the capital needed to do both.”
While the uncertainty of the trade war makes Canada a harder sell in some ways, it becomes a more compelling one at the same time.
“It cuts both ways,” Nadjibulla said. Investors may be wary of projects that depend heavily on the US market. But the turmoil also gives Carney a chance to sell Canada as “a relatively stable, rules-based jurisdiction” in an increasingly volatile world.
Carney has pulled in a large audience for that pitch. Getting roughly 300 major global investors focused on Canada for two days is unprecedented and a political win in itself, Nadjibulla said.
But getting them into the room is the easy part.
“The summit can open doors and create relationships,” she said. “Success will ultimately depend on how many of those conversations turn into serious investment, financing and projects that actually get built.”
What is Carney selling?
He is making the case that Canada has a lot for investors to bet on beyond its access to the US, from energy to critical minerals to skilled workers to connections to markets around the world. Through trade agreements with 51 countries, Canadian businesses have preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers around the world, the government said in a news statement ahead of the summit.
“We’re trusted, because we’re reliable and because we have what the world wants,” Carney said on Sunday. “That’s why the world is coming to our door.”
A leaked prospectus prepared for the summit lays out 167 potential investments across energy, mining, ports, transportation, technology and advanced manufacturing.
They range from satellite technology to some enormous infrastructure projects, including a proposed oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia’s coast.
But the list is heavily weighted towards resources and energy. Minerals and metals alone account for nearly 38 percent of the projects, as per Nadjibulla’s calculations. Add energy and power infrastructure and the share rises to almost 70 percent.
“The summit is fundamentally about financing the physical productive capacity of the Canadian economy,” she said, pointing to mines, processing, energy generation, export infrastructure, ports and manufacturing.
Not all of the projects, however, are ready for investment. Some of those on offer are fully permitted, while others are still at the concept or feasibility stage.
“Some are quite large and expensive and are unlikely to be ready for prime time,” said Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a policy nonprofit.
Canada also has to prove it can build
For investors, getting major projects to that point has long been a sticking point.
Ziemba pointed to lengthy regulatory reviews, particularly for projects that need both federal and provincial approval.
Nadjibulla similarly cited “long and uncertain approval processes” and questions about whether projects can move “from announcement to execution”.
“Investors will want to see a credible pipeline, faster and more predictable permitting, policy stability, clearer revenue models and better coordination across provincial and federal jurisdictions,” Nadjibulla said.
Carney is trying to convince them that things are changing. His government has created a Major Projects Office to speed up approvals for projects it considers to be in the national interest, alongside a “one project, one review” approach aimed at reducing federal-provincial overlap.
The summit is a chance to show investors how that will work, Ziemba said. “But this is still early days.”
What does all of this mean for Canadians?
Even if Carney gets more of these projects financed and built, a bigger debate remains over who ultimately stands to benefit. In an interview with Democracy Now, Avi Lewis, leader of Canada’s New Democratic Party, criticised the prime minister for “selling our airports and our ports and privatising more of our economy to the benefit of foreign investors”.
That debate will be playing out just outside the summit. Labour, Indigenous, housing and climate groups are planning a Monday rally under the banner “The Many vs. the Money,” arguing that Canada’s economic future should not be shaped primarily by corporate executives and global investors.
The trade war has been shifting Canada’s investment focus from manufacturing and other industries built around the North American market to ports, pipelines and logistics that can help Canadian resources reach new markets.
Ziemba also pointed to another potential trade-off – those sectors require a lot of capital without necessarily creating the same number of jobs. That “may limit the benefits to Canadians looking to replace the US-integrated sectors,” she said.
Even if there are any major announcements this week, they will only tell part of the story.
Ziemba said she will be watching how much investors actually commit, the timelines and “clarity on who pays”.
“The summit helps with the first problem, showing investors what is available,” Nadjibulla said. “But execution will determine long-term success and whether the capital actually arrives.”

Leaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'
Twelve European countries on Monday called for the European Union to step up its presence in the Arctic, as melting ice opens new maritime routes while growing tensions with Russia and the United States increasingly put the region in the geopolitical spotlight.
Twelve European countries meeting in Finland on Monday urged the European Union (EU) to beef up its presence in the Arctic – a contentious geopolitical battleground caught between Russia and US President Donald Trump.
"We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic," the countries' leaders wrote in a joint statement following a European Arctic Summit in the town of Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, attended by Denmark, France, Germany, Greece and Sweden, among others.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc was in need of icebreakers, but it was not immediately clear if she was proposing joint acquisition or urging member states to bolster their own capacities.
Given "the situation that we are in, and considering climate change and the opening of maritime routes, we need icebreakers or ships that are able to navigate in these very difficult" conditions, Kallas told reporters.

In January, EU chief Ursula von der Leyen suggested the EU could direct part of its ongoing surge in defence spending on a "European icebreaker capability," which is traditionally considered a civilian capability, among other equipment vital to Arctic security.
Interest in the Arctic has grown substantially since the adoption in 2021 of the EU's latest policy strategy for the region.
Read moreEU to boost Greenland investment amid Trump annexation claims
Trump's repeated threats to bring Greenland – a vast, autonomous Danish territory – under US control have since then triggered a diplomatic crisis among Washington's allies.
While his tone has cooled since the beginning of the year, EU countries are determined to increase their presence in the region – well aware of a hostile neighbour on the other side of Finland's long eastern border.
Mounting tensions
Pointing to "the significant and long-term threat Russia poses", countries said Moscow's ambitions to increase its influence in the Arctic and its "hostility towards Europe, including the increase in hybrid activities, highlight the need to strengthen the EU's Arctic policy".
Officials present included Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, EU foreign policy chief Kallas and EU Council President Antonio Costa, as well as leaders from countries such as Romania and Greece.
"What happens here is not a regional story. It is a European one," Costa said.
No formal decisions were taken at the summit.
But the European Commission is expected to present a new Arctic strategy in a matter of weeks, which will steer the union's approach to the Arctic over the coming years.
Read moreTensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil compan
Countries and leaders can still have a say on the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," Tuomas Tikkanen, senior adviser on European Affairs to Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who initiated the summit, told AFP.
"The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," he said.
Melting ice
Interest in the region has increased significantly since the EU's last Arctic policy was adopted in 2021, reflected in the number of high-level guests from non-Arctic countries in attendance.
"The security environment has changed a great deal, and there has been a lot of interest in the region recently," Tikkanen said.
Leaders discussed topics ranging from economic interests to security.
The Arctic region is warming nearly four times faster than the global average as a result of climate change, according to experts, leading to severe consequences for both the environment and local livelihoods.

As sea ice melts, countries such as Russia, China and the United States have been ramping up activity in the region, racing to claim natural resources and new maritime routes.
China and South Korea sent container ships to attempt to transit the Northern Sea Route in Russian waters in August, testing its viability as the passage remains free of ice longer each year.
Trump insisted earlier this year that Washington needed to control Greenland for national security reasons, though he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
Soon after, in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.
During a visit to the vast island on September 7, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a 200-million-euro ($232-million) package for Greenland, vowing to "be more present and to be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic".

A French police officer is under investigation after a video emerged showing him violently throwing a man to the ground in Carcassonne in southern France, days after a separate scandal involving recordings of officers in the city making racist, misogynistic and conspiracy-related remarks.
A judicial investigation was opened on Sunday for "intentional violence by a person vested with public authority."
The footage, shared on social media by MP Thomas Portes, shows several police officers standing around before one walks up behind a young man and hurls him to the ground.
Once down, the man can be seen holding his head in his arms as other people appear and protest, while someone says: "It's being filmed."
"In Carcassonne, the police are out of control!" Portes wrote.
The incident occurred on 21 June during the Fête de la musique music festival. The police officers were responding to reports of "noise disturbance".
In a statement issued on Monday, the public prosecutor's office said the man, identified as a 29-year-old homeless person, was not the subject of the intervention. He was not arrested and did not lodge a complaint.
On 3 July, he was found "in cardiac arrest" at his camp. An investigation was then opened to determine the cause of his death. But according to the findings of the autopsy carried out on 9 July, "any suspicious traumatic injury pointing to the involvement of a third party" has been ruled out.
The Inspectorate General of the National Police (IGPN) has also been called in.
The prosecutor's office said it had referred the case to the Marseille branch of the IGPN on Sunday, "as soon as it became aware of this video".
César R., one of the four officers suspended following the release of a previous video by the newspaper Midi Libre on 8 September, also appears in the new footage.
He is a witness at the scene but does not intervene.
In the first video, he was reportedly responsible for nearly 90% of the hateful remarks recorded during the patrol. He was a volunteer with the National Rally's security detail.
Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella's party has condemned the remarks made by the police officers, which included racist insults, a call for a coup and the repetition of a transphobic conspiracy theory targeting Brigitte Macron.
In a statement sent to several media outlets, including Euronews, the National Rally announced that the officer had been expelled from the party and removed from its security team.

As concerns grow around the direction that unfettered Artificial Intelligence development may be taking, a report by the AI safety and research company Anthropic underlines the need for oversight of the use and development of AI technology if the doomsday scenario is to be avoided.
Who used the Claude coding agent to develop killer drones?
In its quarterly report “Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI,” published earlier this month, the company identified a group of Russia-linked developers, with the designation GTG-27005, that was using its used Claude coding agent to create software for autonomous kamikaze drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Anthropic believes that, although the system was being developed for military use, the group’s members were likely independent, university-based specialists. It had not identified any specific links with the Russian Armed Forces as the group used a number of virtual servers to avoid geographic restrictions. It said the group showed qualities consistent with the Russian hacking group “Midnight Blizzard,” which had used generative AI tools to prepare cyberattacks. The move to the development of autonomous combat systems was a new departure for the group.
What were the developers hoping to achieve?
The Anthropic report said the operation, was known as “DroneDoc” and “Seraphim.” The group registered its accounts in late 2025 but began in earnest in mid-May 2026. It used the Claude Coding agent to write and review software code and to store the resulting components directly in their project files.
China, India, Turkey Remain Top Buyers of Russian Fossil Fuels
The code was integrated with drone simulation software and computing resource training models rented from commercial suppliers. The resulting system was designed to select targets, including people, and issue attack commands without further operator intervention.
The ultimate aim seems to be to operate attack drones as a swarm and to make decisions autonomously. The use of Claude would allow the development of shared memory for the swarm in a fault-tolerant coordination system – a distributed network architecture that maintains synchronization, and task allocation even when individual drones or components fail and communications were lost or individual components failed.
The team was also developing an onboard compact language model that would determine the drone’s next action after swarm members engage a target: attack another target, continue surveillance, or return to base.
Trained using real combat footage from Ukraine
The developers used combat footage from the fighting in Ukraine gained through social media to train a computer vision system, in which Ukrainian personnel and equipment was designated as hostile, while Russian military systems were added to a list of targets that could not be attacked.
Demonstration simulations were carried out in Ukraine’s Donetsk region Ukrainian frontline cities and transportation corridors.
Anthropic battles the illicit use of AI in the war in Ukraine
In total, the company identified and subsequently blocked nine accounts linked to the project. Along with a regional university Anthropic also found connections with the Russian Academy of Sciences.
The report also describes the growing use of AI to organize cyberattacks against Ukrainian government officials and military targets. One Russia-linked group used AI in phishing campaigns, malware distribution, WhatsApp account takeovers, and attacks conducted through compromised hotel Wi-Fi networks.
The slogan of the US National Rifle Association (NRA): “Guns don’t kill people, people kill people,” could just as easily apply to AI, based on this latest incident. It underlines that calls for vigilance over the development of AI are not overstated but it is the user rather than the technology that needs to be controlled.

How The Early Spring Ends—And Sets the Stage for More Chinese Dramas on Netflix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:36:01 UTC
02:36:01 KST

A happy ending for Shang Zhitao (Sun Qian) and Luan Nian (Jing Boran) on Netflix’s Chinese workplace romance The Early Spring was incredibly hard-won. At the start of the 24-episode series based on a web novel by Gu Niang Bie Ku, recent college graduate Zhitao is hired by Beijing advertising agency Lime—against bigwig Nian’s wishes. The initial power imbalance between ordinary office worker Zhitao and her boss Nian is significant, and there is a company policy against romantic entanglements between co-workers. Still, they quickly fall into bed together. Over the next six years, the two are on-again, off-again as a prideful, emotionally repressed Nian struggles to say nice things to Zhitao and Zhitao struggles to balance her love for Nian with her commitment to her career.
Why does Shang Zhitao leave Beijing?
For Zhitao, Beijing isn’t just a place—it is a symbol of her career ambitions, and the kind of life she aspires to. While The Early Spring’s central focus is romance, the C-drama also delves into other aspects of Zhitao’s character and journey. A major throughline of the show is Zhitao’s efforts to make Beijing a home, and to succeed not just at a company or in a bustling metropolis, but in one of the most prestigious companies in one of China’s most global cities. So, when Zhitao chooses to leave Beijing in Episode 21, “A Grand Retreat,” she isn’t just retreating from Nian, she is retreating from the lifestyle that Beijing demands for success.
It’s not just one event that informs Zhitao’s decision to leave Beijing. When she tells Nian that she wants to get married and he tells her he doesn’t really think about it, Zhitao begins to reconsider their relationship. Then, one of Zhitao’s best friends dies by suicide. Finally, she gets passed over for a promotion in favor of a less experienced, nepo-baby co-worker. When she seeks comfort from Nian, he offers none. It’s the final straw for Zhitao, who begins to feel like all the time and energy she has committed to their relationship might not have been worth it.
The Early Spring’s happy ending
Heading into the final installments of the drama, Zhitao has finally called it quits on her toxic dynamic with Nian, moving home to Harbin and starting her own advertising agency in the snowy, northeastern city where she grew up. A few years pass before a bereft Nian attempts to reconcile. Zhitao’s company has partnered with Lime for a local project, and Nian uses it as an excuse to see Zhitao again. Zhitao is understandably reluctant to let Nian back into her life, but Nian uses the excuse of their dog, a Samoyed named Luke, to spend time with his ex-girlfriend.
Over the following months, Nian elbows his way into Zhitao’s life and attempts to show her that he has changed. He apologizes for his past behavior, and mostly listens to her when she asks for space. Eventually, Zhitao’s love for Nian wins out and she lets him back into her heart and her life. Nian makes it clear to Zhitao’s parents that he intends to marry their daughter, and then proposes to Zhitao by decorating an art gallery with photos from their time together. He calls it Flora’s Museum of Time and Eternity, using the English name Zhitao used when she worked at Lime. Lian gifts Zhitao a necklace with the “L” key from the typewriter Zhitao knocked over in his office during their first in-person meeting. He invites Zhitao’s closest friends and family, and asks the woman he has loved for almost a decade to marry him. She says yes, finally believing that the two can have a relationship as equals. In the final scenes of the show, we see Zhitao and Nian splitting their time between Harbin and Beijing, happy together.
Will there be a second season of The Early Spring?
The Early Spring has done incredibly well on Youku and Netflix, where the C-drama has steadily been in the Global Top Ten list. East Asian dramas don’t tend to have second seasons, but The Early Spring could easily be extended with the adaptation of the second book in the web novel series. Titled Miss Talkative, the sequel novel follows the unlikely romance between Zhitao’s work bestie Lumi and her stoic, more traditional co-worker Will. A developing relationship between the two is hinted at in The Early Spring TV series, but the plot line is left unresolved.
Netflix’s increasing commitment to Chinese dramas
Though Netflix has become known as a home for Korean dramas, with the U.S. streamer investing billions of dollars into the East Asian country’s TV and film industries, the same has not been true for Chinese dramas.
China is not interested in giving any U.S. company too much power in its economy, which has kept the streamer from setting up shop in the country. In 2016, Netflix released a letter to shareholders alongside a quarterly earnings report stating: “The regulatory environment for foreign digital content services in China has become challenging. We now plan to license content to existing online service providers in China rather than operate our own service in China in the near term.” That same year, the Chinese government implemented a de facto ban on South Korean entertainment in China following the announcement that the U.S. would be installing an anti-missile system in South Korea. Netflix is still not legally available in China.
In the decade since, Netflix’s catalogue and business model have become increasingly international. As Netflix focuses on expansion into international markets, C-dramas have become an increasingly valuable asset. While C-dramas have a growing audience in the U.S., they are even more popular in countries like Pakistan, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Vietnam. “Audiences in Asia have long loved this category, but we're making them accessible to an even bigger global viewership,” Maya Huang, Head of Chinese-Language Content at Netflix, tells TIME.
Netflix has been growing their Mainland China offerings since 2024. Recent hits have included historical fantasy romance Pursuit of Jade and costume drama Ashes to Crown, adding to the organic popularity of earlier series like The Untamed, a historical fantasy romance based on a BL web novel that blew up in popularity during the pandemic. As Netflix looks towards the future, C-dramas are part of their plan, with “a team dedicated to finding the most authentic and best-in-class Chinese language stories” including ones—like The Early Spring—that are simulcast with a Chinese streamer. “With Netflix's reach, dubs and subtitles, and our ability to release titles simultaneously worldwide, we're seeing audiences discover these stories in the U.S., South America, Europe and the Middle East,” says Huang. “We want to give these fans more of what they love—so there's plenty more to come from our Chinese language slate.”

Tunisia extends 'Sumud 4' flotilla activists' detention to 10 months, little international outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:31:51 UTC
02:31:51 KST

While Israel’s detention of Global Sumud Flotilla activists drew widespread international attention earlier this year, the months-long imprisonment of four members of the movement by Tunisian authorities has received comparatively little notice.
On Friday, the investigating judge of the Judicial, Economic and Financial Division of the Tunisian court system extended the detention of four activists who participated in the 2025 Flotilla to Gaza by a further four months.
Wael Naouar, Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri, and Nabil Chennoufi, the “Sumud 4,” have been imprisoned since March 2026 and are accused of money laundering and misappropriating funds received through donations.
One of them, Naouar, has been on hunger strike since August 16. The other three went on hunger strike on September 17.
The lawyers representing the four activists said that the accusations against them are bogus and that such charges are frequently imposed to silence political opponents in Tunisia. Defenders of the activists say this reflects a dichotomy in the country, which outwardly supports the Palestinian cause but simultaneously represses activists who support it.
Global Sumud Flotilla says Naouar 'in critical condition'
Global Sumud Flotilla said that Tunisian authorities were “caving to US and Zionist pressure.”
“The imprisonment of the Sumud 4 must be understood within a broader transnational offensive against Palestine solidarity, driven in part by sustained political pressure from the United States and an increasingly aggressive Zionist campaign to criminalize, intimidate and silence those mobilizing against Israel’s genocide and impunity,” it said in a statement.
It added that Naouar is in “critical condition” and at “acute risk of cardiac arrest.”
“By choosing to lock away four organizers while quietly extending an empty investigation, the Tunisian state is tarnishing its historical legacy as a champion of Palestinian solidarity,” Global Sumud Flotilla said.
The movement drew attention to a new Human Rights Watch report, released last week, that said Tunisian authorities are “escalating repression of local and international civil society organizations and their members, as authorities target them with arbitrary arrests and detention, financial and criminal investigations, [and] arbitrary suspensions.”
The HRW report said at least 47 people connected to NGOs in Tunisia had been prosecuted and around 14 convicted and sentenced to prison since 2025.
Where is the international outrage?
An interesting angle of this story is its under-reported nature.
While the brief detention of flotilla members by Israeli authorities sparked international outrage, condemnation, and diplomatic involvement, the six-month detention (now extended to 10 months) of four activists by Tunisian authorities has been barely mentioned by international media.
In the past week, the only English-language media outlets to report on the detention are Al Jazeera English, The New Arab, and the Saudi Gazette.
Within Arabic media, the detention extension has been covered by Anadolu, Al Jazeera, Arab 48, Al Mayadeen, and a few other smaller or local Arab outlets.
In French media (the other main language in Tunisia), the issue has been covered by RFI, Mediapart, TV5MONDE, and Ici Grenoble.
This is extremely sparse in comparison to the reporting of Israeli detentions of flotilla activists.
Israel detained flotilla activists on three main occasions.
During May-July 2025, Israel intercepted the Madleen in June and the Handala in July, detaining and deporting their passengers. The July detention included 18 activists.
In October 2025, during the first Global Sumud Flotilla, Israel intercepted the large flotilla, detaining some 430-440 activists. This was covered by almost every major international outlet. Major NGOs such as Amnesty International published reports about “Israel’s abduction and torture.”
And in April this year, Israel intercepted vessels in international waters and detained the activists aboard the second Global Sumud Flotilla – including Spanish Palestinian Saif Abu Keshek and Brazilian Thiago Ávila – all of whom were subsequently deported. NGOs such as Reporters Without Borders condemned Israel for “kidnapping” three journalists. The matter was reported by ABC, the BBC, The Washington Post and The Guardian, and foreign ministers globally condemned the alleged mistreatment of the activists.
Yet when the same activists are detained in other countries – especially in an Arab country – there is minimal outrage.
The comparison does not suggest that the circumstances of the Israeli and Tunisian detentions are identical.
It does, however, raise a question about the disparity in international attention: Why did the detention of activists associated with the same movement generate such extensive condemnation when carried out by Israel, yet the months-long pretrial detention by Tunisian authorities has attracted comparatively little international scrutiny?
For a movement that describes itself as defending the rights of activists and Palestinian solidarity regardless of where they are detained, the relative silence surrounding the “Sumud 4” is striking.

The joint statement emphasized that "this cannot be the welcome Jewish students receive when they come to university," adding that "students have a right to feel safe and secure in their residences and to express their Jewish identity openly and proudly without fear of being targeted."
The organizations noted that the timing amplified the gravity of the incident, stating that "this occurred over Rosh Hashanah, making it all the more disturbing," and that "at a time when Jewish students should have been marking the beginning of a new year with pride, renewal, and hope, they were targeted by despicable hate."
Addressing the institutional response, the groups stressed that "there can be no tolerance for antisemitism on campus," and noted that "Hillel has been in touch with university leadership to ensure this matter is dealt with decisively."
Jewish students 'will not be intimidated into hiding who they are'
The organizations asserted that "Jewish students are not going anywhere," and that "they will not be intimidated into hiding who they are or removing the symbols of their Jewish identity" because "they are proud, they belong at Laurier, and they deserve to be safe being openly Jewish on campus."
In a statement to the Jerusalem Post, Jay Solomon, CEO of Hillel Ontario, said, “We condemn this act of antisemitism in the strongest possible terms. It is not an isolated incident, but part of a broader pattern of escalating hostility toward Jewish students that we have seen across campuses in Ontario and Canada. We have been in touch with university leadership and expressed our alarm at this incident, which follows similar violations on other campuses since October 7. The administration has assured us the matter is under investigation.”
“This cannot continue. All institutions of higher learning have an obligation to keep Jews safe, and we urge all schools to enforce their policies and hold perpetrators to account swiftly and transparently,” Solomon said.
In a statement to the Post, Laurier said the university “is aware of an incident of vandalism that involved widespread damage along various residence hallways. We are treating this matter very seriously, and our Special Constable Service is leading the investigation.”
The university added, “The students have connected with university residence staff, and appropriate supports are in place and available to them. We take the safety of our students very seriously. We strongly condemn acts of antisemitism and have zero tolerance for hate speech, racism, threats, and harassment.”
The incident comes amidst a surge in hate incidents targeting the Jewish community throughout Canada in recent months, including on university campuses, mirroring findings from a federal report released in August by the Department of Canadian Heritage and produced by the Association for Canadian Studies and the Metropolis Institute.
Known as the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experience (CASE) report, the study documented that over 95 percent of surveyed Jewish students experienced or witnessed antisemitism on post-secondary campuses nationwide.

EU states to raise game as Arctic becomes strategic geopolitical frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

EU states to raise game as Arctic becomes strategic geopolitical frontier
Europe racing Russia, China and US to seize security and economic opportunities.
European Union member states have agreed to increase investment in the Arctic amid a growing scramble for security advantages and vast natural resources.
Labelling the Arctic a “geopolitical hotspot”, a Monday meeting involving 12 countries called for the EU to “take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic”, meeting participants said in a joint statement.
The meeting, which featured the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden, focused on the race for influence over the Arctic as receding ice opens opportunities in the northern region. The discussion identified Russia as the largest threat to the European Arctic, but also noted the ambitions of China and the United States.
“This region has become a geopolitical hotspot,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told a news conference.
Despite Germany not being an Arctic country, Merz said his presence at the summit testified to the importance of the region to overall European security and suggested years of relative neglect should end.
“Let me put it this way: High north – and low attention – is over,” he said.
Russia, Canada, Iceland, Norway and the United States are considered Arctic countries, in addition to EU members Finland, Sweden and Denmark.
All have become involved in increasing geopolitical competition over the region as the retreat of ice sheets – spurred by climate change – has exposed its security and economic opportunities.
Russia has beefed up its military presence in recent years, reopening and modernising bases abandoned since the Soviet Union collapsed.
“Russia poses the most significant and long-term threat to Arctic security and stability. In order to respond to the threat posed by Russia, the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier,” said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo after the meeting.
The warming climate is opening up the Arctic for shipping, fishing, drilling and mining. China has made no secret of its interest in the territory, which is rich in natural resources.
The race has also stirred tension among NATO allies. Greenland, which is not part of the EU but overseen by Denmark, has become a bone of contention between the EU and the United States, with US President Trump claiming that Denmark cannot protect the Arctic island from Russia and China.
“I think everybody recognised that Greenland has been under a big pressure,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Last week, the European Union signed a declaration with Greenland, promising a stronger partnership and announcing a 200-million-euro ($232m) investment package to soothe anxiety caused by repeated threats from Trump to annex the self-governing territory.

Russia's cinemas may lose their backdoor access to Hollywood blockbusters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:29:09 UTC
02:29:09 KST

Russia's cinemas may lose their backdoor access to Hollywood blockbusters
Few people are pictured in a screening room of the Oktyabr cinema in Moscow, Russia, on March 29, 2022. (Natalia Kolesnikova / AFP via Getty Images)
After years of illegal screenings, Russians may soon lose access to major foreign films in their cinemas.
Since 2022, "pre-screening entertainment" — as the practice is known locally — has allowed Russian cinema-goers to watch Hollywood blockbusters, even as these cannot be legally distributed due to international sanctions imposed after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Essentially, people buy tickets for a domestic film, but are shown an American blockbuster, technically for free, in violation of (international) copyright laws, before the start of the (Russian) film," explained a Russian film industry specialist who spoke to the Kyiv Independent on the condition of anonymity.
Alexey Voronkov, the president of Russia's Association of Cinema Owners, said on Sept. 7 that the situation might soon change, with upcoming installments of the Dune and Avengers sagas, as well as other new Hollywood blockbusters, unlikely to be screened anytime soon.
"I think this practice will end in the next two to three months," Voronkov told Russian media, explaining that the screenings were unlikely to resume anytime soon.
Why are Russians still watching Western hits?
Voronkov's announcement comes weeks after the monumental box office flop of Kolobok, a Russian animated film released in early August. Instead of the domestic movie featuring a bread-like creature, Russians appear to have massively watched Hollywood's new Spider-Man sequel.
To watch the film, however, they needed to wait a few extra weeks: Russia's Spider-Man premiere was postponed on government orders, Russian media reported, to give Kolobok a chance to reap at least some box office sales.
The Russian film received poor reviews domestically and was widely regarded as unpopular.
In the first weekend following its official premiere, the picture barely recouped the 250 million rubles ($3 million) in state subsidies that it received. In comparison, the new Spider-Man film is estimated to have grossed up to 900 million rubles ($10.7 million) at Russian box offices in its first days of screening, even with government-imposed restrictions.
In theory, U.S. blockbusters cannot be legally shown in Russia: all films must obtain a screening license from Russia's Culture Ministry, and this license can only be granted to companies that hold the copyright. And as all Hollywood distributors left the Russian market in 2022, obtaining such a copyright in Russia is not technically possible.
read also
Hollywood films no more?
Since its introduction in 2022, pre-screening entertainment has been a legally dubious concept, with the practice also locally known as "gray" screenings, in reference to its unclear legal basis.
The practice clearly violates international copyright regulations because Russian film distributors typically buy copies in neighboring countries — such as Kazakhstan — from companies not authorized to conduct such sales.
The practice also violates Russian laws, even if, up till now, authorities have turned a blind eye to it. All films shown in local cinemas technically need to obtain a screening license — which, for Hollywood films, no company in Russia is legally entitled to request, due to copyright restrictions.
Despite these legal barriers, "pre-screening entertainment" seemed to have worked for years in Russia.
This situation, however, is set to change, with "no Russian film distributors" planning screenings of Dune 3 or Avengers: Doomsday, two Hollywood films which are supposed to premiere globally later this year, Voronkov said.
Recent legal changes have also made it harder to organize "gray" screenings. Since March 2026, Russia's Culture Ministry has been granted new regulatory competencies and can now more easily interfere with cinemas' operations.
Until recently, the strictest punishment theaters faced for screening a film without a license was a symbolic fine of up to 50,000 rubles ($590).
Under the new scheme, however, Russia's Culture Ministry will be able to conduct full-fledged investigations, and theaters could face more serious consequences, such as a 90-day forced closure.
read also
More legal tricks — that are unlikely to change anything
As restrictions tighten, Voronkov noted that Russian cinemas could adopt an alternative approach to bypass legal obstacles to screening foreign blockbusters.
This would involve cinemas renting out their screening rooms to shell companies, which could then show Hollywood films, theoretically without the cinemas bearing any legal responsibility for the screenings.
That scheme might not work either, though, as renting companies would in any case need to use the cinema's equipment for screenings, meaning that the cinemas could not claim they are not participating in the scheme.
In any case, Russia's policy of imposing unpopular domestic films — at the expense of international blockbusters in cinemas — is already making theaters worry about how to keep their businesses running.
"This will mainly hit small, independent cinemas in Russia," the film industry specialist said. "For them, it will be more difficult to compensate for losses if 'pre-screening entertainment' (of Hollywood blockbusters) is banned, in one way or another. But for now, we're only hearing announcements; no decisions have been made on this yet."

“We will continue to stand by Syria throughout this process,” he added.

Female athletes, including Olympic champions, have criticized a viral sports gambling advertisement starring US actor Sydney Sweeney, accusing the campaign of sexualizing women’s sports and reducing athletic imagery to a marketing device.
 
The criticism centers on the “Just Sports” campaign for US sports prediction-market company Novig, released Sept. 9. The advertisement shows Sweeney wearing little or no clothing while sports equipment is positioned across her body as she imitates activities including tennis, hockey, golf, basketball and American football.
 
Sweeney repeatedly says “sports” during the advertisement, which ends by inviting viewers to test their sporting knowledge on Novig’s platform.
 
The campaign quickly attracted tens of millions of views online, but athletes from several sports began responding with footage of themselves training and competing under variations of the message: “This is what a woman in sport looks like.”

“There’s a big difference between looking ‘sexy’ because you do sport compared to use sex to sell ‘sport’,” Nicolson wrote on Instagram.
 
She said the campaign made a “mockery” of women in sports and disregarded generations of athletes who had fought to be recognized for their performances.
 
Sweeney is not only the campaign's public face. Novig announced she had joined the company as a strategic partner and equity holder.
 
She also told Complex that she had been involved in creative discussions from the beginning, saying she did not want simply to attach her name to a company without having a role in the project.
 
Novig defended the concept as an attempt to emphasize that its prediction market focuses exclusively on sports.
 
“The campaign was about embracing a fun idea,” Sweeney said in the company’s announcement, describing its approach as one of “confidence, humor and a playful edge.”
Sweeney appeared to respond indirectly to the criticism Sunday by sharing previous ESPN Body Issue covers featuring nude or partially clothed female and male athletes.
 
She did not directly respond to the athletes’ criticism or explain whether the ESPN covers were intended as a defense of the campaign.

Air Force Plans Hundreds of Autonomous Fighter and ISR Drones by 2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:25:53 UTC
02:25:53 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force plans to field at least 500 semi-autonomous fighter drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft by 2032, and another 500 cheap reconnaissance and strike drones known as Massed Modular Aircraft that same year, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14.
In his keynote address to open AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Meink said the service would bolster its combat capability—which for decades has mostly come from crewed aircraft such as fighters and bombers—with lower-cost drones that operate with minimal direction from Airmen.
And that future is coming fast, Meink said.
“Because of the steps we are taking today, we will have a significantly different force by 2032,” Meink said. “By then, our special operators will have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCAs.”
The first iteration of CCAs—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A—are now rolling off the assembly line and will specialize in air-to-air missions. Future “increments” of CCA could focus on other missions, such as air-to-ground strikes, reconnaissance, or electronic warfare operations.
“We intend to have at least 500 of these in service by 2032,” Meink said, and by that time the drones will be performing many of the same missions crewed fighters perform today, he added.
Meink’s projection is the most ambitious target the Air Force has yet to announce for the CCA program. In 2024, his predecessor as Secretary, Frank Kendall, said the service would have 100 CCAs by 2029. Earlier this year, Meink said he expected to have 150 by the end of the decade.
The Air Force is also accelerating a program called Massed Modular Aircraft, which will field drones to take on some of the missions the MQ-9A Reaper performs today. The service in recent months has grown concerned over the pace of Reaper losses in operations against Iran—roughly 45 have been lost so far, or about a quarter of the Air Force’s fleet—and moved to speed up its plans to field MMAs.
Like CCAs, MMA drones will have autonomous capabilities, but they will be cheaper and less complex than CCAs. Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that the air vehicle of an MMAs will cost roughly $10 million, without sensors or other systems included, while CCAs will cost twice as much, at $20 million per air vehicle.
Meink said the Air Force plans to field 100 MMA drones by 2029 and 500 by 2032—higher than previous estimates from Air Force officials.
In a roundtable with reporters later, Meink also said the the Air Force plans to have multiple types of MMA drones from different contractors in its fleet, similar to how its CCA program is working with multiple vendors.
Asked about the expanded plans for the MMA program, Meink pointed to the program’s relatively low cost and the importance of the MQ-9’s combined strike and recon mission.
“That [ISR and strike] mission is a very important mission,” Meink said. “We’re looking at how we do that with a mix of different platforms. … The ability to bring low-cost mass is a driver here, and we expect these to be significantly cheaper than even the MQ-9s or the CCA.”
When asked if the Air Force could buy more than 500 MMA drones, Meink said that will depend on how much money Congress provides in the budget, but added “I think it should probably be much higher than that.”
When the two autonomous drones—MMA and CCA—are in the field, Meink said, they will transform the way the Air Force fights wars.
The sixth-generation F-47 fighter and B-21 Raider stealth bomber are “phenomenal aircraft” that “will be able to do things no other aircraft has ever done before,” Meink said. But they won’t be able to deliver the “massive scale of combat power we need” on their own, he warned. That’s where lower-cost, uncrewed autonomous platforms like CCA and MMA come in.
“When we pair manned aircraft with lower-cost autonomous systems, we will be able to unlock combat power at scale,” Meink said.
Both CCAs and MMAs are being built around an open systems architecture approach that will make it easier to swap different sensors or other capabilities into the drones, using standardized interfaces. Emphasizing the modularity that comes with open systems architecture will accelerate procurement of the systems, Meink said, and increase competition from industry, which will ultimately lower prices, give the Air Force more choices, and improve the drones’ combat power.
Meink told reporters in the roundtable that CCAs will continually evolve, even within the same increment, but that it was too soon to predict what the fleet of 500 will look like by 2032.
“It depends on how the current ones perform, and what additional capabilities the users are saying they need,” Meink said. “Can we evolve that into the current iteration? Do we need a different iteration? We’re working our way through that right now.”
Meink also said the Air Force plans to have “tens of thousands” of the new low-cost Family of Affordable Mass Munition, or FAMM, weapons in its inventory by 2030, and that they are already being used today.
Meink also revealed a name change for General Atomics’ CCA, which the company had been calling Dark Merlin. The FQ-42 will now be called Vengeance, he said. Anduril’s FQ-44 will continue with the name Fury.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a text to Air & Space Forces Magazine that the company will cease using the Dark Merlin name now that the Air Force has chosen its own moniker.
“We love when our customers name their aircraft,” Brinkley said. “Vengeance pretty much sums up what the FQ-42 brings to the fight.”

Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:25:13 UTC
02:25:13 KST

Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery
Anger rises in Syrian cities as fuel price hikes burden struggling households amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis.
The sight of protesters blocking roads and burning tyres on the streets of several Syrian cities and towns has highlighted popular anger over a government decision to increase fuel prices and a wider cost-of-living crisis.
The protests, which erupted on Sunday, come after months of complaints about soaring energy costs and criticisms that the lives of many Syrians have not improved since the fall of former Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Protests break out across Syria over fuel price increases
- list 2 of 3Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
- list 3 of 3At least seven killed in fire at prison in northern Syria
The Syrian government has defended its efforts, arguing that it will take time to overcome decades of economic stagnation and international isolation.
The trigger for Sunday’s protests was a government announcement that diesel prices would rise by 40 percent, petrol by at least 25 percent and cooking gas around nine percent.
The government said the increases were temporary and caused by a spike in refined petroleum products following the US-Israeli war on Iran and renewed hostilities in Yemen. However, the Syrian parliament has summoned Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir for a hearing on rising fuel costs, a sign that officials were concerned by the public outcry.
Public anger
When anti-regime forces overthrew al-Assad’s government, much of the country erupted in celebration.
It came after more than a decade of war and the 50-year rule of the al-Assad family, which had led to international sanctions on the country.
Aside from expectations that freedoms would increase after the fall of the regime, which operated as a police state, many Syrians also hoped the country’s dire economic conditions would improve.
That has been a tough task for the new Syrian government, led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Since coming to power 21 months ago, the government has focussed on securing international legitimacy and lifting the complex network of sanctions placed on Syria.
On that front, it has largely been successful.
In August, Syria was removed from the US state sponsors of terrorism list, building on earlier decisions to lift sanctions by the US, the European Union and other world powers. This allowed for Syria to be reintegrated into the world economy and receive increased foreign investment.
There has been optimism in Syria, but while the government insists that the positive impact of the removal of sanctions and other government actions will take time, patience has run out for some.
“Fuel itself is not an isolated energy issue right now; it’s related to the cost of living crisis for every household and business in Syria,” Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst at Karam Shaar Advisory, told Al Jazeera. “The anger right now reflects a deeper concern that the recovery stemming from the sanctions relief and Syria’s gradual reconnection with the global financial system is not yet translating into affordable [prices].”
“The protests show that Syrians increasingly hold their own government responsible for what they pay,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions relief weakened the argument that hardship comes from outside and raised expectations at the same time. Much of the anger is also coming from areas that backed the change of government, making this the kind of discontent a government can answer only with results.”
Syria’s poverty rate is around 90 percent, according to the UN’s World Food Programme. The rise in fuel costs has a universal impact, affecting the price of transport but also food and other services.
“A 40 percent diesel hike is not just inconvenient; it is really a threat to [people’s] economic survival on a daily basis,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.
Syria remains highly dependent on energy imports. The country produces around 102,000 barrels of oil per day, compared with domestic needs of around 325,000 barrels per day, al-Bashir said. Syria refines some of its crude domestically but its refineries cannot produce enough petroleum products to meet demands, forcing it to import substantial quantities of diesel, petrol and other fuels.
The Syrian government said it was working on an overhaul of the Baniyas refinery – the country’s largest – in the hope that it will raise processing capacity at the facility from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Energy said prices would continue to be reviewed as global market conditions change. It also said it would work over the long term to expand refining and storage capacity.
Government action
Authorities will now look for ways to temper public anger.
Hawach suggested a “protected diesel price for public transport and farmers”, as well as the government announcing dates for when temporary price increases would end.
“[This] would likely cost the treasury less than the concessions it has tended to make after protesters block roads, and would give people a reason to wait rather than take to the streets,” he said.
The protests have come about as the Syrian government attempts to rebuild the country after a war that devastated much of the country and killed hundreds of thousands of people.
Sanctions removal has borne some fruit: the World Bank approved around $491m in grants to Syria to support infrastructure and economic development since last year.
Still, after a July visit, the International Monetary Fund recommended that the Syrian government collect more revenue and be more selective about what it spends money on “to create the fiscal space needed to create room for development spending and to enhance the social safety net to protect the most vulnerable segments of the population”.
So far, the government has benefited from a degree of patience among Syrians. But despite the progress made over the past year, that patience is beginning to wear thin – particularly among the country’s most vulnerable, who have yet to feel the benefits of economic growth.
“The question is whether this whole process of recovery will translate into credible relief for households, workers, small businesses and farmers facing the knock-on effects of inflation and higher energy prices,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.
