Private schools become a costly choice for struggling parents in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:22:48 UTC
02:22:48 KST

Private schools become a costly choice for struggling parents in Gaza
Gaza families face difficult choices: send children to schools in tents with few resources to pay for private school.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — In their tent in central Gaza, Khadija Abu Qados gets her 11-year-old daughter, Jouri, ready for another day at school amid the ongoing Israeli air raids and crippling financial crisis.
The family has been living in a camp for displaced Palestinians in Deir el-Balah since their neighbourhood, Sheikh Radwan, in northern Gaza, was destroyed in the Israeli offensive in Gaza City last September.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
- list 2 of 3Burnham must establish an inquiry into Britain’s role in the Gaza genocide
- list 3 of 3‘Silent Cold War’: Why calls to slow AI have sparked new US–China frontier
Like their home, the classrooms for Jouri and her 14-year-old sister, Ritaj, at Elyaa’ School are also tents. There are few chairs or desks, so children usually sit on mattresses and carpets when they learn. There is no air conditioning or fans, so the heat makes it difficult for children to focus.
The children have already spent long periods out of school since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Online classes were a challenge due to difficulties in internet access during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Now, Jouri and two of her siblings attend a nearby school run by volunteer teachers near their camp, which charges 30 shekels ($8) a month. Even though it is far cheaper than private schools, the modest fee is difficult for the family to afford when food, water and other basic needs come first.
“If I could afford it, I would send them to private school,” 39-year-old Khadija told Al Jazeera.
Before the war, her daughters attended an UNRWA school in Gaza City, where her children performed well and were praised for their achievements.
Now, she watches them study in tents. The conditions may be difficult, but the teachers are helping her children catch up with missed school time.
“The teaching here is excellent [but] I feel sad for my children because they are studying in these difficult circumstances. There are no chairs and no proper seats. This is not an educational environment at all,” she said.
“Even the stationery is something I can barely afford because prices have become so high. A single notebook costs between four and six shekels.”
The family’s experiences reflect a wider education crisis in Gaza after nearly three years of war.
Around 700,000 children aged between four and 17 had missed formal, face-to-face schooling for almost three consecutive school years during Israel’s war on Gaza, UNICEF said in May.
Just two percent of all school buildings are undamaged and 93 percent of them require major repairs or complete reconstruction. About 420,000 children – three in five – had no access to face-to-face learning.
Israeli air raids are a constant threat, with at least 300 children killed since last October’s “ceasefire”. Last week, eight-year-old Wafaa Akila and her father were killed when their car was struck on the way back home from school in western Gaza.
With the formal education system in ruins, parents and teachers have stepped in, opening temporary learning spaces in tents and volunteer initiatives.
Noha Khadra, who spent 10 years as a teacher, opened the Elyaa’ School in January, operating under the supervision of the Ministry of Education.
Pupils learn in tents with a few desks and not enough chairs, while other essentials such as blackboards are in poor condition.
More than 1,100 students have enrolled in the ‘field school, but there are only 40 volunteer teachers and administrative staff.
Despite the obstacles, she said there is high demand for places in the school, but a lack of resources and staff has meant a gruelling initial nine months for the principal.
“At the beginning, there were no tables. The children were sitting on mattresses. Many students come to us without stationery… so we buy it for them ourselves as much as we can,” she told Al Jazeera.
“I am honestly upset about the classroom conditions. This project has drained my energy, and I cannot provide more than what I am already doing.”
The school provides children with a place away from the everyday pressures of displacement and also access to essentials for survival, such as water.
Private schools
The situation in private schools is better than the voluntary centres, but the high costs make them affordable only to a minority of parents in Gaza.
Zahra Saleh, 25, enrolled her six-year-old son, Ibrahim, in first grade and her five-year-old son, Karam, in kindergarten at the Abdul Aziz Private School in the west of Gaza City.
After finding most private schools too expensive, she finally found one she could afford. Zahra’s husband, like many men in Gaza, is unemployed, so paying the 400 shekels ($131) monthly school fees is difficult. But she did not want Ibrahim, who was beginning his first year of formal schooling, to lose any more education.
She also wanted her children to have a regular routine, with classes from 7am to noon. Learning subjects such as Arabic, English and Mathematics as they would have done before the war, was also her hope.
“I’m in a very difficult financial situation. I had to work at the school so I could reduce the cost of the fees for my children,” Zahra told Al Jazeera.
“I taught him at home as much as I could, but children don’t learn everything at home. In the end, we had to send him to a school. It’s just a normal school environment. That’s what I want.”
Families are also struggling with the growing costs of school supplies, with 12 notepads selling for six shekels ($1.96) before the war but now costing four shekels ($1.31) for just one.
Financial crisis
The schooling crisis comes at a time of acute financial hardship for almost every Palestinian in Gaza.
Abdul Aziz began as a field school in tents with volunteer teachers in 2024, before moving to its current rented building in Shujaiya, west of Gaza City, for the new school year starting this month.
Around 20 staff teach 300 students, aged between three and 15, a much lower student-to-teacher ratio than in non-private schools.
Gaza’s labour market is now “largely nonfunctional”, with more than 90 percent of working-age people without a job. The World Bank estimated in May that $71.5bn was needed for Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction.
The financial pressure facing families is part of a broader economic collapse in the Strip. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics said Gaza’s GDP contracted by 84 percent in 2025 compared with 2023, while unemployment reached 78 percent.
Doaa Qdeih, Abdul Aziz Private School’s director, is mindful of the financial difficulties families face, so has some leeway on payments with parents, including Zahra.
“I found a lot of flexibility. They welcomed me, supported me and understood my circumstances,” she said.
The school does not have one fixed fee for every student. Qdeih said she considers each family’s circumstances before deciding what it can pay.
“I don’t set a fixed amount. Before I set the amount, I look at the situation of the people — what they do for work and what the child’s circumstances are — and then we decide what they can afford,” she said.
“We have families who support each other. You find someone who can afford to pay 300 shekels ($80) contributing, while another family cannot pay anything. There is solidarity among us.”
Almost all this money from the fees goes towards rent and operating costs. Qdeih also used profits from another business she owns to furnish and repair the building the school now uses. But she does not see private schools as the solution to Gaza’s education crisis.
“I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: if the government or the ministry provides places for education, we are ready to volunteer,” she said.
“We don’t want anything in return. We just want to continue serving the children and give them the education they deserve.”

Ukrainian Drone Crew Hits Four Russian Grad Rocket Launchers in One Mission, One 45 Km Away
A Ukrainian drone crew destroyed two Russian BM-21 Grad multiple rocket launchers and damaged two more during a single deployment, with one of the strikes carried out after a 45-kilometer drone flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade on September 14, the operation was conducted by a crew from the Perun Unmanned Systems Battalion. The crew commander, who uses the call sign “Zhulyk,” said the four Grad systems were the first targets of this type struck by the battalion.

The crew reached the position in roughly half a day, while leaving it after the two-month deployment took nearly two days and required stops along the route.

As Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy? | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:19:46 UTC
02:19:46 KST

As £72m in donations makes its way to Reform UK’s bank accounts, consider what Nigel Farage said on the eve of Britain’s vote to leave the European Union a decade ago. “This referendum is the people versus the establishment,” he declared. “It is the vested interest, it’s the rich, it’s the big business.”
Just two years ago, Farage assailed “an unholy alliance of big business, big banks and big government”. He is also the same man who, when he debated with the then Liberal Democrat leader, Nick Clegg, in 2014, claimed to “represent the mercantile, trading, entrepreneurial end of society”, while his opponent “represents big banks, big government and big business”.
To be clear, Farage’s political outfit is being bankrolled by two cryptobillionaires. One of them is Ben Delo, who once developed high-frequency trading systems for JP Morgan. That investment bank was a particular bete noire of Farage: when it backed the Remain campaign, he savaged “the unholy alliance of big banks and big politics”. The other is the Thailand-based cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Farage his pre-election £5m gift and provided two-thirds of Reform’s funding – until now, that is.
Neither of them is the plucky small merchant evoked by Farage’s rhetoric. The man who denounced banks buying political influence is now dependent on two wealthy figures from the world of finance. Predictably, Reform says its benefactors want “nothing” in return for their colossal donations. Yet the two businessmen who have just coughed up the biggest donations in British political history will surely be delighted with Reform’s plans to slash taxes on crypto assets and set up a “bitcoin reserve”.
The political fraud that is rightwing “populism” is quite something to behold. These movements claim to champion the little guy against the elites. Whether embodied by wealthy tycoon Donald Trump, whose relatives and friends are making a killing from his administration, or the privately educated millionaire ex-City broker Farage, the formula is straightforward. Dupe struggling people into believing their problems are caused by migrants, refugees and minorities – while championing the interests of the mega-rich who actually hold the power.
Sure, British democracy has always come with heavy caveats. Political parties and politicians have always received hefty donations from an economic elite that, to be clear, does not give money away without expecting a return. They can also rely on powerful lobbyists to advance their interests. Then there’s the “revolving door” through which politicians and civil servants leave public office for lucrative jobs with companies in the very industries they were previously responsible for overseeing and regulating. And there’s a British newspaper industry mostly owned by rich moguls with a vested interest in defending a status quo they profit from.
But these latest donations take the corruption of our democracy to a whole new level. That two donations to Reform in a single weekend now eclipse the total amount spent by all political parties at the last general election tells its own story. Indeed, these donations amount to about 14 times the total spent by Farage’s party at the last election – when, it should be noted, it won more than 4m votes, or one in seven votes cast.
The party can now pay for hundreds of full-time staff, build local political hubs and massively expand its polling and research infrastructure. Crucially, it can throw vast sums at digital advertising, which can be uniquely tailored to the interests and concerns of individual voters. We know from research in the US that digital ads can shift voting intention. The more money a political party has, the more it can afford to experiment until it finds the ads that work.
Indeed, all the evidence suggests that money wins votes. A recent peer-reviewed study examined every British general election between 1857 and 2017, and found a strong relationship between relative campaign spending and votes. Rich donors really do shower political parties with money for a reason. Reform’s mega-donations underline that democracy is for sale.
But could this spectacularly backfire? Reform is, after all, already embroiled in multiple controversies over gifts and donations from wealthy donors, and its ratings have taken a bad beating. Polling earlier this year found that 83% of Brits believe that “wealthy individuals use political donations to influence the government to further their own personal interests”. That figure was only four points lower among Reform voters, who were also nearly 10 times as likely to say they would view a party more favourably if it promised to cap donations as to view it less favourably.
It would be naive, alas, to believe that this will finally burst the gilded Reform bubble. What it does do depends on what the national political conversation is about. Labour has had long enough in government to change the law to block such donations, and tragically Andy Burnham has retreated from his stated desire to cap them at £500,000.
But that would mean a Labour party that was determined to confront wealthy vested interests. Because Starmerism had no desire to replace an economic order rigged in favour of elites, it was unable to redirect anger away from the scapegoating of migrants. Instead, it simply replicated Farage’s xenophobia, which only ever legitimises the arguments of the anti-migrant right.
A different approach, based on redistributing wealth and power, would force a different conversation. So far, thanks to pressure from Zack Polanski’s Green party, Burnham has shifted some of the rhetoric. But if Labour were to, say, hike taxes on wealth in order to invest in crumbling services, it could pair that with a sustained attack on Farage as the plaything of wealthy vested interests.
Otherwise, the outrage over these donations will fade. The old poison will remain – and this time it comes with £72m behind it.

EU envoys extend Russia sanctions by seven days to debate six-month renewal, EU presidency says
BRUSSELS, Sept 14 - European Union envoys have pushed back the expiry of EU Russia sanctions listings by seven days until September 22, a spokesperson for the EU's Irish presidency said on Monday, after failing to agree on a six-month renewal.
At issue is whether to de-list Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov. France has joined Slovakia in a call to remove him, citing national security concerns, EU diplomats said.
"France is one of the countries most committed to increasing pressure — by all means — on the Russian war machine, as well as to supporting Ukraine," a French diplomatic source said. "We face a specific national security issue and wish to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov."
France's foreign ministry spokesperson declined to comment.
The designations, which target nearly 3,000 companies and individuals with asset freezes and travel bans, had been due to expire on September 15.
"In order to allow additional time for member states to comprehensively examine proposals for the renewal, Coreper has agreed to prolong the regime by a period of 7 days, until midnight Tuesday 22 September," the spokesperson said, referring to the Comité des Représentants Permanents — the body of EU ambassadors that prepares work for the 27 heads of member states.
EU sanctions require unanimous approval from all 27 member states and must be renewed every six months.
Usmanov had a net worth of $18.8 billion as of early 2026, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and is subject to EU and U.S. sanctions and a travel ban.
Usmanov, a metals and mining mogul, has launched multiple lawsuits in Europe with the ultimate goal of having the sanctions lifted. In some, his lawyers contested statements in the media that were used as grounds for the sanctions.
The billionaire also holds assets in telecoms, internet companies and media, and he owns Russian business daily Kommersant.
EU countries frequently debate Russia sanctions renewals until the last moment, in the past largely due to demands from Hungary's former leader, Viktor Orban, and Slovakia, which has better relations with Moscow than most other EU states.
In June, EU countries agreed for the first time to renew the bloc's sectoral sanctions, such as those on energy, for a year to reduce the opportunity for such debates. REUTERS

The legal, ethical war which NAZA highlights and Israel is still barely showing up for - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:12:53 UTC
02:12:53 KST

Movies are always sensationalized and simplified. Anonymous accusations are always problematic. But no one should understate the legal and ethical harm that Israel and the IDF now face following the launch of the NAZA film, which frames the 2023-2025 war in Gaza as a genocide.
It is not the first video footage or detailed, specific accusations against Israel.
Those have been pouring in since nearly the start of the war.
And Breaking the Silence, 972 Magazine, The New York Times, and other media have occasionally gotten Israeli soldiers on the record making accusations against the IDF.
But here are 24 (presumed) Israeli soldiers on camera (even if anonymous) from a variety of different roles, especially relating to artificial intelligence and targeting, making genocide and war crimes accusations in a film made by two Israelis.
These accusers in the NAZA film know all or many of these facts and are still making the accusations, and that is why they are so problematic for Israel legally and ethically.
Going after the IDF accusers legally will not solve any problems, because they are just adding credibility to already seriously researched allegations.
An April 2024 report by 972 Magazine and a December 2024 report by The New York Times brought some of the targeting and AI issues that NAZA seems to raise (even if without specifics) into clear contrast.
Past Israeli commission set a high threshold for proportionality
Simply stated: assuming Hamas systematically uses human shields and that the Israeli military was going to have to kill far more Gazans in this war than in prior ones in order to decisively beat Hamas militarily after the terror group’s October 7 slaughter of around 1,200 Israelis and its taking of 250 hostages, when does the ratio of terrorists to civilians in a particular attack, and as a matter of policy, violate even the most extreme interpretation of proportionality?
Can killing 100 civilians (as claimed by past media reports) or 500 civilians (as claimed by NAZA) be justified to kill even the most senior single terrorist? Can Israel say it is justified to kill 20 civilians “merely” to kill mid-level terrorists?
The 2024 New York Times report contended that the IDF assassination of senior Hamas terrorist, Jabalya Central Battalion Commander Ibrahim Biari, in late October 2023, had a 100-to-1 ratio.
According to reports – no Israeli government or IDF officials have yet been allowed to see the film – the NAZA film, without identifying a specific date or incident, sends the ratio up to the stratosphere of 500 to 1.
IDF needs clearer communication regarding AI-targeting
The IDF needs to respond to the AI targeting accusations with much more transparency both in general and to specific incidents that prior reports raised, which the NAZA film merely dramatized.
In fact, shockingly, the IDF did not put out its first report responding to specific war crimes allegation files until August 19 of this year – nearly three years after the start of the war.
The fact is that The Jerusalem Post has received repeated messages throughout the Israeli legal establishment that there was pressure from Israeli government officials to delay publications of many of the decisions.
Some of this pressure was due to the fear of government officials that portions of their constituency would hold them partially accountable for probing and prosecuting IDF soldiers, something that is very unpopular domestically.
Another source of pressure was the self-defeating concern that publicizing details of probing and prosecuting IDF officials would be used against soldiers by the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
Meanwhile, as former deputy attorney-general for international affairs Roy Schondorf already pointed out in May 2024, the delay in publicizing details of the probes and prosecutions is exactly one of the mistakes Israel made that allowed the ICC and ICJ to jump forward, wrongfully claiming that Israel was not probing or prosecuting anyone.
In December 2024, the Post learned from off-record IDF sources that there are no set ratios and that the IDF viewed the New York Times report message at the time that these ratios are essentially part of a factory-style free-for-all blow everyone up strategy as inaccurate.
Rather, the Post understands that the IDF’s view is that the New York Times report confused various minimal parameters, which may exist for setting at what level different senior-ranked IDF officials are mandated to sign off on certain strikes, with being the end to the process of approving or not approving a strike.
An unanswered question is whether the IDF really lived up to these standards as much at the start of the war in October-November 2023. The Post learned in December 2024 that the IDF would acknowledge that it had less time and fewer resources available to evaluate each target during that time period than in other time periods.
However, the IDF would still contend that it properly checked its targets for civilian casualties, including with multiple tools.
This last point leads into the various reports, which have also raised questions about the IDF’s target bank and AI warfare methods for incriminating some Gazans and for estimating how many civilians are nearby.
On November 16, 2023, the IDF allegedly killed dozens of members of the Malaka family, including a number of women and minors. According to the 2024 New York Times report, the IDF’s estimate of civilian harm was around 16 based on cell phone use and former records. Yet cell phone use was out, and dozens of additional people had come to shelter in the same area due to a lack of other non-bombed areas to take shelter in. Unlike earlier wars, the report said the IDF did not invest in localized resources to check if its civilian estimates were correct.
If the IDF misestimated civilians by the dozens not only this time but many times, at one point does such an error carry a new level of responsibility, potentially even criminal?
Airwars, a London-based conflict monitor, documented 136 IDF strikes that it said each killed at least 15 people in October 2023 alone.
Presumably, a certain number of these people were Hamas terrorists, and the Airwars numbers may have other deficiencies, but until now, the IDF has only addressed five controversial cases with specific decisions and details, and only on August 19.
The Post has learned that the IDF’s view is that overgeneralizations that it was overly reliant on AI and cell phone tracking to determine potential civilian harm are inaccurate. But even now the IDF has continued the mistake of refusing to publicize what its other tools have been for checking potential civilian casualties.
Previously, the Post has reported that drones are regularly used to follow the status of civilians in a target area and that there have been hundreds, if not thousands, of cases where the IDF called off an attack when the drones revealed that too many civilians were in an area about to be struck.
Maybe that has been the tool that has been used to check for civilians, maybe Palestinian collaborators or pro-Israeli gangs who were revealed in 2025, or maybe Israeli special forces on the ground. But the impact that these charges are having on national security already far exceeds whatever tactical losses might come out from revealing some of Israel’s techniques for reducing civilian harm.
Viewers who applauded the NAZA film for 25 minutes at its opening probably are not going to take the time to review Israel’s detailed rebuttal. Most probably presumed Israel committed genocide before the film started.
But many fair-minded Americans and Europeans still will, and Israel and the IDF need to go into overdrive, putting out detailed responses to two- and three-year-old allegations before even those fence-sitters shut off any willingness to hear the other side of the story.
AI targeting is not only under new scrutiny in Israel but worldwide.
And Israelis, after three years of militarily defeating and clobbering enemies on all fronts, should also be ready for an honest look at instances in which individual soldiers departed from the open fire rules.
Even if most soldiers followed the rules, some will need to pay a legal price for their actions, both because that is the IDF’s values and because such accountability may yet save the Jewish state as a whole.

A recipe for disaster: Edward Miliband, Britain, and relations with Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:12:21 UTC
02:12:21 KST

Britain’s House of Commons has been the place where many outstanding speeches have been delivered.
The September 8 statement of policy that Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs Edward Miliband delivered was most certainly not one of them.
In fact, it was not only an embarrassing presentation of lies in place of facts, but he made assertions about the future which are unsubstantiated.
Worse, he predicated Britain’s new policy decision on his being Jewish, saying, “I do so as a proud British Jew.”
He then continued, expressing “the deepest gratitude to the State of Israel for giving a home to my grandmother” after she lost her husband and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis.
Complacently and blindly, in declaring sanctions to force Israel to accept a political solution Israel has decided for itself that would endanger its very survival, a solution the Arab side has itself rejected for at least 90 years, he ignores the distinct probability that he is facilitating a version of Islamist Nazism in its goals to eliminate the Jewish state he once picked oranges in at a kibbutz.
The veterans of that kibbutz, Nahshonim, just south of Rosh Ha’ayin, could surely relate to Miliband, if they didn’t when he visited, to the dangers they faced in the early 1950s.
In that decade, Israel did not possess any “occupied territory” of the “West Bank.” And yet infiltrators from Jordan caused havoc, crossing the former Green Line, stealing livestock and crops, and also murdering Israeli civilians.
As Abba Eban declared in his British-accented English to his Der Spiegel interviewer, those 1967 lines carried “something of an Auschwitz memory” regarding Israel’s existential vulnerability.
For Miliband to state, “if there is one lesson of recent decades, it is that we will never have stability in the Middle East without a two-state solution,” is displaying abject ignorance.
Miliband should know that, by demanding, by force of sanctions, that Israel return to that period of topographical nightmare, without detailing the solutions to Israel’s security needs, as if they even exist in 2026 after October 7 and Hamas’ invasion from Gaza, he is prepping another Arab chance at their own version of a holocaust.
Jake Wallis-Simpson is correct in his comment, on the spiked magazine website, that Labour has committed a “shameful surrender to the anti-Israel mob… sacrificing the UK’s economic and security interests to appease an anti-Zionist fringe.”
Blogger/activist Jonathan Hoffman noted that Miliband was being a “disgrace” – not only for using charged inflammatory language but basing himself on “stories” he was told by unidentified “human-rights activists.” The kingdom’s cabinet is but a branch of the Labour Friends of Palestine.
Simon Schama, the historian, tweeted that the sanctions “will certainly help Netanyahu’s election chances, perhaps decisively,” but he received some oppositional feedback on that aspect.
Nevertheless, the British move surely assists Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s possibility of, if not gaining votes, retaining those who would, at the least, remain within the bloc of right-wing parties as they see a threat to Israel’s security and rights to its homeland.
A sharper criticism was penned by Lord Jon Mendelsohn in The Spectator on September 8. He saw problems in that Miliband’s policy does not deal with the actual violence that is preventing peace.
There is no reference to who disarms Hamas or prevents the rebuilding of its military infrastructure. Neither is there a plan to ensure that a future Palestinian state possesses a monopoly of legitimate force and that that “security guarantee” is “capable of sustaining Israeli withdrawal.”
A second all-Arab Islamist state in historic Palestine as proposed, the first being the monarchical and dictatorial Jordan, true ethno-nationalist states the progressive camp fulminates over when they reference Israel, while Israel yields territory but maintains its not insignificant Arab minority, is patently a recipe for continued violence rather than peace.
Can we at least solve Gaza first? That was, in essence, a two-state solution paradigm, and we have witnessed the calamitous failure of that idea.
Perhaps applying sanctions to persons, businesses, banks, and governing institutions that support anti-Jewish Arab terror? If not in Israel and the Palestinian Authority, then at least in the United Kingdom?
If Britain is struggling with anti-Jewish violence and refusing to deal with the underlying prop-ups of the shootings, stabbings, and the fire bombings, is it not hubris to presume the Arab wars against Israel are a problem England can solve with sanctions on Israel?
Recipe for disaster
Miliband's crutch of declaring himself a “good Jew” with a good Jewish family in Israel, while admitting he is an atheist with a non-Jewish wife, is an unworthy trick of seeking to lull Jews into trusting his policy.
Despite him being “proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” there is very much a contradiction between that and support for the state of Palestine, as he posited.
I, too, am a proud Jew, and I proudly suggest to Miliband and to Andy Burnham that it’s about time that supporters of an Arab Palestine realize that Jewish rights must be acknowledged, among them Jewish national identity and our historic national home, as the League of Nations decided in 1922 and as Lord Balfour wrote in 1917.
Proposed solutions that ignore the roots of Arab violence, their rejectionism, their jihadist mentality, and their anti-Jewish sentiment are a recipe for disaster.
Calumnies such as “ethnic cleansing,” “dehumanization,” and “settler terrorism,” even if quoting Israeli political figures, are not, as such, true.
“Jewish settlement” in the land where Jews lived for millennia, since at least 1250 BCE, is a natural right, and the League of Nations recognized it as such.
Britain and its government have erred terribly. How long until the error is realized and corrected?

Phases of Objects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:12:00 UTC
02:12:00 KST

What happens to a clay statue after you squash it? Some say it ceases to exist, but the lump of clay—a distinct object that had been co-located with it—continues to exist. Others say that the statue ceases to exist and is replaced with a new object, a squashed lump of clay. Here’s a different answer. The statue, which is also a lump of clay, continues to exist and merely ceases to be a statue. Being a statue, the idea goes, is just a phase that the lump of clay passes through, just as being a teenager is a phase that a person passes through. This natural, “phasalist” treatment of the statue-clay puzzle has not received the attention it deserves. There are no representatives of phasalism in Rea’s landmark anthology Material Constitution, for instance, and the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on material constitution devotes only one sentence to it.
In Phases of Objects, Justin Mooney rectifies this neglect. He defends a general metaphysics of material objects that delivers the phasalist account of statues and lumps, while also rendering verdicts on a wide variety of other puzzling cases. For example, his view entails that a human being can become a corpse, that the Ship of Theseus can become a cabin in the woods, and much more besides. The book is full of careful, fine-grained engagement with metaphysical subtleties and thoughtful analyses of hard cases. And it’s a refreshing and invigorating return to the golden age of material-object metaphysics, before it was dominated by universalism vs. nihilism, metametaphysics, and grounding.
This is a terrific book, and we recommend it enthusiastically to anyone with an interest in persistence and coincidence puzzles. In what follows, we present Mooney’s view in greater detail (§1), examine some of its unappealing implications (§2), and discuss some alternative versions of phasalism that may be more palatable (§3).
1. Phasalism and Spatiotemporalism
Mooney’s primary innovation is filling out the basic phasalist picture with a carefully crafted spatiotemporal criterion of identity (43-50), applied across the board to any material object of any sort, people included. According to this criterion, a material object will persist just in case two conditions are met. First, there’s a continuity condition: the object must follow a spatiotemporal path that includes no excessive causal or spatiotemporal discontinuities. Second, there’s a closest-continuer condition: the object must follow a spatiotemporal path that exhibits greater continuity than any rival path. We’ll call his thesis that all material objects are subject to this sort of criterion spatiotemporalism.
Spatiotemporalism delivers the phasalist treatment across a wide range of cases. The statue merely ceases to be a statue when squashed, but continues to exist since the squashing exhibits the needed unrivaled spatiotemporal continuity. When a long piece of yarn is knitted into a sweater, unraveled, and then knitted into a scarf, there all along was just the one material object, which was a sweater and a piece of yarn, then was just a piece of yarn, and is now a scarf and a piece of yarn (87-89). A pumpkin can become a carriage (44). A terrier can become an amorphous mass of cells (70).
Spatiotemporalism is similarly liberal about part loss and replacement. In some cases, this liberalism has attractive consequences. Clay statues and, thus, the pieces of clay with which they are identical, can gain and lose parts without ceasing to exist (66-67). (Here we applaud Mooney for breaking with the bizarre dogma that lumps have all their parts essentially.) In other cases, the results are more surprising. For example, material objects can survive the replacement of all of their parts. And not just organisms and ships: a piece of lead can become a piece of gold (68). That’s the good news for alchemists. The bad news is that you need to already have the gold and the patience to swap it out one piece at a time. Spatiotemporalism also has the surprising consequence that, if we were to dismantle the Empire State Building by removing one small portion after another, we might finally arrive at a situation in which the Empire State Building is a small piece of steel that fits comfortably in a breast pocket (cf. 62-65).
So how do material objects cease to exist on Mooney’s view? Sometimes they cease to exist when they break into pieces. A windowpane ceases to exist when it’s shattered—unless one piece is over half the size of the original windowpane, in which case the windowpane survives as the largest shard (62). This is also how people normally cease to exist on his view: not when they die, but at some point in the process of cremation or decomposition (186-188). Though, depending on the order of events, your end might be later than you think, and, like the Empire State Building, you might wind up as a piece of bone that comfortably fits in a breast pocket.
Objects also cease to exist when, as a result of part loss, they would otherwise shrink down to a region already occupied by one of their parts. For instance, when a door composed of a board and a knob loses its knob, the door ceases to exist, not because it isn’t spatiotemporally continuous with the board, but because the post-knob-loss board is a closer continuer of something else, namely the pre-knob-loss board (104-106). (As Mooney sees it, part loss doesn’t always result in shrinking down to a region already occupied by a part, since he doesn’t believe in arbitrary undetached parts.)
2. Remnant Survival
To our minds, the hardest cases for spatiotemporalism involve what Mooney calls “remnant survival”, where an object is split into differently sized pieces, the smaller of which seems to have the better claim to being the original object. One such case that Mooney addresses involves a vining plant that covers an entire brick wall, and that is later snipped right at the base (69-71). The living plant, now just a couple of inches high, continues to grow. Intuitively, this very plant (pointing to the two-inch remnant) once covered the wall. But according to spatiotemporalism, the two-inch-high plant cannot be the plant that once covered the wall. No material object can survive that sort of abrupt spatial discontinuity. Mooney bites the bullet, and you might think that’s not so bad. But there are more troubling cases of remnant survival. We will mention two.
First, suppose the Statue of Liberty—a hollow, copper statue—is seamlessly filled with copper, one small bit at a time, until it is completely solid. Imagine that we were to remove the internal “core” all at once, apparently returning the Statue of Liberty to its initial state. Surprisingly, spatiotemporalism entails that the Statue of Liberty is the removed core in this case (97-98). The hollow statue that remains is a perfect duplicate of the statue we started with, made of exactly the same copper atoms, which were (we may suppose) never disturbed. Nevertheless, spatiotemporalism entails that it is not the Statue of Liberty. Indeed, despite the fact that there’s a piece of copper there that is made of exactly the same copper atoms as the original piece, arranged in exactly the same way, this piece is not identical to the original piece according to spatiotemporalism.
Second, and in our view most troublingly, are cases of remnant survival involving people. Take the real-life case of Jasmine Ramirez. At the age of 14, Jasmine’s tumor-ridden leg was removed after it had grown to 174 pounds, leaving behind a roughly 100-pound one-legged amputee. Mooney cannot say that Jasmine becomes the amputee, since no material object (on his view) can survive such an abrupt spatial discontinuity. Nor, for that matter, does Jasmine become the severed leg (since that’s what the pre-surgery leg becomes). Nor will Mooney identify Jasmine with a scattered object composed of the amputee and the severed leg, since Mooney thinks there are no such scattered objects (3-4). Rather, Mooney is forced to say that Jasmine simply ceases to exist when the leg is removed.
It gets worse. We just saw that the amputee can’t be Jasmine herself according to spatiotemporalism, so what was the amputee up to prior to the surgery? The spatiotemporalist is faced with various options, none of which is especially attractive. For example, one option is to say that the amputee was a second person co-located with Jasmine prior to the amputation. But, as Mooney acknowledges in connection with disembodied brains (192-196), this option runs directly into the familiar problem of “too many thinkers”. Mooney could instead embrace immaterialism about people, something he is understandably reluctant to do (162-163), and which would in any case not answer the question of what to say about the history of the one-legged organism. Another option is to say that the amputee came into existence at the time of the surgery. But it seems obvious that, if there’s a conscious person at all where the amputee is, that person is Jasmine, the person who once had two legs. In light of this, we suppose the spatiotemporalist might try simply denying that there’s a conscious person where the amputee is. This is in effect Mooney’s line on brains in vats, but it strikes us as intolerable when applied to our relieved amputee.
3. Other Phasalisms
Some metaphysicians may be inclined to dismiss the whole phasalist approach on account of the counterintuitive implications we’ve highlighted here. But you know what they say about throwing stones in glass houses. (We’re looking at you universalists, nihilists, mereological essentialists, plenitudinists, and all Lewisians.) What’s more, Mooney does attempt to ameliorate some of his troubles by developing a nonstandard account of what it means to be “the same F” (125-133). This account allows him to say that the tiny vining plant is the same plant as the (numerically distinct) massive plant that was once covering the wall (153), that the piece of lead is not the same piece of matter as the piece of gold that it becomes (cf. 139), and that the filled-in Statue of Liberty is the same statue as the (distinct) statue with the core removed (140). In any case, whether or not these efforts to render the view more palatable succeed, it really is a tidy picture that Mooney gives us: all material objects are ultimately the same sort of thing, all with the same persistence conditions, and within Mooney’s system it is always clear which object is which.
But even for those who, like us, are unconvinced, there is great value in the book. In the course of developing his own tidy and extreme (tidy because extreme!) metaphysics of material objects, Mooney touches on various decision points for the phasalist, and in doing so, effectively illuminates a whole family of underexplored phasalist approaches. We see his book as a helpful jumping-off point for a fruitful investigation of the different versions of phasalism.
Indeed, Mooney himself at times contemplates departing from spatiotemporalism in ways that could secure a more intuitive treatment of some of the cases we’ve mentioned. In connection with the vine case, he makes an intriguing suggestion that the spatiotemporal continuity condition could in principle be relaxed in cases where some other robust form of continuity is present (71). If biological and psychological continuity are permitted to trump spatiotemporal continuity in this way, the phasalist could say that Jasmine survives as the amputee, since the one-legged girl exhibits significant continuity of both sorts with Jasmine pre-amputation. The downside of such adjustments is that the view gets messier, and is unable to deliver clear verdicts about the full range of cases unless supplemented with guidelines for what trumps spatiotemporal continuity and under what conditions. But for those (like us) who doubt that a tidy metaphysics can capture the messiness of our world, this is a promising avenue to explore.
Another version of phasalism pairs it with a view on which there are two fundamentally different types of material objects, only one of which is subject to the spatiotemporal criterion. For instance, Carmichael (2015) develops a view on which there are, at bottom, two kinds of material objects. First, there are “lump-like objects”, which include stones, statues, sweaters, lumps, and pieces of yarn. Second, there are “event-based objects”, paradigmatically, organisms. By adopting the spatiotemporal criterion just for the former, and applying, e.g., a biological criterion to the latter, we can retain the phasalist treatment of statues and sweaters, while also securing the intuitively correct result in the various remnant survival cases (including Jasmine). This view would also, for better or worse, entail that living organisms do not persist as corpses.
Finally, it’s worth exploring what we might call a “pure immanence” view. As indicated above, persistence (on Mooney’s view) requires a sort of causal continuity: an object persists partly in virtue of the fact that there being something that’s a certain way at the later time is “immanently caused” by there being something that was (largely) that way at the immediately preceding time (44-46). Perhaps this causal constraint can stand on its own, without any spatial or temporal constraints. When multiple objects at some later time are immanently caused to have some range of properties by O having those properties at the earlier time, O survives as whichever object is immanently caused to have O’s properties to a greater (and sufficient) extent. This would, among other things, open the door to persistence across a temporal gap (see Zimmerman, 1999).
4. Concluding Remarks
Two thumbs up! An impressive debut from Mooney.

Helsinki stocks recorded their largest one-day decline of 2026 on Monday, with Nokia losing more than 10 per cent as a global technology sell-off spread to Finland.
The Helsinki Stock Exchange’s general index closed 2.99 per cent lower. The fall exceeded the previous largest daily decline this year, recorded in March when the index dropped 2.7 per cent following the US and Israeli attack on Iran.
Nokia led trading volumes and suffered its largest one-day decline of the year. The network equipment maker’s shares fell more than 10 per cent.
Finnish industrial companies also lost ground. Wärtsilä closed 6.9 per cent lower and Metso fell 5.2 per cent.
Technology shares came under pressure worldwide after executives at US artificial intelligence companies called for a slower pace of AI development over safety concerns.
Anthropic chief Dario Amodei wrote on Saturday that companies should slow advances in AI model capabilities and increase monitoring. Other AI executives have also backed tighter safety measures.
Wall Street also opened lower on Monday, led by technology shares. Rising oil prices and expectations of a US Federal Reserve interest-rate increase this week added to pressure on markets.
Summa Defence faces bankruptcy risk
Summa Defence recorded a separate fall after the Finnish defence and security technology company announced that its working capital had run out and its liquidity had deteriorated.
Its shares fell about 47 per cent to €0.20 during Monday trading, according to Ilta-Sanomat.
Summa Defence said it had no confirmed additional financing sufficient to secure operations under its previous plans. The company said it was unable to meet payment obligations as they fell due without immediate financing or other liquidity arrangements.
The company is considering options involving subsidiaries IntLog, Lightspace Group and Aquamec, alongside possible asset sales and additional financing. It is also assessing whether it meets the conditions for corporate restructuring.
Summa Defence warned that its parent company faces bankruptcy if it fails to secure enough financing or another solution. The company listed on the Helsinki Stock Exchange in June 2025. Its shares have lost about 90 per cent since the start of this year, Verkkouutiset reported.
Despite Monday’s decline, the Helsinki market’s general index remains about 9.6 per cent higher since the beginning of 2026, according to Helsingin Sanomat.

Richard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’ | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:05:50 UTC
02:05:50 KST

Never in the field of British politics has so much been given to so many by so few. You’d have thought Nigel Farage would have wanted to explain Reform’s sudden windfall from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo himself. To bask in the glory of the donations from two down-to-earth, anti-establishment crypto billionaires. Men who know what it’s like to graft, who know the meaning of an honest day’s work for an honest day’s pay.
There again, Nige is keen not to appear as a one-man band these days and he could do with some downtime to enjoy his own £5m handout. And besides, he’s got a police investigation into Reform party funding to worry about. Even so, it wasn’t the best of looks to send Richard Tice out on to the morning media round. Dicky may have his talents, but he keeps them well concealed. His main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy. But he does always leave you guessing. Is he being wilfully stupid or is he naturally that half witted?
Dicky began with a howl of protest. No rules had been broken. He made that sound as if it came as a surprise to him. I guess that’s an easy mistake for anyone to make. Everything was in the rules as they exist. Labour was mounting a coup against Reform for having passed legislation through the Commons that would prevent donors living overseas from giving more than £100,000 until they had lived in the UK for more than a calendar year, backdated to March 2026. You’d have thought Nige might have clocked this. But he probably hadn’t been in Westminster that day. And you can’t trust Dicky to be over the details.
“Our money comes with no demands,” Dicky told Nick Robinson on the Today programme. Harborne and Delo were patriots. All they wanted was to save the country from being ruined by socialists and the rightwing Tories. Quite where he thought Reform fitted in on this particular continuum wasn’t clear. Presumably in the centre ground of British politics. Ordinary men and women who want to rescue their country from the do-goodery of the RNLI.
“Patriots” was doing some heavy lifting here. Harborne had decamped to Thailand in the 90s, had become a Thai citizen in 2011 and had taken a Thai name. Now we learned that Dicky believed in dialectics. The more someone looked as if they were trying to put as much distance between themselves and the UK, the greater their commitment to the UK really was. Chris had just been playing very hard to get. The reality was he had been begging HMRC to ask him back so he could pay his fair share to the exchequer.
Fine, said Robinson. When did he move back to the UK and does he now pay UK tax? Dicky was understandably clueless. He had no idea he was going to be asked whether Harborne complied with the law as it was going through parliament. I’m not his tax adviser, he protested, though if he was he would make sure he paid as little as possible. Dicky has always been upfront in his belief that only the little people pay tax. And as for Harborne’s whereabouts, he wasn’t his diary secretary. He just telepathically knew that Chris had complied with the law as it was and as it was proposed.
It was the same with Delo. No man had ever loved his country more. From Hong Kong. Who wouldn’t want to receive money from a billionaire who had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with money-laundering laws and had been pardoned by Donald Trump? Dicky had no idea when Ben had come back to the country. That sort of level of detail was well above his pay grade. He was just here for the front-of-house stuff. The meet and greet. No one should expect any more from him than that.
Then the killer line. “I hope you will trust the word of our compliance team,” said Dicky. They would assure listeners everything was above board. So touching. So sweet. Up till now, no one had any idea Reform even had a compliance team. They certainly hadn’t been much in evidence while James Orr and Dan Jukes had been negotiating a possible £500,000 gift from an overseas donor. And in the taped conversation, which Nige insisted he hadn’t been listening to, Farage had said, “it’s all above board”.
So, if it’s all the same, we won’t be taking the word of an imaginary compliance team. Nick pressed on. What did Dicky think had attracted two crypto billionaires to a party that had promised to cut taxes on crypto, to limit regulation of the industry and had threatened to remove the governor of the Bank of England if he didn’t play ball?
Dicky couldn’t quite put his finger on it. But he thought it was probably something to do with them really caring about a £500 tax break. And the pleasure of paying for Nige’s hideous suit. Champagne and oysters all round.
There was just time for Robinson to point out that, far from getting nothing for their donations, the two men had already got everything they wanted and more. “Not at all,” Dicky insisted. Because Reform had promised to deregulate and cut tax before the two men had handed over the £72m. Where can you go with someone as dim as Dicky? A tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity. Though Harborne and Delo just have.
It was left to Farage himself to clear up Tice’s mess later in the day in a BBC interview. Well, sort of. Yes, Delo and Harborne’s donations probably wouldn’t meet the necessary deadlines for the legislation going through parliament. But you couldn’t blame Reform for taking the cash. Rather it was the fault of the government for putting in place regulations that Reform might not now be able to get round. As so often with Nige, there was always someone else to blame.
Not that Labour was immune from a little hypocrisy. It had been Burnham who had tried to bury the plan to limit donations to all parties. Something the unions had pushed back against. But the £72m has rather concentrated everyone’s minds. Once the current legislation was through parliament there would still be a good year to pass another law to impose a cap. Down in Brighton, Angela Rayner wanted the TUC to know she was on their side. There was no equivalence between Labour funding from the unions and money from two crypto billionaires. Politics could be bought. Just by the right sort of people.

Bolsonaro 2.0: Brazil braces for the return of the far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:04:05 UTC
02:04:05 KST

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.
“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.
With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.
Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.
Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”
“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.
Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.
A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.
Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.
Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.
But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.
“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.
“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.
Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.
Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.
“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.
For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.
Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.
Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.
Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.
Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.
“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”
As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.
César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”
A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

Türkiye to test first homegrown lunar spacecraft ahead of 2027 mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:02:52 UTC
02:02:52 KST

Türkiye completed the production and assembly of its first lunar spacecraft, transferring the 3.5-metric-tonne craft to Turkish Aerospace Industries (TAI) for environmental testing, the industry and technology minister said in a recent statement.
Mehmet Fatih Kacir said the craft is scheduled for launch from the Kennedy Space Center in early 2027 and will take around two months to reach a 100-kilometer (62.13-mile) polar orbit around the Moon.
The craft will operate in lunar orbit for three months, with the potential to extend its operation to a year and a half, during which solar winds, water formation, magnetic fields and surface radiation will be evaluated through homegrown scientific instruments.
Kacir stated that these efforts have been made to realise “a fully independent Türkiye in critical technologies,” following the country’s similar approach in its defence industry.
The spacecraft includes critical flight, communications and power systems developed for the previous Imece and Turksat 6A satellite projects, boasting an 80% domestic production rate.
“The further tests will verify the spacecraft’s ability to withstand the harsh conditions it will encounter during launch and in the space environment,” he said. The craft will then be transferred to a new cleanroom facility of the Turkish Scientific and Technological Research Institution (Tubitak) Space for final inspections.
The craft will use a homegrown hybrid propulsion system for orbit-raising maneuvers and a final controlled deceleration burn to reach the lunar surface at the end of the primary scientific mission.
“Only eight countries have carried out lunar missions so far, and when we implement our programme, Türkiye will become the ninth country,” the minister noted.
These developments follow the country’s recent accession to the Artemis Accords, signed to promote global cooperation in the peaceful exploration of the Moon and deep space.
Kacir stated that development of the Turksat 7A communications satellite has begun alongside the design phases of the Imece-2 and Imece-3 Earth observation satellite constellations.
Meanwhile, Ankara is constructing a spaceport in Somalia to eventually provide independent access to space and reduce reliance on foreign launch facilities.
The Turkish government is also collaborating with the Turkish Space Agency and the Middle East Technical University (METU) to establish a space tech development zone in Ankara to extend the rapid growth of Turkish defence into the country’s space sector by integrating more tech startups with the national space manufacturing ecosystem.
The southwestern coastal city of Antalya will host the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) from Oct. 5-9 to showcase these expanding capabilities to nearly 10,000 global participants.

Germany to deploy remaining soldiers to Lithuania after volunteer shortfall
Unknown

2026-09-14
17:00:20 UTC
02:00:20 KST

By the end of 2027, around 4,800 German troops are expected to be stationed permanently in Lithuania as part of the 45th Panzer Brigade, on NATO's eastern flank.
The German military is turning to compulsory assignments to fill positions in a brigade stationed in Lithuania. The move is said to be necessary because of difficulties recruiting enough volunteers, leaving a shortage of specialist personnel. According to information obtained by Bild, the first soldiers could be ordered to serve in Lithuania from the end of September, with up to 1,000 Bundeswehr personnel potentially affected.
By the end of 2027, the 45th Panzer Brigade is expected to have around 4,800 German troops and be permanently based in Lithuania, on NATO's eastern flank. The brigade's main base will be in Rūdninkai, around 30 kilometres from Belarus. It's aim: deterrence against Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at this year's Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland, that "most likely we are seeing the most decicive moments, perhaps weeks or months, ahead of us in defending the freedom and peace of our continent."
"This is what I see and what I mean. If Russia succeeds, this will have unpredicted and unprecedented consequences for all of us, including Germany," he continued, adding that that "that's the reason why I'm standing here, very firm, very clear and not willing to go back one centimetre. this is now our historic duty to do what we can, to help this country to preserve peace and freedom in Europe."
Bild was the first to report on the planned compulsory assignments, the Defence Ministry has since confirmed the measures. Almost 80% of the brigade's positions are currently filled by volunteers.
"According to current forecasts, and in view of the continued influx of volunteer applications, the number of compulsory postings is expected to be in the mid three-figure range," the ministry said in a press release. "Maintaining the Bundeswehr's operational readiness is the top priority and the decisive criterion for all measures," it continued.
"In all decisions, the personal interests of service personnel will be taken into account as far as possible." Germany's Defence Ministry plans to brief members of the Defence Committee on Monday on the next steps. For those affected, a compulsory posting means additional notice. They also have the right to challenge the decision in court.
German troops in Lithuania: tanks, drones and deterrence
Euronews accompanied two soldiers from Panzer Battalion 203 during the "Freedom Shield" exercise last June. Their battalion is to be redeployed to NATO’s eastern flank by the end of 2027.
In an interview with Euronews, the battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Oliver Kaufmann, said that Panzer Battalion 203 has "actually a very high proportion of volunteers."
"I can speak for my battalion, and the majority of soldiers are willing to go to Lithuania voluntarily, and that is exactly what I want: I want soldiers by my side who are convinced of the mission and who, as part of the Panzer Battalion 203 team, take on this responsible task," said Kaufmann.
Among the forces already stationed in Lithuania, the staffing rate is about 92%. These forces include, in particular, the multinational battlegroup that has been stationed there since 2017.
Panzer Battalion 203 and Panzergrenadier Battalion 122 are not due to be moved to Lithuania until 2027. According to the investigation, around 40% of the personnel required for those units are still missing.
Watch the Euronews exclusive documentary German troops in Lithuania: tanks, drones and deterrence to see how Germany is strengthening NATO's eastern flank.

Feeling nervous? Work the system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Feeling nervous? Work the system
Take a deep breath — there are tons of ways to regulate your nervous system
When you’re stressed, you lose control. Your sympathetic nervous system takes over, triggering the release of stress hormones into the bloodstream, which increases heart rate, blood pressure and breathing pace. These changes happen involuntarily, whether you’re facing true danger or just an overflowing email inbox. But scientists are learning how to regain some control, guiding the nervous system out of fight-or-flight mode and into relaxation.
Some techniques for doing so are probably already second nature, like recentering yourself with slow, deep breaths. But there’s also mounting data to support a range of zany-sounding practices, including humming, tapping on the skin and cold-water immersion. “Consciously, you can’t tell your heart to slow down,” says neurologist Patricio Millar Vernetti of NYU Langone Health. “But by doing these interventions, you have a little bit more control.”
On social media, these practices are often described as ways to “regulate” the nervous system. They’re actually ways to call off the sympathetic nervous system and let the calming parasympathetic nervous system take over, leading to lower stress hormone levels, heart rate and blood pressure. Doing so successfully may yield significant health benefits, since an over- active stress response can, over time, contribute to hypertension, strain on the heart, excess inflammation and other issues.
Stimulating the vagus nerve, which runs from the brain stem to the abdomen, is one way to activate the parasympathetic nervous system. Breathing exercises can stimulate the nerve. A trendier approach, cold therapy, might too, research suggests. In a small study, scientists observed 25 people as they performed mental math. Twelve participants wore a facial cooling mask beforehand, meant to mimic submerging the face in cold water —a known way to stimulate the vagus nerve. Their levels of the stress hormone cortisol spiked lower and returned to baseline faster than those of people who hadn’t worn the mask, the team reported in 2022 in Scientific Reports.
Techniques like humming and tapping on the skin also seem to activate the parasympathetic nervous system. Slow breathing plus humming can increase heart rate variability, a measure of the fluctuating time between heartbeats, scientists reported last year in Physiology & Behavior. High heart rate variability is a marker of a well-regulated nervous system. It signals that “your body is doing less fighting itself on the inside” and is seamlessly switching between stress and relaxation, says physical therapist Karin Steere of the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Wash.
Tapping on specific spots on the skin, meanwhile, may generate electrochemical signals that travel from nerves to the brain, telling the parasympathetic nervous system that it’s time to take over, argued a 2025 research review. Existing data suggests tapping can lead to drops in stress hormone levels as well as declines in heart rate and blood pressure. The practice is also one element of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing therapy, a treatment for conditions such as PTSD.
There are small, one-off pilot studies supporting nearly every viral nervous system regulation technique, says Darshan Mehta, medical director of the Benson-Henry Institute for Mind Body Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. That means it’s hard to identify one superior tactic. “It’s not important which practice [people adopt],” Mehta says. “It’s important that people do practice.”
Modern science isn’t the only support for these practices, Vernetti says. Chanting and humming, for instance, are part of some ancient spiritual practices. “This is one of those things that science has caught up with relatively recently,” he says, “but people have been doing for centuries.”
