Will strategic Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:58:17 UTC
01:58:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Will the strategic province of Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
Amid the renewed fighting between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and government forces and the Houthis’ capture of the whole of the country’s Red Sea coast, there is increasing speculation that the oil-rich province of Marib will be the next major theatre of conflict.
For many years, Marib has served as an impenetrable barrier against the expansion of the Houthi movement. It is one of the last strongholds of the internationally recognised government in northern Yemen and occupies a strategically important position 120 kilometres east of the capital Sana’a, which was captured by the Houthis in 2014.
Government forces in the area have so far adopted a defensive strategy, but amid the renewed fighting, it could become a base for them to seize the initiative and launch offensive operations.
This strategic shift has already been reflected on the ground in recent developments. Last week, government forces announced the launch of a wide-ranging military operation to take control of Houthi-held areas of the province.
These included an intensive assault by units of the Seventh Military Region, which broke through Houthi defences and recaptured strategic positions northwest of Marib city, alongside a successful flanking operation in the Mahzam Mas area.
In the south, government forces also took control of the Al-Akad Al-Ramli area and positions near Mount Al-Balaq amid fierce fighting that resulted in many deaths and the capture of Houthi prisoners as well as the seizure of military vehicles.
These operations coincided with the Yemeni armed forces repelling two major attacks launched by the Houthis against military positions in the south and west of the province. 
The fighting was described as the most severe since 2021 and has marked the beginning of a new phase on the battlefield, in which the government is on the attack.
The government currently maintains full control over the province’s heartland and all its strategic points.
The tipping point of the Yemeni conflict
Marib is seen as the tipping point of the balance of power in Yemen – a key area on which the entire structure of the internationally recognised government rests.
It covers 17,478 square kilometres, with terrain ranging from rugged mountainous areas to vast desert plains.
Its population before the war was around 348,000, but around two million internally displaced people have fled there, living in hundreds of camps and shelters.
This places enormous pressure on its infrastructure and public services.
As the last major stronghold of the government in northern Yemen, it has become a key administrative centre where state institutions and military and security forces are concentrated.
Its survival is seen as key to the continuation of the Yemeni national project. 
Militarily, Marib is a highly complex and vital geographical hub. It forms a strategic link between Al-Jawf, Sanaa, Al-Bayda, Shabwa and Hadramawt province, while also acting as a fortress that has repelled some of the Houthis’ fiercest attacks. 
The fronts surrounding it have therefore become the first line of defence for Yemen’s east and south.
Financial and military lifeline
Economically, Marib is the country’s most important financial lifeline. It contains the major oil and gas fields in Safer, as well as a key power station, which supplies large areas of the country with electricity. It also generates sovereign revenues that finance a significant portion of state expenditure and essential services.
The military control map in Marib is characterised by considerable geographical complexity, with front lines intersecting and defensive and offensive positions overlapping between government forces and tribes on one side and the Houthi movement on the other.
While the government controls most of the province, including Marib city and the strategically important Al-Wadi district, the Houthis are present in peripheral mountain and desert areas, including areas bordering Al-Jawf governorate to the north and Al-Bayda and Shabwa governorates to the south and west.
This military overlap makes Marib an open front, with every possibility still on the table. Government forces are attempting to secure their security perimeter by taking control of  high ground in frontline districts, thereby cutting off potential routes for Houthi missile launches and ground attacks on the province’s population centres.
The potential military and strategic objectives of a government offensive appear clearly defined.
Military and political objectives
One major objective is to recapture the remaining districts under Houthi control, as well as secure and clear the western and northwestern areas bordering Sanaa and Al-Jawf. 
These areas have served for years as major launching platforms for missile and drone attacks against residential neighbourhoods and critical infrastructure in Marib city.
Government forces are supported by a paramilitary organisation called the Popular Resistance, made up of residents of Houthi-controlled governorates who have been displaced to Marib. 
Government-allied tribal fighters also constitute an active force, possessing heavy weapons and extensive knowledge of the terrain. 
On the Houthi side, the movement relies on mobilising ideological and regional military formations belonging to what it calls the “Central Military Region.” These are stationed at strategic camps that the Houthis have seized and converted into advanced offensive platforms.
The most prominent include Mas Camp in northwestern Marib, as well as the Tamah and Khashm Al-Jafina camps.
The Houthis rely heavily on a war of attrition, using an arsenal of ballistic missiles and drones to attack government positions.
Government camps and fronts constitute the final defensive shields protecting the population centres, economy and energy facilities, while Houthi camps serve as major launch bases for threatening the front lines and attempting to penetrate the defensive perimeter around Marib city.
If the government does manage to make major advances in Marib, taking control of some or all of the Houthi positions in the province, this would represent a major turning point capable of redrawing the map of Yemen’s conflict and altering the balance of power.
Politically, it would likely push the Houthis toward serious engagement with peace negotiations while militarily opening routes towards the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Most importantly, it would constitute clear confirmation of the internationally recognised government’s ability to determine the outcome of the conflict and restore confidence in the Yemeni national project.

DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday reviewed the functioning of the CM Helpline 1905 at the Secretariat and directed officials to ensure the swift, time-bound and satisfactory resolution of public grievances.The chief minister said that the CM Helpline is an important mechanism for addressing the problems of the common people. The chief minister directed the chief development officer, Haridwar, to inspect the site and ensure immediate commencement of the water supply.The chief minister spoke to Dehradun resident Shilpi Saxena, who informed him that a streetlight had been installed in her area within the stipulated timeframe after she lodged a complaint on the CM Helpline. She thanked the chief minister for resolving the issue.Similarly, Almora resident Ayush Bisht informed the chief minister that his complaint related to a scholarship had been resolved by the department. Dr Andreas Krieg, a Middle East security expert at King's College London, told The New Arab that US reluctance did create an opening for Israel "in a narrow military sense", but warned against interpreting this as the beginning of a new Saudi-Israeli security alignment.
"Riyadh does not want to move from dependence on Washington to dependence on an Israeli security architecture," Krieg said.
"The Saudis increasingly regard Israel itself as one of the actors generating regional instability. They may see tactical convergence against Iran or the Houthis, but that is very different from trusting Israel with the defence of the Kingdom."
Israel has a direct interest in preventing the Houthis from consolidating their position around Bab al-Mandab.
The strait, just under 30 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and is one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints.
For Israel, it is also the maritime gateway connecting the southern port of Eilat with the Indian Ocean.
Houthi attacks on commercial shipping following the outbreak of Israel's war on Gaza had already severely disrupted Red Sea traffic, while Israel has repeatedly struck Yemen in response to Houthi missile and drone attacks.
Krieg said Israel could potentially offer sophisticated intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare, cyber and targeting capabilities, as well as its experience attacking Houthi missile, drone and command infrastructure.
But the fundamental Saudi problem, he said, was not a shortage of military firepower.
"The Saudi problem is therefore not primarily a lack of aircraft or bombs. It is political and strategic," Krieg said.
"Air strikes can destroy launchers, warehouses and command centres, but they cannot permanently remove the Houthis from Bab al-Mandab or govern territory in Yemen. Saudi Arabia discovered this painfully during its previous intervention."
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis beginning in 2015, but years of airstrikes and fighting failed to defeat the Houthis, who consolidated control over much of northern Yemen while developing increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities.
Renewed Houthi advances now confront Riyadh with a difficult strategic problem as insecurity affects both of the principal maritime routes connecting Gulf energy exports with international markets.
Iran threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi control around Bab al-Mandab puts additional pressure on the Red Sea route. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, designed to bypass Hormuz by carrying oil to the Red Sea coast, has also demonstrated its vulnerability after coming under drone attack.
Yet direct Israeli involvement could potentially worsen Saudi Arabia's predicament.
Krieg said overt Israeli assistance could bolster the Houthi claim that Riyadh was fighting as part of an Israeli-American coalition, while increasing the domestic and regional political costs for Saudi Arabia.
It could also make Saudi infrastructure appear an increasingly legitimate target to Iran and its regional allies.
Some indirect cooperation remains conceivable, particularly intelligence passed through American channels, Krieg said, while Saudi and Israeli forces could separately operate against the same threat.
But he cautioned that parallel operations "should not automatically be interpreted as an alliance or even close coordination".
Instead, Riyadh appears to be seeking a more diversified security architecture as doubts grow about Washington's willingness to bear the costs of defending its Gulf partners.
Krieg pointed to Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, alongside European maritime partners and greater Gulf and Arab-Islamic security cooperation, as more likely components of Saudi Arabia's attempt to reduce its dependence on Washington.
"The lesson Riyadh appears to be drawing is not that Israel should replace the United States," he said.
"The lesson is that Saudi Arabia needs a much more diversified security system in which it has greater agency."
Israel's willingness to intervene against the Houthis therefore exposes a convergence of Israeli and Saudi interests, particularly around Red Sea security, without necessarily bringing the two countries strategically closer.
"Replacing American dependency with Israeli dependency would not represent strategic autonomy," Krieg said.
"From the Saudi perspective, it would simply exchange one vulnerability for another, and potentially for a much more politically dangerous one."

Why has university become such a scam? | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:55:50 UTC
01:55:50 KST

It wasn’t in relation to university that I first came across the organisation Rethink Repayment, which campaigns for a fairer settlement on student debt. I was looking into the astronomical numbers of young people who still live with their parents. It’s now more than a third of young men and more than a fifth of young women, statistics that get even crunchier when you realise that “young” describes anyone under 35.
There were various reasons – some had gone home after a health crisis, some really liked their parents, some were battling unemployment, but the single unifying theme was student debt. Those on incomes too low to start repaying couldn’t make rent; those in the lower repayment bracket (an annual income of £25,000 or thereabouts, depending on your loan plan) still couldn’t make rent, because they were spending 9% of their income repaying. And those on more than £50,000 were keeping less than 50p in every pound they earn because of their marginal tax rate. It’s always been sold to students when they take on this debt that it won’t count against their mortgage raising capacity, which technically it won’t – but any affordability check by a mortgage company or letting agent will factor in the monthly repayments.
It feels tactless to bring this up, just as a fresh wave of students heads off, with bigger, more exciting things on their minds than long-term debt. Yet it also feels remiss not to mention the fact that they’re being absolutely had. Florence, 29, who works as a solicitor in commercial litigation, is still living at home. She told me: “A lot of the time I’m reviewing contracts, and saying: ‘This is enforceable, sue them.’ The holes in what we were told are shocking. If student loans had come from an institutional lender, we would have a class action lawsuit.”
Without lingering on the unedifying details, such as how we’re all feeling about Nick Clegg nowadays, a quick recap on what the debate around student fees looked like when they were first hiked to £9,000 in 2012. There was a lot of anxiety about whether the government would ever get its money back, or whether a huge amount of this debt would have to be written off – what we didn’t factor in back then was that, this being the government, they could make the rules. If they wanted the interest on student loans to be set at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3%, they could simply snap their fingers and make it so. We talked a lot, too, about what those capped fees meant for universities – 10 years ago, £9,000 wasn’t enough for some courses but it was more than they needed for “classroom subjects” (a lot of humanities), which could then cross-subsidise. Now, with fees only increased to £9,790 in more than a decade, they often don’t even cover humanities courses – so worries about the sheer viability of what was previously one of the nation’s most successful sectors were well founded.
The students themselves were almost a side issue in this debate: the promise was that the debt would be more than offset by their increased earning capacity, once they had a degree, and, anyway, wouldn’t affect them until they could well afford it. This has turned out to be wildly untrue. Graduates are leaving with an average burden of £53,000, four or five times what it was in 2009, and the interest rates mean they can spend years repaying without making a dent in that amount. Graduate vacancies, meanwhile, were down 45% in August, compared with the same month last year, which is casually blamed on AI wiping out entry level jobs. Responsibility would be better situated with employers, who are choosing short-term cost-saving over their duty to their own companies, their society and the future.
It’s one thing to deprioritise the younger generation, it’s another to straight up scam them. I don’t want to tell any political party its business, but the one that makes a better offer than “pretend the problem doesn’t exist” stands to make enormous headway, and not just with the under-35s.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:54:45 UTC
01:54:45 KST

Breadcrumb
After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
Damascus, Syria - The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were dissolved by their commander-in-chief, Mazloum Abdi, on 25 August, bringing an end to Rojava, a 14-year-old experiment in autonomous self-administration in northeast Syria.
Abdi is to take up a new role as a special adviser to President Ahmed al-Sharaa, whilst the senior leadership will occupy various positions within the government.
Sipan Hamo, the former head of the YPG - the primary fighting force of the SDF - had already taken up a position as Deputy Defence Minister for the Eastern Region. Ilham Ahmed, the head of the SDF’s civilian administration, is reported to have been offered a position in parliament.
The dissolution comes seven months after a surprise government offensive in January against the SDF, which saw the armed group lose large swathes of its northeastern territory and be forced into an integration agreement.
Since then, the integration has been advancing on the ground, with this latest development being “largely symbolic” according to Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the This Week in Northern Syria newsletter.
“Although the SDF is technically dissolved, on the ground its military and civilian structures continue to operate,” he explained to The New Arab.
“They work in parallel to the government structures that are increasingly visible as integration continues.”
The future for female Kurdish fighters
As part of the dissolution, Mazloum Abdi announced that the SDF’s military had been entirely integrated into the Ministry of Defence.
However, there was one major oversight. Seated next to Abdi during his meeting with al-Sharaa was Nowruz Ahmed, the commander of the YPJ - the SDF’s all-female fighting force.
The YPJ were prohibited from joining the Ministry of Defence because the “government simply has a perspective that women don’t belong in the military,” says McKeever.
Following the announcement, the YPJ released a statement about a meeting with the Ministry of Interior saying, “it was emphasised that the YPJ could be integrated, as a distinct organised force, into the Ministry of Interior”.
There had been previous reports that the YPJ had been offered a role as a counter-terror unit within the Ministry of Defence, but this was denied by Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, a week before the announcement.
She acknowledged that previously they had been offered to integrate into the Interior Ministry as administrative staff, which they rejected outright.
“It should not have reached a point where the dissolution was announced before a solution to the YPJ issue was found,” Muaz Al-Abdullah, a Middle East Research Manager at ACLED, a conflict tracking organisation, told The New Arab.
“It reflects the balance of power between the two sides, where Damascus is largely able to dictate terms in negotiations.”
However, this strategy presents a danger, he adds, “it will ultimately give a group of trained fighters the reasoning to go against the government either as a group or as lone wolves”.
What role for the Kurdish language?
Another bone of contention surrounds the future role of the Kurdish language within the northeast’s education system.
Many Kurds fear a return to the situation under the Assad regime, before the ‘Rojava Revolution’ in 2012, in which “the state did not recognise Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian identity. Kurdish language instruction and Kurdish cultural expression were banned,” explains McKeever.
As a result, al-Sharaa has sought to assuage Kurdish fears. In January, following the offensive against the SDF, he announced the recognition of Kurdish as a ‘national language’.
However, McKeever notes that this does not make Kurdish an ‘official’ language of Syria. Syria doesn’t currently have a full constitution, with the law either operating on old Assad-era mandates or 2025’s constitutional declaration.
“Full recognition of Kurdish as an official language may come with the drafting of the constitution but, for now, we cannot know,” he says.
As part of the integration agreement between the SDF and the government, Damascus has stipulated a one-year transition period in which Kurdish language classes are offered for three hours per week, alongside one hour for an elective class on a number of topics like women's history, sociology, or philosophy.
The system for the years after has yet to be decided upon. However, for the last 14 years, Kurdish has been the medium of education and so the disagreement between the SDF and Damascus “comes down to whether there will be a fully translated curriculum”.
Effect on the Turkish peace process
The dissolution of the SDF would have been considerably harder to achieve without the parallel peace process between Turkey and the PKK.
In October 2024, Ankara announced that it was commencing negotiations with the PKK, a Kurdish armed group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the government.
In May 2025, following a call by its leader Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK announced that it would destroy its weapons and dissolve.
Turkey considered the SDF as the Syrian branch of the PKK, and so “Turkey is the biggest winner in this whole situation,” Al-Abdullah tells The New Arab.
“The whole Kurdish situation is shifting regionally with Kurdish non-state actors increasingly having to engage with their relative states,” he adds.
“The dissolution of the SDF will only add onus on the PKK to reach a settlement with the Turks.”
However, it is regarding language rights that Turkey’s Kurds might have the most to gain from the SDF integration agreement.
“Turkey completely banned the Kurdish language, and has struggled with the Kurdish file for decades, partly as a result,” Henri Barkey, an Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The New Arab.
“Whilst the deal that was signed in Syria is bad on language rights, it is far better than what Turkish Kurds have, and so they might look to Syria as a model for their own aims in negotiations.”
Managing Kurdish fears
The Syrian government is seeking to simultaneously entrench its control over the northeast whilst allaying Kurdish fears and distrust of the government.
According to analysts, many Kurds are sceptical of the government's Islamist roots, and its history of violence against minority groups, including a series of massacres targeting Alawite and Druze minorities.
For Barkey, “Sharaa can’t afford to alienate the Kurds as they have over a decade of experience organising and fighting”.
Equally, many in the local Arab communities distrust the SDF and its leadership, due to the perception that, despite the SDF’s official support for ethnic pluralism, it developed a system that centralised power in the hands of Kurdish communities at the expense of local Arabs.
The “greatest challenge” lies in knitting together a social fabric between “communities that have often lived separately for the last decade, with displaced Kurds now returning to areas with large Arab populations and displaced Arabs doing the same in reverse,” says Mckeever.
In August, a convoy of displaced Kurds, who were returning to Ras Al-Ain, were attacked by local Arabs, which triggered a day of riots by Kurds against the government in Hasakah and Qamishli.
A day later, an attack by unknown elements on a security point manned by former SDF fighters who had been recently integrated into the Ministry of Defence killed three and injured several.
“This is the same pattern that you see across Syria along these social fault lines, where you have old grievances and a lack of security,” Mckeever adds.
Whereas for ACLED’s Al-Abdullah, the primary risk is that integration “will remain political, and that Kurds won't actually be brought into the national community and so will continue to identify as Kurdish more so than Syrian”.
The government has offered senior SDF leadership positions, likely so they can play the role of “intermediary between the state and the Kurdish communities within which they still have a lot of support”.
What next?
Whilst integration is far from finished, the dissolution of the SDF has “expedited certain things on the ground,” explains Mckeever.
The government’s internal security forces, previously only deployed within the grounds of a few government compounds, have reportedly deployed to a number of Arab neighbourhoods in Hasakah city.
Equally, certain SDF internal security units have begun the integration process and will likely begin patrols under the Syrian flag.
For al-Sharaa, with integration and the Kurdish file moving from a major political issue to one more technical and bureaucratic, he can likely turn his attention to the last holdout beyond the control of the state - Suweida.
The dissolution of the SDF represents the death knell for a vision for Syria, advocated by Israel and the Druze militias in Suweida, of fragmentation.
“With the government empowered domestically and backed internationally by the US and Turkey, it will be looking towards resolving the Suweida situation,” Al-Abdullah says.
“Israel is using Suweida as a card, and will likely abandon it when its interests require,” says Al-Abdullah.
“The Syrian government now needs to be working on winning back the people of Suweida, who felt so betrayed by the government's actions against them.”
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward

French candidates race to claim the cost-of-living issue ahead of 2027 vote
A new Ipsos survey reveals a country gripped by pessimism, with soaring prices the top worry for French voters ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. Candidates from far-right leader Marine Le Pen, to the far-left's Jean-Luc Mélenchon are racing to make the cost of living the defining issue of their campaigns.
With seven months to go before the presidential election in France, a wave of pessimism seems to be gripping voters.
Only 17 percent feel hopeful, according to a poll of 13,060 registered voters released on Sunday by Ipsos France. The vast majority – 91 percent – of respondents reported negative sentiments regarding the current state of affairs, citing emotions dominated by worry, uncertainty and anger. This year, 59 percent of voters specifically said they felt worried, compared to 38 percent in 2021.
“The direct consequences of these negative emotions, of this worry, is a much deeper desire for radical change than in 2022,” Ipsos director Brice Teinturier told French daily Le Monde in an interview on Monday.
Voters increasingly want concrete action. And they want to see change in what arguably affects their daily lives the most – the cost of living.
“What concerns voters most of all is the issue of purchasing power,” Teinturier explained. “It is economic and social issues, far more than immigration, that are of concern.”

Breaking point
It is not the first time the cost of living has been a central concern for voters. It was a major issue ahead of both the 2017 and 2022 presidential elections in France. But with the cost of necessities like housing, fuel and food continuing to rise, the issue has hit a breaking point.
“The anger people feel is towards the political elite, who they feel don’t take care of them or address their daily concerns,” explained Jean-Yves Camus, French political scientist and research fellow at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs.
“Even the middle class understands there is an issue. I consider myself upper middle class and I am not sure that my two children will be able to live in Paris a few years from now. They earn a decent income. [...] But when there are four or five people in the family, you need to go quite far from the city to be able to afford a decent living," Camus said.
Read moreThe price of Paris: What does it cost to live in the French capital?
As successive heatwaves have damaged crop yields and driven up agricultural costs, and the war in Iran has pushed up fuel and energy prices, "the price in supermarkets has surged so much that big families or single people really have to watch what they're buying," Camus explained.
“Many people in the country need to take their car to work every day. Most households even need to own two cars. That’s quite a cost,” he added. And with fuel prices unlikely to ease up at the pump anytime soon, those costs may keep climbing.
Eroded not only by inflation but by a drop in employment levels, the purchasing power of French households is expected to decline 0.4 percent this year, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
The rate is similar to that of 2025, except a larger portion of the French population is feeling the effects this year.
The fall in purchasing power in 2025 stemmed mainly from a drop in dividend income, which usually affects more affluent households.
How candidates are responding
France’s presidential candidates are already homing in on the topic to rally support.
Far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen, flanked by National Rally (Rassemblement national or RN) party president, Jordan Bardella, kicked off the political "rentrée" (France’s post-summer return to politics) with an event in the northern Pas-de-Calais region, last weekend. Before giving a speech in the RN stronghold of Henin-Beaumont to about 2,000 supporters, she posted on X that the cost of living was in a “state of absolute emergency”.
Championing her campaign's central tenet of "national preference" – which would prioritise French nationals over immigrants – she turned to housing policy, pledging to "give French nationals priority access to social housing" and to "reserve" housing subsidies for them.
Le Pen also promised the crowd she would cut VAT from 20 to 5.5 percent for gas, electricity and heating oil.
“Le Pen has convinced a lot of people that everything is due to immigration. She has a magic wand that makes people believe if you stop immigration, everything will be OK,” Camus said. “A lot of disgruntled voters in the working and middle class think that closing the country to immigration will enable the state to spend less on pension reform or make huge gains in the social security system. But that’s not true. Immigrants are also consumers. They pay their rent, they pay taxes.”
Meanwhile, far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon of France Unbowed and Communist party leader, Fabien Roussel made their case at the “Fête de l’Humanité”, an annual festival that brings together left-wing political figures and musical performances.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Roussel, who announced his bid to run for president a week ago, focused on tackling gas prices. He urged people to “gather at roundabouts and outside Total’s headquarters" to force fuel prices to come down.
Mélenchon chose to point to oil supergiants like Total or BP who are benefitting from high prices per barrel. The far-left leader also promised that if elected, he would introduce a “social state of emergency” that would include capping the price of essential goods and profit margins, but also freeze rent increases.
Mélenchon also took the opportunity to reiterate his intention to establish a sliding scale for wages, directly indexing them to inflation.
Read more‘Rain man’ to the rescue? France’s ex-president Hollande plots unlikely comeback
Former interior minister and head of the conservative Les Républicains (LR) party, Bruno Retailleau, spoke to young members of his party at a rally in Nogent-sur-Marne, an eastern suburb of Paris, on Saturday. Though a close associate told French daily Libération that the cost of living would be “the focus of the campaign”, Retailleau chose to direct his speech at his adversaries, slinging insults at “charlatans” Le Pen and Mélenchon or the “patch-and-mend types” like centre-right Horizons candidate, Edouard Philippe, or Gabriel Attal, of President Emmanuel Macron's Renaissance party.
But in his campaign promises, Retailleau has vowed to make “work” his priority. He proposes that French employees work 30 minutes more each day on average in order to earn “one or even two” extra months' salary per year.
Centre-right candidates Philippe and Attal both made public appearances over the weekend, but did not address the cost of living.
“Philippe and Attal don’t offer much choice [on solutions to the cost of living] because they think that the only problem is public spending. For them, the French are more or less OK and France is a free market economy that’s running pretty well,” Camus said.
For now, Le Pen is still largely the favourite in the 2027 election: Between 33-35 percent of French voters intend to cast their ballot for the far-right National Rally candidate.
That combination of negative sentiment and a powerful appetite for radical change means France "ticks many boxes for a populist shift", Teinturier told AFP
"But the shift isn't inevitable," he said. Still, it is already reshaping the race, pushing even "traditional candidates to put forward radical measures".

How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:53:11 UTC
01:53:11 KST

How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
Israeli rights group B’Tselem argues that settlement expansion, displacement and restrictions are not isolated abuses, but a decades-old, coordinated system.
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – On any given week, Palestinians across the occupied West Bank can experience dozens of what appear to be isolated acts of Israeli violence and suppression.
In early September, Israeli forces killed two teenagers during a military raid in al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah. Days later in Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban, leaving about 70 people, including 30 children, without shelter. In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers have kept three families under siege inside their homes for more than a month, cutting off their water and power.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli demolitions threaten schools and homes in Masafer Yatta
- list 2 of 3Animated map shows spread of illegal Israeli settlements across Palestine
- list 3 of 3Israel working to eliminate Palestinian presence from West Bank, NGO warns
In a new report published on Monday, Israeli rights group B’Tselem argued these are not separate incidents. Together, they work towards a single end: Making Palestinian life on the land unsustainable and replacing it with permanent Israeli control. The reality in the West Bank, the group said, is “neither a temporary crisis nor a collection of random human rights violations”.
Instead, it is “an accelerated and explicit phase in an ongoing project of elimination that operates within the Israeli apartheid regime and is driven by a settler-colonial logic of dispossession, displacement, and the establishment of Jewish-Israeli sovereignty”, the publication – called The Elimination Project – added.
‘The Elimination Project’
Drawing on nearly 2,000 Palestinian testimonies, the report said that seemingly separate Israeli violations are part of what it called “a comprehensive mechanism of elimination”.
By “elimination”, B’Tselem referred to the systematic dismantling of Palestinian society, eroding its institutions, economy, freedom of movement and social life.
The report placed this within what it called the “basic logic of settler colonialism”: Establishing “permanent settler sovereignty over a territory already inhabited by an Indigenous people” by “pushing them out, dispossessing them and dismantling their collective existence”.
It identifies five interconnected fronts through which that process operates: Violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.
B’Tselem traced that logic to the 2017 “Decisive Plan” authored by Bezalel Smotrich, now Israel’s finance minister. The plan, the group said, gave Palestinians three choices: Accept Jewish supremacy while giving up their national claims, leave, or face violent suppression.
None of this is new, the report argued; the mechanism has run for decades. What has changed is that it has grown far more severe and open, escalating since the current far-right government took office in late 2022 and sharply after the start of the genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The reality on the ground
For roughly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, that system is felt in the steady narrowing of daily life: Roads they cannot use, land they cannot reach, and fewer places where they can safely live, work and move.
By December 2025, Israel had at least 925 physical obstacles set up across the West Bank, the most the United Nations has recorded in two decades.
Yusef Kashur, a driver and father of six from Dura, south of Hebron, told B’Tselem that the growing network of gates and checkpoints had turned his work into a “torment”, forcing him onto long, dangerous backroads and to turn down fares he once relied on.
“These drives are exhausting, take a very long time, and the fuel costs so much that I don’t make enough to cover our household needs,” he said.
The restrictions feed a wider collapse. Under an occupation that controls its borders, trade and revenue, the West Bank economy has little room of its own, and it has buckled: Unemployment at the end of last year had roughly doubled to 27.5 percent compared to October 2023, driven in part by the freezing of work permits for about 115,000 Palestinians.
The squeeze is deliberate, the report argued: A family that cannot earn is easier to uproot, and when Palestinians fall back on their own land, the pressure follows them there.
After losing his job inside Israel, Jamil Abu Rayan turned to his grapevines near Halhul, only to find settlers had established an illegal outpost at his main plot. Soldiers also barred him from another plot, calling it “[Israeli] state land”.
He told B’Tselem he lost about 60 percent of his 2025 grape harvest and that he can no longer properly work his land.
Recounting a late January attack in the South Hebron Hills, where entire communities face forcible displacement, Isma’il Khalayleh told the rights group earlier this year that a settler pressed a rifle to his forehead and gave him a deadline: “I’m giving you 24 hours to leave this place.”
Agricultural and grazing outposts have “violently taken control” of nearly 20 percent of the West Bank, according to Israeli settlement-watchdog group Peace Now. More than 1,600 settler attacks were recorded by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) last year.
The same pressure extends to where Palestinians can build; Israeli authorities make it “virtually impossible for Palestinians to obtain building permits”, according to OCHA, leaving many families who build without them under constant threat of Israeli demolition.
As Palestinian communities are cleared, more illegal Israeli settlements expand. The current government has approved a record 104 new settlements since 2022.
The suppression also extends to the institutions that hold Palestinian society together, with B’Tselem documenting a series of raids and closure orders faced by charities, trade unions and universities.
Ahmad Dweikat told the rights group that in May 2026, soldiers ransacked a Nablus association he co-founded to help women, children and families, confiscating computers and cash, including money set aside for orphans.
Running beneath all of it is the military’s lethal force. B’Tselem counted about 1,087 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since October 2023, roughly a quarter of them children.
Among them was Jamil Hanani, a 17-year-old boy from Beit Furik who was shot during an army raid on the town. “It’s as if they go out hunting, only they’re hunting human beings,” his father, ‘Atef Hanani, told B’Tselem.
The system behind the violence
For years, foreign governments have urged Israel to show restraint. That framing misses the point, B’Tselem argued: The violence, closures and demolitions are not failures of the system, but the system working as intended.
Sanctioning an individual settler, reopening a road or freezing a single settlement plan would “leave intact the structure that produces violence, dispossession, and oppression”, it said.
Seen this way, the question is not whether each individual act is an isolated violation, but what they produce together: A steadily shrinking space for Palestinians to live, work, build and remain on their land.
And the West Bank, the report argued, cannot be read apart from Gaza. The two are “different manifestations of the same regime project, directed against Palestinians’ ability to exist as a people”.

Ukraine has enacted a National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) decision to impose sanctions on 10 individuals, including former presidential press secretary Iuliia Mendel and nine Russian citizens.
The relevant decree, No. 901/2026, was published on the Presidential Office’s website on Sept. 13.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
President Volodymyr Zelensky signed the decree enacting the NSDC decision, dated the same day, on the application of personal sanctions.
The restrictions were introduced at the proposal of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and will remain in effect for 10 years, with some measures, such as the revocation of state awards, applying indefinitely.
Most of those named are subject to the full range of restrictions, including asset freezes, a ban on trade operations, measures to prevent capital flight, a ban on entry into Ukraine and other measures stipulated by the Law “On Sanctions.”
Mendel is the only Ukrainian citizen on the list.
Mendel served as Zelensky’s press secretary from 2019 to 2021 after winning a competition for the position.
Before joining the presidential administration, she worked as a journalist and contributor for several Ukrainian and international outlets.
In addition to the standard restrictions, Mendel is also barred from accessing her social media pages on Instagram, X and Facebook from within Ukraine.
The remaining nine individuals are Russian citizens.
They include Svetlana Larina, Izabella Liberman, Diana Malyk, Aleksandr Minieiev, Aleksei Plotnykov, Oleg Rezepkin, Mariia Rumiantseva, Sofiia Sambulova and Yevheniy Strunkin.
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Leaves Country Amid Anti-Corruption Showdown
After leaving her post in 2021, which Mendel said was on “good terms,” she published a book in September 2022 titled “The Fight of Our Lives: My Time with Zelensky, Ukraine’s Battle for Democracy, and What It Means for the World.”
After resigning, she worked as a columnist and commented on Ukrainian politics for foreign media.
In mid-2026, Mendel found herself at the center of a controversy following a May interview with US talk show host Tucker Carlson.
Notably, the accusations she made in that interview were not present in the book, in which she praised Zelensky as a leader who had transformed Ukraine for the better.
Kyiv Post fact-checked a series of claims made by Mendel, including allegations that Zelensky is a dictator, uses mobilization as punishment and had agreed to give up the Donbas in 2022.
Several of Mendel’s claims were found to be misleading or unsupported.
Ukraine’s wartime restrictions on men leaving the country are based on martial law and legislation that predates Zelenskyy’s presidency, while lawmakers detained for treason were arrested over alleged ties to Russia or other criminal activity, rather than simply for criticizing Zelensky or opposing the war.
The fact-check also found no evidence that Zelensky agreed to surrender the Donbas during the 2022 Istanbul negotiations.
Mendel’s claim that Zelensky privately promised Russian president Vladimir Putin that Ukraine would never join NATO could not be independently verified. Ukraine’s NATO aspirations, however, had already been enshrined in the Constitution before Zelensky took office.
Other allegations, including claims that Zelenskyy uses drugs or ordered Nazi-style propaganda, were excluded from the fact-check because they were unsubstantiated and based solely on Mendel’s statements about alleged private conversations.

Netanyahu says Gaza documentary 'NAZA' is 'shocking incitement'
JERUSALEM, Sept 14 - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that a new documentary film which alleges that mass civilian deaths were routinely built into targeting decisions in Gaza was part of a wave of global incitement against Jews.
"NAZA", directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday and received a 25-minute standing ovation when it was screened on Thursday.
The film takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected "collateral casualties" and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the war.

Netanyahu's comments followed a statement from the Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir, who said the film constituted an attack on the state of Israel.
"Based on what has been published thus far, this is not a film offering criticism of the IDF, nor is it an attempt to establish the truth. It is based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality, and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders," Zamir said.
The military said that Zamir has instructed the Military Advocate General, whose legal powers are confined within the military, "to examine and advance possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it."
The filmmakers could not immediately be reached for comment.
"We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist and this is why it is especially important for us that Israelis watch this film, it is our country that is doing these crimes," Abraham said in his acceptance speech on Saturday.

Butter late than never: Paris gets its first boutique entirely dedicated to butter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:51:39 UTC
01:51:39 KST

From croissants to sauces, crêpes to kouign-amann (the Breton butter cake which will make any gourmand melt), France knows a thing or two about butter. Now, its capital has its own dedicated butter shop. And some of the varieties may surprise you...
“If you have extraordinary bread and extraordinary butter, it's hard to beat bread and butter.”
How right French chef and author Jacques Pépin was when he said those enduring words. And a boutique in Paris is further proving him right. About the butter part, at least.
Billed as the French capital’s first shop entirely dedicated to butter, Le Butter Shop opened its doors last month and offers 30 varieties of France’s favourite fat - from small family producers in Brittany, the Loire Valley and northern France, with varieties including flavoured kinds like shallot, pepper, seaweed, wild garlic and lemon with green pepper.
France eats around 8 kilograms of butter per person a year, according to the agriculture ministry, so it was about damn time.
Customers can taste by the spoonful before buying anything from a 10-gram pat to a kilogram block. And if the aforementioned varieties didn’t appeal, there are sweet ones too, including vanilla, raspberry, strawberry and chocolate.
“Most people don’t expect to like a raspberry butter or to like chocolate butter,” said owner Erwan Leo. “And when they try it, this is where they’re just like, ‘Oh wow, OK.'”
Leo, who also runs a wine-tasting business, said butter should be used like wine, to make a meal better. “The goal isn’t to get drunk,” he cautions, adding that tasting butter works like tasting wine.
“You have to grab your spoon, you put it on your palate, on your tongue, it has to melt a little bit, and then the flavours are going to start coming one by one.”
Leo adds that the secret to savoring fatty butter is to be like Parisians: Walk a lot, and practice moderation.
“We don’t go beyond four tartines a day,” he said.
“The Italians choose olive oil, we choose butter. We learn how to master it.”
Leo’s producers churn from selected cows and higher-fat milk; an extra 2 or 3 percentage points, he said, “really makes a huge difference.”
The tiny shop has drawn crowds through social media and now has a staff of four.
“From day one, it’s been crazy,” Leo said. “Most people come in with wanting to try one or two butters, they end up trying 25 butters because they’re just so curious.”
Next up: a croissant-flavored butter, and perhaps violet.
“This is limitless,” Leo said.
If you’re not thinking “butter me up”, we don’t know how to help you.
Le Butter Shop is located at 5 Rue Bouchut in Paris, a stone’s throw away from the Champ de Mars and the Eiffel Tower.

How Syria's fuel protests could challenge Sharaa's government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:51:17 UTC
01:51:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Fuel protests sweep through Syria, posing growing challenge for Damascus
Protests have erupted across Syria, particularly in the north and northeast, after the government’s decision to raise fuel prices for a second time in nine days – putting further strain on an already war-battered society, especially farmers.
Diesel rose by 40% to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.32) a litre, while petrol increased by 28% to 195 pounds ($1.47) a litre, according to the state-run news agency SANA. The country’s Energy Ministry described the hike as a "temporary measure" imposed by rising costs of securing fuel on global markets amid the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz crisis.
The ministry said Syria is currently being affected by higher global costs for securing petrol, diesel and fuel oil, while the shutdown of the Baniyas refinery for maintenance has increased the need to source petroleum products from abroad during the maintenance period.
It said the price adjustment "aims to ensure the continued flow of petroleum products and their availability in the local market, amid higher supply costs and the need to secure requirements while the refinery is shut down."
Syria produces around 100,000 barrels of oil per day, while domestic demand is estimated at around 300,000 barrels per day.
Heavy impact in Syria’s agricultural heartland
As soon as the government announced the new prices, protests broke out in several Syrian provinces, with demonstrators blocking major roads and intercepting oil tankers heading towards the Homs refinery.
The latest protests also come amid a broader rise in demonstrations over economic conditions. According to ACLED data cited by Syrian analyst Muaz al-Abdullah, 45% of protests recorded in Syria during the first week of September were driven by economic demands.
But the protests have been particularly prominent in northeast Syria, where demonstrations in Hasakah and Deir Ezzor have taken on a more confrontational character.
Abdullah said protests had become "more violent", with demonstrators burning tyres and erecting barricades to block major roads, including the M5 highway linking northern and southern Syria.
"Barricades were being used to cut off roads, and this is something that we didn't used to see a lot in Syria," Abdullah told The New Arab, noting that demonstrations since the fall of former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024 had mostly been peaceful.
The protests are also significant because they come after a second fuel price increase in just nine days. The first hike was announced on 4 September, followed by another on 13 September.
Abdullah said the protests should be viewed as part of a broader accumulation of economic and social grievances rather than simply a reaction to the latest fuel prices.
"Of course these protests might turn into a challenge for the government, they are super significant. This is a result of accumulating crises and worsening socioeconomic conditions in Syria," he said.
Fuel prices affect virtually every aspect of daily life, from transport and food production to heating and basic services.
The impact is likely to be felt even more heavily in northeast Syria, which includes Hasakah, Deir Ezzor and Raqqa – areas that form the country’s agricultural heartland and produce much of its wheat.
"The northeast of Syria, specifically Hasaka and Deir Ezzor, these regions produce oil in Syria, but now they’re unable to receive basic services and carry out day-to-day affairs because of the fuel price hike," Abdullah said.
The region is also approaching a crucial agricultural period, with farmers expected to begin cultivation in late September and early October.
"Irrigating and cultivating lands and transport can’t happen without fuel," Abdullah said, adding that Hasakeh, Deir and Raqqa produce Syria’s main agricultural product, wheat.
An already fragile state
The fuel hike comes after existing tensions between farmers and the government in the northeast, where protests had already taken place over the price set by Damascus for purchasing wheat and delays in payments.
The timing is particularly sensitive because northeast Syria is undergoing a major political transition as the authorities in Damascus seek to integrate the region and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces into the Syrian state.
The Kurdish-led SDF and Damascus forces fought deadly clashes for weeks earlier this year, with government forces overrunning areas formerly under SDF control. A deal to integrate the SDF into the government is now underway.
"It’s not in the government’s interest, with the transition happening in Kurdish-majority areas, to increase fuel prices," Abdullah said.
He said accumulating economic grievances and deteriorating conditions could delay the integration of northeast Syria into the wider state and social fabric of the country.
The danger for Damascus is that economic frustration could become tied to the region’s broader political transition, reinforcing perceptions among some residents that their situation has worsened as the northeast comes under greater control of the central government.
Such sentiment could prove particularly damaging as Damascus seeks to reunite a country that remains deeply divided after more than 13 years of civil war.
A growing challenge for Damascus
But the unrest is not confined to the northeast.
Protests have also been reported in Hama, Aleppo and Idlib, with agriculture again emerging as a common factor.
"There is one primary thing in common for all these regions – agriculture," Abdullah said.
The protests are among the most significant anti-government demonstrations since Assad’s fall, according to Robin Yassin-Kassab, an author and political commentator.
"There’s been a lot of protests in Syria since the liberation, most of them over economic conditions, price rises, so on, but these are by far the most significant," Yassin-Kassab told The New Arab.
He said the protests were particularly worrying for the government because they were occurring in areas where support for the new authorities might otherwise be expected to be strong. In some demonstrations, protesters chanted: "the people want the fall of Jolani," President Ahmed al-Sharaa's nom de guerre, while others called on the energy minister to resign.
"They could absolutely develop into a broader challenge to the government," Yassin-Kassab said.
While the immediate trigger is the fuel price increase, it is also exposing much deeper frustrations with living conditions across the country.
"It’s both – it’s definitely about fuel prices," he said, pointing to the impact of the war in Iran and the resulting global rise in fuel costs. "But of course in Syria there’s a huge amount of rebuilding to do," he added.
Patience wearing thin
The conflict, which began in March 2011 after Assad’s forces violently cracked down on protesters, left much of the country in ruins. Millions of Syrians remain without adequate housing or employment, while large parts of the country continue to lack reliable electricity, running water and basic civilian infrastructure.
For more than a year, many Syrians have given the new government the benefit of the doubt, Yassin-Kassab said, partly because of their relief at the end of Assad’s rule and partly because they recognise the scale of the task facing the new authorities.
But that patience may not last.
"As we approach two years after the liberation, people’s patience will run out," he said.
Yassin-Kassab said the current protests reflected a population facing a "huge cost of living crisis" while still waiting for the civilian infrastructure needed to rebuild their lives.
For the government, the problem is deepened by its limited resources. Damascus has little income and enormous demands on its finances, particularly as it attempts to rebuild the country and provide basic services after years of war.
Abdullah said the government should explain the decision more clearly and consider measures such as subsidies or other assistance to help struggling households absorb the increased costs.
"The problem isn’t the fuel hike itself, it’s that the government didn’t study this before issuing the price hike. There was no clear study or strategy," he said.
President Sharaa may therefore face pressure to reverse or reduce the increase, at least temporarily, in an attempt to defuse tensions.
But the consequences of the price rise will extend beyond the immediate protests. Abdullah said the problem was beginning to threaten the country’s social peace.
Higher fuel costs are already affecting transport, with taxi drivers increasing fares and disputes emerging with passengers over the new prices. As winter approaches, the cost of heating is also likely to become another source of pressure, with many Syrians relying on mazut to heat their homes.
Yassin-Kassab said the protests showed that the government’s economic difficulties could develop into a much broader political problem, particularly as Syrians become less willing to tolerate worsening living conditions while waiting for the country’s basic infrastructure to be rebuilt.
For a government still trying to stabilise a country emerging from more than a decade of war, the protests offer a warning that economic grievances can quickly become political.
As Yassin-Kassab put it, the economic situation has the potential to "break the [post-Assad] transition."

====================================================================================================

New York Seizes a Dozen Celebrity Deepfake Websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

For the best part of a decade, abusive deepfake “pornography” websites have published thousands of nonconsensual videos depicting women, including high-profile celebrities, politicians, and public figures, into sexual situations. Now, in what is likely the largest takedown of explicit deepfake websites to date, officials in New York have seized more than a dozen of the harmful sites.
On Monday, the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office announced the seizure of 12 domains which it says have been used for “unlawfully” sharing, publishing, and selling celebrity deepfake videos. Around 1,200 people—overwhelmingly women—were depicted in nonconsensual sexual images and videos on the websites, the office says. These included social media influencers, actors, activists, athletes, musicians, and politicians.
“These horrific violations of privacy follow victims into their careers and personal lives and take an immense toll on emotional and mental well-being,” district attorney Alvin Bragg said in a statement, urging potential victims to come forward and contact his office’s cybercrime bureau. The office says its investigations into who is responsible for the websites, plus those who uploaded damaging videos of victims, are ongoing.
The seizures, carried out under New York’s criminal procedure laws, mark perhaps one of the most significant and sweeping actions against websites hosting explicit deepfake videos since the technology first emerged at the end of 2017. As artificial intelligence technology has improved, a dark industry of websites, apps, and bots has appeared: They are designed to “undress” photos of women or create graphic sexual videos that include them. The images and videos are increasingly realistic and can be generated in seconds.
While deepfake technology is widely used against non-famous women and girls—often being shared in private social media groups—celebrities have spoken out about the many harms of being depicted in the content and the challenges of getting it removed. While laws against deepfakes have been slow to emerge, the US Take It Down Act increasingly allows images to be removed, with part of the law allowing law enforcement officials to take down and seize websites.
The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office has not publicly named the websites it has seized. However, ahead of Bragg’s announcement, WIRED independently observed several of the sites’ homepages being replaced by takedown notices—“THIS DOMAIN HAS BEEN SEIZED”—late last week, with the sites now saying they have been taken over following a seizure warrant issued by a New York State Supreme Court.
“The takedowns are a significant win in the fight against synthetic nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII),” says Leonie Oehmig, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), who has studied the deepfake creation ecosystem. Oehmig says that enforcement of state laws shows that the harmful content can be tackled and that the seized sites don’t appear to be accessible if using VPNs to try and access them from other locations. “This shows that meaningful, coordinated enforcement is achievable even where regulation itself remains fragmented across jurisdictions.”
The websites were likely viewed millions of times. Many used names that included phrases such as “sex celebrity” or promised “real deepfakes.” They hosted false videos of some of the world’s most famous celebrities, with one saying, “various actresses’ faces are used for deepfakes.”
Videos could be several minutes in length and include fully sexually explicit scenes—often swapping the faces of celebrities or public figures into existing pornographic videos. Archived versions of the websites show some videos had been watched tens of thousands of times, with one of the websites claiming to have been online since 2018.
“Most videos took the shape of actual pornographic movies, manipulated to instead show targets’ faces instead of the original actors,” says Benjamin Shultz, the lead researcher at the American Sunlight Project, a nonprofit. Shultz, who has been documenting deepfake abuse against political figures and had come across some of the websites during this research, says that many videos appeared to be reposts of content that had originally be shared on the MrDeepFakes website, a notorious deepfake platform that was taken offline after its creators were unmasked by reporters.
“On at least two of the seized websites, elected officials were given profiles containing their name and position, along with a grid of manipulated videos hosting their likeness,” Shultz says. Through recent research, Shultz says that 56 European politicians had been mentioned or appeared on the websites, including 16 US politicians and two based in the UK.
While Oehmig, the ISD researcher, says the takedowns are encouraging, there are many other parts of the deepfake industry that are causing serious harm. “Effective intervention needs to target the ecosystem at multiple points, including the tools used for the creation of synthetic NCII, the discovery and promotion of these, the hosting and technical infrastructure that keeps them online, and the payment and affiliate systems that enable operators to monetize them,” Oehmig says.

Feature: In eastern DR Congo, Bukavu mourns as fire victims laid to rest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:49:34 CST
01:49:34 KST

People grieve during the funeral for victims of a recent fire, in Bukavu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sept. 14, 2026. (Str/Xinhua)
BUKAVU, DR Congo, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Bukavu, a city in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), was in mourning Monday as thousands of residents gathered to bid farewell to victims of a devastating fire that struck a densely populated neighborhood last week.
Silence, tears and grief marked the arrival of bereaved families at a memorial ceremony in the city, where 28 coffins were laid side by side before the victims were taken to their final resting place.
According to those currently in control of the city, the buried included 26 students and two teachers who died after the fire swept through a densely populated neighbourhood crowded with households and schools.
From early morning, large crowds filled roads leading to Alfajiri College, where families, teachers, students and residents gathered for a final farewell. Shops and markets in parts of Bukavu closed during the morning as residents joined the mourning.
For the families, the ceremony brought an unbearable finality to days of shock.
Mwamini Mubwirana, whose family lost children in the fire, said they had left home that morning as they did every school day. "They went out in the morning to go to school because they loved studying so much. They never missed even a single day of school and would refuse to stay at home," she told Xinhua.
"I am very sad. I lack the words to express my pain. These children were pearls of the family. Until now, I still cannot understand their deaths."
At the cemetery, rows of coffins were placed before the graves as inconsolable relatives looked on. Red Cross teams carried them one by one toward the burial sites. Some family members stood silently. Others broke down in tears as the coffins were lowered into the ground.
Anny Badari came to bury her younger sister Bernadette. "We are very sad to have lost our little sister Bernadette," she said. "She was greatly loved because she was always making people laugh, but today we have lost her."
The fire broke out last Thursday, destroying two schools and hundreds of homes in an area where houses are tightly packed together and many are built with highly flammable materials.
Different casualty figures have since been reported by various authorities. Earlier local reports had put the death toll at 29 students, while the authorities administering Bukavu said 28 victims -- 26 students and two teachers -- were buried during Monday's ceremony.
A day after the disaster, Xinhua reporters saw blackened walls, homes reduced to ashes, sheets of metal twisted by the heat and personal belongings scattered among the debris.
On one wall in the devastated neighborhood, 10 photographs from the same family had been placed side by side. Residents stopped before them, exchanging a few words in low voices or simply staring silently at the faces of those who had died.
For residents, the tragedy has been particularly painful because so many of the victims were children who had gone to school only hours before the blaze.
Fires are not uncommon in Bukavu, where rapid urban growth, densely packed housing, narrow access roads and the widespread use of wooden and other combustible building materials have long increased the risk of major fires. But residents interviewed by Xinhua said they could not remember another blaze that had claimed the lives of so many schoolchildren.
"Bukavu may have long been used to fires. We have seen many of them. But Bukavu had never lost so many innocent children in a fire, especially schoolchildren," Bashengzei Chrispin, whose home was destroyed, told Xinhua after the disaster.
According to accounts collected after the fire, the two schools were full of students when the flames spread through the neighborhood. Panic broke out as children tried to flee and parents and residents rushed toward the schools. One teacher interviewed by Xinhua said around 900 students were at the two schools at the time.
Serge Chirimwami, a teacher at Furaha Primary School, recalled the chaos as the flames approached. "Most of the students died in the panic while they were inside the school and the gate was closed," he said. "By the time the teacher arrived, it was already too late for them."
The March 23 Movement rebel group, which has controlled Bukavu since February 2025, declared three days of mourning across South Kivu Province last Friday following the tragedy.
The M23 has also temporarily prohibited new construction on the disaster site and said an assessment committee would be established, pledging to continue investigations to determine the exact cause and circumstances of the fire. ■

China Focus: China fosters birth-friendly environment with better services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:49:22 CST
01:49:22 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China will take further steps to support child-rearing, including making childcare more accessible and affordable, to build a birth-friendly society and boost its birth rate, according to health officials on Monday.
Lei Haichao, head of the National Health Commission (NHC), told a press conference that continuous efforts will be made to promote the integrated development of services at kindergartens and nursery centers, and to support communities and employers in setting up childcare facilities.
The aim is to ensure that families can access childcare services close to their homes or workplaces and at relatively affordable prices, Lei explained.
The country will work to raise coverage of childcare services among young children to effectively reduce families' costs of having, raising and educating children, he said.
The country will also work to improve access to pediatric care at grassroots medical institutions, he noted.
By the end of this year, 1,000 more community-level medical and health institutions will be capable of offering pediatric care compared with 2025, Lei said, adding that by that time, over 95 percent of the country's township-level clinics and community health service centers are expected to have the capacity to provide relevant services.
More than 3,000 pediatricians have been sent from higher-level hospitals to grassroots medical institutions to strengthen pediatric services at the community level, Lei said.
China has developed a full-cycle maternity support system covering pre-pregnancy, pregnancy and childbirth, and child-rearing, with measures that include maternity allowances, childcare subsidies, medical insurance reimbursement and affordable childcare services, to ease the financial burden on families with children.
A total of 12,562 early pregnancy care clinics have been established, covering almost all counties, said Lei. Pregnant women can visit these clinics in the early stages of pregnancy for counseling and other services. If there is a risk of miscarriage, the clinics can help women assess the risk and take preventive measures.
In 2025, China's maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate dropped to 13.4 per 100,000 live births and 3.8 per 1,000 live births, respectively, placing China among the leaders in these indicators among upper-middle- and high-income countries and countries with populations exceeding 100 million.
In terms of incentives, the country introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy program in 2025, offering an annual tax-free subsidy of 3,600 yuan (about 530 U.S. dollars) for each child under the age of three. It also began waiving childcare and education fees for the final year of kindergarten in the 2025 autumn semester.
As of August, more than 25 million infants and toddlers had received childcare subsidies for 2026, and roughly 24 million children enrolled in kindergartens had benefited from the fee-waiving policy.
Also, 260 million people are currently covered by maternity insurance, and many regions are expanding coverage to allow flexible workers to enroll in maternity insurance alongside employee medical insurance.
These policies are among China's broader efforts to build a birth-friendly society amid declining birth rates and an aging population.
Building a "birth-friendly society" has become a key focus of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). The outline sets out measures, including incentives to encourage births and efforts to reduce the costs of childbirth, childcare and education.
It says the goal is to stabilize the number of newborns and support long-term balanced population development.
"China's population currently stands at 1.405 billion, and the fundamentals of China as a populous country remain unchanged," said Lei.
Although the number of newborns has declined in recent years, it has remained at around 8 million, a number very few countries can match, he added.
BETTER HEALTH FOR ALL
Officials at the press conference also expounded on other key aspects of a national health plan for the 2026-2030 period unveiled in July, including making health services more accessible, inclusive, comprehensive and continuous.
China has built the world's largest healthcare service system, with more than 1.1 million medical and health institutions nationwide, while over 90 percent of residents can reach their nearest healthcare facility within 15 minutes, said Guo Yanhong, deputy head of the NHC.
However, the system still falls short of people's needs in some respects, Guo noted, urging a shift of efforts from ensuring access to improving quality, with faster progress in developing a high-quality, efficient and integrated healthcare service system.
For instance, community health centers and health centers in central townships should gradually expand their medical service capabilities, develop specialty departments suited to local needs, and improve their capacity to diagnose and treat common and frequently occurring diseases and provide health management services.
Efforts should also be made to further strengthen the workforce of rehabilitation and nursing professionals and step up the training of rehabilitation nurses and therapists, to have seven rehabilitation physicians and 16 rehabilitation therapists per 100,000 people across the country by the end of 2030, Guo said.
Lei noted that the demographic trend of the growing divergence in population changes across regions, with population development becoming increasingly uneven. With various factors considered, over the next five years, demand for healthcare services, particularly for healthcare professionals, is expected to continue growing in China, he said.
China will therefore expand the training of medical students via increased enrollment in high-quality undergraduate and master's programs, targeted training programs for medical students to serve in rural areas, and a special program for university graduates to work as rural doctors, the official said.
Through closer coordination between medical education and healthcare, China will continue to increase its number of medical professionals while making healthcare positions more attractive via improvements in remuneration and personnel incentive systems, so that medical workers are willing to build long-term, stable careers. Efforts will also be made to foster a social environment that respects medical professionals and values healthcare workers, said Lei. ■
