Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan’s territorial claims: A map no administration is willing to redraw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:55 UTC
01:44:55 KST

For a small nation, Taiwan has an unusually long list of territorial disputes. In part or in whole, it has disputes over the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) with Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. It also has another territorial dispute with Vietnam over the Paracel Islands, and with Japan over the Senkaku Islands (Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台).
Of course, the biggest territorial disputes are with the People’s Republic of China (PRC), which not only claims all of the above, but also Pratas Island (Dongsha, 東沙島), Kinmen, Penghu and all of Taiwan itself.
This creates considerable headaches politically for the government, especially — but not exclusively — administrations led by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
Photo: AP
ROOT OF THE PROBLEM
The root of the problem is that when the Republic of China (ROC) fled to Taiwan after losing the Chinese Civil War in 1949, they brought along ROC territorial claims.
Constitutional reforms beginning in 1991 distinguished the ROC’s “free area” from the mainland and cleared the way for a fully elected legislature. Previously, ROC maps included not only China, but also Manchuria, Tibet, East Turkestan and Mongolia. The primary difference between the ROC’s territorial claims and the PRC’s is that the Soviet Union pressured Beijing into recognizing the Mongolian People’s Republic as independent.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Conservation Administration
In a very colonial mindset, the ROC released a map in the late 1940s showing an 11-dash line, claiming sovereignty over roughly 90 percent of the South China Sea. The PRC’s current 10-dash line (formerly nine-dash), with a few minor tweaks, is based on the ROC’s claims.
While the 1991 constitutional changes put to rest the absurdist fantasy of “reclaiming the mainland,” they said nothing about the South China Sea or the Senkakus. Those claims remain official even today.
The claim to Pratas as Chinese was strong, and the Taiwan Coast Guard occupies it today as a component of the Cijin District (旗津) of Kaohsiung City. Only the PRC disputes this.
Both the Vietnamese and Chinese have reasonable claims to the Paracels, but the ROC lost control in the civil war.
Claims to the Spratlys are far weaker, but both Taiwan and the PRC have bases there. Taiwan occupies Itu Aba (Taiping Island 太平島) today, but lost Thitu Island (中業島) in 1971 when ROC troops evacuated due to a typhoon and the Philippines swept in and took control. People forget, but at the time the Philippines was one of the most advanced countries in Asia. President Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) decided not to mess with them.
THE KMT APPROACH
Chinese nationalism has historically been central to the KMT, while the DPP developed from Taiwan-centered nationalism and the democracy movement.
The KMT’s core ideology is Chinese ethnonationalism, and hardliners take a very absolutist stance on sovereignty. When out of power, they use it to attack the DPP.
Sometimes, this can go so far as to extend to supporting the PRC over other countries in the region on the theory that it is better for Han Chinese to occupy territory than for others.
This was recently demonstrated when KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chairman Chen Yi-hsin (陳以信) attacked President William Lai (賴清德) of the DPP for not defending sovereignty and referred to Scarborough Shoal as Huangyan Island (黃岩島), Beijing’s preferred name, rather than the ROC’s official name, Democracy Reef (民主礁) — language that closely echoed the PRC position.
Yet, as the Thitu Island loss demonstrates, in power the party is more realistic and pragmatic.
The mix of ideology and pragmatism is probably best exemplified by former president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) over the Senkakus.
After World War II, the US maintained control of the Ryukyu and Senkaku Islands until handing them over to Japanese administrative control in 1972. As the handover approached, Chinese nationalists from Taiwan and Hong Kong protested over the Senkakus being given to Japan instead of the ROC. Protests started in the US, but eventually spread to Taiwan. See: “Taiwan in Time: A tale of two protests over specks of land” (April 7, 2019).
According to an interesting 2017 paper by Yoshiyuki Ogasawara (“Ma Ying-jeou’s Doctoral Thesis and Its Impact on the Japan-Taiwan Fisheries Negotiations), a group of protestors in 1971 marched to deliver a written protest to the American and Japanese embassies in Taipei. Ma “was one of the leaders who led this protest and allegedly yelled statements to the effect of, ‘Japan has no principles, America talks nonsense.’”
Ma cared about the issue so deeply that he wrote his Harvard doctoral dissertation on the Senkakus.
Periodically over the years, nationalistic activists would sail to the Senkakus to attempt to plant the ROC flag, sometimes successfully, sometimes not. In office in 2012, Ma met with and praised one such group who were fighting for fishing rights in the region.
Yet, just a few weeks before, he had sent a proposal to the Japanese, and in 2013 signed a joint fisheries agreement allowing Taiwanese access to some of the waters around the Senkakus. The agreement carefully sidestepped sovereignty issues.
THE DPP APPROACH
The DPP are Taiwanese nationalists. They have accepted the ROC framework for the pragmatic reason that voters do not want a war with the PRC over a name, constitution and flag.
By accepting this framework, they inherit the ROC’s territorial claims. Their lack of enthusiasm is palpable, but always reiterate these claims when pressed.
Less than two months into president Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) first term in 2016, the Taipei Times reported that a Presidential Office source stated that the administration had reached an internal resolution on Taiwan’s territorial claims over the South China Sea, which stressed the nation’s sovereignty over islands in the area, but made no mention of the so-called (11-dash) “U-shaped line” and “historical waters.”
When the presidential office was questioned publicly on this, they dodged the issue, stating: “The ROC government stands firm on its claim of sovereignty over islands in the South China Sea and their relevant waters, which are rightfully our rights in accordance with international law.”
A tribunal rejected China’s claim to historic resource rights within the nine-dash line beyond the maritime entitlements provided by UNCLOS. Because the ROC line had the same historical origin, the ruling also undermined expansive Taiwanese claims to historic waters, but it did not decide sovereignty over any island. The Tsai administration was obliged to condemn the ruling, and Tsai rushed to give a speech on a navy frigate.
In July, when claims of sovereignty over the Philippines’ Batanes Islands started appearing in state-owned media that China had a claim as they were historically part of “China’s Taiwan,” Domino Theory pressed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), and they replied, “There is no territorial dispute between Taiwan and the Philippines regarding Batan Island. It is the unrealistic fantasy of Chinese scholars.”
Despite repeated attempts to get MOFA to specifically state that the ROC recognizes Filipino sovereignty over the islands, they dodged the question. I laughed; of course, they would not answer that, but I admired the audacity in asking.
One exposition of this argument appeared in a 2004 paper by Tamkang University professor Chen Hurng-yu (陳鴻瑜). Chen’s case was also made in an editorial in this newspaper, “Manila’s weak claim to the Batanes” (Dec. 23, 2007).
The DPP has no interest in pressing them, and likely would rather drop them altogether, but they will not.
That would mire the administration in controversy, sucking up valuable political capital. That political capital is desperately needed elsewhere, including on defense.
If they look weak on sovereignty, this will give the opposition a vector to further question why they need bigger defense budgets.
It is easier to dodge questions and give boilerplate answers, because everyone is aware that in the real world, no administration — whether DPP or KMT — is in any position militarily to press the ROC’s territorial claims.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

One approach to handling this obstruction is to circumvent it by building robust drone capabilities across a wide swathe of the population. Taiwan is doing just that, but more is needed. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash

Its exterior is painted in a yellow-green gradient intended to blend harmoniously with the ripening rice paddies of the East

Average wages climbing, but median wages low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:55 UTC
01:44:55 KST

The average monthly regular wage in July was NT$49,491, a 3.32 percent increase from a year earlier and up 0.3 percent from the month before, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.
Including overtime, bonuses and other commissions, the overall monthly wage averaged NT$71,165, an annual increase of 8.25 percent and a monthly growth of 17.86 percent, the DGBAS said in a report.
In July, the median monthly wage — generally considered a more accurate measure of people’s income as extremely high or low wages do not skew it — increased 3.47 percent year-on-year and 0.3 percent month-on-month to NT$39,629, indicating that most workers still earned less than the average, the report said.
Photo: CNA
The wage data were based on the agency’s survey of employees in the nation’s industrial and service sectors. The total number of employees, including full-time and part-time employees from Taiwan or abroad, as of July 31 was 8.627 million, up 87,000 or 1.01 percent from a year earlier, the DGBAS said.
From January to July, the average monthly regular wage was NT$49,054, up 2.94 percent from the same period last year, and the median monthly wage was NT$39,341, up 3.06 percent, the report said.
After adjusting for inflation, which increased 1.8 percent annually in the first seven months, the average monthly regular wage was NT$44,113, up 1.12 percent from a year earlier and the largest increase for the same period in six years, while the median figure was NT$35,379, up 1.24 percent, it showed.
In the first seven months, cumulative total earnings (including overtime, bonuses and other non-regular earnings) grew 4.18 percent to NT$483,077 on average in the first seven months, the report said. After adjusting for inflation, the figure grew 2.33 percent, the biggest growth in 11 years, to NT$434,420, it said.
Regarding overtime hours, a key indicator of economic activity, the manufacturing sector averaged 18 hours of overtime in July, an increase of 1 hour year-on-year and reaching a nearly 16-year high for the same month, the report said.
The electronic components industry averaged 28.7 hours of overtime in July, an increase of 0.8 hours year-on-year and the highest for the same month in 47 years, while the average overtime hours in the computer, electronic products and optical products industry reached 17.1 hours, an increase of 1.3 hours year-on-year and a 43-year high for the same month, it said.
DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said that data on the number of employees, regular wage, total wage and overtime hours all showed the overall labor market is moving in a generally positive direction.
However, with consumer inflation ticking up in the past few months and exceeding 2 percent, it could squeeze future real wage growth, she said.

More EU-Taiwan cooperation needed on disaster preparedness: EU envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:54 UTC
01:44:54 KST

The European Union’s top envoy to Taiwan on Monday called for greater bilateral cooperation to boost civil society preparedness for natural and man-made disasters, saying such efforts were crucial for both the EU and Taiwan to enhance resilience.
Lutz Gullner, head of the European Economic and Trade Office (EETO) in Taiwan, said at an EETO-funded workshop in Taipei that the EU believes "resilience and preparedness" are crucial for any society facing natural and man-made disasters, particularly in times of geopolitical uncertainty.
Over the past several years, Europe has been strengthening its civil protection mechanisms, particularly in light of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, he said.
Photo: CNA
"Taiwan obviously is one of the reference points for anything related to natural disasters already for a long time, and we envy many of your systems," he said.
The EU, meanwhile, has more experience dealing with disasters such as wildfires and civil protection mechanisms, he said.
"It’s really about learning together, developing together and, most importantly, not just between governments but between civil society, people and communities, to build a real culture of resilience," he said.
"Taiwan needs partners. The European Union needs partners," he said, adding that such cooperation matters enormously and "can strengthen resilience in Taiwan and in Europe."
Gullner made the remarks during the opening ceremony of a workshop organized by the Taipei-based Forward Alliance, a Taiwanese national security and civil defense think tank.
The workshop was joined by representatives from Samaritan International, a European network of nonprofit, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) focused on social and emergency services.
Paul Wardenga of Samaritan International said at the opening ceremony that by bringing together Taiwanese NGO volunteers and their European counterparts, the seminar will enable the two sides to learn from each other about volunteer management and how to train volunteers for civil protection purposes.

The victory is the duo’s first BWF Tour event win since they paired up in 2024.

Bears get closer to human settlements than thought, trackers show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:51 UTC
01:44:51 KST

The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency yesterday released tracking records of released Formosan black bears for the first time, showing that they get much closer to human settlements than previously thought.
The agency said it had captured two bears, Da Qu-ali (達古阿里) and Aziman (阿里曼), in indigenous villages in Hualien County and began to track them with a camera-mounted satellite collar after releasing them back into the wild.
The results confirmed that the bears have moved from deep mountain areas into lowland hills closer to human communities, leading to an increase in human-bear conflicts, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency
The agency has introduced artificial intelligence-assisted early warning and monitoring systems in high-risk areas to predict bear intrusions, including Taitung County’s Jiaming Lake Lodge (嘉明湖山屋) and Siangyang Cabin (向陽山屋), and Taichung’s Dasyueshan National Forest Recreation Area (大雪山森林遊樂區), agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) said.
The system would issue alerts within two minutes after detecting bear activity, he said.
Bear-resistant trash cans and electric fences have also been set up around human communities in mountainous areas, Lin said.
To help people address potential bear encounters, the agency would distribute guidelines to communities and schools around hot spots for bear activity, he said.
The footage showed Da Qu-ali eating a sambar deer carcass and leg remains of a Formosan serow, and rummaging through garbage, eating lunchbox leftovers and roaming around betel nut gardens, work sheds and orchards.
Lin urged people visiting mountainous areas to manage their garbage, especially food scraps and kitchen waste, to prevent attracting bears.
Bear sightings used to be concentrated in areas governed by the agency’s Hualien, Taitung and Taichung branches, but they have extended to the Hsinchu branch area, Lin said, adding that the frequency of sightings has also increased.
Some people mistakenly believe that human-bear conflicts are driven by indigenous people intruding into bear habitats, he said.
However, indigenous people help conserve the primary and secondary forests that serve as bear habitats, he said.
Another clip released by the agency showed Aziman after he was released in December 2024 entering a cave and remaining there for as long as 70 days.
It was the first record of a Formosan black bear’s overwintering behavior, the agency said, adding that Da Qu-ali did not engage in similar seasonal activities.
Formosan Wild Sound Conservation Science Center founder Chiang Po-jen (姜博仁), who was in charge of the bear tracking efforts, said that bears are smart enough to learn where to easily find food.
The center recorded a black bear catching a chicken from a large coop within a minute after it entered, he said, adding that the bear stayed around the coop over the following 15 days.
Black bears also have good navigational capabilities and spatial memory, Chiang said.
For example, Aziman traveled a long distance after being released, but later returned to its original area of activity, he said.
This was especially likely when food was available, he said, adding that it is crucial to sever bears’ association with human food sources.
Tunghai University life science professor Lin Liang-kong (林良恭) cited Japanese research as showing that if a bear approaches human settlements, it would take three generations for its descendants to distance themselves from humans again.
Japan’s annual budget for addressing bear conflicts has been boosted from ￥100 million to ￥6 billion (US$646,600 to US$38.8 million), he said, calling on the government to invest more in bear research and conflict prevention.
The agency in March estimated that Taiwan has about 1,200 Formosan black bears, but said it would announce a more precise figure by the end of the year.
According to the agency’s guidelines, human-bear encounters can be categorized into three types: sightings, nuisances and physical attacks.
Graded response measures include recording and tracking, protection and monitoring, active deterrence and trapping, the guidelines state.

Academia Historica head vows to fight historical distortion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:50 UTC
01:44:50 KST

Newly appointed Academia Historica director Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮) yesterday said she would prioritize research into Taiwan’s democratization, saying that historical distortion has become more serious in the past few years.
The agency held a handover ceremony yesterday for its outgoing and incoming directors.
Chen, a distinguished professor in National Taiwan University’s Department of History, said President William Lai (賴清德) unexpectedly summoned her in June and asked why, more than 30 years after Taiwan’s democratization, many people’s understanding of history remained rooted in narratives from the authoritarian era.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
Lai asked why political identities remain so deeply divided and whether something had gone wrong during the transition to democracy, she said.
Chen said the invitation was unexpected, as she had been enjoying a comfortable academic career.
Moving into public service could mean having to “wear a helmet,” she said, but added that after 30 years of peaceful life and benefiting from state support for her education, she felt a responsibility to give back.
Chen said her first priority would be to continue research into Taiwan’s democratization, including examining what authoritarian rule means and why it harms society.
Such work should help society remember the struggle for democracy and freedom, and encourage people to cherish the democratic system, she said.
However, recent political events have shown a deliberate trend of bad-faith historical distortion, Chen said.
Some people have portrayed the elected government, whose powers are subject to checks and oversight, as authoritarian or dictatorial, while others have described Taiwan as a “terror state,” she said, adding that such claims could cause irreparable harm to society.
The democratic system can be defended only through continued remembrance and efforts to clarify the historical record, she said.
Chen also said the institution should promote research into Taiwan’s history and confront difficult aspects of the past.
The release of political surveillance records has helped society better understand Taiwan’s history, but has raised difficult questions, she said.
People identified as informants should not be regarded as perpetrators automatically, she said, adding that their roles, whether they harmed others and the reliability of intelligence records all require consideration.
The records contain extensive private information about people who were surveilled, she said, warning that its publication could cause harm.
Transitional justice has entered deeper and more difficult territory, she said, adding that these issues must be confronted.

Sweden’s election too close to call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:49 UTC
01:44:49 KST

Sweden’s general election was too close to call early yesterday, as the incumbent prime minister and the left-wing opposition leader both said they were ready to govern and the far right was seen losing ground.
With more than 90 percent of votes counted, four opposition parties led by Swedish Social Democratic Party Chairwoman Magdalena Andersson, held a three-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
“For now, we are in the lead, and if that is confirmed, Sweden will have a new government,” 59-year-old Andersson, who was Sweden’s first female prime minister in 2021 and 2022, told her supporters.
Photo: TT News Agency via AFP
However, her party — which ruled the Scandinavian country for most of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest — also looked to be heading for its worst score in more than a century with 28 percent of the vote.
Kristersson, whose Moderate Party was credited with 19.9 percent of the counted votes, said that if the result stood, he would respect Andersson’s attempts to form a government with the three other parties on the left.
However, he said that the four had irreconcilable differences, primarily between the Left Party and the Centre Party, and were unlikely to agree on a government program.
“I will therefore, even if tonight’s result stands, examine whether there are any possibilities within this non-socialist parliamentary majority to find some workable government constellation,” Kristersson told his supporters.
“Which government is going to govern Sweden in the coming years is still an open question,” he added.
In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which entered parliament in 2010, lost support for the first time, garnering 17.6 percent of the vote, down from 20.6 percent in 2022.
“We don’t yet have the full election result, but it’s obvious that we’ve lost a few percentage points compared with our result four years ago,” party Chairman Jimmie Akesson told an election night watch party.
However, he said it was a success that supporters were no longer afraid to show their support for the party long seen as a political pariah.
“There are now so many more people around our country who no longer find it difficult to say that they are Sweden Democrats,” Akesson said.
The final outcome might not be clear for a few days, several party leaders said.

BIS says global market AI momentum showing signs of vulnerability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

The artificial intelligence (AI)-linked rally that has seen world stock markets soar over the last two years is showing growing signs of vulnerability, global central bank umbrella body, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), said yesterday.
Investors were becoming "increasingly cautious" about the profitability of future AI investments, especially as the leverage of major US tech firms continued to rise, the BIS said in a report.
"The AI momentum, which had propelled equity markets and contributed to the resilience of the global economy of the last year, has begun to show growing signs of vulnerability," BIS economic analysis head Frank Smets told reporters on Friday ahead of the report’s publication.
Photo: Ng Han Guan, AP
AI-connected stocks were down sharply yesterday after the heads of a number of top AI firms warned at the weekend that the pace of the technology’s development needed to be slowed to prevent threats to humanity.
The BIS report also pointed to an uncertain global backdrop of strains on public finances, exacerbated by geopolitical tensions and volatile energy prices.
The hundreds of billions of dollars worth of debt AI firms have been issuing could also be contributing to the rise in government bond market borrowing costs, known as yields, on top of the long-held concerns about the sustainability of debt levels.
"It’s related to the fiscal fragility that comes also with higher uncertainty in the world economy," Smets said referring to the recent pressures in bond markets.
Nevertheless, he added that there were "no signs of stress" overall and that investors’ risk appetite had remained "remarkably resilient" in recent months.
Dubbed the central bank to the world’s central banks, the BIS has given regular warnings about both global debt levels and potential stock market bubbles in recent years.
"Whether this resilience (in markets) can be sustained, especially if upward pressures on yields continue, remains, however, uncertain," Smets said.
He also echoed BIS chief Pablo Hernandez de Cos’ warning last week of the financial stability risks posed by AI.
"What we are most concerned on in this (AI) area is the rapid increase in debt and leverage," Smets said. "And the fact that many of these financing deals are quite opaque. They’re often off balance sheet. They have sort of circularity in them."
The report also looked in depth at the private market funding that has been pouring into AI in recent years.
Aggregate borrowing by tech firms has risen from around US$22 billion, or 22 percent of total private credit, in 2010 to over US$1 trillion, or 44 percent, by last year. In total, outstanding loans of any type amount to almost US$2.5 trillion, it added.
Another of its studies used AI to analyse thousands of central bank speeches and reports. It showed that "core inflation" metrics that strip out energy price peaks and troughs are being cited more frequently and in greater variety.
While the trend reflected changing economic conditions, it said "the growing complexity of central bank messaging may pose challenges for effective communication with the public."

Slowdown calls deflate AI stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:45 UTC
01:44:45 KST

Stocks related to artificial intelligence (AI) fell sharply yesterday after the CEOs of the US companies developing the most advanced AI models warned the pace of development must slow to prevent threats to humanity.
Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei, in a lengthy essay shared on social media on Saturday, called on AI companies to slow the rate at which they advance model capabilities amid mounting fears of AI misuse. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who runs xAI, said that they agree with Amodei.
In Japan, shares in ChatGPT maker OpenAI’s investor Softbank Group Corp tumbled as much as 13.2 percent, and memory maker Kioxia Holdings Corp plunged 9.8 percent initially, while chip supply chain company Tokyo Electron Ltd fell 3.7 percent.
Photo: CNA
In Taipei, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) slipped 1.2 percent, while in South Korea SK Hynix Inc slid 5.3 percent and Samsung Electronics Co fell 3.7 percent.
“Selling pressure is likely to hit AI and semiconductor-related stocks in Tokyo following a series of weekend comments calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development,” Sony Financial Group Inc senior economist Takayuki Miyajima said in a note. “Additionally, uncertainty surrounding the situation in the Middle East continues to weigh on sentiment.”
In Shanghai, memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies Inc (長鑫存儲) dropped as much as 3.6 percent, while Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (中芯) fell 2.6 percent.
In Hong Kong, Zhongji Innolight Co (中際旭創) shed as much as 6.7 percent at one point, while MiniMax Group Inc (稀宇科技) dropped as much as 7.8 percent. Shares of Z.AI Co (智譜), the developer of the GLM AI series, tumbled as much as 10.5 percent after making a discounted share placement.
San Francisco-based Anthropic released a threat intelligence report on Thursday detailing how several actors had used its Claude AI models for activities ranging from weapons development and cyber operations to surveillance and fraud.
Alarm about the harm from AI grew when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, saying that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
While several US lawmakers have raised concern about AI’s rapid progress and called for new rules, US President Donald Trump on Sunday likened AI critics to “very negative forces” bringing up scenarios that would not happen, and said he wanted to make sure that the US remains the industry leader.
China’s state-backed Global Times called the Anthropic essay a “Cold War playbook” in an editorial, one intended to curb the country’s technological development.
Some investors dismissed the warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI.
Michael Burry, whose prescient bets against the US housing market before the 2008 financial crisis were chronicled in the movie The Big Short, said in a message on social media the warnings were “hype and puffery” and “cover for real uncontrollable slowing growth.”
Others said the warnings would be an overhang.
“In the short term, these warnings could still weigh on AI and chip stocks,” Saxo Bank A/S chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said. “Their valuations assume both strong demand and a relentless pace of technological progress,” she said. “When expectations are this high, even a possible delay can trigger profit-taking.”
The bigger question for markets around AI was who would ultimately earn the return on all the capital being spent on building new capacity, T Rowe Price Group Inc portfolio manager Sebastien Mallet said.
“There is little doubt that AI will change the world,” he said. “But that does not necessarily mean every investment being made today will generate an attractive return.”

MAC cautions travelers on China entry/exit rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:45 UTC
01:44:45 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday urged groups traveling to China to exercise extra caution as local officials implementing new border controls, which take effect today, could be inconsistent or overly strict.
The council has reviewed the new regulations and found five main groups at risk, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) told reporters before attending a Taipei forum held by the Asia-Pacific Elite Interchange Association to discuss the implications of the new entry and exit regulations.
Shen urged Taiwanese travelers to register online before traveling to China as an additional safety precaution.
Photo: Lin Cheng-kun, Taipei Times
Businesspeople, executives, high-tech professionals, lower-level government officials and followers of certain religions could face additional risks under the new regulations, he said.
Over the past few years, the number of people questioned, detained or reported missing in China has increased, he said, adding that it was “abnormal.”
The rules give border authorities at the county level more responsibility, which could lead to inconsistent or overly strict enforcement, as local officials could take a “better safe than sorry” approach when the rules are first implemented, Shen said.
In addition, people could be barred from leaving China based on authorities’ unilateral determination that they might endanger national interests, even without being formally convicted of an offense, he said.
Immigration authorities could also demand documents, data and electronic evidence from devices such as phones, tablets and laptops, and require travelers to unlock them, posing risks to information security, commercial and technological data, and people who have expressed certain political views, he added.
Strict new controls on the high-tech sector are particularly concerning, Central Police University Department of Border Police professor Arthur Wang (王智盛) said.
Taiwanese tech professionals traveling to China could be targeted for possessing sensitive information, and authorities could make it difficult for them to leave or require them to provide information, he said.
Under the new rules, Chinese authorities could demand electronic evidence and information about relatives who have expressed support for Taiwan, participated in international organizations or practice certain religions, he added.
Similar rules have already been implemented, Taipei District Court judge Hsu Kai-chieh (許凱傑) said, citing China’s 2023 revision of its counterespionage law, which allows authorities to bar people from leaving the country if they are suspected of spying.
The new regulations are an additional layer of restrictions, placing greater emphasis on export and technology controls, Hsu said.
They could also become a legal tool for controlling entry and exit from China, barring people who might “cause trouble” from entering and key people already in China from leaving, he said.

Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) yesterday said that she saw a growing number of international friends willing to learn about Taiwan and hear its story during her visit to the Italian island of Ventotene last week.
“Throughout this journey, I have once again felt the international community’s concern for Taiwan, and encountered a growing number of good friends willing to learn about Taiwan and hear its story,” Hsiao said at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport upon returning from Italy.
The most significant part of the trip was “having Taiwan’s voice heard by so many more people in a place of such historical significance,” Hsiao said, referring to the Second Ventotene European Conference for Freedom and Democracy, which she attended last week.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Hsiao said that Ventotene has an extraordinary history.
During World War II, the island was used to detain political dissidents, including Altiero Spinelli, who coauthored a text there that later became known as the Ventotene Manifesto, advocating a federal Europe after the war.
Hsiao cited remarks from her Friday address at the Italian conference, saying: “Whether it is Ventotene or Taiwan, no island is too small to have a voice, and no island or society is too small to deserve respect.”
Although Europe today is vastly different from the Europe of World War II, democracies around the world continue to face similar challenges, she said.
“Authoritarianism, ‘gray zone’ threats, and challenges involving coercion and attempts to alter the ‘status quo’ continue to arise in various forms and locations — challenges with which Taiwan is all too familiar,” she said.
Hsiao said that is why she told at the conference that Taiwan, like its European friends, would remain steadfast in upholding a free and democratic way of life, and committed to maintaining regional peace and prosperity.
The trip was not announced in advance to avoid “unnecessary interference,” she said, referring to China’s objections.
Hsiao was invited by European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, the main initiator of the conference, and Carlo Corazza, head of the European Parliament Liaison Office in Italy, to speak at the meeting, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a news release yesterday.
Aside from meeting Picierno and Corazza, Hsiao and Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) also met with Sandro Gozi, chair of the European Parliament’s Delegation to the EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly; European Parliament member Valerie Hayer; and Ventotene Mayor Carmine Caputo while on the Italian island.
Before returning to Taiwan, Hsiao and Lin toured the renowned Roman cisterns and the Museo Storico Archeologico, which houses archeological discoveries from the island, the ministry said.

China can invent new drugs; paying for them is harder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:38 UTC
01:44:38 KST

China now rivals the US as a global center for pharmaceutical innovation, but its health insurance system struggles to keep pace with the cost of breakthroughs, leaving many patients unable to access top new drugs.
That is why a healthcare law passed last month is important. It restores explicit support for private medical insurance that was dropped from an earlier draft. It would allow private insurers to play a vital role in closing the gap between what the country’s basic medical insurance system can afford to cover and the expensive treatments its drugmakers are producing.
The benefits could eventually be far-reaching. For China’s innovative drugmakers — such as Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals Co (恆瑞醫藥), BeOne Medicines Ltd (now headquartered in Switzerland) and Innovent Biologics Inc — a more developed private insurance market could help lift demand and profitability by making new treatments for everything from cancer to diabetes to insomnia more accessible.
The obstacles remain formidable. Insurers struggle to price coverage for novel treatments because they have little claims history and limited visibility into the clinical and real-world data needed to predict demand and costs, an industry white paper published in May said. Even when drugs are insured, people might find it hard to get them.
The need for an alternative source of financing comes from the limitations of China’s near-universal system, which covers about 95 percent of the population. The state insurance scheme is funded mainly by payroll contributions for urban employees and a combination of individual payments and government subsidies for everyone else. Even for covered treatments, patients can be left to shoulder about 30 percent of the bill, making affordability a major challenge.
There is an inherent tension. Expensive treatments added to the reimbursement list of covered drugs — which was introduced in 2000 — compete with cheaper, more mainstream ones. China has traditionally dealt with this trade-off by using access to its enormous publicly insured market to extract steep price cuts from drugmakers — basically telling companies to cut prices if they want to be on the list. That works well to contain costs, but it inevitably influences the care that patients receive.
Budget considerations mean newer, more effective medicines that have become standard therapies in wealthier countries remain out of reach for many Chinese. For example, Merck & Co’s blockbuster cancer treatment Keytruda (pembrolizumab) is used to treat everything from lung cancer to melanoma, but it has less than 15 percent of market share in China because it is not on the list for public reimbursement, Bernstein SG senior China biopharma analyst Rebecca Liang (梁玥) said.
That gap is what a stronger commercial insurance industry could help fill. At the moment, its role is limited. Private health insurers paid for 7.8 percent of China’s innovative drugs and medical devices last year, the industry paper said. Patients themselves picked up almost 46 percent of the tab, with the balance covered by the public sector. The just-approved healthcare law, which is to take effect next year, aims to shift that burden by putting existing policies on a firmer legal footing while setting out how the system should develop further.
The direction is clear. Last year, China published an inaugural list of two dozen high-end drugs, including costly cancer therapies and treatments for Alzheimer’s, that aren’t paid for by state coverage. Instead, the list gives official endorsement for coverage under low-cost private insurance policies supported by regional governments.
However, creating a pathway for private insurers is only a first step; they also need the tools to make it work. Beijing should make it easier for insurers to access the data they need to price insurance risks, improve information-sharing among hospitals, drugmakers and payers, and develop ways to spread the cost of exceptionally expensive treatments among multiple parties.
Some Chinese drugmakers struggle to turn promising discoveries into profitable products at home. That makes licensing them to overseas pharmaceutical companies, which can commercialize the medicines in more lucrative markets, an important source of revenue for the industry.
China’s biotech success has created a problem that is worth having. The country is producing medicines that its healthcare system was not designed to finance. Private insurers offer a way to resolve that contradiction. Now Beijing needs to make sure the insurance market can actually solve it.

US transport chief misunderstands Ford’s China ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:36 UTC
01:44:36 KST

Genius is only 1 percent inspiration, Thomas Edison said, but that 1 percent is crucial to making the other, sweaty 99 percent worthwhile when it comes to innovation. US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy appears to have missed this in sending a strongly worded letter to Ford Motor Co about its dealings with Chinese companies.
Duffy expressed “profound concern” at what he sees as an iconic US company tying its future too closely to companies from the US’ great strategic rival. Exhibit A is Ford’s plant in Marshall, Michigan, where it licenses technology to produce lithium iron phosphate batteries from Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL), the world leader in that field.
Duffy also does not like Ford’s joint venture with China’s Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd (吉利汽車) to build electric vehicles (EV) in Spain, nor its talks with China’s BYD Co (比亞迪), the largest EV maker in the world, about supplying components. Duffy claims Ford proposed forming joint ventures in the US with Chinese automakers and rebuked the company for doing so.
It is a strange letter. Duffy does not cite a law that Ford is breaking, nor explicitly tell the company to end its agreements based on some statutory authority. Rather, it is a tapestry of concern, alarm and disappointment, prodding Ford to self-police itself out of any dealings with Chinese companies.
It is also somewhat at odds with reality.
“Iconic American companies, like Ford, are also expected to out-innovate competitors. To that end, they need to chart clear paths to technological self-reliance,” Duffy wrote, as if out-innovating competitors is a novel and easily achieved objective.
He ignores that Ford’s Chinese competitors are setting the pace in the global auto industry in critical fields like vehicle design and manufacturing timescales, user experience and electrification. A keystone of that leadership is the learning and technology Chinese companies obtained over the years through domestic joint ventures imposed on foreign automakers when they opened operations there. Duffy is demanding that Detroit out-innovate without being able to learn from the industry’s arch-innovators.
Ford licensed technology from CATL because it needed that to have a chance of building a competitive lithium iron phosphate battery operation in the US. It formed a joint venture, in which Ford is the majority owner, with Geely to boost production at an underutilized plant in Spain that might otherwise have ultimately faced closure.
Ford’s talks with BYD are reportedly centered on batteries for hybrid vehicles, toward which it has pivoted after Duffy’s boss, US President Donald Trump, led a Republican backlash against EVs.
In other words, Ford is working with what it can in the world as it is. The Trump administration’s objectives of reducing reliance on Chinese supply chains and reshoring industrial capacity are fair enough and relatively bipartisan. However, objectives must dovetail with reality to some degree.
Shutting out Chinese battery technology altogether, even the licensing of it, would not create an all-US, world-beating battery industry; it would prevent one from forming. Similarly, there is an inherent tension between making vehicles affordable and making them entirely on US soil.
The letter echoes Trump’s executive order banning imports of bulk-power equipment from certain countries of concern, with China at the top of the list. Again, addressing security concerns around critical infrastructure is a legitimate pursuit, but for certain types of electrical transformers, China is a key supplier to an industry that, like autos, Trump nominally favors: data centers. Depending on how aggressively the order is implemented, it could exacerbate backlogs, with the market for transformers 15 percent short this year, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy.
The gap between politicking and pragmatism might be why Ford, unusually, hit back at Duffy in public. Ford disputed the claim that it proposed US joint ventures with Chinese automakers, although that would actually be a good idea. Ford also pointed out, embarrassingly, that the same battery plant Duffy lambasts in his letter was singled out for praise in terms of creating jobs by Duffy’s own boss less than two weeks ago.
Ford has already endured huge losses stemming from Trump’s EV crackdown and erratic tariffs. Its huge US manufacturing base still seems to not be enough for the White House — the same White House disrupting auto supply chains with its trade war against Canada and renegotiation of Trump’s own North America free-trade agreement. Duffy’s letter might be short on inspiration, but delivers exasperation in spades.

SkyGuardian drones bought from US tested, source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

The first two of the four MQ-9B “SkyGuardian” drones Taiwan purchased from the US underwent their first flight tests at an air base in eastern Taiwan early yesterday, a source familiar with the matter said.
The unnamed source did not disclose further details about the test flights, saying that they were conducted at Hualien Air Base.
The tests were conducted after the military and the drone manufacturer completed the assembly of the two drones delivered to Taiwan earlier this year, the source added.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
On March 17, Deputy Minister of National Defense Hsu Szu-chien (徐斯儉) and Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?) attended a handover ceremony in the US for two of the MQ-9Bs.
The US has agreed to deliver the four MQ-9Bs to Taiwan in two batches this year and next year.
The MQ-9Bs would provide Taiwan with “intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, target acquisition, and counter-land, counter-sea and anti-submarine strike capabilities,” according to the US Defense Security Cooperation Agency.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), a research fellow at the government-funded Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR), previously said that the role of the MQ-9Bs in Taiwan is to enhance battlefield reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities rather than serve as a primary offensive weapon.
INDSR researcher Hsieh Pei-shiue (謝沛學) wrote in 2020, when the US first approved the sale to Taiwan, that the drone is capable of linking to satellite communications networks shared among US allies.
That means Taiwan and the US could share battlefield intelligence instantly, providing opportunities for the two sides to cooperate during a conflict.
For example, if a cross-strait conflict breaks out, Washington could take advantage of anti-ship missile systems deployed along the First Island Chain to prevent Chinese People’s Liberation Army vessels from sailing into waters east of Taiwan to blockade the nation, Hsieh said.
MQ-9Bs are capable of long-term, long-range surveillance, meaning the drones could fly near Chinese vessels and provide critical intelligence for US forces to target them, Hsieh wrote at the time.
Another INDSR researcher, Kao Chih-jung (高志榮), yesterday cautioned that while the MQ-9B can detect and classify a large number of targets at once, it still requires final visual identification by human operators.
That limits the drone to conducting detailed, continuous surveillance on only two or three targets simultaneously, Kao said.
Consequently, the military should not rely solely on a handful of large drones, but should instead utilize the MQ-9B to conduct wide-area scans and designate high-value targets, he said.
That intelligence could then be distributed to small and medium-sized drones, shore-based radars and other combat units to build a more resilient “integrated reconnaissance and strike” network, he added.

Hurts had his moments for the two-time reigning NFC East champions in Sean Mannion’s debut as offensive coordinator. Mannion is Hurts’ fifth coordinator in the last five seasons and their partnership showed early promise for the former Super Bowl MVP.

The early big play came late in the first quarter when Hurts had multiple targets open on a play-action and connected with Dontayvion Wicks for a 64-yard reception. Wicks, acquired in an April trade from Green Bay, had the longest reception of his career and gave the first signal that perhaps the Eagles would be just fine at wideout after trading disgruntled star AJ Brown to New England.
Hurts finished the drive with a dart down the middle to Goedert for a 17-yard score and a 7-3 lead. If the Eagles had questions at wide receiver — and new No. 1 receiver DeVonta Smith had only two targets in the first half, and just three catches overall — they are fine at tight end. Goedert, who had a career-high 11 TD catches last season, again proved himself a trusted target.
Hurts added a 9-yard TD pass to Wicks in the second quarter for a 14-3 lead as the Eagles ran a clean, crisp offense under Mannion. Saquon Barkley, who tailed off last season after rushing for more than 2,000 yards in 2024 when the Eagles won the Super Bowl, ripped off a 42-yard run to set up Wicks’ TD.
Yet the offense largely cooled off behind a shaky line that gave Hurts little time to throw. Meanwhile, the defense — anchored by all-everywhere linebacker Zack Baun — rarely let Daniels break free long enough to sting the Eagles until the fourth.
Daniels — who went 18 of 34 for 164 yards — avoided a sack, spun and scrambled for a 13-yard gain on the final play of the third quarter. He had time in the pocket to hit a wide-open Williams for a 33-yard gain and then hit Stefon Diggs after the veteran receiver beat Cooper DeJean in the slot for a 10-yard touchdown.
Diggs, whose string of personal issues made him available even after he had 99 catches for 1,123 yards for the AFC champion New England Patriots, was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct when he jumped and bear-hugged the goal post before he landed on his back.
The Commanders might have gone for 2, but the 15-yard penalty forced them to settle for the extra point that made it 17-16.

Minister accuses directors of treason over Gaza film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:34 UTC
01:44:34 KST

Israeli Minister of Culture Miki Zohar on Sunday called for the award-winning directors of an Israeli-made Gaza documentary to be stripped of citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state.”
In NAZA, Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistle-blowers who outlined the artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza that have killed tens of thousands of civilians.
The 80-minute documentary won a special jury prize at this year’s Venice Film Festival in Italy.
Photo: EPA
Zohar accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from anti-Semites around the world.”
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” he added on social media.
Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who last year won an Oscar for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” far-right Israeli Ministry of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir wrote on social media.
“I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms,” he wrote.
The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied.
In 2022, the Israeli Supreme Court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty,” for example by committing acts of espionage or treason.
The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism.”
The law requires the Israeli minister of the interior to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it.
Abraham said that “the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanization of Palestinians.”
The Israeli military has criticized the use of anonymous testimonies in the film, saying on Friday that the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified.”
Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians.

Asian Games housing concerns grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:30 UTC
01:44:30 KST

Accommodation at the Asian Games starting this week in Japan is the “worst ever,” South Korean officials said on Monday, adding there was “a serious shortage” of rooms.
Beds in shipping container-style accommodations are too short for players to stretch out, a South Korean basketball chief said, while officials from the Philippines resorted to Airbnb.
There is no dedicated athletes’ village at the Games, with organizers using a cruise ship, temporary cabins and hotels in a bid to cut costs.
Photo: Reuters
The Games in the city of Nagoya and Aichi prefecture officially open on Saturday but soccer and basketball matches are already under way.
Jung Jae-yong, vice president of the Korea Basketball Association, said he was deeply unhappy with the cabins where the men’s basketball team are staying.
“Based on my experience this is the worst it has ever been,” he said. “Athletes who are over two metres tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It’s unreasonable.”
Byeon Jun-hyeong, from the basketball team, posted a video on social media showing a leaking sink and soaked floor in his hut, captioning it “Please help us.”
The huts are meant to house 2,000 athletes and officials over the more than two weeks of the Games.
Indian sports chiefs are so worried about the cabins that they built replicas to help get their athletes used to them.
Jung said organizers had not responded to South Korea’s concerns.
“The organizers have still not said anything,” Jung said. “We are very concerned and are discussing extensively with the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee what to do about this.”
Hundreds of athletes were temporarily evacuated from their accommodation last week as record rainfall lashed Nagoya. More rain has been forecast in the coming days.
More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected at the Games — a larger number than the Olympics.
Local organizers were expecting 15,000 and said last month that they had “neither the manpower nor the budget” to deal with ballooning numbers.
The Olympic Council of Asia said that everyone would get a place to stay.
Star cricketers have voiced fears about a lack of top-notch hotels.
A South Korean Olympic committee official said that, with the Games just days away, there are problems.
“At the moment there is a serious shortage of accommodation not only for the entire South Korean delegation to the Asian Games, but for delegations from around the world in the Aichi-Nagoya area,” the official said.
“We are doing everything we can to resolve the issue and ensure there are no such problems.”
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino said that all his country’s athletes had been given a room, but “some officials, like coaches, were moved to different hotels and Airbnbs.”
Asian Games organizers did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
The Italian cruise ship Costa Serena is due to arrive in Nagoya on Tuesday.
Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes would stay aboard the vessel.
The rest would be in hotels, including in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events would take place.

Russia hits Ukraine train line used by foreign officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:30 UTC
01:44:30 KST

The locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw was on Sunday morning hit by a Russian drone just kilometers from the Polish border, the Ukrainian minister of foreign affairs said, as Moscow’s airstrikes push closer to NATO territory.
The attack happened minutes after another train carrying European officials including former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and former UK British prime minister Boris Johnson left the station on the way back from an annual conference in Kyiv. Former CIA director David Petraeus was at the station when the drone hit, the New York Times reported.
The strike marked the latest escalation by Russia in the war — in its fifth year — as acts of sabotage, arson and drone incursions proliferate across the continent.
Photo: Ukrzaliznytsia Press Office via AP
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said in a post on social media, calling for Europe to increase sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine’s state railway operator confirmed a strike on a train in Volyn, about 2km from the Ukraine-Poland border in northwestern Ukraine.
Russian authorities have not yet commented.
Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs Radoslaw Sikorski said there was no violation of the border, but called the incident “escalation” by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The drones involved in the incident were Geran-5 jet-powered drones, Polish authorities said.
Kremlin forces “struck a passenger train locomotive,” the railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Telegram.
“The monitoring group warned the train crew about the threat in advance, thanks to which no one was injured,” it said.
The train, which had 208 people aboard, would continue on to Poland after a delay at the border of about six hours, the Polish railways said.
Sunday’s strike was the second this weekend, Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Sybiha late on Saturday posted images of railway facilities struck in Lutsk in northwestern Ukraine and Fastiv, southwest of Kyiv.
“Unable to achieve its goals on the battlefield, Russia attempts to make the entire territory of Ukraine a battlefield and turns to systematic attacks against civilians, trains, and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving,” he said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, speaking after an emergency meeting with top civilian and military leaders, said he cannot exclude the potential of escalation by Russia to Poland’s territories in the next weeks or months, including attempts to disrupt or paralyze border crossings.
Poland would consider how to mobilize allies to be prepared for a common response if needed, he said.
Images on social media also showed a large fire at a gasoline filling station close to the border crossing between Yahodyn in Ukraine and Dorohusk in Poland.
Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna said on social media that members of his team had been “stuck at this very border crossing, unable to leave Ukraine because of the Russian drone threat.”

China Airlines ups SAF use in Amsterdam flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

China Airlines yesterday completed its showcase flight for its fifth participation in the SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge, operating a direct flight from Taipei to Amsterdam with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) equivalent to 40 percent of the flight’s fuel use.
It was the first time the airline had used such a high proportion of SAF on a long-haul flight. In last year’s challenge, it used the same percentage on a regional flight to Bangkok.
China Airlines used a “book and claim” model to raise the SAF use on the Amsterdam flight, which was estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 93.2 tonnes, equivalent to about one-quarter of the amount absorbed annually by Taipei’s Daan Park, the airline said.
Photo: Shelley Shan, Taipei Times
The airline has used SAF on eight flights since 2022, collectively reducing at least 600 tonnes of carbon emissions, China Airlines president Kevin Chen (陳漢銘) said.
“The use of SAF on flights is key to helping the aviation industry transition toward net zero carbon emissions. We are committed to expanding the use of SAF on flights to Europe, North America and Asia, while incorporating low-carbon initiatives into our operations and passenger services,” he said.
The Amsterdam flight also featured several low-carbon initiatives, Chen said.
The airline used tableware in premium business class that is 30 percent lighter than previous versions to help reduce fuel consumption, he said.
The business-class menu and wine list were also printed on recycled paper using soy-based inks, he added.
Passengers were encouraged to check-in online before arriving at the airport and save their boarding passes on their mobile phones instead of printing them on paper, Chen said.
“We send text messages to our members encouraging them to preorder their meals before boarding. This not only helps us better understand passengers’ preferences, but also helps reduce food waste and the fuel required to carry excess food,” he said.
Gourmet plant-based meals developed by Taipei-based Michelin Green Star restaurant Little Tree Food (小小樹食) were served in all classes on the flight, the airline said.
The new Marc Jacobs cobranded travel kits also feature sustainable beauty products and toiletries developed in collaboration with Copenhagen-based design brand FRAMA, it said.
The airline’s Dynasty Sky Reading service has reduced the amount of reading material carried on flights by more than 4,300 tonnes since its introduction, it said.
Meanwhile, the airline expects to receive two Boeing 787-9 aircraft by the end of this year, which are expected to reduce fuel consumption by 20 percent and noise levels by 30 percent, Chen said.
The company aims to have 14 Boeing 787-9 aircraft delivered by the end of next year.
The Taipei-Amsterdam flight was exclusively sponsored by CTBC Bank, which also sponsored China Airlines’ aviation challenge in 2024.

Australia brace to take on South Africa at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:27 UTC
01:44:27 KST

Wallabies coach Les Kiss has said Australia need to take a big step up in physicality and intensity when they play world champions South Africa in Perth this month.
Kiss named his squad for the Test on Monday, bringing in uncapped flyhalf Harry McLaughlin-Phillips in place of the injured Carter Gordon and recalling Jordan Petaia after three years in the Test wilderness.
Having watched the Springboks go hammer and tongs with the All Blacks over four Tests, Kiss said the world champions would offer a different level of challenge to the opposition in his first four matches in charge, Japan and Argentina.
Photo: AFP
“The intensity and the physicality of the matches, we’re a little bit removed from that,” he told reporters in Canberra yesterday.
“Certainly, over the last four games, we’ve had some good, intense matches but we’re certainly stepping up another level when we come up against Springboks in a fortnight,” Kiss said. “We’re aware of that. We know we have to be better in certain areas, and we’re working hard to make sure we can improve in that. But, look, they’re in our backyard, so we’ll be up for the fight.”
Kiss said 22-year-old McLaughlin-Phillips had earned his call-up as a replacement for Carter, who fractured his leg in the 28-28 draw with Argentina last week that kept the Wallabies unbeaten in five Tests.
Veterans James O’Connor and Bernard Foley, along with Noah Lolesio, had been touted as possible flyhalf options given the lack of experience in the playmaker role in the squad.
“We did our due diligence, that’s for sure, and it landed that Harry had earned this right, and he’s waiting on our doorstep,” Kiss added. “These younger guys, we’re trying to make sure we get them upskilled, get them to understand how they can lead the game and drive it forward.”
“And we know that we can always lean back into the experience if we need to,” he added.
Outside back Petaia won the first of his 31 caps as a teenager at the 2019 World Cup and was last included in the Wallabies squad for the 2023 edition before moving abroad and having a crack at making it in the NFL.
“We just wanted to have a touch base with him,” Kiss said of the 26-year-old, who after his NFL stint played for a season for USA Perpignan in France before joining Japanese club Urayasu D-Rocks.
“There’s a lot of good back three players in our country at the moment that are playing here. Jordy being a bit further away in France recently, we just felt it was an opportunity to bring him in and have a good look at him.”
The Wallabies face South Africa on September 27 before home-and-away Tests against the All Blacks in October.

Automakers sign US$147m in deals at German show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:26 UTC
01:44:26 KST

Taiwanese auto parts and accessory makers signed US$147 million in business deals while participating in Automechanika Frankfurt held over the weekend, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
About 324 Taiwanese auto parts and accessory suppliers, including manufacturers of car door handles, bumpers, metal components and automotive electronics, took part in the Frankfurt trade exhibition, demonstrating Taiwan’s innovation and research and development capabilities at the Taiwan Pavilion, the ministry said in a statement.
The Taiwan Pavilion showcased Taiwan’s comprehensive automotive parts supply chain and industrial strength through immersive concept cars and smart maintenance scenarios. It featured a “Digital Zone,” business meeting and product display areas, and product launches aimed at connecting Taiwanese businesses with international buyers, the ministry said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Economic Affairs
The five-day exhibition attracted 1,970 potential buyers and visitors to the Taiwan Pavilion and generated deals worth US$147 million, it said.
In addition, the Taiwan Pavilion invited Aumovio, a German autonomous driving systems supplier, and the European Association of Automotive Suppliers to hold a session on industry trends, discussing developments in the automotive industry and green solutions in response to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the ministry said.
The Taiwan Pavilion promoted Taiwanese products through short videos produced by influencers and held a “Taiwan Night” on the exhibition’s opening day, where 350 international buyers and representatives of automotive industry associations met with Taiwanese firms to exchange ideas and discuss cross-border cooperation, it said.
The EU is the second-largest buyer of Taiwan-made auto parts and accessories, ministry data showed.
The ministry said that with the global auto industry accelerating its digital transformation and the European market emphasizing high-quality, innovative and sustainable products, Taiwan should cooperate with Europe on auto component and automotive electronics development as well as aftermarket services.

Why CPC, Taipower need subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:24 UTC
01:44:24 KST

The core principle of economics lies in pursuing the greatest possible collective welfare under the constraint of limited resources. When addressing a controversial issue, it is therefore best practice to disclose as much information as possible in an open, fair and impartial manner to all stakeholders. This can help alleviate concerns on all sides and minimize unnecessary disputes. The following provides answers for common questions to assuage public concerns about government subsidies to CPC Corp, Taiwan and Taiwan Power Co (Taipower).
Since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war, electricity rates in Taiwan have never fully reflected their cost. The expectation is Taipower would be able to make up for its cumulative losses by cutting expenditures and improving efficiency. However, the US-Iran war since late February has sent international oil and gas prices soaring, and Taipower’s finances have further deteriorated. This is why CPC and Taipower still need government support.
There is also the question of why the public has to pay for the government’s policy errors: If Taiwan had not phased out nuclear power, CPC and Taipower would not have needed to import so much natural gas and would not have sustained massive losses. However, the best course is to seek the solutions rather than dwell on what could have been. The task ahead is to think long-term and provide appropriate subsidies to CPC and Taipower, enabling Taiwan’s semiconductor industry to ride the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. This in turn could propel the stock market higher and generate additional tax revenue, which could then be returned to the public.
Taiwan’s economy grew 8.76 percent last year, the highest in 15 years. In the first half of this year, GDP growth further soared to 13.72 percent — about 4.3 times the average of the previous 13 years. This exceptionally high growth rate was primarily driven by the semiconductor and information and communications technology (ICT) supply chains as AI demand soared.
About 90 percent of the world’s advanced chips are dependent on Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain. This creates significant electricity demand. Last year, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC) domestic facilities consumed 25.8 terawatt-hours (TWh), or 9.1 percent of Taiwan’s total annual electricity consumption of 283TWh. As TSMC and related companies complete more new facilities, electricity demand would rise further. Providing appropriate subsidies to CPC and Taipower could ensure stable power supply, giving greater momentum to the semiconductor and ICT supply chains. This would allow the public to share in the economic prosperity and stock-market gains generated by the AI industry.
Given the limited time to rapidly increase electricity supply, Taiwan must rely on CPC and Taipower, which already possess the know-how. Before 2030, they are the only companies in Taiwan capable of quickly purchasing large quantities of crude oil and natural gas on international markets during a global shortage, and then rapidly convert them into electricity for domestic consumption.
Does this mean the public has to tolerate all the problems associated with subsidizing CPC and Taipower? The international trade system as it stands today is essentially about leveraging comparative advantage to try and obtain the largest possible share of the pie. In a rapidly advancing world, our first priority should be to secure and protect Taiwan’s readily available share of the AI boom, making full use of our own comparative advantage.
To this end, Taiwan urgently needs an adequate supply of electricity. The fastest and most effective approach is to turn to our experts and industry leaders to resolve this key problem as quickly as possible; everything else is secondary. Even if these experts have their shortcomings, the bigger picture must come first. For now, providing subsidies to CPC and Taipower is still the government’s best strategy.
Liao Huei-chu is a professor at Tamkang University’s Department of Economics.

Flash memory prices expected to climb further soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:23 UTC
01:44:23 KST

Prices of high-capacity NOR flash memory chips are projected to increase 90 to 110 percent in the second half of this year amid growing demand and slower capacity expansion, after jumping 100 to 120 percent on average in the first half, TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) said yesterday.
“Emerging applications such as AI servers and aerospace communications are propelling demand in 2026, aside from existing applications such as advanced driver assistance, digital cockpit systems and industrial devices,” the Taipei-based research group said in a report.
Demand from AI servers is exceptionally strong as each AI server requires three to five times more NOR flash memory capacity of a general-purpose server, TrendForce said. Edge-AI devices such as computers and robots with AI features are fueling demand for high-density NOR flash memory chips, it said.
Photo: AFP
“As NOR flash memory makers’ capacity expansions remain scant, demand-supply mismatch will carry into the second half of 2026,” TrendForce said. “NOR flash memory chip prices continue to hover at high levels, with high-capacity 256-megabit chips likely to double.”
While major memory makers have dramatically raised capital expenditures, it takes time to translate new capacity into available supply because of challenges in process shrinking, yield ramp-up, product validation and customer design-in, TrendForce said. The supply gap in the mid-to-high- capacity segment would remain unmet in the short term, it said.
However, prices of 128-megabit NOR flash memory and low-to-mid-capacity chips should see much milder increases of 10 to 20 percent in the fourth quarter, as capacity from Chinese suppliers comes online, it added.
TrendForce said Hsinchu-based Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電), the world’s largest NOR flash memory supplier, outgrew its rivals in capacity expansion, thanks to the production ramp-up of its 45-nanometer technology and efforts to upgrade to 25 and 20-nanometer technologies.
China’s GigaDevices Semiconductor Inc (兆易創新), the second-largest NOR flash memory maker, is optimizing its product portfolio to those with capacity higher than 32 megabit, TrendForce said. The company would not see a capacity pickup until its production outsourcing efforts bear fruit in the second half of this year, it said.
Macronix International Co (旺宏), also based in Hsinchu, would see very limited capacity growth in NOR flash memory as it is strategically pivoting its 12-inch capacity to favor embedded MultiMediaCard (eMMC) products and NAND flash, a segment that is experiencing far more severe supply constraints, the researcher said.
