OPINION - Iran's last card: The Houthis and Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:17:19 UTC
01:17:19 KST

- Dr. Ali Bakir is an assistant professor of International Affairs, Security, and Defense at Qatar University and senior nonresident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.
When the Israel/US-Iran war began on Feb. 28, the Houthis offered largely nothing but statements of support. The restraint had nothing to do with a shortage of missiles or of will. They were waiting for Tehran to decide when and how to best use its regional militias. That decision has now come. Over the past few days, Houthi forces overran Mocha and Dhubab and seized Perim Island (Mayyun), which splits the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They now hold Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the gate to it.
The strait carries roughly 12% of global trade, 11% of seaborne oil, and 8% of LNG. On their own, those figures are survivable. Ships can go around the Cape, freight costs rise, and the world absorbs it. What makes this moment different is that the other great oil chokepoint has been effectively closed during the war. With the Strait of Hormuz shut and Bab el-Mandeb under threat, Saudi Arabia has lost its fallback.
Calculated strategic shift
For years, the Houthis targeted Riyadh as part of the Saudi-Iranian contest across the region. After the two countries normalized relations, the Houthis scaled down their operations and moved to an entirely different theater. They focused their attacks on Israel before deciding to shift their focus and target Saudi Arabia, its infrastructure, energy facilities, and export routes. Seen from inside Yemen, this cycle of escalation, retreat, silence, and sudden redeployment makes little sense. Seen as one arm of Iran's regional network, it makes perfect sense.
Missiles, drones, and guided shells have always given the Houthis more reach than a conventional army of their size. They can strike Saudi energy sites, southern cities, and shipping cheaply and with very little warning. Control of the coast and Perim now adds weapons that are hard to counter. Artillery, anti-tank missiles and mines all work at close range and line of sight.
The implications of the Houthis' move are already visible. Riyadh has shut its East-West Pipeline after drone attacks. Jazan, Abha, and Najran are under repeated alert. Seventy-three civilians have been wounded in strikes on civilian and economic sites. Read from Tehran, the move serves three purposes.
First, it gives Iran a second lever over energy flows without committing its own forces to another high-intensity front. Houthi gains narrow Saudi export options, raise the political cost of American operations against Iran, and show that Tehran still has cards to play while it is under pressure. This returns to Iran's opening plan, which was to drive oil prices to levels the global economy cannot absorb and force Trump to stop the war under pressure from home and from the major importers and exporters.
Second, it weakens Saudi Arabia's standing and widens the split inside the Gulf Cooperation Council over Yemen, the Strait of Hormuz, and the war itself. Iran has been distributing the financial, human, and infrastructural costs of the conflict selectively among the Gulf States. At one point, the UAE carried the heaviest exposure, then Kuwait took its place, and now Saudi Arabia will bear the largest share. The Emiratis are already implicitly blaming Riyadh for the Houthis' progress in areas that were held before by pro-UAE forces. This comes at a time when Iran and the United Arab Emirates have agreed – according to the Iranian president – to turn the page and rebuild strained relations.
Defining test for the alliance
Third, it undermines the Mecca defense alliance. Ironically, the first test to the alliance has come from Iran rather than Israel. Saudi Arabia now faces three fronts at once: the Houthis in the south, Iraqi militias in the north, and Iran to the east. Iran using the Houthis against Riyadh acts as a catalyst for Pakistan and Türkiye to solidify their commitments. Tehran hopes to create an illusion for smaller states that this alliance lacks practical force, aiming to present appeasement as the safer alternative.
Throughout the war, Saudi Arabia has pushed for de-escalation while both belligerents preferred the opposite. By using the Houthis as a claw, Iran risks turning every one of its neighbors against it. The paradox is that Israel started this war and is the one state Tehran avoids. Israel's defense minister boasted recently that Iran knows American jets take off from Israeli soil to bomb it and still does not dare respond, which he offered as proof that Israeli deterrence holds.
The move in Yemen ends up serving Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has been pressing Saudi Arabia to join the Abraham Accords, and when the Houthis moved, he presented himself as a savior whose services are available on request. A wider war and higher oil prices also strain Türkiye and Pakistan and pull their attention elsewhere. For Türkiye in particular, the Israeli threat is not something that can set aside.
The open question is whether the Houthis can hold what they have taken, or whether their newly acquired positions will leave them highly vulnerable if Saudi Arabia and its allies decide to push back decisively.

Government moves to nationalise Speciality Steel UK to protect 1,300 jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:17:17 UTC
01:17:17 KST

One of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK).
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said officials would “work towards” acquiring the company to protect the jobs of its 1,300 workers in Rotherham, Stocksbridge and Brinsworth in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in the West Midlands.
The insolvent steelmaker, formerly part of the tycoon Sanjeev Gupta’s industrial empire, fell into administration last year and its day-to-day operations have since been run by the government’s official receiver.
The Norwegian steel startup Blastr Green Steel had been in talks to buy SSUK, but hopes had faded over the summer for a private sector takeover after a deadline to finalise a deal passed in June.
The steelworks and its staff have been described by Reynolds as important strategic assets for the UK. SSUK is the largest producer of “green steel”, made using less-polluting electric arc furnaces.
Reynolds said: “We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default.
“Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our industrial strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing.
SSUK went bust last year after longstanding financial issues under previous ownership, particularly after the collapse of its primary lender Greensill Capital in 2021. A high court judge at the time found the company was “hopelessly insolvent”, with only £650,000 in the bank after running down its reserves.
Since then, the government has been funding the wages of its workers, costing £3.5m a month. The plants have not been producing steel for the last year, though some staff remain on its sites to maintain equipment.
Ministers’ preference was for a private sector buyer, but after what were described as “extensive discussions” with Blastr, officials decided the company’s offer could not provide the desired long-term stability for SSUK.
A Blastr spokesperson said: “We are disappointed by the government’s decision today concerning Speciality Steel UK, and we were not informed in advance. Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK – and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners. We have a fully-funded proposal – at no cost to the British taxpayer – that is ready to complete within 12 weeks.”
Mark Bula, the Blastr chief executive, quit the company unexpectedly at the end of last month, with its finance boss, David Morant, taking his place.
The shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said it was “surprising” that the government had moved away from a private sector buyer after picking a preferred bidder. Speaking in parliament, he asked Reynolds: “Other than a new prime minister who’s committed ideologically to nationalisation, what has changed
Reynolds added there was “nothing ideological” about the move and that he would “not go into the detail” about why Blastr’s bid fell through. He accused the Conservatives of a “legacy of neglect” during their 14 years in government.
The government has committed to spending up to £2.5bn on the steel industry through the national wealth fund. About £500m of that was put towards converting Tata Steel’s blast furnaces into electric arc furnaces.
The South Yorkshire mayor, Oliver Coppard, said he was pleased the government had taken action, adding: “It’s the next important step forward, giving us more time to find the best possible outcome for our steelmaking communities – places where people have faced economic challenges and real barriers to opportunity for far too long.”
Roy Rickhuss, the general secretary of the Community union, welcomed the intervention but said the lack of a credible buyer was “a disappointing outcome”.
He added: “SSUK is a unique and integral component of the UK’s steelmaking capabilities, without which we would be entirely reliant on foreign suppliers for high-value speciality inputs to our critical energy infrastructure and our advanced manufacturing base, including the defence industries. We cannot allow British industrial sovereignty in these areas to be lost.”

NATO officers are now learning from Ukraine’s combat experience in UAVs, electronic warfare, and intelligence. Ukrainian military personnel have held a series of seminars for officers from the Polish and German armies on applying lessons from modern warfare to military command and decision-making, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said.
No NATO army has fought a modern war. Because Ukraine's soldiers are the only ones with years of combat under saturating drones and jamming, their experience is now reshaping how the alliance plans and trains, not the reverse.
The seminars have mixed theory with live exercises and set Ukrainian operational practice against NATO's written doctrine, exposing where the alliance's assumptions about maneuver, command, and the use of force no longer fit a battlefield run by technology.
Ukraine teaches the lessons of drone war

He is Ukraine's senior representative at the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC), the first joint civil-military institution between NATO and Ukraine.
The course runs through a joint centre
The three-week event took place in Lublin, at the base of the Lithuanian-Polish-Ukrainian Brigade, which provided the facilities. It was part of JATEC's support for a program called Captains' Training, intended to facilitate the exchange of tactical-level lessons between Ukraine's forces and NATO. The officers worked through Troop Leading Procedures for planning a company's actions and the Military Decision Making Process, used by a battalion staff.
In Ukraine, the Come Back Alive foundation has backed the same course since 2022.

Mahmoud Abbas: Do not reverse your most popular decision, extinguish our last bit of hope - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:16:59 UTC
01:16:59 KST

Masar Jadid party list for the Palestinian legislative elections calls to President Mahmoud Abbas
Voices within different circles of the Palestinian leadership are increasingly calling for the legislative elections scheduled for November 28 to be postponed, citing the complexity of the situation and the difficulty of the present circumstances.
Yet millions of Palestinians continue to cling to the glimmer of hope created by the presidential decree calling for the elections to be held on time.
Allow me to be the voice of all those who cannot make themselves heard before you, President Mahmoud Abbas: the young people waiting for an opportunity to help shape their future; the women demanding their rightful place in public life; the people of Gaza seeking an end to war and destruction; and Palestinians in the West Bank, Jerusalem, and the diaspora who are weary of division, paralysis, and their inability to influence the decisions affecting their lives.
Since the decision to hold elections was announced, nearly two million Palestinians have responded with renewed hope and registered to participate – close to 90 % of eligible voters.
Opinion polls may indicate that a large Palestinian majority, approaching 80%, disagrees with the policies of the current Palestinian Authority and demands change.
But another reality is equally clear: an overwhelming majority of our people now stand behind you and support your decision to hold the elections on schedule.
This may be the most popular and widely supported decision of your political and national career – not because it guarantees victory for any particular side, but because it returns the decision to the people and gives them the right to choose their representatives, hold them accountable, and renew the legitimacy of their institutions.
Holding elections is neither an administrative procedure nor a ceremonial milestone in the life of a political system. It is a historic event capable of uniting a people torn apart by a long and painful division.
It can restore effectiveness to Palestinian politics and open the doors of our institutions to new blood and to generations long denied the opportunity to participate.
History will record that you made this decision during one of the most difficult and complicated periods in the modern Palestinian experience.
You will be the president who addresses the newly elected Legislative Council at its first session and entrusts a new government emerging from that council with the responsibility of governing: a national unity government of the kind we have lacked for far too long, and a government responsible for rebuilding a devastated Gaza and restoring human dignity to its people as they prepare to endure their third consecutive winter among tents and rubble.
Palestinians need a government that offers them more than slogans: a government that improves their lives, protects their rights, restores the world’s confidence in them, opens the door to financial and political relief, and rebuilds their institutions on the foundations of law, accountability, and popular legitimacy.
You recently succeeded in overseeing local elections and in enabling Fatah to convene its conference and elect its Central Committee. Fatah’s youth movement was also given the opportunity to elect its leadership.
I was one of those young activists when I first met you following your return to Ramallah in the 1990s. Just as those processes were successfully completed, you can protect the most important electoral process of all and ensure that it takes place on time.
Do not repeat the mistake
The senior figures now advising you to postpone the elections because of the circumstances – and working hard to present alternative scenarios and “Plan Bs” – are, in many cases, the same voices that offered you similar advice in 2021.
The elections were postponed then, but none of the promised alternatives materialized.
While the Palestinian “Plan B” amounted to little more than promises and delays, other plans were being formulated elsewhere, beyond our sight. They exploded in all our faces on October 7, 2023, and our people paid a catastrophic price.
The most dangerous course today would be to repeat that mistake: to cancel the political process without providing a credible democratic alternative, and to allow the resulting vacuum to expand until it is filled by extremism, chaos, and violence.
When ballot boxes are closed, the gates of despair are opened. When young people are denied the ability to change their reality through politics, the entire society becomes more vulnerable to the next earthquake.
Perfect conditions for elections do not exist – especially in the Palestinian context. If we make perfect conditions a prerequisite for democracy, elections will never take place.
The challenges involving Gaza, Jerusalem, the internal division and the occupation are real, but they are additional reasons to insist on holding the elections and to work for their success – not justifications for canceling them.
Jerusalem must not become a pretext for obstructing the Palestinian people’s democratic will once again.
We must fight to hold elections there using every political, legal, and diplomatic instrument available to us – and, most importantly, every technological one.
If certain actors within Israel place obstacles in the way, we must confront them with innovative solutions that guarantee the participation of Palestinian Jerusalemites, rather than granting those actors in Israel veto power over Palestinian democratic life as a whole.
I have been among those who criticized and opposed the PA’s policies on many occasions, expressing my views clearly in Palestinian, Arab, and international forums.
Today, however, I stand with the overwhelming majority of the Palestinian people – beside you and behind your decision to hold these elections on time.
This is not a political alignment behind an individual or a party. It is a stand in defense of the Palestinian people’s right to choose, and in support of legitimacy, democracy, and peaceful change.
Your determination to uphold this decision – even if you find yourself standing alone against pressure, calculations, and competing interests – will give millions of Palestinians a new reason to believe that politics can still change their lives.
When you stand before the elected Legislative Council at its first session, you may hear applause unlike any you have heard throughout your long national career.
It will not be the applause of courtesy or protocol. It will come from hearts in which hope has been restored, and from a people who will respect you for returning to them the right to determine their own future.
Mr. President, do not allow anyone to extinguish the glimmer of hope your decision has ignited. Do not surrender our people’s future to those offering excuses and alternative plans that have already been tried and have failed.
Stand firm on November 28, and make it a date with history – not another date postponed.
The writer is a Palestinian political leader from Jerusalem and the founder and head of Masar Jadid (New Path), a new Palestinian party committed to democracy, nonviolence, accountable government, dialogue with Israel, and improving the daily lives of Palestinians. He is a longtime advocate of a negotiated two-state solution and sustained engagement between Palestinians and Israelis.

A good deal in bad neighborhoods: Why the Gulf’s best bet remains in Jerusalem - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:16:51 UTC
01:16:51 KST

Every year, just a few days before Rosh Hashanah, Israel’s Finance Ministry publishes the outgoing year’s economic balance sheet. Entering a fourth year of war, what Israel has pulled off is nothing short of remarkable.
With a 3.3% unemployment rate (well below the OECD average), a rising GDP per capita of around $60,000, inflation under 2%, and foreign investment nearly doubling over the past year, Israelis have a lot to be proud of.
Through what is its longest war, Israel has done what few thought possible three years ago: cemented itself as an undisputed, stable economic powerhouse in the world’s most dangerous and unstable neighborhood.
Just look across the borders. Every single one of Israel’s neighbors faces crippling water and energy deficits, but their problems don’t end there.
Lebanon can barely call itself a sovereign state, having long since surrendered what sociologist and political philosopher Max Weber defined as a government’s baseline test: a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force.
Syria, even as its new transitional authorities attempt to piece together the post-Assad state, remains fragmented and fragile. Egypt and Jordan maintain a cold peace with Israel, but both are in economic shambles.
Cairo splurges tens of billions on megaprojects, a glittering new administrative capital and sprawling sports cities, while its citizens face soaring unemployment and poverty.
In Jordan, millions remain classified as refugees despite living in the kingdom for generations, maintaining a persistent resentment toward the crown.
Not many know this, but the most coveted prize for a growing subset of Jordanians today is simply a daily work visa to cross the border and sweep floors in Eilat.
Further south, the siege on Hormuz shattered another illusion: the promise of a unified Arab Ummah (nation).
Despite the so-called Sunni alliance, these states failed to protect their skies from an Iranian missile onslaught, or safeguard their two main economic engines – commercial aviation and oil exports – from Iranian and Houthi strikes, simply because they never established a joint and proactive preventative defense.
Meanwhile, Israel is doing, at least in an economic sense, pretty damn well for itself. This simple fact puts the region in a spot where, no matter what MENA governments say or do publicly, doing business with Israel remains their best bet.
The survival of the Abraham Accords proves it. Anti-Israel sentiment may be rampant on the Arab streets, but the Accords’ primary beneficiaries, the UAE and Morocco, continue to expand their trade and investment ties with the Jewish state.
Trade with the Emiratis has surpassed $3 billion this year. Morocco’s trade numbers look smaller at around $400 million, but you mustn’t tell their masses that over 10% of their defense imports now originate in Israel – for fear of sparking a riot.
The past
As we enter the seventh year of the Abraham Accords, it is easy to see why the diplomats can’t stop congratulating themselves.
Grafting a hyper-productive tech economy onto a volatile neighborhood yields what economists call a synergistic surplus – and what real-world operators simply call a damn good deal.
The sight of Arab ministers gathering at Sde Boker for the 2022 Negev Summit to talk supply chains, desalination, and Iranian drones was the ultimate proof of concept.
Just months prior, the idea of foreign dignitaries chatting over coffee in David Ben-Gurion’s backyard was pure fan fiction.
Yet for all the anti-Israel rhetoric echoing through their capitals, regional leaders recognized that Israel’s structural stability is too useful to ignore.
Nowhere is this truer than in the defense sector. Under pressure from Iranian proxies and domestic instability, Arab monarchies are quietly doing joint drills and sharing radar data with the Israelis.
Washington, ever keen on maintaining Pax Americana on the cheap, essentially forced the marriage by shifting Israel into CENTCOM’s jurisdiction.
This presumably bland administrative reshuffle placed Israel and its Arab neighbors at the very same war room table, locking off-the-books security hookups into a permanent military apparatus.
Yet the Accords were never flawless. Lasting, mutually beneficial peace relies on three distinct tiers, and so far, the foundation remains uneven.
The first tier belongs to top-level elites: state officials and mega-corporations.
Opening an embassy in Abu Dhabi or watching business tycoons mingle at Negev resorts makes for great photo-ops, but these backchannels existed long before formal normalization, and they would survive a diplomatic rupture just as easily.
Sovereign governments don’t need a physical flag in Tel Aviv to move capital; an offshore shell company in Cyprus does the job with far less political noise.
The second tier is seemingly impossible to shift: the Arab street. Decades of entrenched anti-Israel sentiment do not vanish overnight. Look at the tourism numbers.
While hundreds of thousands of Israelis flooded Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Marrakech, incoming visitors from the Gulf or Morocco were virtually nonexistent. But a lagging public does not cap the potential for a synergistic surplus.
The third tier is where the cheese lies: the middle-layer elites.
These are the agile, high-potential enterprises positioned just below the global giants – agrotech ventures, AI and semiconductor startups, independent energy developers, and cross-border logistics operators.
By stitching regional talent, capital, and technology directly into everyday commercial incentives, this middle tier builds the structural connective tissue that renders diplomatic peace not just symbolic, but unbreakable.
The future
Israel has an urgent incentive to anchor regional stability.
In a fracturing world order, supply chain disruptions and maritime chokeholds are becoming erratic and unpredictable. Expanding regional trade infrastructure is becoming a strategic imperative for Israel and its neighbors alike.
Executing this requires pursuing imperfect, high-stakes megaprojects.
Yet the risk of ambitious regional integration pales in comparison to the alternative: degenerating into an economic island tethered to over-regulated, low-growth European trading partners whose own geopolitical trajectory offers shrinking returns.
As I have argued previously in these pages, energy infrastructure is the ultimate lever for anchoring Israel’s regional standing.
The playbook is sitting right in front of us: combine capital-flush, tech-hungry Gulf states with the vast, sun-drenched, and labor-rich landscapes of Egypt and Jordan.
Consider an audacious proposition: a cross-border energy and compute hub in the Gulf of Aqaba.
Combine Saudi oil, Egyptian and Jordanian land and labor, and Israeli science and innovation. The resulting synergy unlocks a once-in-a-generation play: constructing and powering massive AI data centers using a hybrid blend of solar and oil for unbroken, 24/7 operations right in our backyard.
While the US and Western Europe collapse under acute grid constraints and local NIMBY resistance, a Middle Eastern AI corridor – with Israel as a load-bearing partner – would transform the region into one of the most indispensable nodes of the global economy.
This is not a project for the faint of heart – and neither are the alternative proposals on the table, whether a pan-Middle Eastern rail network linking the region to India or joint large-scale scientific endeavors.
Each requires Israel to have a hard-headed strategy and a serious appetite for risk.
Nor is it an easy pill for Arab governments to swallow, relying as it does on an “outside-in” peace model that prioritizes state-level alignment before resolving the Palestinian issue. Yet both sides would do well to take a cue from Alexander Hamilton.
Facing fierce opposition, Hamilton championed an imperfect framework because it was vastly superior to the status quo and flexible enough to evolve over time.
The document he fought for was the US Constitution – a deeply contested compromise that went on to power the most prosperous nation in human history.
The writer is a geopolitical analyst and former director of operations at Hashiloach, a policy journal. He can be reached at eewachs@gmail.com

Russian convoy resupplies Syria coastal facilities for first time since Moscow-Damascus deal
TARTOUS, Syria, Sept 14 - A convoy of Russian naval and cargo vessels delivered supplies last week to coastal facilities long used by Moscow’s military, two sources familiar with the operation said, in the first such mission since Damascus and Moscow agreed last month on the future of Russia’s military presence in the country.
The operation offers an early indication that Moscow is continuing to resupply facilities at Tartous port and the Hmeimim airbase under the new deal, which provides for civilian facilities used by Russia to be transferred to Syrian control and military sites to be turned into joint training centres.
Russian forces are to remain at the bases under the agreement. Russia has used Hmeimim and Tartous to project power across the Mediterranean, Middle East and Africa. Tartous provides Moscow with its only naval repair and replenishment facility in the Mediterranean.
Moscow has supplied both sites in recent months but last week's was the first since the August 9 agreement was announced.
The four-vessel convoy arrived at the Mediterranean port of Tartous on September 7, according to movements tracked by Reuters and maritime intelligence firm SynMax.
Satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed the Russian Ro-Ro cargo ship Sparta and navy replenishment oiler Akademik Pashin docked on September 8 in Tartous at piers 3 and 4, respectively.
A Reuters reporter saw the two vessels docked there on September 9, while Russian tanker General Skobelev remained offshore. A surveillance balloon was seen flying over the port during the unloading operation.
A Syrian military source and a Russian-Syrian businessman familiar with the operation said Sparta unloaded supplies including ammunition destined for Hmeimim and Tartous. Reuters could not independently confirm the contents of the shipment or their intended recipients.
SynMax identified the fourth vessel in the convoy as Admiral Levchenko, a Russian Udaloy-class destroyer.
Syria’s General Authority of Ports and Customs and Russia's embassy in Damascus did not respond to requests for comment.
VESSELS SAILED DARK
The vessels stopped transmitting their signal shortly after crossing Strait of Gibraltar towards the Mediterranean. Reuters tracked the group via satellite imagery as it continued east and ultimately reached the Syrian coast.
Sparta has long been used in Russian military logistics in Syria and is under U.S. sanctions. General Skobelev is also under Western sanctions over transporting Russian oil.
Damascus and Moscow reached the agreement over Hmeimim and Tartous after 18 months of negotiations following the December 2024 overthrow of former President Bashar al-Assad, a close Russian ally. REUTERS

‘Fauda’ is Lebanon’s top show on Netflix as it thrives across Arab world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:16:33 UTC
01:16:33 KST

The new season of Fauda, released on September 8 on Netflix, is a hit around the world, as the series tends to be – but the big news is that, even as anti-Israel sentiment mounts around the world, it is the number one show in Lebanon, according to tracking sites such as FlixPatrol.
Not only is it the top show in Lebanon, which has been in a state of war with Israel since 1948, but it is or has been in the top 10 in nine other Arab countries that have different relationships with Israel.
At the time of writing, it ranks fourth in Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar; sixth in Bahrain and Morocco; seventh in Oman; eighth in Kuwait; and tenth in Egypt.
Earlier in the week, it reached number two in Jordan, the UAE, and Bahrain; number three in Qatar, Kuwait, Morocco, and Oman; and number four in Egypt. In Saudi Arabia, it reached number eight, but has since dropped out of the Top 10.
The tracking sites, which release statistics before Netflix releases its own figures, are considered reliable.
The show's success in the Arab world
Two Israelis, Lior Raz (who also stars in it) and Avi Issacharoff, created Fauda, and Yes Studios produced it. It is about an Israeli counterterrorism commando unit and is based on true stories.
The show has frequently won praise for its depiction of Palestinian characters, some of whom are portrayed with great sympathy, such as Dr. Shirin (Laëtitia Eïdo), a West Bank physician caught between various factions.
The success of the new season in the Arab world is not unprecedented; the fourth season of Fauda, released in 2022, performed similarly well across the Middle East.
Reportedly, it has long been a guilty pleasure among Palestinians in the West Bank and even in Gaza.
What is remarkable about the release of the fifth and final season is that despite the waves of hatred against Zionism and Israel, Arabs are still tuning in – and in large numbers, especially since two episodes of the new season present a detailed flashback to the events of October 7, 2023, when Hamas terrorists massacred 1,200 in southern Israel.
The family members of one of the main characters are slaughtered graphically, and members of the unit try and fail to save many others across the region.
Issacharoff said, in an interview with Ynet, ahead of the release of this season, “People asked whether Fauda would still try to present both sides. But this event is different. Here, you want to tell the story from an Israeli perspective.”
That may be, but Arabs around the Middle East are still tuning in, and the press is writing about the series respectfully in many of these countries.
In the Lebanese newspaper Al Joumhouria, a mainstream Center-Right Arabic-language daily, its reviewer wrote about the show from the perspective of someone who knows and likes it: “Ironically, Fauda becomes more compelling when it stops trying to be exciting all the time.
“Its best moments aren’t necessarily those where cars explode, or characters exchange gunfire, but rather those where the series leaves its characters lingering in the silence following the explosion …
“The plot sometimes feels smaller than the reality it’s trying to represent. This makes some storylines feel all too familiar. … This is where the series’ limitations become apparent.
“Fauda aims to be simultaneously a special operations series, a psychological drama, and a commentary on post-October 7 Israel. It can succeed in each of these roles individually, but it doesn’t always manage to weave them into a cohesive plot.”
Just like many reviewers in Israel, this Lebanese reviewer asked the question: “When a real trauma is transformed into dramatic material, the question becomes bigger than the quality of the scene: Who is telling the story?
“Who has the right to define the victim and the perpetrator? And where does the drama end and the construction of the political narrative begin?”
That’s a question that can only be answered by those who watch Fauda, and it’s clear that, whatever their political beliefs about Israel, many Arab viewers are debating such questions among themselves.

Leaders of Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland unite for self-determination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:16:19 UTC
01:16:19 KST

Leaders of Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland unite for self-determination
Leaders of nationalist parties from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland say Westminster has ‘no right’ to block democracy.
The leaders of the main political parties in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have declared their right to “self-determination” in a joint agreement signed at a rare meeting in the Welsh capital, Cardiff.
All three parties – the Scottish National Party (SNP), Plaid Cymru in Wales and the pro-Irish unity Sinn Fein in Northern Ireland – want greater autonomy and eventually independence from the United Kingdom, but have different views on issues such as referendums and timelines.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘War on terror’: How 9/11 changed the language of conflict
- list 2 of 39/11 at 25: How the ‘War on Terror’ helped mainstream Europe’s far right
- list 3 of 3Trump says a unified Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during Irish visit
The SNP’s John Swinney, Sinn Fein’s Michelle O’Neill and Plaid Cymru’s Rhun ap Iorwerth attended in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments.
Laura McAllister from Cardiff University told Al Jazeera that the wording of the agreement was “deliberately” couched in the broader “constitutional language of self-determination”.
“This is the first time that the nations of the United Kingdom are attempting to drive the constitutional question,” she said. “They also covered some of the more practical policy areas where they may wish to share stances, such as renewable energy, relationships with Europe, economic development.”
What does the three-party joint agreement say, exactly?
“Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future,” the group said on Monday, referring to the UK-wide parliament in London.
“For the first time ever, people across these islands have first ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom,” the memorandum of understanding continued.
“The future of our nations belongs in the European Union … For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end.
“Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the agreement said.
What has the UK PM said on pro-independence movements?
Sinn Fein wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and join a united Ireland.
The forum happened after US President Donald Trump weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK. He told reporters that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” during a visit to Ireland on Saturday. “Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.
Indeed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had something to say on Trump’s comment – that his position on Irish unification remained unchanged.
On August 27, Britain’s newly-elected leader said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the UK was “off the table”.
Burnham has also dashed hopes among some for a second vote on Scottish independence, saying recently that another referendum was “off limits”.
What is the legal status of the three regions?
Constitutionally, the UK has four constituent countries: England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Within these four jurisdictions, there are three legal systems:
- England and Wales have a combined legal system.
- Scotland operates as a distinct legal system based on Scots law.
- Northern Ireland has its own distinct, independent legal system based on English common law and its own legislation.
Power is shared in a system known as devolution, unlike in the federal system of the United States or Germany. It means power is not constitutionally divided on an equal basis between a central government and the four nations.
Elected institutions have some powers with their own legislatures and governments, but defence and foreign affairs, among other issues, remain controlled by London.
Crucially, none of the states has the right to unilaterally leave the UK.
Scotland held an independence referendum in 2014 after Westminster gave the green light. Independence was rejected by 55 percent to 45 percent. Wales similarly has no existing legal mechanism allowing the Senedd (Welsh parliament) to call an independence referendum on its own.
For Northern Ireland, the rules are different. Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, the British government must call a referendum if the UK secretary for Northern Ireland believes it is “likely” that a majority would vote for a united Ireland.
Has the mood for greater autonomy grown?
Recent polling points to significant, though varying, support for constitutional change.
A Survation poll found 47 percent backing Scottish independence, while a University of Liverpool survey found 36 percent in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish reunification.
In Wales, a Survation poll put support for independence at 32 percent.
“Plaid Cymru was elected with heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence,” explained McAllister. “The situation in Scotland is very different” and “fundamentally” so in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, she added, describing Monday’s meeting as “very tactical and very strategic”.

Keeping women out of prison must be the focus | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:14:44 UTC
01:14:44 KST

Your editorial (The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer, 10 September) is right to argue that the prison capacity crisis cannot be solved through a series of short-term fixes. Victims need confidence that the government has a credible long-term strategy for the criminal justice system, not another piecemeal intervention designed to buy time.
I share your concern about the pressures facing probation services. There are also legitimate questions about the impact on policing, but we cannot discuss the prisons crisis without confronting the crisis in our courts.
About one in five prisoners are now awaiting trial, often because cases are taking so long to be heard. Some defendants spend so long on remand that by the time they are sentenced, they are released from court, having effectively already served their sentence. Victims will rightly ask whether that is justice, and the public will rightly ask what it means for public safety.
The government points to the removal of foreign offenders as part of the solution to prison overcrowding. Yet a third are held on remand awaiting their day in court due to a court system in crisis.
Prisons, courts, probation and policing are interconnected. The government cannot hope to resolve the prisons crisis if it does not also resolve the crisis in our courts. Delays leave victims waiting years for justice, drive up the remand population and place further pressure on an overcrowded prison estate. As victims’ commissioner, I need assurances that the prime minister is focused on pursuing a strategy for the whole justice system, not simply responding to the latest emergency.
Claire Waxman 
Victims’ commissioner for England and Wales
We are a collective of women’s charities, frontline services and women with lived experience of prison. We saw first-hand the devastating impact that Holloway prison’s closure had 10 years ago. For 170 years, it was a paradoxical space – a place of trauma, but also a crucible of feminist resistance and home to dozens of frontline services. From the suffragettes to the activist Chris Tchaikovsky, women’s history unfolded there. Now it has been razed.
This invites the question: what could we build instead? Your editorial offers some answers when it references the Corston review. However, one crucial element is missing: women’s centres. These are spaces where women’s services are brought together under one roof, offering support with housing, domestic abuse, employment, childcare, therapy and more. They help women holistically, rather than simply fixing one area of their lives. Women in Prison reports that for every £1 invested in a women’s centre, £2.75 is saved.
Women’s centres stop women entering the criminal justice system, keep children out of care and relieve pressure on emergency services. We’ve spent a decade campaigning for one on the Holloway prison site. The public are supportive and building work is under way, but funding is still not secured.
If Andy Burnham wanted to pursue a visionary policy, he could champion a women’s centre programme across the UK, starting with the Holloway Women’s Building.
Polly Creed
Holloway Women’s Building Collective, London
Measures to reduce the number of women behind bars are long overdue, but it must be more than a short-term fix to try to free up capacity (Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men, 7 September).
Women in, and leaving, prison face particular challenges. Many have also been victims of crime or have children they hope to be reunited with. Rates of homelessness are higher among women than men when they leave prison.
These challenges also lead to higher numbers of women being recalled to prison. Our analysis found that there was one recall for every four women under post-release supervision in the community in the first three months of this year, compared with one recall for every five men.
In some cases, recall will have been needed to protect the public. But in others, better community support could and should be put in place.
If the government is serious about a long-term reduction in the number of women in prison, it should start by ensuring that women leaving prison are supported to stay out.
Enver Solomon
Chief executive, Nacro
The reported proposal to convert parts of the women’s prison estate to accommodate male prisoners may initially sound controversial, but the more important question is why so many women need to be imprisoned in the first place.
A pilot women’s court in Bristol offers a potentially much more constructive answer. By taking a trauma-informed, problem-solving approach, the court seeks to address the circumstances underlying offending – including domestic abuse, addiction, mental ill health and homelessness – while still holding women accountable for their crimes.
This seems preferable to the familiar cycle of short prison sentences, release and reoffending. It also recognises something often overlooked in the debate: imprisoning women can have consequences far beyond the offender herself. Many are mothers and primary carers, so custody can profoundly disrupt children’s lives and family relationships.
If the Bristol experiment demonstrates that intensive community supervision and properly funded support can reduce reoffending while keeping women safely out of prison, it deserves to be expanded.
The real test of a successful prison policy should not be whether we can find more cells, but whether we can reduce the need for them.
Stuart Harrington
Burnham-on-Sea, Somerset

Not Just Remote Learning: What Scenarios for Organizing the Educational Process Were Proposed to Schools During Air Raids
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:13:25 EEST
01:13:25 KST

Not Just Remote Learning: What Scenarios for Organizing the Educational Process Were Proposed to Schools During Air Raids
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Education and Science recommends that schools determine in-person, blended, and remote learning scenarios depending on the security situation. The transition between formats should be planned in advance.
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine recommends that schools determine several scenarios for organizing education in advance, depending on the security situation, including in-person, blended, and distance-learning formats. This was reported by the press service of the Ministry of Education and Science, as reported by UNN.
The conditions under which schools organize the educational process differ significantly depending on the security situation, the characteristics of the area, and the capacity of a particular institution. Therefore, there cannot be a single model that works equally well for all schools. Each educational institution must determine the learning format taking into account its own conditions and capabilities, the availability and capacity of a shelter, infrastructure, and readiness to organize distance learning. At the same time, the school must approve possible scenarios and an algorithm for switching between them in advance, depending on changes in the security situation. To help schools organize this process, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine has developed methodological recommendations on organizing the educational process in general secondary education institutions under martial law
The document contains common approaches that schools can use to assess their own capacity and prepare several scenarios for organizing the educational process in advance, depending on changes in the security situation.
Organization of the educational process
The founder or an authorized body must ensure the necessary conditions for organizing the educational process and assess the institution's capacity. The school principal organizes the educational process, determines the basic and alternative models, and approves a practical algorithm for switching between them.
Such an algorithm must be prepared in advance. It must take into account scenarios involving changes in the security situation, prolonged alerts, problems with electricity or communications, as well as other circumstances that may affect the possibility of studying in person.
The school must assess its own capacity. The first step is to determine whether it can ensure safe and uninterrupted in-person education, including assessing:
-  the capacity and capabilities of the shelter; 
-  the number of students and staff the school can safely accommodate; 
-  the possibility of staying in the shelter for an extended period; 
-  the availability of electricity, heating, water, and other necessary utilities; 
-  backup power sources; 
-  access to the internet and communications; 
-  the readiness of teachers and students for distance learning; 
-  the possibility of organizing education using other educational spaces in the community. 
At the same time, the total number of people simultaneously present at the school cannot exceed the shelter's capacity. If the shelter is used not only for staying during an alert but also as a learning space, the school must also take into account the actual number of equipped learning places.
Several learning scenarios
Based on its assessment of its own capacity, the school determines a basic learning model and alternative scenarios between which it can switch depending on the security situation.
Possible models include:
In-person learning with a transition to the shelter during an alert. This is the optimal model for situations when alerts are short or infrequent. After the all-clear is given, students and teachers can return to classes.
In-person learning using the shelter as an educational space. If alerts are frequent or prolonged, the shelter can be prepared for continuing education, with places for students, a teacher's workstation, lighting, power supply, and, where possible, internet access.
A combination of in-person and distance learning. If the school cannot safely accommodate all students at the same time, education can be organized on a rotating basis—for different groups on different days, weeks, shifts, or according to another schedule.
Distance learning. This format is used if students cannot safely travel to or stay at the school, or if the security situation requires it.
"At the same time, the transition to another format should not happen spontaneously. The school determines in advance the conditions under which the transition takes place, who makes the decision, how the schedule changes, how teachers work, and how communication with students and parents is conducted. Where possible, lessons should begin immediately in safe locations," the Ministry of Education and Science reported.
As noted by the Ministry of Education and Science, an air raid alert does not mean the automatic suspension of the educational process. If staying in a shelter is safe and the necessary conditions are available there, learning may continue in forms appropriate to the situation. This may include continuing the lesson, independent work, reading, consultations, completing project or research assignments, reviewing material, or other pedagogically appropriate activities.
At the same time, if alerts become systematic or last for a total of more than two hours during the school day for several consecutive days, the school is advised to switch to a pre-prepared model of learning in a shelter or to a remote format.
The school must also determine how to work with different subjects. Not all learning activities can be transferred to a shelter or online with equal ease. Therefore, when planning, the school must decide which classes require direct interaction between the teacher and students, special equipment, laboratories, or workshops; which can be held in a shelter; and which learning outcomes can be achieved through independent, project-based, or research work. If some students do not have safe conditions or the technical ability to study remotely at home, the school may organize safe learning areas or groups for them.
At the same time, during a single lesson, one teacher should not simultaneously conduct an in-person class for some students and a synchronous online class for others. Instead, during the day or week, different groups may study in different formats according to the schedule established by the school.
We remind you
In Kyiv, ahead of the start of the new school year and amid prolonged air raid alerts caused by the ongoing attacks by the Russian Federation on the capital region, including with jet-powered drones, different learning formats were prepared depending on the security situation.

The relevant parliamentary committee has backed the request, with lawmakers expected to vote on Kravchenko’s dismissal on Tuesday.
Kravchenko submitted his resignation on 7 September after NABU and SAPO uncovered an alleged criminal organisation involving officials in the Prosecutor General’s Office.
Investigators allege that members of the group regularly received bribes from fraudulent call centres in return for not interfering with their activities, and laundered millions in criminal proceeds.

Middle-class parenting neglects life skills that are essential for students | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:12:02 UTC
01:12:02 KST

Zoe Williams’ university-bound son won’t be the only one among his peers not to know how, or indeed why, bed sheets are laundered (I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures, 8 September).
Modern day, middle-class parenting tends to direct kids away from domestic pursuits, focusing instead on academic achievements and sporting prowess or music grades, scouting activities and Duke of Edinburgh awards. With their waking hours consumed by so many outside interests, there’s little time for learning life skills such as cooking, cleaning and laundering.
I visit schools giving talks to sixth-form students about preparing for university. In advance, I invite the students to share any questions or concerns they may have. Alongside issues such as finding their future friends and whether they’ll cope academically, they often question how they’ll live independently. Many of them have never had to do a full supermarket shop, prepare a meal from scratch, wash a kitchen floor or iron a shirt.
They anticipate focusing on their studies and socialising with their flatmates, coursemates and people they meet through clubs and societies. They do worry about how they’ll also take care of themselves and how they’ll juggle everything.
We owe it to our young people to teach them essential life skills along the way – not just in the week before they head off to university – so they have one less thing to worry about. After all, conjuring up a decent chilli, cleaning a loo properly and washing a sheet without it shrinking, fading or changing shape, are lifelong useful skills.
Melissa Scallan
Author, Starting University
 Five minutes after dropping my son off at his Birmingham halls of residence, we received a WhatsApp message: “I cut my hand on a knife when I opened the packaging. There’s quite a lot of blood. Any advice?” As we turned the car round, while rummaging for plasters in the glove box, we got another message. “It’s OK, my new flatmates have bandaged me up.” All six are still close mates, 10 years later.
Pippa Keech
Lyndhurst, Hampshire

Severe mental illness and the risk of violence | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:10:13 UTC
01:10:13 KST

Your report of Sarah Hughes’s acknowledgment that mental health organisations have sometimes “softened the truth” about the relationship between serious mental illness and violence marks an important change in the public debate (Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief, 5 September).
There is some historical irony here. Mind grew from the National Association for Mental Health, an organisation in which psychiatrists and other mental health professionals played an important part. From the 1970s onwards, Mind increasingly defined itself as an independent campaigning organisation and, at times, a vigorous critic of psychiatric practice and authority.
As a psychiatrist who previously chaired the Royal College of Psychiatrists group concerned with risk, and who gave evidence to the Nottingham inquiry, I have seen the consequences of our difficulty in discussing this subject plainly.
Psychiatrists have long had to hold two propositions together. The overwhelming majority of people with mental illness are not violent and should not be stigmatised as such. But some severe mental disorders, particularly when accompanied by factors such as substance misuse, disengagement from treatment or a previous history of violence, can materially increase risk. Acknowledging the second proposition does not contradict the first.
Indeed, avoiding discussion of risk for fear of stigma can itself have consequences for patients, families and the wider public. Properly resourced services, continuity of care, assertive follow-up and thoughtful risk assessment protect patients as well as others.
It is therefore significant that Mind is now prepared to say publicly that the mental health charity sector has sometimes been too reluctant to acknowledge an uncomfortable reality. This should not become an argument between psychiatry and its critics. It is an opportunity for clinicians, patients and campaigning organisations to recover a more mature position: opposing stigma while being equally willing to speak honestly about risk.
Prof John F Morgan
Consultant psychiatrist, Harrogate, North Yorkshire

Top civil servant sacked by Starmer received record £860,000 payout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:09:15 UTC
01:09:15 KST

The former head of the civil service Chris Wormald received a record payout of almost £860,000 when he was forced out of the top job in Whitehall by Keir Starmer.
Cabinet Office accounts have revealed that the former cabinet secretary, who was sacked earlier this year, was paid £859,496 upon departure. The figure is an unprecedented amount, which required civil servants to seek a special direction from ministers to approve it because it was “greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to”.
Wormald has since been made a member of the House of Lords, after serving as cabinet secretary for just 14 months. He was replaced by Antonia Romeo earlier this year.
It was revealed earlier this summer that the size of the payout to Wormald was so vast that Cat Little, the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office, had to request a ministerial direction from Starmer in February to override value-for-money concerns before she could approve it.
In her letter to the prime minister at the time, Little wrote that she needed special permission to grant such a high award, saying “in respect of value for money, I have consulted civil service HR and legal advisers and have had due regard to managing public money and the consideration of Sir Chris Wormald’s employment rights in the circumstances. The proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to.”
Little said she had been informed a settlement of that level was “necessary given that this is a departure from a high-profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice”.
She said the prime minister could take into account “the public interest in bringing this matter to a conclusion and the prevention of distraction from the effective operation of government”.
The Conservatives said the payout was an “appalling waste”. The shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: “Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.
“This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers’ money by Labour. Whether it’s big payouts for fall guys, or gimmicky giveaways, this government is always happy to spend our money if it thinks it will benefit the Labour party.”
The settlement with Wormald dwarfs the previous record amount given to the former Treasury permanent secretary Tom Scholar, who was forced out by Liz Truss in one of her first acts as prime minister. He was given £457,000, including severance pay and compensation in lieu of notice and leave.
Wormald became a crossbench peer after he was nominated by Starmer as the former prime minister left office.
At the time, No 10 had been criticised over its handling of Wormald’s departure, with his allies saying he had been badly treated and learned of his fate through the media.
Dave Penman, the general secretary of the senior civil servants’ union the FDA, said the briefing against Wormald had been extraordinary and that it was “no way to run a country”.

Dancing with the enemy: Lebanese platform partners with Israeli channel
A Lebanese media platform owned by disgraced banker and businessman Antoun Sehnaoui has announced a media partnership with Israeli broadcaster i24NEWS, amid Israel's ongoing attacks on Lebanon and its occupation of parts of the country's south.
The Washington-based This Is Beirut platform and i24NEWS released a video on Sunday announcing the new collaboration, presenting it as an effort to bring together Israeli and Lebanese newsrooms.
In the video, two Israeli presenters appeared alongside a group of Jewish, Muslim and Druze Israelis, as well as Lebanese-Israeli activist Miriam Younes, who has promoted Israeli messaging among Arabic-speaking audiences for years.
The presenters danced with the group before addressing the Lebanese public, inviting people to visit Israel while expressing a desire to visit Beirut.
i24NEWS accompanied the video with a message asking: "What if Israel and Lebanon could tell a different story?"
"In one moment in Jaffa, two newsrooms from different sides of different borders came together and chose to listen to each other," it said, describing the encounter as an opportunity for "people, music, culture, and a conversation about what could be possible".
The broadcaster added that such moments could be the beginning of "a different future".
Neither i24NEWS nor This Is Beirut provided details about the nature of the partnership, including whether it would involve jointly produced journalism or the exchange and republication of reports and articles.
The announcement comes as Israeli forces continue to attack southern Lebanon and maintain control over parts of the country's territory, despite a ceasefire agreement and Lebanese demands for an end to Israeli attacks and a withdrawal from occupied areas.
Sehnaoui has publicly expressed support for Zionism on several occasions. In 2025, he funded a New York opera about the life of Theodor Herzl, the founder of the Zionist movement.
He also met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for dinner in Washington in July.
Following that meeting, Lebanese judicial authorities issued a search and investigation notice against Sehnaoui over alleged dealings with Israel, according to the report.
i24NEWS was founded in 2013 by Israeli-French businessman Patrick Drahi and broadcasts in English, Arabic and French from Jaffa.

Refined product deficits, not crude supply, strain energy market — US Energy Secretary

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:04:53 UTC
01:04:53 KST

WASHINGTON, September 14. /TASS/. Disruption in the global energy market is driven primarily by a shortage of diesel fuel and other refined petroleum products rather than crude oil supply volumes, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said, explicitly linking the tightness to the global impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russian fuel and energy infrastructure.
"World oil supplies will continue to grow, and that'll ease some of the pressure on oil prices," Wright predicted at a press conference at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) headquarters in Vienna.
"But the bigger challenge has been on oil refining. This is a tighter market than the oil market, and there's a lot of causes for the tight refining market. But maybe the one I'd highlight the most is the Russia Ukraine conflict," the US Energy Secretary noted.
He pointed out that Russia is currently not exporting any diesel fuel.
"That [market] is too tight right now. We are working with American refiners to expand their capacity," Wright said.
Responding to reporters' questions on September 13, US President Donald Trump effectively demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries to prevent further escalation in the global energy market, adding that Washington had already conveyed this position to Kiev.
Commenting on Trump's remarks, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted that "any call for the Kiev regime to cease strikes on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed." On July 30, the Russian government imposed a new temporary ban on exports of gasoline, diesel, and other fuels, running until January 31, 2027.

SO arquitetura stacks tiny azores home onto 13 square-meter footprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:03:11 UTC
01:03:11 KST

On the south coast of São Miguel, Portugal, SO Arquitetura & Design has turned a tiny storage building into a complete home. Mini Atalhada began with a footprint of just 13 square meters, inside a concrete structure too small to accommodate even a car. The architects bought the building themselves, using it as a chance to test their own ideas about how little space a house really needs. With very little room to expand across the site, they went upward, bringing the total interior area to around 35 square meters.
The stair became the central problem almost immediately. In a house this small, a conventional staircase could consume a large share of usable floor space, so the studio designed a compact structure from perforated metal sheet with timber treads. Light passes through it, as do views from one level to another. The stair still takes up space, of course, but its porous construction keeps it from cutting the house into isolated floors.
The team at SO Arquitetura & Design organizes the home’s program to follow the building upward. The lowest level meets the street and contains the entrance with supporting functions, while the sleeping area sits through the intermediate levels. The main living space occupies the top floor alongside the kitchen, with a work area incorporated into the same level. Here, the house gains more daylight and a stronger relationship with the surrounding landscape and sea.
At 35 square meters, every element has to earn its place. Built-in furniture absorbs storage and domestic functions, while structure and lighting are worked into the same spatial logic. The interior feels connected across floors instead of being broken into a collection of tiny rooms. Even the stair participates in that idea, allowing sightlines and light to continue through the center of the house.
Mini Atalhada converts a 13-square-meter storage structure into a compact home in the Azores
concrete and timber give depth to a tiny interior
Exposed reinforced concrete stays visible throughout the interior, giving the small house a fairly direct material character. Pale timber brings warmth against those harder surfaces, while black window frames and dark ceramic finishes sharpen the edges of the rooms. There is very little excess here. The interest comes from how those surfaces sit close together, changing as daylight moves through the narrow volume.
Light does a surprising amount of spatial work. Openings visually extend the rooms toward the landscape, while daylight travels through the perforated stair and across several levels. After dark, integrated lighting makes the stacked occupation of the house visible through its facade.
SO Arquitetura & Design also sees Mini Atalhada as a response to rising land and construction costs, but the strongest argument is already built into the house itself: an awkward 13-square-meter footprint has become a complete home whose compactness shapes almost every architectural decision.

timber treads soften the metal stair running through the center of the house
the top floor places the main living space beside views toward the sea
exposed concrete meets pale timber throughout the compact interior
custom built-in furniture concentrates storage along the walls

2026-09-15
00:01:43 CST
01:01:43 KST

MOGADISHU, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A total of 171 Somali migrants stranded in Libya returned home safely on Monday aboard a charter flight organized by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
According to the IOM, the returnees, including three minors, were stranded in Libya after surviving hazardous journeys across several countries, only to face severe hardship, exploitation and abuse at the hands of smugglers.
"Migration should never compromise a person's safety, dignity or future. By supporting voluntary returns and reintegration, the government, the European Union and IOM are enabling Somali migrants to turn a challenging chapter into an opportunity to rebuild their lives at home, in safety, with dignity, and integrated in their communities," Manuel Marques Pereira, chief of mission for IOM Somalia, said in a statement issued in Mogadishu.
Supported by the EU through the Migrant Protection, Return and Reintegration in Sub-Saharan Africa (MPRR-SSA) program, and in coordination with the Somali government, the charter flight first landed in Hargeisa, northern Somalia, where 42 returnees disembarked.
The remaining returnees arrived in Somalia's capital, Mogadishu, where authorities and families welcomed them before they received immediate post-arrival assistance.
Many returnees had been separated from their families and lacked access to basic services, leaving them in urgent need of humanitarian assistance and protection support.
Since August 2022, the EU-IOM partnership with the Somali government has facilitated the voluntary return of about 2,000 Somali migrants from Libya, with additional charter flights scheduled for late 2026, according to the IOM.
According to the IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), hundreds remain stranded in Libya under dangerous conditions.
Severe insecurity and a lack of necessities, including food, shelter and medical care, leave thousands in urgent need of protection and humanitarian assistance.
The MPRR-SSA initiative enables safe and voluntary returns for Somali migrants. After arrival, returnees receive housing, medical and mental health care, as well as transport to their home regions.
They later receive individualized financial assistance to help them rebuild their lives and reintegrate into local communities. ■

Finland has joined the French nuclear initiative in Europe
Kyiv • UNN
Finland has joined France’s initiative to expand nuclear deterrence through cooperation with European partners. It has already been supported by Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
Finland has joined France’s initiative to expand the scope of its nuclear deterrence through cooperation with partner countries in Europe. Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
In March, France announced the "Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative" in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s concerns about the United States’ security commitments to Europe and the implications of the war in Ukraine for regional security.
"This initiative is primarily aimed at strengthening European security. It enhances Europe’s responsibility for its own defense and helps prevent escalation," Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a post on the social network X.
Under the initiative, the exclusive right to make decisions on the use of nuclear weapons belongs to the president of France, unlike the NATO model, where a shared Nuclear Planning Group operates.
At the same time, the initiative provides for joint exercises, the possibility of temporarily stationing nuclear-capable assets on the territory of allies, as well as in-depth consultations.
Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a "natural step" after other Nordic countries — Norway, Sweden and Denmark — joined the initiative earlier this year.

BUDAPEST, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Hungary and Germany agreed on Monday to strengthen bilateral cooperation and open a new chapter in their relations, following talks between Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orban and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Budapest.
In a joint statement issued after the meeting, the two ministers said the countries aimed to deepen their long-standing partnership and jointly contribute to a strong, secure and competitive Europe.
Anita Orban said preparations had begun for Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar's visit to Berlin on Nov. 9-10.
The two sides agreed to strengthen the Hungarian-German Forum, establish regular consultations between their foreign ministries and deepen exchanges between young diplomats. They also agreed to intensify cooperation between think tanks while examining the possibility of holding a German-Hungarian cultural year in 2028.
On economic ties, the ministers said bilateral cooperation has contributed significantly to both economies, particularly in the automotive industry, and pledged to expand the cooperation. They called for strengthening the EU single market, improving European industrial competitiveness and coordinating efforts to safeguard energy security.
On migration, Hungary and Germany said their region faced significant pressure and identified stopping illegal migration and strengthening the protection of the EU's external borders as common goals.
The two sides also reaffirmed their commitment to EU enlargement and the integration of the Western Balkans, while highlighting Hungary's recent accession to the European Public Prosecutor's Office as part of the efforts to strengthen the rule of law. ■

Nepal's flood warning network crippled as key monitoring stations swept away: gov't report

KATHMANDU, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Nepal's ability to monitor sudden rises in river levels suffered a major setback after the Aug. 26 flood swept away several hydrological monitoring stations, a government report said.
The report released on Sunday by the Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research (CHWRR) under the Water and Energy Commission Secretariat (WECS) said the loss of these stations highlights the extreme nature of the flood and poses challenges for future monitoring in the region.
The report has found that monitoring stations located at Rasuwagadhi and Syaphru Besi in Rasuwa district, Betrawati in Nuwakot and Phurke Khola in Dhading were destroyed or rendered inoperative as the flood moved rapidly through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors.
The destruction of the stations meant that water levels could no longer be continuously recorded at several critical points as the flood intensified downstream.
Seven days after the devastating flood, the Nepali authorities installed a flood monitoring system with a CCTV camera at Timure in Rasuwa to provide visual surveillance of river conditions.
According to the report, this is the first time Nepal has initiated a CCTV-based real-time river monitoring system, aimed at strengthening the country's capacity to detect sudden changes in river conditions and issue timely flood warnings. ■
