Nepal disaster: Swiss expert urges lessons for future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:12:32 UTC
22:12:32 KST

Nepal disaster: Swiss expert urges lessons for future
Nearly three weeks after devastating floods struck Nepal and Tibet, Swiss engineer Eric Bardou says conditions on the ground remain challenging and calls for a better understanding of such events to help prevent future disasters.
“You could say it almost feels like an earthquake,” said Eric Bardou, a member of the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA), in a telephone call to the Keystone-ATS news agency from Kathmandu on Saturday. On the ground he saw buildings destroyed or displaced by the force of the wave, some of which appeared to have been pushed sideways.
The 57-year-old engineer, who specialises in geotechnical engineering, hydrology and mountain risks, was sent to Nepal by Switzerland on September 5. He was integrated into the mission of the United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), where his role involved assessing risks related to water and terrain.
On his arrival, two lakes that had formed as a result of landslides raised fears of a new wave. “They drained on their own, but it is the sort of situation that still needed to be monitored,” he explained. The teams had to set up observation points and adjust their movements to ensure they were not caught off guard by a new rise in water levels.
Preserving evidence
The Swiss expert, who is soon returning from Nepal, highlights another, less visible urgency: preserving the traces of the disaster before they disappear.
“If we don’t do it now, we will never be able to understand what happened,” he stresses. But behind these traces lies, above all, a human tragedy.
Bardou said he was deeply moved seeing people wandering along the riverbanks, searching for missing relatives or for items that might be salvaged from the rubble. International organisations on the ground are meanwhile focused on trying to rescue those still alive beneath the rubble.
More
Switzerland sends more aid funding, experts to Nepal
The hope to be able to document the disaster, however, is confronted with a fundamental difficulty: estimates vary widely depending on the methods used, particularly concerning the volume of collapsed material.
“The volume swept downstream is estimated at between 100 and almost 300 million cubic metres,” Bardou explains. He claims to have seen various estimates and is unable to determine which is the most reliable, especially as he has been unable to access the area where the deluge began.
On August 26, rock and ice broke away at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres on the north face of the Langtang Lirung massif. Debris quickly descended downstream along the Lhende Khola river valley, situated some 20 kilometres upstream of the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi border pass, completely obliterating the Sino-Nepalese border at that point. The deluge killed nearly 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.
More
Himalayan flood sparks concern among Nepalese and Tibetans in Switzerland
Another unknown factor is the exact composition of the mass that poured down the valley. The traces observed downstream indicate a particularly fluid flow containing vast volumes of water and boulders, some of which were several metres in diameter.
‘Fluid’ torrential debris flow
By comparing marks left on trees and buildings with the deposits on the ground, Bardou estimates that 80% of the mass consisted of water.
The disaster has also left behind a considerable amount of sediment and caused heavy erosion. Some bodies have been found downstream as far as India, at a distance of between 150 and 240 kilometres, demonstrating the enormous power.
Bardou says the challenge is to better understand the mechanisms behind this disaster rather than settling for a simple explanation linked to climate change. “To say that it’s hot, that the ice is melting and that everything is collapsing is a bit too simplistic,” he said.
More
Why do Swiss mountains collapse? It’s complicated
Climate change can cause rapid transformations to which the mountains must adapt, he said. Permafrost, which acts like a cement holding certain rocks and soil together, may play a special role. But he says he’s not totally satisfied with this as the sole explanation. Society needs to determine exactly what happened in order to identify and prevent such events, he adds.
Prevention is difficult
Prevention measures, however, are hampered by the sheer scale of the Himalayas: 600,000 km² compared with the 25,000 km² of the Swiss Alps. “The scale radically changes the situation,” he said.
In Switzerland, the large number of observers, guides, engineers and sensors makes it easier to detect mountain movements and changes.
In Nepal, institutions and specialists have been working on glaciers and mountain risks for some time. But even with satellite images showing a possible acceleration in an area prior to the event, you still needs to know where to look among the vast amounts of data, says the Valais native.
The glacier at the root of the disaster is now a central focus. Until then, the priority had been to rescue those who could still be saved.

He said the vessel would enable authorities to examine previously inaccessible sections of the wreck and conduct a detailed inspection of its interior.

The Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger vessel operating between Kyrenia and Taşucu in Türkiye’s Mersin province, began taking on water from its bow shortly after departing Kyrenia Port around noon on Aug. 30. The vessel sank as it attempted to return to the port.
There were 267 passengers and crew members aboard. A total of 239 people were rescued, while 14 people died and another 14 remain missing. The wreck lies at a depth of approximately 554 meters off Kyrenia.

America’s AI boom needs $140b in new power plants, new estimate shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:11:18 UTC
22:11:18 KST

America’s AI boom needs $140b in new power plants, new estimate shows
NEW YORK – America’s data centre boom will need US$110 billion (S$140 billion) to build 45 gigawatts (GW) of new power generation through 2030, according to an analysis by Moody’s Ratings.
The vast majority of that new supply – more than 30 GW – will come from natural gas-fired units and represents about 4 billion cu ft of incremental gas supply, according to a report on Sept 14.
The bulk of the remaining supply will come from solar and energy storage, with nuclear restarts accounting for less than 5 per cent. One GW is roughly equivalent to the output of a traditional nuclear reactor.
The projection is based on the International Energy Agency’s forecast that data centres will consume 426 terawatt-hours in 2030, doubling its share of US electricity usage to 10 per cent from 2025 levels.
Moody’s forecast quantifies what it would take to produce enough megawatts to feed the data centres needed for artificial intelligence and cloud computing that are driving the biggest expansion in US electricity demand in decades, fueling a massive buildout of infrastructure to support it.
The White House has called the AI race a national imperative, backing some of the world’s biggest companies as they compete for potentially enormous profits.
But the buildout comes at a cost, drawing opposition from Americans worried that the average household and business is subsidising AI through rising power bills, pollution, water shortages and threats to public lands and private property.
The US$110 billion buildout of new power plants alone could add US$25 billion to US$30 billion a year to electricity costs in the US. How that is passed on to consumers will depend on the rate-making process and other rules for allocating costs in each area, Ryan Wobbrock, senior vice-president of ratings at Moody’s Ratings’ global infrastructure finance group, said in an e-mail.
Data centres will pay for as much as US$15 billion of those costs directly because they are paying for power plants to be built on their AI campuses, he said. These behind-the-meter projects at data centres represent about 30 per cent of the total buildout through 2030.
After two decades of lacklustre demand growth, the US has been struggling to jumpstart the construction of gas generators in an industry that typically moves with years of lead time. These gas generators are coveted because they can be ordered to ramp up, unlike renewables that are beholden to sunshine and wind speeds.
Amid affordability concerns, “federal and state politicians and regulators are requiring more time to review and structure rates, creating a new source of potential delays for new data centre developments”, according to the report led by Wobbrock.
“The pace of data centre development is increasingly exceeding the speed at which the electric grid can add generation, transmission and interconnection capacity,” he said. BLOOMBERG

Hungary moves to amend controversial child protection law after EU court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:11:11 UTC
22:11:11 KST

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced amendments to the country’s child protection law, which the EU’s top court ruled discriminatory in April. The changes could end discrimination against sexual minorities and help unlock further EU funding for Hungary.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced amendments to the country’s so-called child protection law, which has faced longstanding criticism from Brussels and LGBTQ+ rights groups over its discriminatory provisions.
The law was initially adopted in 2021 under Viktor Orbán’s government as a measure to protect minors from paedophilia. It was subsequently amended to effectively prohibit the depiction of homosexuality to minors, on the grounds that such content could pose a risk of paedophilia.
The legislation led to books, newspapers and films being pulled from shelves and television schedules. Following protests from international gay rights organisations, the European Commission launched an infringement procedure against Hungary.
In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that the law breached EU law, finding that it treated LGBTIQ+ people as a threat to society, violated their human dignity, and risked contributing to their social exclusion.
Speaking to a national radio on Monday morning, Magyar said the amended law would restrict minors' access to violent and sexual content while removing discrimination against sexual minorities.
"There is a good chance that the amendment of the law, in addition to much stronger protection of children, will also allow Hungary to avoid the fine," Magyar said.
In a separate 2024 ruling, the European Court of Justice fined Hungary €1 million a day for systemic breaches of its migration system, which restricted access to asylum. The ruling has so far cost Hungary around €1 billion.
Magyar said that child protection, healthcare and education remained key priorities for his government, which took office in April after bringing 16 years of rule by Orbán’s right-wing, Eurosceptic Fidesz party to an end.
Magyar, who has made restoring relations with the EU and NATO a key priority, struck a deal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in May to release €16.4 billion in previously frozen EU funds for Hungary. He said the amendments to the child protection law were aimed at unlocking further funding.
"We could unlock half a billion euros for educational support," he said.
In response to a request for comment from Euronews, the European Commission said it was too early to assess the proposed amendments, but confirmed that it remained in close contact with the Hungarian government on the issue. The amendments are expected to be presented to parliament later on Monday.
Over the weekend, Magyar also announced plans to relax restrictions on adoption by same-sex couples, which had been effectively prohibited under Orbán’s government.

UN rights chief calls for action on growing risks from AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:10:18 UTC
22:10:18 KST

Beril Canakci
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
 UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk on Monday called on governments and leading artificial intelligence companies to take urgent action to address the growing risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
“We are on the cusp of irreversible change, affecting not just us but generations of humanity to come,” Turk said in a letter addressed to governments and AI developers.
He warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful AI is creating “greater existential risks” and said failures involving agentic AI systems — AI systems capable of carrying out tasks with limited human intervention — could bring essential services to a standstill, disrupt communications and critical infrastructure, and threaten democratic institutions.
“Entire populations could be cut off from clean water, heating, and financial services,” Turk said, adding that AI is already accelerating warfare and weakening safeguards against the launch of weapons of mass destruction.
Turk said AI-related harms are already occurring, pointing to the automation of essential services, large-scale data collection and surveillance, and AI-powered disinformation campaigns.
“AI harms are not hypothetical — they are already occurring, front and centre,” he said.
The UN rights chief urged governments and frontier AI companies to establish common safety standards, conduct ongoing human rights assessments, and introduce independent monitoring.
He also called on states hosting leading AI companies to ensure they are held accountable and to require independent technical checks of AI systems capable of acting autonomously.
“No country can govern this technology alone. No company should be able to decide by itself which risks the world must accept. No person should be required to surrender their human rights in exchange for claims of technological progress,” Turk said.
He urged governments and companies to work through multilateral forums to develop rules for advanced AI based on international human rights law.
The statement comes in the wake of recent incidents of AI agents going beyond what many experts thought possible, spurring industry insiders to issue warnings and calls for stricter regulation of the sector.

"Allocating 0.25% of GDP annually to support Ukraine is not just a figure. It is a very concrete expression of friendship, solidarity and an understanding that our security today is shared," he said.
Stefanchuk emphasized Ukraine's readiness to share its acquired experience, primarily in the defense and security spheres.
"Ukraine and Lithuania are connected by more than partnership. We share close ties between our peoples, a common understanding of threats and a shared vision of Europe's future," Stefanchuk said.

South Korea and Arctic Shipping: A Game Changer on Thin Ice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

On September 16, 2025, South Korea’s Lee Jae-myung administration formally adopted Arctic shipping development as a national policy. The Ministry of Ocean and Fisheries has subsequently moved to Busan, aiming to establish the city as South Korea’s maritime hub for Arctic shipping.
South Korea sent its first trial container, the PanStar Acro (under the flag of Panama), via the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to Europe in August 2026, following a few weeks behind the Chinese container ship Dubai Tower (under the flag of Liberia).
On September 11, 2026, Hanwha Ocean, one of Korea’s big three shipbuilders, began constructing the country’s second ice-breaker, which is expected to be more than twice the size and 50 percent better than the existing RV Araon.
South Korea, an Asian middle power, is clearly ambitious about seizing potential economic and strategic opportunities of the development of Arctic shipping. The challenges and prospects for South Korea’s Arctic ambitions hold insights for other interested countries as well.
The Arctic is warming at an alarming rate due to human-induced climate change. According to NASA, in September, when the Arctic sea ice reaches its minimum extent, the ice-covered area is now “shrinking at a rate of 12.2 percent per decade, compared to its average extent during the period from 1981 to 2010.” A decrease in the extent of sea ice and the loss of older, thick ice makes longer navigation seasons possible and generates new access to previously difficult to reach regions of the Arctic.
According to the Arctic Council, the number of ships operating in the Arctic reached a record high in 2025, with 1,812 unique ships entered the Arctic Polar Code area. This is a 40 percent increase compared to 2013. The shipping activities in the Arctic are likely to further increase in years to come, since the Arctic Ocean could possibly have its first ice-free day in summer 2027.
The Arctic shipping routes, especially the NSR along the Russian Arctic coastline, could cut shipping times by 10-20 days between East Asia and Europe, compared to traditional routes via the Strait Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope. Moreover, the freedom of navigation in “strategic chokepoints,” such as the Strait of Hormuz, is being shaken by geopolitics. This makes Arctic shipping routes strategically attractive for East Asian economies as an alternative for their foreign trade and energy security. China is so far the most active user of the NSR. And here comes South Korea.
In my view, the development of the NSR must be considered in the context of the China-Russia-U.S. strategic triangle. Both Russia and the United States are Arctic states, but they hold divergent views about the legal status of the NSR. Article 234 (“Ice-Covered Areas”) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea provides a legal basis for Russia to exert jurisdiction over the NSR. However, Russia actually treats the NSR as its domestic waters. The United States, on the contrary, views the NSR as straits used for international navigation. Under this view, ships should have free transit rather than needing to apply for a permit from Russia’s Northern Sea Route General Administration.
China is in a tense geopolitical rivalry with the U.S., while Russia is now China’s most important partner in international affairs. Nevertheless, Russia and China have profound differences about how the Arctic should be governed. China is not openly challenging Russian regulation of the NSR, but that does not mean China is satisfied with Russia’s position. China wants to be seen as an equal partner with Arctic states and have a bigger say in Arctic governance.
Therefore, when South Korea enters into the scene as an active user of the NSR, there are potential risks and challenges from three aspects.
First, there is geopolitical risk. Russia is interested in increasing the use of the NSR and welcomes foreign investment and technology to develop the Russian Arctic. However, since the Ukraine War, national security concerns now supersede economic development and environmental protection in many parts of the Arctic. The region has sadly become confrontational again. Any future geopolitical incident, such as a Freedom of Navigation Operation (FONOP) by the U.S. against Russia’s “excessive claims” of the NSR, could spark fierce Russian retaliation. South Korea, as a U.S. ally, might be caught in the crossfire.
Second, and related, is the sanctions risk. The U.S. has introduced massive sanctions against Russian entities, both primary sanctions and secondary sanctions. Those sanctions paid special attention to Russia’s oil and gas industry as well as the banking system, to cut the Russian economy off from the West and reduce Russia’s revenue to fund its war. Secondary sanctions are particularly powerful. They are used to maintain or put additional pressure on the sanctions target by penalizing third parties that engage with the primary sanctions target in activities that could undermine or evade the purpose of the primary sanctions.
Therefore, Chinese and Japanese enterprises have become very cautious about doing business with Russia. For example, according to the website of Northern Sea Route General Administration, in 2025,only one Chinese-flagged ship submitted an application for a navigation permit on the NSR. The R/V Tan Suo San Hao is a scientific vessel owned by the Institute of Deep-sea Science and Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, which was delivered in 2024 with capacity to conduct scientific expedition in the Russian Arctic. China’s state-owned global shipping giant, COSCO, has tempered its enthusiasm about using the NSR. Rather, unknown shipping companies, such as New New Shipping and Sea Legend (which runs Dubai Tower), were established to provide regular container service only between Russian and Chinese ports, using the NSR. The U.S. secondary sanctions are applied universally. South Korea’s status as a U.S. ally does not necessarily shield its companies from future U.S. sanctions.
Third is the competition South Korea will face in Arctic shipping. China is the most active user state of the NSR so far. The Polar Silk Road was officially announced by China’s 2018 Arctic Policy White Paper. Originally, the PSR aimed to cover the whole Arctic as China’s overall strategy in the region. However, due to what I call a “push and pull effect” between the U.S., Russia, and China, the PSR has evolved to focus on collaboration with Russia.
Building upon China’s “unlimited” bilateral cooperation with Russia, the PSR has two dimensions. It reflects China’s strong interest in developing and using Arctic shipping routes, not only connecting the Chinese and Western European markets, but also China and the resource-rich Russian Arctic for China’s energy security. Therefore, South Korean companies will be facing economic and technological competition from Chinese companies in the Russian Arctic.
That being said, I think South Korea’s ambitions for Arctic shipping should be lauded. The NSR has potential to serve South Korea’s national interest as an alternative, strategic shipping route. Moreover, because Russia wants to diversify sources of foreign investment and increase the usage of NSR, South Korea’s interest in the Arctic shipping is likely to be welcomed by Russia. Therefore, South Korea could become a game changer in the Arctic amid geopolitical headwinds.
As a middle power that has been thriving in the epicenter of East Asian geopolitics for decades, South Korea has a proven record for managing great powers relations for national security and prosperity. Now it will try to make use of that experience in the Arctic.

What’s Behind One Nation’s Attacks on Andrew Hastie?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

What populist nationalists find most offensive about liberal democracy is the rule of law. The idea that there should be an equal and impartial exercise of laws is an affront to both their belief in social hierarchies, and also their desire to exercise power in an arbitrary manner. To them, the law should be used to advance their concept of the nation, and privilege or discriminate based on who represents or challenges their beliefs. This hostility toward the rule of law intensifies when they find a prominent symbolic vehicle for their political ambitions.
This attempt to bend the country to their will is now being demonstrated in Australia through the One Nation party and its relentless attacks on Liberal Party MP Andrew Hastie. The party has commissioned cartoons that refer to Hastie as a “traitor” and a “gutless maggot.” The social media swamp that One Nation swims in and facilitates has become so aggressive and threatening that Hastie has had to employ security at both his electorate office and his home – something incredibly rare in Australia.
Hastie’s crime, in One Nation’s eyes, is that he testified in the defamation case that Ben Roberts-Smith, a former corporal in the Special Air Service (SAS) Regiment, launched against the publishers of The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, and The Canberra Times, after they reported on allegations that he had committed war crimes in Afghanistan.
Hastie, a former SAS captain himself, and 20 other SAS veterans were subpoenaed to provide evidence in the case. A Federal Court judge found that on the balance of probabilities, Roberts-Smith was responsible for, or complicit in, unlawful killings in Afghanistan. The full bench of the Federal Court subsequently unanimously dismissed Roberts-Smith’s appeal. A criminal trial for Roberts-Smith remains pending.
For One Nation, the question of Roberts-Smith’s guilt is irrelevant because they believe the law itself to be fraudulent. The idea that there should be rules of engagement that the Australian Defense Force (ADF) is held to is something One Nation rejects. The military is considered an institution that sits above both domestic and international law.
For the ADF to investigate itself – as it did over allegations of war crimes committed in Afghanistan – is evidence to One Nation that it has been captured by a weak and “woke” series of ideas that have no place on a battlefield. Roberts-Smith has therefore become a symbol of the unrestrained manhood that the military should be a demonstration of. Those SAS soldiers – and especially Hastie – who testified in the defamation case therefore are guilty of betrayal.
It is here that “patriotism” in One Nation’s view has shifted from loyalty to the country’s institutions and principles toward loyalty to an individual who is deemed to embody what they see as a national virtue. This has also become bound to an immense sense of victimhood that One Nation cultivates. The rule of law is victimizing not just Roberts-Smith, but the nation itself. And if this is the case, then the rule of law must go. What is being challenged is whether Australian institutions have the authority to determine what conduct in war actually means.
Hastie has also become a perfect target for One Nation because he is a Liberal Party MP. One Nation may be mired in dystopian fantasies about global left-wing conspiracies, but the electoral threat they pose is actually to the Liberal Party. This is the party they want to replace, and it is the Liberal Party’s traditional voters from which One Nation are drawing most support. Bringing down Hastie therefore also has an electorally symbolic value. One Nation just won a by-election in a Western Australian state seat that overlaps with Hastie’s federal seat. It was another shot over Hastie’s bow.
One Nation’s attempt to replace the Liberal Party has further symbolic value because as the party that claims to be the holder of the classical liberal tradition in Australian politics, belief in the rule of law should be central to the Liberals political project. Theoretically, it should make the Liberals the party most resolutely opposed to One Nation and its radical objectives. Bizarrely, however, the Liberal Party seems to be a willing participant in its own decline. The party’s psychology is bound to its opposition to the Labor Party; it can’t comprehend threats from anywhere else.
Yet the threat here is not just against the electoral fortunes of the Liberal Party, or the reputation and physical personhood of Andrew Hastie. There is a wider battle taking place over what “patriotism” actually means. One Nation’s political strategy is to wrap itself in the flag and present its politics as an expression of national loyalty, while directing its hostility toward the institutions and principles that actually constitute the nation’s liberal democracy.

Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
Unknown

Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
A Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on September 14, photographs published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Project 1331M corvette, known by NATO as the Parchim II class, with painted outlines resembling windows and doors across its hull. Netting has also been installed above parts of the deck as a physical barrier against incoming drones.
The vessel was photographed at the Leningrad Naval Base in Kronstadt on August 22. Frantarelli said the ship could be either the Zelenodolsk or Kazanets, although its exact identity has not been confirmed. Russia operates roughly six of the East German-built anti-submarine corvettes, each displacing about 800 tons.
The modified vessel is part of a broader effort to alter the appearance of Russian warships based at Kronstadt. Naval analyst H I Sutton has documented several Baltic Fleet ships using black-painted bows and sterns, checkerboard patterns, and other disruptive designs since mid-2026.
Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, were also seen in July with unusual paint schemes and anti-drone netting.
The measures followed successful Ukrainian strikes against Russian naval assets in the Baltic region. On June 3, Ukrainian forces struck the corvette Boikiy while it was undergoing work in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing significant fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the vessel may have been damaged beyond repair.
In March, Ukrainian drones also sank the Russian patrol ship Purga near Vyborg, northwest of St. Petersburg. According to Defence Blog, neither vessel had protective anti-drone netting installed when it was targeted.
Similar techniques have historical precedent. During World War Two, warships were sometimes painted to distort their outline or blend into nearby infrastructure. Germany’s battleship Tirpitz reportedly carried a scheme during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven that included painted features intended to make the hull resemble buildings along the waterfront.

Russian strikes will cost Ukraine’s economy up to $10 billion this year, ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:07:49 UTC
22:07:49 KST

Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year and plans to submit a three-part business support package to the Cabinet next week, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.
Russia has escalated its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine through 2026, striking first at power plants, substations, and residential blocks, then widening the target list to trains, factories, retailer warehouses, and medicine depots. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said on 28 August that Russia had destroyed about 90% of retail chains' food logistics, but that supply would shift to direct deliveries, with no shortage of basic foods expected.
Kravchenko said business is an absolutely important source of funding for the defense forces, and that it ensures critical goods are supplied and communities can function.
Three-part package aims to support businesses affected by Russian strikes
- The package has three elements, Kravchenko said. The first would extend the geographic coverage of existing damage compensation programs to include Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, and simplify the application process so affected companies do not wait months for support.
- The second would expand subsidized lending for large businesses, with loans of up to about $22 million (UAH 1 billion) and an interest-rate subsidy of about 5 percentage points. The loans could fund investment projects, including fortification and protection, as well as working capital.
- The third would expand the state's 5-7-9 lending program, which sets the borrower's rate at 5%, 7%, or 9% depending on the purpose of the loan and the size of the business, to suppliers whose large retail clients are losing money to strikes.
He said all three programs had been finalized and hoped businesses would begin receiving substantial support within the coming weeks. The package followed a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and discussions with businesses, he said.
Russian strikes have damaged logistics networks and businesses across Ukraine
An overnight strike on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast on 5 August killed 17 people and destroyed or damaged warehouses and distribution centers belonging to Rozetka, Epicentr, Nova Poshta, Silpo, and other major companies. Co-founder Iryna Chechotkina described Rozetka's warehouse complex in Brovary, valued at $70 million, as beyond repair. The same strike killed six Silpo employees.
Further strikes through early September hit Auchan, Nova Poshta again, Varus, Dnipro-M, and Coca-Cola.

Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:06:01 UTC
22:06:01 KST

As Russian long-range drone attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure intensify, Kyiv has explored every avenue available to strengthen its air defense capabilities. In November this led to a plan to add civilian air defense groups to supplement the existing multilayered system of military mobile fire teams armed with machine guns, interceptor drone equipped units, conventional missile and cannon air defense crews and military aviation.
There has been a rapid upsurge in the numbers of private security and defense firms specializing in “Mala PPO” – localized anti-drone protection, as the system is colloquially known.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rules of engagement
These private teams operate under strict coordination with and under command of the Ukrainian Air Force, which retains the sole authority to approve providers and on target authorization and firing decisions.
As well as protecting their own facilities the capability is viewed as an extension of Ukraine’s existing early-warning network which can identify the direction being taken and by which types of Russian drone – the ability to take shelter from attacks is, in many ways, as vital as having the ability to engage drones.
Between November and the end of March, 24 companies in Kharkiv, Odesa, Kyiv, Poltava, Zakarpattia, and other regions had received authorization to combat drones, which had expanded to 51 by the end of August. Licensed operators include major Ukrainian companies that have trained and equipped their own internal or are engaging private security companies to safeguard critical economic infrastructure.
Ukraine Has Leverage Over Trump Now
For obvious physical and commercial security reasons companies reveal little information on how they plan or and with what systems they implement their air defense – many do not even confirm they take such measures at all for fear that will make them a target. The main exception to this is the larger security providers who advertise their general capability and number of businesses with which they are engaged to drive and expand their own business.
For example, a report in Le Monde at the weekend highlighted the prominent private air defense company Carmine Sky which claims to employ hundreds of personnel and has contracts with around 40 Ukrainian businesses. Carmine Sky says it can offer an arsenal that includes anti-aircraft turrets with remotely operated heavy machine guns, electronic jamming, and interceptor drones managed from secure control rooms.
Addressing the technological challenge
It is not only the numbers of private users of air defense systems that have expanded to face the threat but those who are developing the necessary countermeasures as Russia develops the capability of its attack drones – particularly its Geran and Banderol jet-powered drones.
According to media reports these drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kph (375 mph), with payloads of 90 kilograms (200 pounds) over a range of 800-1,000 kilometers (500-625 miles).
This is forcing a need to rapidly develop faster interceptors capable of engaging incoming drones at longer ranges and higher altitudes with the overarching limitation that the cost of any interceptor must remain (considerably) lower than the incoming target.
Several Ukrainian manufacturers showcased their solutions at this year’s MSPO defense industry show in Kielce, Poland.
Representatives of General Cherry and GrimTech, both current interceptor manufacturers, told Defense News that they were working on a new versions of their interceptors to tackle the jet drone problem.
                                                                                                                                                                         
To do so, they said, would require changes to the existing designs, and the use of materials capable of withstanding higher flight temperatures. They indicated that testing was underway with the goal to have the new weapons enter service before the end of the year.
The private defense companies, both users and manufacturers, have respondeded to those who have criticized the “privatization” of air defense by pointing out much of the funding to develop these countermeasures comes from the income streams their activities generate.

Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:05:04 UTC
22:05:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
In a highly consequential development for Yemen and the region, the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha from the internationally recognised Yemeni government, along with a strategic Red Sea island.
The lightning advance over the past week puts them in a prime position to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait more easily than ever before.
The loss of Mocha on 10 September cuts the government’s direct access to the Red Sea, while the capture of the strategic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, a day later enables them to effectively close the Bab al-Mandab in tandem with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The offensive, which displaced almost 50,000 people, represents one of the biggest strategic setbacks for the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in several years.
The Houthis captured Yemen’s capital Sanaa and the major port city of Hodeidah in 2014. The Zaydi Shia group fought the government, which relocated to the southern port city of Aden, and its Saudi backers in a devastating war that from 2015 until 2022.
Approximately 150,000 Yemenis have perished, and the country endured a severe humanitarian crisis that pushed it to the brink of famine.
A 2022 Saudi-Houthi ceasefire largely held until July, when fighting resumed after Riyadh attempted to block a direct Mahan Air flight from Tehran to Sanaa, the first since 2015.
The official purpose of that Iranian flight was to pick up and return a Houthi delegation attending the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Riyadh and the Yemeni government feared an unopposed air bridge would enable Tehran to conveniently fly military equipment directly to its Houthi allies.
The emboldened Houthis have since resumed striking Saudi infrastructure and energy sites with drones and missiles. The kingdom now faces Iran-backed militia attacks from Yemen to its south and Iraq to its north. The latest advance inside Yemen marks the most significant escalation with Aden and its Saudi backer in years.
Serious territorial gains
“The Houthi advance into Mocha is a strong indicator that Iran is seeking to undermine the US-led coalition in its strategic rear, which is the Bab al-Mandab,” Nicholas Heras, Interim Executive Director at the Middle East Policy Council and Senior Director at the New Lines Institute, told The New Arab.
According to reports, Iran told the Houthis to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising them more funding and weapons, and Tehran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) paramilitary directly guided the group’s coastal offensive.
“Saudi Arabia is a wavering member of the American coalition against Iran and the resumption of the war in Yemen with rapid Houthi gains is an embarrassing predicament for Saudi Arabia,” Heras said.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, pointed out that Mocha “certainly matters” to the Houthis since it expands the “buffer zone” for Hodeidah.
Additionally, it opens up a route for any subsequent attempts to encircle the southwestern city of Taiz, entrenches their influence over the Red Sea, and provides “new launch positions” for striking shipping passing through that vital but narrow Bab al-Mandab.
“I think the Houthis will continue to advance so long as there is military opportunism,” Bohl told The New Arab. “They can always trade away territory for a final settlement since there is the suggestion that they may only be interested in controlling those Zaydi portions of Yemen,” he noted.
“The most likely block on further advances will be the almost certain furious counterattacks by the IRG (Yemen’s Internationally Recognised Government) and the Saudis who will do whatever they can to prevent the fall of a major city like Marib or Taiz or an advance on Aden,” Bohl added.
More broadly, the RANE analyst noted, these advances certainly help the Houthis with their broader Red Sea strategy and potentially give them additional territory which they can trade for a future settlement with Riyadh and the Yemeni government.
Heras echoed this assessment. “The Houthis understand the limits of their power in Yemen beyond the core areas of Zaydi population concentration and are instead seeking to improve their ability to pressure the Saudis to pressure the Americans to support Iran,” he said.
“This Houthi campaign along Yemen’s coast is a declaration that the Houthis are key actors in global geopolitics who are able to undermine the US geostrategy in the Middle East.”
Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), assesses that these Houthi advances mark the “most serious territorial gain” the group has made in years, putting the entire Hodeidah governorate under its effective control.
“This is a major defeat for the IRG - which just a few days ago was boasting of military advances in the very same governorate - and a sign of the extreme unpredictability of the current escalation," he told The New Arab.
Saudi support
RANE’s Bohl expects Saudi air support will prove critical for blunting any further Houthi advance and supporting IRG counterattacks.
“At the same time, so will unity amongst the IRG's ground forces,” he said. “This latter element is the most critical because without a sense of unity these counteroffensives will be stuck being localised and unable to comprehensively roll the Houthis back.”
According to an Axios report, Saudi Arabia’s powerful Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump during the Houthi advance, requesting renewed US strikes against them.
Trump declined. Nevertheless, US military advisors in Saudi Arabia are providing expanded intelligence and targeting support for the kingdom’s operations against the Iran-backed group, according to a CNN report.
Bohl noted that Saudi Arabia is already responding to Houthi attacks and advances and is “likely to be drawn into further involvement” in the civil war raging over its southern border. That further involvement could potentially lead to a deployment of Saudi forces into Yemen alongside “enhanced airstrikes” against the group.
The escalation, and ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, come a little over a month after the kingdom signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan on 7 August.
Pakistan has already clarified that it hasn’t planned any military response against the Houthis for their attacks.
“There is no such thing under discussion right now … When the time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on 10 September, the same day Mocha fell.
“As for other members of the Mecca pact, they will remain wary of conducting military operations inside of Yemen given the distant geographies from Turkey and Pakistan, as well as the prospect of trapping their forces in an intractable conflict,” Bohl said.
“But most notably, the change in the Trump administration from the first to the second term may prove to be important.”
He recalled that in its first term at the end of the 2010s, the Trump administration focused on “containment and mitigating the humanitarian impacts” of the Yemen conflict.
Now, in its second term, it perceives Yemen as “part of the struggle” against Iran. Consequently, it may be more likely to support broader Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed group while making “fewer demands” to change tactics that could have a significant humanitarian impact.
Potential scenarios
ACLED’s Yemen analyst Ali sees several potential scenarios for Yemen after these latest Houthi advances.
“The Houthis may press their advantage and launch more attacks to seize the coast of Taiz governorate just south of Hodeideh, bringing the entirety of the Yemeni Red Sea coast under their control,” he said.
“Alternatively, IRG forces may regroup to carry out a counterattack and attempt to reclaim lost territories.”
Both scenarios would mean a “heightened level of violence” and “increased risk for civilians” in Yemen in the coming weeks in addition to “hundreds of military casualties” from “deadlier clashes” along other internal frontlines. Ali anticipates fighting focused in al-Jawf in the east, which borders Saudi Arabia.
Both sides are engaged in heavy clashes there, with strategic sites “changing hands” at a rapid rate.
“Alternatively, the Houthi blitzing may force Saudi Arabia - which is the IRG’s main backer - back to negotiating with the group to avoid further potential losses for their Yemeni allies in the IRG, which could mean an abrupt end to the current round of escalation,” he said.

WATCH: Estonian National Symphony Orchestra's 100th season opening concert
The Estonian National Symphony Orchestra (ERSO) opened its 100th season Friday with a festive concert featuring works by Beethoven, Schumann and Estonia's own Heino Eller.
Conducted by Olari Elts, Friday's program began with Eller's symphonic poem "Dawn" ("Koit"), one of the Estonian composer's most frequently performed works.
South Korean pianist Yekwon Sunwoo then joined the orchestra for Schumann's Piano Concerto in A minor, often described as a musical love letter to his wife, Clara Schumann, who premiered the work.
Sunwoo, an alum of the Curtis Institute of Music and Juilliard, rose to international prominence after winning the 2017 Van Cliburn International Piano Competition and has since performed with leading orchestras and on major stages worldwide.
The evening concluded with Ludwig van Beethoven's iconic Symphony No. 5 in C minor.
More concerts to come
ERSO's season opening concert was broadcast in cooperation with Klassikaraadio, with Nele-Eva Steinfeld hosting.
The award-winning Estonian orchestra's centennial season continues with a South Korean tour featuring works by Schumann and Beethoven alongside Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits' "Hymns to the Northern Lights."
In early October, ERSO will perform at the Festival TubIN with conductor Mihhail Gerts and violinist Hans Christian Aavik.
ERR's culture portal will stream more ERSO concerts in full throughout the fall.

The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:00:58 UTC
22:00:58 KST

Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.
The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.
The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.
It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.
Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.
The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.
Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.
Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.
Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.
The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.
The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.
Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.
Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.
These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.
His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.
After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.
The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.
He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.
Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.
Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.
St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.
A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.
“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”
A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”
In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

These neutrinos from the sun have the lowest energies ever seen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

These neutrinos from the sun have the lowest energies ever seen
The ethereal subatomic particles were born in the sun’s main type of fusion reaction
Barely-there particles called neutrinos just got caught acting even more ethereal.
With tiny masses and no electric charge, the subatomic particles rarely interact with anything, making them difficult to detect. Scientists have now spotted neutrinos with lower energies than any they’ve seen before. And they did it using a detector meant for another purpose entirely.
XENONnT, at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy, is designed to search for dark matter, the mysterious substance that is needed to explain the behavior of galaxies across the universe. It has yet to find any — although a similar detector has seen a tantalizing hint. What it has found, instead, are neutrinos — hundreds of them, researchers report in a paper submitted August 29 to arXiv.org.
Neutrinos are born in vast numbers in the sun — about 100 billion of them pass through your thumbnail every second. Some of those solar neutrinos are expected to interact in XENONnT. So the researchers went neutrino hunting.
The team found evidence of neutrinos smacking into electrons within the detector, producing light that revealed their presence. It’s the first time a dark matter detector has spotted neutrinos based on their electron-jostling antics. The detection met a statistical benchmark of 5 sigma, which physicists typically consider the threshold for a definitive detection.
Other dark matter detectors have seen hints of this process. In July, PandaX-4T, at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory in Liangshan, saw evidence of low-energy neutrinos, but at a statistical significance of about 2.2 sigma — not enough to make the detection a sure thing.
The neutrinos have energies as low as 17 kiloelectron volts. That’s about a tenth the energy of the wimpiest neutrinos previously detected. The newfound low-energy neutrinos are produced in the main fusion reaction that powers the sun, in which two protons merge to form a larger atomic nucleus.
The particles could carry the sun’s secrets. With a proposed, more advanced detector, “we expect to be able to extract valuable knowledge about the sun’s composition,” says XENONnT physicist Florian Jörg of the University of Zurich.
In 2024, XENONnT saw higher energy neutrinos from the sun, as did PandaX-4T. Those neutrinos are by-products of a different, less predominant type of fusion reaction, making them less numerous, but easier to spot. Detectors can catch these higher-energy neutrinos interacting with an entire nucleus instead of just a single electron.
The signature of a low-energy neutrino bouncing off an electron is easily confused with hordes of other interactions that can mimic it, called background. “The difficulty is picking the neutrino needles out of the background haystack,” says neutrino physicist Kate Scholberg of Duke University, who was not involved with the study. The researchers “look to have done a pretty heroic job on this.”

"The Culmination of a Lifetime" — Media Star Oprah Winfrey Announces a Series of Live Performances in Las Vegas
Kyiv • UNN
Oprah Winfrey will perform at Sphere in Las Vegas on April 2–4, 2027. Her show will combine music, poetry, storytelling, and visual art.
In 2027, American media star Oprah Winfrey will hold a series of live performances at the Sphere arena in Las Vegas. According to her, these events will be the culmination of decades of work dedicated to encouraging self-discovery and personal growth through television, publishing, and public events, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The three performances, scheduled for April 2–4, are part of a project titled "Oprah Winfrey's AHA." The name refers to moments of sudden insight, which Winfrey has long called "AHA" moments and which have become a recurring theme throughout her work.

"I was standing there alone, looking up, and thinking: 'What was that just now?'" she said, describing the moment when her idea began to take concrete shape.

Israel working to eliminate Palestinian presence from West Bank, NGO warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Israel working to eliminate Palestinian presence from West Bank, NGO warns
Israeli human rights group B’Tselem details five mechanisms used by Israel to dismantle Palestinian collective life.
Israel is executing a systematic and accelerated campaign to dismantle “Palestinian collective life” and establish permanent Jewish-Israeli sovereignty across the occupied West Bank, an Israeli human rights group has warned.
The “Elimination Project”, published on Monday by B’Tselem, details several tactics used by the Israeli government to help it achieve its overall objective of “erasing the Palestinian presence” from the occupied West Bank.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank are choking the Palestinian economy
- list 2 of 3Israel arrests 100 Palestinians in a week as West Bank pogroms continue
- list 3 of 3How significant are new European sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements?
The report argues that while Israeli policies have been rooted in a long-term settler colonial framework, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has entered an accelerated phase of this objective since late 2022, particularly after the Hamas-led October 2023 attack on southern Israel.
“What Palestinians are living through in the West Bank is not a series of separate incidents. It is a single political project that reaches into every part of life,” said B’Tselem executive director Yuli Novak.
The report outlines five interconnected mechanisms Israel uses to advance its West Bank project, drawing from roughly 2,000 testimonies given by Palestinians.
Firstly, Israel is “using military forces and armed settler militias to impose violence, fear and coercion”, according to the report.
Between October 2023 and September 2026, Israel killed at least 1,107 Palestinians in attacks across the occupied West Bank, the NGO said.
The Israeli army uses military operations and demolitions and assists armed settlers in driving Palestinians from their land to expand its presence in the territory, the report said.
To date, at least 75 Palestinian communities have been forcibly displaced, it said. Israel has, via armed settlers, taken control of more than 1,070,000 dunams of land, equivalent to 18 percent of the West Bank as of July, 2026, it said. A dunam is a unit of land area commonly used in the region, equal to 1,000 square meters (about 0.247 acres or 0.1 hectare). Furthermore, about 33,000 Palestinians have been displaced from refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
Israel also actively restricts Palestinians’ movement, with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs documenting 925 movement obstacles, including roadblocks and unmanned checkpoints, throughout the territory by the end of last year.
The Israeli government has purposefully stifled the West Bank’s economy, with unemployment rising from 13.1 percent in 2022 to more than 31 percent in 2024.
Lastly, Israel actively criminalises political organising, suppressing protests and arresting activists, students and journalists.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, it has arrested at least 60 Palestinian journalists working in the occupied West Bank.
B’Tselem urged the international community to stop viewing Israel’s violations as isolated incidents and to end complicity in its actions.
It also called for immediate global action to protect Palestinians and dismantle Israel’s military rule and apartheid system.
“Palestinians are being left exposed to escalating violence while Israel advances its project of elimination in the West Bank. Governments cannot condemn these crimes while granting Israel the impunity to continue,” said Novak.
“Together with international institutions, they must use every means available under international law to stop Israel’s crimes and halt the machinery of violence and destruction that is tearing Palestinian life apart.”

Russian Drones Just Miss Former CIA Director David Petraeus: a View From a Train Near the Polish Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:56:31 UTC
21:56:31 KST

The third evacuation was different.
The first two times our train from Kyiv toward Poland stopped because of Russian drone attacks, passengers moved quickly but relatively calmly away from the cars. The third time, the urgency in the railway official’s voice had changed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
People were shouting, “Run!”
So we ran.
We had been told to get at least 200 meters from the train, away from anything that might attract a Russian drone or send shrapnel flying if it were hit. We crossed a dark, marshy field, sometimes over old wooden planks. Then came the sound I will remember: the whine of a jet-powered drone somewhere above us.
I’m 85, and after running for a while my lungs went from burning to feeling as though they might burst. Eventually I couldn’t keep up with the younger passengers, but I kept moving.
We reached the edge of a lake, where people dispersed into bushes and under trees. The advice was to stay low, partly to reduce exposure to shrapnel and partly to be less visible from the air.
Some passengers were crying. A few small dogs looked as unhappy about the proceedings as the rest of us.
Two young women remained standing. Other passengers shouted at them in Ukrainian to get down. I didn’t need a translation. The tone was approximately: Sit down immediately or we will personally kill you before the Russians have a chance.
No one thought this was a drill.
Then we heard another explosion.
Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
My companion Clara Kaluderovic was receiving information from Ukrainian security contacts about drones in the area. At one point we were told that an interceptor had brought one down. Others were still somewhere nearby.
This happened after a week in Kyiv during which air-raid alerts had become almost part of the background noise. Ukrainians know this experience far better than I ever will. But for a foreign journalist, being hunted out of a train and into the bushes near the Polish border made something very clear: Russia’s effort to make normal life impossible does not stop at the front.
Railways matter enormously in Ukraine. With civilian airspace closed, trains are the principal arteries connecting Ukraine with Europe. Diplomats take them. Journalists take them. Aid workers take them. Families take them. So do Ukrainians leaving the country and Ukrainians determined to return.
Make those trains frightening enough and you begin to isolate Ukraine.
After one of the attacks we could see heavy smoke. Initially, from my angle, I thought a church near the railway had been struck. Later, after comparing photographs and talking with others, I learned that I had been wrong. The drone had hit the locomotive of a train standing beside ours, behind the church.
That correction matters. One obligation of eyewitness journalism is to distinguish what you thought you saw during chaos from what the evidence later shows. It was an exercise in humility.
We also saw damaged railway track. Another strike hit near a gas station. Trains began collecting in the area as movement toward the border stopped. At one point there were passenger trains around us and, beyond one of them, a long line of fuel cars.
Looking at the fuel cars I could see from my train window, sitting in a stationary railway carriage suddenly seemed considerably less attractive than it ordinarily does.
Gen. David Petraeus was also traveling in our group. Earlier in Kyiv, he had told me that Ukraine and Russia are “redefining the very nature of warfare.” He was talking primarily about drones, sensors, electronic warfare and the extraordinary speed at which battlefield technology is evolving.
Now we were experiencing one small part of that revolution ourselves.
The important question was not whether Russia knew precisely who was on our train. I cannot establish that, and speculation is not fact.
What can be established is the effect.
Hundreds of civilians were repeatedly driven from trains in the middle of the night. Rail traffic on one of Ukraine’s essential connections with Europe was disrupted. A locomotive was damaged. Railway infrastructure was hit. And passengers who had thought they were nearly safely across the border discovered that the war could follow them almost to Poland.
One Ukrainian woman I met while we were outside was surprised and seemed deeply appreciative that an American had come to Ukraine during the war. Of course I loved what she said, but, I found myself thinking the sentiment should run the other way.
Ukrainians have been living with versions of this for more than four years. For me, hiding under bushes while Russian drones passed nearby was extraordinary. For millions of Ukrainians, calculating where the nearest shelter is, listening for drones and waiting for the all-clear have become grotesquely ordinary.
Eventually, electricity returned to our carriage. My laptop began charging. Someone produced hot water and I made a cup of Earl Grey tea.
Civilization restored, at least temporarily.
Russia may be trying to persuade foreigners that traveling to Ukraine is too dangerous, too inconvenient and simply not worth it.
If that was the message, it failed with me.
I came away with more resolve and more energy than ever. I cannot wait to return to Ukraine.
And when I do, I intend to come back on that same rail line.

The department said the partnership would extend beyond access to facilities to include professional training, technical exchanges, and new technology.

Ukraine Has Leverage Over Trump Now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

Notable to hear President Trump announce that he had been in contact with President Zelensky of Ukraine to call on him to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump suggested that these Ukrainian attacks had been behind the ramp up in diesel prices in recent weeks. This appeared to repeat a narrative from Treasury Secretary Bessent that it was Ukrainian attacks on Russia, and not the war effort on Iran, which had driven US diesel prices to record prices - over $6 a gallon.
Obviously, it’s politically useful for Trump to blame the war in Ukraine for the elevation in global energy prices since the war in Iran given the proximity of midterms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It’s true that Ukraine has been increasingly successful in hitting Russian energy infrastructure. Ukrainian deep strike drone attacks have hit 30-40% of Russian refineries. It is hard to determine how much capacity has been taken out of action, but it’s been so significant that Russia, which was a significant diesel and refined product exporter, has banned exports. There have, meanwhile, been significant shortages at the pumps across Russia.
Trump might be eager to deflect blame for the global spike in energy, and particularly from the war in Iran, but he cannot escape from some of the blame even for Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Important here to note that under the Biden presidency when US was providing significant military support to Ukraine – particularly long-range HIMARS and ATACMSs systems – it had leverage over Ukraine. It could threaten to pull those systems unless Ukraine held to certain red lines – particularly limiting attacks on Russian assets with global market impact. Ukraine generally complied.
Russia Launches Kalibr Cruise Missiles Directly From Base, Ukraine Says
But things changed under Trump. He pulled financial support from Ukraine and limited delivery of key weapons systems. Ukraine was forced to develop its own – and therein put much effort into the development of deep strike drone capability to replace the US systems. These systems are now proving so effective against Russian energy infrastructure. And as they are home made Ukraine feels little need to ask for US permission to hit longer range targets in Russia.
Ukraine still exercised some restraint, however. Because it remained dependent on European financing, Kyiv was inclined to limit actions that could disrupt global energy markets and hurt energy-importing Europe. Ukraine held back.
But what changed with Trump’s attack on Iran was that Ukraine saw the US acted on its own interests – attacking Iran and forcing up global energy prices against the interests of key allies in Europe, and Asia. Ukraine saw that what was good enough for the US was good enough for it. States, like the US act in their own national interest, and Ukraine saw the green light to do the same, even though they were hurting the interests of allies. Ukraine took the gloves off.
So I would argue that in his management (or mismanagement) of support for Ukraine and then the attack on Iran, Trump cannot get away from significant blame for current high oil, energy and diesel prices.
And surely if Ukraine is to stop these attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, then the question is what Trump will supply in return? What’s the quid pro quo? Ukraine now has leverage, or cards. Ukraine will likely demand an uptick in delivery of key air defense systems –Patriot interceptors if it is to pull punches in attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

Taiwan’s China Airlines cuts emissions with sustainable fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:54:38 UTC
21:54:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China Airlines said Monday that it used a 40% blend of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) on a long-haul flight to Amsterdam for the first time, cutting an estimated 93.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
The Sunday flight from Taoyuan to Amsterdam marked China Airlines’ fifth participation in SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge and its first use of a 40% SAF blend on a long-haul route, per CNA. The airline said the emissions reduction was equivalent to one-quarter of Daan Forest Park’s annual carbon absorption or the emissions produced by 40 passenger cars.
China Airlines President Chen Han-ming (陳漢銘) said the airline had used SAF eight times since 2022, with the latest flight using about 36.3 tonnes, per Liberty Times. He said Amsterdam was chosen because the Netherlands had extensive experience with sustainability initiatives.
The demonstration flight also used meal trays and cutlery that were 30% lighter than previous versions, as well as lower-carbon meals and soy-based ink for printed materials. Michelin Green Star restaurant Little Tree Food provided vegetarian meals, while passengers were encouraged to use digital boarding passes.
Chen said SAF had historically cost about 2.5 to three times as much as conventional jet fuel, although the difference varied with oil prices. He said China Airlines hoped to reach a more advanced level of sustainability before considering whether the higher cost of SAF could be passed on to passengers.
This year’s Aviation Challenge focuses on bringing airlines and supply-chain companies together to support the transition to net-zero emissions, CNA reported. China Airlines has also cooperated with Formosa Plastics and Foxconn on sustainability projects.

Former agency head: Defense minister actively involved in Datasel dealings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Former agency head: Defense minister actively involved in Datasel dealings
Former Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar has alleged that outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur personally pushed for several defense procurement deals and rejected a proposal to halt the arrangement.
Former Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar and outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) were due to attend a special parliamentary committee hearing on Monday, but neither appeared. Saar said that because the European Public Prosecutor's Office has launched an investigation and he is unable to verify facts against documents, he would prefer to answer questions in writing.
The most significant part of Saar's eight-page explanation concerns Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's role. Saar claims that the defense minister was not a hands-off client in this area who simply waited for reports.
"He personally brought forward and actively proposed deals, intervened in negotiations over contract terms, delivery schedules, the size of advance payments and prices in at least one major case, in some instances negotiated directly with the supplier, urged that payments be expedited after contracts had been signed and gave the contracting authority guidance during discussions held practically every week."
Responding later to follow-up questions, Saar said the final two deals in the Datasel case were concluded at Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's personal initiative.
"The minister also had a specific interest in concluding the deals through the Greek company Nordeto. RKIK was urged to conclude the contracts quickly, with the short validity period of the offer cited as the reason. By that point, delays in deliveries under the first contracts had already been reported."
According to Saar, Nordeto was unknown to RKIK and, to his knowledge, its business activities were not connected with ammunition or defense-related goods.
"The offer had been sent privately to Defense Minister Pevkur. I am not aware of how the defense minister satisfied himself as to the partner's reliability and capabilities. RKIK did not enter into a contract with this intermediary. RKIK entered into a contract with the business entity as close as possible to the origin and ownership of the goods (the general principle), which in this case meant Datasel."
Saar was also asked whether businessman and Reform Party member Jaanus Rahumägi may have played any role in the matter.
Special committee chair Urmas Reinsalu asked: "Delfi has reported on Jaanus Rahumägi's ties to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur and reported in August 2025 that Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur was in Greece where he spent time at Jaanus Rahumägi's villa and, among other things, met with the Greek defense minister. To your knowledge, were arms deals discussed during this visit, and if so, which ones?"
Saar replied briefly: "I had left office by then and am not familiar with the topics that were discussed."
Minister reluctant to stop mediation
Saar's explanation also shows that, while serving as RKIK director general, he made a formally recorded proposal to end the intermediary arrangement and return funds not covered by contracts.
"In late winter/early spring 2025, RKIK submitted a written proposal to a defense minister's decision-making meeting to stop concluding contracts in this manner and return funds not covered by contracts. Defense Minister Pevkur rejected the proposal and ordered procurement to continue. The minutes of the relevant decision-making meeting are held by the Ministry of Defense and I assume the committee will have an opportunity to review them in writing."
Saar added that the decision showed the minister clearly understood both the need to support Ukraine and the risks associated with providing that support and was by no means unaware of the details of how the aid was being brokered.
ERR was unable to reach Hanno Pevkur for comment by phone.

Experts expect Brent crude at $95-115 per barrel in near term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
