21:51:39 KST

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. The price of Brent crude will hover around $95-115 per barrel in the near term, while a surge to $150 is not currently seen as a base-case scenario, experts surveyed by TASS believe.
Alexey Belogoryev, Research Director at the Institute for Energy and Finance, noted that many oil futures traders were "badly burned" in the spring and summer of 2026 after betting on a much stronger and more sustained price rally, leaving them skeptical about prospects for further growth.
"Therefore, I would expect prices to hold within the $95-115 per barrel range for Brent for now. If the situation does not improve fundamentally by the end of the year, a move toward $150 is indeed possible, though it is far from the base-case scenario at this stage," he said.
Nikolay Dudchenko, an analyst at Finam Financial Group, also downplayed the likelihood of prices hitting $150, though he admitted a potential rise to $120. "It appears that national oil reserves may still be sufficient to curb further price growth. Moreover, high oil prices could eventually impact demand itself, leading to its gradual destruction," he explained.
The average oil price for 2026 is projected at $93-95 per barrel by Belogoryev, and $80-90 under Finam's base-case scenario, according to Dudchenko.
Analysts explained that the Middle East conflict and the lack of progress toward its resolution remain the key factors driving prices, alongside declining crude and petroleum product inventories and upward pressure from rising refined product costs. Brent crude futures for November delivery on the ICE currently trade at $107.9, up 3.15% from the previous close.

The band’s line-up has changed several times since 2013. Today, alongside Krustev, No More Many More are Radoslav Gergov on vocals and percussion, Vladimir Ivanov on drums, Grisha Georgiev on bass and Kamen Aleksandrov on guitar.
Their September 18 concert will also feature special guests, including the band Taraleshta, known for their three albums and for supporting Manu Chao and S.A.R.S. last year. This summer, they will also be part of The Wailers’ upcoming concert in Sofia on July 15.
PHOTO Facebook /No More Many More
Another guest will be actor Valeri Yordanov, with whom No More Many More created the powerful song “Nyama bivshi hashove” (“Once a Rebel, Always a Rebel”). The band are also working on “Pesenta na zhabite” (“The Song of the Frogs”) for Yordanov’s next film, which is due to begin shooting in the spring. Metodi Krustev says of the song:
“The song is about the eternal soldier. The film is pretty heavy – mud, war, battles... I wrote it after reading the script Valeri sent me. Cellist Tanya Nedkova also plays on it. I think it turned out really well. We used special film sounds, sound design. The interesting thing was that I re-recorded the vocals because I got ill during the recording. The next morning, when I heard myself speak, I immediately called to record the vocals while I was ill, because I wanted the song to sound that way – as heavy as possible, since the film is really brutal.”

Sixty-six-million-year-old fossil unearthed in Türkiye's capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:48:25 UTC
21:48:25 KST

A fossil belonging to a gastropod that lived along the shores of the Tethys Sea 66 million years ago has been discovered at an archaeological site in Ankara, Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said.
The fossil was unearthed during excavations at Kulhoyuk in the Oyaca neighbourhood of Ankara’s Golbasi district.
Ersoy said on social media on Monday that the specimen was believed to date from the final phases of the Tethys Sea, a prehistoric body of water that once covered parts of what is now central Anatolia.
Researchers are examining whether residents of Kulhoyuk found the fossil elsewhere and deliberately brought it to the settlement thousands of years ago.
The possibility could offer new insights into how the object reached the site and what significance it may have held for its inhabitants.
Gastropods are a class of molluscs that includes snails and slugs.
Ancient settlement
Kulhoyuk is a roughly 5,000-year-old settlement associated with the Hattian and Hittite civilisations. The fossilised creature therefore did not live alongside the settlement’s inhabitants.
The discovery follows the identification of what archaeologists described as the earliest-known seed remains of Ankara’s distinctive “Sevgi Cicegi”, or Love Flower, inside a 4,000-year-old Hittite vessel at the same site.
Excavations at Kulhoyuk have been ongoing since 2021 under a long-term archaeological programme backed by the Turkish presidency.
The work is led by Associate Professor Derya Yilmaz Tekin on behalf of Ankara University and the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
Ersoy said excavations would continue to shed light on Kulhoyuk’s history through further discoveries.

Rublev’s ‘Trinity’ Icon Removed From Display After Climate Control Failure – RBC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:48:23 UTC
21:48:23 KST

Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century masterpiece “Trinity,” one of Russia’s most sacred icons, has been removed from public view following a climate control failure at the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius outside Moscow, the news outlet RBC reported Monday, citing a source in the Russian Orthodox Church and an art conservator.
President Vladimir Putin ordered the icon to be transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church in 2023, defying warnings from art experts at the Tretyakov Gallery — where it had been housed since 1929 — who cautioned that relocating the fragile relic could cause irreversible damage.
The Church confirmed on Sunday that the icon was taken out of its specialized climate-controlled display case into a Tretyakov-compliant inspection room on the monastery grounds for a “routine inspection” of its condition.
“The icon will continue to be studied and treated in the Lavra’s restoration workshops, while the display case is being repaired,” art historian Ksenia Korobeynikova wrote on Telegram.
The exiled news outlet Echo, citing an anonymous source, reported Saturday that the sealed protective glass case housing the “Trinity” broke some time ago, leaving internal humidity levels at around 80%, which is above the safe range of 50-55%.
A specialized technician flown in from Germany reportedly repaired the case, but the unit failed again shortly after their departure.
Museum experts have said that the high humidity causes the antique wood that the “Trinity” was painted on to swell and warp.
“The icon is curling up into a tube,” Echo quoted its source as saying.

Parliament pushes tougher energy permit deadlines, setting up clash with EU countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:47:49 UTC
21:47:49 KST

The European Parliament is trying to turn permitting reform into a stronger, common EU rulebook, while capitals seek flexibility to accommodate national legal systems, environmental constraints and administrative structures, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The European Parliament is pushing for tougher EU-wide deadlines and automatic approvals to speed up energy infrastructure, setting the stage for a clash with EU countries seeking more flexibility over how their national permitting systems work, according to an internal document seen by Euronews.
The divide is emerging as EU lawmakers negotiate new permitting rules designed to cut years of delays — sometimes up to ten years — that have held back renewable energy, electricity grids, storage and other infrastructure needed for the bloc's energy transition.
The Parliament's position is more rigid than the Commission proposal and the Council's mandate, particularly on electricity grids. While the Commission proposed a maximum two-year authorisation period for transmission and distribution infrastructure, Parliament wants distribution projects approved within one year and transmission projects within two years. The Council would retain a two-year ceiling for both, with extensions allowed in extraordinary circumstances.
However, the sharper dispute is over what happens when authorities miss those deadlines.
The Parliament backs a stronger use of tacit approval, under which certain administrative steps are deemed approved if authorities fail to respond on time. But the Council has narrowed this approach, saying EU countries may provide for tacit approval for specific intermediary administrative steps, while excluding environmental decisions and grid-connection permits.
EU lawmaker Niels Fuglsang (S&D/Denmark), leading the file in Parliament, said the bloc's power grids need to be built faster if the EU is serious about the climate and energy transition and lowering electricity and fuel bills.
"The European Parliament’s position delivers faster permitting without compromising legal certainty or public confidence. I will defend that approach in the negotiations, and I don’t think weakening the rules on tacit approval is the right solution,” Fuglsang told Euronews.
Overriding public interest
The co-legislators also differ on how far energy projects should be prioritised when they conflict with other interests. Both sides want faster permitting and support tighter deadlines, digitalisation and simpler procedures. However, they differ over how much discretion should remain with national authorities.
The Parliament mandate seeks to broaden the presumption that renewable energy projects and related infrastructure are of overriding public interest, limiting member states' ability to create exceptions.
On the other hand, the Council retains the broader presumption but allows more explicit exceptions — including where cultural heritage needs protection or where a project would have significant environmental effects that cannot be mitigated or compensated for.
The Parliament also wants a more standardised administrative system, including stronger requirements for a single point of contact for project developers, while the Council is more willing to let EU governments decide how to combine existing national authorities and contact points.
Nonetheless, the Council goes further than the Commission in some areas.
According to the document, the Council mandate raises the threshold for some small-scale installations benefiting from simplified permitting, including small solar systems, to 200 kW from the Commission's 100-kW level.
Ultimately, the emerging compromise will go beyond a political battle between faster and slower permitting and be about who controls the clock.
Parliament wants EU rules to make missed deadlines costly and approvals more predictable, while EU governments want to accelerate projects without giving Brussels —or the automatic approval mechanism — too much power over national permitting decisions, avoiding undesired precedents.
The next political talks on the permitting rules under the Grids Package are scheduled for early October.

Passengers evacuated after train hits lorry on level crossing

Passengers evacuated after train hits lorry on level crossing
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Around 150 passengers have been evacuated from a train after it collided with a lorry on a level crossing in Gelderland.
Two people on the train and the lorry driver suffered minor injuries in the collision on Horsterweg, Elmelo, train operator NS said.
The Sprinter train was heading towards Harderwijk when the crash happened just after 10am on Monday. The passengers were escorted to the station before buses were arranged to take them to their destinations.
The lorry was transporting concrete blocks on a low loader. NS said the clean-up operation would take several hours and all trains between Amersfoort and Zwolle have been cancelled for the rest of the day. Replacement buses are running between Putten and Nunspeet.
Police said the lorry driver was taken to hospital for treatment. The investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing.

Ukraine: AfD questions German aid, Berlin remains committed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

AfD puts pressure on German aid to Ukraine
September 14, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament.
He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing."
US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace.
On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward."
She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack.
How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin," who posed no threat of war to NATO.
East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid
The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently.
Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it.
According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate."
In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR).
"The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW.
"I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win."
Fear in Germany of Russian threats
On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine.
Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship.
According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this.
Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident.
"It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments."
Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine.
Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly
Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future."
But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%.
Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that."
Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'?
His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'."
Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan, which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power.
But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up."
So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate.
This article was translated from German.

Low-Deposit Online Casinos: How to Play Big on a Small Budget  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:45:38 UTC
21:45:38 KST

Low-deposit online casinos are designed for players who want to try real-money games without committing a large amount upfront. Instead of requiring a £20, £30, or £50 first payment, these sites may allow deposits from as little as £1 to £10.
That lower entry point can be useful if you are new to online casinos, testing a payment method, or simply setting a strict entertainment budget. It does not make gambling risk-free, though. A smaller deposit limits the amount you put in, but every wager still carries a chance of losing money.
How low-deposit casinos work
The basic process is the same as at any other licensed online casino. You create an account, confirm your age and identity where required, choose a payment method, and deposit money into your casino balance. The difference is the minimum amount the casino accepts. Comparisons of vetted low deposit casinos can help show how those minimums, payment methods, and offers vary between sites.
For example, a site might set a £5 minimum deposit for debit cards but allow £1 deposits through an e-wallet. Another may advertise a £10 minimum deposit because that is the lowest amount needed to qualify for its welcome offer.
The minimum deposit is not the same as the minimum bet. Many slot games offer spins from 10p or 20p, while table games can have different stake levels depending on the provider and game variant. A £5 deposit may therefore last for a number of small slot spins, but it will not go far at a £5-per-hand blackjack table.
Payment methods also matter. Debit cards, PayPal, Apple Pay, bank transfers, and e-wallets may each have their own minimum and maximum transaction limits. Always check the cashier page before registering, as the advertised figure may apply only to selected methods.
The advantages of a small first deposit
The main benefit is budget control. Depositing £5 rather than £50 makes it easier to decide in advance what you are comfortable spending. If that amount is lost, the financial impact is smaller.
Low deposits can also be a practical way to assess a casino before using it more regularly. You can test how quickly the site loads, whether games run smoothly on your phone, how the cashier works, and how responsive customer support is. It is also a chance to see whether the available games suit you.
For players who prefer occasional entertainment rather than long sessions, a small balance can be enough. A few low-stake spins or hands may be all you intended to play.
Finally, low minimum deposits can make payment methods more accessible. If you use a digital wallet or prefer not to leave a larger sum in a gaming account, the ability to deposit only what you plan to spend is useful.
The limitations to keep in mind
A low deposit does not necessarily mean low overall cost. A £1 or £5 payment can disappear quickly if you choose high-stake games or chase losses. The amount deposited should be treated as the total budget for that session, not a reason to keep topping up.
Bonuses can be another complication. A casino may promote a welcome bonus after a small deposit, but the terms can make it difficult to turn that bonus into withdrawable cash. Wagering requirements, maximum bet rules, excluded games, and withdrawal caps all affect the real value of an offer.
Game selection may also be narrower for bonus play. Slots usually contribute fully or nearly fully towards wagering requirements, while roulette, blackjack, baccarat, and live casino games often contribute less or not at all. The exact rules vary between operators.
Small deposits can create a mismatch with withdrawal limits too. You may deposit £5, win £12, and then find that the casino requires a £20 minimum withdrawal. That does not mean the money is lost, but it may mean you need to keep the balance in the account until it reaches the withdrawal threshold. Read that rule before depositing.
What to check before signing up
Start with licensing and safety. In the UK, use casinos licensed by the Gambling Commission. A licensed operator should display its licence information and provide clear links to safer gambling tools, terms and conditions, complaints procedures, and identity verification information.
Next, check the actual minimum deposit for your chosen payment method. The headline figure on a promotion page may not apply to every option in the cashier.
Then read the bonus terms carefully, especially these points:
- Wagering requirement: This is the number of times you must stake the bonus, and sometimes the deposit as well, before withdrawing bonus-related winnings. A £10 bonus with 35x wagering requires £350 in qualifying bets.
- Time limit: Bonuses often expire after a set number of days.
- Maximum bet: Many offers restrict the amount you can stake per spin or hand while wagering.
- Maximum withdrawal: Some low-deposit or no-deposit offers cap the amount you can cash out.
- Game eligibility: Check which games count towards wagering and at what percentage.
Also review the minimum withdrawal, withdrawal processing times, and any fees. Reputable UK casinos generally do not charge a fee for standard withdrawals, but payment providers can have their own rules. You should also expect identity checks before a withdrawal, and sometimes before you can deposit or play. This is a standard part of regulated gambling.
How to stretch a small bankroll
A small bankroll is not about finding a way to guarantee a win. It is about making a limited budget last longer.
Choose lower stakes. If you deposit £5, 10p or 20p slot spins give you more time than £1 spins. Set a fixed session limit before you begin and do not add more money once it is reached.
Avoid treating bonus funds as free money. Read the terms first and skip the offer if the wagering requirement does not suit your budget. A straightforward cash deposit can sometimes be easier to manage than a complicated promotion.
Use the casino’s deposit limits, time reminders, and self-exclusion tools if needed. Taking breaks is sensible, particularly after a quick loss or an unexpected win. Neither result is a reason to increase your stake. The World Health Organization’s ICD-11 entry on gambling disorder also reflects the importance of recognising gambling-related harm and using available safeguards where needed.

Tips For Organizing Financial Documents Before A Divorce Case Begins  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:45:36 UTC
21:45:36 KST

In Washington and California, a divorce can require spouses to reconstruct years of financial decisions at a time when communication is already strained. Separate bank access, frequent job changes, business ownership, or a move between states can leave records scattered across online portals and old devices. The result is often a financial history that feels clear in memory but becomes difficult to explain once questions arise.
Good preparation begins by turning that history into a record another person can follow. You don’t need to understand every legal consequence before starting, but you should know what exists, where it came from, and what gaps remain. The legal team at Envision Family Law can then review the material under the rules that apply in Washington or California and focus attention where it is most useful. This approach gives early discussions more structure and helps prevent incomplete assumptions from shaping important decisions.
1. Start With a Financial Inventory
Before a divorce case begins, organized financial records give an attorney a clearer view of income, property, debt, and spending. They also help identify missing information before deadlines create pressure. A complete file reduces repeated requests and supports accurate financial disclosures. Begin by gathering records from the past three years, then separate current documents from older files. This first review creates a reliable foundation for the steps that follow.
2. Gather Income Records
Collect recent pay stubs, annual tax returns, bonus statements, commission records, employment contracts, and records showing other income. Self-employed spouses should include profit-and-loss statements, business tax returns, invoices, and expense records.
A clear income file helps your legal team review household earnings and assess financial issues tied to support, property division, and cash flow. The firm serves clients in Washington and California, where state rules affect how courts evaluate financial information. Organized records help the legal team spot inconsistencies before they affect negotiations or court filings.
3. Separate Assets From Debts
Create two lists, one for assets and another for debts. Include bank accounts, investment accounts, retirement plans, real estate, vehicles, business interests, stock options, credit cards, personal loans, mortgages, and tax obligations.
Record the institution, account number’s last four digits, current balance, ownership name, and date of the statement. Property acquired before marriage, during marriage, or after separation may be treated differently under state law. Mark the acquisition date and source of funds whenever the records show that information.
4. Preserve Tax And Banking Records
Download complete bank statements rather than relying on account summaries. Monthly statements show transfers, withdrawals, recurring payments, and unusual spending that summary pages often omit. Keep federal and state tax returns with every schedule, attachment, and amended filing.
Also save records for business income, rental income, capital gains, and large deductions. Use a consistent file naming system, such as “2024 Checking January” or “2023 Federal Tax Return.” Consistent labels make searches faster and reduce confusion during document review.
5. Document Real Estate And Personal Property
For each home or other property, collect the purchase agreement, deed, mortgage statement, refinancing documents, appraisal, property tax bill, insurance record, and repair receipts. Note the purchase price, down payment source, loan balance, and estimated current value.
Photograph valuable personal property, including jewelry, artwork, firearms, collectibles, equipment, and vehicles. Add purchase dates, receipts, serial numbers, and insurance schedules when available. These records help establish ownership and reduce disputes about missing or undervalued items.
6. Review Retirement And Investment Accounts
Retirement and investment records require careful attention because account balances often change through contributions, withdrawals, gains, and losses. Gather statements from the date of marriage, the date of separation, and the current date when those documents exist.
Include 401(k) statements, pension summaries, individual retirement account records, brokerage statements, stock option documents, and beneficiary forms. Highlight deposits made before marriage or after separation. A clear timeline helps distinguish separate contributions from marital growth.
7. Protect Digital And Paper Files
Store copies in a secure location that the other spouse cannot alter or delete. Use a private email account or encrypted storage that does not depend on a shared device. Keep original paper records in a safe place and scan them into clearly labeled folders.
Do not alter statements, delete messages, or move money to conceal information. Preserve relevant emails, financial messages, account alerts, and records of major purchases. A document log should list the file name, date received, account involved, and any missing pages.
8. Track Monthly Expenses
Prepare a realistic household budget using bank statements, bills, payment records, and receipts. Include housing, utilities, food, transportation, insurance, medical care, child-related costs, subscriptions, tuition, and debt payments.
Separate recurring expenses from one-time purchases. Note payments made for either spouse, children, shared property, or separate property. This budget gives the legal team a practical view of household needs and helps identify expenses that require immediate attention after separation.
Conclusion
Financial preparation should begin before a divorce petition, response, or settlement discussion creates urgent deadlines. A person who gathers complete records, builds an asset-and-debt list, protects digital files, and tracks household expenses gives counsel usable information sooner. Next, create dated folders for income, accounts, property, debt, taxes, and expenses, then compare each folder with recent bank activity. List missing documents and request them before the case moves forward.

477.4 million customer non-cash payments totalling 597.1 billion euro were executed in Latvia by Latvian payment service providers in the first half of 2026. This averaged 2.6 million payments worth 3.3 billion euro per day.
The total volume and value of non-cash payments made by customers in the first half of 2026 increased by 6% and 2% respectively in comparison with the first half of 2025.
In the first half of 2026, the use of non-cash payments in Latvia continued its upward trend. Compared with the first half of 2025, both the volume and the value of non-cash payments increased, confirming the growing role of non-cash payments in everyday transactions.
As in previous years, the most popular non-cash payments were card payments and customer credit transfers, constituting 59% and 36% of the total volume of non-cash payments respectively.
The volume and the value of credit transfers, excluding intrabank payments, reached 58 million payments totalling 85 billion euro (increases of 9% and 12% respectively).
With the growing number of customer credit transfers, instant payments are becoming increasingly important in everyday transactions, accounting for more than one quarter of all customer credit transfers.
To ensure card payments, 2.3 million payment cards had been issued by Latvian payment service providers by the end of the first half of 2026 (1.2 cards per capita on average).
Residents had access to 62.8 thousand points of sale (POS), 869 ATMs in Latvia, as well as 7 ATMs operated by Latvian payment service providers abroad. At the end of the first half of 2026, the number of customer payment accounts opened by Latvian payment service providers totalled 3.2 million or 1.7 payment accounts per capita on average.
A detailed report on the operation of interbank payment systems, the development of payment instruments, and other areas vital for non-cash payments is available on Latvijas Banka's website (https://www.bank.lv/en/statistics/stat-data/payment-statistics).

What a Car Accident Attorney Does to Help You Pursue Compensation  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:45:04 UTC
21:45:04 KST

For drivers in Wesley Chapel, a collision can disrupt everything from a daily commute to work, family responsibilities, and access to essential activities. The financial consequences may also continue after a damaged vehicle has been repaired, particularly when an injury requires ongoing care or prevents someone from working. Florida recorded 3,184 traffic fatalities in 2024, according to the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, underscoring the potentially severe consequences of roadway collisions across the state.
A car accident attorney at Distasio Firm can help an injured person evaluate the full scope of a potential compensation claim. This may include investigating how the collision occurred, establishing who was responsible, gathering medical evidence, documenting lost income, and communicating with insurers. The attorney can also help distinguish immediate expenses from losses that may continue. By building the claim around documented consequences rather than only the initial accident, legal counsel can help present a more complete picture of the compensation being sought.
Why Legal Help Matters
People often seek legal advice after an insurer requests a recorded statement or sends a quick settlement proposal. A car accident attorney reviews crash facts, explains available options, and manages communications that could affect the claim. This support gives an injured person time to follow medical advice and assess losses before accepting payment.
Investigating the Collision
An attorney begins by examining how the crash occurred and who caused it. This review can include police reports, photographs, witness accounts, vehicle damage, and available video footage.
The investigation also considers road conditions, traffic signals, vehicle positions, and driver behavior. These details help establish negligence and connect the other driver’s conduct to the injuries.
A lawyer preserves evidence before repairs, vehicle removal, or fading memories weaken the claim. Prompt action also helps identify other responsible parties when the facts support their involvement.
Documenting Injuries and Losses
Medical records show the nature of an injury, the treatment received, and the care doctors expect. An attorney collects those records and tracks appointments, prescriptions, therapy, and related expenses.
Lost wages require separate documentation. Pay records, employer statements, work restrictions, and reduced earning capacity can show how the collision affected employment.
A claim can also include pain and suffering. Legal counsel connects physical limitations, emotional distress, and daily disruptions to the documented injuries.
Calculating a Fair Claim Value
Insurance companies often focus on current bills instead of future consequences. An attorney reviews expected medical treatment, rehabilitation, permanent limitations, and future income losses before valuing a claim.
The calculation also includes property damage and other accident-related expenses. Careful documentation helps prevent a settlement from overlooking losses that appear later.
Each case has different facts. Injury severity, available insurance, fault evidence, and recovery time all affect the compensation a person can pursue.
Managing Insurance Companies
An attorney handles calls, letters, document requests, and settlement discussions with the insurer. This process reduces the risk of an injured person making statements that weaken the claim.
Adjusters often seek information that limits liability or reduces the reported effect of an injury. Legal counsel reviews communications and provides accurate responses based on the evidence.
A settlement proposal requires careful review before acceptance. Once a person signs a release, the insurer usually closes the claim and ends further payment discussions.
Negotiating and Filing a Lawsuit
Most car accident claims involve negotiations before a lawsuit becomes necessary. An attorney presents the evidence, calculates damages, and responds to the insurer’s position.
If negotiations fail, legal counsel prepares the required court documents and manages the litigation process. This work includes discovery, depositions, motions, and trial preparation when necessary.
The attorney also monitors applicable deadlines. Missing a filing deadline can prevent an injured person from pursuing compensation through the courts.
Taking Steps After a Crash
An injured driver should report the collision to law enforcement and request a copy of the police report. Medical attention should follow, even though symptoms seem minor after the impact.
Photographs should capture vehicle damage, road conditions, traffic signals, visible injuries, and the surrounding scene. An injured person should also collect contact information from drivers, insurers, and witnesses.
An injured person should avoid discussing fault on social media or giving a recorded statement without legal advice. Preserving evidence early gives the claim a clearer factual foundation.
Conclusion
A car accident attorney investigates the collision, documents injuries, calculates present and future losses, and handles insurer communications. Legal counsel also protects filing deadlines and prepares the case for court when negotiations fail. After a Florida crash, an injured person should seek medical care, preserve photographs and records, and avoid signing a release before reviewing the claim’s full value. A prompt case evaluation can clarify available options and the next practical step.

Cyprus raised its corporate tax rate to 15%. The incentives that determine what you actually pay were left untouched  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

Cyprus enacted the most significant reform of its tax system in more than two decades, effective 1 January 2026. The headline is the corporate income tax rate, which rose from 12.5 to 15 per cent in line with the OECD global minimum.
That figure is being reported as though it settles the question. It does not. The 15 per cent rate is a starting point, and the two regimes that reduce it for holding, financing and IP-owning companies survived the reform intact.
The notional interest deduction
A Cyprus company funded with new equity rather than debt can claim a notional interest deduction against its taxable profit, without any interest actually being paid. The deduction is capped at 80 per cent of the taxable profit generated by that equity, which brings the effective rate on qualifying profit down to 3 per cent.
The reference rate is based on the ten-year government bond yield of the country where the capital is employed, plus a fixed premium, and the Tax Department publishes the applicable rates each year. The deduction is claimed annually for as long as the capital remains productively deployed. It cannot create or increase a tax loss, and anything unused in a year is lost rather than carried forward.
For an international group capitalising a Cyprus financing or holding vehicle with fresh equity, this is the single most valuable feature of the system, and the reform did not touch it.
the IP box
Qualifying profit from qualifying intellectual property, including patented inventions and copyrighted software, benefits from an 80 per cent exemption. Only the remaining 20 per cent is taxed, which produces an effective rate of 3 per cent on income within the regime.
The regime is nexus-based and follows the OECD modified nexus approach, so the benefit is proportionate to the qualifying development expenditure actually incurred by the Cyprus company. It rewards genuine development activity rather than the acquisition of an intangible. Alongside it, Cyprus continues to offer a 120 per cent deduction for qualifying research and development expenditure, extended to 2030.
the holding structure
The features that make Cyprus work as a holding jurisdiction are unchanged and, taken together, are more important than the headline rate.
Dividends received from subsidiaries are exempt from corporate income tax, subject to anti-avoidance conditions. Gains on the disposal of securities are exempt, with the position on property-rich companies tightened by the reform and worth checking where real estate sits in the structure. Cyprus imposes no withholding tax on dividends or interest paid to non-residents, and none on royalties where the right is used outside Cyprus. Royalties for rights used in Cyprus bear 10%, and payments to companies in EU blacklisted jurisdictions have carried withholding tax since 2022. From 1 January 2026 the defensive measures extend to low-tax jurisdictions, where interest and royalties paid to associated companies are no longer deductible. The destination of every payment therefore needs checking rather than assuming.
Furthermore, stamp duty has been abolished entirely from 1 January 2026. That removes a cost and an administrative step from share transfers, loan agreements and intra-group documentation. The treaty network remains extensive and includes all three Baltic states.
the compliance timetable tightened
For tax years from 2026 onwards, the corporate income tax return and the final tax payment both fall due by 31 January of the second year following the tax year, rather than 31 March with payment later. The first return under the new date is the 2026 return, due 31 January 2028. Supporting records must be kept for six years.
The reform also extended the carry-forward period for trading losses from five years to seven, applying to set-off from tax year 2026. For groups with loss-making years behind them, that is worth modelling before the next return.
The return depends on audited financial statements, so the audit is the binding constraint rather than the tax deadline. A group that appoints its auditor late in the cycle compresses everything downstream, and Cyprus has a finite number of licensed audit firms with capacity concentrated around filing season.
the practical position
Cyprus is no longer competing on headline rate. It competes on what sits underneath it, and for equity-funded holding and financing structures, or companies owning genuine intellectual property, the effective outcome is materially lower than 15 per cent.
Structures set up before this year should still be reviewed. The corporate residency test was widened, the property-rich threshold for securities disposals was revised, and the filing calendar moved. None of those are difficult to address, but they are easier to address now than at the next deadline.

What Evidence Can Link Workplace Retaliation to a Prior Complaint  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:44:52 UTC
21:44:52 KST

New York’s diverse workplaces bring together employees and employers across industries, from large corporate offices and public institutions to family-owned businesses and professional practices. In these environments, employees may sometimes speak up when they believe workplace conduct has crossed a legal or professional boundary. What happens afterward can become just as important as the original complaint, particularly when an employee suddenly faces unfavorable treatment.
Determining whether that treatment was ordinary workplace management or a response to protected activity often depends on the surrounding facts rather than on a single isolated event. For New York employees, recognizing these connections early can make it easier to understand what happened and what information may matter. The lawyers at Derek Smith Law Group can help assess the circumstances and identify evidence that may support a retaliation claim.
Evidence That Shows Employer Knowledge
A retaliation claim usually begins with proof that the employer knew about the prior complaint. Employees can use emails, human resources reports, hotline submissions, written grievances, meeting notes, or testimony from supervisors who received the report.
The complaint should identify what happened, when it occurred, and who received the report. A dated written record reduces disputes about notice. If the report occurred during a meeting, the employee should create a follow-up email that describes the discussion and retain any responses. Employees who need help with complaints can seek legal guidance, particularly when retaliation follows a complaint of discrimination or harassment. Legal counsel can compare the complaint with later employment actions, identify missing records, and preserve evidence before routine business systems delete messages or scheduling data.
Timing Between the Complaint and Adverse Action
Close timing between protected activity and adverse treatment can support an inference of retaliation. Examples include a reprimand issued days after a complaint, a schedule cut immediately after an investigation begins, or termination soon after an employee reports misconduct. A timeline should include the complaint date, investigation dates, supervisor contacts, performance reviews, disciplinary notices, schedule changes, and termination date. Exact dates help reveal whether the employer acted before or after learning about the complaint.
Inconsistent Explanations and Unequal Treatment
An employer’s shifting explanation can support a retaliation claim. For example, a manager might first cite poor performance, later cite attendance, and eventually cite a policy violation. Written records that conflict with those explanations can show that the stated reason lacks credibility. Comparators also provide useful evidence. An employee can compare the discipline imposed after the complaint with the treatment given to workers who committed similar violations without making a complaint. Relevant comparisons include attendance records, performance history, sales results, policy violations, and prior warnings.
Changes in Work Conditions
Retaliation does not always involve termination. An employer can retaliate by reducing hours, assigning undesirable work, excluding from meetings, denying promotions, issuing negative evaluations, transferring, threatening, or increasing monitoring. The action must be serious enough to discourage a reasonable employee from reporting misconduct.
Evidence becomes more persuasive when working conditions changed after the complaint without a documented business reason. Calendar invitations, shift schedules, assignment records, text messages, and performance metrics can show the difference between conditions before and after the report. Employees should preserve evidence lawfully and avoid accessing restricted files. Personal copies of relevant communications, schedules, evaluations, and notices can help establish the timeline without creating separate workplace policy issues.
Statements That Reveal Retaliatory Motive
Comments by supervisors can directly connect the complaint to later action. Statements such as “this is what happens when someone complains” or warnings against contacting human resources can provide direct evidence of retaliatory intent. Messages can also reveal motive indirectly. A manager’s email questioning why an employee reported conduct, discussing the complaint before imposing discipline, or directing closer scrutiny can help establish the connection.
The speaker, date, location, and witnesses matter. Employees should write down the exact words as soon as possible, rather than relying on memory months later. A contemporaneous account should identify who was present and what happened before and after the statement.
Conclusion
A retaliation case becomes clearer when the evidence forms a dated sequence: the employee reports protected conduct, decision-makers learn about it, workplace treatment changes, and the employer gives an inconsistent explanation. Employees should preserve emails, schedules, evaluations, notices, witness names, and personal timeline notes before records disappear. A prompt legal review can identify filing deadlines, separate lawful management decisions from retaliatory conduct, and determine which documents best connect the complaint to the adverse action.

Andy Burnham has cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday after his father, Roy, died.
Among other plans, the prime minister had been due to speak to the TUC conference in Brighton on Tuesday.
Burnham’s father had Alzheimer’s and was in a care home. In an interview Burnham gave in July, he said his father’s condition meant he was unaware that his son was about to become prime minister.
“That’s a sadness because he would be [proud],” Burnham told the Times. “But the way I look at it, it’s his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn’t know it.”
Burnham has talked about wanting to improve social care, in part because of his experiences with his father.
In one of his first speeches as prime minister, Burnham said it was humbling to see the “skill and the care and the professionalism” of care workers like those looking after his father, and that they should be paid more.
Among those expressing their condolences was Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who posted: “My thoughts are with Andy and his family at this terribly difficult and sad time.”
In her own post on X, Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, offered her condolences to Burnham and his family, adding: “No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.
“A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won’t ever be the same again.”
At the start of the Commons session on Monday afternoon, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said: “I am sure the whole house will want to send our best wishes to him and his family at this sad time.”
In Head North, the 2024 book he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor, Burnham described what he said had been a happy upbringing with his father, his mother, Eileen, and his two brothers in Culcheth, near Warrington in Cheshire. Roy worked as a telephone engineer, while Eileen was a GP’s receptionist.
“Neither my dad, Roy, nor my mum, Eileen, went to university. But both could have done if they had grown up in a different time and in a different place,” he wrote.
“Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go. But that did not make them pushy parents in any way.
“Their approach was one of quiet encouragement and confidence-building. Our family home in Culcheth was always full of music, life, laughter, love and support.”

The ranking of Turkish students in science, mathematics and reading -- the three core subjects assessed under the 2025 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) -- rose 50%, said the nation’s president on Monday.

According to the PISA 2025 report, which included 91 countries, Türkiye saw the largest increase in scores among OECD countries in science, mathematics, and reading, he said.

He said the share allocated to education more than doubled from 7.6% of the central government budget in 2002 to 15.33% in 2026.

In Ankara alone, 30 new schools with a total investment value of 1.989 billion Turkish liras have opened over the past two years, adding 544 new classrooms, Erdogan said.
 
He said the investments seek to ensure equal and fair access to education for all children, regardless of their income level, while providing better conditions for teachers to do their work.

The himalayan flash flood that devastated northern Nepal on August 26 was an unprecedented disaster. The death toll continues to rise, with nearly 1,400 people now confirmed dead and 5,130 still missing, including around 600 foreign nationals from 35 countries.

Kathmandu now wants to change its message on the international stage. Rather than simply calling for emergency aid, it is demanding compensation for the losses and damage caused by climate change.

Japan’s Failed Centrist Experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

The Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), once thought to pose a significant threat to Takaichi Sanae’s hold on power, came to an unremarkable end. After nearly seven months of negotiations among the CRA and its sister parties, the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito – both of which had dissolved in the lower house but continued to exist in the upper chamber – the three parties concluded that a complete merger would not proceed. As a result, the CRA is set to split into two groups, with former Komeito members returning to their former party and former CDP-affiliated members launching a new party. One member of the latter group will remain in the CRA to oversee its dissolution.
While the process of ending the CRA is already complicated enough, what makes it even more difficult for voters to grasp is that former CRA members will form a parliamentary group in the lower house. In other words, while the two parties have decided that they cannot be part of the same party, they still believe that they need to act as one, at least within the lower house.
The main cause of the breakdown in negotiations has been said to be the CDP’s reluctance. While Komeito was willing to join the CDP, which essentially shared its policy positions, the CDP ultimately could not reconcile its policies with those of Komeito. Komeito is more right-wing than the CDP’s positions on national security and nuclear energy.
Moreover, with local elections approaching next spring and the CRA having performed poorly at the February 2026 polls, local branches of the CDP have grown concerned that joining the party could put them at a disadvantage electorally. With the CDP having the largest number of local legislators among the opposition parties, second only to the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), it had much to lose by alienating its local candidates and organizations.
However, confidence may also have factored into the CDP’s calculations. While the CRA had consistently struggled in the polls, the CDP has significantly outperformed the alliance in some polls. According to an August poll by TV Asahi, the CDP recorded 4.7 percent support, compared with just 1.8 percent for the CRA. Similarly, an NHK poll put support for the CDP at 2.8 percent, compared with 1.7 percent for the CRA. These figures may have reinforced the CDP’s belief that it could perform better on its own than as part of a broader alliance.
Nevertheless, the CDP’s record in national elections tells a different story. Since its reorganization in 2020, the CDP has either lost seats or significantly underperformed other opposition parties in terms of changes in its parliamentary strength. In both the 2021 lower house election and the 2022 upper house election, the CDP ended up with fewer seats than it had before the election.
Although the party surged from 98 to 148 seats in the 2024 lower house election, the increase came overwhelmingly from single-member districts, where the CDP benefited from a favorable electoral environment, including the political-funds scandal involving LDP candidates. By contrast, its performance in the proportional ballot barely improved from the previous election: its proportional vote total increased only marginally, despite higher voter turnout.
In the 2025 upper house election, the CDP’s parliamentary representation remained essentially flat, while it fell to third place among the opposition parties in the proportional vote, behind the Democratic Party for the People and Sanseito.
Before the 2026 lower house election, the CDP’s alignment with, and eventual incorporation into, the CRA alongside Komeito was intended to reverse the party’s declining appeal among younger voters. Younger Japanese were thought to favor tangible policy outcomes – from lower costs of living to robust national security measures – over simply opposing the governing party. However, the electoral strategy failed.
This does not mean that so-called “resistance opposition,” a label that some pundits have come to associate with the CDP brand, lacks sufficient appeal to give the party staying power. Especially among older generations, opposing the LDP on normative issues such as the interpretation of Article 9 of the constitution and a zero-tolerance stance on nuclear energy – both core issues on which the CDP has refused to compromise – remains essential to their political orientation. However, as past election results make manifestly clear, those who could be described as “resistance liberals” do not constitute a majority, while parties that have performed well electorally in recent elections are gaining ground among younger voters.
With a weakening yen driving up prices across the board and a deteriorating security environment not only across the region but around the globe leading to abandonment of strict application of pacifism, resistance-oriented politics is increasingly seen as an unrealistic approach to governing a country. The CDP may be playing it safe by relying on tactics that succeeded in a different era, but by going it alone, it risks doing a disservice to its constituents and diminishing the political standing it might otherwise have strengthened through its alignment with the CRA.

Italy and wolves: living with a growing population amid myths and alarmism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:41:26 UTC
21:41:26 KST

The latest data put Italy's wolf population at around 3,500 animals spread nationwide, and experts say it has since grown. Amid sightings and scares, what is being done and what must be known so farmers, residents and wolves can live side by side?
From the attacks in Puglia to sightings in Emilia-Romagna, Umbria and Lazio, the summer of 2026 was dominated by alarmism about wolves.
The wolves currently present in Italy are around 3,500 according to the data from the latest national monitoring exercise carried out by Ispra (source in Italian), the Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research, which dates back to 2022. Since then the population has increased by around 150 animals, mainly in the Alpine area.
However, it is not only the growing number of wolves or the sightings near built-up areas that have reopened the debate about the species.
In March 2026 Italy transposed the 2025 EU directive on the wolf's protection status, which amends the previous 1992 rules. The animal has thus gone from "highly protected species" to "protected species", raising questions among experts about how useful this downgrading really is.
Are there too many wolves in Italy? How real is the risk for people living in towns and cities and how should they behave? Euronews asked experts in the field to respond, debunking myths and scaremongering.
Should we be afraid of wolves?
"Wolf attacks remain an extremely rare phenomenon, so there is no real risk to people, but in recent years we have seen an increase in these cases, which we monitor very closely," says Piero Genovesi, head of the wildlife coordination service at Ispra, speaking to Euronews.
The institute was the first to carry out nationwide monitoring of the number and distribution of wolves in Italy using rigorous scientific methods. In the past, animals were counted at local and regional level on the basis of sightings and estimates, but the methods were not standardised.
Ispra's study was conducted between 2018 and 2022 and used a single protocol for sampling and data analysis across the country, as well as the most sophisticated statistical methods currently available. The figure of 3,500 animals is therefore an accurate estimate of the number of wolves actually present in the country; it is not a minimum figure, the experts stress.
"Numbers tell only part of the story: wolves are territorial animals that live in packs and they do not accept other animals in their territory. This means that numerical increases are not explosive, but that the species tends to colonise any area left free," explains Genovesi, noting that the wolf has gone from being a species almost extinct 50 years ago to one that is now found virtually everywhere, from the beaches of Rome and Puglia to the Po Valley.
The species' remarkable adaptability is the reason why sightings near cities are no longer so rare.
There were 19 incidents of wolves attacking humans between 2017 and 2024, according to Ispra data gathered thanks to cooperation with Life Wild Wolf, (source in Italian) an EU co-financed project that supports the authorities in preventing and managing interactions between humans and wolves.
The most significant figure, however, concerns the number of wolves involved in these attacks: only seven animals were responsible for all the cases, and a single female wolf committed 11 of them. Looking at the numbers, it is clear that these episodes are exceptional and that these particular wolves have developed abnormal behaviour, as confirmed by experts and by studies that have been focusing on this species for decades.
What is "confident behaviour"?
"In reality there is no need to be afraid of wolves: it is a species that keeps its distance; it is a shy, nocturnal animal that tends to avoid coming into contact with humans," says Marco Antonelli, zoologist and large carnivore specialist for WWF Italy.
Ispra has drawn up a specific protocol for the management of urban and 'confident' wolves, classifying wolf behaviour according to the level of risk it poses. While sightings near homes have always occurred and pose no risk, permanent settlements close to people carry a higher level of risk, up to increasingly worrying behaviour such as the predation of domestic animals and, ultimately, aggressive reactions towards humans.
"There may be different reasons why this kind of behaviour develops: certain human actions lead wolves to become used to and comfortable around people," explains Antonelli, adding that in some cases these are individual traits of specific animals that develop behaviour that departs from the norm.
Downlisting and legislation in other European countries
The major novelty in 2026 is the so-called "downlisting", the move from the category of "highly protected" species to "protected" species. The difference is just a single word, but we will have to wait and see what changes in practice.
In March Italy approved the transposition of the 2025 EU directive and will have to bring previous rules into line with it by January 2027. The decision is triggering a wave of changes at national level: Germany, for example, has already transposed the new directive and is preparing to amend its national hunting law.
"It was a political choice, pushed by President von der Leyen. It was not necessary; wolves could already be culled under derogation, as provided for in the legislation," says Luigi Boitani, emeritus professor at La Sapienza University in Rome and one of the world's leading wolf experts.
His view is backed up by some figures: in Italy there have been cases of culls authorised as derogations from the rules, and there are countries where they took place regularly, such as France, which culled 250 wolves every year.
According to Piero Genovesi, by contrast, in the Italian system the downgrading brings technical changes, as it simplifies the bureaucratic procedure.
"Whereas previously authorisation from the Environment Ministry was required, based on a technical opinion from Ispra, now the regions can decide autonomously, still on the basis of a technical opinion," says Genovesi.
The current system should therefore be much more flexible, but it does not solve the real problem created by the growing number of wolves in Europe.
"The downgrading was essentially a political decision driven by very powerful farming lobbies at European level, in an attempt to solve the age-old issue of conflict between wolves and livestock farming," says Marco Antonelli, speaking to Euronews.
The difficult coexistence between wolves and farmers
Zootechnics is the science that deals with livestock breeding. And it is livestock farmers who have always been on the front line in denouncing the damage caused by wolves to their sector and the dangers faced by farm animals.
"Over the past 10 years, wolves are thought to have been responsible for preying on 0.6% of the livestock present in Europe, and the figures for Italy are very similar," says Antonelli, adding that the phenomenon should not be underestimated and should in fact be tackled with appropriate prevention strategies.
One of the most effective strategies is the use of so-called livestock guardian dogs, specially selected breeds of sheepdogs that look after and guard flocks. One of the best breeds for this job is found in Italy: the Maremma-Abruzzese sheepdog.
Other, more modern strategies include electrified and buried fences or raised night shelters, which provide effective protection for animals. Culls can be a solution to deal with animals that develop abnormal behaviour, but taken together these protective measures can ensure everyday coexistence between wolves and farmers.
"The data show that prevention strategies are much more effective than any culling strategy. A solution does exist, but it is not as simple as many make out, which is why the commitment of the authorities is also needed," Antonelli concludes.
Beyond polarisation: "coexistence means compromise"
City dwellers can also play a part and need to know the right preventive behaviour to adopt. Above all, it is essential to ensure proper waste disposal, as rubbish is highly attractive to all kinds of wildlife.
Another important factor is the management of pets: in areas where sightings are frequent, experts advise against leaving pets unattended and, above all, against leaving pet food on the street, as it could attract wolves.
"The most dramatic change we are seeing today is the polarisation of opinion about wolves: the number of people wanting to defend them has grown a lot, and so has the number of people wanting to see them culled," says Luigi Boitani.
"The middle ground is still very small, yet that is what we should be aiming for: coexistence means compromise," the professor concludes. Knowledge of the species beyond opinions and myths is still limited, but pursuing it is the only long-term solution.

Joyce dismisses threats of 'tanked economy' from negative migration rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:40:21 UTC
21:40:21 KST

Barnaby Joyce says One Nation will follow 'will of the people' over economist warnings on migration
In short:
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says voters are "tired" of economists, dismissing warnings about the impacts his party's migration policy could have on the economy.
The party has proposed sending migration to net negative rates for three years by heavily restricting student visas and blocking visas for family members of skilled workers.
What's next?
Labor and the Coalition are also proposing to slash migration, but have not detailed their policies.
One Nation is "not afraid" to drive migration to negative levels, with its Treasury spokesman saying he will follow the will of the people, not warnings from economists, in deciding how deeply to cut migration rates.
Business and the university sector have warned One Nation's proposal to cut migration by about 750,000 places over three years would devastate the economy.
Speaking on ABC National Forum, Mr Joyce said voter concerns on migration had to be respected.
"The will of the Australian people is so pronounced, this has to be dealt with, we will deal with it," Mr Joyce said.
Political commentator George Megalogenis said no government had ever purposefully caused a net outflow of migrants.
He said migration had been negative only four times in Australia's history: twice during the depressions of the 1890s and 1930s, and twice during the deployment of soldiers during the first and second world wars.
"If you're going to take … 766,000 people out of the Australian economy and society for three years, you have tanked the economy in a way that is on the scale of the depression of the 1890s and 1930s," Mr Megalogenis said.
Net overseas migration has been falling from its peak in mid-2023, when international borders reopened after the COVID-19 pandemic.
While the surge of migrant arrivals has slowed to pre-COVID rates, the number of migrants departing has also remained flat, leading to migration rates still above the government's long-term forecasts and above the pace of housing construction.
Joyce: People 'tired' of economists
The National Forum heard views on migration amid a raging debate on the issue — while Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all taken a position to cut migration rates, the details of which visa categories should be cut often prompts fierce reactions from sectors where there are sometimes already workforce shortages.
One Nation yesterday announced its plan to heavily restrict the number of international students allowed to study in Australia and block skilled workers from bringing family to Australia.
Net migration would be net negative for three years — meaning more people leaving the country than arriving — until an ongoing cap of 130,000 places a year took effect.
Mr Joyce defended One Nation's proposal, but dismissed questions about the economic impact it could have.
"The issue of what it is going to cost I think is contentious, but I have no concern about following the will of the Australian people," Mr Joyce said.
"I think the Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with public policy, to go to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and, to be quite frank, I have been around this game for a while and I have never seen a forward estimates in any budgetary paper be even close to the mark."
Mr Joyce said he was not worried about what the Parliamentary Budget Office or another office might conclude about One Nation's migration policy "because they're not elected, I am".
He noted that the party's policy did not touch demand-driven visa programs, like the Pacific worker program which many farmers relied on, or visas for skilled workers themselves — just those that would allow them to bring family.
Earlier, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) warned that pursuing a pre-determined migration target was a mistake.
"If you are basing the outcome on a set of arbitrary numbers and an arbitrary target, which is not achievable without across-the-board cuts in a whole range of categories, then you are going to do long-term damage to the Australian economy," ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar said.
Speaking on National Forum, former deputy prime minister and Nationals MP John Anderson said Australia had only avoided recession because of high migration rates.
But he said that voters were being drawn away from the major parties by a concern about migration.
"A balanced, reasonable immigration rate is good economically," Mr Anderson told National Forum.
"It's good socially, whilst we agree 'the law of the land' really does apply, but we need to realise how badly broken [the migration system] is."
"We are here because One Nation has captured the initiative, because vast numbers of Australians think the system is now not working for them."
Labor and Coalition yet to settle migration policy
Both Labor and the Coalition have announced their own intentions to cut migration as One Nation's popularity has surged.
The federal government has a target to reach a net migration rate of 225,000 a year by 2028, but is yet to detail new policy intended to bring down migration from the current rate of about 300,000 a year.
Labor's planned changes to migration were postponed several weeks ago, and continue to be debated by cabinet.
The Coalition, meanwhile, has signalled its intention to tie Australia's migration program to housing construction rates to ensure that migration does not outpace housing supply — though it has not yet detailed that proposal.
Frontbencher Andrew Hastie said cutting migration would require "trade-offs", which was why his party was still working through its position.
"We are committed to this, to getting it right, though — that is the difference between us and One Nation," Mr Hastie said.
Mr Hastie said he agreed with One Nation's proposal to reduce temporary graduate visas, as was "stopping the visa hopping", but he said it was unclear how One Nation intended to do that.
Loading...
Nyadol Nyuon: Migration debate a proxy for race
While much of the debate has focused on what level to cut migration by, and population pressures on housing and infrastructure, there has also been a question around who should be allowed to migrate to Australia.
One Nation has proposed banning some migrants by preventing travel from countries where the Department of Foreign Affairs has issued a "do not travel" advisory due to terrorism or other security risks.
The Coalition has proposed tightening the test for prospective migrants to make compliance with a statement of Australian values a binding visa condition, and delaying access to social security supports for non-citizens.
Human rights advocate and lawyer Nyadol Nyuon said trying to pin criminality on certain communities was the kind of thing dividing Australians.
Ms Nyuon said the migration debate was often used as a placeholder for conversations around race.
"I don't have to look a particular way to love this country, but whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," Ms Nyuon said.
Loading...
Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly said she feared losing the Australia she grew up in.
"I grew up playing cricket in a street with kids from Greece and Yugoslavia at the time, Italian, Chinese, and nobody cared. Nobody cared what language your mum spoke," Ms Aly said.
"Nobody cared that my skin got darker as the sun was over us. Nobody cared about any of that. And that's the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we're losing."

Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.
The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).
That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.
Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”
Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.
His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.
The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.
Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.
“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”
After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.
