Nepal: Thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

Nepal: thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
September 14, 2026
Nearly three weeks after deadly flash floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border, the Himalayan nation is shifting from search-and-rescue operations to relief and reconstruction efforts.
Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,386 bodies have been recovered across five affected districts, while more than 5,130 people are still missing. The latter figure includes 587 foreign nationals and around 900 workers employed in hydropower tunnels and other energy facilities.
The deluge, which authorities say was triggered by a glacier collapse, devastated communities and swept away more than a dozen hydropower facilities. As search operations continue in submerged tunnels and along muddy riverbanks, families are growing increasingly desperate for news of missing loved ones.
Villages wiped out in minutes
The scale of human loss is particularly stark in the upper river basins, where entire settlements vanished within minutes. In many places, destroyed roads and bridges have cut off access, forcing rescue and relief teams to rely on helicopters to deliver essential supplies.
Niranjan Paudyal, a resident of Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District who lost his parents, uncle, aunt and sister in the flash floods, said the flood took away even the chance of burying his family members.
"We spent days searching through debris, hoping for signs of my missing parents and family," he told DW. "Sadly, the disaster left us with no choice but to perform their final rites without their bodies."
Public land in Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa District has either been washed away or rendered unsafe.
"There is not even land left after the flood to perform the final rites of those who lost their lives," Chameli Gurung, the municipality's deputy chair, told DW. "Relatives have to travel to Kathmandu's Pashupati Aryaghat to perform the final rites."
In Uttargaya alone, at least 618 houses were swept away or buried and 877 people remain missing. Only 12 bodies have been recovered. Gurung said local authorities are exploring the possibility of leasing private land to accommodate displaced families before winter.
Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, told DW that affected people are being resettled close to their original homes by securing nearby public or private land and providing financial assistance based on household size until they can become self-reliant.
Nepal faced with a colossal recovery bill
As emergency relief efforts begin to stabilize, Nepal faces a massive financial burden. A preliminary rapid damage and needs assessment (RDNA) puts the total reconstruction requirement at about 723.3 billion Nepalese rupees ($4.78 billion, €4.1 billion), according to local media reports.
The RDNA estimates that nearly two thirds of the funds will go into restoring energy and transport networks and academic facilities.
Hydropower, which supplies almost all of Nepal's electricity, had become a fast-growing source of the country's export revenue. The flood damage has deepened concerns about how Nepal will finance its recovery.
On Monday, neighboring India approved the export of power to Nepal for 18 hours a day until at least December 31, Reuters news agency reported.
"We will try to utilize all of our domestic resources and seek international support to manage the funding gaps," Timilsina, the communication minister, told DW.
Nepal wants to grow resilient
Nepal has formally approached the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed Loss and Damage Fund for assistance. However, the fund, established to help countries deal with the impacts of climate change, has yet to begin distributing its limited resources.
Nepal is seeking to turn reconstruction into part of a broader economic recovery strategy, with an emphasis on climate-resilient infrastructure rather than simply replacing what was destroyed.
"Given our previous experience with post-disaster management, what matters most is how effectively we can use the funds to restore lives and livelihoods and build disaster-resilient infrastructure," Roshee Lamichhane, an associate professor at Kathmandu University, told DW.
Demand for climate justice
Beyond recovery finance, Nepal is making a broader climate justice argument on the international stage.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 24, where he is expected to call for global responsibility for mitigating climate impacts.
Despite contributing less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards.
"Reconstruction would be used as an opportunity to build climate-resilient infrastructure," Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division at Nepal's Ministry of Forests and Environment, told DW. "We will develop a guideline with the motto of 'tomorrow for a better future.'"
Climate scientists caution against attributing any single extreme event solely to global warming without detailed studies, but they agree that rising temperatures are accelerating glacial melt across the Himalayas.
Manjeet Dhakal, director of Climate Analytics South Asia, says the scale of the disaster highlights the growing consequences of rising global temperatures and gives Nepal an opportunity to advocate for cuts in global carbon emissions on the international stage.
"How many more disasters should we wait for before there is a global response to address the impacts of climate change?" he asked, adding that developed and advanced countries, alongside other nations, should take greater responsibility.

The weapons were allegedly distributed to other criminal organizations, including groups linked to drug trafficking and kidnappings. Investigators said parcels were sent through courier services using false or stolen identities in an effort to conceal those involved.
According to Europa Press, the investigation began in early 2026 after authorities detected a series of suspicious shipments originating in Spain’s Valencia region and being sent to other parts of the country.
In June, police intercepted one parcel containing a handgun, a submachine gun, a silencer, and a high-capacity drum magazine. Subsequent arrests helped investigators trace the distribution network and identify the workshop in Figueres.
A key development came on August 25, when officers intercepted another package containing a submachine gun with its serial number removed. Surveillance later connected the shipment to a storage facility used as the illegal workshop.
Six people were arrested during searches in Girona, Valencia, Badajoz, and Barcelona. The suspected head of the network remains in custody.
In February 2026, Belgian authorities arrested Viktor Labin, a suspected Russian GRU operative accused of supplying coordinate-measuring machines used by Russia’s defense industry. According to The Insider, his company allegedly helped channel military equipment to Russian contractors linked to at least 18 defense enterprises.

NAJAF – An Iraqi court on Sept 14 sentenced a butcher to 10 years in prison for selling pork that he claimed was beef in the holy Muslim city of Najaf.
Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council said the man was caught with 75kg of pork that he was selling as beef in Najaf, home to one of the world’s most revered Shi’ite Muslim shrines.
“Najaf Criminal Court has sentenced a convicted person to 10 years in prison for selling meat not suitable for human consumption,” it said.
Although Islam forbids pork as it is believed to be impure, Iraqi law does not explicitly ban its sale in the Muslim-majority country, which has a Christian minority.
The court based its ruling on a 1998 law that criminalises the sale of “dog or donkey or other meat... that is unfit for human consumption”.
Millions of pilgrims from around the world flock to Najaf every year to visit the mausoleum of Imam Ali – the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law, the fourth Islamic caliph and the first Shi’ite Imam.
The butcher, who was arrested earlier in September, attracted widespread attention on social media, with some Iraqis calling for better food safety and others sharing funny videos of pigs captioned “here is Najaf”.
Najaf resident Ahmad al-Mansouri said jokingly: “I think I have eaten more pork than beef or lamb over the past years.”
He was among many residents who were deceived. After buying a kilogram of ground meat and finding it was of “excellent quality” and cheaper than the market rate, he started visiting the butcher more often.
“We were surprised when he was arrested on charges of selling pork,” Mansouri said. AFP

Iran censures US deliberate destruction of development at Human Rights Council
TEHRAN –The Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO has elaborated on the deliberate destruction of development by the US through adopting coercive sanctions and launching military aggressions against the country.
“Forty years after the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, its promise remains unfulfilled for millions. The question is no longer whether development is a human right, but why some states are still allowed to systematically deprive other people of that right,” IRNA quoted Hassan Fartousi as saying while addressing the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council, being held from September 7 to October 7.
Recognizing the right to development becomes meaningful only when the international community can offer effective and actionable solutions to the obstacles that practically prevent nations from accessing the resources, opportunities, and infrastructure necessary for development, the official added.
“For decades, the United States has subjected the Iranian people to extensive unilateral coercive measures, obstructing access to financial resources, technology, medicine, and essential goods, and deliberately constraining our development. Today, the same United States has added military aggression to the economic coercion.
The impact of these illegal measures is not limited to economic indicators; it also affects health, education, infrastructure, and human capital, he added.
“When hospitals are attacked, when schools are destroyed, when children are killed in their classrooms, we are not merely witnessing casualties of war. We are witnessing the deliberate destruction of development itself. A school destroyed in seconds represents years of trauma for the students and challenges in education. A hospital struck means not only a damaged building, but the destruction of health, human capital, and future generations,” Fartousi further noted.
The official went on to say that “Forty years after the declaration, commemoration is not enough. Those who destroy development through unlawful coercion and military aggression must be held accountable. Hereby, as the Secretary General of the Iranian National Commission for UNESCO in Iran, the right to development must be a right for all people, especially the people who are living in the developing countries.”
The 63rd session of the Human Rights Council biennial panel discussion on the right to development was held under the theme ‘Commemoration of the fortieth anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development’.
The panel aimed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development (DRTD), and to reaffirm the commitment of the international community to the effective realization of the right to development as an inalienable human right for all; take stock of the achievements, obstacles and challenges encountered over the past four decades in the implementation of the Declaration on the Right to Development at the national, regional and international levels, including lessons learned; and identify elements towards a road map for the concrete operationalization of the right to development including through adoption of the draft International Covenant on the Right to Development.
It also aimed to explore the contribution of the right to development framework to the implementation of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development and beyond, including by proposing principles, policy recommendations and institutional pathways; and to catalyse a forward-looking dialogue on the future of the right to development as it enters its fifth decade.

What did EU leaders say about the train attack?

"He is wrong."

Lockheed Martin expands secretive Vectis drone program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:11:22 UTC
21:11:22 KST

- Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works is building four additional Vectis combat drones, bringing the program's total to five aircraft.
- The tailless, stealth-focused drone is designed to fly alongside crewed fighters like the F-35, with a first flight targeted by the end of 2027.
Lockheed Martin is building four more of its newest combat drones, the company announced September 14, doubling down on a program that’s still more than a year away from ever leaving the ground.
The news came from the company’s secretive Skunk Works division, following a major Air Force conference near Washington, D.C., where Skunk Works also unveiled a full-scale model of the aircraft, called Vectis, for the first time.
If you haven’t heard of Vectis yet, here’s the short version: it’s a drone designed to fly into combat alongside piloted fighter jets like the F-35, acting as a kind of robotic wingman. The Air Force calls this category of aircraft a “Collaborative Combat Aircraft,” or CCA, and the idea is straightforward even if the acronym isn’t. Building more fighter jets with pilots inside them is expensive and slow. Building smart, semi-autonomous drones that can fly in formation with those jets, carry weapons or sensors, and take on some of the riskier parts of a mission is, at least in theory, cheaper and faster to scale up.
Lockheed first showed off Vectis a year ago, in September 2025, but the design has changed since then. The version unveiled this week has no tail and a deeply recessed air intake built into the top of the fuselage, both features meant to make the aircraft harder to spot on radar. Ron Fehlen, the vice president and general manager of Skunk Works, told reporters the team is eager to see the pieces coming together.
“The team is extremely excited as these parts start to come together, to actually get the wheels off the ramp by the end of 2027,” Fehlen said.
That end-of-2027 target is when Lockheed expects the first Vectis prototype to actually fly. In the meantime, the company is now building four additional aircraft, bringing the total to five once the original prototype is included. Lockheed hasn’t said publicly what those extra four aircraft will be used for, whether that’s more flight testing, demonstrations for potential buyers, or something else.
For scale, Vectis is about 34 feet long with a 38-foot wingspan, which puts it roughly in the same size class as the Air Force’s MQ-9 Reaper drone in length, with wings about as wide as an F-35’s. It falls into a weight and altitude category the Air Force calls Group 5, meaning it weighs more than 1,320 pounds and is built to fly above 18,000 feet, the same bracket as the two CCA drones already chosen for the Air Force’s first round of the program. Lockheed hasn’t said what weapons Vectis might carry, what kind of engine powers it, or how much each aircraft is expected to cost.
That first round of the CCA program didn’t go to Lockheed. The Air Force picked General Atomics and Anduril Industries instead, and their aircraft, known as the YFQ-42A and YFQ-44A, are being built mainly for air-to-air combat missions. The Air Force has said it eventually wants at least 1,000 of these drones total, built out over several future rounds, and it’s aiming to keep the cost of each aircraft around $20 million, not counting the sensors and other equipment that would go inside. Fehlen said Vectis isn’t necessarily being built for one specific future round of the competition, but that Lockheed sees potential customers well beyond the Air Force, including the Navy and militaries overseas.
One thing Lockheed has been eager to talk about is how quickly the Vectis team has been moving. According to the company, engineers went from an initial sketch to testing a model in a wind tunnel in under two months. The first complete digital design of the aircraft came together in six months, and the team had manufactured its first physical part within eight months of starting the program. Lockheed says that speed comes from manufacturing and design tools built up over years of other Skunk Works projects, not from cutting corners on this one specifically.
Whether Vectis ends up winning a future Air Force contract, getting picked up by the Navy, or drawing interest from an allied country overseas is still an open question. For now, what’s confirmed is that Lockheed is putting real money and staff behind five aircraft instead of one, with a flight test still more than a year away.

====================================================================================================

“Fairly disciplined workers”: Russia’s prison service is replacing penal colonies with forced labor centers — and making money from it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:11:20 UTC
21:11:20 KST

As the military recruitment of prisoners reduces the population of penal colonies across Russia, the country’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) is expanding another branch of its system: correctional centers for convicts sentenced to forced labor. By the end of 2025, Russia had created 400 of these centers, with space for up to 50,000 people. This past June, FSIN even unveiled a “quickly deployable” center that can be installed directly at businesses nationwide. The new system is more profitable than traditional penal colonies, providing FSIN with fresh revenue streams and companies with access to a workforce almost entirely devoid of rights.
You’re not prisoners, but you can’t leave
Russian law does not classify forced labor as imprisonment, but a person sentenced to forced labor is nevertheless obligated to live in a closed FSIN facility. They must work wherever the administration sends them and cannot freely leave the correctional center.
“You can sit there and not go anywhere for a year,” Olga [name changed], a former convict who spent time in correctional centers from Perm to Volgograd, told The Insider. After a penal colony, Olga said, a correctional center can genuinely feel “almost like home.” People there can wear their own clothes, use a phone, read the news online, and communicate with relatives every day through messaging apps. But the relative improvement in quality of life that Olga experienced only applies to those who have previously spent time in a penal colony, where prisoners must wear standardized uniforms, communication with relatives usually happens by letter, and phones are banned.
For someone sent to a correctional center directly from life outside prison, the experience looks different: living by a schedule set by the FSIN, leaving the center only with permission, working forced overtime, and being subject to the administration’s will.
“People who were sent to a correctional center straight from home were somewhat shocked,” Olga recalled.
“A model correctional center with a sports ground and park”
According to Olga, life becomes especially hard when a correctional center is set up directly at a production site — with a dormitory next to the workshop and the employer working together with the administration to reduce inmates’ lives to moving between bed and the workplace. That is exactly the model FSIN now wants to replicate: fast-deployable correctional centers that can be built next to enterprises.
“At the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, FSIN presented a model correctional center with a sports ground and a park. The project was sent to the regions as a recommendation,” TASS wrote in late June. In FSIN photographs, the model does not look like a prison but like a tidy workers’ dormitory: a long two-story modular building, lawns, bushes, streetlights, a separate sports ground, and a walking area with benches.
The TASS report also listed other elements of the project: a parking lot, a diesel power station, a transformer substation, and a separate yard where those who have violated prison rules can still get a chance to walk. But the presentation itself showed that the most attractive parts of the image — the park and sports ground — aren’t mandatory. A FSIN representative clarified that they are only “optional facilities.”
In other words, what was sent to the regions was not a plan for a center with a park but an easily replicable solution for quickly housing people sentenced to forced labor. The FSIN website describes it even more directly: the facilities can be built quickly “at any enterprise,” and the project can be used by representatives of large and medium-sized businesses interested in creating dormitories for convicts at their facilities.
That detail is crucial, Olga explained. She served her sentence both in a correctional center where she had to walk down the street to get to work and in a center where the dormitory was effectively on the production site.
“If it’s a closed-system correctional center, then the employer works in very close coordination with FSIN. No one’s getting away from them. FSIN plays the way the employer needs it to,” Olga said.
Employers work in very close coordination with FSIN in closed-system correctional centers
In that model, a person does not simply live near work — work becomes an extension of the prison regime.
“The conditions were always more lenient where the employer wasn’t in the same building as the dormitory. But where you live right in the workshop, right at the production site, that was where things were the hardest,” Olga recalled.
At one correctional center in the Moscow region, Olga said, the living quarters resembled a hangar or garage, with a workshop on the floor below. The facility had poor ventilation and was plagued by dirt, rats and cockroaches.
“It's legalized slavery,” she said. “They force people to work and use every tool of pressure and punishment available to make sure they keep working and don’t complain.”
30,000 workers with no rights
Forced labor as a new type of criminal punishment began to be used on Jan. 1, 2017, when FSIN opened its first four correctional centers and seven sections attached to its penal colonies, with a total capacity of fewer than 900 people. The first convicts arrived in March of that year. Now, a small network of facilities that was previously being tested as an alternative to colonies has turned into a separate and growing branch of the penal system.
By the end of 2025, according to FSIN Director Arkady Gostev, Russia had created 400 correctional centers and sections operating as correctional centers, with capacity for 50,000 people — and more than 30,000 convicts were actually being held there.
Given the overall decline in Russia’s prison population, those figures are especially notable. In May 2026, Gostev said that since the end of 2021 the number of people in places of detention had fallen from 465,000 to 282,000. About 85,000 of them were held in pretrial detention centers (SIZO) and PFRSI, a Russian abbreviation for facilities operating as pretrial detention centers, leaving about 197,000 in penal colonies and prisons.
The rise of correctional centers, whose inhabitants are not counted among the country’s prison statistics, do not explain that decline. Instead, the main reason for the drop in the population of penal colonies was the recruitment of prisoners for the war in Ukraine — first by the Wagner private military company, then by the Defense Ministry. In May, FSIN itself acknowledged for the first time that “efforts to recruit contract soldiers” for the armed forces was affecting the number of prisoners.
But at the same time, the agency is expanding the part of the system that is formally not considered imprisonment — exploiting the labor of convicts rather than simply isolating them away from society. The more than 30,000 people actually held in correctional centers already amount to about 15% of the current number of people under FSIN’s jurisdiction. The centers’ total capacity — 50,000 places — is comparable to about a quarter of that population.
The agency is expanding the part of the system focused not on isolation, but on exploiting convicts’ labor
At the same time, legal changes are making it easier to fill correctional centers. Since 2026, forced labor can be imposed as a standalone punishment, without a prior sentence involving imprisonment. The penalties under dozens of articles of the Criminal Code have also been expanded to include forced labor.
A “dormitory” behind a fence: What life is like in a correctional center
Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code describes correctional centers as special institutions for people sentenced to forced labor. They can exist separately, as sections attached to penal colonies, or directly at enterprises that use convict labor. Inside such centers, internal rules apply, and convicts are kept under supervision.
In correctional centers, people are allowed to have money, wear ordinary clothes, use a phone, access the internet, and keep personal belongings. At the same time, a convict must remain on the correctional center’s grounds, they may not leave without permission from the administration, they must carry an ID card at all times, they must follow internal rules, and they must take part in unpaid maintenance and improvement work for up to two hours a week. The person and the room where they live may be searched, and their belongings may be inspected. In effect, it is the same kind of closed institution as a penal colony, only with a softer internal regime.
The word “dormitory,” which is used to describe the living quarters in correctional centers, says little about the real conditions. Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code uses the same word for the places where convicts live in general-regime, strict-regime, and special-regime colonies. In practice, these are usually not separate rooms for a few people but buildings divided into large sections, each housing several dozen people. Even in the model FSIN showed at the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, a large room with rows of beds can be seen inside the modular building. It looks more like a barracks-style sleeping hall than a regular dormitory.
Olga said conditions varied widely by region. In some places, the administration turned a blind eye to the rules, while in others, it used them as a tool of pressure. Still, the routine in forced labor facilities, she said, resembled the “Groundhog Day” rhythm of life in a penal colony:
“Wake-up, breakfast, go to work, a little lunch at work, and then at around 8 or 9 p.m. we come back from work, wash, have a bite to eat, and go to sleep. That’s basically every day.”
In some correctional centers, Olga said, people could go into town for a few hours on weekends. However, on others, people had to go months without leaving the grounds.
“If there are no problems, if the employer does not say they are working badly, then everything goes normally,” she said. “But if someone starts, for example, filing complaints against the employer, then the administration first of all restricts outings.”
Grigory Mumrikov, an artist who served a forced labor sentence in Zelenograd, just outside Moscow, after being convicted of participating in the organization of an anti-war protest, shared similar impressions. Compared with pretrial detention, the correctional center seemed to him like “great happiness,” even if he was still in captivity. From evening to morning, he was in the correctional center, and from morning to evening, he worked as a laborer at Aksakovo, a sanatorium run by FSIN. Mumrikov spent the couple of free hours he had after work walking around a lake.
“I could simply sit on a bench, just to avoid being on that territory,” he said, referring to the correctional center.
That was possible because the convicts worked outside the correctional center and traveled to and from Aksakovo on their own. But by 8 p.m., Mumrikov had to return to the center for the evening roll call.
“Everyone was rounded up and told to work weekends”
Under the law, people sentenced to forced labor must work wherever the correctional center’s administration sends them. Formally, their labor is supposed to be regulated by labor law. But convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer.
Convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer
In some correctional centers, Olga said, there was still some choice — the administration could offer two or three potential employers, and the person would choose where to work based on their skills and health. But that was not the case everywhere. In the correctional center in Leninsk, in the Volgograd region, where she was held in the winter of 2023-2024, there was only one employer: a canned goods factory.
“You cannot refuse to work, because that is considered a malicious violation,” Olga said.
According to her, people worked 10 to 12 hours a day, and weekends could be turned into workdays. However, if inspections began, the employer would show a normal schedule.
“The employers drew up a good schedule and pretended that no one had been forced to come in on weekends and that the working day was what it should be,” she said. “Accordingly, as soon as the inspectors leave, everything goes back to the way it was: longer working days and mandatory weekend work.”
The order to work on weekends, she said, usually came not directly from FSIN but from the production site. A foreman would gather the convicts, make sure no one had phones to record the conversation, and then announce the new schedule: “We work on weekends. We work until such-and-such time. And whoever complains will make things worse for themselves.”
That is what makes a convict’s position in a correctional center fundamentally different from that of an ordinary worker. In a correctional center, an employer’s demand almost automatically becomes an FSIN demand. The administration begins applying pressure, and complaints or refusal to work can result in disciplinary penalties.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system,” Olga said. If a person refuses to work for pennies or complains about conditions, she said, the administration can begin “catching them on small things” to find grounds for punishment. Accumulating such penalties creates the risk of transfer to a penal colony.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system”
Similar complaints have emerged in other regions. In Zelenograd, convicts in a correctional center said they worked without a proper schedule, faced overtime, and were threatened with tougher conditions if they reminded officials of their rights.
“We differ from undocumented migrants on a construction site only in that we are Russian,” forced laborers said.
Konstantin, a former prisoner who served his sentence in Kabardino-Balkaria in Russia’s north Caucasus, told the independent outlet Cherta that he was sent to sort household waste — eight hours in the heat at a rural dump that included hides of slaughtered cows and sheep, a terrible smell, large numbers of insects, and no ability to refuse the work.
Another person interviewed by the outlet, from the Voronezh Region in central Russia, worked at an agricultural complex growing mushrooms and said regular hired employees earned significantly more than convicts got from the correctional center.
These examples do not mean that people in every correctional center are forced to work overtime or are sent to the hardest jobs. Former convicts themselves also describe centers with decent working conditions and normal schedules. But all cases have one thing in common: a person cannot resign if they are unhappy with the conditions.
There is pay, but people support themselves
Officially, labor in correctional centers is paid. In any sentence, between 5% and 20% of a convict’s salary is withheld for the state, and the inmate is free to use the rest of the money. But unlike a penal colony, where prisoners have to be fed and issued uniforms, people in correctional centers are almost entirely self-supporting.
Convicts are given a bed and bedding, but they usually buy their food, clothes, shoes, hygiene products, medicine, and other everyday items while also reimbursing the correctional center each month for utilities and household services.
In Leninsk, in the Volgograd Region, Olga said, about 3,000 to 4,000 rubles ($35-$46) were withheld from her wages for utilities, and after all the deductions were made, convicts were typically left with about 9,000 to 10,000 rubles ($104-$116) a month to live on.
“And you have to take into account that this is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers provide food,” she said.
“This is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers have food”
Formally, if a convict has no money, the correctional center has to provide them with food, clothing, and shoes at the state’s expense. But in practice, Olga said, getting that support can be difficult.
“You go to the management and say: I have nothing to eat, you are supposed to provide me with food. And they say: ‘Well, where am I going to get it? You can see there is no kitchen,’” she said, describing life at a correctional center in the Moscow Region.
At the same time, Olga stressed that low pay is not an inevitable feature of correctional centers. In the Perm Region, where she worked at a private garment factory, the business was properly organized, and convicts’ wages could be comparable to ordinary wages outside the prison.
Olga earned about 40,000 to 50,000 rubles ($460-$580), while women who sewed well made up to 100,000 ($1,160), even after the deductions. “It was a fairly good place,” she said.
That contrast shows that the problem with correctional centers is not simply that they always pay poorly. With a decent employer, convicts can earn close to what they would outside prison. But if the employer is dishonest, the fact that a person is trapped means they are forced to survive on less than the national subsistence minimum.
What can lead to punishment in a correctional center
Under the Penal Enforcement Code, violations committed by people serving forced labor can lead to them being placed in an internal isolation cell inside the correctional center for up to 15 days. Olga said anyone sent there can only bring a minimum of belongings, and there is a ban on phones. “Not as frightening as in a colony, but the point is the same — to isolate you and show what they can do to you,” she explained.
The law separately defines “malicious violations,” which include refusal to work, disobeying the administration, participating in a strike or collective disobedience, possessing banned items, leaving the center without authorization, or returning more than 24 hours late. If a person is declared a malicious violator — for one “malicious” violation or for three ordinary violations within a year — the head of the correctional center submits a request to a court to transfer the person to a colony.
In practice, Olga said, these rules become a method of control. The administration may ignore minor violations for a long time, then use them against those who complain about an employer or refuse to work in poor conditions.
“They may treat you relatively well for a long time, but once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do,” she said.
“Once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do”
An everyday minor infraction can thus become part of a chain that ends in a person being packed off to a penal colony. “For those who came from a colony, that's the main fear,” Olga said. “They tell you: ‘if you don't want to work, you'll go back.’”
Who benefits from the new system
In public statements, FSIN describes correctional centers as a more humane alternative to colonies: a person is not completely isolated from society, and they can work, earn a salary, use a phone, and gradually return to normal life. In an explanatory note to the law expanding the use of forced labor, its authors wrote that such punishment allows convicts to maintain social ties, restore work skills, and compensate victims.
But this humanization also has an economic aspect. Under the Penal Enforcement Code, sections of correctional centers can be created directly at enterprises that use convict labor. The standard contract between a correctional center and a company describes the arrangement as a ready-made production scheme: the correctional center sends convicts, and the organization agrees to employ them at its site and report violations of labor discipline to the administration.
For businesses, this means access to workers whose minimal privileges depend on their successful fulfillment of assigned tasks. A convict cannot simply quit and leave for another employer, and as a FSIN representative told TASS, commercial entities are interested in creating such sections because people sentenced to forced labor are “fairly disciplined workers.”
“They are interested in doing their work well, because if they violate labor discipline or the procedure and conditions for serving their sentence, there is a risk that the punishment will be replaced with a harsher one — imprisonment,” the representative said.
The state additionally encourages businesses to take part in the scheme. Since 2026, organizations have been exempt from property tax on premises, territories, and other real estate they provide free of charge to house correctional centers.
The model is also convenient for FSIN. The agency does not need to build a traditional penal colony, as businesses provide part of the infrastructure while paying convicts enough that the state is not obliged to provide them with food, clothes, or medicine — 5% to 20% of their wages also go directly to the state.
In the end, businesses get workers whose discipline is backed by FSIN, while the agency gets infrastructure and a “contingent” — the official bureaucratic term used for prisoners and other people under state supervision — whose burden of support can largely be shifted onto the convicts themselves. At the same time, for FSIN and the state as a whole, this is a form of punishment that can be presented as humane resocialization.
A Gulag without isolation
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But direct comparisons between modern correctional centers and the Gulag would be misleading because the scale, conditions and level of violence are vastly different. Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
Correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet tradition of forced labor — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now for Russia’s business sector
The state does not need to fully isolate a person in order to control them. It is enough to link their place of residence, their type of work, their salary, and the threat of transfer to a penal colony into a single system. As a result, correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet tradition of forced labor — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now, also, for Russia’s business sector.
Not humanization, but a pragmatic move by FSIN
Correctional centers may offer better conditions than penal colonies, but they are still a form of deprivation of liberty, no matter what the paperwork says. In the end, they create even more opportunities to exploit prisoner labor than colonies do, and FSIN directly describes people sentenced to forced labor as a convenient labor resource.
Putin’s war in Ukraine is draining prisoners from Russia’s penal colonies, and dozens of institutions have closed down due to the lack of inmates. That could have led to FSIN losing bureaucratic influence (and with it, staff and funding from the state budget). Instead, the agency’s leadership appears to have found an effective way out: it can now report growth in the number of institutions providing a more humane form of punishment, and it can do so in a way that certainly pleases Russian businesses.

Biosphere reserve management regulations under final review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

21:10:47 KST

Biosphere reserve management regulations under final review
TEHRAN - The judicial and legal committee of the cabinet of ministers is conducting a final review of the executive regulations for biosphere reserves, which will establish the framework for managing the country’s biosphere reserves.
Once approved by the Cabinet, the regulations will establish the specific management framework for the country’s biosphere reserves, IRNA quoted Hamid Zohrabi, an official with the Department of Environment, as saying.
The regulations constitute the country’s first comprehensive framework specifically dedicated to biosphere reserve management. They aim to establish clear management mechanisms, enhance coordination among relevant agencies, and strengthen local community participation, he added.
They also enable the Natural Resources and Watershed Management Organization to establish biosphere reserves, which would contribute to the development of the country’s biodiversity conservation capacities, the official noted.
Referring to the differences between biosphere reserves and protected areas, Zohrabi said that the former seeks to strike a balance between biodiversity conservation and sustainable resource use, as well as promote the socio-economic development of local communities and research activities.
Moreover, it will pave the way for the integrated management of biosphere reserves, the utilization of indigenous knowledge from rural and nomadic communities, and the attraction of targeted investments.
The official went on to say that the implementation of the law will strengthen Iran’s position within the global network of biosphere reserves, and contribute to achieving the goals of the Hangzhou Strategic Action Plan.
Biosphere reserves are territories of outstanding ecological value where people and nature grow harmoniously alongside each other, conserving biological and cultural diversity, advancing sustainable development, and connecting communities across a global network.
Iran, with 14 biosphere reserves, has always been among pioneering member states in the World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
 
 According to the head of the DOE, Shina Ansari, biosphere reserves cover less than four percent of our national territory, which is not enough, so we are committed to expanding the network by the establishment of four more biosphere reserves.

"Potato production is expected to total about 12.5 million tonnes this year. The available volume is more than enough for the domestic market. The population consumes a maximum of 2-2.5 million tonnes a year. The rest of the harvest is traditionally used for seed and livestock feed," Vysotsky said.

Final harvest figures will be available once the harvesting campaign is complete, the ministry said.

Iran seizes assets of 240 dissidents and journalists as protest arrests top 6,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:09:14 UTC
21:09:14 KST

The judiciary froze 182 bank accounts and confiscated property belonging to journalists, activists and public figures accused of acting in favour of "hostile governments". Tehran has executed at least 532 people since January, including 29 linked to the protests.
Iran's judiciary has seized assets belonging to 240 dissidents, journalists and public figures and frozen 182 of their bank accounts, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported, as Police Chief Ahmadreza Radan announced on Sunday that more than 6,000 people had been arrested over the January protests.
Of the asset seizures, 143 took place in Tehran. Those targeted were accused of "propaganda activities or actions against the country and in favour of hostile governments," according to Mizan.
The agency said some of the assets belonged to journalists working for Persian-language opposition broadcasters Iran International and Manoto, as well as activists and public figures living abroad.
The asset seizures include the case of Sadegh Saeedi-nia, whom Iranian media described as an entrepreneur, whose property was confiscated and who received a custodial sentence in one of the most high-profile proceedings against regime opponents.
The judiciary has also made more than 2,000 inquiries to Iran's Central Bank regarding defendants' accounts and warned that additional seizures and proceedings are under way.
Radan said his forces had arrested three members of the Mojahedin-e Khalq (MEK), an exiled Iranian opposition organisation seeking to overthrow the Tehran regime, in an operation the previous night.
He said MEK members had played a role in what Iranian authorities describe as a coup, the term the Islamic Republic uses for the December-January protests.
"We will not forget the rioters and coup-plotters, we continue to monitor them and take action against them," Radan said.
He also said security forces had prevented a repeat of Chaharshanbe Suri — the Persian fire festival marking the last Wednesday of the year — from being used to trigger further unrest.
"One of the enemy's extensive plans was to use the last Wednesday of the year to create a scenario similar to the incidents (in January), but that did not happen," he said.
Iran has executed at least 532 people since January, according to Iran Human Rights, a Norway-based monitoring group, including at least 29 people in connection with the January protests. The rate has accelerated since the start of the war with the US in late February.
The late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed in a US strike on his residence at the start of the war, had been among those who publicly described the protests as a coup attempt.

Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:09:02 UTC
21:09:02 KST

Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
Marib is home to Yemen’s oil and gas sector. Whoever controls it secures major economic gains. Taiz’s location makes it strategically critical.
Yemen’s government forces have carried out air attacks against the Iran-backed Houthis to repel their advances, as the rebel group has been gaining ground in government-held positions in the past week.
The focus of the fighting is now shifting to the region of Marib – the government’s last remaining stronghold in the north and a major oil and gas hub. Should the Houthis gain control of it, it could decisively turn the tide of the war in their favour, say analysts.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Yemen’s Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island in Red Sea
- list 3 of 3More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies
Heated battles are also taking place in western Taiz, on the western coast, where reports suggest government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia, are now on the counteroffensive after losing some ground there last week. A video released on Monday by the Yemeni army purports to show Houthi positions and vehicles being bombed there.
Trapped in the middle are the civilians. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has reported that more than 85,000 have been forced to flee their homes since the beginning of September. More than 2,000 have fled into Djibouti’s northern shores.
So why does Marib matter?
It is the last remaining stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in northern Yemen. A Houthi expansion there would threaten government presence and weaken its leverage in the north.
Marib also hosts the country’s largest gas and oil fields, meaning that whoever controls it holds some of Yemen’s most important energy infrastructure and a potentially crucial source of revenue.
“Dominating Marib’s oil and gas resources has been a Houthi goal for more than a decade. Without facing a crushing defeat in Marib, they would keep fighting to achieve that goal,” Saddam al-Huraibi, a Yemeni political commentator, told Al Jazeera. Should they gain control of it, the group could earn great leverage to negotiate favourable terms in any future mediation effort.
A Houthi capture of Marib would be a “watershed moment” in terms of the country’s internal dynamics, said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Future Security Program of the New America think tank. Still, he said, it will be a tough fight as government forces will see this battle as an existential war. “Losing Marib would be an absolute crushing defeat” for the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, he added.
Marib is also geographically significant because it lies on the easiest road that runs from northern Yemen to Shabwa Governorate in the south – a seafront on the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea – and al-Mahra Governorate.
The optics of a win in Marib would also be a powerful propaganda tool for the Houthis, helping them convince many Yemenis that the group is on a roll militarily and is poised for even greater victories, said Nabil Hetari, a Yemeni writer and human rights activist.
There is also a humanitarian dimension. Over the years, the city has been welcoming displaced people from areas which have fallen under Houthi control since the fall of the capital Sanaa in 2014. According to IOM figures from 2023, Yemen recorded nearly 2.8 million internally displaced people, more than half of whom (58 percent) are in Marib.
“All the parties involved in the battle are focused on Marib as a potential decider in the nature of their exit from this war,” said Hetari.
And why does Taiz matter?
The strategic importance of Taiz lies in its geography.
The governorate forms a bridge between the Houthi-held north and the government-held south and the Red Sea coast. Thus, whoever controls it gains the upper hand in the movement of weapons and supplies between the interior and the southern port city of Aden.
Taiz also carries considerable political weight. One of Yemen’s largest population centres, the city became an important centre of resistance to the Houthis after they seized Sanaa in 2014 and has endured years of fighting and restrictions on access. A major Houthi breakthrough there would therefore carry symbolic significance far beyond the territory captured.
Its western coast also stretches towards Mocha, a historic town that the Houthis captured last week, and towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Bab al-Mandeb is one of the world’s most important shipping routes. The 20km- (12-mile-)wide waterway lies between Yemen and Djibouti, connecting Europe to Asia. Before fighting resumed, about 12 percent of global trade passed through it. In recent days, the Houthis have grabbed most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including Mayyun (Perim) Island, which lies in the strait.
“The Houthis seek to move closer to this vital waterway to threaten maritime traffic. Such a move aims to keep the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb under the influence of Iran and use them as leverage against regional and international powers,” said Fuad Mussed, a Yemeni analyst and author. “This is a strategy Tehran has been pursuing for years.”
This is a serious concern for Saudi Arabia, which has been relying on the Red Sea route to export its oil, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian woman shines at BRICS Startup Contest 2026
TEHRAN – Iranian female entrepreneur Azam Karami has secured first place in the Energy, Infrastructure and Mobility category of the BRICS Women’s Startup Contest 2026.
Led by the BRICS Women’s Business Alliance (BRICS WBA), the contest aimed at empowering and accelerating women-led startups across BRICS nations.
The event was held from September 9 to11 in New Delhi, India, with over 506 projects from BRICS member countries competing in six areas: “Health and Wellness,” “Agriculture and Food Security,” “Education,” “Energy and Infrastructure,” “Trade and Digital Transformation,” and “Sustainable Development.” Ultimately, only 18 projects reached the final stage.
Titled ‘Smart Monitoring of Railway Track and Bridge Errors Using Drones and Artificial Intelligence’, her project was developed with the aim of increasing safety, reducing maintenance costs, and improving productivity in transportation infrastructure management.
Karami is a faculty member at Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman. In the BRICS Women’s Startups Contest 2024, she received the award in the nomination ‘Artificial Intelligence’ for her project titled ‘Automatic Fault Detection in Power Transmission Lines’.
The 2026 edition of Women’s Startup Contest continued to spotlight innovative, high-impact women-led enterprises, fostering cross-border economic integration, collaboration, and knowledge exchange within the BRICS ecosystem. The initiative provided a dynamic platform for visibility, networking, and business expansion, enabling women entrepreneurs to scale their ventures and engage with investors, industry leaders, and policymakers across BRICS countries.
Fostering sustainable development, promoting economic inclusion, strengthening integration among BRICS markets, supporting innovation in key sectors, building entrepreneurial resilience, highlighting women-led solutions for global challenges, enhancing collaboration between BRICS nations, raising awareness of sustainable business practices, promoting technological adoption and digital transformation, and strengthening local economies through global connections are among the key objectives of the contest.
Iran outlines policies on women, family at BRICS WWG
In July, Narjes Abolqasemi, an official with the Vice-Presidency for Women and Family Affairs, elaborated on the country’s macro-level policies on women and family at the BRICS Working Women Group (WWG) held in Kerala, India, on July 6-7.
The empowerment of women requires a transition from sporadic measures to strategic and sustainable policies; in Iran, women’s entrepreneurship and economic development serve as driving forces for strengthening national resilience and the family foundation. Therefore, the policies are designed and implemented with a family-centered approach, IRNA quoted Abolqasemi as saying.
She also highlighted the importance of the four priority areas of the meeting, which included promoting women’s participation in governance and leadership, advancing digital and financial inclusion, strengthening women’s entrepreneurship and skill development, and enhancing the role of women in climate action, food security and nutrition.
Referring to the country’s experience in expanding the women entrepreneurship ecosystem, she said Iran focuses on establishing support models for women-led innovative businesses, developing modern skills, and benefiting from the potential of the digital economy.
Iran’s participation in the WWG meeting provided a great opportunity to share indigenous experiences, expand joint efforts, and develop new initiatives to achieve economic justice and sustainable development among BRICS member states, Abolqasemi noted.
Underscoring the significance of fostering specialized collaboration among BRICS member states, the official announced Iran’s readiness to utilize its scientific, policy, and executive capabilities to assume an effective role in the design of innovative models for women’s economic empowerment and expanding multilateral cooperation within the BRICS framework.
The WWG Meeting was held under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” which reflects a people-centric and humanity-first approach to global cooperation.
It brought together senior government officials from BRICS member countries in the two-day event to discuss key issues related to women’s empowerment, women-led development and enhanced cooperation across shared priorities.

Satellite imagery shows extensive damage to a Saudi Aramco fuel depot and apparent damage to a military site in southern Saudi Arabia following recent Yemen's Houthi attacks, according to analyses by satellite imagery platform Soar.
Satellite images of Saudi Aramco’s bulk fuel plant in Abha show at least six storage tanks completely destroyed, while eight others sustained varying degrees of damage, according to the analysis.
The facility, a major fuel distribution hub for southwestern Saudi Arabia, appears to be largely out of operation, Soar said.
Separately, satellite imagery dated Sept. 13 shows two burn marks on a military hardstand in Sharurah in the southern Najran province.
The area is used to park armored personnel carriers and military pickup trucks, suggesting that the site may have been targeted in a Houthi strike, according to Soar.
The analyses are based on modified Copernicus Sentinel satellite data. Saudi authorities have not provided a detailed assessment of the damage shown in the imagery.
The findings come amid a sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, which has launched a series of missile and drone attacks against the kingdom in recent days.
On Sept. 8, Houthi missile and drone attacks targeted Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring 73 civilians, including women and children, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attacks caused fires at energy facilities in the south of the kingdom and temporarily halted some operations at the targeted sites.
The Houthis have continued their attacks, saying Sunday that they carried out a large-scale missile and drone operation against Saudi military targets, including facilities in Khamis Mushait.
Saudi authorities also issued emergency warnings over potential threats in Abha and Khamis Mushait on Sunday before later announcing that the danger had passed.
The Houthis say their operations are in response to Saudi military strikes in Yemen, while Riyadh has condemned the attacks as violations of its sovereignty and warned that they threaten civilians and critical infrastructure.

UK unions split over donations cap as TUC chief says ‘super-rich’ corrupting politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:07:27 UTC
21:07:27 KST

Trade unions are set to launch an intervention on Tuesday on political donations after the head of Britain’s trade union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics.”
Union leaders met on Monday to discuss possible support for a domestic cap on donations. Discussions are expected to continue but sources said general secretaries were likely to back strong words calling for further action on political donations from wealthy individuals – but arguing that trade union members should be treated as individual donors giving small amounts.
Union leaders had been split on the prospect of limiting domestic donations to political parties, with many including the GMB fearing it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.
Labour-affiliated unions are working on a statement on political donations that is expected to be put before the TUC general council on Tuesday, the Guardian understands. But union sources said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.
Many of the trade unions that are not affiliated to Labour are keen to go further on limits – but would themselves not be affected by measures that could curb party donations.
On Sunday, Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, broke ranks and backed a limit, after two crypto billionaires, Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, donated £72m to Reform UK within 24 hours.
Asked about the possibility of an overall cap on donations, Gary Smith, the general secretary of the GMB, said “we’ll work that through” but added that amendments to the representation of the people bill, aimed at enacting a limit, “felt ill-thought-through”.
However, Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, which is not affiliated to Labour, said the government should be doing more on political donations. “The government’s going to have to step in here. Citizens have noticed this. This is buying and distorting democracy, and in a way that ultimately will impact working people adversely,” he said.
In his annual address to the TUC conference in Brighton, Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said the donations were “a crisis for our democracy”.
“Tell me, why is it that two crypto billionaires have donated £72m to Reform in just two days?” he said. “The evidence is clear: Reform UK is a party for sale. Nigel Farage is a politician for sale. And given half the chance, they’d sell our country down the river.
“Make no mistake, this is a crisis for our democracy. We cannot allow our political system to be captured by corporate interests.”
He said there was no similarity “between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires”.
“We need a proper conversation about how we clean up our politics that doesn’t push workers to the margins – but does stop the super-rich corrupting our politics,” he added.
Nowak said no donations at all should be allowed from those who did not live and pay taxes in Britain. A bill currently before parliament would limit donations from overseas British donors to £100,000. He said the government must also go further on foreign funding for political ads. “Elon Musk, keep your grubby hands out of British politics,” he said.
Smith said that despite qualms about a donations cap it was clear that the government had to “clean up the money going into politics”.
But he said he was concerned about trade union funding being caught in the crossfire. “Care workers, school, support staff, energy workers, they need a political voice. And they deserve a stake in the country, in politics, and we do that through pennies that our members donate to a political fund, some of which we use to support the Labour party.
“So our money’s clean, it’s declared, it’s transparent. People know where it comes from, and we’re unequivocal and unashamed about advancing the interests of our members.”
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said union donations were “the cleanest money in politics”, adding: “We must make sure we reflect the difference between our donations and other donations.”
Thomas also urged the government to look again at election spending limits, as a way to help level the playing field.
The bill currently in the House of Lords puts significant limitations on overseas donors, including for a calendar year after they return to the UK.
Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Harborne spent in Britain.
The two separate donations of £36m by Harborne and Delo are unprecedented in UK political history and will give Reform enormously boosted resources before the next election.
Delo was based in Hong Kong but has returned to the UK. Asked when, Tice said it was “many, many months ago”. Harborne is registered to vote in the UK but also lives in Thailand.
The former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson said on Monday that he thought the retrospective nature of the cap was “pathetic” and unfair.
“Just because some people want to support one party very generously, Labour kicks up a huge fuss and says they’re going to cap donations,” he told GB News. “I think the next election is going to be fought on the shape of the British economy and on British society and the government that has the most credible [plan] and I think it’s the Conservatives.”
But he said he questioned the motives of Reform’s donors. “The problem with Reform … whatever the motives of these guys, these crypto kings, in funding Reform with squillions. I wonder whether they want Reform to be pro-crypto,” he said. “Reform is weak on welfare, and I think weak on the economy.”

Baltic export: The Insider identifies the Russian agents of influence working to destabilize Latvia&#039;s upcoming elections

Latvia's upcoming parliamentary elections, scheduled for Oct. 3, will feature fourteen political parties competing for 100 seats in the Saeima. Roughly a third of the candidates consider Russian their native language — some studied at Russian educational institutions, while others frequently travel to Russia. Moscow is closely monitoring the campaign, and pro-Kremlin propagandists are spreading a range of falsehoods in an effort to influence Latvian voters. The Insider has identified the figures in the Russian Embassy in Riga and the presidential administration who oversee the Kremlin's network of agents in Latvia responsible for election interference.
Vladimir Balobayev, the Kremlin’s Baltic handler
Sources identify 38-year-old Kaliningrad native Vladimir Balobayev as the Russian Presidential Administration's point man on issues involving Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania.
In 2015, Balobayev was general director of the Baltic Information and Analytical Center, which channeled funding to so-called independent journalists in the Baltic states. Among those who received payments from him was Andrei Solopenko, editor of the Baltnews portal, which is now banned in the EU. In 2025, a Riga court sentenced Solopenko to 280 hours of community service for violating anti-Russian sanctions.
In 2016, Balobayev became deputy director of the Center for Eastern European Studies at Immanuel Kant Baltic Federal University in Kaliningrad, where he published a paper titled “Transformation of Poland’s Political System.” In 2019, Balobayev moved from Kaliningrad to Moscow and joined the Presidential Administration. He soon became head of the Department for Interaction with Civil Society Institutions within the presidential office responsible for cultural ties with former Soviet states. In December 2020, Putin awarded him the rank of Active State Councillor of the Russian Federation, 3rd Class.
At the time, the “cultural” directorate's Baltic desk was headed by Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) colonel Yevgeny Umerenkov. In the 1990s, Umerenkov had used a Komsomolskaya Pravda press pass as cover to spy in the United States and Mexico, and in 2020 he returned to the Kremlin-friendly tabloid after effectively being sent into retirement. The desk was taken over by Umerenkov's aide, Vadim Smirnov, who reported directly to Dmitry Kozak.
In the early 2000s, Smirnov had trained at the Moscow office of the American Council for International Education, which is funded by U.S. taxpayers. He later worked for RIA Novosti, served as press secretary to Kaliningrad Region Governor Vadim Tsukanov, and became a political columnist for Kaliningradskaya Pravda. In 2013, Lithuanian authorities barred “journalist” Smirnov from entering the country due to suspicions that he was involved in espionage activities. In 2024, due to poor performance, Smirnov lost his position as the Presidential Administration's overseer of the Baltic states. Balobayev took his place.
In August 2025, following a series of spy scandals, Putin scrapped the “cultural” approach and created the Directorate for Strategic Partnership and Cooperation (USPS) in its place (as The Insider previously reported). In the new directorate, Balobayev oversees a range of Kremlin-backed organizations: the Foreign Ministry’s Third European Department, Rossotrudnichestvo, the Russian International Affairs Council, the Foundation for Support and Protection of the Rights of Compatriots Living Abroad, the Russkiy Mir Foundation, the Baltnews news portal, and a team of propagandists.
Among Balobayev’s better-known actors promoting narratives about NATO’s “cunning” plans to seize the Baltic Sea while spreading “Russophobia” in the Baltic states are propagandist Andrei Mamykin (who is internationally wanted at Latvia’s request), former Riga City Council member Ruslan Pankratov (who fled to Russia), Belarus-based blogger Roman Samul (formerly active in the “Antifascists of the Baltics” movement), “historian” Alexander Dyukov (who predicts the imminent extinction of the populations of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania), and Konstantin Khudoley (head of the Department of European Studies at St. Petersburg State University’s School of International Relations).
One of Khudoley’s students at St. Petersburg State University, Vyacheslav Morozov, moved to Estonia in 2016 to teach at the University of Tartu, where he gave numerous lectures on Russia’s role in the modern world before being caught spying for the GRU. During the investigation, Morozov admitted to working for Russian military intelligence; he was sentenced to six years and three months in prison.
SVR station chief in Riga Igor Sorokopud
In 2023, in the midst of Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine, Latvia downgraded diplomatic relations with Moscow and cut embassy staff by 60%. The ambassadors were replaced by chargés d’affaires. Today, the Russian embassy’s work in Riga looks more like the activities of a school patriotic club: on commemorative dates, diplomats visit the graves of Soviet soldiers and present certificates to the few surviving World War II veterans who have made it to almost 100.
But that is only the visible side. Closely monitoring the Saeima elections is the SVR station chief in Riga, 43-year-old embassy first secretary Igor Sorokopud.
Born in Moscow, Sorokopud studied Middle Eastern languages at Department No. 38 of the Military University of the Russian Defense Ministry (VUMO), an institution currently headed by Colonel Vladimir Bykovtsev, who spied in Yemen back in Soviet times. After graduating from VUMO, Sorokopud enrolled at the SVR Academy, where he underwent specialized training for work at stations in the Middle East.
In 2018, he was posted to Iran, where he worked under the cover of the embassy’s third secretary. The Insider obtained an invoice from the Peter Justesen store in Tehran — part of the international duty free chain serving diplomats — made out to Sorokopud. According to the invoice, in January 2020 the Russian official spent $2,944.45 at the store (the sale of alcohol is strictly prohibited in Iran, and it appears that Sorokupud resold bottles on the side).
In 2024, Sorokopud was transferred to Latvia, where he took charge of the local SVR station. His main operational interests are Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, Western military aid to Ukraine, and people with access to the country’s leadership, the Defense and Foreign ministries, and other centers of decision-making.
Sorokopud’s operational focus: Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, military aid to Ukraine, and people in positions of power
The SVR’s agent network in Latvia is made up primarily of former Soviet military personnel and Russian-speaking residents who are susceptible to pro-Kremlin propaganda due to dissatisfaction with their personal economic circumstances.
In Latvia, Sorokopud lives with his wife, Yekaterina Vostrikova, a St. Petersburg native who previously worked as a financial analyst at Aton, a Russian company that manages the assets of private investors. Until 2024, Vostrikova went by the name "Gretchen" and the surname of her then-husband, American Chad Anthony.After divorcing him, Yekaterina reverted to her maiden name, Vostrikova, and joined Sorokopud in Iran. The Insider has found that Vostrikova herself has access to classified information, suggesting that she may be more than simply a spy’s wife.
The SVR is actively engaged in disinformation operations in Latvia. In May, for example, the agency claimed —falsely, by all available indications — that Ukraine had reached a deal with Latvia to launch strikes on Russia from Latvian territory: “Despite concerns on the Latvian side that it could become the target of a retaliatory Russian strike, the authorities in Kyiv persuaded Riga to approve the operation. The Ukrainians emphasized that it would be impossible to determine the exact launch site of the drones.”
However, Sorokopud does not appear to be responsible for producing that particular disinformation narrative. Instead, the false claim in question was apparently orchestrated by SVR press bureau chief Sergei Guskov, whom The Insider previously reported on.
The “Russian world” in Latvia
Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, support for the “Russian world” in Latvia has declined noticeably. Moscow, however, still appears to be betting on the Russian Union of Latvia (RSL), despite the high-profile espionage scandal involving former Latvian MEP Tatjana Ždanoka, who, as The Insider revealed, worked for the Russian intelligence services for several years. (Notably, the RSL’s governing board also includes the aforementioned Baltnews “journalist” Andrei Solopenko.)
In Strasbourg, Ždanoka served as leader of the RSL, promoted claims that Russian-speaking residents of the Baltic states were being persecuted, and voted against resolutions condemning Russia over the annexation of Crimea, its war in Syria, and its aggression against Ukraine. Leaked correspondence indicates that since at least 2005, Ždanoka had been in operational contact with the FSB, received money from Moscow, and sent reports to her Russian handlers. She also advised Russian intelligence on how to intervene more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries.
MEP Zdanoka advised Russian intelligence on how to interfere more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries
In 2024, amid the espionage scandal, Ždanoka stepped down from the RSL leadership. The party was then taken over by co-leaders Andrei Pagor and Yevgeny Osipov. Pagor, a former police officer, was forced to resign after suspecion arose that he had been soliciting bribes from drug dealers. He is currently running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket.
The other co-leader, Osipov, was responsible for founding the Latvian branch of the neo-Nazi Russian National Unity (RNE) organization back in the 1990s. Osipov says that he went underground at the age of 16 and spent his nights putting up RNE leaflets. In 2000, fellow members accused him of disloyalty to RNE leader Alexander Barkashov and expelled him from the organization, after which Osipov joined the Latvian National Democratic Party (LNDP). In 2013, he was sentenced to community service for desecrating the Latvian flag.
Elena Osipova, Osipov’s wife, is also on the RSL’s governing board and heads the Russian Community in Liepaja. In 2023, she ran for the European Parliament alongside Ždanoka but failed to win a seat. She is now a regular participant in RSL protests and has had repeated run-ins with police. In 2024, Elena challenged the results of the Liepaja municipal elections, demanding a recount; the court rejected her request.
“Not so fast!”
Another former Ždanoka aide, Anna Bondere, is running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket — alongside former police officer Pagor. She presents herself as a defender of the Russian language and a fighter against neo-Nazism. Bondere regularly attends RSL rallies and is frequently quoted by the propaganda website of the Russkiy Mir Foundation, established by Putin’s decree.
“Do you think the Russian Union of Latvia has ceased to exist? No! Not so fast!” she wrote in a Facebook post.
Bondere graduated from Moscow State Industrial University in 2003. After returning to Riga, she worked in education before joining the RSL. Russian border-crossing data show that Bondere travels to Russia almost every year and has visited the country particularly frequently since the start of the so-called “special military operation.” While in Russia, she stayed at expensive hotels, citing “business” as the purpose of her trips and using a Sberbank card to pay for her expenses.
The Insider sent Bondere questions via social media, but she did not respond.
Among the other pro-Putin candidates running for the Saeima is Aleksejs Rosļikovs, founder of the Stability! party. However, Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against Rosļikovs for inciting ethnic hatred, prompting him to flee to Belarus.
Rosļikovs was previously involved in business, and local journalists have reported that he evaded taxes and repeatedly set up new companies. Whenever one of his companies accumulated debts, he would promptly change its founders. Rosļikovs has served as a member of both the Saeima and Riga City Council, but in 2026 he lost his mandate for repeatedly failing to attend meetings.
While lying low in Belarus, Rosļikovs has been waging an anti-Latvian propaganda campaign, portraying Russian-speaking people as victims of discrimination in the Baltic states. In his statements, the fugitive candidate says that if elected to the Saeima, “Ukraine will not receive another cent.” In April, Rosļikovs also spread a false claim that Latvian schools had purportedly banned students from speaking Russian even during recess.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Ministry has joined the disinformation campaign. Grigory Lukyantsev, director of the ministry’s Department for Multilateral Cooperation in Human Rights, claimed that authorities in the Baltic states were preparing mass deportations of Russian-speaking residents. The “sensation” was picked up by all major pro-government Russian media outlets. Unsurprisingly, the news turned out to be fake.
