Exclusive: Egypt rejects Houthi bid for Red Sea shipping talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:55:23 UTC
20:55:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Egypt rejects Houthi proposal for direct talks over Red Sea navigation
Egypt has rejected a Houthi proposal for direct talks with Egyptian maritime authorities over navigation through the Bab al-Mandab and Red Sea, amid concerns that engaging officially with the group could amount to implicit recognition of its authority.
The proposal was conveyed by Yemen's Houthi movement through the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) in London and sought direct communication with Egyptian officials to coordinate with the Suez Canal Authority and maritime ports, sources told The New Arab.
The request concerned establishing arrangements governing maritime safety and navigation around Bab al-Mandab following Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and their control of strategically important islands and coastal areas overlooking the strait.
A senior Egyptian source told The New Arab that Suez Canal Authority chairman Osama Rabie had categorically rejected official communication with the Houthis.
Rabie would not give "a party that is not internationally recognised an opportunity to obtain implicit recognition merely by responding to its message, even by telephone", the source said.
Egypt recognises Yemen's internationally recognised government and has sought to avoid steps that could formally legitimise Houthi rule over territory under the group's control.
However, Cairo has not ruled out indirect contact with the Houthis as it attempts to protect shipping through the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
The Egyptian authorities instead referred the proposal received by the ICS to security agencies, allowing communications to be handled outside official state institutions, according to the source.
The aim is to secure an end to attacks on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab, restore freedom of navigation and protect crews regardless of nationality, while preventing the Houthis or another actor from establishing recognised authority over the international waterway.
Egyptian sovereign security agencies have already maintained channels with both sides of Yemen's conflict without granting the Houthis official recognition, the source said.
Cairo is particularly concerned that instability around Bab al-Mandab could further damage traffic through the Suez Canal, whose revenues have been severely affected by the Red Sea shipping crisis.
The Houthis had previously approached the London-based shipping body after taking control of Yemeni coastal cities, seeking an international conference on regulating navigation through Bab al-Mandab during their exchange of missile attacks with Israel in 2025, according to a Suez Canal Authority source.
That proposal was rejected because participating states did not recognise the Houthis and because internationally unrecognised political entities cannot participate in setting international maritime rules.
Egyptian officials fear that accepting the Houthis as a party capable of negotiating rules for passage through Bab al-Mandab could establish a new reality in which an internationally unrecognised armed group exercises de facto authority over one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.
Mohamed Shireen al-Naggar, a transport expert and board member of the Alexandria Chamber of Shipping, told The New Arab that Houthi control around the entrance to Bab al-Mandab would not necessarily result in the strait being closed, but could leave shipping exposed to heightened risks even after active warfare ends.
"Shipping companies will not wait for another attack on vessels," he said, explaining that the presence of an armed force on islands and in coastal cities surrounding the strait would itself raise security risks.
This could push shipping companies towards the much longer route around the Cape of Good Hope, increasing fuel consumption as well as shipping and insurance costs.
Despite Houthi assurances that vessels would be allowed through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea, with the exception of Saudi-linked ships, al-Naggar said current conditions posed a serious threat to maritime traffic.
Continued fighting would make companies reluctant to send cargo through the area, particularly highly flammable shipments of oil, gas and petroleum products, he said.
Oil and gas tankers travelling from the Gulf towards Europe and the Mediterranean could consequently face risks at two crucial chokepoints - the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.
Disruption at both would have significant consequences for Red Sea and Suez Canal traffic, while higher fuel, insurance and freight costs would ultimately feed into global transport, industrial and consumer prices.
Al-Naggar said Cairo's contacts through its security agencies with the Houthis and Iran, alongside official communication with Saudi Arabia and the US, were intended to prevent Houthi battlefield control around Bab al-Mandab from becoming a permanent threat to Red Sea navigation.
The risks could become particularly acute during the European winter, when demand for Gulf oil and gas rises.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reiterated Cairo's position during the latest BRICS meetings in New Delhi, saying that "Egypt rejects any attempts to militarise the Red Sea".
Sisi said developments in the Middle East and their impact on global trade, energy and supply chains demonstrated the "close interconnection between security and development", stressing the importance of maintaining the stability and freedom of international navigation.

Ramesh’s remarks came after the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) for all commodities stood at 110.8 in August 2026, with annual wholesale inflation rising to 9.92 per cent year-on-year (YoY), according to official data released by the Ministry of Commerce & Industry.
The figure marked a marginal increase from July 2026, when headline wholesale inflation stood at 9.78 per cent. The all-commodities index also edged up from 110.0 recorded in the previous month.The rise reflected price pressures across major industrial and energy segments. Fuel and power recorded the sharpest increase, with YoY inflation accelerating to 22.93 per cent in August from 20.05 per cent in July.In contrast, inflation in primary articles moderated to 7.76 per cent from 8.52 per cent in the preceding month. Inflation in manufactured products edged up to 8.37 per cent from 8.29 per cent over the same period.

Iran protests as US prevents its nuclear chief attending IAEA meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:51:38 UTC
20:51:38 KST

Iran protests as US prevents its nuclear chief attending IAEA meeting
VIENNA, Sept 14 - The United States blocked Iran's nuclear chief from attending this week's U.N. atomic watchdog meeting in Vienna by opposing an exemption from so-called "snapback" U.N. sanctions, prompting protests from Tehran on Monday.
Iranian nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami had been due to attend and address this week's International Atomic Energy Agency General Conference, an annual meeting of IAEA member states that began on Monday. At the opening, however, Iran said Austria had revoked Eslami's visa after originally granting him one.
"The cancellation and so-called legal justification advanced for it are a stark indication of a political act and advanced formal politicisation of this organisation," Iran's ambassador to the IAEA told the conference.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the United States had pressured Austria into the move, while Iran and Russia said it formed part of a broader effort to prevent Iranian officials from obtaining visas for international travel.
The United States said it had objected to an exemption that would have allowed Eslami to travel despite sanctions reimposed under the so-called "snapback" mechanism at the U.N. Security Council.
Eslami was among those targeted by sanctions lifted under a 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and major powers and the United States. The deal unravelled after President Donald Trump pulled the U.S. out of it in 2018, and Western powers triggered the "snapback" mechanism last year to re-impose those sanctions.
Iran and allies including Russia do not recognise the reimposed sanctions. Austria said it had requested an exemption for Eslami.
"Austria, although being only the host state, submitted a request for an exemption to the travel ban to the Security Council sanctions committee, which was rejected," Ambassador Christian Ebner told the conference.
"As a consequence, Austria was obliged to deny one member of the Iranian delegation the entry into its territory," he said.
U.S. Ambassador Preston Wells Griffith III said his country had objected in New York to an exemption being granted, and that was why the application was denied.
"The United States objected to the exemption request, which per the rules of the U.N. sanctions committee resulted in the U.N. Security Council denying the request," he said.
"His (Eslami's) participation would have only resulted in Iran exploiting IAEA proceedings as a stage for propaganda while sidestepping substantive cooperation, undermining the credibility of the very body charged with verifying its nuclear commitments," he said, referring to a standoff over inspections. Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:50:44 UTC
20:50:44 KST

Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through
Saudi Arabia asked for the meeting to be postponed, but Tehran says it will continue to seek a regionally backed bill.
Tehran, Iran – Another attempt to clinch a deal between Iran and Oman to restore some traffic to the Strait of Hormuz has been set back by a lack of regional consensus on the future of the waterway.
Officials from Iran, Iraq and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations – minus objecting Bahrain – were scheduled to meet in Oman’s port city of Salalah on Monday to confer on new temporary routes in the Strait of Hormuz amid Tehran’s ongoing hot-and-cold war with the United States.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Red Sea nations watch as Houthis seize Bab al-Mandeb strait
- list 2 of 4Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 3 of 4Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
- list 4 of 4Yemen forces advance in Taiz; Houthis take key islands, attack Saudi Arabia
On Sunday night, the region’s officials announced the postponement of the meeting, without giving a new date. None of the stakeholders gave any indication that the postponement was directly linked to recent Houthi and Iraqi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia.
However, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Saudi objection was the reason for the postponement, without providing further details.
US media outlets Axios and CNN reported that Saudi Arabia had submitted amendments to the Iran-Oman proposal for Hormuz because it had concerns that the wording would establish a new status quo which would be unacceptable to Riyadh.
It comes days after Saudi Arabia shut down its critical East-West oil pipeline – the kingdom’s key route for energy exports – after drone attacks in the area originating from Iraq. US President Donald Trump said these attacks were likely conducted at Tehran’s behest.
Saudi Arabia has also faced repeated attacks by the Houthis, who took control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast over the weekend.
Hours after the Salalah meeting was postponed, the Saudi civil defence issued alerts for Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran in southern and western parts of the kingdom. The Houthis claimed to have fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military facilities in Khamis Mushait, in retaliation for air strikes across Yemen, which it blames on Saudi Arabia.
What comes next?
Iran has said it will engage with the US on the future of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war only if there are tangible moves to lift Washington’s naval blockade on the country and return to the June memorandum of understanding.
With continued disruptions to the passage of vessels through the strait, Iran has signalled that it intends to continue pursuing the bilateral agreement with Oman over Hormuz, which it said was finalised last month.
“In consultation with Oman, in the next step, we will make a decision on how to announce or register the agreement,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters during a weekly news conference on Monday.
When the two countries initially advanced the bilateral deal, Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of US talks with Iran.
Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Tehran wants to use its leverage over Hormuz for regional legitimacy – and ultimately to pressure the US.
“The broader the regional buy-in, the harder it becomes for the US to dismiss the arrangement as an Iranian diktat,” he told Al Jazeera.
GCC states, suffering from a sharp decrease in energy receipts, want ships moving and their economies insulated from a war they neither started nor can end. But Vaez said Washington is unlikely to lift the blockade on Iran even if the region blesses the arrangement between Muscat and Tehran.
“[The US] will find it much harder to sustain a policy that its own partners increasingly see as perpetuating the crisis,” Vaez said
Temporary entry and exit
The Omani-Iranian planned agreement envisions temporary entry and exit routes for commercial vessels in the strait, with Tehran repeatedly stating that this would not mean that the Strait of Hormuz has reopened.
Iran and Oman are the only two countries with territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. The proposed inbound corridor reportedly goes through Iranian waters, while the outbound corridor mostly passes through Omani waters, with small parts still in Iranian territory.
During Monday’s scheduled meeting, Iran and Oman were supposed to share precise maps and discuss the details of the routes with GCC members Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait, and Iraq, which is outside the bloc. The deal could reportedly include voluntary tolls to fund navigation, environmental protection and search-and-rescue operations.
Bahrain, which has borne the brunt of Iranian attacks since the US-Israel war on Iran started at the end of February, said it would not participate in the forum since it would amount to “appeasement”. The Tasnim news outlet, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), claimed Israel pushed Bahrain to refuse participation.
How does Yemen fit in this picture?
The latest diplomatic movement comes after days of explosive developments in Yemen, when the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, essentially took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea after a lightning offensive against government forces.
Thomas Juneau, assistant professor in the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa, said the Houthi advances represent a significant gain for Iran. Its Yemeni allies’ position in the Red Sea offers Iran an important new bargaining chip in future negotiations with the US.
“The Houthis are not a simple arm of Iranian foreign policy. They operate largely based on their own interests, and do not take and execute Iranian commands,” he told Al Jazeera. “But Houthi and Iranian interests are largely, if not always fully, aligned. They cooperate closely on the basis of those shared interests.”
Juneau sees the ability for Iran and the Houthis to potentially partially block traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb – two of the world’s most crucial maritime bottlenecks – would give them tremendous influence over the global economy, and thus the US.
The Houthis are trying to seize the opportunity to “institutionalise the de facto reality of their veto on maritime traffic” in the southern Red Sea and replicate partial Iranian success in doing the same in the Strait of Hormuz, Juneau said.
Iran has stressed that their allies’ gains in the Red Sea cannot be separated from the Saudi-led blockade and attacks on Houthi areas in Yemen since 2015.
“We know very well that continued war between Islamic countries in the region only has one winner, and that winner is no one but the Zionist regime, which is after persisting tensions and conflict in our region and between Islamic countries,” Iranian spokesperson Baghaei said.

The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.
Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.
The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”
Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.
The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to the rail operator.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.
He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.

Ukraine’s FLYCAT strike drone is built to fly without satellite signals. Its bigger new sibling is designed to reach 200 km behind the front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:45:14 UTC
20:45:14 KST

A Ukrainian company has unveiled a homegrown strike drone built to fly deep behind Russian lines, Militarnyi reported on 13 September. Octava Defence showed the new long-range aircraft—a bigger version of a drone already used in combat—at the MSPO 2026 defense expo in Kielce, Poland. The company says the smaller drone is built to keep working in electronic warfare conditions without a reliable satellite signal.
Russian jamming is one of the biggest obstacles to Ukrainian strikes deep in the rear, which is why Ukrainian makers keep building guidance that does not depend on satellite signals.
The workhorse is already in the fight
The base FLYCAT, presented in January 2026 by another Ukrainian firm, Venator Technologies, is a strike drone Ukrainian forces have used in combat since March. An improved model went into action in July and August and is now undergoing codification—entry into Ukraine's official weapons register.
Watch first naval battle in history fought entirely by drones: Ukrainian uncrewed boat spots, fires on, and sinks Russian one in Black Sea
The company says the updated drone can fly more than 80 km, stay in the air for an hour, and carry a warhead weighing up to 3.7 kg. It is built to hunt armored vehicles, artillery, radars, and air-defense systems, as well as lighter shelters and communications gear. It can pair with a scout drone that finds the target and passes the coordinates. Several FLYCATs can also strike a single target together or hit multiple targets at once.
Nearly everything on it is built in Ukraine—the communications, navigation, guidance, and warhead. Only the engines come from abroad. Its two cameras—day-only or day-and-night—feed a terminal-guidance module that picks out the target from 2,000 m as it closes in.
The one that reaches deeper
The FLYCAT SL is a bigger, longer-range version, and it is still in testing. The company says it is built to fly more than 200 km, stay airborne for over two and a half hours, and carry a heavier load of up to 7 kg.
That range is meant to let it go after command posts, armored vehicles, artillery, and air defenses far behind the front line.

How Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces assign combat roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

How Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces assign combat roles
Major Volodymyr Baiduzhyi, head of the training and laboratory support group at the 199th Training Center of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Age and physical capabilities matter when selecting a military specialty, while the instructors’ approach varies significantly depending on the stage of training,” Baiduzhyi said.
According to him, during basic military training, instructors try to adapt the workload to individual recruits so that everyone acquires the necessary minimum of skills or reaches the maximum of what they are capable of.
“Specialized training requires a completely different approach. Age, physical capabilities and previous civilian experience become critically important. For example, a 50-year-old welder is unlikely to become an effective UAV operator, as learning new technological skills becomes more difficult with age. Such a person is also no longer suited for reconnaissance, where endurance and physical fitness play the primary role,” the officer added.
Baiduzhyi noted that the main goal of basic military training is to turn recruits into versatile infantry soldiers who are proficient in basic weapons and can operate alongside the military equipment used by the Air Assault Forces.
“We have all the main types of both crew-served and small arms used by the Air Assault Forces. We train service members to operate both Soviet-era equipment and modern equipment made in Ukraine and abroad. They learn to operate ground equipment and how to properly deploy from it,” the officer explained.
According to Baiduzhyi, basic weapons include an assault rifle, either an AK-74 (the 1974 Kalashnikov assault rifle – ed.) or a foreign-made rifle. Recruits train with various types of weapons, but each has a primary weapon that they study more intensively and may later receive in their combat brigade.
Everyone also learns to use grenade launchers, including single-use launchers, Carl Gustaf and RPG-7 systems, as well as machine guns. A recruit may not become a grenade launcher operator or machine gunner, but they must understand what these weapons are and how to use them, the officer noted.
Baiduzhyi added that recruits also have the opportunity to train on FPV drone simulators and operate various unmanned systems. This does not mean everyone will become a UAV operator, but they should understand how these systems work.
“After completing specialized training, a service member will consolidate the skills they have acquired and become well versed in the type of weaponry they will subsequently operate on a permanent basis,” the officer concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Armed Forces of Ukraine currently have the greatest need for service members aged 23–45.

Brainwash: Anatomy of a Dutch language course
Ready to start speaking Dutch? The Dutch Brainwash school, which sponsored this piece, invited DutchNews’ Lauren Comiteau to visit a class.
On the sweltering August day I visit Albert Both’s Brainwash class on the Keizersgracht in the heart of the Jordaan, you can hear the laughter before you even enter the room.
During this last class of Both’s current one-week intensive Dutch language course, eight students – Both’s maximum per course – sit around a huge white table that takes up most of the room. Amidst the organised chaos are stuffed animals, books and games, all props to help the students learn Dutch, or as Albert says, “they’re part of the story to get people talking”.
Armed with fans, water bottles and notebooks full of the handouts they’ve been given throughout the week, all eyes are on Both, who is working a whiteboard via his computer and talking about the past tense.
“It’s the first thing people teach you when you’re learning Dutch,” says Both, “but it’s like giving cauliflower to a baby. The past tense is akin to opening Pandora’s box. If I show it too soon, it will be pure quicksand.”
Instead, after a week of talking and learning, Both gets to the past tense, telling his students the secret to faking it until they make it.
“The trick is you can use the present tense to talk about the past,” he says. You do that, he continues, by saying one sentence in the past tense, pausing, and then continuing in the present tense. “If you do it with elegance and grace, no one knows you’re cheating. I’ve been doing it for a very long time.”
Informal, fun and funny
“I’ve done six different types of courses trying to learn Dutch,” says American independent researcher Lauren Vargas (45), who currently lives in Leiden. “This is the first one where I’ve learned more in seven days than I have in six years.”
She chalks that up to Albert’s teaching style, a far cry, she says, from her other classes where teachers focused too much on structure without theory and application. “Here, you build up to better understand the mechanics, and we’re encouraged to be playful with the language, to make mistakes, to accept that we can actually speak more and understand more than we think we do.”
They can do that because of the informal atmosphere Albert has honed over the years. “We sit around a table like a group of friends,” he says. “My students inspire each other to learn. We create a safe and fun atmosphere, as compared to their past traumatic experiences learning Dutch, which were often impersonal and had students sitting there like they were in a factory.”
The casual conversations – which focus on anything the students want, including the sex toy a sex worker once brought in or a headlining murder investigation that led to a murder-themed discussion – uniquely bind the students. The stuffed Jesus toy is to stimulate conversations about religion.
“That really helped break the ice and get us more comfortable with each other,” says student Jamie Tipelto. “Then we’re able to be more open and freer about speaking and making mistakes. It’s a safe space.”
Fellow student Jesse Corcoran (47), an American researcher at UMC Utecht, who’s lived in the Netherlands for only four months, ditched her more structured and academic Dutch class and followed her husband into Albert’s Brainwash.
“My old class always filled me with anxiety because there wasn’t a lot of ice-breaking, and I wasn’t really comfortable with the people that I was in class with,” she says. “Here, from the first day, the ice is broken, and then you’re more comfortable making mistakes and trying new things.”
“It’s definitely given me more confidence to speak to my neighbours. And that’s a big thing for my husband and I because we want to integrate and become part of the culture. So getting that courage and that confidence to speak to Dutch people is paramount.”
65,000 mistakes
Even for those who have been in the Netherlands longer, like Romanian product manager Sudi (46), who has lived here for 15 years, Albert’s class was a gamechanger.
“I’d taken inburgering classes before, but they created a fear in me of making mistakes,” she says. “Coming to this course made a big difference, because we signed a contract to make 65,000 mistakes. I think I’ve made 30,000, so I still have 30,000 to go!”
Sudi had been following Albert on social media and related to his postings that seemed to echo her situation – getting over the speaking-Dutch hump.
“Now, in the process of making my mistake quota, I’m more confident speaking Dutch and being part of the community. It was a great choice.”
For American Shemby Nagel, who took the course with her friend Lauren Vargas, Albert’s class gave her an unexpected energy boost. “With every language course I’ve tried to take in the past, after about an hour or two, your energy level just goes down. You tank and you’re just dreading coming in the next day. You don’t have time or energy for homework,” she says.
“This is the very first language class – or any class – I’ve taken where my energy level has just gone up and up and up. So by the time I finish, Lauren and I travel back to Leiden and continually work on what we learned in class. And when I get home, I’ll have conversations with my partner and my daughter in Dutch, which I never would have done before.”
Ongelooflijk!
“We have an amazing time together,” says Sandra from Mexico, a procurement manager who has lived in the Netherlands for 10 years.
Albert is legendary among those looking to learn Dutch, and she liked the reviews that talked about his jokes and non-traditional way of teaching. She made the daily commute from Rotterdam, “feeling so happy to be here and excited that he broke through my fear of speaking”.
At the same time, she says his class “opened her ears” to listening to Dutch on the streets, something she had previously avoided because she didn’t understand the language. “That’s how I found my new favourite word: ongelooflijk (unbelievable)!”
Only the beginning
As class winds down, Albert reminds his students one last time to keep on talking. “You can do more than you think,” he tells them. “You must! At some point, you must just say it, even if you think it’s wrong. That’s the reality.”
One by one, the students go around the table saying, “Ik spreek Nederlands,” or “I speak Dutch”.
Albert hands them their diplomas, and then they gather their belongings and head out to a local café for a well-earned drink.
“Het is niet het einde, maar het begin,” he tells them. “It is not the end, but the beginning.”
For anyone looking for a Dutch refresher class, struggling with stalled motivation or wanting to start truly speaking Dutch, Both’s class has proven invaluable. You can sign up here for the next Dutch Brainwash!

Melike Pala
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
The European Commission said on Monday that it supports innovation and the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) services in Europe but stressed that companies must comply fully with the bloc's safety and security rules.
"We are for innovation in Europe. We welcome AI services in Europe, as long, of course, this is done fully in line with the AI Act and the safeguards that we have put in place," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters at a midday briefing in Brussels.
"We are all in favor of having innovative and the latest models in the European Union, but we are not compromising on our security standards," he added.
Regnier was responding to a question about a proposal by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling on AI companies to slow the pace of frontier AI development amid growing concerns about the ability to control increasingly advanced systems.
He said the EU was "definitely playing a role" in AI development and described the bloc as a "front runner" in putting safeguards in place for the development and deployment of artificial intelligence.
Regnier said the EU's AI Act is fully enforced and that authorities have already sent their first requests for information as part of efforts to ensure compliance.
Asked whether Anthropic had engaged with the commission over its proposal to pace frontier AI development, Regnier said he was not aware of any such engagement and stressed that the commission would not enter into bilateral discussions of that nature.
AI development concerns came to the fore following a statement by Amodei urging AI firms to slow down the pace of model development amid growing concerns over controlling AI systems.
Billionaire Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed support for Amodei on their social media accounts.

Estonia's Robert Virves inches closer to WRC2 2026 drivers' title

Estonia's Robert Virves inches closer to WRC2 2026 drivers' title
Robert Virves has secured the World Rally Championship WRC2 Challenger title after finishing second at the weekend's Rally Chile.
The result also moved Virves, 26, and co-driver Jakko Viilo one step closer in the Škoda to bagging the full WRC2 drivers' title for 2026.
The Challenger title is a subcategory of WRC2 for those rally drivers who have not previously won a world championship title in the second-tier category.
The Estonian is on course to win his first full WRC2 title in any case, with 117 points and two races to go: He would need to drop out of both races while Finland's Teemu Suninen would have to win both of them, for the title not to go to Virves.
Virves has won four Rally2 WRC races this year, in Kenya, and Greece, along with his home rally in Estonia, and the following round in neighboring Finland.
In Chile, the Estonia duo started Sunday firmly in second place and won the final two of the four stages, a bit under a minute behind Frenchman Yohan Rossel (Lancia), who took first place and ahead of the third-placer, Briton Gus Greensmith (Toyota).
Virves is eligible to score points in one more round of the two remaining, in Sardinia (October 1-4) and in the season closing Saudi Arabian race (November 11.14).
A positive result would be the first WRC title for an Estonian driver since Ott Tänak and co-driver Martin Järveoja in the Toyota Yaris won the senior WRC titles in 2019, the first Estonians to do so.
The WRC title for this year is still wide open with Welshman Elfyn Evans chasing his maiden title on 230 points, with Toyota teammates Sami Pajari (Finland, 213 points) and winner in Chile Oliver Solberg (Sweden/Norway, 209 points) snapping at his heels and both after their own senior titles too.

ICE arrests keep soaring. Here’s why they are not leading to more deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:41:42 UTC
20:41:42 KST

ICE arrests keep soaring. Here’s why they are not leading to more deportations
Sept 14 - Immigration arrests in the U.S. have soared in recent months, aided by more local law enforcement cooperation with ICE, increased use of technology to track and process people, as well as enhanced data sharing between federal agencies.
But the mass arrest campaign this summer did not lead to a commensurate increase in deportations -- according to preliminary U.S. government data reviewed by Reuters -- a reflection of the legal and logistical limits faced by President Donald Trump as he attempts to hit his mass deportation goals.
Even as arrests jumped to nearly 51,000 in August, setting a record for a third straight month, deportation numbers held mostly steady, averaging around 1,200 per day, the preliminary government data showed.
About the same number of people were deported per day in May, for example, when there were around 19,000 fewer arrests, according to arrests data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a public records request and analyzed by Reuters.
The disconnect is partly due to who is being targeted, five current and former officials said. The arrests include a growing number of people with no criminal conviction or charge and without deportation orders, according to the Deportation Data Project figures.
Many of those picked up had pending asylum or other legal claims – meaning they could not be immediately removed from the country unless they agreed to waive their rights and voluntarily depart.
A lack of available flights and limits set by receiving countries have also capped Trump’s deportation ambitions, former officials said.
"This is a false narrative," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in response to questions from Reuters. "Thanks to President Trump’s strong immigration enforcement policies, three million illegals have left the United States.”
A WIDENING DRAGNET
The nationwide crackdown in recent months was not as high profile as past operations in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, but it was more widespread.
"ICE Officers are herewith ordered ... to do all in their power to achieve the very important goal of delivering the single largest Mass Deportation Program in History," Trump declared on Truth Social in June.
Current and former officials said immigration officers are under growing pressure from the White House to hit a goal of 3,000 arrests per day.
"There are no quotas for arrests," DHS said in a statement to Reuters.
Throughout the summer, ICE agents partnered with local police to conduct traffic stops and picked up people at homes and job sites. Others were detained at immigration courts or routine immigration appointments.
The administration continues to assert it is focused on the “worst of the worst,” but people with criminal convictions accounted for less than a quarter of arrests in July, the Deportation Data Project figures show. That figure was nearly 60% in December 2024, the month before Trump took office for a second time.
Among the easiest people to find are those who have shared their personal information with the U.S. government, hoping to achieve legal status. These include immigrants being sponsored for green cards by U.S. citizen family members, those with asylum claims – and the more than a million people who have had their temporary legal status revoked during Trump’s second term.
But those people often have active cases to stay in the United States, which can make it more difficult to quickly deport them.
Many also “have long roots in the United States and may be more likely to be able to quickly find a lawyer through their U.S. family members and may be more aware of their rights,” said Julia Gelatt, an associate director at the Migration Policy Institute think tank.
At airports, following tips shared by the Transportation Security Administration, ICE has targeted people who had previously overstayed visas, even if they subsequently applied for asylum or married a U.S. citizen and had a path to legal status. More than 1,200 people were arrested by ICE following tips from TSA through early June, according to internal government data shared with Reuters.
Dolores Mendoza, 62, and Roberto Avalos, 64, were detained last week at an airport in Birmingham, Alabama, after returning from a trip to California to visit family. The couple entered the country on tourist visas in 2015, and stayed and adopted their three U.S. citizen grandchildren after their daughter died of breast cancer.
Neither has a criminal record. Both obtained work authorization and have pending petitions for permanent U.S. residence through their eldest grandchild, Marvin, who is now 22 and able to sponsor them.
Marvin said his younger brothers, ages 15 and 16, are struggling with their grandparents gone.
The youngest “hasn’t come out of his room often,” Marvin said. His other brother is “more angry than anything.”The couple's lawyer has filed a case in federal court contesting the detention as unlawful.
NOT ENOUGH PLANES
Some who can't afford a lawyer have languished in detention.
Yajaira Moran, 50, has been held for the past five months despite having a pending claim for a crime victim visa as a survivor of domestic violence.
In early September, she gave up and asked to go back to her home country of Nicaragua. She remains in detention as she waits to be deported.
Even when people are eligible for deportation, the logistics are complex, requiring coordination with receiving countries and transfers around a vast network of detention centers.
“Getting people on planes is really hard, and the actual number of available planes has historically been a choke point,” said Blas Nuñez-Neto, a former Biden administration official.
While the Trump administration signed a deal last year to purchase six Boeing 737 planes for deportations, those planes are still undergoing FAA checks and are not yet in use, according to a person briefed on the matter.
Planes in the existing fleet often depart without being at capacity, due to logistical, legal and diplomatic issues, former officials said, or because the receiving country has limited the number of people it can accept.
Recent deportation flights to the Haitian coastal city of Cap Haitien have carried as few as 57 people, according to the Human Rights First advocacy group. REUTERS

Ban defectors from public office: CJP backs Kapil Sibal's anti-defection proposal
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Monday endorsed senior advocate and Rajya Sabha member Kapil Sibal's proposal to bar MPs and MLAs who defect from their political parties from holding public office. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke described the proposal as the "need of the hour".Sibal, speaking at a talk titled 'Horse Trade and Democracy' in Kerala's Kochi, called for amendments to the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution to prevent party mergers from becoming "loopholes for mass walkouts".Under the existing law, legislators who defect are protected from disqualification if at least two-thirds of the members of their legislative party cross over to another party, with the move being treated as a merger.
Sibal called for changes to the Tenth Schedule to close this "loophole" and ensure that "a merger is a merger of political parties and not a collective walkout by legislators".CJP co-convener Saurav Das backed Sibal's proposal, saying it was in line with the forum's first demand charter."Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal's proposal to ban any MP and MLA who gets elected on Party X's symbol and later defects to Party Y for money or under pressure should be welcomed.
He calls for a 10-year ban," he said.Das said point 5 of CJP's first demand charter, released by Dipke, proposed an even stricter provision: barring defectors from holding any public office or contesting elections for 20 years."Breaking political parties, bribing MPs with 50-100 crore, toppling governments is a fraud committed on the country. Such fraud should never happen. The Anti-Defection law is outdated. The ruling party has ensured its misuse in its lust for eternal power. The young will change this," he said.Dipke reiterated the demand, calling it the "need of the hour". In a post on X, he said, "Any elected representative who switches parties after being elected should be barred from holding public office."The call for changes to the anti-defection law comes amid the ongoing political developments within the Trinamool Congress in the Lok Sabha and West Bengal Assembly.In the Lok Sabha, 20 of the TMC's 28 MPs have announced that they are leaving the party to form a separate Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), while extending support to the BJP-led NDA.The move has brought renewed attention to the anti-defection law and its two-thirds merger provision.In West Bengal, the faction led by Ritabrata Banerjee has sought recognition as the TMC and staked claim to the party's name, organisational control, assets and election symbol. The faction has also claimed the support of a majority of the party's newly elected MLAs.The Election Commission has begun examining the competing claims of the Ritabrata and Mamata Banerjee factions.The developments have focused attention on the Tenth Schedule provision that protects legislators from disqualification when two-thirds of a legislature party is deemed to have merged with another political party.
The TMC developments come after seven Aam Aadmi Party Rajya Sabha members joined the BJP earlier this year, with the group also invoking the two-thirds merger provision.The issue has also featured prominently in earlier splits involving the Shiv Sena and the Nationalist Congress Party in Maharashtra.In 2022, Eknath Shinde led a majority of Shiv Sena MLAs away from Uddhav Thackeray, triggering a change of government. In 2023, Ajit Pawar split the NCP and joined the BJP-led government along with a group of party legislators.

EU halves cheap parcel influx in bid to rein in Chinese e-commerce giants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:40:36 UTC
20:40:36 KST

The EU has cut the number of low-value parcels entering the region by half, following the introduction of a €3 flat fee. The measure is part of a broader effort to curb the growing dominance of Chinese e-commerce platforms.
The number of small parcels valued below €150 arriving in Europe has fallen by nearly 50% since 1 July following the EU’s introduction of a €3 flat tax on such shipments, according to data from Dutch and Belgian customs.
In Belgium, the number of small parcels have decreased by 53% compared to the previous year, according to data from the Belgian authorities. Dutch customs present similar data, finding that e-commerce parcels, particularly from China, decreased by 46%. Together, the two countries make up almost 50% of the total low value parcels arriving from outside the EU.
However, the Dutch customs said that the decrease might represent a change in the working methods due to the levy.
"More and more companies appear to be opting for bulk import and storage within the EU to resell their goods to consumers from there," they said in a press statement in early September, specifying that they will investigate the matter further.
The temporary levy was introduced after policymakers noted the overwhelming dominance of Chinese e-commerce in Europe, which has led to an influx of billions of low-value parcels into the single market.
According to European Commission data, some €4.6 billion low-value items under €150 were imported to the EU in 2024, representing an average of 12 million parcels per day. That was a major increase from the €2.3 billion that entered in 2023 and €1.4 billion in 2022.
The sheer volume of packages and the fragmentation of the current European customs structure make it harder for the EU to have an adequate monitoring system.
Checks would prevent the entrance of illegal products, which already represents a major problem in Europe. A 2025 peer-reviewed laboratory study published in Contact Dermatitis analysed 111 clothing items across Italy and the EU, and found that 63% contained carcinogenic, endocrine-disrupting, or sensitising chemicals.
Similar findings have been released by Greenpeace and the European Consumer Organisation.
"The temporary €3 import duty that has been in force since July 1 has already significantly reduced the flow of parcels, but we are not there yet," Dutch MEP Dirk Gotink, responsible for the custom reform on behalf of the European Parliament, told Euronews.
"With the new law, the EU and national customs authorities will finally receive the tools to effectively protect businesses and consumers. European customs work will also be modernised, with a single central data hub, a European Customs Authority in Lille, more risk-based checks, and closer cooperation between authorities," the MEP said.
Gotink was referring to the overall custom reform the EU is about to implement, which aims at facilitating the tracking of items arriving from outside the EU.
As part of the reform, the EU will set up a data hub in the French city of Lille, where custom data are expected to be gathered and analysed. The new tax authority is expected to be operational by 2028.

Finland joins France's nuclear deterrence initiative
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:39:31 CST
20:39:31 KST

HELSINKI, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Finland has decided to join France's nuclear deterrence initiative, Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen announced on Monday, describing the initiative as "significant for security in Europe."
"This is a natural step, as our close allies Norway, Sweden and Denmark have already joined the initiative," he said in a statement.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb reaffirmed on Monday that Finland does not intend to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime.
"The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe's responsibility for its own defense and helps prevent escalation," Stubb said on social media platform X.
He stressed that the French initiative does not replace or overlap with NATO's nuclear deterrence, adding that Finland's foremost priority is to act as part of NATO and the European Union.
French President Emmanuel Macron unveiled the "forward deterrence" initiative in March, opening closer cooperation with European partners on France's nuclear deterrence. Germany, Britain, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Sweden and Denmark initially joined the initiative. Norway joined later, and Finland's participation brings the total number of participating countries, including France, to 11.
Under the initiative, participating countries may take part in deterrence exercises, while conventional forces may also participate in French nuclear activities. France has also raised the possibility of temporarily deploying elements of its strategic air forces to allied countries.
Finland and France are also due to sign a strategic partnership document in Helsinki on Monday. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot is visiting Helsinki after attending a meeting of European leaders in Rovaniemi, northern Finland, hosted by Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo.
According to the Finnish Foreign Ministry, the Finland-France partnership covers security and defense, energy, climate and environmental issues, science, innovation and technology, and bilateral trade and investment. ■

China's yuan loans increase by 10.44 trln yuan in Jan.-Aug. period
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:39:01 CST
20:39:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.44 trillion yuan (about 1.54 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, central bank data showed on Monday.
At the end of August, outstanding yuan loans stood at 282.35 trillion yuan, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China.
M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, had increased by 7.5 percent year on year to 356.81 trillion yuan by the end of last month.
M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 115.77 trillion yuan at the end of August, a rise of 4.1 percent from a year earlier.
China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 464.8 trillion yuan at the end of August, up 7.2 percent year on year, the central bank noted.
"At present, China's aggregate financial volume is growing at a reasonable pace, and social financing conditions have remained relatively loose," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management.
The central bank said in its latest monetary policy report that it will continue to implement a moderately loose monetary policy in the second half of 2026, strengthen counter-cyclical adjustment, and take solid steps to promote sustained and improved economic development.
It will also maintain ample liquidity, guide financial institutions to enhance the balance of credit supply, and align the growth of social financing and money supply with expected targets for economic growth and overall price levels.
Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said that looking ahead, the country's monetary policy will strengthen coordination with fiscal and industrial policies and step up counter-cyclical adjustment.
Structural monetary policy tools are expected to see further price cuts, increased quotas and expanded coverage, to boost financing support for tech companies and private enterprises, facilitate the shift to new growth drivers, and stabilize overall employment, Wang said. ■

Economic Watch: China's services trade fair emerges as institutional platform for open, innovative cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:38:58 CST
20:38:58 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) is turning China's market momentum into shared global opportunities, mirroring a broader trend of Chinese trade fairs becoming dynamic platforms for global innovation and open trade.
Held annually in Beijing, this year's CIFTIS concluded on Sunday with more than 1,200 outcomes achieved, facilitating resource matching, exchanges and cooperation, according to Lu Huiling, deputy head and spokesperson of the Beijing municipal commerce bureau.
"China's opening-up in the services sector provides vital certainty to global trade in services," said Yang Zhengwei, vice president of the Development Research Center of the State Council, who attended the fair.
CATALYST FOR CROSS-BORDER SYNERGY
As one of the world's largest platforms for trade in services, CIFTIS serves as a key institutional platform for China's opening-up and a crucial window for the world to see opportunities in China's increasingly open services sector.
This year's CIFTIS, its 13th edition, attracted participants from 90 countries, regions and international organizations, with more than 1,800 enterprises displaying their industry solutions.
"For Norwegian companies, the Chinese market holds many opportunities," said Henning Kristoffersen, commercial counsellor at the Norwegian Embassy in China. Norway, the guest country of honor for 2026 CIFTIS, utilized its 260-square-meter pavilion to move beyond traditional exports, exploring deep cooperation with China in emerging fields such as green maritime transition, marine nutrition and digital technologies.
Kristoffersen said the fair provides an essential platform for Norwegian firms to assess market demand, match with Chinese partners and establish long-term strategic collaborations in these specialized sectors. While Norway's land-based aquaculture, recirculating aquaculture systems and other technologies in its fisheries are attracting increasing attention from China, China's emerging technologies and services in AI and robotics are drawing in Norwegian businesses.
At the fair, Klaus Hoseth, CEO of a Norwegian aquaculture tech company, showcased a highly-automated salmon processing line. Noting that manual feeding remains labor-intensive during peak volumes, Hoseth saw a solution in China. "Chinese robotics might come in handy," he said, having visited a Beijing-based start-up specializing in both hardware and software for embodied AI robots ahead of the fair.
Beyond technology, CIFTIS is catalyzing a broader form of cross-border synergy -- one driven by China's expanding market access in telecom, allowing global network resources and AI services to better meet local enterprise demands.
As one of the first batch of Hong Kong-invested enterprises in China's pilot program for expanding the opening-up of value-added telecommunications services, Hong Kong Telecommunications (HKT) positioned itself as an "international connector" at the exhibition, with a focus on showcasing its AI product operations and global network resource services.
Mak Chi-fai, general manager of the China Business of the Commercial Customer Business of HKT, said the company is bringing its seasoned international telecommunications operations and AI service experience into the Chinese mainland to empower enterprises to achieve intelligent and efficient operations.
BRIDGE FOR GLOBAL INNOVATION
Beyond showcasing China's open market, CIFTIS serves as a powerful catalyst for collaborative global innovation. This role is reflected by initiatives like the China-Europe Innovation Industrial Park, launched at this year's fair to directly translate conceptual agreements into long-term cross-border projects between European and Chinese enterprises.
Huzur Devletsah, U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly's vice president and China general manager, highlighted the country's pivotal role in the company's global strategy. Leveraging China's policy incentives and research strengths, Lilly is accelerating the rollout of an integrated chain covering R&D, manufacturing and commercialization, deeply integrating into China's pharmaceutical innovation ecosystem.
"Looking ahead, Lilly will continue to use CIFTIS as a bridge to unite industry, academia, and research partners, accelerate the commercialization of cutting-edge global innovations in China, and support the Healthy China 2030 initiative," Devletsah said.
The collaborative innovation is supported by an increasingly enabling regulatory environment. Wu Xuchu, vice chairman of KPMG China, noted that institutional opening-up in areas like cross-border data flows has turned China into a vital "innovation testing ground" for global services firms.
"This provides an opportunity both for Chinese professional firms to grow alongside businesses and for global counterparts to participate in China's development," Wu said.
Reinforcing this commitment to high-standard innovation frameworks, the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) served as a co-host of the Global Trade in Services Summit at the 2026 CIFTIS for the first time, addressing IP protection -- a core compliance priority for multinationals establishing local R&D centers.
Trade data tells the same story about cross-border innovation. The Ministry of Commerce said that in 2025, China's total trade in knowledge-intensive services grew by 6.6 percent. In the first seven months of 2026, knowledge-intensive services accounted for 53.5 percent of China's total services exports, up 3 percentage points compared to last year.
PLATFORM FOR SHARING CHINESE SOLUTIONS
CIFTIS also acts as a platform promoting China's global service practices, which are transferable, replicable and open to cooperation. Even after the physical exhibition halls of CIFTIS close, its global impact continues.
A dedicated exhibition area for Chinese service cases was set up for the first time at the core of the thematic exhibition, offering a window into the development of China's services.
One example is PowerChina's work on the Kananga-Kalamba Mbuji road project in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the company integrated infrastructure delivery with human capital development, training nearly 700 local workers and facilitating technology transfer to foster enduring local capabilities.
Fintech cooperation is another area highlighted at CIFTIS. China's strengths in digital services are playing a key role in helping developing nations bridge the digital divide. By sharing digital capabilities and infrastructure, China is helping to make financial services more accessible and inclusive across emerging economies.
"Trade in services is increasingly becoming trade in knowledge," said Benjamin Hung, President of International at Standard Chartered. He added that China's sharing of expertise in fintech, AI, payment systems and digital platforms can significantly empower innovation across the Global South and throughout the broader global economy.
Alongside CIFTIS, other Chinese trade fairs serve as institutional mechanisms to promote trade and advance multilateralism, amid mounting global trade uncertainties.
The recently concluded China International Fair for Investment and Trade in Xiamen facilitated two-way investment. The Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou next week is poised to set new benchmarks for digital commerce, while the China International Import Expo in November, the world's first national-level import-themed expo, is expected to further turn China's vast market into a shared market for the world.
Together, these fairs form a broader network of Chinese trade expositions that bridges economies and champions open cooperation. Within this network, CIFTIS is being seen as driving proven service models into long-term cross-border collaboration, extending its impact beyond each exhibition.
"CIFTIS will increasingly move beyond being simply an exhibition and become a marketplace for ideas, technology, investment and international partnerships," said Simphiwe Madikizela, professor of economics at the University of South Africa. ■

German investment in China rises by a third in H1: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:38:44 CST
20:38:44 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- German companies increased their investment in China by around a third in the first half of 2026, while investment in the United States plunged 65 percent, according to analyses by the German Economic Institute (IW).
German companies' direct investment in China increased by around 5.6 billion euros (6.5 billion U.S. dollars) in the first six months of the year, about a third more compared with the same period last year, IW said in a report on Monday, citing data from the German central bank.
The report found that German companies' reinvested profits amounted to 7.8 billion euros (9 billion dollars) in 2025, during which year the companies, according to IW's earlier analysis, invested around 7 billion euros (8.1 billion dollars) in China.
Over the longer term, German investment in China has remained broadly stable at a relatively high level, with the average half-year figure between 2020 and 2025 also standing at around 5.6 billion euros, the report showed.
Most German companies remain committed to the Chinese market, said Juergen Matthes, an IW expert and author of the report.
More than 85 percent of German companies operating in China plan to maintain or expand their current level of engagement, while more than half intend to increase investment, Matthes said, citing a survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China.
"China is an important sales market (for German companies), and some use it as a 'fitness center,'" Matthes said. Companies that can maintain their position in the Chinese market are also more likely to succeed globally, he added.
German investment in the United States, meanwhile, moved sharply in the opposite direction.
A separate IW analysis showed that German companies invested around 4.3 billion euros (4.96 billion U.S. dollars) in the United States in the first half of 2026, down 65 percent from a year earlier and nearly 80 percent from the first half of 2024, the final such period before U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House.
Heightened economic policy uncertainty in the United States was holding back German companies' new investment decisions, IW noted. ■

Finland enters French-led European nuclear deterrence initiative
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:36:04 EEST
20:36:04 KST

Finland has joined France’s European nuclear deterrence initiative, expanding defence cooperation with Paris while ruling out the stationing of nuclear weapons on Finnish territory in peacetime.
President Alexander Stubb said on Monday that the initiative was intended to strengthen European security, increase Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and reduce the risk of escalation.
Finland and France issued a joint statement confirming the decision after confidential talks at political and official level.
The initiative, launched by French President Emmanuel Macron in March, extends the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Finland becomes the tenth country to join, alongside Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
Stubb stressed that Finland would not host nuclear weapons in peacetime.
“There would be no sense in that,” he told reporters. He declined to speculate about possible arrangements during a war.
France will retain full control over its nuclear arsenal and will continue to decide what constitutes a threat to its vital interests. The initiative does not provide participating countries with a French nuclear umbrella or collective defence guarantees.
Finland’s main nuclear deterrence remains based on NATO and the extended deterrence provided by the United States, Stubb said.
The French initiative does not replace Nato’s nuclear deterrence and is not intended to duplicate it.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Finland’s participation would deepen bilateral defence ties with France and strengthen national security.
“The French initiative is different from Nato’s nuclear deterrence,” Häkkänen said in a ministry statement. “The participating countries will not have obligations comparable to Nato’s collective defence.”
France is also not asking participating countries to contribute to the cost of maintaining its nuclear arsenal.
A joint working group will be established to define the practical forms of cooperation. Stubb said the process could last between 10 and 15 years.
Stubb said access to information about French nuclear deterrence was one reason Finland chose to participate.
He also said the involvement of Sweden, Norway and Denmark had influenced Finland’s decision, as the Nordic countries share security interests in northern Europe.
Russia has opposed the French initiative. Asked about Moscow’s likely response to Finland’s participation, Stubb said there was no need to overstate the situation.
“Keep a cool head,” he said.
The decision received broad parliamentary backing, according to Stubb, although the Left Alliance has said it opposes Finland joining the initiative.
The announcement comes as Finland and France expand defence cooperation in other areas. Stubb said France had already committed forces to activities in Finland and that the nuclear deterrence initiative added another element to the relationship.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot are also due to sign a strategic partnership document in Helsinki on Monday.

Russia says Gulf instability rapidly worsening global oil market situation

Elena Teslova
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
The situation in global oil markets is rapidly deteriorating amid instability in the Persian Gulf, with major volumes of oil being removed from international supply, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.
Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov pointed out that "a huge amount of oil is dropping out of the market."
"Just with the disruption of the oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, more than 4% of global supplies have been knocked out of the global market. This cannot but have the most serious consequences, and it cannot but cause concern among the world’s economies," he said.
Peskov said Russia had introduced a ban on exports of oil products in order to ensure adequate supplies for its domestic market.
"As our domestic market becomes reliably saturated, the issue of lifting such a ban will come onto the agenda, and then an additional volume [of oil products] will again be directed to global markets," he noted.
Peskov said the removal of Russian oil products from international exports was also affecting global markets.
The comments came as Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline remained shut following an attack, threatening to further reduce global supplies and push energy prices higher. The pipeline has been carrying about 4 million to 5 million barrels per day, equivalent to roughly 4%-5% of global supply.
 
Ukraine conflict, Finland, BRICS
Peskov also welcomed calls for Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian civilian economic infrastructure, including an appeal by US President Donald Trump to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on Russian diesel production amid concerns over the impact on the US economy.
"Any call to the Kyiv regime to stop strikes on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed," he said.
Asked about reports in Western media saying Ukraine was losing the conflict, Peskov said he believed the course of developments on the battlefield was increasingly clear to Western analysts and professionals.
"It is becoming increasingly obvious to Western analysts and professionals that Russia, based on the dynamics on the fronts, is consistently moving toward achieving its goals," he said.
According to the official, it had previously been a "big misconception" to argue that Ukraine had the potential to withstand Russian pressure.
He added that some people still held that view, arguing that "serious analysts and professionals were increasingly drawing a different conclusion from developments on the battlefield."
"Some still retain this erroneous point of view. But professionals and truly serious analysts are increasingly realizing, based on the dynamics observed on the fronts, that Russia is indeed improving its positions day by day and consistently moving toward achieving its goals," he said.
Peskov said Russian President Vladimir Putin had positively assessed China’s and India’s readiness to contribute to efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict.
He added that any country could use its influence with Kyiv to encourage greater flexibility and contribute to bringing the conflict closer to a settlement.
"In general, any country can use its influence on the Kyiv regime to encourage it toward greater flexibility, which would be a significant contribution to the settlement," he said.
Peskov declined to comment on Finland’s decision to join a French-backed project for an advanced nuclear deterrence concept.
"I don’t quite understand what this concept is, to be honest. I still have to learn some details. Therefore, I would refrain from making any comments," he said.
Peskov said the expansion of BRICS bloc and specific candidates for membership had not been discussed at the group’s recent summit in New Delhi.
Russia, he added, supported Cuba’s desire to join the group and welcomed Havana’s intention to work within the group.

20:33:00 KST

Six months after seven foreign nationals, including an American and six Ukrainians, were arrested in India and booked under the anti-terrorism law Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), the government has charged them under the less stringent Immigration and Foreigners Act.
U.S. national Matthew Aaron Van Dyke, and Ukrainian nationals Hurba Petro, Slyviak Taras, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Stefankiv Marian, Honcharuk Maksim, and Kaminskyi Viktor were arrested in March from different parts of the country and charged under section 18 of the UAPA, which deals with offences amounting to conspiracy for terrorist activities and organizing terror camps.
They have now been charged under sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act for illegal entry and violations of visa conditions.
The dropping of terror charges against the foreign nationals has triggered speculation that the Indian government was under severe pressure from the U.S. government to release them. Van Dyke’s family had reportedly made a case before the U.S. government to intervene diplomatically in the issue to secure his release from prison. The opposition Congress has slammed the BJP-led government for bowing to American pressure.
Government sources were quoted in the media as saying that the National Investigation Agency (NIA) booked the foreign nationals under the Immigration and Foreigners Act (IFA) because the charges under this law have already been established during the investigation.
Foreign and even Indian nationals must obtain a Protected Area Permit or Restricted Area Permit to visit some border districts and states in the country. Violation of the law could mean imprisonment for up to three years.
The NIA has alleged that the seven foreign nationals went to Mizoram without the requisite permit and then crossed the border into Myanmar, where they held training sessions for Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations (EROs) in drone warfare and jamming technology. The agency claimed that their trip to India’s Northeast and then to Myanmar was not merely a violation of immigration laws but was part of “a larger conspiracy” involving a few Indian insurgent groups active in the region.
NIA has clarified that the probe into offences under the UAPA is continuing against all seven foreign nationals.
Under the UAPA, the NIA must complete the probe within 180 days, during which the accused remains in custody. The accused can apply for bail if the chargesheet is not submitted within this period.
In March, The Diplomat reported that the foreign nationals were not involved in any terror plot against India. In all likelihood, they were probably looking to reap profits from the sale of drones to resistance groups in Myanmar.
Drones have been widely utilized both by the military and resistance groups in Myanmar in the ongoing civil war. According to some functionaries of resistance groups active along the India-Myanmar border, most of these groups had been exploring diverse options to purchase drones after the supplies from Thailand and China were disrupted.
It was at this juncture that the seven foreign nationals landed in the camps of some resistance groups in Myanmar and offered demonstrations of drones and jamming technology with the objective of supplying the equipment in the coming months.
In addition, the likelihood of a mission being executed by these seven men to gather information on resistance groups in Myanmar on a mandate by some foreign agencies cannot be ruled out.
The illegal entry of foreign nationals to the border states in the northeastern region and their onward journey to the conflict hotspots in Myanmar has been a cause of concern for the Indian government. In 2025, Mizoram Chief Minister Lalduhoma stated that around 2,000 foreigners visited the border state, of whom several had crossed the border into Myanmar and entered the Chin Hills to provide military training to some resistance groups there. Last year, a Belgian journalist was arrested in Mizoram on flimsy charges but acquitted three months later.
The Indian government will be hoping that the arrest of the seven foreign nationals will deter others from indulging in similar adventurism in the future. Whether terror charges are slapped on them remains to be seen.
