Chancellor Merz’s party won the local elections in Lower Saxony
Kyiv • UNN
The CDU received 27.2% of the vote and remained the strongest force in Lower Saxony. The AfD came in third with a record 15.9% for the party.
The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) remained the strongest political force at the district level in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony after local elections were held there, according to preliminary results released on Monday. DW reports, UNN writes.
Details
Sunday's elections attracted unusually high attention because they were seen as an indicator of the level of support for the far-right "Alternative for Germany" (AfD) after its convincing victory in elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt last week.
Mayors, district chiefs and local councils in the state were elected.
Results of the elections in Lower Saxony
For Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is under pressure, the result was undoubtedly a relief: his CDU came in first, receiving 27.2% of the vote. This is slightly less than the 31.7% the party received in the last local elections in Lower Saxony in 2021.
The Social Democratic Party (SPD), which leads the coalition government at the state level, came in second with 24.6% support — a sharp decline from 30% in 2021.
The AfD came in third with 15.9%, more than tripling its 2021 result.
The Greens, the junior partner in the state-level coalition, received 14.1% of the vote, compared with 15.9% in 2021.
Rounding out the list are the Left Party and the Free Democratic Party (FDP), with 6% and 3.7%, respectively.

During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 460 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, up to 290 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and some 40 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: A new face, old baggage and a fresh scandal – what is ZZS taking into the election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:18:04 UTC
20:18:04 KST

Ilona Bērziņa/BNN
With less than three weeks to go until the 15th Saeima election on the 3rd of October, BNN is taking a closer look at the political forces competing for seats in parliament. We begin with a party that, according to August polling, still has a chance of clearing the 5% threshold.
Reputation, an attempt to break free from the “old mould” and the green dragon. What are ZZS’s chances?
As recently as Friday, the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) had little reason to worry about making it into the 15th Saeima. Although an August SKDS poll showed support for ZZS at just 2.8%, a survey conducted at the end of August by Latvijas fakti in cooperation with SIA Faktu logs put the party at 6.9%. Then Saturday arrived, and now-former Welfare Minister Reinis Uzulnieks managed to gamble away his political career – and perhaps more than a few ZZS supporters – to the “green dragon” of alcohol.
An extraordinary meeting of the ZZS board has already pulled the emergency brake on the situation, recalling Uzulnieks from his post as Welfare Minister and expelling him from the party. In doing so, ZZS is demonstrating zero tolerance for drunk driving and showing that it is prepared to sacrifice any “sheep” that strays, regardless of their previous achievements.
Politically, however, this display of values does not solve the problem. No matter how much controversy erupts, ZZS cannot remove Uzulnieks from its candidate list. Registered candidate lists cannot be withdrawn, and amendments can be made only in specific cases laid down by law by the Central Election Commission (CVK). A party’s desire to rid itself of a “scapegoat”, or a candidate’s excessive fondness for the “green dragon”, is not among them.
This creates a grotesque situation: the party says this person no longer belongs to our political force, yet voters in Zemgale will still see him as number one on the ZZS list. It is difficult to believe that voters will start studying the Saeima Election Law to understand how this happened.
This is an issue lawmakers should consider during the next Saeima. Perhaps the Saeima Election Law does need to be amended so that a candidate can be removed in this or another exceptional situation even relatively shortly before an election. Requiring candidates to produce a certificate from an addiction specialist confirming that they are free from addictions would probably make little sense. One can only imagine the chorus of outrage over privacy, human rights and everything else that would follow.
For the sake of fairness, it should be said that in certain circles it is hardly a secret how many people at various levels of power and influence enjoy a stronger drink. The only difference between them and Uzulnieks is that they have not been caught.
Meanwhile, one poll has ZZS standing outside the doors of the Saeima, while another has it safely inside parliament. The Uzulnieks scandal has not yet been measured by either survey. Claims that it has already cost ZZS one, two or three percentage points – or, conversely, nothing at all – therefore cannot be taken seriously at this stage. Its impact will only become visible in September.
Generational change. An ambition or reality?
In this election, ZZS is trying to prove that a generational shift is taking place within the party. So far, it is visible mainly in the advertising.
The party’s candidate for prime minister is no longer Aivars Lembergs, but Economy Minister Viktors Valainis. He is also the number one candidate on the ZZS list in Riga.
With Valainis as its public face, the party may be trying to break free from the image of the “old ZZS”. He talks about investment, economic growth and entrepreneurship, while the ZZS programme itself is highly ambitious. By 2030, the party promises a minimum wage of 1,250 euros, an average salary of 2,500 euros, an average pension of 1,000 euros, 5% VAT on essential food products, zero property tax on primary residences and at least one billion euros in foreign investment every year.
And now let us remember that classic line, uttered long ago by a representative of a different political force: “Well, how can you not make promises?”
In an interview with Jānis Domburs, Valainis did not provide financial calculations for a number of the programme’s promises. ZZS’s economic offer could therefore work either as a positive vision for the future or as yet another generous pre-election catalogue.
In recent weeks, Valainis, who served as Economy Minister in both Evika Siliņa’s and Andris Kulbergs’ governments, has become increasingly critical of Prime Minister Kulbergs’ performance and the pace of the government’s spending review.
And here a fair question arises: Mr Valainis, what have you personally done since September 2023, right up to the present day, to address these issues? Where is the substantial reduction of the bureaucratic apparatus, the trimming of supervisory and management boards at state-owned companies, and the elimination of other entirely unnecessary spending?
The Krauze forestry case and the Uldis Augulis phenomenon
ZZS already has a reputation problem involving one of its party leaders. In May, prosecutors carried out procedural actions against then-Agriculture Minister and ZZS leader Armands Krauze in the so-called forestry industry case. He was given the status of a person against whom criminal proceedings had been initiated, and then-Prime Minister Evika Siliņa dismissed him from office literally in the final minutes of her term.
The National Audit Office’s finding that the support mechanism for forestry companies reduced Latvijas valsts meži revenue by 49.4 million euros certainly sounds severe. However, it should not be forgotten that the decision to support domestic forestry companies was adopted and approved by the entire government, not Krauze alone. The argument that the government was full of fools who understood nothing about forestry hardly withstands scrutiny. For now, the matter continues to grind through the extremely slow mills of Latvia’s law enforcement institutions.
Uldis Augulis is one of Latvia’s most experienced ministers, having headed both the Ministry of Transport and the Ministry of Welfare several times. In the Kulbergs government, he became Agriculture Minister in place of Krauze.
His political experience is genuinely valuable to ZZS at a time of crisis. Yet Augulis, much like Augusts Brigmanis, represents precisely the political generation from which Valainis is trying to distance the party’s image. Augulis is an experienced politician who knows the system well, but at the same time he is an almost perfect symbol of ZZS’s political continuity – someone who might bring a tear to the eye of the party’s more conservative supporters as they remember the “good old days” when no one in ZZS tried to hide Aivars Lembergs’ involvement and influence.
ZZS and its problem with political consistency
The issue, of course, is the Istanbul Convention.
When Evika Siliņa’s government was being formed in 2023, ZZS was among the political forces prepared to ratify the Istanbul Convention with an accompanying declaration on the values enshrined in Latvia’s Constitution. In reality, this was the price the party paid for a seat at Siliņa’s government table.
At the time, Viktors Valainis publicly spoke about the need to dispel the fears and political intrigue surrounding the document. Less than two years later, ZZS had completely reversed its position. Together with the opposition, the party supported Latvia’s withdrawal from the Convention, while Uldis Augulis spoke of the “promotion of left-wing ideology” – even though, when he himself served as Welfare Minister, he had publicly explained that the concept of “social gender” did not oblige Latvia to change how its legal or education systems understand gender.
From an electoral perspective, this reversal could help ZZS compete for conservative voters. But ZZS is far from alone in that political space, and the competition for voters is fierce. The National Alliance, Latvia First (LPV), to some extent the United List (AS), and other political forces are already competing for the same electorate.
Moreover, an SKDS poll conducted after all the controversy surrounding the Convention showed that the issue was largely unimportant to ZZS voters: 16% were not interested in it at all, 38% were rather uninterested, while only 7% were very interested.
In essence, ZZS paid a high political price over an issue that is not a priority for its traditional electorate.
GKR – a stepping stone for ZZS in Riga
More than a few observers also see a lack of principle in ZZS’s cooperation with Oļegs Burovs’ Honor to Serve Riga (GKR), although the partnership is rooted in pragmatism.
GKR and ZZS already ran together in the 2025 Riga City Council election, while in this Saeima election Burovs is number three on the ZZS candidate list in Riga. Burovs can give ZZS something it has historically lacked – a recognisable Riga politician and access to voters for whom the traditional identity of a farmers’ party means very little. When a party is hovering around the 5% threshold, even a relatively modest boost in Riga can be extremely valuable.
However, the more representatives of different political groups ZZS brings into its ranks, the harder it becomes to answer a basic question: what exactly is ZZS?
Is it a party representing rural and farmers’ interests? A conservative force? A centrist party of pragmatic managers? Lembergs’ partner? Burovs’ Riga platform? A modernised economic party led by Valainis? Does the voter even understand who lives in this ZZS garden and what the party’s ideology ultimately is?
ZZS should not be written off yet. Latvian voters have survived even bigger political scandals. The party also has a powerful traditional trump card – a strong regional organisation, well-known municipal politicians and an electorate that tends to be more disciplined than opinion polls sometimes suggest.
Yet if one had to name a ZZS achievement that is easy for everyone to understand, ironically it would be the raising of minimum income thresholds and benefits, which Uzulnieks actively championed, efforts to introduce a basic pension, opposition to raising the retirement age, and the party’s willingness to freeze public officials’ salaries.

Kravchenko publishes video, documents on suspicions against NABU director
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:17:38 EEST
20:17:38 KST

(Updated version)
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has released a video and the text of a notice of suspicion addressed to National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) Director Semen Kryvonos. The video addresses the alleged falsification of paternity documents to evade punishment, while the text of the suspicion also details an episode concerning a land scheme.
"Episode No. 1. Part One. The court established the fact of a crime in Semen Kryvonos's actions. But no punishment followed: he fictitiously adopted a child and unlawfully obtained grounds for exemption from liability—an amnesty. Subsequently, with this past behind him, he successfully passed a competition involving international experts and headed NABU," Kravchenko commented on the video.
The video itself features an interrogation record of a woman whose child was allegedly adopted by the NABU Director. The woman in the video claims she has no relationship with Kryvonos.
"In June 2009, Holosiyivsky District Court... considered a case charging Kryvonos... with committing an intentional crime against the voting rights of citizens acting by prior conspiracy of a group of persons," the video states.
The video then presents a snippet of an interview with Kryvonos during the competitive selection process for the position of NABU Director. In particular, in the excerpted fragment, Kryvonos explains to a member of the competition committee the circumstances surrounding the closure in 2010 of a case against him concerning the transfer of UAH 15,000 to students for voting for the BYT political party.
In the video, Kryvonos recounts his civic activism as a student and the fabricated accusations: "Law enforcement representatives were basically set on us at the time. They acted very crudely, several students were detained. There were no bribes—that is all nonsense. I had no idea about any search, I was not hiding."
At the same time, according to the report published by Kravchenko, Kryvonos "knowingly misled the members of the competition committee" and developed "a criminal plan, the implementation of which subsequently allowed him to be released from criminal liability."
According to the information in the video, "Semen Kryvonos's criminal plan consisted of creating an artificial ground under which he would obtain the right to fall under an amnesty. One such legislative ground at that time was an individual having a minor child."
The video goes on to state that Kryvonos's accomplice "found him an unmarried woman who had a child, whose father's details in the birth registration book were entered at the mother's direction."
According to the video, the mother of the minor child was misled; she was persuaded to help Kryvonos under the pretext that his employer allegedly needed documents confirming that he had a dependent child.
"As established by the investigation, after legally acquiring paternity over someone else's child, Semen Kryvonos had no intention whatsoever of fulfilling parental duties," the video states.
Subsequently, as claimed in the clip, based on the paternity documents, Kryvonos filed a motion for amnesty, and on June 25, 2009, the court released Kryvonos from criminal liability in connection with the application of the Law "On Amnesty." "In the same way, the case charging Kryvonos with bribing students was closed," the video clip states.
In May 2018, as asserted in the video published by the Prosecutor General, Kryvonos applied to the court with a claim to exclude information listing him as the father, and the court granted the claim.
The clip summarizes that in this manner Kryvonos, with the aim of evading criminal liability for bribing students, "developed and implemented a criminal intent consisting of falsifying the birth certificate and misleading the court."
The video clarifies that under this episode, Kryvonos has been notified of suspicion under Parts 2 and 3 of Article 358 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
Later, Kravchenko published a PDF file of the text of the suspicion against Kryvonos on his Telegram channel. In addition to what was stated in the video, the document indicates that in 2014, while serving as the head of the registration service of Obukhiv City-District Department of Justice in Kyiv region, Kryvonos agreed to accept a bribe for the allocation of a plot of land. Thus, according to the text of the document, he is suspected of falsifying official documents to obtain a bribe. However, as the text of the document notes, the crime was not carried out to the end.
Shortly afterward, Kravchenko published another post on his Telegram channel. "Today, NABU and SAPO stated that they 'did not seize any criminal proceedings mentioned in the statements of the Prosecutor General.' This statement is another lie, which is refuted by their own procedural documents," he wrote.
He published a copy of the search protocol from the official offices of the Office of the Prosecutor General. "It records in black and white the seizure of materials from criminal proceedings against NABU and SAPO employees, including covert investigative actions materials," the Prosecutor General explained.

Turkish top diplomat due in Baku for strategic talks

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan (R) and his Azerbaijani counterpart Ceyhun Bayramov, from a former meeting. (AA Photo)
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will travel to Azerbaijan for a two-day visit to discuss strategic ties between the two nations as well as regional and global developments, diplomatic sources have informed.
Fidan will be in Baku on Sept. 15 and 16, where he will meet Azerbaijan Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov and Defense Minister Zakir Hasanov. He will also be received by Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev, the sources said.
The visit comes after Fidan’s important trip to Syria, where he discussed regional developments and Israel’s continued aggression.
The talks in Baku will address the growing strategic bilateral relationship between the two countries. Fidan will also reiterate the need to intensify efforts to increase the trade volume from the current $7 billion to $15 billion, as agreed by both presidents.
Fidan and Bayramov will also review energy and transportation projects, sources said.
The Turkish top diplomat will also raise cooperation in the field of defense industry, security and military ties during his meetings with Bayramov and Hasanov.
Top diplomats from Türkiye and Azerbaijan will assess ongoing cooperation within multilateral platforms, particularly the Organization of Turkic States, as Türkiye prepares to host the upcoming leaders’ summit.
Fidan will also reiterate Ankara’s support for the ongoing normalization process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, emphasizing that a historic opportunity for regional peace has emerged.
Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a peace agreement in 2025 under the mediation of United States President Donald Trump. Armenia is expected to amend its constitution for the finalization of the process with Azerbaijan.
Türkiye is also running a separate normalization process with Armenia.
Fidan will also reiterate Türkiye’s support for Azerbaijan’s reconstruction efforts in the Karabakh region and for making key energy and trade routes fully operational.
Türkiye and Azerbaijan enjoy excellent relations under the motto of “one nation, two states” since the latter’s independence in 1991. The two countries established the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council in 2010, which paved the way for further strengthening and deepening ties.
Roughly 5,800 Turkish firms currently operate in Azerbaijan, accounting for an estimated $18 billion in capital investments. Conversely, Azerbaijan’s total investments in Türkiye have exceeded $20 billion, supported by roughly 2,600 active companies.

TUC leader calls for ban on crypto donations and says Reform’s £72m shows democracy ‘in crisis’ - UK politics live
Unknown

2026-09-14
11:17:06 UTC
20:17:06 KST

Farage hints £72m donations to Reform UK won't be legal under retrospective measures in elections bill when it becomes law
Nigel Farage has hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tighten elections law currently going through parliament.
He made the apparent concession in an interview with the BBC in which he strongly objected to the government’s plan to make a new law banning Britons who live abroad, or who have recently relocated to the UK, from giving more than £100,000 a year to political parties retrospective.
It seems likely that the law would apply to Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, the two cryptocurrency billionaires who have each pledged £36m to Reform UK.
In an interview, Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, asked Farage if he was sure that both donations were compliant with the law now, and “how we expect it soon to be”.
Farage replied:
Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today. Of that there is no question whatsoever.
Mason pointed out that Farage was saying “today” and he asked if Delo and Harborne were both resident in the UK on 25 March – after which the retrospective restrictions on donations by new arrivals will kick in when the representation of the people bill becomes law.
Farage replied:
I’m not going to go into their particular details. All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.
Now there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally.
Well, that simply cannot be. If a government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There’d be a response the other way. We or the Conservatives would say, right, if you’re going to stop legitimate donors like this, we will then say to the trade unions, you can’t give money. And if you do that, you have collapsed the whole political system.
In fact, there has not just been “talk” of making the cap retrospective. The bill legislating for this has gone through the Commons, and MPs debated amendments creating these exact laws on Wednesday 2 September.
While laws applying retrospectively are rare, they are not unprecedented. Reform UK wants to pass retrospective legislation itself. For example, it plans to abolish indefinite leave to remain as an immigration status, including for people who already have it.
Farage’s position is different from the one adopted by his party over the weekend when Robert Jenrick, the Treasury spokesperson, said that Reform UK was confident the Delo and Harborne donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it’s going to be in the future”.
Nigel Farage has hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tighten elections law currently going through parliament. (See 2.04pm.) For more comment on this story, do listen to the latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast, featuring Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey.
Official who headed review into influence of foreign money in politics calls for cap on amount any person can donate
Philip Rycroft is former permanent secretary who carried out the government review on the infuence of foreign money on British politics that led to the government deciding to impose a cap on the amount that can be donated by Britons living abroad, and a moratorium on donations in the form of cryptocurrency.
Wider reforms of the donation rules were outside his remit. But, in interviews today, he has said there should be a cap on the amount any person can donate.
He told Times Radio:
It is absolutely true that political parties are essential for the democratic process and they need to raise money from private sources until we get to a point which is, I think a very long way off, when we have significant state funding.
So how do you square the circle? In my view the way you could do that is to have donation caps but to set them at least initially at a really quite a high level, for the sake of argument £1m a year from any individual, corporation or indeed trade union and that would allow the parties still to function without requiring state funding.
Rycroft also that if the government reduced spending limits during election periods, and impose spending limits outside election periods, that would also help because it would “so parties don’t need to raise so much money”.
The Labour MP Phil Brickell has written to the Electoral Commission asking it to investigate if the donations given to Reform UK by Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne worth a total of £72m are legitimate, HuffPost UK is reporting.

Trump Says He Backs a United Ireland, Stoking a Divisive Debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:15:03 UTC
20:15:03 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would “love to see” a united Ireland and believed it was “going to happen eventually,” breaking with decades of careful neutrality by U.S. presidents over Northern Ireland’s constitutional status.
“You have Northern Ireland, and you have Ireland,” Trump told reporters on Sunday while visiting a golf tournament at one of his resorts in the Irish village of Doonbeg. “It would seem to me that one of the ‘naturals’ of all time is to put them together.”
It’s also not the first time Trump has discussed Northern Ireland and the Irish Republic: he joked about a “merger” of the two in March, though the Northern Ireland official he was addressing at the time, who opposes unification, emphasized that the comment was clearly in jest only.
The President seemed aware that his recent remarks would garner backlash, particularly from the British. “The U.K. would have something to say about it obviously, but I think it would be a great thing,” he said Saturday, while in conversation with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin. “I mean, how can it be bad?”
Trump’s statements come weeks after newly installed U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there was not enough public support for a referendum on Northern Ireland’s future. Other British politicians have balked at Trump’s statements, arguing that Northern Ireland is indisputably part of the U.K.
Martin also downplayed the U.S. leader’s remarks. “It shouldn't be a surprise,” Martin told reporters on Sunday, adding that Trump “takes a different sort of perspective on things.” The Irish leader said that some responses to Trump, however, were an overreaction.
“They asked me about Scotland—that one I won't talk about yet,” Trump said Sunday, referencing another country divided on leaving the U.K. The Trump family also owns a golf resort in Scotland, which voted against independence from the rest of Great Britain in 2014. “I’ll save that for another day.”
Why Ireland is divided—and how reunification could happen
The island of Ireland was divided in 1921 following the Irish War of Independence. While a northern region of six counties remained part of the U.K., the rest of the island, comprising 26 counties, became the Irish Free State, which eventually became a sovereign republic in 1949.
From the 1960s, tensions in the north between largely Catholic Irish nationalists, or republicans, who wish to reunite with the Republic of Ireland, and mainly Protestant unionists who want to stay with Britain culminated in a three-decade, violent period known as the Troubles.
A 1998 peace agreement—dubbed the Good Friday Agreement and mediated in large part by the U.S.—ended the violence and recognized the right of those in Northern Ireland to recognize themselves as British, Irish, or both. It also recognized that Northern Ireland’s status must be based on democratic consent.
Following the agreement, Northern Ireland has not yet held a referendum. But Irish nationalism gained momentum when Sinn Féin, the predominant Irish republican party, won the most seats in the Northern Ireland Assembly in 2022. It was the first time a republican party dominated the assembly since Northern Ireland’s formation, though Sinn Féin must still share power with unionists under local laws. Polls, however, show that the Northern Irish public is still divided on whether it should leave the U.K., and Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland has focused on socioeconomic issues over reunification in recent years.
In the Republic of Ireland, Sinn Féin is the largest single party, but it belongs to the opposition after two more moderate center-right parties formed the government following the 2024 election, with Martin as the current leader. Some have criticized the Irish government under Martin for its slow uptake of the unification issue. Ireland’s Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald said after Trump’s comments: “The conversation on Irish unity has shifted, and the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.”
Claire Hanna, who leads the small nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party in Northern Ireland, also welcomed Trump’s support. “Turns out he’s not as orange as he looks,” Hanna said, in reference to the political color associated with the Protestant and unionist community in Ireland.
How British politicians responded to Trump’s remarks
The 1998 Good Friday Agreement stipulates that the U.K.’s Northern Ireland secretary can decide to hold a poll and must call one if they believe a majority would vote for Irish reunification. Chris Bryant, the incumbent secretary, posted this section of the agreement on social media amid Trump’s unification remarks, adding: “Just in case anyone should need a quick refresher course on constitutional matters in Northern Ireland.”
In a visit to Northern Ireland last month, Burnham said that calling for such a poll is “off the table,” citing the divisiveness of past votes on Brexit and Scottish independence. “We’ve got to focus on bringing people together as best we can,” the British Prime Minister told the BBC.
The U.S. President also rankled some on the British far-right who usually side with him. “Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, a known Trump ally, wrote on social media, explaining that “the people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification.” Rupert Lowe, another British parliamentarian who heads the Restore Britain party, called Trump’s statements “unacceptable” and “insulting,” and suggested that the President “should not be aiming to permanently damage our country to get back at the current malign Labour Government.”
Lowe’s claims come as Trump has expressed frustration over the U.K.'s refusal to get involved in the U.S.’s war against Iran.
Kemi Badenoch, who leads the opposition Conservative Party, posted on social media that Trump was “shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state,” though she argued that “this sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”
Scottish, Welsh, and Northern Irish leaders meet to discuss potential break-up of United Kingdom
The First Ministers of the U.K.’s devolved nations—Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland—signed a Memorandum of Understanding Monday, calling for each country to have the “right to determine its own future.”
Michelle O'Neill of Sinn Féin joined Scotland's John Swinney of the Scottish National Party (SNP) and Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth of Plaid Cymru as they insisted no Westminster government has the right to “block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.”
“What unites us is a determination to ensure that the voices of our nations are heard, that our people have the opportunity to thrive, and that cooperation between Scotland, Wales, and Ireland can be strengthened," the agreement read.
O’Neil wants Ireland to be reunited. Swinney and ap Iorwerth are open to calls for independence from their nations. O’Neil and Swinney urged for referendums in their respective countries, while ap Iorwerth declined to set a timetable for a Welsh independence vote.

Taichung streetlight upgrades cut electricity costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung City Government said Saturday that its ongoing streetlight upgrades are expected to save more than NT$140 million (US$4.4 million) in electricity costs this year, according to a press release.
The city had saved NT$93.45 million by the end of August and expects to exceed its original NT$130 million target. The new LED lights have increased road illumination from about 12 lux to more than 40 lux.
Construction Bureau Director-General Chen Ta-tien (陳大田) said the project saved NT$16.31 million during the second half of 2025 after it began in July. It saved another NT$64.9 million in the first half of 2026.
Chen said replacing older streetlights would reduce electricity costs and improve road safety. He added that the project had been registered by the Ministry of Environment as a voluntary emissions-reduction initiative.
The project is expected to generate carbon credits equivalent to about 20,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide. Based on current market prices, the credits could bring the city an estimated NT$60 million to NT$80 million over 10 years.
The bureau said residents could report streetlight problems through a 24-hour QR-code system. Major repairs can now be completed within nine hours, it added.

In The Belly of AI | Storyteller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:12:20 UTC
20:12:20 KST

[NOTE: In The Belly of AI available until October 12, 2026.]
The Human Cost Behind the Magic of AI
Henri Poulain’s documentary In the Belly of AI looks beyond the promise of artificial intelligence to reveal the workers, resources and inequalities hidden behind the technology.
Artificial intelligence has a branding problem. There is considerably more human intelligence inside it than its name suggests.
We experience AI through the illusion of effortlessness. A question produces an answer in seconds. A few words become an image. Algorithms recognise faces, filter content and increasingly influence what we watch, buy and read. But behind this apparent magic lies an enormous infrastructure of human labour, natural resources and physical machinery.
This film turns its attention away from what artificial intelligence can do and towards a less frequently asked question: What, and who, makes it possible?
AI systems learn from vast quantities of data, but that data does not simply organise itself. Across the world, workers label photographs, categorise objects, transcribe recordings, evaluate responses and moderate disturbing content. Their work helps train and refine increasingly sophisticated AI systems. In the Belly of AI brings these largely invisible workers into view.
The paradox is striking. The more seamless AI appears to the user, the easier it becomes to forget the human labour behind it.
There is also a geographical imbalance. The public face of the AI revolution is dominated by billion-dollar companies, celebrated entrepreneurs and powerful new models, largely concentrated in the world's wealthiest economies. Much of the labour supporting those systems, however, takes place far from the companies and consumers benefiting most from them. The film places AI within a much older economic story, in which some of the least visible people in a global supply chain are also among its most essential.
AI has a geography, and so does the infrastructure powering it. The "cloud" sounds weightless and immaterial. In reality, it exists in enormous data centres requiring land, electricity and water. Artificial intelligence therefore has an environmental footprint as well as a human one.
Perhaps the film's most unsettling idea is how rarely users are required to think about any of this. Technology is most seductive when complexity disappears. AI takes this abstraction particularly far because the product itself appears intelligent, while the people and physical infrastructure behind it recede from view.
Much of today's debate focuses on what AI might eventually do to workers: which jobs it will replace and which professions it will transform. In the Belly of AI asks us instead to consider the workers who are already part of that future.
Recognising these costs does not mean rejecting artificial intelligence or its potential. But technological progress deserves a more complete accounting.
The greatest trick of AI may not be that machines have learned to appear human. It may be how successfully we have made the humans behind them disappear.

Syria fuel price hikes trigger widest protests since Assad fall

Syria fuel price hikes trigger widest protests since Assad fall
ALEPPO, Syria, Sept 14 - A sharp rise in fuel prices at the weekend has sparked protests across Syria, in the country's most widespread demonstrations since the toppling of Bashar al-Assad almost two years ago.
Demonstrators burned tyres and blocked key roads, including the highway linking the capital Damascus to the industrial hub of Aleppo, after Syria's government on Saturday raised diesel prices by 40% to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.32) a litre.
The price increases piled further pressure on Syrians facing years of economic crisis. The United Nations Development Programme estimates 90% of Syrians live below the poverty line, compared with about a third before the Syrian civil war began in 2011.
In the steepest of several price hikes announced since the Iran war began, the government also raised household and industrial gas prices by about 9%, 95-octane gasoline by 28% to 195 pounds and 90-octane gasoline by 26% to 185 pounds.
Protesters also blocked convoys of crude tankers travelling towards refineries in central Syria, with some demanding the dismissal of the energy and economy ministers and the head of the Syrian Petroleum Company.
"We don't want higher wages. All we want is lower diesel and other fuel prices," Yasser Salim told Reuters in Aleppo.
Bassam al-Ali, also protesting in Aleppo, appealed directly to President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying the situation was untenable.
"Border crossings bring in millions of dollars. We don't want new roundabouts or malls. We just want to live," he said.
RUSSIAN SUPPLY UNDER PRESSURE
Energy Ministry spokesperson Abdulhamid Salat said on Sunday that the price increases were a temporary measure driven by higher global procurement costs and Syria's heavy dependence on imports, and could be revised up or down as conditions changed.
Syria has relied heavily on Russian crude, importing around 60,000 bpd this year, although Damascus has told Washington it is willing to sharply reduce those purchases.
That supply has come under growing pressure as Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have reduced production, prompting Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline and diesel.
Prices reflected not only crude costs but shortages of refined products and higher refining, transport and supply costs, Salat said in a statement.
The supply crunch has been compounded by the three-month closure of Syria's Baniyas refinery, the country's largest, for its first comprehensive maintenance operation.
The increase means 95-octane gasoline has risen about 86% since February, while diesel has more than doubled. Benchmark Brent crude rose about 44%, from $72.48 to $104.61 a barrel.
Imad Abu Ras, a 44-year-old taxi driver, said passengers had already begun objecting to higher fares, adding: "Now vegetables and everything else will go up with fuel prices. What is the solution? Steal? We can't steal". REUTERS

Muslim students accuse Lebanon university of crackdown on prayer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:09:05 UTC
20:09:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Muslim students accuse Lebanese university of discrimination over prayer
A lack of prayer spaces at the Lebanese American University (LAU) campus in Byblos has sparked controversy in Lebanon, with Muslim students accusing the university of discriminating against them.
Byblos, also known as Jbeil, is a majority-Christian city north of Beirut, but hundreds of Muslim students study at the university's campus.
Students have accused LAU of preventing Muslim students from praying on campus and closing spaces previously used for prayer. They have also pointed out that there is no mosque within walking distance of the university.
An LAU student who gave only his first name, Suleiman, told The New Arab: "The students were praying in an unused locker room but then the university said they wanted to convert it to a lab. This never happened."
"When the students asked if they could get [another] space to pray, the university ignored them. The students began praying underneath a staircase in the parking garage but the university said they couldn't do that either. A LAU student asked [LAU] president Chaouki Abdalla for another space to pray but the students were told to forget about this request," Suleiman added.
Around 300 students recently signed a petition calling on LAU to provide prayer spaces for Muslims. Suleiman said, however, that many Muslim students feared speaking out over concerns that they could be expelled.
Local imam Sheikh Ahmed Al-Laqis accused LAU of preventing students from exercising their right to pray, saying that if the university continued to do so, "people would be forced to seek other solutions".
The controversy has continued to generate debate in Lebanon, with LAU issuing a statement "regretting that this issue is being amplified".
"LAU is a secular, private, not-for-profit institution. Its mission and values are clearly communicated to all students, faculty and staff," the statement said.
"The matter concerns requests for dedicated physical spaces for prayer. Consistent with its secular character, the university does not designate physical spaces for religious observance. This policy applies equitably to all members of the LAU community," it added.
However, students have pointed to LAU's mission statement, which includes a commitment to "enable individuals to find their own spiritual and personal fulfilment".
They have also pointed out that universities in Lebanon and other countries where Muslims make up a much smaller proportion of the population provide prayer spaces for Muslims and members of other faiths.
The New Arab contacted LAU for further comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Sectarian tensions
Some secular Lebanese media outlets have defended the university's policy.
"It is true that under Lebanese law every citizen has the right to practice their religious rituals but is the university the appropriate place for that?" the social media platform Political Pen commented in a video.
The issue has also fuelled sectarian tensions between Muslims and Christians, with Ibrahim al-Saqr, a prominent figure in the right-wing Christian Lebanese Forces party, sarcastically suggesting that Muslim students should establish their own Islamic university if they wanted to pray.
Some students have linked the controversy to other alleged instances of discrimination against Muslims in Lebanon, including previous reports of Lebanese Muslims being denied the opportunity to rent homes in Christian areas and women wearing hijab being denied access to beaches.
Sectarian tensions in Lebanon have intensified amid Israel's war, which has forced hundreds of thousands of mostly Shia Muslim Lebanese to flee their homes in southern Lebanon and seek shelter in Sunni and Christian areas.

Hormuz diplomacy stalls as Gulf states suspend meeting with Iran

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:09:00 UTC
20:09:00 KST

Gulf Arab states canceled planned talks with Iran on Monday as Yemen’s Houthis launched a fresh attack on Saudi Arabia, widening a conflict that has further threatened global oil supplies.
The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen said they fired dozens of missiles and drones Monday at a Saudi military airbase in Khamis Mushait, near the border, hitting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots. They described the attack as retaliation for hundreds of Saudi airstrikes on Yemen in recent days.
Saudi authorities announced brief emergency alerts there and in three other southern cities which have previously come under Houthi fire.
The Houthis launched a lightning advance last week in Yemen, culminating in the seizure of an island in the mouth of the Red Sea on Friday. A separate attack that day, which Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed fighters in Iraq, knocked out Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline, the main route for Middle East oil bypassing the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
Crude oil prices rose more than 3% Monday, when the market reopened after the weekend, while the politically sensitive average retail price of diesel in the United States hit a new all-time high above $6.23 a gallon.
Traders say the closure of the Saudi pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply unless it is reopened within days. Images from space show sections of the pipeline damaged by blazes. Riyadh has not given a firm estimate for how long it will be shut.
Oman had been due to host a meeting Monday with Iran and Gulf states to discuss negotiations aimed at reopening Hormuz, the world's most important oil shipping lane, largely closed since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February.
But Oman's Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi announced overnight that the meeting had been postponed "in the interests of consensus." Iran said the postponement was at the request of Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, Iran issued a list of 77 ships it said had violated its protocols for operating in the Strait of Hormuz. Any ship on the list would face "restrictions on future passages, including fines, detention, or confiscation," and other ships that assisted them by accepting transfers of cargo would be added to the list.
The upsurge of fighting in Yemen poses a dilemma for Washington, which is under pressure to aid its Saudi allies but anxious not to expand the costly war to a new theater.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis for more than a decade, after the mountain fighters captured Yemen's capital in 2014. The war there had largely been quiet under a ceasefire for the past few years, but fighting has now resumed, with the Houthis driving back forces from a Saudi-backed government based in the south.
Thousands of Yemenis have fled inland from the coast to escape fighting as the Houthis swept into cities including the historic Red Sea port of Mokha last week.
Aisha Muhammad, an elderly woman burning twigs to heat a kettle in government-held territory near Taiz, told Reuters she had left behind two daughters and three sons who had been unable to escape.
"They can't even go out to the market to get food and drinking water. They are being blocked and shot at, so they are trapped inside their homes," she said. "They cannot reach us, and we cannot return to them. This is a trial from God."
On Friday, the Houthis captured Perim Island, inside the Bab el-Mandeb, the "Gate of Tears" strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea.
U.S. President Donald Trump is under pressure to end the war to relieve the global energy shortage and lower prices that are hurting the fortunes of his Republican Party ahead of mid-term elections in November.
Three sources have told Reuters that Washington has so far rebuffed calls from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to intervene in Yemen.
Trump confirmed over the weekend that he had spoken to the prince, and said the Houthis had also phoned asking Washington to keep out of the dispute.
The United States bombed the Houthis in 2025 for two months, but Trump called off that campaign after reaching a cease-fire with the group, which he said had promised not to attack ships in the Red Sea.
Trump, who attended a golf tournament at one of his resorts in Ireland, said he expected the Iran war to end shortly after the elections in November, after which the price of oil would "drop like a rock."

What is Ilona W. accused of?

She allegedly had contact with a full-time Russian intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin from at least October 2023.

Ilona W. is also accused of attending events herself to identify useful contacts and potential targets.
Prosecutors say she tried to recruit people from Germany's Defense Ministry and the arms industry.
She also allegedly sought information on German defense policy and the defense industry on behalf of her Russian contact, particularly in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine.
The charges were filed last week before the state security division of Berlin's Higher Regional Court.
Germany expelled the suspected Russian intelligence officer linked to the case shortly after W.'s arrest, prompting Moscow to retaliate by expelling a German diplomat.

Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:08:42 UTC
20:08:42 KST

Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Researchers in Nijmegen have set up a laboratory to try to answer one of the oldest questions known to science: why are people ticklish?
Aristotle, Erasmus, Galileo and Darwin all tried to put their finger on the purpose of tickling, or gargalesis to use its scientific name, without finding a definitive reason.
Now two researchers at Radboud University in Nijmegen are using robots and sensors to try to shed more light on the phenomenon.
Tickling exists across cultures and throughout history, but with few variations and little difference between men and women, indicating that it has its roots in biology. Tickling has been observed in other primates such as bonobos and chimpanzees.
Ziliang Xiong and Konstantina Kilteni have set up their lab in a windowless basement in the Maria Montessori building, an environment stripped of any other stimuli that could make their test subjects laugh.
The robot uses a metal pin to simulate tickling, with settings that can be adjusted to measure the effect of different types of contact from gentle stroking to prodding. The participants wear a cap equipped with electrodes that measure their brain responses.
Families and partners
The researchers also asked the 448 subjects to fill in surveys about how they experienced tickling, which revealed strong similiarities.
Most tickling is by adults on children, usually within families, or between siblings. Partners and friends also tickle each other, but this is less common.
Most respondents said they reacted to tickling by laughing, squirming or trying to turn away. The vast majority named the same body parts as most susceptible to tickling: the sides, armpits, belly and the soles of the feet.
The researchers noted that while tickling is associated with play and laughter, many people find it unpleasant and it can quickly become overwhelming. The Nazis even used it as a torture method.
There are indications that people diagnosed with autism are more sensitive to tickling and that ticklish people may even live longer.
Other theories suggest a link between tickling and sexual stimulation, given that couples often tickle each other and it tends to be directed at body parts that are rarely exposed.
Thin skinned
Darwin speculated that tickling felt uncomfortable because it involved touching parts of the body that are unused to being touch, while Aristotle believed it worked on places where the skin is thinner.
But the researchers in Nijmegen said none of the theories provided a complete answer to the reasons why people are sensitive to tickling. “You rarely get touched on your back, but the back is pretty resistant to tickling,” Xiong pointed out.

UK MPs and Lords call for new laws to tackle AI threat to human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:07:24 UTC
20:07:24 KST

OpenAI has urged British lawmakers to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology.
The company behind ChatGPT said the UK government should act immediately, following a call by its arch-rival Anthropic to curb AI development.
“We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon.
However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems.
In a separate interview with the online publication Politico, Duff Gordon said the government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to legislate.
OpenAI’s intervention came as a UK parliamentary committee demanded more restrictions on the power of AI, warning that the world was unprepared for the “potentially dire” consequences of the technology, in the latest sign of rising global concern.
A new regulatory framework is needed for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public, according to the cross-party joint committee on human rights, comprising MPs and Lords.
It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause.
The call for action came after Anthropic, a leading AI company, urged its competitors and governments at the weekend to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development – a call that received immediate support from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk.
It follows a series of serious safety incidents in which swarms of AI agents broke out of testing environments and hacked into third-party infrastructure, as well as evidence some users have dodged controls to use models in ways that could support biological weapons development.
Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology.
“Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said.
A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries.
“We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson.
On Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology. Downing Street rejected the call for a ban, but said it was exploring additional targeted interventions “to address the most significant AI-related national security risks”.
Sobel said: “New legislation is needed to establish a comprehensive set of protections that deal with the entire AI supply chain and its life cycle.
“A single AI regulator should be established to set policy, monitor performance and ensure enforcement.”
Donald Trump has played down warnings of dire risks to humanity. “We’re leading China in AI,” the US president said on Sunday. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
In his weekend call for the main AI companies to “pace the frontier”, the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the US government should grant the leading AI companies a waiver to allow them to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday night that while he would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”, there was no “need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence”.
He said: “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.”
Sobel, who has also proposed a bill to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK, said protections were needed now to ensure that potential human rights risks do not “become reality”.
The committee said a new AI bill should establish a regulatory regime that mandates more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models, and prohibit some uses of AI which are incompatible with human rights.
It also called for mandatory transparency requirements across all levels of the technology’s life cycle, and the establishment of an independent AI oversight body to monitor AI harms and risks, with strong powers to hold AI providers to account.
The UK government has already established the AI Security Institute (AISI), which subjects advanced models to safety tests – but does not have the power to compel AI developers such as Anthropic to submit their technology for scrutiny. Last week, it was reported that Anthropic had declined to send its latest model to AISI for testing.

US says it’s clearing Hormuz traffic: Why are oil futures beyond $100?
Brent crude crosses $107 as Hormuz disruptions and Saudi pipeline shutdown threaten global oil supply.
President Donald Trump says the United States is making progress in reopening the Strait of Hormuz and escorting more oil through the waterway, yet oil prices have jumped in recent days.
The recent attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure have also pushed crude prices up, with Brent crude rising $3.21 to $107.82 a barrel.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iraq seizes drone-launching platform used for targeting Saudi oil pipeline
- list 2 of 3A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
- list 3 of 3Red Sea nations watch as Houthis seize Bab al-Mandeb strait
The apparent contradiction between US claims and surging oil prices shows the reality on the ground is complicated at best.
So, what do we know about shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, and where are oil prices headed?
What are the US, Iran and others claiming about the Strait of Hormuz?
Washington says traffic through Hormuz has been improving despite the two sides being in a diplomatic deadlock.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday said 10 million barrels of oil per day, on average over the past week, were passing through Hormuz, adding that “we’re back to two-thirds or north of two-thirds of the previous flows.
“So the world oil markets are tighter than we’d like today, but they’re not overly tight,” Wright added, according to US media outlet Bloomberg News.
President Trump has made similar claims, stating that the US is in “total control” of the strait and asserting that its forces are escorting ships carrying millions of barrels of oil through the waterway, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes.
Iran has, however, disputed the US claims. Tehran says it controls access to Hormuz and has warned ships against using routes it has not authorised. Last week, Iran announced a new restricted shipping zone around the crucial waterway.
Shipping data from tanker trackers also suggests traffic remains well below normal levels. Preliminary ship-tracking data shows vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz falling to single digits a day over the weekend, remaining well below the 10-day average of 14 a day, the Reuters news agency reported.
Reuters said a total of 14 vessels transited the waterway, with four exiting the Gulf and 10 entering it.
More than 100 vessels passed through the strait daily, carrying an estimated 20 million barrels of oil, before the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February.
The data is preliminary and subject to updates, as some vessels navigate the passage with their Automatic Identification System transponders switched off, meaning they are excluded from the official counts, Reuters added.
What is the latest with oil prices?
Oil prices jumped more than 3 percent on Monday after an Iranian ship was attacked on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West oil pipeline was damaged in a drone attack.
Brent crude rose $3.21 to $107.82 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate gained $3.17 to $103.22.
The rise came after Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was temporarily shut by a drone attack originating from Iraq, according to Saudi officials.
Riyadh has been using the pipeline to export oil via the Red Sea amid the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Four percent of the global oil supply will be threatened if the pipeline remains shut.
A series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on southern Saudi Arabia in recent days has further added to the uncertainty about oil supply originating from the world’s largest oil producer.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni group hit civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring 73 people, among them women and children.
The assault on the kingdom marks a sharp escalation in Yemen’s long-running war, which flared up again in July after nearly four years of relative calm under a United Nations-brokered truce.
Why are oil prices climbing, despite US assurances?
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, says oil prices are likely to remain under upward pressure as disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues, despite US claims that it is clearing traffic through the waterway.
“Despite US claims to the contrary, Hormuz is not under its control, and oil is not flowing freely,” he said.
Beauchamp says passage through Hormuz remains severely limited and ships continue to face attacks, while Houthi attacks on infrastructure have added another source of concern for energy markets.
“Near-month futures continue to trade at a premium to the spot price, a recognition that disruption is expected to continue, ratcheting up the pressure on the global economy,” he added.
Christopher Haines, the Global Head of Oil, Energy Aspects, says crude prices will continue to rise, pointing out that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are still notably lower than pre-conflict levels and the global oil reserves, which helped steady the market over the last six months, have dwindled.
“The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has little to give with announced releases having ended… while China will not be able to reduce their buying as they did in the summer due to higher seasonal demand in the winter,” Haines told Al Jazeera.
“Crude buying has been robust as refiners have to run harder to produce the fuels the northern hemisphere needs for heating.
“We believe oil prices can continue to rise, as without the buffers we have had over recent months, prices will have to increase to curb demand.”
Early on Sunday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Monday said it had intercepted and destroyed an advanced MQ-1 drone that was flying over the Strait of Hormuz.
“With no one in a hurry to talk, it seems that oil prices will continue to rise, and a return to March’s highs seems to be a matter of when, not if,” Beauchamp said.
A meeting in Oman between Gulf countries and Iran to discuss possible agreements on the Strait of Hormuz, which had been scheduled for Monday, was postponed, further delivering a blow to diplomatic overtures to end the six-month war.
Iran on Monday said the planned meeting was postponed by Saudi Arabia over the recent events in Yemen.
US Energy Secretary Wright also poured water over any hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough, saying “counting on a consensual agreement with Iran today is certainly not a good bet,” according to Bloomberg.
Meanwhile, Abdul Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, said the Houthi group’s growing presence along Yemen’s western coast, next to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, was also a reason for a surge in oil prices.
“The Bab al-Mandeb strait is now largely under Houthi control,” Khalique told Al Jazeera, referring to the vital shipping route connecting Asia with Europe.
“Having already taken the port of Mocha and the islands of Hanish and Zuqar earlier in the week, Iran-aligned Houthi forces seized the strategically vital Perim (Mayyun) Island and the mainland town of Dhubab, giving them effective control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline.”
Khalique added that war risk insurance for Hormuz transits, which stood at about 0.25 percent of hull value before the war, has climbed as high as 3 to 10 percent of hull value, depending on the vessel and route.
“For a $100m tanker, that range translates to a war risk premium of $3m to $10m for a single transit, before cargo cover and freight costs are added on top,” he said.
“The US may hold substantial military control over the battlespace, but it has not restored the conditions needed for a resumption of normal commercial shipping, and that gap is precisely why oil prices continue to climb even as Washington declares victory.”

Russian attacks kill 6, injure 43 across Ukraine over past day, Donetsk Oblast among hardest hit

Shark attacks, seriously injures surfer at popular beach in Australia
A surfer in his 50s was rushed to a hospital on Monday after being bitten by a shark at a popular beach in Western Australia, the state government and local ambulance service said.
Authorities said they received a report of a "shark incident" around 9:45 a.m. at Glenfield Beach, just over 400 kilometers (250 miles) north of Perth.
The man is in a "serious but stable condition," national broadcaster ABC reported, citing local health authorities. The outlet identified the injured man as Mel Ismail and released images of a damaged surfboard, which will be tested to determine the species of shark involved.
Locals were advised to take additional caution around the beach.
Australian scientists believe increasingly crowded waters and rising ocean temperatures are shifting sharks' migratory patterns, which may be contributing to a rise in attacks.
A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten by a shark while swimming in Sydney Harbour in January. The attack that killed the boy was one of four recorded in the span of two days, which prompted officials to close dozens of the city's beaches.
Three divers were also fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June — two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.
Also in June, a woman was mauled by a shark at one of Australia's most popular beaches in Sydney.
The woman — a schoolteacher — last month recalled swinging a "left hook" at the predator before it dragged her underwater.
She was placed in an induced coma and had part of her left arm amputated after the June 13 attack.
Last November, a shark killed a woman and seriously wounded a man at a national park beach on Australia's east coast in a rare instance of the predator attacking two people.
The International Shark Attack File, a database of global shark attacks maintained by the University of Florida, has recorded more than 1,280 shark incidents around Australia since 1791, including more than 250 fatal incidents. Such incidents have become more common as the population has grown and activities such as surfing and scuba diving have gained popularity.

Real-world problem-solving is at the heart of the education of the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:02:23 UTC
20:02:23 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
Real-world problem-solving is at the heart of the education of the future
"Life is not divided into separate subjects. It is essential to integrate multidisciplinary learning into the educational environment," says Georgi Ivanov, co-founder of the Educational Factory
Monday 14 September 2026 12:25
Monday, 14 September 2026, 12:25
Georgi Ivanov
PHOTO Diana Tsankova
Font size
Memorising facts without understanding them or gaining practical experience is a legacy of the past that distances young people from fulfilling their potential in an increasingly dynamic and demanding world. As the new school year approaches, Georgi Ivanov, co-founder of the Educational Factory organisation, raises the question of what education of the future should look like, linking the acquisition of knowledge to the purpose of the learning process and its application in real life.
According to the expert, one of the main challenges facing children and young people is seeing meaning in what they are taught in the classroom.
"The key problem is not a lack of knowledge," says Georgi Ivanov. "In the world of new technologies, we already have access to every kind of information and can easily retrieve it at any time. The problem is rather a lack of context, and if education fails to address this issue, we will lose students' attention. Meaning emerges when knowledge is applied within a system of cause-and-effect relationships and consequences. That is why it needs to be connected to a real-life scenario, whether in business, science or everyday life, while also demonstrating its practical application, results and impact in the real world."
PHOTO Technical University, Sofia
Leading educational models around the world are based on learning through solving existing problems, thereby creating a connection with the world around us. One example in Bulgaria, Georgi Ivanov notes, is the Technical University. According to him, the institution places a strong emphasis on practice, giving young people the opportunity to create value and present what they have achieved.
But how can the connection between education and the reality around us be established?
"Here we are perhaps talking about the greatest systemic deficit: education is isolated from life," Georgi Ivanov replies. Although national curricula provide a certain framework, the key role remains with teachers, he stresses, adding that he is increasingly encountering highly motivated and proactive educators. Despite the obstacles they face, they find ways to connect what is taught at school with its practical application.
"This leads to very good results among students who have such teachers and inspiring mentors in front of them," the expert concludes.
PHOTO Facebook/ Educational Factory
"There are three key supporting mechanisms, and the first is working on real-world projects," he continues. "When students solve problems that exist outside the school environment, they gain a much clearer idea of what they can apply in the future. There is a great deal of discussion today about professions that may disappear because of artificial intelligence and new technologies. That is why developing soft skills is becoming increasingly important."
Soft skills, he explains, are the abilities that enable people to interact with one another and manage their behaviour. Thanks to these skills, people can adapt and learn quickly, allowing them to succeed and develop in a positive direction.
"The second condition is contact with professionals, because no matter how much you read and how interested you are, if you do not have a mentor to inspire you, give you the right guidance and provide feedback, it will be much more difficult to navigate this world. And the third key mechanism is interdisciplinarity, because life is not divided into subjects and every project involves different elements, such as mathematics, communication, technology, critical thinking and teamwork. That is why it is important to integrate interdisciplinarity into our educational environment."
PHOTO Technical University - Sofia
Georgi Ivanov points out that although new technologies are increasingly entering education as tools, the key remains the human context.
"We need to adapt new technologies to the human context. The real world is not created by simply adding practice to theory. It is created by turning learning itself into practice. This is precisely why we place such emphasis on the practical side of things."
An argument in support of this approach is that experience is more powerful than theory because it simultaneously activates emotion, action and memory, turning them into one of the strongest mechanisms for learning.
PHOTO Facebook/ "Educational Factory"
"Theory is the foundation on which we need to build, but experience is linked to transformation, and that is the most important thing," Georgi Ivanov says. "When a person learns by doing, processes take place in the brain that are different from those involved in passively receiving information. Instead of activating a limited number of cognitive areas, as happens when we listen or read, a broader neural network is engaged, bringing together thought, emotions and action and leading to the creation of more deeply integrated knowledge.
This, in fact, 'anchors' information more firmly, because it is no longer abstract. It carries meaning and context and becomes something we personally own."
In conclusion, Georgi Ivanov admits that his favourite way of learning is precisely through experience, because the things that we experience ourselves are the ones we remember longest. Through memory, the context, the time, the place and the people resurface, and it is as if everything comes alive once again.

Russia will temporarily halt natural gas supplies to Armenia for scheduled maintenance and repair work in Russia, Gazprom Armenia announced.

The company stated that domestic reserves and additional natural gas volumes from Iran will ensure that, during this period, “uninterrupted and reliable gas supply to consumers in the republic will be provided without restrictions.”
Russian natural gas supplies to Armenia were also suspended for scheduled repair work a year earlier, in the second half of September.
Relations between Moscow and Yerevan deteriorated sharply shortly before Armenia’s parliamentary elections in early June. Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan are also demanding that Armenia hold a referendum on whether to remain in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or continue pursuing EU membership.
On September 11, Pashinyan said Armenia is looking for alternatives to Russian gas. “Gas isn’t cheap in Armenia. Compared to other countries, Armenia sees the largest markup in pricing from the border to the consumer. Gazprom Armenia is making large profits, and that’s also a fact we need to note,” he said. Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov had previously said Russia could offer Armenia a preferential gas price on a market basis if Yerevan decides to leave the EAEU.
