Houthis capture more Yemeni Red Sea islands, tightening grip on Bab el-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:01:18 UTC
20:01:18 KST

The Hanish archipelago fell after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew, adding to Houthi control of Mokha and Perim Island. More than 80,000 people have been displaced in two weeks of fighting, as the internationally recognised government vows to regroup.
Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis captured more islands in the southern Red Sea, government and Houthi officials said Monday, strengthening their control of a major maritime shipping route.
The capture of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the group's swift advance around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key passage for oil shipments that has become even more crucial during the Iran war as the Strait of Hormuz remains under US and Iranian blockades.
Like Hormuz, located at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula — is a chokepoint that connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea, making it a key waterway for cargo traffic to the Mediterranean Sea.
For more than a month, the Houthis have been striking Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, stepping up pressure on global oil prices and boosting Iran's leverage in its war with the US.
Forces of the internationally recognised Yemeni government have been attempting to rally and fight back, but the Houthi gains have seemingly come with little resistance.
The Houthis deployed on the Hanish islands, 160 kilometres north of Bab el-Mandeb, after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official.
The group officially known as Ansar Allah captured the archipelago after seizing the nearby mainland port city of Mokha and the island of Perim, inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In parallel, they waged an offensive further inland, particularly in the longtime battleground province of Taiz.
The Houthis also launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets on Monday.
The Houthis said they fired dozens of drones and missiles at the kingdom — which backs the Yemeni government — prompting the Saudi Civil Defence to issue brief alerts in the neighbouring cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha.
The Saudi Civil Defence overnight said a Houthi projectile fell in a different area near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings.
Riyadh did not announce any new attacks targeting the Houthis.
Thousands fleeing fighting in Yemen
The Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.
The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July after a UN truce that had largely maintained quiet since 2022, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, prompting the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.
Some 150 civilians have been killed in fighting since 3 September, the government's Human Rights Ministry said. More than 200 civilians have been wounded, it said.
Thousands of families have fled their homes in Taiz and nearby provinces in the past day alone, said Khanzad Shah, acting head of Islamic Relief, a charity that operates in the area.
"Many of them don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied," he said.
The UN has estimated that more than 80,000 people have been displaced in the past two weeks, including over 2,000 people who fled by boat to Djibouti.
The fighting threatens to reignite a war that for more than a decade brought disaster to Yemen, killing more than 150,000 people and driving the country to the brink of famine.
The internationally recognised government supported by an array of disparate militias controls the south and east, including the key southern port of Aden.
The Hanish islands, newly captured by the Houthis, had been controlled by the UAE-backed allies. However, the UAE dismantled its military infrastructure there earlier this year.
For years, Saudi Arabia waged an air campaign against the Houthis, while backing the government and allied militias, yet it has appeared reluctant to throw itself fully back into the war, despite the Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping.
The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
Yemeni government forces to regroup?
On Sunday, the Yemeni government's military said it launched airstrikes on Houthi positions in the port city of Mokha, the coastal town of Dhubab and elsewhere in Taiz province.
The Houthis reported strikes by the Saudi-backed forces in Taiz province and artillery shelling in Saada province, the birthplace of the Houthi movement on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia.
Sultan al-Arada, a member of the government's presidential leadership council, described the collapse of government forces in Mokha, about 80 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and elsewhere on Yemen's west coast as "painful and regrettable."
He said in a televised interview aired late Saturday that forces "are currently regrouping and will return to the battle."
Rashad al-Alimi, who leads the presidential council, sought on Sunday to downplay the defeats as "incidental," according to comments published by the country's state-run SABA news agency.
The government "will remain clear and fixed on the goal of retrieving institutions and of reclaiming sovereignty over all national territories," al-Alimi said.

‘Carbon fever’ threatens hard-won Indigenous rights in Bolivian Amazon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:57 UTC
20:00:57 KST

In the village plazas of Pando, a remote northern Amazonian region of Bolivia, the main talk is no longer just about the next harvest. One pressing issue is the “invisible air” being sold to foreigners who regularly visit their communities.
In June 2024, the country’s constitutional court struck down the ban on a funding mechanism linked to carbon markets. Since then, Indigenous leaders of three ethnic groups – the Tacana, Ese Ejja and Cabineño – have complained about companies and foundations that arrive with offers of “climate solutions”, often during the ever more frequent droughts or floods.
“We heard about this [carbon] business and nobody understood what it was,” says Julio Mayo, from the Cabineña nation. “Even today, I don’t think people understand. We’re still in doubt.”
In this corner of the Amazon, the air is a heavy blanket, scented with damp earth, and rivers snake through some of the world’s most pristine rainforest. For Mayo and others, the forest is not a carbon sink or a commodity – it is their living pharmacy, a guarantee of food security and a sacred ancestor.
Bolivia, where more than 40% of the population identifies as Indigenous, and whose consent to any proposed laws or development of their land and resources is protected by the International Labour Organization’s Indigenous and tribal peoples convention, was until recently Latin America’s staunchest opponent of carbon markets. A law passed in 2010 on the “rights of Mother Earth” in effect banned the “commodification of nature”.
Yet that had changed even before the court decision. Months before the ban was overturned in June 2024, disputed carbon contracts were already being signed. On 12 March 2024, a handful of Indigenous leaders in the Pando region signed a contract with the Federico Hecker Foundation.
The agreement handed the foundation control over carbon credits, audits and sales across 440,000 hectares (about 1m-acre) of the Multi-ethnic Indigenous Territory II (TIM II) for 30 years. Lucio Ayala, TIM II’s president, says: “They just told us that we were going to receive money, a lot of money, but they didn’t explain what it was about.”
TIM II is shared by the Cavineña, Tacana and Ese Ejja nations – each with its own authority, but held under a single collective land title. After the Cavineña, the Ese Ejja signed the foundation’s contract in September 2024.
Mayo says: “They spoke nicely about the project, the benefits, but it wasn’t in the contract.”
Leaders of a different community who did sign the agreement say they were swayed less by an understanding of carbon markets than by promises of food aid and better housing, which never materialised.
The foundation “categorically denies that it offered money, bribes or personal benefits to obtain signatures”, and says it put forward “from the outset a comprehensive proposal for conservation and community development” that would go beyond “simply generating carbon credits”.
It added: “Food security, housing and basic services were not isolated promises – they were part of a multidimensional development proposal designed to ensure that forest conservation would also lead to social and economic improvements and contribute to various SDGs [sustainable development goals].”
Leaders of the Tacana say they refused the offer specifically because they recognised the Hecker name. Federico Hecker was a Swiss immigrant who arrived in Bolivia’s northern Amazon during the late 19th-century extractive boom and rose within the rubber empire. His son, Peter Hecker, later served as a senator for Beni and became a Brazil nut trader.
Tacana families remember the Heckers not as conservationists but as patrones – bosses under Bolivia’s old debt-peonage system. “Many families were bonded to the Heckers,” one community member recalled.
Although debt peonage, known in Bolivia as Pongueaje or Pongueaje, was formally abolished under agrarian reforms decreed in 1953, Indigenous people maintained only precarious control over their ancestral lands. That arrangement ended only when Indigenous pressure for land reform won the collective title to TIM II in 2001. Another Indigenous leader claims the contracts are “the way they [the Heckers] are trying to get back what they consider their land”.
Referring to the large Bolivian estates geared to the extraction of rubber and then Brazil nuts, the foundation acknowledged that “the general history of the Amazonian barraquera economy … went through periods of highly asymmetrical labour relations and mechanisms of empowerment, indebtedness and economic dependence that gradually changed throughout the 20th century”, but states that “this context does not lend credence to allegations against the Hecker family regarding members of TIM II”.
By March 2025, TIM II’s board and the Ese Ejja nation had formally rejected the agreement, saying their representatives had been “surprised, pressured and manipulated” into signing a document that “should never have existed”. The foundation rejected the allegations.
Opposition to the agreement was not confined to TIM II. At the National Forum on Land, Territory and Environment in Santa Cruz in October 2025, Indigenous organisations from across Bolivia issued a joint statement saying: “We reject carbon bonds for promoting the commodification of nature and undermining territorial sovereignty and Indigenous rights.” They also pointed to deals such as the Hecker contract as examples of what they feared.
Critics warn that the carbon market, meant to fund environmental projects and cut emissions, often worsens inequalities. Problems include unfair contracts that remove community control, land grabs, displacement, limited access to traditional lands, conflicts with food production, and false promises of jobs, income and infrastructure.
The deal may have been signed in Bolivia’s remote fringes, but it has direct ties to the country’s parliament. Aimé Hecker Urresti was elected in 2025 as a national MP and has been working with the centre-right government of Rodrigo Paz Pereira to advance carbon markets.
The foundation’s website lists Hecker Urresti as chairman and credits him with the “groundbreaking political and legal effort” that opened Bolivia to carbon markets. He is one of four MPs who formally presented a bill in 2025 to congress to regulate the market his own foundation wants to operate in.
“It cannot be that a lawmaker is now promoting a law that will regulate an initiative in which his own family is involved,” says Miguel Vargas, a lawyer for Indigenous rights and a former director of the Centre for Legal and Social Studies (CEJIS), a non-profit Bolivian human rights organisation based in Santa Cruz de la Sierra.
Hecker Urresti says all parties to the foundation’s contracts were fully informed of the stipulations in advance and that the foundation respects their right to annul the agreements.
“The communities were not regarded as passive recipients. The contracts assigned roles to the Indigenous councils and authorities for outreach, coordination, providing information to the communities, and monitoring and oversight,” the foundation said in a statement.
Hecker Urresti also denied any conflict of interest and stressed that the bill had been substantially revised since the initial draft.
Bolivia’s supreme decree 5264, issued in October 2024, centralises control of the market in the national government but excludes Indigenous authorities from its structure and sets no binding rules on consent, carbon ownership or benefit-sharing on Indigenous land. A new bill, which is reportedly intended to address this, mentions consultation but grants no veto rights and bears Hecker’s signature.
“The draft bill is not intended to establish privileges but to define general, transparent, verifiable rules that apply equally to all participants in the carbon-credit market,” he says.
Ayala says he learned about the new bill only when reporters told him. “Now the worry is with the current government. I’ve just heard about it; they’re drafting a law so carbon can be sold. If it passes, what are we supposed to do? We no longer have a voice or a vote,” he says.
However, Hecker Urresti says: “Comments [were] gathered during the consultation process with Indigenous organisations, public bodies, sub-national governments, specialists and other stakeholders involved in climate finance.”
Struggling economically and battling loss of forest, the country’s president is now touting Bolivia as a new source of carbon credits, with the pro-business government saying it aims to sell billions of dollars’ worth in the coming years.
European governments and initiatives are also involved. The EU says it has never directly funded carbon-credit projects in Bolivia, yet an internal planning document for a joint €24m (£21m) EU-Swedish climate programme states that Bolivia’s opening to carbon markets took place “with significant support from the EU-Sweden initiative”.
The EU delegation in Bolivia maintains it “did not influence or participate directly” in adopting the decree. Since 2021, the EU has allocated approximately €104m for environmental programmes in Bolivia. Last year, the EU officially incorporated credits into its emissions-reduction targets by 2040.
Deep in the Amazon, local communities are gathering the last of the season’s nuts and preparing their small plots of yucca. They have survived the rubber fever, the timber fever and the gold fever. Now they fear that “carbon fever” will deprive them of full rights to their lands.

Zuckerberg says the science isn’t settled. But the harms of short-form video on the brain are starting to show | Caty Enders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:57 UTC
20:00:57 KST

A few years ago, when I’d just started graduate work, I was waiting with a grandmother finishing a questionnaire I’d handed her about her 19-year-old granddaughter who was in the testing room next door. They were participating in a study that used brain imaging to look at adolescent development. The older woman had a soft southern accent and a warm laugh.
“What’s funny?” I asked.
“Cellphone use,” she said, gesturing at a question about how much time her granddaughter spent on her device. “When is she not on it? And my younger granddaughter, she just turned 18 – I mean, I think she’d die if you took the phone away from her.”
I told her that’s what I studied – “well,” I said. “Mostly social media.”
“Social media!” She shook her head. “Sometimes I think that’s the worst thing that ever happened to us.”
In the years since, that sense of broad, far-reaching harm has worked its way from our collective consciousness into thousands of high-profile lawsuits currently making their way through US courts. Last week, yet another began in New Mexico, focused on user data and the Cambridge Analytica scandal. In October, teenagers in Los Angeles will argue that Meta, YouTube and Snap caused serious mental health issues.
The most high-profile suits have focused on adolescent mental health, child sexual exploitation and, to a lesser extent, data privacy.
But in the years I’ve been researching how digital media is changing us, I’ve been increasingly concerned with how little we know about its cognitive effects, particularly those of short-form video, the format that now dominates every social media platform.
The vague sense that we are being cognitively hollowed out, dulled and diminished by our latest technology is captured in the term “brain rot”, recognized by the makers of the Oxford English Dictionary as the 2024 word of the year. And the more researchers look at it, the more it seems to describe distinct cognitive changes that are now being borne out by science.
The literature is still limited, but the most recent meta-analysis, published in Psychological Bulletin, examined the roughly 70 quantitative studies focused on the mental health and cognitive effects of short-form video. The majority of this research comes from China, where platforms are heavily regulated. Still the authors found an association with negative cognitive changes – stronger, in fact, than the association with poorer mental health.
The strongest relationships were with attention and impulse control. But relatively few studies looked at anything else, such as memory, decision-making, language or reasoning. In that analysis, the available research on memory amounted to a single study.
Whether individuals described their use as compulsive – or something they couldn’t control – predicted the worst cognitive outcomes.
Mark Zuckerberg and other social media executives have repeatedly argued that current science doesn’t back up public concern. And it’s true that active social media use – connecting with friends and family, sharing updates, writing and creating content – can be psychologically and cognitively beneficial.
The trouble is, tech companies have increasingly ignored the preferences of their users and promoted passive engagement, pushing the zombie-making infinite scroll and time-dissolving short-video feed – a digital format that seems almost universally damaging.
In my own research, I’ve found surprising relationships between memory and both cellphone use and short-form video. These early findings call for replication, but they held even after accounting for depression and anxiety.
The more time young adults spent on their phones, the worse they performed on a test of working memory, the system that holds information in mind while you’re using it. What you rely on to follow an argument or carry out a plan.
And in study participants who described their short-form video use as out of control, episodic memory was measurably weaker. This form of memory might be thought of as the internal record of your own life – the ability to travel back and revisit various moments. It is how we develop our sense of self in relationship to the world over time.
I’ve been dogged by the idea that, due to my own digital media habits, I might be moving through my days with a befogged sense of what I just did. What I should do next.
Even more alarming is the possibility that we are becoming less and less self-aware and creative in our own internal lives. Memory and imagination run on the same circuitry. In a 2007 study, patients with damage to the hippocampus, the brain’s memory hub, struggled to construct imagined scenes. Remembering the past and picturing a reality you haven’t lived appear to be the same act, run in opposite directions. If we are degrading the one, we might be degrading the other, damaging our ability to envision and enact a new future.
Perhaps these cognitive relationships feed on themselves as a sort of cyclone, driving diminished capacity that in turn results in more helpless digital media consumption. Perhaps collective cognitive changes could have large sociological or political implications.
The head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said in a state trial in California last February that he doesn’t think Meta products are “clinically addictive”. And on semantics, he’s right. The only behavioral addiction the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders currently recognizes is gambling.
But clinical addiction doesn’t have to be the mechanism behind what we observe as problematic use. With all my concerns about the cognitive effects of short-form video, I’ve still been unable to quit Meta platforms. After many rounds of locking myself out, I always come back for the flickers of old Facebook, where I might stay connected to people and communities I care about. Where I can see a friend launch a brilliant new mosaics venture, or my mother organize events for her town’s bike community, thousands of miles away.
A peace negotiator and member of a working group I convened at the Santa Fe Institute described social media platforms as holding our most important relationships hostage. To access them, we wade daily through brain-rotting media we would otherwise choose to avoid.
The price we pay for connection is our own minds.
In its most recent legal settlement, Meta agreed to pay $17bn and make design modifications to better protect 13- to 17-year-olds: a two-hour daily cap across Facebook and Instagram; a lockout between midnight and 6am, with notifications silenced from 10pm; hidden “like” counts; a ban on cosmetic-surgery filters; and the option to return to an un-optimized-for-your-attention news feed.
The settlement doesn’t include rationales or any admissions of culpability. But implicit in the changes is the idea that short-form video, lack of choice, and passive, mindless consumption are the main culprits. Direct messages with personal contacts and long-form content are excluded – the things users both want and that we know are relatively safe.
Though the settlement is only geared towards protecting a subset of adolescents, what research we have suggests social media’s cognitive risks affect teenagers and adults equally. We all have grounds for wanting greater control over our digital environment.
It may be just a matter of time before cognitive research can do for social media what decades of epidemiology did for lead in the 1960s, 70s and 80s: allow concerned citizens to push for corporate changes that make the world safer for everyone.
Science and litigation will continue to lag behind the relentless pace of big tech. Knowing this, perhaps the safest way to approach the digital world, where we now spend most of our time, is to listen to our own minds and bodies. The science is telling us that teens – and their grandmothers – knew intuitively that something was wrong, even if research will take years to prove exactly what it was.
- 
  Caty Enders is a journalist and researcher exploring our relationship to technology. She writes the newsletter Standing in the Current

Islamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling it | Arun Kundnani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:56 UTC
20:00:56 KST

Five years ago, many Muslims wondered if the prejudices they faced were set to fade away. The “war on terror” was dwindling in prominence, and new enemies such as Russia seemed to be displacing fears of Islamic terrorism. Yet Britain’s Islamophobia has only intensified since then. A poll published in July found that two out of five Britons believe Muslims cannot integrate into British society. Earlier in the summer, it was reported that more than half of Muslims in Britain had personally experienced anti-Islam prejudice in the last year, and a quarter in a public place.
The evidence of a worsening climate for Muslims has been mounting since two summers ago, when racist riots erupted across the UK, targeting mosques and asylum hostels. Watching videos of those events, I was disturbed by the parents who brought their young children to watch while mobs attempted, with apparently murderous intent, to break into the buildings. It was not only hardened far-right activists but a much broader cross-section of British society that was willing to participate in racist violence directed at Muslims or asylum seekers assumed to be Muslim.
But it is the widespread indifference to anti-Muslim racist violence that is most distressing. Last October, a white man raped a Sikh woman in her Walsall home while shouting Islamophobic abuse, believing her to be Muslim, and telling her he was a “British master”. The case attracted little public comment, despite seeming to be part of a pattern of racist sexual crimes in the region. Likewise, there was only modest coverage of the rampaging knife attack that began at an Edinburgh mosque in June that left a number of men injured.
To understand why Islamophobia is so pervasive, we need to grasp the deeper forces that enable it. The first is a bedrock of anti-Islam attitudes set during the 1990s when, with the cold war over, neoconservative intellectuals began to see in Islam a new enemy to replace communism. After Muslim protests against Salman Rushdie’s The Satanic Verses, some liberal commentators also began to declare that Islam was incompatible with western values. That all might have remained a problem of cultural adaptation to be solved through community-building, but during the “war on terror”, anti-Muslim racism was institutionalised in the daily functioning of the British state by the Labour government. Ministers made regular speeches singling out Muslim communities as threats, while under the Prevent policy, thousands of public sector workers were trained to regard ordinary Muslim political and religious behaviours as indicators of extremism.
The second has to do with Palestine. The groundswell of opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza has been profoundly disconcerting to Britain’s foreign policy establishment. In turn, the hundreds of thousands of people who marched on demonstrations have been depicted as supporters of, or aligned with, Islamic extremism. That has restored a virulent atmosphere of animosity towards Muslims, who are again seen as dangerous and disloyal.
We might think, for example, of Keir Starmer’s description of planned protests on 7 October 2025 as “un-British”, his suggestion that further protests could be banned and his call for prosecution against demonstrators using contested phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – despite repeated explanations that such slogans are not calls for violence. His comments reflect a widespread belief that ordinary protest – against a genocide! – is actually something else: the importing by Muslims and their allies of dangerous foreign ideologies. But to say that is to demonise the bond of allegiance between Muslims in the west and Muslims in other parts of the world fighting colonial occupations. That community-based international solidarity, of the kind that Britain used to hold up as evidence of its tolerance, should only be welcomed.
Third, there are the barriers that make it hard to even raise the issue of anti-Muslim racism in a fruitful way. Talk about Islamophobia in the mainstream of British public life and you will face the ritual demand that you also condemn Islamic extremism and acknowledge antisemitism among Muslims. Of course, an attack on a synagogue is to be condemned as forcefully as an attack on a mosque. But the harder political question is how to create the conditions in which neither one of those attacks is made likely. In this, Jewish communities have the resolute support of the British government. Muslims do not. For decades, they have been on the receiving end of official disdain, and when they attempt to assert a modicum of political representation they are accused of “family voting”.
This matters because racism is about power. Its function is to divide society so that certain groups can be subjected to exceptional forms of exploitation or elimination. It is typically experienced as routine and structured powerlessness: the daily struggle to eke out a living in the face of discriminatory employers, public services riddled with suspicion, oppressive policing, immigration enforcement. Twenty-five years ago, policymakers at least paid lip service to racism as “institutional”, which helped to make visible some of its structural features. But that is no longer true. Racism is nowadays framed mainly as a problem of extremist individuals radicalised by hateful and polarising ideologies.
Tackling racism means overcoming that lack of power. But the opposite is happening as governing elites continuously reinforce racist attitudes. A decision, for instance, to allow Ukrainians fleeing war preferential entry to the UK while many Afghans fleeing war have to risk their lives in dangerous sea crossings – a policy of racial segregation that is as absolute and violent as those of the Jim Crow south of the US – is also a form of public messaging. Policymakers can hardly be surprised when ordinary people take their cue from such policies and decide that non-white immigrants must indeed be a threat to national identity. Racism applied at the border inevitably seeps into other areas of public life.
Then there is the other response to talking about Islamophobia: to switch the conversation to a victimhood competition, the never-ending game of fighting over whose oppression is greater, as if there were some way to rank Black people, Jews and Muslims by the scale of horrors they have experienced. What this misses is that the fate of Muslims is inseparable from the fate of all people of colour in the UK. What Britain does to Muslims today it is likely to do to Black people tomorrow, and vice versa. And if a future government of Britain decided to carry out the mass deportation of Muslims from the country, I have no doubt it would decide soon afterwards to do the same to Jews. When supporters of Israel promote Islamophobia, they are playing with fascist fires that will end up engulfing us all.
For decades, Britain’s mainstream political leaders have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties. They continue to do so, sleepwalking to social disaster with an unconscionable recklessness and complacency. It is high time they woke up.
- 
  Arun Kundnani is editorial director of Monthly Review Press

What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:56 UTC
20:00:56 KST

What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
The Chinese leader cares very little about personal rapport.
President Trump will host Xi Jinping for a state visit on September 24, once again putting his claimed bonhomie with the Chinese leader at the center of the relations between the two superpowers. But Trump’s insistence on the importance of this personal rapport shows just how little he understands his adversary.
I have been studying Xi ever since he became China’s heir apparent, and I became an analyst at the CIA in the waning days of the George W. Bush administration. I spent years deciphering Xi for U.S. presidents as the intelligence community’s top expert on Xi. And I spent two years as the director for China at the National Security Council, where I staffed all of President Biden’s interactions with Xi and coordinated diplomacy with China across the U.S. government.
For a decade now, Trump has oscillated between courting and skirmishing with Xi. After his first term, Trump called Xi a friend and described him as someone he knew well. His experience with Xi seems to have led him to believe that he has unique, firsthand insights into China’s leader that his staff and advisers lack; in the past year, he has excluded even his close confidants, such as Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, from intensive diplomacy with China, and has acted practically as his own China desk officer.
Trump’s go-to stratagem for gaining leverage with Xi has been to be unpredictable, or at least to try to be. Yet in Trump’s second term, Xi has surprised Trump more often than Trump has surprised him. That is because Xi’s modus operandi, at home and abroad, is that of a jack-in-the-box: He winds up patiently over years, sometimes decades, and then pops at the propitious moment. The result is always startling.
Xi rose to become China’s leader in large part by presenting himself as having the steady hands needed to restart stalled economic reforms without upsetting the comfortable gentlemen’s agreements that kept the Communist Party’s factional rivalries in check. But once Xi secured power, he launched a blistering campaign against the very party elites who had pulled him up.
Xi’s steeliness has caught Trump off guard, just as it did his Chinese colleagues. At the time of Trump’s first term, Xi was accustomed to playing politics as a quiet, intense poker match, in which the Chinese leader read the opposing players and considered his own cards with characteristic subtlety. Trump, meanwhile, approached politics and policy making more like a gambler on a hot streak at one of the casinos he owned. During his first encounter with Trump, at Mar-a-Lago in 2017, Xi learned about U.S. air strikes on Syria over a beautiful piece of chocolate cake. He spent the years in between Trump’s first and second terms winding up to deal with a president whose M.O. he now understood—and preparing to pop up when the moment was right.
That moment came early in Trump’s second term. In April 2025, the U.S. president rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs, which included some that amounted to a de facto embargo on China. Xi surprised Trump by being the only world leader to retaliate rather than conciliate. Trump was ultimately forced to fold.
In the run-up to the two leaders’ summit in Seoul last fall, Xi again surprised Trump’s team—this time by unfurling an expansive set of export controls on rare earth elements, which ultimately prompted the U.S. to roll back its own export controls on China. Beijing’s willingness to escalate was a remarkable departure from a previous pattern of downplaying differences ahead of such summits, and it underscored that Xi was more interested in curtailing Washington’s ability to target China than in striking a deal.
Accordingly, the meeting in Seoul, and Trump’s subsequent visit to Beijing in May, produced little beyond relatively minor commercial agreements affecting specific firms and sectors. The Trump administration, undoubtedly disappointed by the lack of any meaningful deal to emerge from these summits, chose to emphasize Trump’s efforts to deepen his rapport with Xi. The president evidently believes this personal relationship will allow him to secure deals that advance American interests.
This expectation has no observable foundation in Xi’s 14-year rule. Even by the standards of authoritarian rulers, such as Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Xi has shown himself to be unsentimental about personal relationships—including those with members of his own inner circle, to say nothing of the leader of China’s principal geopolitical rival. Xi is very different from Putin in this regard. Whereas Putin takes extravagant risks on the international stage but is loath to hold his associates accountable for incompetence, Xi is just the opposite. He is calculating and measured in international politics but pitiless in jettisoning even longtime associates for perceived malfeasance.
In January, Xi dismissed his military’s top officer, General Zhang Youxia. The relationship between Xi and Zhang went back decades, extending not just to their childhoods but all the way back to their fathers, who were comrades in arms in China’s ferocious civil war. Four years ago, Xi deferred Zhang’s retirement, keeping him on board to help manage the world’s largest and second-most-capable military. We do not know what motivated Xi to oust Zhang, but given the history between the two men, the act was as brutal and unexpected as anything in a season finale of Game of Thrones.
Xi’s approach to Washington has been similarly dispassionate. During Trump’s visit to Beijing, the American president lavished praise on Xi, only for the Chinese leader to respond with stoic indifference.
Trump’s desire to parlay personal charisma into deals may be one of his least idiosyncratic qualities. In fact, there is something about the impulse that is quintessentially American. Even—perhaps especially—for a Beltway outsider, ascending the American political ladder requires a tremendous amount of glad-handing and personal magnetism, if not charm. Those who reach its pinnacle often assume that the same qualities will serve them on the international stage. Joe Biden rose through the Senate, which required cordiality and the ability to strike deals with rivals. George W. Bush and Bill Clinton were known for their affability. Overbearing friendliness might even be described as our national affect.
By contrast, Xi grew up in a system that punished openness and personal dynamism. His father’s boss and mentor, the reformer Hu Yaobang, whose death in 1989 sparked the protests in Tiananmen Square, was known for his outspokenness, which played a crucial role in his political demise. Hu’s ouster extinguished freewheeling politicking from the ranks of China’s leadership ever after.
Going into his next encounter with Xi, Trump seems to genuinely believe that he has the upper hand. Yet an unsettling split screen has accompanied every summit of his second term. In Seoul, Xi walked into the meeting having just outlined the five-year plan for China’s development through 2030. By contrast, Trump was in the midst of the longest government shutdown in U.S. history. In May, Xi hosted Trump for a meeting that Trump had earlier postponed because of the war in Iran, which was going badly. Xi now plans to follow his state visit to Washington with a major party meeting to lay the groundwork for his fourth five-year term, which will start next year. Trump, meanwhile, will be at best a lame-duck president within weeks of the summit—or worse, if the Democrats are able to take back the House or the Senate.
The contrast evident at these meetings with Trump has surely reinforced Xi’s view of the United States as a declining but dangerous power, and of China as an ascendant one. Xi believes that time is on his side, so he does not need a deal. He’s happy to perpetuate an uneasy stalemate through a pantomime of rapport with Trump. In the meantime, Xi is winding up for the fifth U.S presidential administration of his tenure, whatever it may bring.

Nothing in the contents should be construed as asserting or implying U.S.-government authentication of information or endorsement of the author's views.

Top tennis players end public campaign after Grand Slams agree to advisory council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:27 UTC
20:00:27 KST

Dilara Hamit
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
The world’s leading tennis players have ended their 18-month public campaign against the four Grand Slam tournaments after organizers agreed to establish a formal council to give players a role in negotiations and decision-making.
The campaign sought a larger share of tournament revenue as prize money, greater financial support for player welfare and pensions, and direct consultation over decisions affecting competitors.
“Now that a formal council exists to carry this work forward, the public phase of the campaign led by the unified group of top players comes to a close,” the players’ representatives said in a statement reported by The Guardian.
They cautioned, however, that the campaign could resume if the newly created Grand Slam Player Advisory Council fails to produce results.
“The players will now work directly with the Grand Slams to establish the council, through which players themselves will be directly consulted and able to negotiate on an ongoing basis,” the statement said.
The Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and US Open agreed in August to create the council, a move that proved central to resolving the dispute.
Jannik Sinner and Aryna Sabalenka were among the most prominent players involved in the campaign, which began after a formal proposal was presented to the tournaments in July 2025. Carlos Alcaraz withdrew his support last month.
The dispute intensified during this year’s French Open, when players limited their media duties in protest. A similar action planned for Wimbledon was abandoned following talks with the All England Lawn Tennis Club.
The players said progress had been made across the campaign’s three central areas. The US Tennis Association committed $2 million to player welfare during this year’s US Open, while prize money increased across all four major tournaments.
Total Grand Slam prize money has risen to $415.6 million since the formal proposal was submitted, according to the statement. Players estimate that more than $30 million of the total represents additional growth beyond the increases that would have been expected based on previous years.
Their main financial demand, however, remains unmet. Players have called for prize money to reach 22% of Grand Slam revenues by 2030, while the current proportion remains at about 15%. The French Open is so far the only major tournament to indicate that it will introduce a revenue-sharing formula.
The players described the gains as evidence of what coordinated action could achieve in an individual sport, adding that they expected the new council to build on the progress and continue pursuing objectives that had not yet been fully realized.

What It Was Like to Know Gloria Steinem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

I was a 33-year-old organizer when I first met Gloria Steinem in 2007. Despite being a women’s studies major in college, I had not fully grasped Gloria’s role in supporting grassroots women's organizations. She had created the Ms. Foundation for Women to do just that, to fund and amplify women’s organizing, like the work I was doing with domestic workers in New York. Meeting her at their annual fundraising gala, I was moved by how kind, warm, and genuinely excited she was to learn about and support our efforts.
“Do you know about Carolyn Reed?” she asked me.
Reed founded the Household Technicians of America in 1971. Her organizing, along with the work of Dorothy Bolden and the National Domestic Workers Union in the South, catalyzed the inclusion of domestic workers in federal minimum wage laws after 40 years of exclusion from Roosevelt’s New Deal.
I had never heard of Carolyn Reed or Dorothy Bolden. None of my women’s history classes had taught me about these two Black women who helped pave the way before me. But Gloria knew Ms. Reed well; she frequently enlisted Gloria in domestic workers’ efforts to gain respect and recognition as professionals.
At the time, together with organizers from around the country, I was planning what would become the founding meeting of the National Domestic Workers Alliance. Gloria’s prompt helped us find our roots in the legacy of Black domestic workers organizing and leadership throughout the country, whose bravery has made our economy better for women generation after generation, a legacy our organization was founded to carry forward.
This is who Gloria was. She recognized value and power where others didn’t. She corrected the omissions that kept us from finding one another.
A year after we met, I reached out to Gloria to let her know that we were at an important point in our efforts to pass the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights in New York State, the first comprehensive state-level legislation to extend labor rights to domestic workers, including new protections such as paid leave. We were planning a 24-hour vigil in front of the governor’s office. We communicated by email; she formatted her emails like letters, with all the accompanying formalities and indentations.
“Dear Ai-jen,
Ok, I’ll see you there.
Love, Gloria.”
We were five years into our campaign. Dozens of domestic workers had taken time away from work and sacrificed their wages to hold vigil. When Gloria arrived, she joined our circle on the sidewalk across from the governor’s office, listened to everyone’s stories, and when it was her turn to speak on our little red and white battery-operated bullhorn, she spoke of Carolyn Reed, how she was applauding our campaign from heaven, and would be walking alongside us on our march to victory.
This was the beginning of a long friendship and mentorship. But Gloria’s specific form of mentorship included listening and sharing what she learned from other women, curated by her strategic mind and communicated with her unparalleled way with words. She did not give advice; she shared stories. She never saw herself as a mentor, as much as she felt mentored by others, always learning from the women she met, especially younger women.
Gloria identified as an organizer more than an activist, because organizers re-organize relations of power to be more equal, and put power in the hands of everyday people. When I told her we were experimenting with neighborhood-based organizing circles to reach more domestic workers, she told me that previous movements of women gathered in circles of 13—small enough that everyone felt seen and heard, but large enough to feel the power of the collective.
Like any good organizer, Gloria appreciated the chance to roll up her sleeves: she wrote letters to governors to help us get across the finish line in our legislative campaigns and called mayors to ensure that domestic workers would not be excluded from paid sick days legislation. If she was invited to speak at a press conference related to labor legislation, she would check with me to see how the bill impacted domestic workers.
Several years into our friendship, I found her essay “Revaluing Economics” in Moving Beyond Words. Published in 1994—years before the National Domestic Workers Alliance was even the germ of an idea—she wrote about care as an essential resource that our economic model has never adequately valued, in no small part because of its association with women. She argued that if we are to not only survive but thrive in the future, we must fundamentally protect and revalue care. The last 15 years of my work have been deeply shaped by these ideas.
More recently, I spent much of my time with Gloria through an intergenerational, multi-racial circle of women who affectionately call ourselves the “G Squad”—composed of a writer, two artists, a pro-democracy organizer, me, and Gloria. We gathered over the years to celebrate Gloria’s birthday, to strategize big moments in the women’s movement, or vet a new love interest in the mix. We learned about Gloria’s life and adventures from one another, and we learned about other women through Gloria.
Much has been shared about the talking circles Gloria hosted in her home, but Gloria was part of dozens of ongoing circles of relationships with women like ours around the world. I wondered how she had the time for so many, including us. She was one of the first people to send me a note when she learned I would be joining the Board of Trustees of the Ford Foundation.
“I can't tell you how happy it makes me to know that your understanding and way of organizing will be there—you who don't hold a finger to the wind, but become the wind,” Gloria wrote. “It also makes me feel a little better about the way too early loss of Wilma.”
She was referring to her close friend and former principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, Wilma Mankiller, who died of cancer with Gloria at her side. Wilma was a legendary organizer and leader who also served as a trustee of the Ford Foundation. Gloria urged me to read Wilma’s speech, Context Is Everything.
Gloria changed the context for women like me, our choices and our understanding of them. It was as if she lived on a different time and space continuum, one composed of circles of women throughout history, all “linked, not ranked.”
Her true gift was helping so many of us see the hidden stories, ideas, lives, and contributions of women. She helped us locate our place in the story. In this world sorted by hierarchies of human value, at a moment when too many of our stories are being erased, may her memory be a reminder that we are not alone in the world or in history.
We are part of a proud and vast legacy of women, seen and unseen, that continues to change the world. And that is exactly what Gloria would have wanted.

The Best Soundbars (2026): Sonos, LG, TCL, Bose, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

A soundbar is one of the smartest upgrades you can make for your entertainment room. The latest models sound loud, clear, and distinct, with realistic sound that is truly transportive—a thunderstorm sounds like rain from every direction, a sword fight reverberates with every clang.
There are tons of options to choose from, but all of my top picks went through rigorous hands-on (and ears open) testing. I chose the best models in a few categories, including ones that are ideal for bass, small spaces, or expandability.
For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the Best RGB TVs, Best OLED TVs, Best Cheap TVs, Best Home Theater Projectors, and Best Streaming Devices,
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Overall Soundbar
Specs
The Sonos Arc Ultra launched in 2024, but it’s still my soundbar champion, with the most pristine sound for movies, games, and music. With some of my other top picks outclass it in specific areas like surround sound or bass, the Arc Ultra’s great all-around performance makes it easy to recommend.
This model is a prime example of why soundbars are a great addition to any home theater. Dolby Atmos and DTS:X surround sound are convincing— the upward fighting and side channels make spear clanks and grunts in Predator: Badlands appropriately spatial. Play a song like Want Want by Maggie Rogers and you can feel the pounding electric guitars and synth in your bones.
And while the Sonos app has gone through ups and downs, room calibration just works without a lot of tedious tweaks and adjustments, especially compared to other brands I’ve tested.
While it’s not perfect—I would have liked an extra HDMI input and audio that is not quite so bright in the upper register—this is one powerful and sublime soundbar that’s an easy recommendation.
Best Soundbar for Surround Sound
Specs
You won’t find a better surround sound experience than the one the LG Sound Suite H7 provides, especially if you add the optional LG W7 subwoofer and LG M7 satellite speakers. They aren’t cheap additions, but they create a very immersive experience all together.
The system uses Dolby Atmos FlexConnect so you can place the extra speakers anywhere you want. Using the LG ThinQ app, you can then group the speakers for Dolby Atmos surround sound that’s ultra-realistic. When I watched The Last House, which has an exceptional audio design, the system placed creepy sound effects across every corner of the room.
Setup takes a little patience—you have to configure each individual speaker, add it to your network, group them together, and calibrate the sound to your room. But it’s worth the effort. I’ve never heard planes sound so realistic in my viewing room than watching Unbroken with this system.
It’s not as bass-heavy as some of my other picks from Focal and Klipsch, and the full system of soundbar, speakers, and subwoofer is pricey, but it delivers an excellent surround sound experience.
Best Compact Soundbar With Subwoofer
Specs
The TCL A65K soundbar is much shorter, thinner, and cheaper than most on my list, but it still packs a punch, especially for music and dialogue. It includes a subwoofer that connects wirelessly without any complicated setup. It’s a huge step up from any built-in TV or projector speakers, with much clearer dialogue, louder bass, and more detailed vocals. But with its small size, it can’t quite match the bombastic, spatial sound of my (admittedly much pricier) other top picks.
There is an included remote, but I actually found the TCL app great for controlling inputs and adjusting settings. It doesn’t support Wi-Fi connectivity, which surprised me, but HDMI eARC and Bluetooth connectivity is enough for most situations.
Most Compact Soundbar
Specs
Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata is a big fan of the Bose Smart Soundbar for its incredibly sleek and small design—it’s the most compact soundbar on this list by far at just over 27 inches across. Despite its small size, it has central, side-firing, and up-firing drivers, meaning more convincing spatial audio than rivals like the Sonos Beam Gen 2.
It’s got wide connectivity, HDMI eARC, optical IN, IR repeater, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth, plus the Bose Connect app for setup, network connectivity, EQ, streaming, and swapping between inputs. It lacks overall power and bass, but if space is tight, this is a great solution over built-in speakers.
Best Soundbar for Bass and Dialogue
Specs
Once I heard the soundtrack to The Odyssey on the Klipsch Flexus Core 300 soundbar, I was convinced it was the loudest and bassiest model around. But dialogue is also a strength—TV shows sounded crisp and clear even in chaotic scenes which can sometimes cause issues with lower quality soundbars.
You can also easily expand the system by adding up to two subs and side speakers, similar to how you can build out the Sonos and LG soundbars. The Klipsch app is a pleasure to use, and makes it easy to tweak inputs and settings.
Why is it not my top pick? The Dolby Atmos surround sound is not that convincing. In epic aerial combat scenes watching Unbroken and Masters of the Air, the planes didn’t sound like they were flying from back to front (like they should) compared to some of my other picks. Also, room calibration took a lot of effort and time.
Best Premium Soundbar
Specs
Loud and powerful, the Focal Mu-So Hekla soundbar is a 34-pound behemoth you want for explosive set pieces in movies, (think anything with Tom Cruise flying airplanes or jumping off of buildings). There are 15 speakers inside, including three woofers that deliver powerful bass that matches the Klipsch Flexus Core 300.
A big plus is the upfiring audio drivers for Dolby Atmos. It was the first time I noticed a loud clank sound up by my ceiling when the main character in Predator: Badlands extends a spear to the sky. Only the LG Sound Suite H7 has better surround sound, but the Mu-So Hekla is louder and boomier (in a good way).
I loved the Focal app as well—it’s easy to use for selecting inputs, adjusting settings and room calibration.
For music, I played Fleetwood Mac at high volume and never heard any distortion or hiss. A test track by Maggie Rogers called “Want Want” sounds like a nightclub has come alive.
This is a large, heavy, premium soundbar with a premium price tag. With such a big upfront investment, it’s disappointing that it isn’t more expandable—you can only add a subwoofer, not side or rear speakers like the Sonos, LG, and Klipsch.
Still, for sheer sonic superiority, the Focal Mu-So Hekla is one of my all-time favorite soundbars.
Honorable Mentions
Sonos Beam Gen 2 for $499: The Sonos Beam Gen 2 is an excellent compact soundbar options, especially if you have other Sonos speakers in your home. It doesn’t quite beat the Bose Smart Soundbar in terms of sound quality—the Bose has upfiring speakers, which gives it a fuller sound than the Beam. But with the recently announced Sonos Beam Ultra, I’m expecting the Beam Gen 2 to go on sale (or at least get discounted soon).
Sony Bravia Theatre Trio for $2,200: The Sony Theatre Trio has several outstanding features, even if it can’t quite keep pace with the Sonos, Focal, or other high-end models. A flagship from Sony, this package comes with a soundbar and two speakers (plus an optional sub), and has excellent center channel audio for clear and rich dialogue. The setup is easy and the room calibration actually makes a difference in terms of room-filling bass. Dolby Atmos was not super convincing, though. The Last House creepy sound effects didn’t emanate from above or the sides enough.
Bluesound Pulse Cinema for $1,499: Bluesound is better known for its small, high-res audio speakers, but this 47-inch-long soundbar sounds stunning for music too. While Dolby Atmos support is good, playing dream-like synth rock tracks like “I Will Wait” by Phoebe Bridgers reveals a truly amazing spatial audio experience. The mix seems to emulate all around the room. On “Walk Walk” by Maggie Rogers, the driving bass and drums sound ultra-realistic. This is a pricey soundbar, though, and others like the Sonos Arc Ultra sound more realistic, especially its upfiring drivers.
Polk Audio Signa S4 for $449: Former WIRED senior editor Parker Hall says that, despite its age, the Polk Signa S4 is an excellent-sounding soundbar, especially for the price. It’s simple to use, easy to setup, has a few modes to choose from (Movie, Music, and Night), and versatile 3.1.2-channel Atmos-enables speakers. It’s a little dated, though, and doesn’t have Wi-Fi connectivity. You can learn more in his Polk Signa S4 review.
KEF XIO for $2,500: For a true audiophile experience, consider the Kef XIO. Music and movies sound incredibly balanced, clear, and loud, which makes sense—Kef is known for its high quality stereo speakers. Compared to lesser soundbars, you’ll notice the uptick in quality right away, which is expected at this $2,500 price point.
Bose Lifestyle Ultra for $1,099: During my testing, I kept going back to the Bose Lifestyle Ultra to play music. While the Focal and Sonos models have more of a bone-crunching bass and slightly better Dolby Atmos sound effects, for music, this Bose soundbar filled the room better. A nice bonus is that the Atmos support worked for albums like Rumors by Fleetwood Mac on TIDAL, which plays in surround sound.
Samsung Q990H for $2,000: An updated version of their flagship soundbar (the Samsung Q990D), the Samsung Q990H uses a new Sound Elevation feature to enhance dialogue. Not hearing what people say is annoying and one reason some of us enable subtitles, but the Q990H alleviated that pain point somewhat. Samsung also added new software optimizations for sound leveling and more distinct audio at lower frequencies.
Why would you want to expand with more speakers?
Several soundbars like the Sonos Arc Ultra and the Klipsch Flexus Core 300 allow you to add extra speakers and even a sub (or two!) to the standalone soundbar. While this might seem like overkill since the soundbar itself is capable of simulating surround sound effects, adding more speakers will help with realism. Spaceships will sound like they are flying from the back of the room and gunfire will ricochet from the left to the right.
Why is Dolby Atmos so important?
Dolby Atmos is the gold standard for surround sound audio, competing with the less common DTS:X specification. Soundbars use upfiring speakers to give you the impression that music and movie audio is coming from above you or from the sides. Note that Dolby Atmos is often only available at the premium tier level of streaming apps like Prime Video and Netflix.
What is room calibration?
Audio tends to bounce all around the room, echo down hallways, and escape through open windows. If you are in a tiny space, the sound won’t have anywhere to go. Room calibration is one way to compensate for room size and unusual architectural features. A soundbar like the Sonos Arc Ultra has a calibrate feature, where it emits a tone and then listens on its microphone, adjusting its audio for that particular room. Having tested many soundbars, good calibration can make a huge difference.

AI Leaders Are Calling for a Slowdown. Trump’s Team Says It’s on Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

As calls for artificial intelligence regulation intensify, US President Donald Trump’s team have made it clear that if lab leaders want to implement an industry-wide slowdown, they’re going to have to do it themselves.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on the US government to regulate AI companies within a wider effort to slow the pace of the technology’s development in an essay published Saturday. The essay received rare endorsement from both OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns chatbot Grok, following a week of intense debate about the technology’s threats to human safety. Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella also called for pacing development.
Calls for AI slowdown and regulation have intensified after a number of researchers voiced major concerns in the last week about the speed of the technology’s advance. “AI progress is increasing,” former DeepMind researcher Rishub Jain told WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.”
But David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X, “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel … Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”
Amodei had requested the government enable competing AI companies to work together on standards without breaching antitrust law, either by participating in discussions or issuing a waiver for the companies involved. He also called for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party, though critics wondered how effective this would be. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know,” Sacks wrote.
Concerns about the US ceding its lead in the technology to China have caused the US government to mostly push back against the notion of slowing the pace of its development. “You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We’re leading China on AI,” he added, “and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
The US largely views China’s AI ecosystem as an economic and national security threat and has previously been caught short by the country’s advances in the technology. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday. “So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.”
In the meantime, companies say they are going to start taking voluntary steps to reestablish public trust that they are acting responsibly. On Sunday night, OpenAI’s Altman committed to a proposal by Amodei to give embedded third-party evaluators employee-level access to their firms to check that practices and products are safe and to report incidents. While these measures will have “significant costs,” he wrote on X: “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

Sexually Explicit Deepfake Sites Target 100-Plus Politicians in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Almost 150 politicians across Europe have been included on harmful deepfake pornography websites over the last few years, according to new research seen by WIRED. Some of the politicians, who are overwhelmingly women, have had their likeness included in explicit videos, while others have names and photos listed in disturbing database-like entries that can link to deepfake creation tools.
Analysis of around 160 domains that host deepfake abuse and other nonconsensual sexual content, by researcher Benjamin Shultz, has found that at least 138 women members of parliament (MPs) from 22 European Union countries have appeared or been mentioned on the sites. In contrast, only nine male MPs were referenced in any way. By Shultz’s calculations, it is 33 times more likely for women MPs to be targeted by deepfake ecosystems.
“Deepfake porn is part of a much bigger trend of online hate and intimidation against women and female politicians,” says Suzanne Kröger, a Dutch member of parliament with the Progressive Netherlands group, who was impacted. Kröger, who expressed anger at what the research uncovered, says the findings are “really deeply disturbing” and help to reveal the scale of abuse. “We are politicians, we have a platform and speak out,” Kröger says. “But meanwhile, there are millions of women victims of these criminal acts.”
The research, which has been published by German digital democracy think tank Agora Digitale Transformation, focuses on national members of parliament from all 27 countries in the European Union. Shultz, a fellow at Agora and the lead researcher at the American Sunlight Project, compiled the details of more than 5,800 members of parliaments across Europe in July and then used custom search engines to find where they appeared across the deepfake websites. (The research does not include members of the European Parliament).
Politicians from Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, and France appeared on the websites the most, according to the findings, and the more senior a politician is, the more likely they were to be targeted. Shultz alerted all of the MPs individually and provided guidance on how the content may be removed. The websites also include depictions of celebrities, journalists, and other public figures, he says. WIRED is not naming the websites in order to not drive further attention to the abusive images.
Multiple researchers and lawmakers say that while politicians have been targeted with deepfakes for years, it can damage democratic practices and create chilling effects that may stop women and girls from becoming public figures. “This discourages women from taking office in the first place and also crowds these women out of public life,” Shultz says. “There’s so much evidence to support that this does real psychological damage. This also does reputational damage for the future if they want to fade out of politics and have another career.”
“Deepfake videos are used to intimidate politicians but also to belittle women,” says Sarah Dobbe, a Dutch Socialist Party MP, who was impacted. “It is very important that if a woman or girl is victimized in this way, she can get direct support if needed, and that the content is removed quickly.”
Across the sites he monitored, Shultz categorized multiple categories of abusive content or behavior. His results include instances where MPs appeared in content that was actively being hosted by the sites, indexed results where content had been removed, and also a number of profiles and “gateways” where potentially new content could be created.
Multiple websites hosted pages that include the names of MPs, official photos, and in some cases their social media profiles or personal information. Some included sections “rating” the women’s bodies, Shultz’s report says. Often next to these MP biographies were links to so-called nudifier apps or the websites’ own tools that claimed to digitally undress people. “It has all the images, all the information, and a direct link to the tool, and in three clicks you can generate,” Shultz says. “That’s just as bad as actually hosting the content.”
Since AI-created deepfakes first emerged at the end of 2017, the underlying technology to produce them has become much more accessible, and the output of the tools has become more realistic. Over time, millions of nonconsensual AI images and videos have been created, mostly by men and boys, and are often used to harass, intimidate, or blackmail women and girls, including at almost 100 schools around the world.
“These platforms are designed to run like businesses,” says Henry Ajder, an AI adviser and deepfake expert who has been tracking the ecosystem since 2018. He says that while it is not surprising that politicians are being targeted in this way, the findings are helpful for officials in Europe to understand the severity of the issue. “The whole infrastructure is set up to do this at scale with ease,” he says.
In general, lawmakers have been slow to introduce legislation to tackle the growing array of harms caused by deepfakes. However, in recent months, some laws have started to be introduced. Both the UK and EU are planning bans on nudify services, while under the US Take It Down Act, at least two major deepfake websites publishing thousands of images and videos of celebrities have been taken offline. Reporting by journalists unmasking those behind the websites has also led to major sites being taken offline. Ahead of this story being published, WIRED found that at least half a dozen of the domains that appear in the research have recently been removed from the web—reducing the total number of depictions of the European MPs.
Shultz, who is also researching the number of depictions of UK and US politicians, previously analyzed how many US senators and members of Congress appeared on deepfake sites in 2024. After the websites were taken down, Shultz says, there has been a “significant decrease” in the number of depictions of those American politicians that appeared on the websites two years ago.
“It’s a priority to ensure that these images are taken down, but that also there’s strong regulation on this type of technology,” says Kröger.
