How Escalating Attacks in Yemen Impact Global Oil Trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

An escalating wave of attacks around the Red Sea has pushed oil prices above $100 a barrel, as Houthi territorial gains near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure threaten a route that has become a critical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sunday, Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Saudi Arabia, launched attacks against the Iran-backed Houthis along the Red Sea. The strikes were part of an effort to dislodge the Houthis after the rebel group captured the port city of Mokha and Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea, key positions that give the group a vantage point to threaten shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis also launched missiles at several areas in Saudi Arabia, and in recent weeks attacked the kingdom’s oil infrastructure and shipping. The group declared a blockade on Saudi vessels in July, but said other countries’ commercial shipping can continue through the narrow Bab el-Mandeb.
The escalation has pushed up energy prices around the world. It also potentially gives Iran leverage over the U.S. by threatening another maritime chokepoint, putting economic pressure on Washington just before the midterm elections.
The attacks come as diplomatic efforts to end the nearly seven-month-long U.S. and Israeli war with Iran have dropped off. An anticipated diplomatic meeting between Gulf countries and Iran was postponed, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi announced on Sunday. The meeting, meant to take place in Oman on Monday, would have been the first talk between Iran and Gulf Cooperation Council countries to discuss the Strait of Hormuz since a mid-June memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran collapsed.
The attacks have also reignited major fighting in Yemen’s yearslong civil war, which killed 150,000 people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The U.N.’s migration agency said more than 82,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen since the start of September. That includes more than 2,000 Yemenis who fled to Djibouti, which hosts a U.S. base on the other side of Bab el-Mandeb.
Here’s how escalating attacks in the Red Sea have impacted energy prices and what could happen next.
What is the latest escalation?
Saudi authorities said a projectile struck al-Tuwal in Jazan province, wounding two people and damaging a mosque, several buildings and vehicles. Earlier in the week, Saudi Arabia said a large wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks over four southern cities had injured 73 people.
The Houthis said they launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Sharurah military base in Saudi Arabia’s southern Najran region, near the border with Yemen. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed damage at the base.
The group alleged on Sunday evening that Saudi Arabia had conducted 58 airstrikes across Yemen during the preceding 24 hours, and 129 strikes across Yemen over the 48 hours before Saturday evening. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed those strikes.
Inside Yemen, government forces launched strikes near Mokha, Dhubab, and elsewhere in Taiz, claiming they destroyed Houthi vehicles and weapons. After initially retreating from parts of the western coast, government units said they were regrouping late Saturday and would return to battle.
The government-allied National Resistance said more than 500 of its fighters have been killed on the west coast over the past month, while more than 1,000 Houthis were killed in Hodeida and Taiz provinces over the same period.
How have the attacks affected oil and gas?
Oil prices climbed more than 2% on Monday. Brent crude futures opened at $108.23 a barrel in late Sunday trading, up $3.62 or 3.46%, while WTI futures opened at $103.20, up $3.15 or 3.15% from Friday’s close. U.S. diesel prices surpassed $6 a gallon on Friday for the first time on record, while oil gained more than 8% last week, with Brent surging over $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
Saudi Arabia closed its East-West oil pipeline as a precautionary measure after multiple drones from Iraq damaged infrastructure in the Riyadh and Medina regions. No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack, although U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran was “probably” responsible. Saudi Arabia had recently rerouted around 4 million barrels per day—around 4% of global supply—through the pipeline to circumvent Hormuz.
The attacks around the Red Sea have also added a substantial risk premium to transit through Bab el-Mandeb. Increased Houthi activity can discourage shipping even though the group said it will only target Saudi-linked vessels, Allison Minor, the director of the Atlantic Council’s Project for Middle East Integration and former U.S. deputy special envoy for Yemen, warned in a July analysis of the blockade. Tanker owners may weigh delaying voyages or charging higher freight rates, which could quickly raise costs for consumers.
While some shipments could be redirected north through the Suez Canal or Egypt’s SUMED pipeline, both of those routes are estimated to carry smaller capacity than Bab el-Mandeb and could mean longer, possibly costlier, journeys for some cargoes.
Experts say the duration of the disruptions will determine whether the current price increase becomes a sustained supply shock. If operations resume quickly, the pipeline’s effect could remain limited, June Goh, a senior analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Bloomberg. An extended shutdown, however, could force Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude exporter, to cut production, Goh said. Saudi Arabia reportedly has enough oil stored at Yanbu to sustain current exports for five to seven days.
The impact on global energy supply is exacerbated by severe restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz, which already pushed up energy prices around the world. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that Gulf oil exports in August were nearly half their pre-war level. Global oil inventories have fallen by 507 million barrels since February, the agency said.
Thye May Ting, an analyst at Hong Leong Investment Bank, wrote in a research note that Brent is likely to remain elevated because of the combined pressure at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, forecasting prices of $95 to $100 a barrel toward the end of the year.
Using a baseline of $110 a barrel, economist Mohamed Shadi projected Brent could reach a peak of $120 a barrel if 25% of oil flows through Bab el-Mandeb were halted, $145 if 50% of flows were impacted, and $229 under a complete shutdown.
Meanwhile, fighting near Hormuz has continued. A vessel transiting the Strait was struck by a projectile, causing a fire to break out onboard, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Sunday. Iranian state media said an Iranian commercial vessel was struck off its coast, killing one and wounding four.
The IEA projects world oil supply to average 100.7 million barrels per day this year, a decline of 5.7 million barrels per day from last year, according to its September report. It had previously forecast a year-over-year decline of 4.3 million barrels per day in August.
What could Saudi Arabia do?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly pressed Washington for more military support, but the Trump Administration has so far resisted direct participation. Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice on Thursday urging him to authorize U.S. strikes as the Houthis advanced along the Red Sea coast, but Trump refused. The U.S. had sent more than 100 military advisers to Saudi Arabia to provide military intelligence, according to CNN.
Trump said Saturday that the Houthis had called his Administration. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with, and we’ll get that straightened out,” Trump said.
The kingdom could independently intensify its air campaign and provide more support to Yemeni government forces on the ground, although Saudi air support reportedly failed to arrive during Thursday’s battle for Mokha despite requests from Yemen. A larger campaign could expose Saudi Arabia to more missile and drone retaliation from the Houthis, which it is likely keen to avoid after its costly intervention between 2015 and 2022 failed to defeat the group and prompted repeated attacks on Saudi cities, airports, and energy facilities.
Saudi Arabia could also turn to Pakistan and Turkey for help under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed last month. Riyadh has not formally invoked the pact before, but it could request additional intelligence and technological support, Riaz Khokhar, a researcher at Islamabad’s Institute of Regional Studies, wrote in Al Jazeera. Islamabad, however, may be wary of domestic opposition and a confrontation with Iran, Khokhar wrote. Instead, it might push for a multinational naval coalition to protect Bab el-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia could also pursue diplomatic efforts to negotiate a cease-fire. Minor suggested in July that the Houthi campaign may be aimed at extracting concessions from Riyadh rather than creating an all-out war. Other analysts told Reuters that the Houthi gains could push Gulf governments toward accommodation with Tehran, especially since Iran’s talks with the U.S. have tapered off while fighting has intensified.
Trump said Sunday that he still expects the Iran War to end this year, and that gas prices would “drop like a rock” once it did. Last week, Trump accused the Iranian government of prolonging the war in order to sabotage Republicans’ midterm prospects, but said Iran “can’t hold out any longer” and that the war would end “immediately after” the elections.
He also floated the possibility of maintaining a U.S. presence to control Iranian oil.
“We’ll ultimately get out [of Iran], unless we decide to stay and keep the oil like Venezuela,” Trump said. U.S. revenue from Venezuela, he added, “paid for the war many times.”

U.S. Navy’s San Diego heads out from Naval Base Guam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:59:58 UTC
19:59:58 KST

- USS San Diego (LPD 22), a San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock, departed Naval Base Guam on September 12, 2026, after a routine stop.
- The ship is forward-deployed to Sasebo, Japan, and assigned to Expeditionary Strike Group 7/Task Force 76, the 7th Fleet's amphibious command.
A U.S. Navy warship built to carry Marines ashore just wrapped up a stop at one of America’s most important Pacific outposts. USS San Diego (LPD 22), an amphibious transport dock, departed Naval Base Guam on September 12, 2026, after transiting Apra Harbor during what the Navy described as routine operations in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of responsibility.
Navy amphibious ship movements like this one are drawing closer reader attention these days, as the United States remains engaged in an open-ended war with Iran that has strained the fleet’s resources in the Middle East.
There’s nothing dramatic about a port call, but the ship itself does an unusual job. San Diego belongs to the San Antonio class, a type of vessel the Navy built specifically to move Marines and their gear from sea to shore. Below the flight deck sits a well deck, a flooded compartment that can launch air-cushioned landing craft or a conventional landing craft straight out the stern. Above deck, the ship can land helicopters or tiltrotor MV-22 Ospreys. Put those pieces together and you get a floating staging base that can put a battalion of roughly 700 Marines onto a beach without needing a port.
San Diego is the fourth Navy ship to carry the city’s name, following an armored cruiser from 1914, a World War II-era light cruiser, and a combat stores ship commissioned in 1969. This version was built at Northrop Grumman’s Ingalls shipyard in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and commissioned in 2012. Rather than being based stateside, it’s forward-deployed to Sasebo, Japan, meaning it’s stationed in the region full time instead of sailing over from the United States for each deployment. That arrangement lets the Navy keep amphibious ships closer to potential trouble spots in the Indo-Pacific and cuts down the weeks it would otherwise take to steam from California or Virginia.
The ship falls under Expeditionary Strike Group 7, also known as Task Force 76, which serves as the Navy’s amphibious arm within 7th Fleet. The command is headquartered at White Beach Naval Facility on Okinawa, though most of its ships, San Diego included, are actually based at Sasebo and travel south to pick up embarked Marines before heading out on patrol. Task Force 76 oversees a mix of amphibious ships, helicopter squadrons and beach landing units, and it’s the Navy’s go-to organization whenever the 7th Fleet needs to move Marines by sea, whether for an exercise, a disaster-relief mission, or something more serious.
That’s where 7th Fleet comes in. Headquartered in Yokosuka, Japan, it’s the largest of the Navy’s forward-deployed numbered fleets, covering an enormous stretch of ocean from the international date line west to the India-Pakistan border. Ships assigned to it spend most of their careers training and operating alongside allied navies in Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and elsewhere in the region, rather than rotating home between deployments the way many U.S.-based ships do.
Guam fits into that picture as a forward staging point. The island, a U.S. territory roughly 1,500 miles east of the Philippines, hosts both Naval Base Guam and Andersen Air Force Base, and it functions as a logistics and refueling hub for American ships and aircraft moving through the western Pacific. Apra Harbor, where San Diego pulled in, is a regular stop for Navy vessels passing between deployments in the region, so a single-day port visit like this one doesn’t typically signal anything beyond routine scheduling.
The Navy did not say what brought San Diego to Guam this time or where the ship is headed next. It’s also unclear whether the stop was tied to a broader deployment involving other ships from Expeditionary Strike Group 7 or Task Force 76, or whether San Diego was traveling largely on its own. Ship movements like this are common enough that the Navy doesn’t always spell out the full itinerary, and unless there’s a specific mission to announce, port visits and transits generally get logged rather than explained in detail.
For now, what’s confirmed is straightforward: an American amphibious ship built to land Marines on a beach spent time at a key Pacific base and then got back underway. Whatever comes next for San Diego hasn’t been made public.

Unknown

10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

(AA Photo)
Solar and wind generated 23.7 percent of Türkiye’s electricity in the first seven months of 2026, according to Energy and Natural Resources Ministry figures.
Solar accounted for 11.6 percent of generation, compared with 0.4 percent in 2016, while wind’s share more than doubled to 12.1 percent from 5.7 percent over the same period.
Solar generation also reached a monthly record of 5.37 billion kilowatt-hours in July, surpassing the previous high set in June.
Combined installed solar and wind capacity reached 42,865 megawatts at the end of July, accounting for about a third of Türkiye’s total electricity generation capacity of 126,476 megawatts. Solar capacity stood at 27,507 megawatts and wind at 15,358 megawatts.
Solar’s share of installed capacity rose to 21.7 percent from 1.1 percent in 2016, while wind’s share increased to 12.1 percent from 7.3 percent.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the expansion supported Türkiye’s goals of energy independence and a cleaner energy supply.
“We have carried out a major transformation in Türkiye’s energy sector over the past 10 years,” Bayraktar said.
He said Türkiye would present new renewable energy targets at the COP31 U.N. climate conference in Antalya and continue investing in infrastructure to make reliable, clean and affordable energy accessible to everyone.

Sweden faces political uncertainty as election deals far-right a blow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:57:52 UTC
19:57:52 KST

Sweden faces political uncertainty as far-right loses some of its vote share in super close election
Sweden faced political uncertainty Monday after an election thriller that saw the left-wing opposition hold on to a slim lead with votes still left to count. Sunday's election also served up a surprise setback for the far-right Sweden Democrats, who lost ground for the first time since entering parliament 16 years ago.
The leader of the left-wing opposition, Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, and outgoing conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson each said they wanted to explore coalition options to secure power and form a new government, but both would have to make major concessions to obtain a majority.
While the left-wing held a slim lead, the bloc was expected to face thorny negotiations to form a government, with the talks expected to drag on for several weeks. Parliament can vote on a new prime minister on Sept. 29, at the earliest.
After Sweden's 2022 national election, it took 37 days to form a government, much shorter than the 134 days it took to do so in 2018.
Political analyst Mats Knutson at public broadcaster SVT said both blocs were likely to end up in a "stalemate that paves the way for a long and troublesome process of forming a government, which could end in a snap election."
"One or several parties may have to abandon their 'red lines,'" he said.
With 95% of the votes counted on Monday, the four opposition parties held a three-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Prime Minister Kristersson's right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration far right.
But observers warned those results could still change, with some votes only due to be counted by Wednesday.
"The situation is really tight, and it's been more and more polarized in Sweden the last years," 48-year-old construction worker Mikko Duvaldt told the AFP news agency on Monday. "It's going to be a tough situation for each side to form a government."
"A culture of negotiation"
If the left-wing majority is confirmed, Andersson, a staunch defender of Sweden's welfare state, will attempt to form a government with the three other parties on the left: the Greens, the left and the center. But the bloc is fractured by deep ideological differences.
The center has said it would refuse to support any government including the left, and the left has said it would not support any government of which it is not a member.
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson is meanwhile expected to court the Center Party — which, until 2019, had been part of the right-wing bloc — to try to build a majority on his side.
"I will therefore, even if tonight's result stands, examine whether there are any possibilities within this non-socialist parliamentary majority to find some workable government constellation," Kristersson told his supporters on election night.
Annika Freden, associate professor in political science at Lund University, said Kristersson could expect to get the cold shoulder from the center.
"Kristersson reaching out to the center is expected, but the center is fundamentally opposed to entering into an alliance with the far-right, so nothing will come of it," she said.
She told AFP she thought the parties would do everything in their power to avoid a new vote.
The negotiations on the left will be about "how much they can get through and will determine if and when the red lines are relaxed," she said. "In Sweden we have a culture of negotiation, and there is a strong reluctance to call a snap election."
Far-right retreats
The anti-immigration Sweden Democrats party fell to 17.6% from the more than 20% of the vote share it won four years ago, relegating it to third place behind the Social Democrats and Kristersson's Moderates.
The Sweden Democrats, a party that traces its roots to Sweden's extreme-right fringe, has spent the past two decades moving steadily toward the center of political power. It first entered parliament in 2010. By 2022, it became the country's second-largest party and agreed to support Kristersson's minority government from outside the cabinet. The arrangement gave the party substantial influence over immigration, crime and other policies without formal responsibility for government departments.
Observers attributed this election's decrease in popularity to the fact that strict policies on migration and crime had now become part of mainstream politics.
"Migration issues were strongest in 2015-2016 and now many parties are in favor of a restrictive policy, and the Sweden Democrats haven't succeeded in being strong on other issues," Freden told AFP.

Jailed Editor, Closed Outlet: The Rapid Demise of Kazakhstan’s Top Independent News Site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:57:00 UTC
19:57:00 KST

Reported by
Orda.kz, one of Kazakhstan’s leading independent news outlets, ceased publication a month after an Almaty court sentenced its editor-in-chief to eight years in prison. Press freedom advocates described the closure as the final step in a months-long state campaign aimed at silencing critical journalism.
The outlet’s majority owner, Maksat Ganiyev, publicly attributed the shutdown to financial losses, telling reporters that six years of investment had failed to yield commercial viability and denying that the decision was driven by political pressure. He described the outlet as a business project. “It has to deliver a certain return. It has to be commercially viable and interesting”, he told OCCRP.
Yet media watchdogs and legal experts view the shuttering as part of a wider, systematic tightening of state control over independent media following the adoption of a new constitution and the election of a single-chamber parliament, the Kurultai, dominated by the ruling Adilet party.
“I don’t think this comes down to finances for the investor,” said Nazira Darimbet, head of the Kazakh human rights organization Adil Soz. “The scheme was designed so that, in the eyes of society, everything would look legal.”
Darimbet drew parallels to the 2016 forced closure of Respublika, another independent outlet whose editor was jailed on criminal libel charges before the publication was forced off the air.
The crisis at Orda.kz escalated dramatically on Aug. 8, when a court found editor-in-chief Gulnara Bazhkenova guilty of spreading false information, embezzlement, and illegal entrepreneurship - charges first leveled by police investigators in late 2025. In addition to the eight-year prison sentence, the court imposed a five-year ban on her practicing journalism, though her imprisonment was deferred for two years because she has a minor child.
Bazhkenova’s conviction forms part of a broader wave of legal action against independent reporters across Kazakhstan. On July 31, a court banned the owner and editor-in-chief of the KazTAG news agency from journalism and placed them under restricted liberty. Elsewhere, video blogger Azamat Omarov was arrested on charges of inciting social discord, while investigative journalists Lukpan Akhmedyarov and Dinara Yegeubayeva were placed under travel bans.
The pressure on the press has also extended to physical access. In the wake of the Aug. 23 parliamentary elections, administration officials at the Kurultai informed reporters that they would no longer be permitted to approach lawmakers in corridors for unscripted questions. Instead, journalists must remain in a designated press room and move through the building only with official escorts.
Rights advocates warn that the combination of criminal prosecutions, outlet closures, and physical barriers risks reducing Kazakh political coverage to little more than state-curated public relations.
“We risk getting clones of state channels with the same questions, the same faces, and the same answers,” said Diana Okremova, director of the Legal Media Center.

Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrent initiative
- Finland has joined France’s Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative to strengthen European security amid concerns over US commitment and the Ukraine war.
- The initiative keeps French presidential authority over nuclear use but promotes joint exercises and potential deployment of nuclear-capable assets among partners.
- Finland follows Nordic countries joining earlier and emphasises the programme complements NATO without hosting nuclear weapons in peacetime.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Finland has joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner European countries, the heads of both countries said on Sept 14.
In response to US President Donald Trump’s expressions of concern about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation,” Finland President Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland's defence minister Antti Hakkanen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” following other Nordic countries, such as Norway, Sweden and Denmark, that joined the initiative earlier in 2026. In total, 10 countries participate, including Finland.
Stubb said the programme does not replace NATO’s nuclear deterrence and that Finland does not intend to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its territory in peacetime. REUTERS

How Israel is reshaping its eastern front along Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:55:50 UTC
19:55:50 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel is reshaping its eastern front along Jordan with security barrier and settlements
Israel is pressing ahead with plans to establish about 40 new illegal settlement outposts along its eastern frontier with Jordan, in addition to a planned 500km (310-mile) barrier and an expanding military and civilian presence in the occupied Jordan Valley.
The developments have prompted warnings from Jordanian analysts that Israel's settlement expansion could create a new security reality along the kingdom's western frontier and put further pressure on Palestinian land and resources.
Jordanian military analyst Jalal al-Abbadi told The New Arab that Israel was continuing its settlement expansion across different border areas, including Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
He said the recent increase in illegal settlement outposts, particularly in central and northern areas, involved armed extremists who effectively reinforce Israeli forces and serve as a first line of defence.
Al-Abbadi said the geographical distribution of the outposts could eventually create a security belt, although "even now it cannot be described as a security belt or a complete buffer zone".
He warned that the outposts could attract extremists and people from abroad and contribute to the displacement of local residents living nearby.
Jordanian expert on Israeli affairs Ayman al-Haniti said Israel's mine clearance operations and construction of the barrier indicated an effort to establish a "human barrier" along the frontier.
He said this could consist of settlements, training camps and military bases.
The border between Jordan and Israel extends for more than 300km, he said, warning that the establishment of farms and more than 40 settlements could put pressure on groundwater and other resources.
"Jordan will be deprived of the resources located along the border strip," he remarked.
A 500km barrier
The settlement expansion is being pursued alongside construction of a security barrier planned to eventually stretch around 500km, from the occupied Syrian Golan Heights to the area north of Eilat.
Initial sections of the project began construction in 2025, with the first phase covering around 80km. The wider project includes physical barriers, surveillance equipment, radars, cameras, communications systems and roads, while mine clearance has taken place along parts of the planned route.
But the project is not simply being built along Israel's internationally recognised border with Jordan.
Parts of the barrier run several kilometres inside the occupied West Bank, cutting across the northern Jordan Valley and separating Palestinian communities from farmland.
The "Crimson Thread" section, in particular, has involved the excavation of Palestinian land and destruction of agricultural infrastructure.
The project has damaged irrigation pipes, farmland and greenhouses and separated farmers from land on the other side of the barrier. Its route was established through nine Israeli land-seizure orders, while Palestinian residents have faced increasing restrictions on their movement as construction advances.
A wider settlement project
The barrier forms part of a broader expansion of Israel's illegal settlement project in the occupied West Bank.
Around 40 new Nahal settlement groups are planned along the eastern border, while agricultural farms are also being established in the area.
The settlement plans come as Israeli settlers expand outposts, farms, roads and fencing elsewhere across the occupied West Bank, further increasing Israeli civilian presence on Palestinian land.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich recently announced the demolition of 35 Palestinian buildings along access routes to new settlements in the northern West Bank, linking the move to strengthening and protecting Israeli settlements.
Although the demolitions are not directly connected to the Jordanian border, they form part of the wider expansion of Israel's settlement presence across the occupied territory.
What does it mean for Jordan?
Jordanian political analyst Amer al-Sabaileh said Israeli activity along the eastern border had intensified after Israel raised concerns about weapons and people being smuggled across the frontier and infiltration.
Israel has conducted military exercises around the border and introduced additional barriers and security measures since 7 October 2023, he said.
"Israel is applying the same security logic it had used in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and Syria to Jordan, seeking to prevent potential attacks and infiltration," he said.
"Israel was working, according to its security doctrine, to redraw the geography of the area in line with its security requirements," he added.
Al-Abbadi said a military confrontation between Jordan and Israel was currently unlikely, with no indications that either side was seeking direct conflict.
"There is no room today to open more conflicts," he said, adding that Jordan remained committed to the two-state solution.
He said Jordan was maintaining its borders and relying on diplomatic efforts to prevent further Israeli settlement expansion, particularly in border areas.
The Jordan Valley's importance as a food-producing area also meant the Israeli moves had economic as well as security implications for Jordan, he added.
The developments along the border would require a degree of coordination, al-Sabaileh said, while Jordan did not want any breach of its territory or smuggling and infiltration across the frontier.

Meeting of the Group of Women Ambassadors with the OPCW leadership

SoftBank shares plunge as calls grow to slow AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:55:07 UTC
19:55:07 KST

AI development should slow down, leading developers have warned, as the industry faces growing calls to put safety ahead of profits. The comments weighed heavily on technology shares on Monday.
Shares in Japanese investment conglomerate SoftBank Group, a major investor in OpenAI, plunged more than 10% on Monday, alongside other technology shares, after executives at some of the world’s leading AI companies backed calls to prioritise “caution over speed and prudence over profit”.
The phrase was used by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called on Saturday for AI companies to “pace the frontier” through a coordinated slowdown in the development of their most advanced models, allowing more time to understand and manage the risks.
Among his main concerns is so-called “recursive self-improvement”, in which AI systems help to build the next generation of AI models.
“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk publicly backed his warning, with Musk saying: “Dario is right.”
Altman also told Fortune in an interview published on Saturday that OpenAI would not proceed with an initial public offering this year, as the company focuses on safety.
OpenAI and Anthropic are both privately owned. Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a possible stock market listing in the coming months.
The comments followed the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that the technology could escape human control.
Evan Hubinger, another Anthropic researcher who remains at the company, subsequently wrote: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” He said he believed the probability was greater than 10% within the next decade.
US President Donald Trump rejected the warnings on Sunday, calling AI critics “very negative forces” and saying the scenarios they raised would not happen. House Speaker Mike Johnson also urged people not to panic.
Investors nevertheless sold technology shares on Monday.
SoftBank’s decline “probably reflects the possibility that AI development may be slowed by regulators to try to avoid the worst-case outcomes that Anthropic and OpenAI have discussed,” said Dan Baker of investment research firm Morningstar.
“And maybe [it] also reflects the possibility that any further examples of loss of control of newer AI models could also slow AI development,” he added.
Other AI-related shares in Asia also fell. South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix lost 5.3%, while Samsung Electronics dropped 2.8%. Japanese chip-equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron fell 0.9%, while memory-chip maker Kioxia Holdings sank 6%.
The race with China
Amodei also called for tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, arguing that chips would largely determine the country’s AI capabilities.
However, he acknowledged to CBS News that the “toughest dilemma” was that China might not join a coordinated slowdown.
China’s state-backed Global Times described his position as “short-sighted” and accused him of trying to restrict China’s development through an “AI Cold War”. Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping has proposed a BRICS open-source AI zone to deepen cooperation on AI models and training.

European spies regain powers denied for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:54:04 UTC
19:54:04 KST

For decades, European intelligence agencies were defined more by what they could not do than by what they could; in Germany, the Nordic countries, and much of Eastern Europe, post-war trauma, the legacy of authoritarian regimes, and a growing commitment to safeguarding civil liberties constrained the operations of spy agencies, reports Politico.
Now, as Russia expands its campaigns of hybrid attacks against critical infrastructure and Chinese espionage intensifies, Europe’s largely dormant intelligence organizations have been granted new powers to protect their interests. Over the past 18 months, the need for change has become more pressing amid growing concerns regarding the reliability of the United States under the Donald Trump administration.
While each country must address the specific combination of its own intelligence services, history, and geographical situation, a shared trend toward granting broader powers is evident. Sometimes this comes at the expense of privacy, but governments are assuming a greater role in safeguarding their security. In recent weeks, the governments of several European countries have granted their intelligence agencies broader powers to disrupt hostile operations and launch defensive cyberattacks, while also authorizing the exchange of intelligence with private companies.
David Omand, former head of the UK’s Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), stated that intelligence communities must be able to provide governments with an understanding of what is actually happening and seek to explain it. They need to determine whether Russian-backed criminal activities are underway or if the situation is something entirely different. Omand noted that this requires intelligence communities to truly function as a unified whole, integrating technical, digital, and human intelligence.
In Sweden, the government is preparing staff for the new Foreign Intelligence Service,
which is set to launch in January. In August, Stockholm announced the appointment of two senior officials to the service: Andreas von Beckerath will serve as the agency’s Director General, while Annika Brändström will be his deputy. Both will assume their new roles as soon as the service becomes operational. Von Beckerath currently serves as the European Union Ambassador to Serbia, whereas Brändström has a long career in government, including experience as a security advisor.
The Swedish government has indicated that separating civilian foreign intelligence from military intelligence will allow for a clearer distinction of responsibilities and improve the country’s ability to assess a wide range of security risks. This restructuring is taking place as Sweden continues to reshape its security architecture following its accession to NATO. This process has been largely driven by threats posed by Russia, which escalated sharply after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On August 28, the Dutch government launched consultations on a proposal to grant its intelligence agencies broader powers under national security law. This would allow them to disrupt the activities of Russian hackers, Chinese spies, and Iranian agents without prior authorization, and enable the sharing of more intelligence with security companies and the military.
Significant legislative changes are also planned in Austria,
a country that has acquired the status of a global hub for espionage. Current laws allow foreign agents to operate with impunity on Austrian soil, provided their spying is not directed against Austria itself. The government is now working to close this legal loophole, thereby complicating matters for the estimated 7,000 spies believed to be operating in Vienna.
The most drastic changes are taking place in Germany. The country has a troubled history with both Nazi-era agencies and, later, the East German secret police, and has been very cautious regarding the powers granted to its intelligence services. Now, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government aims to give these services broader capabilities to counter threats from hostile states. Under the proposed reforms, set to take effect in January, the German foreign intelligence service (BND) will be authorized to conduct sabotage and offensive operations.
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, remarked that this move was long overdue. Europeans had not anticipated that such threats would reach them, and this measure represents a response to the new threat landscape.
Until now, the BND’s activities were limited to intelligence gathering.
This reflected post-war restrictions deliberately put in place to prevent a recurrence of the abuses that occurred under Nazi rule. However, this also meant that Germany was largely ineffective in the digital realm, partly due to a lack of the necessary authority to access certain types of communications data.
In March, Germany’s data protection watchdog warned that it would be unable to adequately protect citizens from surveillance by intelligence agencies. Omend stated that Germany represents a classic case—it will need to rethink its traditional approach of balancing privacy concerns against national security interests.
The need for deeper intelligence cooperation among European nations became increasingly urgent after the Trump administration abruptly halted the sharing of military and combat-related intelligence with Kyiv in March 2025. The US President has also faced accusations of appointing loyalists with limited or no experience to lead these agencies. This has raised concerns among European officials that Washington might be unwilling to share intelligence that contradicts the administration’s political stance.
Ferdinand Gehringer, a senior hybrid threats analyst at FTI Consulting, said that these changes reflect both a growing awareness of threats to Europe and a shift in the methods used by Russian intelligence services, which are increasingly employing low-level agents to carry out acts of sabotage.

Compulsory troop deployments in Lithuania: German Defense Ministry
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will order compulsory troop deployments in Lithuania.
According to the Defense Ministry, this is intended to fill gaps in the German armoured brigade's complement.
Several hundred military personnel would be affected, with the shortages in logisticians and IT specialists being the main reason for the move.
The ministry said that 80% of the Lithuanian brigade's positions are filled with volunteers.
"The principle of voluntariness remains unchanged as our guiding principle," the ministry said. 
 
German finance minister and UniCredit CEO meet over Commerzbank merger
German Finance MinisterLars Klingbeilheld a meeting with the CEO of UniCredit to discuss the future of Commerzbank.
This comes as the German bank's takeover by Italian lender UniCredit edges closer.
After the meeting, Klingbeil said it is "paramount" for the German government that Commerzbank continues to "fulfil its vital role in financing the German economy."
"We expect Commerzbank to remain a listed company headquartered in Frankfurt and to continue its strong focus on financing small and medium-sized businesses," the Social Democratic politician said in a statement.
UniCredit is close to sealing one of Europe's biggest mergers of banks in recent years with it increasing its stake in Commerzbank to nearly 50 percent.
 
Suspended sentence for priest in possession of child pornography
A Catholic priest from North Rhine-Westphalia has received a suspended 14-month jail sentence after being found guilty of possessing of some 24,000 data files containing images and footage of sexual abuse of children and youths.
The district court in Waldbröl, a rural area to the east of Cologne and Bonn in the Westerwald forest, found the man guilty on Monday.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
The defendant had pleaded guilty to all charges, leading to a comparatively quick court process.
As well as the suspended sentence, the man was ordered to pay €10,000 (roughly $11,500) to a local facility providing advice and counsel to those affected by sexualized, psychological and physical abuse.
He was also ordered to complete a therapy course that he had already begun.
The Cologne diocese, of which Waldbröl is a part, had already suspended the priest from various activities after the allegations became public knowledge. Among other things he was stopped from working with minors.
He's also subject to church disciplinary proceedings. These had been put on hold pending the outcome of the court case.
Police called to reprimand man painting house in 'just his shoes'
Police on duty in Kaiserslautern had a more colorful callout than they might have bargained for over the weekend.
Police said on Monday that early on Saturday evening, they had received calls from residents displeased by a man painting a facade in his driveway.
They took exception to the fact that their neighbor was "wearing just his shoes," as police put it, during his travails.
"After officers brought to his attention that he was creating a disturbance in the community with his actions, the 64-year-old became intransigent," police said.
"Only after an explicit order did he put some trousers on. He was told that his behavior constituted a breach of the peace and that he should reckon with a criminal complaint."
Fuel prices hit record high, ADAC considers levels unjustified
Prices for drivers at German filling stations hit the highest levels on record for gasoline on Sunday, while diesel was just shy of April's record prices.
The nationwide average for the cheapest E10 unleaded variant hit €2.27 per liter on Sunday. That equates to roughly $9.92 per US gallon.
Diesel was slightly shy of its record level but still rose to €2.40 per liter, or $10.48 per US gallon.
Germany's largest motoring club the ADAC said that "given the still-rising oil prices it can be assumed that slight increases in the daily average prices for Super E10 and diesel will emerge" on Monday.
Prices for gasoline and diesel have risen quite sharply in September, and more generally since the German government's temporary tax relief introduced in response to the war in Iran expired at the end of June.
Developments in the Gulf have been driving the price upwards, despite claims to the contrary from under-fire US President Donald Trump on Monday.
The ADAC, which is frequently critical of the country's fuel providers and their pricing policies, argued that geopolitics alone still did not explain the latest hikes.
"In the view of the ADAC, the oil price and the euro-dollar exchange rate only partly explain the current price levels at the petrol pumps," the ADAC wrote. "What's particularly noticeable is how Super E10 keeps hitting new record highs, even though crude oil prices are far adrift of their previous highs. For consumers this development is difficult to explain."
The ADAC called on refining and fuel selling companies to be more transparent in their pricing practices.
Light aircraft crashes south of Mönchengladbach, 3 killed
A light aircraft crashed in a field in Erkelenz in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia on Monday.
Police in nearby Heinsberg said three people were killed in the crash; nobody on board the small Cessna survived.
Police said the crash happened before noon in a rural area south of Mönchengladbach and that they were still working to identify the victims.
Firefighters and police were at the scene on Monday. The German body responsible to investigating air traffic accidents had started an invesigation, which police said was liable to take some time.
SPD says coalition is not dependent on Merz staying chancellor
Senior figures in the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) have expressed growing concern about the turmoil inside Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
They also made clear that their party's participation in the coalition is not dependent on Merz's remaining chancellor.
SPD parliamentary manager Dirk Wiese said there was an impression that "nerves are a little frayed within the CDU" and urged the coalition partner to regain its focus and move ahead with reforms agreed by the government.
Asked whether those reforms necessarily had to be implemented with Merz as chancellor, Wiese declined to commit himself, saying instead that Merz needed to adopt a different tone.
SPD parliamentary deputy leader Siemtje Möller was more explicit. She said her party's participation in the governing coalition was not tied to Merz personally.
Merz urges CDU unity as pressure mounts
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to remain disciplined as criticism of his leadership grows following the party's election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.
Speaking at an international Arctic policy meeting in Rovaniemi, Finland, Merz said Germany was playing an important role in determining "the fate of the European continent," particularly on security policy.
He said he was therefore trying to convince "my colleagues, my friends, my party, my parliamentary group that this is much more important than some of the domestic political debates we are currently having."
"I understand this domestic political debate," Merz said.
Merz has faced mounting criticism within the CDU since the party's poor performance in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, with some members openly discussing whether he should be replaced.
Several prominent CDU politicians nevertheless backed the chancellor on Monday.
"I still believe in Friedrich Merz," CDU budget policy spokesman Matthias Middelberg told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, calling the leadership debate "unnecessary."
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Merz could "always rely on the support of the governing parliamentary groups and his Cabinet," describing the government as "really very stable."
Green leader tells Merz coalition: 'Get your s--- together'
Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak has told Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to "get your s--- together" amid growing speculation over a possible change of chancellor.
"I am extremely irritated by all the speculation that is coming from everywhere," Banaszak said in Berlin on Monday. "And my expectation is very clear: Get your s--- together. We are living in such dramatic times."
Banaszak said that, though he had not voted for Merz, the chancellor and his coalition had been elected and had a responsibility to govern the country.
The Green politician pointed to discussions about minority governments, the possible dismissal of ministers from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and scenarios involving an early replacement of Merz.
He said the debates suggested that Merz and the leadership of his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) were losing control both of the coalition and of discussions within their own party.
"That is not a good sign," Banaszak said.
Germany’s largest union calling for nationwide protests over auto sector job cuts
The German union IG Metall is calling for demonstrations in more than 200 locations across the country on September 21. The demonstrations will be held to protest job cuts and other demands being made of workers in the auto industry.
Christiane Benner, leader of IG Metall, said most of the sector's crisis is falling on employees. "We are currently witnessing an unprecedented attack on workers in the auto industry," she said, adding that the union's main concern is the risk of losing the 35-hour workweek, a standard in the German auto sector.
Employers' demands in times of crisis
Due to the current challenges facing the sector, automakers are proposing an increase to a 40-hour workweek with no wage adjustments.
Jens Schäfer, chairman of the ZF Automotive Works Council in Hanover, said this would mean five additional hours of work without extra pay.
"That's driving colleagues crazy," he said, adding that it would also lead to more job losses.
Benner said workers have already made sacrifices, including concessions in collective bargaining agreements and pay concessions worth billions of euros, while companies continue to pay dividends and management has faced no consequences for past mistakes.
IG Metall's goal is to mobilize more than 100,000 people on September 21.
Merz congratulates Zverev on US Open victory
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has congratulated Alexander Zverev on winning the US Open, his second Grand Slam title of the season.
The German defeated Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 in Sunday's final in New York.
"First Paris, now New York: Heartfelt congratulations, dear Alex Zverev, on the well-deserved US Open victory and your second Grand Slam title in a season. Stellar performance!" Merz wrote on X.
Zverev also won the French Open in June. Merz called him after that victory to offer his congratulations.
Nearly half of German schoolchildren report sleep problems
Almost half of schoolchildren in Germany say they regularly have problems sleeping, according to a new survey published by health insurer DAK-Gesundheit.
The survey found that 46% of pupils in grades 5 to 10 experience sleep problems at least once a week, up from 36% in the 2019/2020 school year.
At the same time, 69% said they felt drained or exhausted at least once a week. Three years ago, the figure was 52%.
Michael Hubmann, president of Germany's professional association of pediatricians, pointed to excessive media use as one factor behind the increase in sleep and exhaustion problems.
"Children and adolescents who use social media until late in the evening or consume disturbing videos triggered by algorithms are being kept from healthy sleep," he said.
DAK chief executive Andreas Storm warned that persistent exhaustion and sleep problems could make it harder for children to learn successfully.
"Anyone who is already exhausted at a young age or even suffers from sleep disorders and does not know how to deal with such pressures has worse conditions for successful learning," he said.
Germany to order 4th new signals intelligence ship
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that Germany will acquire a fourth signals intelligence ship.
"These ships can hear and see what others cannot. They are our eyes and ears at sea. They perceive and analyze a vast range of signals and sounds," the minister said during a keel-laying ceremony for the third ship of this type to be built by the German company Rheinmetall.
The acquisition is part of a budget proposal that is pending parliamentary approval, he added.
Pistorius also said the ships were essential for providing situational awareness and enabling precise maneuvering in times of increasing insecurity.
The new class of ships are expected to be delivered to the German Navy from 2029.
Germany sees slowing economic momentum in 3rd quarter
The German Ministry of Economy says the country is experiencing an economic slowdown at the beginning of the third quarter.
"The economic boom in energy-intensive industries, which was driven by increased foreign demand in the wake of the conflict in the Middle East, appears to be slowing down," the ministry said in its monthly report.
High energy costs have caused domestic consumption to decline considerably, a trend also driven by the conflict, the report said.
Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia
German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.
Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said.
She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.

EU to propose KIDS Act on social media safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:51:55 UTC
19:51:55 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Commission will propose new rules to restrict minors' access to social media and video-sharing platforms before the age of 15, according to preparatory documents seen by POLITICO and a person familiar with the matter.
The EU executive on Thursday will unveil a new EU KIDS Act setting out age restrictions, along with new rules requiring covered products, such as social media and AI companions, to be safe by design. The proposal aims to create a tiered system for accessing social media under parental supervision before age 15, the documents said.
The age restrictions are a major step by the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen to better safeguard minors' on social media platforms, amid a fierce backlash from health experts, politicians and parents against the effects of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and others on the mental health of minors.
Advertisement
It comes after months of intense pressure from government leaders, including France's Emmanuel Macron, to put the issue at the top of the political agenda. Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids' access to social media.
Von der Leyen is expected to present more details in her State of the European Union speech to parliament members in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
Commission spokesperson Olof Gil confirmed the act is coming on Thursday at a press conference on Monday.
The EU's new proposal would apply to social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, and AI chatbots and AI companions, but would exclude educational tools. It will also come with a series of education measures for kids, parents and guardians, the documents said.
A panel of health and tech experts convened by von der Leyen presented similar recommendations earlier this year to restrict access to what they called "social media+," including services like AI companions.
The text is still subject to change ahead of its formal presentation on Thursday and will have to be negotiated with European governments and members of the European Parliament afterward.
Advertisement
Kids' accounts before 15
The proposal doesn't set a hard limit on social media access but instead calls for certain types of accounts to be accessible at different ages. These limitations apply to social media and video-sharing platforms that are high-risk, the documents said without clarifying how the category would be determined.
For children under 13, parents can open accounts for their kids that are fully controlled by the guardians and use services that meet strict safety standards.
Between 13 and 15, the proposal calls for introductory accounts with limits on contact with strangers and screen time, as well as parental controls.
After 15, teenagers can set up their own accounts.
The proposal would also require verification technology for social media and video-sharing platforms to verify users' ages, the documents said.
The Commission's proposal will include a new enforcement architecture similar to that of the Digital Services Act and the Artificial Intelligence Act, including supervisory fees to be paid by companies, the documents said. These laws centralize enforcement of the highest-risk companies and services to the Commission, while leaving national regulators to oversee smaller firms.
The Commission declined to comment on the plans.
This article was updated to include new details of the proposal.

Study finds long-term heart rate rhythms in 70 pct of people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:51:36 CST
19:51:36 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The heart rates of 70 percent of people follow weekly, quarterly or even yearly cycles, according to a study by researchers at Australia's University of Melbourne (UniMelb).
The research, published in the journal eBioMedicine, analyzed more than 900 years of smartwatch data from 623 healthy university students. The findings could improve understanding and management of neurological, psychiatric and broader health conditions, according to a UniMelb statement released on Monday.
Researchers found that most participants' heart rates followed multi-day patterns that could not be explained by season, exercise or environmental factors.
"Many people show unique rhythms in their heart rate from weekly and monthly cycles to longer rhythms such as 10 weeks or six months," said UniMelb Associate Professor Pip Karoly, who led the study.
The resting heart rate of 70 percent of participants followed a cyclic pattern over years, suggesting the body has a built-in biological pacemaker controlling heart rate over the long term, Karoly said.
Known as infradian rhythms, these patterns are involved in reproductive cycles, seasonal affective disorder -- which can cause mental health challenges in times of lower light -- and animals shedding fur or skin, the researchers said, adding that the factors governing infradian rhythms in humans remain unclear, but may involve a combination of hormonal, environmental and genetic causes.
"Interestingly though, housemates, siblings and friends had similar rhythms, suggesting people's bodies naturally sync with those they are close to," Karoly said.
The team is developing an app to track infradian rhythms in relation to neurological and psychiatric patterns and is studying the genetics of multiday rhythms. ■

SINGAPORE, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's bond market issuance rose 21.8 percent year on year in 2025 to a record 95 billion U.S. dollars, surpassing the previous high of 77 billion U.S. dollars recorded in 2023, its central bank said on Monday.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said in a report that issuance remained robust, driven by refinancing needs as well as regional demand for capital to fund investments in artificial intelligence, technology and infrastructure.
Singapore's corporate debt market also continued to expand, with new issuance rising 10 percent year on year to 339 billion Singapore dollars (about 267 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025.
The outstanding size of the corporate debt market increased 6.8 percent to 659 billion Singapore dollars at the end of 2025.
Financial institutions remained the most active issuers across both Singapore-dollar and non-Singapore-dollar markets in 2025.
However, their share of total issuance moderated slightly as corporate issuers increased their participation, particularly in the Singapore-dollar market, said the authority. ■

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- At least 21 people were killed in a road accident in South Africa's Western Cape province, authorities said on Monday.
The accident occurred at around 11:30 p.m. (2130 GMT) Sunday on the N1 highway between Prince Albert and Leeu-Gamka in the province, involving two minibus taxis and a station wagon.
Local police confirmed the crash to Xinhua, saying emergency personnel were summoned to the scene after three vehicles collided.

"A total of 18 occupants were declared deceased. Several other occupants were transported to nearby medical facilities for treatment," he said, adding that local police have opened a culpable homicide case and are investigating the cause of the crash.
The Western Cape Mobility Department later confirmed in a statement that the death toll had risen to 21.
The department said the N1 highway remained closed in both directions due to the severity of the crash, urging motorists to avoid the area, exercise extreme caution and use alternative routes. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Southern Europe shows renewed economic resilience amid eurozone slowdown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:51:23 CST
19:51:23 KST

* Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years.
* Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core.
* The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies.
* China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships.
MADRID, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the eurozone faces a subdued growth outlook, a different economic picture has emerged along its southern flank: Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years.
In the second quarter of 2026, seasonally adjusted GDP in the euro area increased by 1.0 percent year-on-year. In contrast, Spain, Portugal and Greece recorded growth of 2.7 percent, 2.5 percent and 1.9 percent, respectively, while Italy matched the eurozone rate.
A report published in June by Allianz, an insurance company, described Southern Europe's post-2021 performance as "a clear shift in the geography of Eurozone growth, with Southern economies moving from chronic underperformance to cyclical leadership."
Analysts and market observers attribute this resilience to three overlapping shifts: a broader mix of growth drivers, financial and institutional repair reinforced by EU investment, and a pragmatic openness to external markets, capital and technology, including expanding industrial partnerships with China.
Together, these factors have helped Southern Europe withstand some of the pressures weighing on the eurozone's traditional industrial core.
SHOCKS SHIFTED SIDES
Recent shocks -- from supply-chain disruptions to energy-price spikes and trade tensions -- have not fallen evenly across the eurozone.
"In the current cycle, the asymmetry of external shocks has, so to speak, shifted sides," Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, said in an interview with Xinhua.
Sanz said Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core.
The difference is also visible in the drivers of growth. In the second quarter of 2026, Spain's economy ministry said growth was supported by domestic demand, investment and industry, while Portugal's rebound was driven mainly by net external demand.
Investment, construction and services have supported Italy in recent years, while investment, consumption and net exports all contributed to Greece's growth in 2025. Tourism also remains an important source of activity, employment and services exports, particularly in Spain, Portugal and Greece.
A changing energy mix has provided another buffer. Eurostat data showed that over 60 percent of gross electricity consumption in Portugal, Greece and Spain came from renewable sources in 2025. The European Commission said growing renewable generation had lowered wholesale electricity prices, with gas influencing prices in only a minority of market hours in the Iberian Peninsula.
Labor supply has provided further support, particularly in Spain. According to Sanz, labor-market reforms that reduced excessive reliance on temporary contracts helped stabilize household incomes, while immigration expanded the workforce and supported employment and domestic demand.
Public investment has added another leg to the recovery. Allianz estimates that Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece together account for almost 60 percent of funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the centerpiece of NextGenerationEU.
"Public capital injected through NextGenerationEU funds has therefore served as a countercyclical firewall, financing green-transition infrastructure, digitalization and key industrial projects without placing excessive strain on national finances," Sanz said.
REFORM DIVIDENDS
The recent divergence also reflects differences in the timing of adjustment. The sovereign debt crisis forced Southern Europe to confront long-standing financial and structural imbalances.
The process varied across countries. Greece and Portugal entered broad assistance programs covering fiscal consolidation, bank repair, pension reform, and changes to labor and product markets. Spain received assistance focused on its banking sector, while Italy remained outside a bailout program and followed a more gradual course.
The adjustment carried a high economic and social cost, as domestic demand contracted and unemployment surged. Over time, however, banks reduced non-performing loans, households and businesses cut debt, and labor- and product-market rules were revised.
Spain and Portugal also broke with a pattern of running external deficits during periods of expansion and began regularly recording current-account surpluses.
A 2026 study by the National Bank of Belgium found that Spain, Portugal and Greece grew at an average annual rate of 1.7 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared with 0.6 percent for Germany, France, the Netherlands and Belgium. It linked their stronger performance partly to post-crisis reforms and fiscal consolidation.
Greece shows how the repair extended to the functioning of public institutions. According to the IMF, measures targeting tax evasion and informality helped narrow its value-added tax compliance gap from 24 percent in 2019 to about 9 percent in 2024.
Reforms have also covered the judiciary, business regulation and tax administration, although weak productivity and judicial delays remain constraints.
After the pandemic, EU conditionality took a different form. Rather than focusing primarily on correcting imbalances, RRF funding was tied to national recovery and resilience plans combining investment projects with reform commitments, with at least 37 percent of the budget allocated to climate and biodiversity and a further minimum of 20 percent to digital measures.
The plans have directed funding toward renewable energy, power grids, sustainable transport, industrial decarbonization and digitalization.
According to Sanz, Spain and Portugal have used EU funding for electric-vehicle value chains, industrial decarbonization and the digitalization of public administrations and small businesses, while Italy has coupled investment with reforms of public administration, the justice system and public procurement.
However, these gains should not be overstated. Sanz cautioned that, except in some technological and renewable-energy niches, Southern Europe's productivity gap with Northern Europe remained substantial.
An analysis published by the Jacques Delors Institute noted that the four countries entered the pandemic on different growth trajectories and have deployed RRF funds at different speeds. Although the facility has supported demand and investment, the analysis said, its lasting impact will depend on whether the projects and reforms raise productivity and potential growth.
The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies.
COOPERATION WITH CHINA
China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships.
In Spain, cooperation with Chinese companies is increasingly moving beyond trade toward local manufacturing in the electric-mobility supply chain. Chery's partnership with Spanish automaker Ebro has revived production at the former Nissan plant in Barcelona, while CATL and Stellantis are jointly investing in a lithium iron phosphate battery plant in Zaragoza.
"Spain has become a gateway not only for distribution but also for manufacturing, taking advantage of the auto manufacturing ecosystem that our country has," said Raul Morales, communications director at Faconauto, Spain's federation of automotive dealers' associations, in an interview with Xinhua.
Portugal is following a similar pattern. Chinese battery manufacturer CALB is developing its first European factory in the Sines Industrial and Logistics Zone. The 2 billion-euro project is expected to create 1,800 direct jobs and help Portugal develop a battery value chain around its lithium resources.
In Greece, China COSCO Shipping Corporation (COSCO) acquired a majority stake in Piraeus Port Authority in 2016, becoming the operator of the entire port. The port has since strengthened its position as a major Mediterranean container hub.
Stefanos Gkikas, Greek deputy minister of maritime affairs and insular policy, described the cooperation between COSCO and the port authority as "productive," saying it had enhanced the port's competitiveness and strengthened Greece's position in global shipping.
In Italy, the Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, Italian renewable-energy developer Renexia and China's MingYang Smart Energy have agreed to work toward establishing wind-turbine manufacturing capacity. The proposed investment, worth around 500 million euros (579.2 million U.S. dollars), is linked to the planned 2.8-GW Med Wind floating offshore wind project off Sicily.
Sanz described the four countries' approach to China as "a form of reasonable industrial pragmatism aligned with their growth needs."
"Greater openness to emerging economies is an undeniable advantage for Southern Europe's economic dynamism, provided that it takes the form of co-investment, technology transfer and local job creation," he said.
"The success of Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece will therefore depend on their ability to manage the complex balance between attracting highly competitive global capital and complying with EU regulations," he added. ■

Snail shells could help reconstruct prehistoric cyclones: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:51:11 CST
19:51:11 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Snails carry weather records on their backs that could be used to map extreme weather events and reconstruct the paths of past cyclones even in prehistoric times, a new study has found.
Researchers examined the rings on the shell of a Biggenden Banded Snail collected from Coalstoun Lakes National Park in Australia's southeast Queensland, linking its bands to weather records, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
Tiny samples taken from the shell at millimeter intervals were analyzed using high-resolution radiocarbon dating, revealing the age of the snail, when it lived and the weather during its lifetime, said Nicholas Patton, lead author of the study published in The Holocene.
"It contained elevated levels of radiocarbon from the nuclear tests in Australia in the 1960s, meaning we could date the growth bands and reveal the snail had lived for about 4.5 years," Patton said, adding that analyzing the oxygen and carbon stable isotopes of the different bands revealed insights into the rainfall the snail experienced.
Researchers found that the shell did not grow continuously during the snail's life, with periods of rapid growth separated by periods of little or no growth. They initially expected rapid growth to correspond to years of heavier rainfall, making more food available for the snail, but found the snail was responding to extreme rainfall events rather than annual wetness.
The study showed the growth spurts were linked to periods immediately following cyclones in 2015 and 2017.
"It shows that snail shells could be used to map extreme weather events for periods before modern meteorological records," said Honorary Professor Jamie Shulmeister in UQ's School of the Environment.
"It was surprising and quite exciting that the humble snail could be a tool to reconstruct the paths of past cyclones even in prehistoric times," he said.
The researchers' next step is to test the method using shells preserved in different sediment layers and combine the individual shell records to extend this information further back in time. ■

Parasitic worms aren’t just a gut problem—they can infest the brain, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:50:52 UTC
19:50:52 KST

Tapeworms are typically thought of as a gut problem: Eat undercooked meat and you could be left with an intestinal parasite. But there’s another, more unsettling way these creatures can enter your body: you can swallow their microscopic eggs in food or water contaminated by an infected person’s feces.
That’s exactly what happened to a 52-year-old woman in the Philippines. She had no idea. For four months, she suffered headaches and visual hallucinations—and she eventually went to the emergency room at her local hospital.
The woman spoke fluently, but her words often did not make sense, resembling a “word salad.” She struggled to understand speech, name objects, repeat words and follow simple commands, says Bonifacio C. Pedregosa II, a neurologist at Jose R. Reyes Memorial Medical Center in the Philippines.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, Pedregosa and a co-author lay out how the woman’s symptoms presented a medical mystery—one with a gory solution.
The woman’s visual hallucinations came and went, Pedregosa says. “She described seeing animals and people who were not actually present during these episodes,” he explains. Doctors initially wondered whether she had a psychiatric disorder, but her pronounced language comprehension problems prompted them to image her brain to get a closer look.
The scans revealed the source of the mystery: cysts scattered throughout her brain. Many contained a tiny bright dot—the scolex, the headlike part of a developing tapeworm larva, armed with suckers and hooks.
That telltale sign led the doctors to diagnose neurocysticercosis, an infection in which larval cysts of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium lodge in the brain.
Brain-wave testing also showed abnormal electrical activity, leading doctors to suspect her hallucinations were related to seizures.
Once swallowed, the tapeworm’s eggs hatch in the intestine, releasing larvae that can enter the bloodstream and travel to other tissues throughout the body—including the brain.
A common route of infection is fecal-oral spread: a person carrying an intestinal tapeworm sheds microscopic eggs in their feces, and poor hand hygiene while preparing food or even touching surfaces can allow those eggs to be swallowed by someone else.
Doctors couldn’t pinpoint where or how the woman became infected. In the previous year, however, she had spent time in evacuation centers where sanitation and food-handling hygiene were poor, Pedregosa says. In this case, the doctors treated the woman for the parasitic infection and suspected seizures. A month later, her symptoms had resolved, and repeat brain scans showed that the cysts had shrunk and the distinctive dots had disappeared.
But neurocysticercosis can be fatal. Dying parasites can trigger swelling in the brain, while cysts in certain locations can block the normal flow of fluid around the brain or cause seizures.
Hallucinations have appeared in other cases. In one case, a 15-year-old in Peru had brain scans resembling Swiss cheese and developed visual and auditory hallucinations, while another patient presented with hallucinations, as well as paranoid delusions.
