The CEO Moment: Airbnb’s Brian Chesky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Next year, Airbnb will mark its 20th anniversary. Through its evolution—from a few air mattresses placed on an apartment floor to one of America’s best-known American technology companies—it has been led by Brian Chesky. And at a time when Silicon Valley doesn’t champion introspection, Chesky, 45, is an outlier: someone who has become a prominent voice on company leadership and a frequent investigator of his own character. “The primary weakness of me as a founder running a company was people had to pay for my immaturity in my thirties,” he told me during a recent interview at Airbnb’s headquarters in San Francisco for our new interview series, The CEO Moment. “But I said it was a good long-term bet,” We spoke as the company, called out by critics as contributing to rising housing costs in the cities where it operates, was set to announce a number of new housing initiatives.
You are one of three people who started the company in 2007.  There aren't that many founders leading Fortune 500 companies. How do you think the fact that you founded this company shapes how you lead it today?
The people that build companies tend to be more in the details, more decisive, bigger authority, …They tend to take bigger, bolder risks partly because they have the moral authority to. For example, I could—I wouldn't—but I could change the name of the company because I came up with the name of the company. Somebody who is a professional manager, I don't think they would ever dare change the name of their company. They would feel like it's not theirs to change.
You’ve said that you think CEOs think about hiring wrong. Why is that?
Because I thought about hiring wrong…When I was starting Airbnb…Sam Altman…said hiring should be 50% of your job. I'm not even sure it was 50% of his job.
Has your thinking about the value of remote work shifted as we’ve gotten further from the pandemic?
I have a view that if your office policy's is easy to explain, it might be wrong because it might be one size fits all.
You’re vocal about the fact that you think leaders don’t need to have regular one on one meetings with their direct reports.
I think it's not only unnecessary, it's probably inferior. And if you go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones…
Now you can get a hotel on Airbnb. Why?
I was ideologically against hotels. In fact, I think our first tag line was “forget hotels.” So why would I ever offer them? And so that was my party line for probably 10 years. In 2018, 2019 my stubbornness got the best of me and many of our customers told us that we want hotels. And ultimately I had to make a decision. You know if you're a brand, just because your customer wants something doesn't mean you sell it to them. You can decide no, go somewhere else…But we noticed there were three types of people. There are people that only book Airbnbs. There are people that only book hotels, but most people are willing to book both. 
You're building your own AI frontier lab separate from Airbnb. Why not build that within Airbnb and what will be the relationship between the two?
I thought about building inside of Airbnb….I like to think that our shareholders know what they get themselves into, and I never sold them on us being a frontier company and spending billions and billions of dollars of capital expenditure and then spending huge sums recruiting these engineers or these AI researchers….The benefit to Airbnb and to me is I'm gonna learn a lot about AI, but it's also a totally different kind of culture. So I wanted to keep them separate.
You’re announcing a number of new initiatives around housing. People say Airbnb makes cities more expensive. What role do you want the company to play in making places more affordable?
I think Airbnb has been a place people pointed to over the last 15 years, especially the last decade…for reasons why cities are expensive. And so we have wanted to be part of the solution, not part of the problem. 
We're creating a $250 million fund to house the last dollar for projects. There's about 750,000 homes in America development projects that are stalled because they don't have the last dollar of completion ... .We want to do something called the City Index. We want to open source data around cities, policies, the cost of living, permitting to basically show the cities that are most successful at lowering housing costs by having the best policies….We want to do the housing prize where we're going to do a million dollar prize every year for five years for any company, private or or nonprofit that has ideas around technology that can make housing development easier.

The High Cost of Winning a Michelin Star
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Two out of every five Michelin-starred restaurants close their doors within a few years of receiving the honor, a statistic so counterintuitive that it forces us to ask what, precisely, the star confers and what it destroys.
A 2024 study by Daniel Sands, then of the UCL School of Management, tracked New York City's elite restaurants that had opened between 2000 and 2014 and earned a glowing review in The New York Times. Sands found that receiving a Michelin star significantly increased a restaurant’s likelihood of closing compared with equally acclaimed restaurants that never received one: 40% of Michelin-starred restaurants had shuttered by 2019, against roughly 20% of their unstarred but similarly lauded peers.
One reason: The arrival of the star and crimson plaque can alter the entire local food ecology around a restaurant. Suppliers and vendors, aware of a kitchen’s new status, often increase prices. Landlords like to raise rents. Staff, suddenly more marketable, must be paid more to be retained. The kitchen, chasing the standard the star implies, tends to reach for costlier and rarer ingredients. Every plate becomes more expensive to produce, yet few diners can absorb the escalating cost of eating there. That change can be lethal.
Fine dining, by its nature, runs on razor-thin margins. Exclusive guest lists cap revenue, rare ingredients inflate costs, and a kitchen brigade requires constant, expensive supervision and training. Consider what a plate costs at a typical three-star establishment: at Alain Ducasse au Plaza Athénée in Paris, Ducasse’s own three-star flagship, a single main course runs €80 to €135, and the tasting menu alone costs €260 to €360 per person, before wine, tax, or service—figures that hold across most three-star houses, where a full tasting menu routinely clears $400 to $600 a head once the bottle list is opened. Even at those prices, industry accounts suggest that margins remain thin once the true cost of labor, rare ingredients, and the theater of service is tallied. After all, the diner is paying as much for craft and spectacle as for food.
To keep the star, a restaurant must submit to a rigid, largely unwritten catalog of expectations—the wine list, the choreography of service, the physical opulence of the room—that locks owners and chefs into an inflexible, high-overhead model precisely when they most need room to adapt to shifting economics and changing appetites.
Chefs who sought the star in pursuit of creativity often find themselves instead locked into an endless rat race simply to preserve the status quo. Michel Roux Jr closed Le Gavroche, London’s pioneering two-Michelin-starred institution, in January 2024 after 56 years, citing the toll of the grind and his need for a different balance of life and work. Magnus Nilsson closed his celebrated two-star Fäviken in rural Sweden in December 2019 after 11 years, confessing that he had simply stopped waking up excited to go to work. Both talented chefs were crushed, at least in part, by Michelin’s expectations.
Chasing a Michelin star takes nerve; keeping one takes a very deep pocket. Atelier, a 22-seat tasting-menu restaurant in Chicago’s Lincoln Square, opened in February 2023 under chef Christian Hunter and won a Michelin star within its first year. But the restaurant could not sustain its costs against rising rent, wages, and inflation, and it closed abruptly in May 2026 with owner Tim Lacey telling staff and guests that the restaurant’s finances had left the team no choice.
A growing, if still informal, collective of chefs worldwide is now actively requesting the removal of their own stars, choosing instead to reclaim food as a site of authentic community, relational care, and cultural survival.
Their conclusion: The economics of the Michelin star simply does not work.
So how did we get here? The Michelin Guide was launched in 1900 by tire manufacturers André and Édouard Michelin as a free promotional roadmap distributed to fewer than three thousand motorists then on French roads—a way to encourage driving, and with it, tire wear.
By 1926, the guide had transformed into an arbiter of taste, awarding a single star to mark exceptional dining; by 1931 it had formalized the now-iconic one-, two-, and three-star hierarchy, alongside the red cover and the roly-poly figure of Bibendum, the Michelin Man. The red-bound guide became, over the following century, shorthand for elite dining the world over. Restaurateurs quake at the prospect of an anonymous inspector’s unannounced visit, yet the status a star confers is so vast that chefs the world over continue to chase it. And when the star finally arrives, the regular, vernacular diners who sustained a kitchen through its lean years are often displaced by gastro-tourists chasing a commodified edible experience and influencers eating for the camera rather than for the plate.
And then are the ways in which the Michelin system has undervalued certain cuisines. For instance, despite Indian cuisine standing among the world’s great culinary traditions, only Indian restaurants located outside India have received a star; only recently, in 2024, did a Mexican establishment—the taco stand Taquería El Califa de León in Mexico City—receive one, becoming the first taquería in the world to do so. I had long assumed this asymmetry was a matter of distinctly European taste and bias. It turns out I was only partly right. It is also a matter of money.
The Michelin Guide is ultimately a business that manufactures and confers value. And to be sure, a Michelin star does come with benefits. So much so that municipal chambers of commerce understand precisely what a Michelin presence does for a city’s status as a gastronomic destination, and in recent years cities have begun paying substantial fees for the privilege of having Michelin inspectors visit their food halls and restaurants.
The issue is that these privileges tend to carry a hefty price tag. While a Michelin star can bring notoriety and exposure, these benefits are often outweighed by unsustainable costs
Michelin figured out how to sell status back to us, one unsustainable plate at a time.

Press Review: EU bolsters Ukraine ahead of talks as BRICS summit shows Global South stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. The European Union is looking to strengthen Ukraine ahead of potential peace talks, and the Republican Party led by US President Donald Trump is bracing for a defeat in November’s midterm elections. Meanwhile, the latest BRICS summit in India highlighted the growing role of the grouping in promoting the interests of the Global South. These stories topped Monday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: EU looks to strengthen Ukraine ahead of potential talks
The EU wants to give Kiev a quantitative and qualitative advantage in working out the terms of any future agreements with Moscow, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told Izvestia. This is why the Europeans are keen to take part in negotiations. The European Commission, for one, has just approved a new €6.1 billion aid package for Kiev to purchase air defenses and other weapons. In addition, European leaders may once again persuade US President Donald Trump to restore pressure on Moscow, experts argue. The Kremlin does not rule out the possibility of reviving trilateral talks involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine in October.
For the time being, European countries continue to consider sending their troops to Ukraine after the conflict. Among other things, the idea was discussed at a meeting of the "coalition of the willing" on September 4. However, a week later, Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a blunt warning that any European troop deployment to Ukraine would mean a war with Russia. Moscow has no reason to enter into conflict with Europe, as everything was resolved following the results of WWII, he added.
Maintaining the current political regime in Ukraine is extremely important for European officials, since Kiev plays the role of a constant threat to Moscow and serves as a distraction for its attention and forces, Vladimir Shapovalov, deputy director of the Institute of History and Politics at Moscow State Pedagogical University, noted. The ultimate goal of Brussels at this stage is to defeat or weaken Russia as much as possible by reducing its global weight, the expert argued.
Kiev’s European allies are currently focused on two key directions: they are urgently trying to find missile interceptors for Ukraine’s air defense system as the Ukrainian army’s combat capabilities have declined amid Russian strikes. The other goal pursued by Brussels and London, Shapovalov argued, is to persuade Russia to resume applying pressure on Russia. European leaders may visit the White House like they did following the Alaska meeting between Putin and US leader Donald Trump in August 2025.
The Ukraine issue was discussed at the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11-13. Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan reaffirmed at a meeting with Putin that the UAE is ready to host Ukraine talks. Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov described the potential venue as "fully acceptable."
According to Oleg Karpovich, department head at the Diplomatic Academy of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, the UAE has repeatedly demonstrated its effectiveness as a neutral platform for the negotiation process, and trust is key in resolving such issues. While the implementation of conditions outlined at the Anchorage summit remains the most urgent topic for negotiations, Karpovich said, today, there are growing doubts about whether Kiev would be ready for compromises. And Ukraine will need to recognize the current realities in the special military operation zone for any 2.0 talks.
Vedomosti: Trump-led GOP party bracing for defeat at midterms
With 50 days to go to the US midterm election, Republican President Donald Trump gives unprecedented pledges to help out his losing party. Addressing a GOP convention on September 9-10, he promised a $5,000 `Trump Dividend’ to every adult American if Republicans retain control of Congress in November. Later, he pledged that the Iran war he launched on February 28 will end but only after the midterms, when he also said gasoline prices will drop.
Despite all these pledges, the Cook Political Report said, only 37, or a small fraction, of the 435 House districts and nine of 35 Senate seats up for election are truly competitive. Calculations by Vedomosti based on up-to-date ratings and electoral track-record show that Democrats will win a House majority by 10 or more seats, and while Republicans still have a chance to retain their Senate majority, they may lose one or two seats.
Meanwhile, the ratings of Trump himself and his party have continued to plunge below 40%: as of September 11, the head of state’s nationwide approval rating stood at 39.3%, or one of the lowest in his second term, and the Republican rating stood at 38.8%, according to a Real Clear Politics survey. For comparison, the majority of Americans, or 48.3%, are ready to vote for Democrats who enjoy a 40% approval rating.
Pavel Dubravsky, a political analyst and CEO of Dubravskiy Consulting, too expects Democrats to win a House majority. The situation in the Senate may be less clear, but House Republicans will have to choose between a bad and a very bad outcome. Yevgeny Minchenko, CEO of Minchenko Consulting, agrees. According to him, Trump has lost economically oriented voters and disappointed his own allies with the Iran war. However, he emphasized, even despite such comfortable conditions, Democrats will not be able to win a crushing House victory or gain a Senate majority. "Democrats don’t have either a bright leader or a unique agenda," the expert said.
The House control transitioning to Democrats would guarantee Trump an insurmountable barrier to his entire agenda, including the election and migration reforms, Vadim Kozlov, Head of the Department for Domestic Policy Studies at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, told Vedomosti. As regards his foreign policy, a Democratic win will not cause any significant changes as the president has the biggest mandate here, the expert stressed.
Media: BRICS summit in India shows where Global South stands
BRICS is strengthening its role as the main platform for promoting the interests of the Global South. Cooperation has not stalled amid the acute conflict around Iran: participants in the New Delhi summit were able to adopt the final declaration, even as the positions of some countries vary. The grouping is now facing a strategic choice between whether to develop full-fledged institutions, becoming an international organization, or to maintain the current flexible format of the forum. BRICS critically needs new mechanisms that can improve living conditions in specific countries to implement major projects.
The latest summit confirmed that a coalition of Asian, African, Middle Eastern and Latin American countries - players seeking to boost their global posture - is forming around BRICS. In the summit declaration, the BRICS leaders highlighted the contribution of partners as they called on them to play a more active role in joint projects.
That the final document was adopted unanimously represents a major diplomatic success for India as BRICS chair. New Delhi managed to bring the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Iran, which became involved in the Middle East conflict due to the policies pursued by the United States and Israel, to the table.
India’s BRICS presidency is successful at least because a star team of global leaders gathered in New Delhi for separate talks, Gleb Makarevich, research fellow at the Center for the Indo-Pacific Region at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO), agreed. And the fact that the declaration was adopted without sparking a row between Iran and the UAE, too, is a positive development for the Indians. Besides, New Delhi’s authority in the Global South was once again confirmed, he told Vedomosti.
BRICS will likely consolidate as a hybrid structure: it will not become a full-fledged political and military pole modeled on a bloc, with its composition being too heterogeneous, and the principle of consensus during any expansion will only make resolving sensitive issues more difficult. Nor will it remain a purely "economic club" either for it is clear already that a common language is being developed on international security, global governance, reform of international institutions, climate and technological agenda through the association, Margarita Lipovataya, a senior lecturer at the Faculty of Global Processes at Lomonosov Moscow State University, explained to Izvestia. And BRICS is likely to adopt a model of electoral consolidation. The association will act more cohesively and institutionally on issues where interests coincide, such as de-dollarization, or reform of the IMF and the UN Security Council, the expert said.
However, the growing role of this grouping is inevitably perceived as a challenge to the previous model of international relations in the West. Washington, for one, is sharply toughening its rhetoric against BRICS members, which in itself suggests that BRICS is becoming a significant irritant for the United States, Lipovataya added.
Vedomosti: What Houthis’ advance in Yemen could spell for Saudi Arabia
The hostilities in Yemen between the pro-Iranian Houthis and pro-Saudi government forces continued, as Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree stated on September 13 that his movement had carried out an attack on the Sharurah military base in southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis targeted Saudi weapons depots, as well as command and control centers, using ballistic missiles and drones, Saree said in a post on X.
The Houthis also warned the Saudi side that attacks inside the kingdom will continue unless Riyadh ends its aggression. And on September 12, Yemen’s government forces with Saudi support carried out a series of strikes on Houthi positions. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday, fielding reporters’ questions, that the movement is not looking to fight with America. According to Trump, the Houthis are only dissatisfied with Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s official government fighting against Ansar Allah.
Axios reported earlier that Saudi de-facto leader Mohammed bin Salman had twice asked Trump to attack Houthi positions over the phone. The US leader refused to provide direct military assistance to the crown prince as he said Washington needed to focus on the conflict with Iran. Nor did Turkey and Pakistan agree to help Saudi Arabia with their troops even as they signed a military bloc with it in early August.
The American position regarding the conflict around the Red Sea is not very clear for a number of reasons, Alexey Yurk, a researcher with the Center for Middle East Studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, told Vedomosti. Firstly, the Trump administration attempted to defeat the Houthis back in 2025, which resulted in a tactical victory in the form of a ceasefire and guarantees that the Houthis would not attack American ships, despite the lack of any strategic success. Moreover, that campaign was the first sign in a series of military failures for the current administration, demonstrating the limitations of US military tools. Secondly, all available resources are currently focused on Iran. Finally, the recent escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia theoretically gives Trump an opportunity to subsequently draw Riyadh into a direct confrontation with Tehran.
And in the wake of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, the current oil crisis in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and the southern Red Sea has spread beyond the oil and shipping industries, Kirill Rodionov, an expert in energy, noted.
The developments clearly benefit Iran, as this eventually distracts Arab, Israeli and potentially US resources away from itself and once again shows to the entire world how unable the US is to achieve the desired results militarily, Yurk argued. All of this, as Tehran views it, should push, if not Washington, then at least its allies, to negotiate with it. At the same time, the expert noted, it should not be forgotten that it was the Saudis who contributed to the latest bout of tensions by attacking the airport where an Iranian delegation was scheduled to arrive in July. That move gave Iran an excellent pretext to escalate the conflict around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Kommersant: Experts weigh in on soaring metallurgical coal prices
The growing shortage of metallurgical coal in Asian markets has boosted demand for Russian commodities. In the first week of September, coal prices Free on Board (FOB) in the Far East reached $176 per metric ton, up by one-third since early 2026. A deal was even signed to supply 40,000 tons of Russian grade K coal to China at $267 per metric ton. Experts believe the shortage is temporary as they await a price correction in the second half of the year.
At the end of 2025, a strong upward trend emerged in the global coking coal market, which, according to Alexander Kotov, partner at NEFT Research, could persist until the end of the first quarter of 2027. The current growth is fundamentally driven by three factors, namely slowing production in China due to strict environmental inspections at mines, strong demand from India, and output problems facing key exporters in Australia, where the slightest deterioration in weather conditions during the rainy season from November to February causes supply disruptions.
Boris Krasnozhenov, head of the investment and industry analysis directorate at Alfa-Bank, warns of the temporary nature of the current shortage. For Russian coal miners, the surge in demand will significantly improve the economic situation in the second half of the year, with senior analyst at T-Investments Akhmed Aliyev predicting a sharp rise in EBITDA compared to the first half of the year.
Kotov expects that growing coal prices will only lead to a decline in metal trade globally, reduced capacity utilization, and a wave of bankruptcies among inefficient players. The global market remains under pressure from Chinese imports that exceed 10 million metric tons per month. Krasnozhenov expects steel prices to remain close to current levels until the end of the year.

How the Iran War Forced the Gulf to Rethink Its Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Showing up at a funeral matters everywhere, but especially in the Arab world and the wider Middle East. When Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, was buried on July 9,just over four months after he was killed in a joint American-Israeli military strike. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Oman sent official delegations to the funeral. The United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, and Bahrain did not. To many analysts, the absence was more telling than any official statement.
Before the war, the Gulf states were diversifying their economies beyond oil, betting on remaining islands of stability in a turbulent Middle East. President Donald Trump’s decision to wage war on Iran, despite their opposition, exposed the fragility of that bet. War-risk insurance costs soared, and Iranian attacks followed.
Saudi facilities at Abqaiq and Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas complex were hit; the UAE intercepted barrages for weeks; Bahrain and Kuwait weren’t spared either. Though it wasn’t widely reported, Saudi Arabia and the UAE struck Iran, as, according to some accounts, did Qatar—though Doha denies it. In private, Gulf officials confirm that most Gulf Arab states retaliated.
The war produced unusual strategic convergence among the Gulf monarchies. There is now widespread recognition that the region’s existing security framework has failed. Though coordination behind the scenes may run deeper, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), created in 1981, has invoked its collective-defense clause only once.
Officials broadly agree on three points: Iran remains a long-term threat; the U.S. security umbrella is no longer dependable; and regional stability has become an existential priority. They also see two clear challenges. One is an Iranian regime that continues to pursue its vision of an “Iranian Axis” across the region. The other is an Israel bent on “regional paramountcy,” the presumption that it alone sets the terms of force while the region adjusts. Yet consensus on diagnosis only sharpened disagreement over the prescription.
Competition among the Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia and the UAE, means that convergence remains a trend rather than a settled fact. But such rivalry is hardly unique to the region. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine forced a fractious Europe into greater cohesion without resolving disagreements over how forcefully to confront Moscow. Iran and Israel are now subjecting the Gulf Arab states to a comparable test.
An unreliable U.S. security umbrella
The war altered the Gulf’s calculus on two fronts at once. Iran proved to be at least as dangerous as the most hawkish Gulf capitals had warned. The other shock was less expected: Washington was willing to start a regional war alongside Israel, despite Gulf objections, and then prove unable or unwilling to manage what followed.
The Gulf states had long since stopped assuming that Washington had a coherent and effective Iran strategy; the war added a new extreme. Objectives shifted by the week, and an administration in a hurry to exit, even as Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, left the Gulf Arab states feeling that they had been taken to war without being warned, consulted, or protected.
Even so, overwhelmingly, Gulf Arab states managed to intercept the overwhelming majority of what Iran fired at them. “Restraint backed by functioning defenses,” Rashid Al-Mohanadi, a Qatari analyst, argued, “is not the same as restraint born of vulnerability.” Privately, Gulf officials also say that they engaged in genuine, if discreet, quiet coordination.
Researchers at the Carnegie Endowment recommended that GCC states could share air-defense stockpiles with each other during the attacks. The GCC’s own mutual-defense clause was never formally invoked, but member states reaffirmed their commitment to it as the war ground on. None of that erases the economic toll of war-risk premiums or the failure of the collective-defense mechanism to activate, but it complicates the picture.
Most Gulf states have reverted to a previous preference: containing and de-escalating rather than confronting Iran. Qatar and Oman pressed Washington toward a memorandum of understanding with Tehran; Saudi Arabia backed the Pakistan-brokered track that produced it; the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain wanted to fight on but came on board within weeks. Even that agreement highlighted the Gulf’s limited influence; it raised the possibility of a $300 billion reconstruction fund for Iran financed by “regional partners” who were not consulted.
For more than a decade, the Gulf states have been working on a diversification strategy to insure against an unreliable Washington and a threatening Tehran at once. This tack gained momentum after the 2015 nuclear deal eased Tehran’s isolation even as Syria and Yemen deepened fears of Iranian regional reach. At the same time, Washington emphasized a pivot to Asia, though the Gulf capitals never quite believed in it. The strategy hardened into doctrine after Trump pulled out of the deal in 2018.
Not every Gulf state draws the same conclusion about how to navigate a region that will see less American dominance over time, a debate that remains unresolved. But all of them expect a new regional security architecture eventually, and the harder question is where diversification stops being hedging and starts being an architecture in its own right.
Old and new alignments in the Gulf
The strategic alignments within the GCC have shifted repeatedly. The Saudi-UAE-Bahrain blockade of Qatar, imposed in 2017, has largely given way to a different configuration, with Riyadh now closer to Doha and Muscat than to Abu Dhabi. But beneath these differences, a growing Gulf consensus is taking shape: a rejection of both an Iranian-led axis and Israeli regional paramountcy, coupled with a willingness to engage pragmatically with both countries.
Israel’s pursuit of “regional paramountcy” has revealed a fundamental divergence over the shape of postwar regional order and helped stall wider normalization in the absence of meaningful progress on Palestinian statehood. Qatar and Oman have maintained channels to Tehran throughout, while Saudi Arabia has adopted a similar posture of strategic restraint, refusing to let its territory be used against Iran and sending a delegation to Khamenei’s funeral.
Every Gulf state is now pursuing some version of the same wager: no single external guarantor can be trusted on its own, so the safer course is to pursue several policies at once rather than commit to a single tack.
The UAE just does it most visibly: striking Iran directly while also trading with it when convenient and walking out of OPEC without consulting Riyadh. Saudi Arabia finds exasperating the UAE’s preference for early, unilateral action rather than waiting to see whether a deteriorating situation might resolve itself. The gap between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi is the clearest sign that the Gulf states remain a considerable distance from genuine strategic cohesion.
Geography constrains every strategy the Gulf has tried. Iran and the Gulf share the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil flows. Decades of mutual suspicion have never severed their economic interdependence; Qatar and Iran still jointly exploit the world’s largest gas field. None of that produces trust, but it hasn’t produced pure passivity either: escalation was available to every Gulf Arab capital here, and each chose restraint and diplomacy instead.
Tehran has learned a new kind of leverage from this war—chokepoints, not proxies—and demonstrated how much strategic leverage control over Hormuz can provide. It has also survived the attempt at regime change, emerging with an economy contracted by 6.1% and inflation near 69%. It cannot sustain an open-ended war against most of its neighbors, and it knows it. That argues for a bargain, unless Tehran’s new leadership judges ending the war on Washington’s terms the greater risk.
Iran cannot be wished away. Increasingly, neither can Israel, which supplies the other side of the problem. The ceasefire that paused the direct U.S.-Iran fighting, brokered largely by Pakistan, never bound Israel at all. Tel Aviv wasn’t a signatory; it kept striking Hezbollah in Lebanon throughout the negotiations and treated the deal’s promise to end hostilities on every front as somebody else’s commitment. Washington backed Israel’s argument. The ceasefire itself came apart on its own terms: talks in Islamabad over access to Hormuz collapsed, and by July, Iranian strikes on commercial vessels that had bypassed Tehran’s approved shipping lane brought the fighting back in earnest.
Iran built the missile and proxy networks that gave the region reason to fear it long before February, and nothing here excuses that record. But Gulf governments are not choosing between two threats. They are managing both at once, and Israel’s demonstrated readiness to ignore arrangements even Washington negotiates makes it just as pressing a strategic problem as Iran, if not more so, depending on the Gulf government in question.
The case for building collective security
None of this amounts to reconciliation with Iran, and no serious figure in Riyadh, Doha or Abu Dhabi calls it that. What is emerging is an uneasy accommodation among adversaries that distrust one another but have run out of cheaper alternatives: an Iran too weakened to sustain war but unable to walk away from it unbeaten, and Gulf states too exposed to keep outsourcing their security to a Washington whose steadfastness in their defense has proved limited.
Tehran’s leverage over Hormuz, perhaps its only tangible gain, will last, and it leaves the Gulf states with a long-deferred choice: credible collective defense, or continued diversification. Oman is still negotiating to restore navigation through the strait and a meeting on the subject between Gulf Arab states and Iran was postponed on Sunday.
The challenges for Saudi Arabia have increased after the Houthis in Yemen took control of the Perim Island in the Bab El-Mandeb strait that would allow them to disrupt maritime traffic through the Red Sea and weaponize it as a chokepoint. Saudi Arabia has signed the Mecca Pact, a mutual defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan, though its strength remains untested.
These initiatives suggest the emergence of not one alliance, but overlapping partnerships: a diminished but enduring American partnership; Turkish and Pakistani security ties; bilateral arrangements among Gulf states; and channels of engagement with both Iran and Israel.
The Gulf Arab states are not trying to replace Washington but are layering a series of relationships to prevent domination by a single power. Yet coordination is not collective security. The Gulf needs standing mechanisms for integrated air and missile defense, intelligence-sharing, maritime security and mutual assistance, and a credible collective defense commitment. The GCC already has much of the institutional skeleton; what it has lacked is the political trust and strategic consensus to make it work.
The Gulf monarchies can keep stacking insurance policies, or begin turning those relationships into a genuine regional security system. The war has shown that the Gulf states can coordinate more effectively than many expected, and the foundations for something more durable may already be there.

The bombarding of childhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
19 minute listen
I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue.
This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media.
Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information.
Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. Does it give children time to follow a story, grasp a concept, identify with a character, regulate emotion or share attention with another person? Or does it continually hurry them toward the next cue, the next reward, the next burst of stimulation?
When media move too quickly, the layers of experience collapse into one another. A child may laugh at someone slipping on a banana peel but imitate only the visible silliness, missing the anticipation and reversal that make the joke work. A character may comfort a friend, but if the scene moves on too quickly, the child has little time to recognise the repair, or imagine doing the same in the kindergarten room. To develop empathy in the early years, a child must notice that another person feels something different. That small act of crossing over takes time.
In this sense, pace is not a minor stylistic feature of children’s media. It is one of the ways media imagine the child. Is the child a consumer to be retained, a nervous system to be stimulated, a vessel to be filled with educational content – or a person whose attention is still forming, and who therefore needs time to arrive?
People who worry about children and screens tend to worry about violent content, advertising, or whether a phonics app calling itself ‘educational’ truly supports phonics. These are reasonable worries and I share them. But spend five minutes watching what many young children watch, and you will see how fast, loud and bright everything on the screen has become. It does not matter whether the child is watching on a smartphone in the car or on a television at home. The screen has inherited the adult logic of media design.
That logic is, for the most part, the logic of the attention economy. It overwhelms and overshouts, making it easier for the screen to steer the viewer. The attention economy has introduced a host of small design features for shortening time. The Like button is faster than writing an appreciative comment. A progress bar tells us how many minutes remain in an article before we have decided whether to read to the end. Increasingly, AI appears beside long documents with an offer that sounds helpful but carries a philosophy: this text is long; would you like a quick summary?
The child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other
There are, of course, features that work in the opposite direction. The delayed message and the pop-up that asks: ‘Are you sure you want to delete this?’ are two examples. Such features interrupt automatic action and return a fragment of judgment to the user. A nature documentary with linearity and the interpretive presence of an adult voice is a great model for children’s media; for example, in the TV show Prehistoric Planet (2022-25), David Attenborough’s voiceover and the camera’s zoom-ins encourage children to look closely and wonder about unfamiliar life. But these are exceptions within a larger system in which speed is treated as the default.
When learning is crowded with content that keeps jumping ahead – a crisis appears, a mission begins, a spaceship launches, a door opens – the child’s attention is restarted as each problem is introduced and immediately solved. Such media may gesture at teamwork or perseverance, but the speed of the format leaves little time for those lessons to sink in. In the animated TV series Paw Patrol (2013-), for instance, a rescue is clear and reassuring: someone is in trouble, pups assemble, each uses a skill, and order is restored. Yet the movement from problem to rescue to resolution is often so efficient that the child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other. Similarly, in the app-based game Hot Wheels Unlimited, building tracks and racing cars may suggest creativity and problem-solving, but the dominant rhythm is acceleration: boost, race, crash, win, unlock, repeat.
Research has told us many useful things about children’s media. We know that some educational television (like Sesame Street) can support learning. We know that some apps are better designed than others. We know that interactive features in digital books can help when they serve the story, and distract when they do not. We know that characters and narratives shape children’s ideas about identity, gender and social life. Pace cuts across all of these questions as the condition under which content becomes experience.
Screen time can run fast or slow. This is partly why merely clocking ‘screen time’ is too crude a measure. Two children may each watch 20 minutes of media and have entirely different encounters with time. In one case, the child is moved through a coherent story with pauses, repetitions and recognisable emotional beats. In another, she is pulled through 10 clips, 30 characters, flashing colours, sudden songs and rewards that arrive before thought has had time to form. The clock records the same duration but the child does not live the same time.
And parents are rightly worried: a four-year-old does not come to media with adult reserves of self-regulation. She is still learning how to stay with a feeling, how to wait for a story to unfold, how to connect one event to another, how to notice that a character’s sadness matters before the joke wipes it away. If a programme moves too quickly, it may encourage a child to expect information to arrive in rapid, constantly shifting bursts, making slower, more sustained forms of attention harder to tolerate. Stopping this vicious cycle starts by asking what exactly makes children’s media fast or slow.
A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think
Don’t get me wrong, I am not saying that slow is always good or better than fast media. Some lively children’s media can be excellent; some slow media can be dull, inert or badly made. The point is that good children’s media give a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keep interrupting that act before it can become a memory or play.
When my research group compared children’s shows, apps and digital stories, we saw that pace can become a set of design choices. A story can move in a way that helps a child anticipate what comes next, or it can jump so quickly between scenes that cause and effect become blurred. A screen can guide the eye toward one important object, or fill the frame with competing movement.
This is why the familiar adult language of ‘engagement’ is so poor for children. A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think. In the Children’s Slow Media Project, we have therefore tried to make these differences visible. We evaluate children’s media by looking at how these media organise time. We ask whether the narrative is coherent enough to follow; whether the sensory field overwhelms meaning-making at specific age junctures; whether the design builds in stopping points, where the story can be digested before it goes on. Does a piece of media allow learning to develop through meaningful repetition? And does a story or piece create openings for a child and adult, or two children, to notice something together?
When in March 2026 the UK Department for Education advised parents of children aged under five to choose ‘slow-paced, age-appropriate’ content, without saying what slow-paced actually is, our group sought to make the term concrete.
What makes a show slow or fast for a given child? It depends. Children differ by age, temperament, language, sensory sensitivity and circumstance; thus, without testing their responses, it is impossible to provide a firm recommendation: a show that suits one four-year-old may overwhelm another. We therefore give ratings only to provide a map for adult judgment. The ratings are illustrations, inviting parents to check whether their child is being given enough time to complete an act of attention.
The shows scoring highest on the slow rubric are those that leave room around the characters’ actions and allow the child to recognise the actions. Often there is a face, a puppet, a song, a greeting, a familiar body on screen that treats attention as a relationship. Indeed, the power of programmes such as the US show Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood (1968-2001), the Norwegian series Fantorangen (2007-), and the British shows In the Night Garden… (2007-09) and Teletubbies (1997-2001) lies in their ability to build a rapport with the child and then repeat, almost as in a ritual. Here, small acts and greetings or songs provide a familiar frame, almost like a safety net, within which new concepts can be introduced. In the Australian animated series Bluey (2018-24), play often begins in an ordinary family situation and develops into imaginative games that involve parents, siblings and friends; the pace can be lively, but it tends to return the child to pretend play, negotiation and emotional understanding. In the animated TV series The Adventures of Paddington (2019-25) – a British-French co-production – gentle mishaps are usually held inside a world of curiosity, politeness, family and repair, so comedy becomes a route into perseverance or social understanding. Such programmes are slow because they leave openings through which the story can travel back into meaning and play.
The child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat
Conversations between characters are another way in which higher-ranked shows convey new concepts with appropriate pace. When introduced with context, a new word or idea might not be immediately clear, but the child can notice and infer. Over time, the child arrives at understanding, and this slow, even arduous process helps the concept stick. For example, in one episode of Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood (2012-) – based on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood – Daniel is nervous about trying the swing. The scene allows that feeling to be acknowledged, sung through, and gradually transformed into confidence, with support from Daniel’s friend Jodi and her grandmother. Similarly, in the Sesame Street-based game app Elmo Loves ABCs, a letter is traced, sounded, repeated, connected to words, and encountered through touch and play.
The lowest-scoring media are those in which the child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat, next loop of familiarity or personalised nudge. Instead of allowing the child to settle into the story, such children’s shows repeatedly pull attention back; the same is true of many preschool game apps built around loops of reward and progression.
Evaluating children’s popular media taught me that pace is a revealing measure of quality but also a proxy for a deeper question about the child’s agency, their own sense of self.
The real distinction is whether a medium leaves room for the child’s own attention or continually redirects it. When every pause is filled, every uncertainty immediately resolved and every wandering thought pulled back by a brighter cue, waiting and reflection can begin to feel intolerable. The child learns to reach for the next stimulus before the previous one has had time to settle. To give space for a child’s attention to drift inward, to reflect, is therefore to leave room for the child’s inner life. Slow media changes the relation between screen and child by saying: you may arrive at your own pace.
Some critics may dismiss slow media as nostalgia: a longing for the children’s television of the previous generation, or a privilege available only to parents with time and large bookshelves and big houses with quiet rooms. But that is a notion we should refuse. The attention economy has trained us to treat a child’s pause as a problem, a wandering gaze as lost engagement, and an unfilled moment as wasted time. The opposite is true – slow time gives children the space to perceive, process, respond and make meaning – and it can be designed for in children’s media.
Like energy drinks, fast media promise more capacity than the child actually has: more attention is supposed to lead to better performance. Fast media feel like an extension of the child’s energy, but the bargain is unsustainable and unhealthy. What looks like support can become dependency, and what promises engagement and learning is actually compulsion.
Children need media that do not merely occupy them, instruct them or keep them quiet. They benefit and grow from stories and shows that preserve children’s capacity for inwardness and their relation to others. In fast media, the child’s attention is continually propped up by the next stimulus. Slow media insist on the opposite. In the end, the aim is not to withdraw children from the digital world, but to make that world more worthy of them.

Best Noise-Canceling Earbuds (2026): Bose, Apple, Samsung, Beats, and More

The best noise-canceling earbuds are indispensable tech we all use daily for listening to any and everything—from phone calls, podcasts, and TV shows to workouts, commuting, and air travel. The list is endless. If you buy only one pair of headphones, you should make it a good pair of noise-canceling earbuds.
Most wireless earbuds come with built-in noise cancellation, but the difference between a good pair and a great pair is vast. Trust me, I’ve tested every one of our top picks in the real world—think busy New York City streets, loud cafes, crowded gyms, and rush-hour subway platforms—and sometimes, the noise cancellation is less effective at doing its one job. My top picks come from brands like Bose, Anker, Apple, and Beats, and while none is best overall, a few great options fit different needs.

Updated September 2026: I've updated WIRED's product recommendations and honorable mentions. I also updated specs, prices, and links.
Best ANC Earbuds
Specs
If you’re seeking the absolute best active noise canceling (ANC), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) should be at the top of your shortlist. In all my testing, I've yet to find a pair of noise-canceling earbuds that can knock these off the throne, though some models come close. In any environment, whether it’s a noisy subway platform or an international flight, these earbuds largely block out noise. Plus, they sound great, with most music and TV shows coming in clearly and with ample detail.
This second-generation version improves upon the original in small but important ways, including enhanced ANC, more stable connectivity, wireless charging, better personalized sound tuning, and improved customization options within the app.
All that noise-canceling comes at a cost. These are big earbuds that, while comfortable, wouldn’t be my first choice for working out or keeping things fast and light. The QuietComfort Ultra is also pricey and doesn’t have very impressive battery life (just six hours). But for ANC alone, it is the gold standard.
Best Budget ANC Earbuds
Specs

They have a similar shape and size to the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (though they are a bit smaller), with similar touch-sensitive controls on each bud.

Best ANC Earbuds for iPhone

They offer the easiest connectivity for Apple users, and you can swap between your devices instantly and seamlessly. Plus, they connect to Apple's Find My network for pinpoint location tracking.
But they’re also just good earbuds, with excellent noise-canceling and a particularly impressive transparency mode. They also have heart rate sensors built into each earbud, meaning you can start and track a workout and get accurate, detailed stats without wearing a fitness tracker. I’ve tested them against wearables from Garmin and Google, and they are surprisingly accurate.
Apple recently introduced ANC into its entry-level AirPods 5, which I will be testing soon.
Best ANC Earbuds for Samsung
Specs
The Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro emulate the magic of AirPods, but only for Samsung fans, says former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata. They have a very similar size, shape, and control scheme (pinch-and-slide controls on the stem). They are also strikingly similar in features, including accurate GPS location tracking, seamless swapping between Samsung devices, and ample control through a Samsung Galaxy phone. Where they stand out is a dual-speaker audio system that delivers rich bass and assertive treble, plus availability in multiple colors. I wouldn’t recommend the Galaxy Buds for anyone outside of Samsung’s ecosystem, though.
Best ANC Earbuds for Android
Specs
For all my Google Pixel Phone readers out there, I’d strongly consider the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2. The noise-canceling is excellent, and while not as strong as Bose, Apple, or Sony, these earbuds are much smaller and lighter. They also have a built-in mini wingtip on each bud, making them a bit more secure than AirPods Pro, in my testing. That, plus a long battery life and solid IP54 dust and water resistance, makes them good for commuting, travel, working out, and most anything you can throw at them.
Best ANC Earbuds for Sound Quality
Specs
If you want excellent noise-canceling and excellent sound quality, the Sony WF-1000XM6 is what you're looking for. With the right fit, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless earbuds that I’ve tested. They use a memory foam ear tip that, once you dial in the fit, provides excellent passive noise isolation. Combined with the near-Bose-level ANC, you can effectively tune out most of your surroundings.
Still, the crown goes to Bose for the best ANC, simply because the 1000XM6 can be tricky to fit perfectly—I had to swap out ear tips a few times before they felt comfortable.
Best ANC Earbuds for Working Out
Specs
The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the long-awaited update to the 2019 originals, with a much-needed redesign and the biggest new addition being strong noise cancellation. A sport-focused design with powerful ANC makes these earbuds excellent for the gym, effectively blocking out most background music and weight-clanging.
The new buds are also smaller, slimmer, and lighter than the originals, but still have an ultra-secure fit thanks to full wraparound ear hooks. I’ve literally smacked my ears around with my hands just to see if they would budge—they did not. Frequently Asked Questions
What Is Noise Canceling and How Does It Work?
When people think of noise cancellation in headphones, two things happen at once. First is passive sound isolation: headphones physically block your ears and block some sound from reaching them. Second is active noise cancellation (ANC), which uses a mix of exterior microphones and software to suppress outside sound before it reaches your eardrums.
ANC has been around since the 1970s, but has been refined to very advanced levels since then. Nowadays, it feels like magic, but the principles of physics haven't changed.
Sound moves through the air as pressure waves. The frequency of a wave (the number of times it oscillates per second) determines the pitch. We perceive low-frequency waves, like from an airplane rumble, as dull, bassy sound. We hear high-frequency waves, like a police siren, as a sharp, treble sound.
ANC uses microphones to hear incoming waves and generate the polar opposite waveform. When you add opposite waveforms together, they cancel each other out, and it's as if there is no sound wave at all, at least to our ears.
It isn't perfect because many sounds surround us at the same time—some constant, like the hum of an AC, while others are varied and sudden, like the human voice. ANC can't cancel every sound in your environment, but the best headphones get impressively close.
What Is Transparency Mode or Ambient Sound Mode?
You don't always want to block out all the sound around you when wearing headphones. That's why most models have a transparency mode (sometimes called ambient sound mode), which does the opposite of noise canceling—it filters in environmental sounds through your headphones so you can hear your surroundings more clearly.
Like with ANC, some headphones accomplish this task better than others. Apple AirPods are some of the best; it can feel like you're not wearing earbuds at all when using their transparency mode.
One limitation with these modes is outside interference, namely wind. I've tried using transparency mode while riding an ebike, and it mostly sounds like a blistering blast of artificial wind noise. If you're looking for headphones for outdoor activities like running or biking, open earbuds are a great alternative, as they leave your ears open to naturally hear the world around you.
How I Test Noise-Canceling Earbuds
I test all kinds of headphones, including noise-canceling ones, the way regular people might use them. I wear them for multiple weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I use them to take calls, listen to music, watch TV shows, scroll social media, and listen to my favorite playlists.
For testing noise cancellation, I use headphones in the real world. Luckily, I live in New York City, where loud traffic, subway platforms, cafes, and crowds of people are ever-present. When I can, I take earbuds on long flights to see how they handle jet engine noise.
For audio, I don't have a set playlist I test every single headphone with. I instead try to sample a wide variety of genres and artists. My main streaming source is Spotify Lossless, but I take time to test other lossless formats and high-resolution audio codecs when possible.

A College Girl Was Exploited on Camera. A Network of Anonymous Men Got to Work
