Officers from Israel Police's Lahav 433 - The National Crime Unit's cyber division concluded an investigation into a 44-year-old Ashkelon resident who had infected hundreds of computers belonging to dozens of companies with malware since 2020, police announced on Monday.
Police officers arrested the suspect on August 18 following a "complex analytical and technological investigation" in order to identify and locate them, police noted.
The suspect used the malware to gain control of the victims' computers, which police say enabled him to capture thousands of screenshots and screen recordings, hijack webcams and computer microphones, and record videos of victims in both their workplaces and their private homes.
Police say the suspect also downloaded files and extracted passwords, credit card details, and other sensitive information from the victims.
The suspect is also accused of recording minors, including capturing and storing nude images of underage victims.
As part of their investigations, police officers took statements from nearly 60 victims, as well as representatives from Incident Response firms that provided services to the companies affected by the breaches, police noted.
Suspected hacker caused over NIS 2 million in damages, Israel Police say
Police calculated that the incident also caused over NIS 2 million in cumulative financial damages to the affected companies.
The State Attorney's Office filed an indictment with the Rishon LeZion Magistrate's Court and a request to extend the detention of the suspect until the conclusion of proceedings, police stated.

Yehuda Widawski, Israel’s oldest Holocaust survivor, dies at 107 on Rosh Hashanah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:56:53 UTC
18:56:53 KST

Yehuda Aharon Widawski, who survived both the Lodz Ghetto and Auschwitz-Birkenau, and later devoted decades to restoring Jewish cemeteries in Poland, died on Sunday night at age 107.
Widawski was Israel's oldest Holocaust survivor and one of the oldest members of the Sochatchov and Modzitz Hasidic communities.
Born in Poland in 1919, Widawski was imprisoned with his family in the Lodz Ghetto following the Nazi invasion. He was later deported to Auschwitz, where he lost his parents and most of his siblings.
Together with his brother, Jehoszua, Widawski survived Josef Mengele's selection. Eight days later, the two brothers were sent to the Friedland work camp, before being liberated by the Red Army in 1945.
After the war, he assisted the Irgun's arms procurement efforts in Europe. He immigrated to Israel in 1950, settled in the country, and built a large family, living to see a fifth generation.
A life's work of memory, revival
Beginning in the late 1970s, Widawski returned to Poland repeatedly, locating and restoring dozens of Jewish cemeteries and mass graves that had been neglected and desecrated. He also worked to preserve historic gravestones.
In 2012, Widawski was chosen to light a torch at the state Holocaust Remembrance Day ceremony at Yad Vashem in recognition of his work preserving historical memory.
He also became a prominent witness at ceremonies held by Jews of Polish origin and remained a leading figure and role model in the Sochatchov and Modzitz Hasidic communities. He retained his mental clarity and warm demeanor until his final days.
His death on the eve of the Jewish New Year marks the passing of one of the most prominent symbols of revival to emerge from the ashes of the Holocaust, a man who endured some of the worst horrors of the 20th century and chose to devote his life to ensuring that future generations would not forget.
President Isaac Herzog paid tribute to Widawski in a post on X/Twitter.
"I was saddened to hear of the passing of Yehuda Aharon Widawski, of blessed memory, a survivor of Auschwitz and the Nazi camps, at the age of 107," Herzog wrote. "When he was 104, I had the privilege of hosting Yehuda at the President's Residence together with his magnificent family. I was moved to hear from him about his life story and about his decision to return to Poland years after immigrating to Israel in order to search for his grandmother's grave."
"That search became a life's work," Herzog said.
"For decades, Yehuda worked to locate and restore Jewish cemeteries and graves in Poland, and helped identify more than 3,000 graves," he went on. "Yehuda once said that his revenge against the Nazis was that they lost, and that we have the State of Israel. Indeed, his life was a remarkable testament to the victory of life, memory, and revival. May Yehuda's memory be blessed.""

'State-led discrimination': Turkey jails 16 people after raids in Izmir on LGBTQ+ groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:56:48 UTC
18:56:48 KST

A Turkish court ordered the detention of 16 people pending trial in the western province of Izmir as part of a government campaign that has included sweeping raids on LGBTQ+ associations, a prosecutor's office said on Monday.
The Izmir chief prosecutor's office said 18 suspects had been detained under the "My Family is Safe" operation, with 16 of them ordered to be remanded in jail and the other two placed under judicial supervision.
Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on Sunday the investigations, coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin, involved 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.
The government says the operation aims to protect children and family values. Authorities detained 26 people in Istanbul and 21 in Ankara over the weekend and raided the offices of several LGBTQ+ associations.
Rights groups accuse the government of increasingly targeting the LGBTQ+ community through rhetoric, restrictions and legal measures.
'State-led discrimination'
The Turkish Human Rights Association described the operation as "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society".
Nacho Sanchez Amor, the European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur, called the arrests "a shocking escalation" of repression.
Prosecutors have said the investigations cover alleged offenses including prostitution and obscenity, and that children and minors were being inappropriately influenced on issues relating to sexual orientation and gender identity.
The operation comes as Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan promotes a "Decade of Family and Population" aimed at tackling falling birth rates and an aging demographic.

Yohanan Elishuv, last surviving fighter who raised Eilat's Ink Flag in 1948, dies at 95
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:56:44 UTC
18:56:44 KST

Yohanan Elishuv, the last surviving fighter who took part in the raising of the Ink Flag at Umm Rashrash, modern-day Eilat, at the end of the 1948 War of Independence, died at age 95.
A Palmach fighter from the generation that fought for Israel’s independence, Elishuv served as a runner and driver, fought in some of the fiercest battles along the road to Jerusalem and in the Negev, and ultimately took part in an event that became one of the enduring symbols of the young State of Israel.
The raising of the makeshift Israeli flag at Umm Rashrash on March 10, 1949, came at the end of Operation Uvda and is generally regarded as marking the conclusion of the War of Independence. The troops reached the abandoned police station without a national flag, prompting soldiers to create what became known as the Ink Flag.
Elishuv was born in Petah Tikva to Haya and Moshe Elishuv. His father hailed from Russia, from a family of Subbotnik converts whose original surname was Sapinkov, while his mother immigrated from Bessarabia.
As a child, Elishuv struggled with severe dyslexia. He left school at 12 and worked in a garage where he developed technical skills that would later prove useful during his military service.
At around age 15, he claimed to be 16 so that he could join the Palmach. He combined work and military training at Givat Ada, where his platoon commander was Rafael “Raful” Eitan, who would later become IDF chief of staff.
Battle for Jerusalem
Elishuv’s connection with Haim Poznanski, known as “Poza,” commander of Company B of the Palmach’s Fourth Battalion, began after Elishuv quickly repaired a mechanical problem in Poznanski’s pickup truck. Impressed, the commander made the young fighter his personal runner during the battles for the road to Jerusalem.
Poznanski was killed in April 1948 at Nabi Samuel, one month after his brother Yitzhak was killed at Beit Keshet. Elishuv survived the bloody battle at Nabi Samuel, escaping under cover of heavy fog, an experience that left him with a lifelong fondness for foggy days. Every year, he visited Poznanski’s grave at Kiryat Anavim and took his children with him to honor his former commander and fellow fighters.
Following the failed Nabi Samuel operation, Elishuv helped organize the retreat, evacuate the wounded, and recover weapons.
During the battle for Jerusalem’s Katamon neighborhood, he was among the fighters who evacuated Eitan and David “Dado” Elazar, both future IDF chiefs of staff, when they were wounded. According to the account of his wartime service, the two wounded commanders had prepared grenades to blow themselves up to avoid being captured.
Elishuv later fought at Beit Siris, helped secure the Jerusalem road in the Sha’ar Hagai area, participated in the capture of Beit Iksa and Beit Mahsir, and took part in an attempt to break into Jerusalem’s Old City through Zion Gate. The battles for Jerusalem and its supply routes were among the central fronts of the 1948 war, with the Palmach and various Hagana units taking part in efforts to break the siege of the city.
During the first truce in June 1948, Elishuv was transferred to the southern front under Uzi Narkiss. He was wounded after driving over a mine, and had to be hospitalized, but returned to combat after recovering.
Elishuv's fight across the Negev
He subsequently fought in the isolated Negev, Operation Yoav, the capture of Beersheba, Operation Lot, Operation Horev, and finally Operation Uvda. Palmach veterans of the Negev Brigade also took part in several of those campaigns, including Operations Yoav, Horev, and Uvda.
During Uvda, Elishuv was appointed driver to Southern Front commander Yigal Allon. According to the account of his life, when Narkiss offered him the position, Elishuv responded irreverently that if Narkiss, with two rank bars, was trouble, then Allon, with three, would be three times as much trouble.
Allon reportedly laughed and said he wanted a man who feared nothing.
Elishuv later drove the command and reconnaissance jeep carrying Negev Brigade commander Nahum Sarig as the brigade raced south in an informal contest with Golani Brigade troops to reach Umm Rashrash first.
He was among the first group of fighters to reach the police station there on March 10, 1949. The Negev Brigade troops raised the improvised Ink Flag; that image became one of the defining photographs of the War of Independence.
Negev Brigade commander Sarig and Golani Brigade commander Nahum Golan later transmitted a message to the Israeli government announcing that the brigades were presenting the Gulf of Eilat to the State of Israel.
After leaving regular service in 1949, Elishuv served in the Artillery Corps reserves and participated in the 1956 Sinai Campaign, the Six-Day War, the Yom Kippur War, and the First Lebanon War.
In civilian life, he worked for about 30 years as a heavy-vehicle driver for Solel Boneh. His work included building roads to Eilat and helping develop southern Israel, the Dead Sea, Sodom, and the Negev’s crater region. He later worked as a purchasing agent in the company’s industrial division.
After retiring, he and his wife volunteered with a diabetes association.
Elishuv survived three bouts of cancer. He leaves behind his three children: Ofer, a doctor at Hadassah; Yoav, who works at Ichilov Hospital; and Merav, a lawyer. In his later years, he was invited to speak at pre-military academies and high schools about the legacy of Israel’s War of Independence.
Elishuv died in bed at his Petah Tikva apartment, built on the same plot of land where he had been born 95 years earlier.
He was buried at Segula Cemetery in Petah Tikva on Monday, in the city where he was born, lived, and died.

Houthis claim to launch large-scale missile, drone attack against Saudi Arabian air base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:56:44 UTC
18:56:44 KST

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi terror group claimed Monday that it carried out a large-scale ballistic missile and drone attack on King Khalid Air Base in southern Saudi Arabia, as the group simultaneously expanded its control over strategic islands along the Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis said dozens of ballistic missiles and drones targeted military infrastructure at the base in Khamis Mushait, including aircraft hangars, radars, runways and ammunition depots.
The group claimed the strikes caused significant damage to the base. The extent of the damage could not be verified immediately.
The Houthis stated that the operation was carried out in response to what they described as more than 300 Saudi airstrikes across Yemen during the previous five days.
The group said Saudi F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets carried out those strikes from Khamis Mushait and Taif airbases.
Saudi Arabia has carried out strikes against Houthi targets amid a sharp renewed escalation between the kingdom and the Iran-backed group, but the Houthi figure of more than 300 strikes was not independently confirmed.
The Houthis threatened further operations inside Saudi territory if the strikes on Yemen continued, saying they would respond to any additional escalation with larger attacks.
The Monday claim followed a major Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia the previous week, when the group used missiles and drones against Khamis Mushait and Saudi energy infrastructure. Saudi authorities said those attacks wounded more than 70 people and caused fires at oil facilities.
Houthis make territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast
At the same time, the Houthis have made significant territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and on islands near the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemeni government and Houthi officials said Monday that the rebels had captured Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish, two islands roughly 160 kilometers north of the strait.
The takeover followed the group’s seizure of Mocha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, during its rapid advance along Yemen’s western coastline.
The Houthis had reached the Hanish Islands several days earlier as government forces withdrew from positions in the area, according to Yemeni military sources.
Government forces backed by Saudi Arabia attempted over the weekend to regroup and launch a counteroffensive following the Houthi advances around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

OpenAI backs binding UK AI legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:55:39 UTC
18:55:39 KST

LONDON — OpenAI’s top European lobbyist is calling for the U.K. to introduce binding rules on AI developers in light of the technology’s rapidly advancing capabilities, and the risks that come with them.
Tom Duff Gordon, the company’s head of policy in EMEA, told POLITICO in an interview that the “U.K. should act now to set up a stronger set of safety rules.”
“OpenAI is in a position to support legislation in the U.K. to establish durable, mandatory, capability-based requirements for frontier AI that would build on the set of voluntary commitments that we currently have,” said Duff Gordon.
Advertisement
He said Andy Burnham’s government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to pursue legislation.
The Labour government is facing mounting pressure from lawmakers to address the risks of AI after leading companies disclosed a spate of safety incidents in recent months. That pressure intensified last week after a researcher at AI company Anthropic resigned and accused Anthropic and OpenAI, where he’d previously worked, of “gambling with our lives.”
In its 2024 manifesto, Labour committed to “introducing binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful AI models,” but has since backed off the idea of comprehensive AI legislation, instead relying on sectoral regulation and safety testing by its AI Security Institute through voluntary partnerships with AI firms.
Duff Gordon said legislation would put the U.K. on an “equal footing” with the EU and emerging state and federal frameworks in the U.S. — where OpenAI has said it backs “mandatory, capability-based national AI safety regulation.”
But he stressed that any U.K. legislation should be narrowly focused on the most serious risks related to national security and cybersecurity, and “the small number of labs and the small number of models that are completely at the frontier.”
He said any legislation should include compulsory independent model testing by third parties, a “strong focus” on cybersecurity, and requirements for monitoring and reporting safety incidents. AISI should play a “central role” in any new regime, he added, saying OpenAI has “high regard for their technical competence and expertise.”
Advertisement
Legislation should also include standards for testing models ahead of their release set out in “flexible and adaptive” technical rules designed for “international interoperability,” he said, so that “as we move, we hope, towards greater global and multilateral consensus on the governance of frontier AI, the U.K. will be well positioned.”
AI safety is expected to be on the agenda when U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping meet later this month, which Duff Gordon said was “a very important conversation for them to have, and we hope that they have it.”
But he said there is also an opportunity for the U.K. — where OpenAI maintains its largest research hub outside of the U.S. — to have “a strong and influential voice on the next stage of policy.”
“We think the U.K. is a leader in AI,” Duff Gordon said. “We want them to continue to be a leader in this new safety-conscious era that we’re going to be moving into.”

India has approved a proposal to supply power to Nepal
India has approved the export of up to 654 MW of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours a day until December 31, following devastating floods that damaged hydropower infrastructure and sharply reduced the Himalayan nation's domestic generation capacity, the Ministry of Power said on Monday.The approval, effective from September 13, allows electricity exports to the Nepal Electricity Authority between midnight and 6 pm, according to the ministry.Up to 600 MW will be supplied through the Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar 400 kV double-circuit line, while another 54 MW can be transmitted through the Tanakpur-Mahendranagar 132 kV single-circuit line, the ministry said.
"The recent floods in Nepal have caused significant damage to hydropower infrastructure, reducing the country's domestic power generation capacity and creating an additional requirement for electricity," the Ministry of Power said in a release."The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal," it added.The ministry said the quantum of electricity to be exported from January 2027 would be reviewed in December 2026. "The quantum of power to be exported from January 2027 will be reviewed in December 2026," it said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated parts of northern and central Nepal.
According to Nepal's national disaster risk rreduction and management authority, the death toll had reached 1,385, while 5,130 people remained missing as of September 11. More than 12 hydropower plants were reportedly swept away or damaged.About 900 power station workers are among those reported missing, further affecting the country's electricity generation capacity. Nepal, where hydropower supplies almost all electricity, had also halted power exports and said it would buy electricity from India to meet domestic requirements.India has separately continued its relief and rescue support. The ministry of external affairs said eight special flights since August 26 had delivered more than 130 tonnes of relief material, while 54 expert personnel had been deployed for rescue, relief and forensic operations.
"The assistance includes standard relief supplies such as temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps and medicines," the MEA said, besides specialised equipment for tunnel and mud rescue operations and DNA profiling.The United States has also approved $1 million to strengthen Nepal Police's DNA and forensic identification capacity. The US State Department said the latest assistance takes Washington's humanitarian, health and forensic support following the floods to more than $5 million.Nepal has meanwhile sought China's assistance to rebuild the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road, a key trade route that was severely damaged. Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal told The Kathmandu Post that "China has given us a verbal commitment to provide assistance, although a written agreement has not yet been signed."

An essay by Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei calling for slowing down AI development may look like a rational statement focused on safety risks, but it is really a "Cold War playbook" targeting China, the state-backed Global Times has said in an editorial.
In the essay published on Saturday and later endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, Amodei outlined a framework to pace the development of frontier AI model capabilities and create more time to manage mounting safety risks.
Amodei also urged the US to strengthen chip export controls on China and crackdown on alleged model distillation by Chinese AI labs. He also told CBS News on Sunday that the "toughest dilemma" over his proposal to slow AI advancement was if China and other nations chose not to do the same.
The Chinese government has not yet issued an official statement specifically responding to Amodei’s remarks.
However, a response has emerged in Chinese state media, with the Global Times, published by the People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, arguing that the true agenda of Amodei's essay was “to attempt to curb China's AI development through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies, uphold Washington's monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology, and exclude China from the global AI governance system.”

‘We're leading China’
US President Donald Trump brushed aside calls to slow down AI on Sunday, saying that "very negative forces" were raising exaggerated concerns.
"We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins," Trump said.
The US president dismissed calls to curb the sector's rapid progress, claiming that "a lot of negative forces" are exaggerating hypothetical risks and raising issues that will never materialise.
While acknowledging that authorities "can put guardrails" on technological systems, Trump maintained that his primary objective centres on preserving America's edge.
The US and China are planning to discuss frontier AI safety risks in mid-September, sources have said, and the issue could be raised during a summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on September 24.
The US leader visited China in May, and later extended an invitation to Xi for a state visit to the US scheduled for September 24.

Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:51:40 UTC
18:51:40 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
Satellite imagery has confirmed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant following a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike, with part of the facility’s main production building destroyed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite images published by the Exilenova+ OSINT project show that one FP-5 missile struck the plant during an attack overnight on September 11, destroying a section of its main workshop measuring approximately 20 by 15 meters.
“One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed part of the main workshop measuring 20 by 15 meters,” Exilenova+ said.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, which produces the Flamingo missile, also confirmed the use of the FP-5 against the facility, according to Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka on September 13.
Fire Point said the strike destroyed an attached section of the building covering approximately 380 square meters.
“As a result of the hit, the building covering an area of about 380 square meters completely collapsed and was destroyed,” the company said. Exilenova+ also reported that another Flamingo missile apparently failed to reach the plant, with satellite imagery showing an impact crater near the facility.
Volgogradpromproekt is located in Volgograd’s Kirovsky district and specializes in small-scale chemical production, including organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins, and other specialized industrial chemicals.
One of the company’s key products is OSF, an organosilicon derivative of ferrocene containing iron compounds. The substance is used as a catalyst and burn-rate modifier in composite solid rocket propellants, allowing manufacturers to regulate how quickly the propellant burns while maintaining required characteristics.
Volgogradpromproekt supplies Russian defense manufacturers, including the Perm Powder Plant, which produces propellants and explosives for more than 100 weapons systems, including Grad and Smerch rockets and surface-to-air missiles.
The plant has also been linked to production chains for Kalibr cruise missiles and air-launched anti-ship missiles. Another major customer, the Kamensky Chemical Plant, produces solid fuel for Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles, as well as Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S rockets.
Volgogradpromproekt also supplies materials used in shipbuilding, including to the Amur Shipbuilding Plant, which builds Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile ships.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces used FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Russia’s Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, the country’s only facility that serially assembles Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.

Left edges ahead in Swedish election thriller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:50:35 UTC
18:50:35 KST

STOCKHOLM — Sweden’s high-stakes general election is heading for a tight finish in a contest to decide whether a new center-left prime minister takes over or the far right enters government for the first time.
With 95% of results now declared, the left-wing bloc of Social Democrat opposition leader Magdalena Andersson has a three-seat lead in the 349-member parliament — ahead of conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party right-wing alliance.
The outcome of Sunday’s vote may not be known until Wednesday. The two candidates for prime minister will now seek talks with other party leaders as they attempt to solidify their blocs into governing majorities.
Advertisement
An official familiar with the matter said Kristersson intends to play hardball — he is expected to try to tempt the small, liberal Center party to leave Andersson’s camp and join his side, before forcing a vote in the new parliament on whether he can stay on as prime minister. That vote is likely to be at least two weeks away.
The finely balanced contest is bittersweet for Andersson and her allies on the left. For months, her bloc had been leading comfortably in the polls, but the race tightened dramatically in the last two weeks of the campaign.
Speaking around midnight, she said the votes counted so far pointed to an “even” outcome. “But right now we are leading and if this holds up, Sweden will get a new government,” she said, to cheers from supporters packed into her party’s glitzy election night reception.
The election is a watershed moment for Sweden: An Andersson victory would restore center-left rule, while a Kristersson win could bring the far-right Sweden Democrats — a strongly anti-immigration party founded in the 1980s by neo-Nazis — into government for the first time. The result will also be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where nationalist movements are gaining ground.
Kristersson has been governing for the past four years with support from the Sweden Democrats in parliament, but without giving them a formal role in the coalition.
He said the closeness of the result would make forming a government “complicated,” but insisted the left had failed to win a majority for its “socialist” economic program. “Where it ends remains to be seen,” he told his supporters at the Moderates’ election night party in central Stockholm. “But we are not in a hurry.”
Advertisement
ABBA and ice-creams
The day began with the betting markets and final polls giving Andersson’s left a narrow but consistent lead in the proportional representation election.
She won a coveted celebrity endorsement on Sunday morning from ABBA’s Benny Andersson, who took the stage at the Social Democrat headquarters to serenade her. As he played the opening chords of “Mamma Mia,” Social Democrat staffers took up the refrain, replacing the chorus line with “Magdalena.”
Wild cheering broke out among the youthful crowd drinking beer and champagne at the Social Democrat election “vigil” when two exit polls gave Andersson’s bloc a clear lead when voting closed at 8 p.m.
But a few hours later, the atmosphere darkened again as forecasts showed the race was far tighter than expected, with just a single seat separating the two blocs. Andersson’s party’s vote share fell and it will likely end up with fewer seats, even if she wins power.
By 9 a.m. on Monday, with 6,273 out of 6,626 districts declared, the Swedish Election Authority projected Andersson’s four-party bloc winning 176 seats — compared with 173 for Kristersson’s side.
Analysis by Swedish public broadcaster SVT showed only about 28,000 votes separate the two blocs — with another 200,000 expected to be counted Wednesday.
Advertisement
“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her campaign bus, posing for selfies with voters and party volunteers. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.”
Andersson accepts that a victory for her left-wing bloc won’t consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final margin is a narrow one. But she has bet big on the belief that Swedish voters will balk at handing power to a party she regards as “extremist.”
“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.
Kristersson’s night was mixed, too. His Moderate party actually increased its vote share, while the Sweden Democrats and their firebrand leader Jimmie Åkesson fell back. But the sitting prime minister may still lose office.
He insists that the Sweden Democrats can be trusted, having worked with them to drive through hard-line policies on immigration and violent crime.
The prime minister told POLITICO on Friday that any Sweden Democrat ministers in his team would have limited room to go rogue — because he would remain in charge.
Advertisement
“Since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government,” he said.
In the coalition-building efforts that determine who gets to run the country, Sweden’s smaller parties often have outsized influence. That will be true again this time if the projections of a razor-thin victory margin are borne out.
On the right, Kristersson leads a settled alliance of four parties, including the Sweden Democrats. Andersson’s path to a coalition, meanwhile, could be complicated by disagreements between the smaller parties in her bloc. Much may depend on her political skills and her ability to force through a power-sharing deal in the days and weeks ahead.

German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.

She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.
What is Ilona W. accused of?
Prosecutors say Ilona W. ran a marketing agency in Berlin and also chaired a lobbying association, giving her extensive contacts in military and political circles.
She allegedly had contact with a full-time Russian intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin from at least October 2023.

Ilona W. is also accused of attending events herself to identify useful contacts and potential targets.
Prosecutors say she tried to recruit people from Germany's Defense Ministry and the arms industry.
She also allegedly sought information on German defense policy and the defense industry on behalf of her Russian contact, particularly in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine.
The charges were filed last week before the state security division of Berlin's Higher Regional Court.
Germany expelled the suspected Russian intelligence officer linked to the case shortly after W.'s arrest, prompting Moscow to retaliate by expelling a German diplomat.

Can Lebanon swap Hezbollah's arms for reconstruction cash?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:47:09 UTC
18:47:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Lebanon swap Hezbollah's arms for reconstruction cash?
There's a phrase attributed to Rafic Hariri that captures Lebanon's postwar bargain, because that's what it is, with almost frightening clarity: "we bought peace with debt." After the 1989 Taif Agreement, the men who had waged war entered the state and began administering peace, because it became more profitable than continuing the war.
Reconstruction contracts, borrowed money, bank deposits, Gulf capital and donor support turned the end of fighting into a financial settlement, giving every major bloc a stake in keeping it alive. The end of the civil war in 1990 safeguarded the political class by handing it a new economic arrangement.
Nearly four decades later, Lebanon is being offered another version of the same bargain: disarm Hezbollah, place the south under state control, and the money returns: an IMF programme, World Bank lending, Gulf investment in a southern economic zone. The first bargain was priced in debt and expired in October 2019, when the banks shut their doors. This one is priced in weapons.
Reconstruction is the word being used. Resuscitation is closer.
The arrangement offered to Lebanon is asymmetrical. Hezbollah is asked to disarm, accept verification, and place the south under Lebanese Army control, while Israeli withdrawal remains gradual and conditional. The Lebanese Armed Forces, Lebanon's principal cross-sectarian institution, must enforce state authority against a movement rooted in the same communities from which many of its soldiers are recruited.
Joseph Aoun, president since January 2025, knows what that asks of the army he once led. Ordering it into direct confrontation with Hezbollah – Lebanon's fear – could lead to the same fracture as in the early years of the civil war. And the country supplying the bombs dropped on the south is also the power that decides how the south gets rebuilt. A government that cannot safely fulfil one demand or compel the other keeps both in motion, and both unresolved.
For nearly thirty years, Lebanon spent more dollars than it earned. Diaspora deposits and Gulf capital entered the banks that financed the state, and Banque du Liban defended an artificial currency peg. Governments borrowed to pay salaries, service debt, and rebuild Beirut, while the fixed lira made imports cheap and incomes look stronger than the economy beneath them.
In 2019 the dollars stopped arriving at the rate the system required. The peg became a fiction, the banks locked depositors out, salaries collapsed, and the life built around the 1,500 lira disappeared.
How the money becomes loyalty
The pattern didn't start in 2019. It started at the 1989 Taif Agreement.
The standard complaint at the time was precise: Taif reconciled the warlords, not the people. Reconstruction began only once the political class had survived the war, and the ministries handed out under the new sectarian formula converted that survival into permanence.
Solidere, the Lebanese Company for the Development and Reconstruction of Beirut Central District, founded in 1994, compelled landowners to trade their property for shares rather than compensation, and was financed through the same treasury bills that paid interest to the same banks partly owned by the political class.
Contracts for roads, power and reconstruction were distributed through ministries now held by the men who had fought each other for those buildings a few years earlier, and each ministry became a channel: deposits into debt, debt into contracts, contracts into the jobs, favours, and protection that bind a constituency to its leader. The war had ended. The economy built to finance its end had relocated the same men into the offices that controlled it.
Hezbollah is no outsider to the post-Taif order; it is one of its armed shareholders. Yet disarmament asks one faction to surrender the instrument of its power while the governing order is asked to surrender none of the institutions through which it reproduces itself. The banks, ministries and confessional formula are absent from every agreement on the table. A binding allocation of banking losses, bank recapitalisation or serious tax reform would force every faction to pay. Disarmament concentrates the bill on Hezbollah.
What returns once that condition is met is the same machine that has been running for four decades. An IMF programme supplies the external seal of approval. The World Bank's existing reconstruction framework can expand; bilateral aid and Gulf capital become easier to mobilise; the money returns through the same state machinery. Hezbollah is weakened. The post-Taif order is refinanced.
Disarmament is the maximum reform the system can absorb without dissolving. Everything the system cannot survive – a law dividing the banking losses, a tax base, the confessional formula itself – stays exactly where it has been since 1989. Past that point, real reform starts touching their own accounts, and none of them will vote for that.
What that refinancing looks like in practice is not abstract. A house in the south does not become a reconstruction project on its own. Someone has to recognise the damage, decide who is eligible for compensation, choose which villages are prioritised over others, design the tender and pick the contractor, approve the payment, and rule on whatever delay or appeal follows. Every one of those decisions is political, and Lebanon has followed this exact sequence twice before.
After Taif, reconstruction aid flowed through the Council for Development and Reconstruction, an agency established in 1977 to sit above politics, but captured by it within two decades. Rafik Hariri and, later, Nabih Berri took command of its board, and it became a byword for sweetheart deals.
Its board went essentially unchanged from 2006 until 2025, extended by a 2009 decree that kept the same members in place indefinitely. Split after Taif between Hariri and Jumblatt, the Central Fund for the Displaced was meant to resettle the displaced from the civil war within three years for $500 million. It took ten years and cost over a billion, while investigators found that residents were compensated for properties that never existed and officials at the Ministry of Displaced had accumulated real estate no salary could explain.
The current round runs the same route. The World Bank's Lebanon Emergency Assistance Project, with $250 million in funding against a $1 billion framework, is implemented through the CDR according to international benchmarks. The ministries distributing that money, and appointing those consultants, are the same ones allocated under the sectarian formula in 1990.
Ask, then, what disarmament actually buys, if the framework is implemented, verified and completed. It buys a state with one gun instead of two. It does not, on its own, buy a different state.
A promise with no deadline
The sovereignty case is real. Lebanon cannot remain a country where Hezbollah decides when war begins. But Lebanon's constitutional order has been promising its own abolition for thirty-six years. The 1990 amendments name the end of political confessionalism as a national goal and assign parliament a staged plan for carrying it out. No deadline was imposed on the people who benefit from delay.
At what point do we stop treating each crisis as a separate malfunction? The banking collapse, the port explosion and the stalled IMF negotiations were different events, yet each ran into the same structure: divided authority, protected officeholders, concealed responsibility, and no institution strong enough to impose a settlement on the others.
Today, new loans diagnose a shortage of money. Reconstruction diagnoses destroyed buildings. Neither diagnosis reaches the political machinery that makes accountability impossible. The post-Taif order receives new money, new legitimacy, and another lease on life.
In Beirut's southern suburbs, a resident named Mohammad has been waiting since the ceasefire for someone to open a file on his damaged home and business. Not the state's reconstruction project, which hasn't reached his street. Not Jihad al-Bina, Hezbollah's own compensation arm, which paid out roughly four hundred million dollars after the 2024 war but has gone largely quiet on this one, with its funding from Tehran disrupted by sanctions and the fall of Assad.
Two authorities spent twenty years competing for the right to be the name a family calls when the roof comes down. For the moment, in Mohammad's street, neither one has come.

Yemen's displaced long for loved ones, stability as Houthis advance

Unknown Publisher

Yemen's displaced long for loved ones, stability as Houthis advance
TAIZ, Yemen, Sept 14 - As Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants swept through the battered country's Red Sea coastline, thousands of panicked people fled to makeshift camps, adding to an already vast population of internally displaced people.
Aisha Muhammad, like others who escaped from coastal areas and arrived in the southwest province of Taiz, left behind her two daughters and three sons, trapped in their homes as fighting turned a once-vital corridor for trade into a route of displacement.
"They are being blocked and shot at. Right now, they cannot reach us, and we cannot return to them. This is a trial from God," said Muhammad, boiling water in an old black teapot placed on rocks over a flame.
More than 82,000 people have been displaced by the fighting since the start of the month, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, including over 2,000 who have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.
The advance by the Houthis, who already control most of the north and Yemen's most populous areas, is strengthening Tehran's hand in its conflict with the U.S.
ANOTHER YEMEN CRISIS
Hardship is not new in Yemen, where a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, despite expiring six months later, but efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified.
The Houthis – mountain fighters in sandals who have transformed into a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones – have opened a second theatre of war with their lightning western offensive.
Their advance has put them in a strong position to tighten their grip over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a vital chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping – more than six months after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
"Behind every number is a family who's lost everything," said Amy Pope, IOM director general. "Many have been displaced multiple times. People are crossing the sea with nothing because they have no other choice left. Yemen is a country torn by poverty and conflict, and it cannot carry this crisis alone."
Video shared by IOM showed Yemenis who arrived in boats on Djibouti's northern coast receiving food and water at a nearby refugee settlement.
Djibouti's finance minister, Ilyas Dawaleh, said on Sunday that the situation was "becoming increasingly difficult for our country, despite our unwavering commitment to humanitarian resources".
Back in Taiz, many, including Abdullah Qaiyd, an elderly man walking with a stick, are once again longing for stability.
"Now, look at us. We are tormented and shaken to our core. We long for a basic livelihood, and we long for safety," he said. REUTERS

French blockade looms over Commission’s plan to fast-track trade deals in English
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:46:21 UTC
18:46:21 KST

Eager to unlock new markets for EU businesses, the European Commission plans to accelerate trade deal ratification by circulating only English versions for approval by EU governments and the European Parliament – but sources told Euronews that Paris is set to oppose the move if it goes ahead.
France will push back against a European Commission plan to fast-track ratification of trade agreements by circulating only English-language versions during talks with EU governments and lawmakers, skipping translation into the bloc’s 24 official languages, according to several sources.
The slow ratification of the contentious EU–Mercosur trade deal has frustrated the Commission, which wants to accelerate negotiations and bring deals into force more quickly as it seeks new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions.
Translating the agreements into every official EU language can take months due to the legal scrubbing required before the ratification process begins.
The EU executive has confirmed to Euronews that trade chief Maroš Šefčovič told EU trade ministers in February that the trade deal with India concluded on 27 January could serve as a test case for using English as the main language during ratification.
“We lost almost €300 billion by not having the Mercosur agreement in place since 2021, if it comes to the GDP, and more than €200 billion in export opportunities,” Šefčovič told journalists after meeting ministers on 20 February, adding that once negotiations end it can take up to 2.5 years before businesses can operate in partner countries.
“In today's world, we cannot simply lose the time,” he said.
Šefčovič said the Commission would ensure the agreements are translated into all 24 official EU languages once published in the Official Journal, i.e. after ratification. He added the proposal was backed by at least seven member states at the meeting, though not all countries had time to speak.
French sources who spoke to Euronews were insistent that Paris would vigorously oppose the move to English-only agreements if necessary.
“As a matter of principle, we defend the use of all the languages of the Union, and in particular French, which is one of the EU’s working languages,” one official told Euronews.
'Transparency, precision and understanding'
Language policy in the bloc’s institutions remains politically sensitive for countries such as France, whose language has declined sharply over the past decades as English massively dominates daily work in the European Union institutions – despite French, German and English being the three official working languages.
“Switching entirely to English raises a legal and democratic issue, and the Commission is well aware of it,” another French official told Euronews.
On its website, the European Commission says linguistic diversity is essential and that the EU promotes multilingualism in its institutional work.
The bloc once even had a commissioner dedicated to multilingualism, though the portfolio was gradually merged with others and eventually disappeared.
"I have the impression that in some cases the Commission seizes the opportunity to push the idea that English has a superior status, and that the other official languages are translation languages that can come later," Michele Gazzola, expert in language policy, said.
He added that relying only on English during ratification could pose problems for members of the European Parliament, and even more so if national parliaments are involved.
“It’s a matter of transparency, precision and understanding."

Iran unveils homegrown catalysts for oil, gas industries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:45:16 UTC
18:45:16 KST

The “chromium-free high-temperature shift catalyst” and “medium-temperature shift catalyst” were unveiled at Iran’s knowledge-based Sarv Oil and Gas Industries Development Company on Sunday.
The two products have been developed for use in key industrial processes, including hydrogen and syngas production, where catalysts play a critical role in converting carbon monoxide and adjusting gas composition for subsequent stages.
In the water-gas shift process, carbon monoxide reacts with steam to produce hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
High- and medium-temperature shift catalysts are used, depending on process design and operating conditions, in hydrogen, ammonia, methanol and syngas production units, as well as in parts of the refining and petrochemical industries.
The domestic production of the catalysts is particularly significant for Iran as sanctions and restrictions on access to foreign technologies and equipment have complicated the country’s supply chains.
One of the newly unveiled products is a chromium-free high-temperature shift catalyst.
 
 Conventional high-temperature shift catalysts may contain chromium compounds as promoters.
Eliminating chromium from the formulation can reduce concerns associated with the handling and management of chromium-containing materials and represents a technological step toward safer catalyst formulations.
The second product is a medium-temperature shift catalyst designed to improve carbon monoxide conversion under intermediate-temperature operating conditions.
The developers say domestic production of such catalysts can go beyond replacing imported products by shortening supply chains, reducing foreign-exchange costs and limiting the impact of sanctions and import restrictions.
It can also facilitate access to technical support and replacement catalyst supplies for industrial operators.
Catalysts are considered strategic components of the oil, gas and petrochemical sectors, and disruptions in their supply can affect the operating capacity and costs of industrial plants.

Türkiye among most popular non-EU destinations for European travelers in 2024

18:45:10 KST

Melike Pala
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Türkiye ranked among the top three destinations for tourism trips made by European Union residents outside the bloc in 2024, according to data released by Eurostat.
The UK, Türkiye and Switzerland were the three most popular destinations outside the European Union by number of trips made by EU residents last year, Eurostat said on Sunday.
EU residents made around 1.2 billion tourism trips in 2024, spending nearly 6 billion nights away from home, while total tourism expenditure reached €618 billion ($713 billion).
According to Eurostat, almost 73% of EU residents' foreign trips were made within the EU, while the remaining trips were to destinations outside the bloc.
The UK, Türkiye and Switzerland were the leading destinations outside the EU by number of trips in 2024.
Destinations outside the European continent accounted for only 13.1% of all foreign trips by EU residents.
Africa represented 4.5%, Asia 4.2% and the Americas 4.1%.
Eurostat noted that proximity remained an important factor in EU residents' choice of foreign destinations, with neighboring or nearby countries generally preferred for trips.
Italy was the most popular foreign destination overall for EU residents, accounting for 10.7% of all foreign trips, followed closely by Spain at 10.4%.

Butenko: Education Ministry recommends 3 learning models for schools amid prolonged air raids
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:42:54 EEST
18:42:54 KST

The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine recommends that schools use three basic models for organizing the educational process—face-to-face, combined, and remote—amid prolonged and repeated air raid alerts, Minister of Education and Science Andriy Butenko has reported.
"The main principle remains unchanged: the safety of children and teachers comes above all. At the same time, we must do everything possible to ensure that children have as many learning opportunities as possible despite the alerts, because every lost hour ultimately affects the quality of education," Butenko wrote on Facebook.
According to him, last week, together with teachers, parent organizations, school principals, and education administration heads, recommendations were developed for organizing the educational process in general secondary education institutions during prolonged and repeated air raid alerts. The recommendations were officially sent to the regions to help schools determine their operational procedures in advance under various security conditions.
According to the guidelines, schools can use face-to-face, combined, or remote learning models and switch between them dynamically depending on the security situation and the capacity of a specific institution.
The framework also defines the procedure for organizing the school day if an air raid alert is active at its start, as well as actions in the event of power or communication outages.
In particular, if a shelter is equipped for conducting classes, the educational process can continue there. If an air raid alert catches children and teachers during remote learning, the lesson can continue online after everyone moves to a safe location.
For regions with prolonged air raid alerts, it is recommended to adapt remote classes so that participants are immediately in safe locations. Asynchronous learning should be available for students who cannot join the classes.
Butenko noted that educational administrators have already reviewed the recommendations, and starting September 15, the educational process must be maximally adapted to the developed approaches.
"It is important to provide schools not with a single rigid instruction for all cases, but with clear tools so they can find the best solution for their conditions, maintaining the main balance: safety always comes first, but we do everything to preserve the quality of education," he emphasized.
According to the minister, the recommendations were developed at the request of educators and take into account the experience and proposals of people who organize education under wartime conditions every day.

The Military Court Service

The Military Court Service
The Military Court Service provides a criminal court for the Royal Navy, Army and Royal Air Force in the Court Martial, Summary Appeal and Service Civilian Court.
Introduction
The Military Court Service (MCS) works closely with, but is independent of: the Office of the Judge Advocate General; the Service Prosecuting Authority, which is equivalent to the Crown Prosecution Service; the Service chains of command, Service and MOD personnel branches; the National Probation Service; and the victim and witness services and military court advocates.
Service Court proceedings are publicised over a two-week assize period. Military court listings. All hearings are open to the public in exactly the same way as civilian courts, unless otherwise directed by the presiding judge.
Service Court results are now published on a monthly basis.
Further information on the Court Martial, Summary Appeal Court and the Service Civilian Court can be found in the Manual of Service Law JSP 830.
HM Crown Prosecution Service Inspectorate - Military Court Service Report - August 2026
This inspection was undertaken at the invitation of the Director of the Military Court Service. Such invitations reflect a commitment to transparency, continuous improvement and independent scrutiny. I welcome the willingness of the MCS to subject itself to external inspection and to seek assurance about the effectiveness and efficiency of the service it provides. This is reflective of a positive approach and demonstrates a mature organisation with a culture that is open to challenge and improvement.
Anthony Rogers HM Chief Inspector of the Crown Prosecution Service
HMCPSI - The Military Court Service, August 2026
Organisation
The MCS is independent of the Service chains of command and is staffed by civil servants employed by the Ministry of Defence (MOD) working from both court centres.
To ensure independence, the Director MCS is appointed by the Defence Council as the Court Administration Officer (CAO). The CAO has a legislated function to give notice of court proceedings and to specify lay members of the court (equivalent to jury selection).
The Court Martial Appeal Court recently clarified the respective roles of the Judge Advocate and the CAO in relation to the constitution of the Court Martial, concluding that the Judge Advocate’s role is to give direction on the composition category, while the CAO is responsible for specifying individual members. These duties are conducted in accordance with the Armed Forces Act 2006 and related Statutory Instruments.
The CAO is a permanent member of both the Service Justice Board (SJB) and the Service Justice Executive Group (SJEG).
The Director MCS operates from the Bulford Court Centre supported by a Senior Management Team and a Court Administration Unit. Each Court Centre has a dedicated Court Officer who is directly responsible for the management of court proceedings, liaison with the Judiciary and court listings.
The current Director of the Military Court Service is Mr Cleaven Faulkner JP:
Military Court Service Strategic Plan 2026-2030
The Strategic Plan, owned by the Director of the Military Court Service (MCS), sets the direction for MCS personnel and partners in delivering Military Court business.
The Service Justice System is a vital public service relied upon by hundreds of victims, witnesses, families, and defendants across the UK and overseas to deliver justice outcomes that matter.
Building on the achievements of the past four years, this plan provides a clear roadmap for delivering an operating model centred on timely, impartial, and efficient administration of Service court proceedings. It aims to strengthen confidence in a justice system that is fair, effective, and accessible to all who depend upon it.
The strategy drives a culture of continuous improvement and ongoing modernisation of our court processes. It recognises the value of embracing technology‑based systems that enhance efficiency, reduce duplication and bureaucracy, and improve integration with our partners and stakeholders. These reforms lay the groundwork for MCS to deliver a new fully integrated Military Court Listing System (MCLS), with its incumbent in‑court digital case management system, Case Center.
Following significant investment in recent years, the MCS is now well placed to consolidate progress, continue to adopt innovative technologies and ensure that the Services have a modern, effective court system that works in the interests of all Service personnel and their families. Looking ahead to 2030, the strategy identifies the areas in which the MCS will continue to modernise and transform, ensuring best value for money and delivering an increasingly efficient and effective criminal court service for the Royal Navy, the Army, and the Royal Air Force.
Through this modernisation, we aim to build greater confidence in and respect for the Service Justice System. We are committed to continue our work in building a leading‑edge service that is open, inclusive, and innovative. Success will be delivered through the professionalism, dedication, and integrity of our people, who work every day to uphold the principles of justice.
Military Court Centres
There are two permanent court centres in the UK. Bulford, Wiltshire and Catterick, North Yorkshire.
A view of the Bulford Military Court Centre
A view of the Catterick Court (BSL Version)
Military Court Centre information and images of our court rooms.
Due to the draw down of British Forces Germany, the permanent court centre at Sennelager has been converted for other use but has been retained as a Court Martial location should one be required. MCS have a permanent Court Martial capability at Episkopi, Cyprus.
The court system is entirely portable, with the ability for MCS to convene trials outside of the MCCs anywhere in the UK or elsewhere. The most recent examples have included Nightingale Courts at Tidworth and Catterick and overseas in Cyprus, Germany and Gibraltar.
MCS have invested in the latest Digital Audio Recording (DAR) technology to meet legal compliance for the recording of proceedings. The capability covers both the four fixed courts and two portable recording equipment sets. The Service Courts have the latest Digital Evidential Presentation System and now have the capability to support the pre-recording of evidence from victims of serious sexual assault (Section 28).
The Service Courts have a state-of-the-art case management system called Case Center. This product is the latest version of the Crown Court system, Caselines and has been operational since September 2023. MCS are moving towards completing the last element of its digital transformation program with Board members using laptops to view evidence, via the Case Center Jury Portal, during proceedings.
Procedure
The Deputy Director MCS oversees the delivery of the MCS assize programme. Cases are listed within ‘assize sessions’, held at the Military Court Centres run by MCS staff. However, a particularly lengthy or complex Court Martial or Service Civilian Court case may be listed as a ‘stand-alone’ outside the assize sessions. Where possible the volume of cases is equally split between both Court Centres.
At the listing phase of case management, the Court officer will work with the resident Judge Advocate to appoint a Judge Advocate to each case.
The MCS policy is to list a case for an initial hearing within 42 days after receipt of directional papers from the Service Prosecuting Authority.
How we select a Court Martial Board
Our Operating procedure for selecting Court Martial Boards
.
On 1 January 2023 legislation delivered changes to the constitution of a Court Martial board. The changes required the CAO to specify Court Martial boards with at least one man and one woman (so far as is reasonably practicable) and to specify an increase from five lay members to six, for proceedings of a prescribed description. Specification of the OR7 rank from the nominated pool of lay members may now also be permitted under the act.
‘OR7 rank’ means any of the following— chief petty officer, staff corporal, staff sergeant, colour sergeant, Royal Marines, flight sergeant, chief technician.
The Armed Forces (Service Court Rules) (Amendment) (No. 2) Rules 2022
Section 155, Armed Forces Act 2006
The Military Court Service case management system, Case Center (formerly Caselines)
The Military Court Service partners with Thomson Reuters using Case Center. The application streamlines the way the courts prepare, manage, and present digital cases within a centralised cloud-based solution.
The court will manage proceedings by sending and sharing case materials from any device, keeping all parties in sync as they prepare for a hearing. In a hearing, purpose-built presentation tools streamlines proceedings so parties can direct others to the right document in a timely manner.

After you enter your details and the role you will be performing within the Service Justice System you will be registered and ready to be invited to your allocated cases.

Once you have been verified by the Military Court Service either directly with the court, or with the Armed Forces Criminal legal Aid Authority, you will be invited to the case. This process mirrors that applied by the Ministry of Justice in the use for the Digital Case System (DCS).

Court Martial and Summary Appeal Court Guidance
Guides are issued under the authority of the Judge Advocate General and the Director of the Military Court Service jointly as an aid to those who practise in the Service Justice System, and it is to be used in all hearings. Volume 1 provides information about procedure generally and it deals with all types of proceedings in the Court Martial as well as in the Summary Appeal Court. Volume 2 provides information specifically for members of boards.
Guidance on practice, procedure and sentencing is issued by the Judge Advocate General.

If published, transcripts will remain on the page for up to 12 months from the date of conviction.

Remote observation of Service Court proceedings
Open justice has been a fundamental principle for centuries. The principle is a broad one, but at its core has always been a right of access to a public hearing. Historically, this has meant access for reporters and other members of the public to the court or other room in which the hearing takes place.
The primary legislation is contained in section 85A of the Courts Act 2003 as inserted by section 198 of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. The regime is implemented by the Remote Observation and Recording (Courts and Tribunals) Regulations 2022. The power is to “direct that images or sounds of the proceedings be transmitted electronically”. It is to be exercised “for the purpose of enabling persons not taking part in the proceedings to watch or listen to” them. It is not designed for those taking part in the proceedings.
Any person wishing to make an application to the Military Court Service to request permission for the remote observation of a hearing can do so:
Applicants must ensure the court are given at least 3 clear working days to process applications.

Swiss prosecutors investigate driver after fatal coach crash

Swiss prosecutors investigate driver after fatal coach crash
The Office of the Attorney General of canton Graubünden has opened proceedings against the driver of a coach involved in a deadly crash in the southeastern Swiss Alps last week that was carrying a Dutch tour group.
Graubünden prosecutors confirmed an earlier report by the online newspaper 20 Minuten. Proceedings are underway against the driver of the Dutch coach on suspicion of multiple counts of manslaughter through negligence. He is also accused of multiple counts of causing bodily harm through negligence.
The coach was travelling from Zernez to Susch in canton Graubünden last Thursday evening when it veered off the road near the village of Less and tipped onto its side.
More
Five killed in Dutch coach crash in Swiss Alps
There were 45 Dutch nationals on board; five were killed and the others suffered injuries ranging from minor to serious. The driver himself was also injured. The attorney general’s office has not provided any information regarding his condition or his current whereabouts.
The accident sparked a wave of sympathy. Dutch authorities travelled to the Engadine region and met with those affected. Victims are being treated in hospitals in several cantons as well as in neighbouring Austria.

Kallas: Russia attacks train near Polish border to “scare” Europe
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said this while speaking to journalists ahead of the European Arctic Summit in Finland, Ukrinform reports.

Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:41:48 UTC
18:41:48 KST

Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A woman has been arrested for allegedly trying to recruit a hitman on the dark web to kill her ex-husband.
Police confirmed that the 45-year-old woman was arrested in Rotterdam at the weekend for being “involved” in organising a contract killing after the case came to light during an investigation by RTL Nieuws.
The website turned out to be a scam that advertised non-existent “contract killing” services and the attack was never carried out, despite the client transferring US$1,400 (€1,200) in bitcoins as a downpayment.
The man, who was given the cover name of Jerom by RTL, told the broadcaster he was “incredibly relieved that the police have identified a suspect”
The client instructed the website “burn him alive and make sure he doesn’t survive.” When told that the attack would cost $9,000, they replied: “OK, how much does it cost to cut off his arms and legs or shoot him?”
Elderly mother
The instructions included Jerom’s home address, a recent photograph and information about the house, including the alarm system and the fact that his elderly mother lived with him.
“The only demand is that he has to die. I don’t care what happens to the mother,” the client wrote.
Police said arranging the killing was still a crime even though the hitman did not exist. They did not confirm if the request had come directly from the businessman’s ex-wife.
In 2021 a man from The Hague was given an eight-year jail sentence for trying to arrange a murder on the same website. A judge said he had acted “coldly and clinically” in instructing the killing and could take no credit for the fact that the victim was still alive.

Why Israel opened its first Slovenia embassy in just three months: ‘Czechia couldn’t stand alone’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:41:37 UTC
18:41:37 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar inaugurated Israel’s first-ever embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday, completing in just three months a diplomatic push driven by Ljubljana’s dramatic change of course toward Jerusalem and Israel’s search for reliable allies inside the European Union.
The embassy, in central Ljubljana, is the fifth Sa’ar has opened in the past year and a half and comes as Slovenia emerges as one of Israel’s closest partners in the EU.
For now, however, the mission is operating from temporary premises.
The permanent embassy is intended to move to another space on a higher floor of the same office building, but that property has not yet become available. Israeli officials said there was an urgent need to establish a diplomatic presence before then, prompting security authorities to approve the temporary arrangement.
A senior diplomatic official said Sa’ar promised the Slovenians in June that Israel would open an embassy after the new government reversed a string of measures adopted by its predecessor.
Those changes included lifting a ban on Israir flights landing in Ljubljana, reversing recognition of a Palestinian state, removing a Palestinian flag from the Slovenian Foreign Ministry building, ending an arms embargo on Israel, revoking the designation of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as persona non grata and declaring an intention to move Slovenia’s embassy in Israel to Jerusalem.
Officials also described a broader transformation in Slovenia’s position inside the European Union, from one of the bloc’s most hostile governments toward Israel to one of its friendliest.
That shift was demonstrated last month when Slovenia and Czechia vetoed an initiative by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to secure a joint condemnation by all 27 member states of Israel’s E1 construction plan.
‘You can’t leave the Czechs alone’
According to the senior official, Slovenia’s importance grew after the political upheaval in Hungary and the fall of Viktor Orban, whose government had been strongly supportive of Jerusalem.
The change, the official said, created an opening for Kallas to seek unanimous EU decisions targeting Israel, including potential sanctions.
“Czechia would not have been able to withstand the pressure alone, so it needed another country to support it,” the official said. “That is why there was urgency in opening the embassy in Ljubljana. You can’t leave the Czechs alone.”
Sa’ar instructed Foreign Ministry Director General Eden Bar Tal to establish the mission, which was completed within three months, a timetable officials described as unprecedented.
Sa’ar later traveled to Ljubljana with a delegation of Israeli businesspeople as part of a broader effort to deepen economic and political ties.
“Israel had to show Slovenia that it was serious,” the official said. “Israel cannot do without Slovenia, and we are going full speed ahead in advancing relations in every field. Sa’ar’s directive is to strengthen the relationship with maximum effort.”
Security officials approved the temporary embassy ahead of the planned relocation in several months.
A senior Foreign Ministry official said Israel would not pay rent on both premises simultaneously. Once the intended space becomes available, the mission will move there without any overlap.
“That was the security authorities’ condition for opening the embassy,” the official said.
Another senior ministry official rejected suggestions that Sa’ar insisted on opening the embassy before Israel’s election for political reasons.
“Sa’ar has established six embassies over the past year and a half, including when elections were not on the horizon,” the official said. “That is his policy. It is his forte.”

A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:41:18 UTC
18:41:18 KST

Russia struck a fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse in two weeks on 14 September, setting fire to the Odesa depot of medicine distributor BaDM, Ekonomichna Pravda reported. Russian forces hit it during an attack they ran across the country through the night.
The fourth depot, and what Russia did to it
The BaDM complex stands on the edge of Odesa. The strike started a fire on the grounds, and the State Emergency Service worked at the site. It left significant damage to the storage buildings.
Preliminarily, nobody was hurt, sources on the pharmaceutical market told Ekonomichna Pravda. BaDM is one of the biggest wholesalers moving medicines to Ukrainian pharmacies.
The three depots Russia hit before it
- Russia opened the run on 3 September, when it damaged the Biokon logistics complex in Boryspil raion, Kyiv Oblast. That site counts as the country's largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouse.
- Overnight on 8 September, Russian forces attacked the Kyiv warehouse of Optima-Pharm with two ballistic missiles. They had already destroyed that site, which belongs to one of the largest distributors, in 2025.
- On 13 September, Russian forces struck Universal Logistic, the second-largest medicine warehouse in Ukraine. Four specialized sites in two weeks is a pattern, and Russia now hits medicine storage as it has hit food, construction materials, and parcels.
The attack the Odesa strike came in
Russia launched 108 strike drones from 18:00 on 13 September, Ukraine's Air Force said. The wave carried Shahed-type drones, among them jet-powered ones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys. Air defense downed or suppressed 85 of them by 08:00. Ukrainian forces recorded hits at seven locations, and the Air Force said the attack was still running when it published that count.

At least one dead, 25 missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

18:40:55 KST

At least one dead, 25 missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Greece
At least 51 people rescued as search operation continues off the island of Gavnos near Crete.
One person has died, 25 are missing and 51 people have been rescued after a boat carrying migrants sank off a Greek island near Crete, according to the country’s coastguard.
“Fifty-one were picked up by two boats that were in the area,” a coastguard spokesman said on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Italy suspends free movement with Spain: Is Schengen in crisis after Ceuta?
- list 2 of 3Greece reopens Syrian and Afghan asylum cases, hoping for returns
- list 3 of 3Eight bodies recovered in Libya, Greece as Mediterranean death toll rises
He said survivors had reported that 77 people were on board when the boat went down near the island of Gavdos.
Search and rescue efforts were ongoing, with four ships, boats, Frontex aircraft and a coastguard helicopter operating in the area, Greece’s public broadcaster ERT News reported.
The 51 rescued people were due to be brought to Crete, “where the prescribed procedures will be followed”, ERT reported.
After arriving in Crete, undocumented migrants generally face immediate arrest and temporary confinement before being transferred to closed detention camps on the Greek mainland. Under Greek law, individuals are subject to extended administrative detention, severe penalties and fast-track deportation.
Strong winds blowing through the area have been hampering the search operation, ERT said.
Crete and Gavdos, about 320km (200 miles) from the Libyan coast, have become the main point of entry for asylum seekers in Greece.
In late August, Greece’s ANA news agency published figures from the Ministry of Migration and Asylum that indicated that migrant arrivals in the country fell from about 61,000 in the year to August 2025 to 42,000 in the following 12 months – a decline of about 31 percent.
Greece’s conservative government in July suspended all asylum claims for migrants arriving by sea from North Africa for three months, a move it argued helped deter crossings.
The ban passed in parliament amid a surge in asylum seekers reaching Crete and after talks with Libya’s Benghazi-based government to stem the flow were cancelled in July.
The government remains at odds with regional authorities in Crete over a plan to build a permanent transit facility on the island. It is preparing draft legislation that would mandate imprisonment for people whose asylum claims are denied and require ankle monitors during a 30-day compliance period before deportation.
Authorities in Europe have tightened their immigration rules over recent years as far-right, anti-immigrant political parties have won increasing support throughout the continent.
Greece has been in discussions with Germany and several other European Union countries on setting up “return hubs” outside the bloc for processing migrants’ claims.
