Iran police chief says 6,000 people arrested so far over January protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:40:37 UTC
18:40:37 KST

Sahin Demir
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Iranian authorities have arrested 6,000 people so far over their alleged involvement in anti-government protests and unrest in January, the country’s police chief said on Monday.
In remarks aired by state broadcaster IRIB, Ahmadreza Radan said the detainees were involved in an attempted coup, and accused them of assisting countries hostile to Iran during the unrest on Jan. 8-9.
“We will not release these people, except those who express regret and repent,” he said.
The protests began on Dec. 28, 2025, at Tehran’s Grand Bazaar amid a sharp depreciation of the Iranian rial and worsening economic conditions before spreading to several cities across the country.
The demonstrations intensified on Jan. 8-9, with Iranian authorities saying some of the protests turned violent and involved attacks on security forces as well as public and private property.
Authorities have accused the US and Israel of supporting the unrest, allegations rejected by Washington and Tel Aviv.
They said the unrest caused extensive damage to public and private property, including government buildings, banks, police stations, schools, mosques, homes, and vehicles.
In a related move, Iran’s judiciary said authorities seized 240 properties and other assets belonging to people accused of acting against the country or supporting hostile governments, including individuals living abroad. As many as 182 bank accounts have also been frozen.
The judiciary said the measures targeted people accused of activities including propaganda against Iran and cooperation with Israel and other countries Tehran considers hostile.
Iranian authorities have put the death toll from the January unrest at 3,117, including civilians and security personnel, while rights groups have reported higher figures.

Monsoon withdrawal from parts of west Rajasthan likely around Sept 19
Conditions are becoming favourable for the Southwest Monsoon to withdraw from some parts of west Rajasthan around September 19, the IMD said in its latest weather bulletin.The weather office said west Rajasthan is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall between September 14 and 18, but the region is forecast to remain dry on September 19 and 20.The IMD said a low-pressure area over southeast Rajasthan and adjoining Gujarat Region and southwest Madhya Pradesh lay over southeast Rajasthan and adjoining north Gujarat. Its associated cyclonic circulation extended up to 7.6 km above mean sea level and tilted southwards with height.The monsoon trough at mean sea level currently passes through Naliya, the centre of the low-pressure area over southeast Rajasthan and adjoining north Gujarat, Rajgarh, Damoh, Pendra Road, Rourkela and Digha before extending southeastwards to the northwest Bay of Bengal.West Rajasthan recorded isolated rainfall in the 24 hours ending 8:30 am on September 14, while east Rajasthan received rainfall at a few places. The IMD has forecast thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph, gusting to 50 kmph, at isolated places over west Rajasthan during September 14-16.The developing dry spell in west Rajasthan comes even as the weather system over the region continues to influence rainfall elsewhere.
The IMD has forecast isolated to scattered rain over east Rajasthan through September 20, while west Madhya Pradesh and east Madhya Pradesh are also likely to receive rainfall during the period.Heavy rainfall activity is meanwhile expected in several parts of the country. Saurashtra and Kutch are likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall with isolated extremely heavy rainfall on September 14, while heavy to very heavy rain is forecast over Gujarat Region.
The IMD has also forecast heavy rainfall at isolated places over East Rajasthan, Kerala and Mahe, Madhya Maharashtra, Odisha, Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttarakhand and West Madhya Pradesh on September 14.

Growth of 'Flock cameras' in US key issue for 2026 midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:39:04 UTC
18:39:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Growth of 'Flock cameras' in US becomes key topic for upcoming 2026 midterms
Flock cameras are increasingly coming up in the news as a bogeyman of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States—along with AIPAC, ICE, data centres, and AI.
Like other issues that started with young protesters, Flock cameras have now entered the mainstream campaign lexicon for the upcoming US midterms, wherein candidates' positions on the surveillance technology are seen as something of a litmus test.
What is 'Flock Safety'?
The privately held surveillance company, which uses image recognition technology to identify people through their license plates, known as automatic license plate readers (ALPR) was established in 2017 and is based in Atlanta. It holds contracts with property owners and law enforcement. Their approximately 120,000 cameras are used in more than 6,000 communities in nearly all 50 states, where they do billions of scans every month.
The company is best known for its automatic license plate readers and CCTV cameras, which are becoming increasingly ubiquitous. It is also working on developing broader surveillance systems.
How are they different than regular license plate readers?
Conventional license plate readers are generally used to detect drivers who are speeding and to identify people with criminal backgrounds. Flock cameras scan passing cars for their make, model, colour, location and other details—essentially creating a vehicle fingerprint—to then use the data at a later date.
Why are Flock cameras under scrutiny?
Their widespread deployment without the use of warrants has raised concerns over privacy violations. There are also questions over the constitutionality of the devices that surveille (without warrants) civilians who don’t necessarily have a criminal record.
The leaders of Flock have argued that their technology, through use by law enforcement, has helped catch criminals and find missing people.
Earlier this month, the American Civil Liberties Union released a statement on Flock cameras, saying, “Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies like Flock Safety are quietly trying to build a nationwide mass surveillance system. If there are Flock cameras in your city, they are tracking, logging, and sharing your movements without a warrant.”
They go on to describe the system of Flock cameras (the largest of a growing number of such companies) as terrifying.
In a recent campaign ad, Connie Chan, who is running for Congress in San Francisco to replace Nancy Pelosi, accused her opponent, Scott Wiener, of being in support of Flock.
“Right now, our federal government is tracking our personal data and selling it without our knowledge and permission,” Chan says in her campaign ad.
“Across the country, Flock system is using AI in mass surveillance, using that technology to assist ICE, stalk women, monitor protesters, and follow people follow people who have never been suspected of a crime,” she continues. Flock have said they don't work with ICE.
She goes on to say that all federal funding for Flock should be stopped and AI and mass surveillance in general should be prohibited. She also says that Flock is influencing the Democratic Party by helping block bills that would require more transparency in the use of surveillance. She notes that Wiener and a Flock employee (a Democratic Party official) have cross-endorsed one another.
How are states responding?
In response to public outrage over Flock cameras, some states have enacted regulations. Florida has banned the cameras from state highways; Washington state has the first statewide regulations on ALPRs; California killed a bill that would regulate Flock cameras.
How are people protesting Flock cameras?
Protests against Flock cameras have largely been led by young people. On social media platforms, such as TikTok, some Flock opponents have given guidance on how to destroy Flock cameras without being detected. The destruction of Flock cameras has led some cities to cancel their contracts with the company.

17 NCPI MPs to join BJP together, 3 to back NDA from outside: Rebel TMC MP Basunia
NEW DELHI: Seventeen of the 20 MPs are likely to join the ruling Bhartiya Janata Party either before or after Durga Puja in October, rebel TMC leader and Cooch Behar MP Jagadish Chandra Barma Basunia claimed Monday.According to Basunia, the MPs have decided to make the switch together, which he said would ensure that they are not disqualified under the anti-defection law."We are 17 MPs going to the BJP together. Since more than two-thirds of the 20 members will be moving, the anti-defection law will not apply to us," Basunia said.The development comes nearly three months after 20 dissident TMC MPs announced their merger with the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) on June 14 and extended support to the ruling NDA.The anti-defection law requires at least two-thirds of members of a legislature party to agree to a merger to avoid disqualification. In the case of the 20-member NCPI group, the threshold is 14 MPs.Basunia said, however, that three of the 20 MPs from the minority community would not formally join the BJP, citing the political and administrative dynamics in their constituencies.He named Abu Taher Khan, Khalilur Rahaman and Yusuf Pathan, saying they would extend support to the NDA from outside.
"They will support the NDA, and may be given important responsibilities or portfolios," Basunia said.Basunia's claim comes days after he and his wife, TMC MLA Sangeeta Roy, faced protests on returning to their ancestral home in Sitai, Cooch Behar.
Locals and BJP workers staged demonstrations against the couple amid criticism of Basunia's political shift. A TMC office near his residence was also allegedly set on fire during the unrest.Basunia has maintained that he has severed ties with the TMC and is now aligned with the NDA.The Mamata Banerjee-led party suffered a massive breakaway of Parliament and assembly strength after its stinging defeat in Bengal polls at the hands of the BJP. Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar led the faction of rebel Lok Sabha members to form a new party NCPI.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

Ukrainian forces struck the 92N6 radar of the S-400 system in Sochi, as well as Russian UAV facilities, radars, command posts, and relay stations.
The Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of Russian military facilities during the night of September 14, including a 92N6 radar from the S-400 system in Sochi, storage and launch sites for attack UAVs, command posts, radars, and repeaters. The General Staff reports this, UNN writes.
On September 13 and during the night of September 14, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of important military facilities of the Russian aggressor
It is noted that in Sochi, Krasnodar Krai, Russia, a 92N6 multifunctional radar station from the S-400 "Triumf" surface-to-air missile system was struck.
Meanwhile, in the areas of Kursk in Russia's Kursk Oblast and the city of Donetsk, storage, preparation, and launch sites for attack UAVs were struck. In Novohrodivka, Donetsk Oblast, a UAV command post of a unit was struck.
In Lityzhy, Trostenchyk, and Lypovets in Russia's Bryansk Oblast, enemy radar stations were struck.
In the area of the "Saki" airfield in the temporarily occupied territory of Crimea, the occupiers' short-range radio navigation system was struck
And in Rokhmanove, Krasnyi Styaz, and Kamen in Russia's Bryansk Oblast, three enemy repeaters were struck.
The extent of the damage is being clarified.
For reference
The 92N6 radar is a multifunctional radar station. It provides tracking of airborne targets and guidance of surface-to-air missiles toward them. As part of the S-400, this station is one of the key elements in the system's direct execution of firing missions.

‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:37:16 UTC
18:37:16 KST

‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
After the Yabloko party — which ran on antiwar slogans and briefly gave hope to many Russians — was barred from the State Duma election, the opposition, both inside Russia and in emigration, has been debating what voting strategies to adopt now. The Bereg cooperative spoke with Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina about the hopes tied to Yabloko, what the election results might actually change, the divide between those who left and those who stayed, and the prospects for a new democracy. Meduza is publishing the interview in full.
— Did you expect the authorities to let Yabloko run its campaign and compete for votes, or did you assume they would block it?
— There was a sense that the Kremlin had its own separate line, or at least an internal debate, about softening the regime. The wavering was obvious: Yabloko was registered and approved, after all. Perhaps [some officials] pinned their hopes on the negotiations that began after Trump took office, hoping for reconciliation. But it’s become clear recently that things are actually headed toward continuing the war, toward finishing it off — and the negotiations have been shelved indefinitely.
The period when negotiations were actually underway was, of course, full of hope, and traces of that hope still lingered this past spring. Yabloko being allowed to run would have signaled that the negotiating track was still being considered — and had they been barred, that would have signaled the opposite.
— Did you notice growing interest in Yabloko?
— Activists really did start talking about voting for Yabloko. There was enthusiasm among a certain segment of society — people who had been to at least one protest in their lives.
— What was the mood among these people after the party’s list was disqualified?
— They hoped for a miracle. It didn’t happen, but life goes on — there’s no sense that life has stopped. Young people who came to politics for the first time probably feel the disappointment more deeply. Those who are older have already lived through so many political disappointments…
— You’ve surely heard the opposition debate various election strategies: boycotting, voting for anyone but United Russia, or backing a specific party like New People or Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF). But this debate mostly plays out outside Russia, among opposition figures abroad. Does it exist inside the country?
— The mood is roughly this: “How much longer can this go on? Nothing depends on this, nothing will change because of it.” Among a certain segment of true Yabloko supporters, there’s talk of spoiling the ballot or not showing up at all.
Protest voting can produce political consequences, but they’re so illusory, let’s say, that it doesn’t feel worth the energy overall. The idea of voting for any party at all, which used to excite people, doesn’t excite me anymore.
— What are these illusory consequences?
— There’s a pragmatic logic to voting for one of the parliamentary parties, but that logic only applies in a crisis scenario. During turbulence, when the system becomes unbalanced, change always happens through institutionalized players, actors within the system. If several establishment parties won a slightly higher share of the vote, that would, in theory, position them to become those players.
The vote share [for them] would have to be large enough that it couldn’t be masked by fraud — and right now, it’s far from certain that’s even possible. With electronic voting, there may be no limit to fraud at all.
There’s also symbolic voting, which doesn’t inspire me at all — going to a polling station and writing in Yabloko on the ballot. That’s unlikely to accomplish anything, and as for a clean conscience… Honestly, I’ve cleansed mine so many times already that I don’t really need to. Especially since it’s not even a unified strategy — “Smart Voting” has shown that, for the most part, it doesn’t produce results.
You’re choosing one cannibal over another. Let everyone decide for themselves — the main message is just: go vote, and decide [who to vote for] on your own, however you want.
— So voters can still show the authorities their discontent?
— I think the government knows all about that discontent. It just no longer takes society into account — its mood is well known. Instead, it works on society through violence, aggression, and a steady drip of one nasty thing after another. They do something nasty, wait a while, make some noise, let people get used to it, then take the next small step. Society manages to adapt, to adjust. People have even somehow adapted to the shortage of gasoline.
— And you?
— We fill up at night and only drive when it’s absolutely necessary. There’s even something environmentally friendly about it — you ride a scooter or walk to the nearest store. Everyone now keeps a gas canister in the trunk, like in the 1990s. And we just keep living.
— Perhaps people started supporting Yabloko precisely because they’re tired of constantly adapting?
— People started supporting Yabloko for another important reason too. I wrote an article called “5 Discourses Around the War,” where I showed how the antiwar and pro-war discourses diverged.
But the largest and most important layer of opinion was never expressed publicly anywhere. Most people were pro-Putin and antiwar. They had no public spokespeople at all, but they could be called pacifists. [In the media space, it’s assumed that] you’re either pro-Putin and pro-war, or anti-Putin and antiwar. There’s also a variant — anti-Putin but pro-war — which exists among Z bloggers.
People who were pro-Putin and antiwar had no talking heads of their own — until Viktoria Bonya. They were a silent majority. When negotiations with Trump began, and there was hope for a ceasefire, they thought: “Fine, we’ll wait — they’ve started negotiating, so it will probably be alright.”
A year passed, the negotiations went nowhere, problems kept mounting, and that silent majority’s voice began to emerge — we saw it in Bonya’s statement and others like it. The authorities tried to silence those voices, and in response, this group’s views began shifting toward an anti-Putin position.
The antiwar discourse split long ago into a pro-Ukrainian strand and a pacifist strand. Lev Shlosberg represents the latter, and so do I. Most people in Russia identify with the pacifist discourse — most citizens were raised as pacifists in the Soviet Union. Everyone sang Let There Always Be Sunshine, and today’s young people sang it in school too.
Not everyone within that broad pacifist discourse is ready to come out against Putin. Some of them supported Yabloko and started moving toward an anti-Putin position. The party doesn’t directly say it’s against Putin — it focuses instead on its opposition to the war.
And that’s a smart approach — it draws in more and more of these people, because they’re for peace but not yet ready to talk about Putin. The next step for them is lifting the taboo on criticizing Putin, the way the taboo on discussing the war was lifted.
— So, to win over public sympathy, you shouldn’t talk about Putin, because it’s still too soon?
— People react to events in bursts. For example, when the gasoline problems began, open rejection of the Russian authorities appeared, in some cases even hatred. But it’s not directed at Putin personally — he’s too sacred a figure. It’s impersonal hatred toward “the bosses” in general.
The position favoring a Ukrainian victory resonates with hardly anyone in Russia. These people exist, but there aren’t many of them. The old opposition can speak loudly because it’s in emigration. But, in my view, this position will never be shared by the majority in Russia.
— And what position could it share? Accepting an outcome, where neither Ukraine nor Russia wins?
— That’s the most likely outcome. But the trend [in Russia] has changed: previously, holding the position “let’s have peace, and it doesn’t matter who wins” wasn’t punished as a matter of principle — now, it seems to me, it’s starting to be. The Shlosberg case showed that, as did [Andrei] Klepach’s dismissal. You can no longer question the idea of victory.
— Does the silent majority need this victory?
— They just want the war to end. It seems the victory narrative isn’t aimed at ordinary citizens but at the most active, pro-war segment of society — maybe at Putin himself too, who probably belongs to that segment as well.
There’s a segment of society that isn’t ready to let this go without a victory — they’ve paid too high a price over these four years: many of their people have died, a great deal has been invested.
But that’s a small share. Most people don’t care, as long as it all ends. And what kind of victory would that even be? What is victory, really? People generally aren’t very interested — they’re ready to accept whatever they’re offered as victory.
— Maxim Katz believes the opposition in emigration is largely to blame for Yabloko being barred — that they showed support at the wrong time. Do you share that view?
— I think it sped up the process, but Yabloko would have been barred anyway — maybe a bit later, and the campaign would have run a little longer. I don’t know whether they would have expanded it [nationwide] or not. In Veliky Novgorod, banners reading “For Peace!” and “For Yabloko!” are still hanging, because they’re running for the regional assembly there and have an active local cell. In Moscow, there was nothing visible at all — zero.
The problem is that no one negotiates with anyone, no one talks things through — just like Putin doesn’t with Volodymyr Zelensky. Yabloko never coordinated with the opposition [in emigration] on whether support was needed, or what kind. And the opposition never approached Yabloko in advance to discuss the form or timing of support.
I never publicly support anyone unless asked to, because I know my support could do harm — even though I’m only designated as a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities, and I live in Russia. When you have “undesirable” status, or something worse, you have to handle this very carefully. It seems to me that some kind of ethic around this should have developed by now, over these years. But it hasn’t, unfortunately — everyone tries to distance themselves from everyone else.
— Maybe the Kremlin is making an effort to set opposition figures against each other?
— The Kremlin didn’t need to make any effort, because Yabloko never really entered into negotiations with anyone — or did so only rarely. I can’t complain here, since I’ve collaborated with Yabloko a great deal and I’m very grateful to them for that. But I know plenty of stories where they simply wouldn’t negotiate with the rest of the opposition. And the rest of the opposition didn’t come to them either.
There’s also an additional factor now: media visibility. The laws of the mass-media market demand an immediate public reaction to the political agenda, and that factor plays a bigger role than the political one.
For many well-known opposition figures in emigration, the public sphere just comes down to mass media — an old model built around a single source of information. There can be competition among several major players, but it’s neither networked nor horizontal. You can only take part in that process as a unit within the mass — through your like.
The public environment needs to be built differently, starting today. Social networks, when they first emerged, offered hope that it could be. But in the end, opposition actors continued to mirror the existing order — the power-based model for organizing the public sphere [and don’t create platforms for discussion, only broadcast their own views].
— In your view, what election strategy is the Kremlin pursuing?
— The authorities used to feel a need to simulate elections more convincingly. In our district, there was genuine competition in the 2021 elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, and strong competition across Moscow generally.
Now the authorities aren’t allowing anything genuine at all. They’re suppressing turnout — it’s very important to them that only their own people show up at the polls. In Moscow, only single-mandate candidates are running any kind of campaign; in our district, an SVO veteran has been at it for months already.
There’s also electronic voting. In my view, the entire electronic vote in the last Moscow City Duma elections was fabricated. I went to my polling station on Sunday at 7 p.m. and voted with a paper ballot — mine was the first one in the ballot box. People did come to the polling station, but everyone there was made to vote electronically.
— Observers say electronic voting can’t be monitored at all.
— There will still be plenty of paper voting in the regions. But the observer movement has grown quite weak — few people volunteer as observers anymore, and all the active organizations have been crushed. It probably takes society some time to understand that no public leaders or organizations are going to appear anymore, and that people need to organize on their own here.
There’s a big open question: are there limits to fraud under current conditions? Observer theory holds that every instance of fraud has its limits — that you can’t falsify more than a certain percentage. But does that rule still hold now?
— If the limits on fraud are loose enough to manufacture any result for United Russia, even an implausible one, and the authorities use that leeway — what reaction would that provoke in society?
— In my view, it’s the youngest part of society — the ones who suddenly believed in something — who could end up demoralized and disillusioned. On the whole, people don’t place much hope in elections and are unlikely to be disappointed. In advanced political thought, which runs a bit ahead of political reality, elections as a symbol of democracy have long been discredited.
The discrediting of elections will help give rise to new forms of democracy in this country. They’re already emerging, and this alternative experience could become the basis for a new political philosophy, practice, and democracy here. But these are lengthy processes.
— Are you talking about horizontal interaction between people?
— Yes, these are horizontal forms. Some communities, for instance, have devised complex combinations of lottery and voting for decision-making. People in small communities choose leaders simply because they know them, and leaders rotate quickly. That includes political communities, women’s communities, and local interest clubs.
I know a theater group that stages its own plays with its own money and tours with them. This amateur theater has its own forms of democracy, its own forms of decision-making. A director originally brought the group together and made the decisions, but after he died, the group decided not to disband and to run things themselves instead. Now they look for directors and make democratic decisions about whom to hire.
Horizontal structures exist all over the country — gardening co-ops, homeowners’ associations. The whole country is threaded through with a variety of democratic formats.
— Do the authorities notice them? The Kremlin is now promoting the concept of “social architecture” — supposedly not a political technology, but engagement with citizens and communities on social projects.
— They have this new term because they consider only geopolitics to be politics. Of course, they’re not going to build real democracy or real democratic institutions — they always build an imitation.
But hijacking the agenda [from the state] was dangerous in the 2010s. Now the top leadership cares about only one thing — the ”special military operation” — and has no time for such games.
I think it’s dangerous that the very people who want to build a different Russia — not a Limonov-style one, but a genuinely different one — don’t fully grasp the importance of real democratic alternatives. They’re still playing by the old rules. Under the old system, you can outplay those in power, break the regime, build another one, but fundamentally it will still rest on all the same original patterns.
In my view, we need to come up with new ideas, find them within society, help them develop — and then a new political event will happen. We need to dream, to build utopias — that’s very important. We’re going through a phase of major historical shift right now. We all sense it. People have been talking about it for 100 years already.
When I was studying cultural studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s, everyone talked about this major shift. I really hoped the changes would come without violence. But, unfortunately, we entered this historical cycle along with it.
— You’re speaking in terms of a broad historical framework. What if we narrow it down to talk about the so-called ones who left and the ones who stayed? People can presumably be divided based on whether they emigrated, but can these groups be generalized by their views and convictions? Is there some essential conflict between them?
— I don’t think there’s any conflict between “those who left” and “those who stayed” — people communicate with each other. But there is a conflict between public discourses. When that gets translated into personal terms — explaining someone’s views and positions by whether they left or stayed, as if that determines who they are, [that’s wrong]…
Your everyday reality probably still shapes your perception. Perhaps a larger share of nonconformists — people willing to break many ties — ended up among those who left. These people often have a hard time accepting others, other ways of life. But claiming that nonconformists left and conformists stayed is an oversimplification. Often, leaving or staying was simply a forced decision.
— On July 2, you published a post on Facebook calling for an end to the cycle of “retaliatory strikes” between Russia and Ukraine. At the time, some politicians and activists criticized you for “abstract pacifism” and “equalizing morality” — or, more gently, for an unfortunate choice of words. How did you feel about those accusations then, and how do you feel about them now?
— It was unpleasant that people resorted to personal attacks instead of debating the ideas.
Naturally, I never intended to equate the aggressor with the victim — I don’t even understand what’s meant by that [in the critical posts]. I was talking about children. They’re not aggressors. Children are always victims.
Not long ago, I talked with some random people about this — about the drones. People were complaining, and I asked them: “You understand why this is happening, who started all of it, right?” They answered: “The main thing is for it all to end soon, for them to somehow reach an agreement. It doesn’t matter how, let them just agree.”
People aren’t demanding “payback” — they’re reacting like pacifists, not militarists bent on revenge. Hatred toward Ukrainians in Russia hasn’t spread as much as I feared back in July, after all. What people have developed instead is hatred toward the war and those who continue it.
— How do you think Russians will discuss these painful topics a year, five years, 10 years after the war ends? Or is this not really a matter of time, but of something else?
— If it all ends within a year — and there is hope for that — people will want to forget all of it. This is a painful experience, a major trauma for society.
Over a 5–10 year horizon, everything will depend on how events unfold. If Russia changes, I think the question of responsibility will come up eventually. But in my view, those changes will be gradual rather than revolutionary. After some time, people will start asking themselves what they did wrong, how they let this happen. I, at least, hope for that.
Right now people are in a state of trauma, and it’s pointless to ask them these questions, especially since ordinary citizens didn’t make the actual decisions. So right now, it seems to me, these conversations just pour fuel on the fire of the war.
Dialogue is possible in principle, even between the most radical people. Except… you know, it’s already a bit of a broken record: “Well, you over there.” — “Well, you should repent.” — “Well, you won’t understand us.” You open Facebook, read all this, and close it again.
We can all understand each other, especially when we want to. Jürgen Habermas called this communicative ethics. A genuine communicative action is an effort to understand another person, not to convince them otherwise, humiliate them, or prove them wrong. Even people who don’t share a common language share common facial expressions — you can smile, and that smile will be understood in every language, by every people.
Communities that work toward understanding others, toward building discussions and debates, are really valuable, and there are plenty of them in Russia right now. Don’t take this as me criticizing “those who left” again — no, I mean public figures in emigration, as political actors.
Unfortunately, many of them are once again resorting to old methods: “Let’s not try to understand the other person — let’s just explain to them that they’re a fool, let’s shut them up.” In doing so, they’re only perpetuating those same old habits: the absence of dialogue, the drive toward total unanimity.
— When the war ends, will Russia change?
— The end of the war will bring relief. It could also become a trigger for change — some kind of democratization movement might begin, which would ultimately turn the wheel. Either that turn will come from above, or it will be some joint movement, from above and below. History is unpredictable. But I’d like the change not to happen too quickly.
If it’s the proverbial short-term “window of opportunity,” it will lead to unfounded changes imposed from above. Someone will appear who says, once again: “We’ll solve everything in 500 days.”
People can’t handle that, which is why I think the pace of change matters. It’s important that changes be rooted, that their direction be shaped with society’s participation. Society needs to be brought into a conversation about its own future — and that can and should start now. Otherwise, we’ll end up again in a situation where one part of society wins and another loses, and on the next turn, revanchism sets in: the losing side will want to replay everything all over again.

Taichung doctor links some hair loss cases to zinc deficiency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:37:09 UTC
18:37:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Taichung dermatologist says zinc deficiency may be an overlooked cause of hair loss after a 37-year-old male patient with a family history of baldness was found to have low zinc levels.
Dr. Ko Wei-li (柯偉立), director of the Department of Dermatology at Taichung Cheng Ching Hospital, said approximately 30% of the hair-loss patients he treats have zinc deficiency, per CNA.
The patient sought treatment because of his father's history of baldness. Blood tests showed he had insufficient zinc levels, which Ko identified as the primary cause of his hair loss.
Zinc is an essential mineral involved in protein synthesis and cell growth. Ko said zinc deficiency can interfere with keratin synthesis, slowing hair growth and leaving hair thinner and more prone to breakage. Hair loss caused by zinc deficiency can also resemble other forms of hair loss, making blood testing and medical evaluation important.
After the patient increased his intake of zinc-rich foods and took zinc supplements, a follow-up examination six weeks later showed increased hair volume and zinc levels within the normal range.
Ko recommends that patients diagnosed with zinc deficiency consume zinc-rich foods such as oysters, beef, and pumpkin seeds. For severe deficiency, he said supplements can also be used following medical evaluation.
The National Institutes of Health notes a tolerable upper intake level of 40 milligrams of zinc per day for adults from food, beverages, and supplements. Excessive zinc intake can interfere with copper absorption and cause other health problems.
Ko advises people experiencing unexplained or persistent hair loss to seek medical evaluation rather than assuming it is solely hereditary or taking supplements without first determining whether they have a deficiency.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index closed below the 46,000-point level on Monday as calls from leading AI executives to slow development weighed on technology shares and tensions in the Middle East continued.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) closed down 322.33 points, or 0.7%, at 45,862.52. Turnover fell to NT$630.9 billion (US$19.8 billion), compared with NT$721.9 billion on Friday, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Among the index’s most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC fell 1.24% to NT$2,380. MediaTek declined 0.55% to NT$4,560, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Foxconn gained 0.2% to NT$248.50. Delta Electronics was unchanged at NT$1,620, and ASE fell 0.97% to NT$612.
Optical component stocks were among the biggest decliners after Morgan Stanley followed UBS in cutting its ratings on Largan Precision and Genius Electronic Optical. Both stocks hit their daily limit-down, closing at NT$5,995 and NT$954, respectively, according to FTNN.
In contrast, cybersecurity stocks extended their gains after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) recently identified the sector as an important area for AI development. Fortune Information Systems, Azion, Ecloudvalley Digital Technology, Metaage, CHT Security, Acer e-Enabling Service Business, and Genesis Technology all reached their daily limits.
Rising power consumption from AI server racks has increased focus on upgrades to data center power infrastructure. SDI hit its limit-up on expectations of new AI power distribution projects, while Superior Plating Technology also reached its daily limit on its in-house production of liquid-cooling components, according to Sinotrade.
Power semiconductor stocks also moved higher on expectations of further price increases in October, driven by rising power consumption from AI servers. Eris Technology hit its daily limit-up, while Panjit, Taiwan Semiconductor, Mosel Vitelic, Advanced Power Electronics, and Episil Technologies also gained, according to Anue.
Looking ahead, analyst Chiang Kuo-chung (江國中) said trading could remain volatile due to market positioning, with the monthly settlement of Taiwan index futures scheduled for Wednesday. Foreign investors continue to hold net short positions, reflecting expectations for lower prices and potentially contributing to larger market swings in the short term, according to CTEE.
Chiang said the market remains highly sensitive to signals from the US Federal Reserve on interest rate policy. Higher rates could put pressure on stock valuations, particularly for companies that have yet to generate strong earnings and rely mainly on investment themes. He advised investors to use market rebounds to consider shifting from theme-driven stocks to AI companies with confirmed orders.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Zhubei City Office said Monday that it has completed the second phase of streetlight upgrades along Xinglong Road.
The project covers sections three to five, with 58 streetlights installed. Nearly 100 dual-height fixtures were also added along sidewalks to improve nighttime safety for drivers, pedestrians, and people exercising in the area.
Zhubei Mayor Cheng Chao-fang (鄭朝方) said Xinglong Road is an important riverside thoroughfare used for commuting and recreation, per CNA. Phase one covered sections one to three, while phase two extended the upgrades to section five, improving nighttime visibility.
Cheng said the older high-pressure sodium lights provided dim lighting for people jogging along the road. He said the dual-height fixtures illuminate both the roadway and sidewalks, improving visibility for drivers and pedestrians.
Cheng said that although Xinglong Road is outside the city office's jurisdiction, the office nevertheless allocated funding for the lighting improvements.
Separately, the city office completed a two-phase LED streetlight upgrade in Zhubei's high-speed rail district in August. More than 1,000 lights along major roads were replaced in the first phase, followed by more than 700 older sodium lights along neighborhood streets in the second phase, per a city office press release.
Cheng said some of the sodium lamps had been in place for more than 20 years. The new LED fixtures can be adjusted according to road width and traffic conditions while reducing electricity costs.
With the high-speed rail district upgrades completed, Cheng said the city plans to extend its streetlight replacement program to other parts of downtown Zhubei and surrounding areas.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Gogoro could achieve its financial targets ahead of schedule, with its 2027 free-cash-flow goal potentially reached as early as this year, CEO Chiang Chia-wei (姜家煒) said Saturday.

The new model will carry the joint venture’s brand and compete with other scooters in the Vietnamese market. Chiang said Gogoro was optimistic about the market, as electric vehicle registrations rose sharply in the first half of the year and the government promoted all-electric scooters.
He added that Gogoro would initially focus on Ho Chi Minh City and take a measured approach to expansion.

DPP defends NT$8.1 billion Cianjhen Fishing Port renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:36:39 UTC
18:36:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the government's NT$8.1 billion (US$255 million) renovation project at Cianjhen Fishing Port on Monday, saying the investment is justified by the hundreds of billions of Taiwan dollars generated by the country's distant-water fishing industry.
Chuang said Taiwan's distant-water fishing industry had previously received a warning under the European Union's illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing rules, adding that extensive legislative work was required to avert potential EU sanctions, per FTNN. He also said the newly built facilities were intended to improve living conditions for foreign fishing crews, adding that suggestions for further improvements to the port are welcome.
A series of reports by UDN identified major problems with the renovation, including issues involving the new crew quarters and fish market. A common theme in the reports was a disconnect between the facilities' designs and the needs of their intended users.
The crew quarters were designed to improve conditions for foreign workers by providing free amenities, including prayer rooms, showers, and Wi-Fi, as well as hotel rooms available for a fee, per UDN. However, an insufficient number of showers and washing machines has prompted some crews to avoid the facility, instead using container-based shower facilities and washing their clothes by hand.
Philippine crew members pointed out that, with an average monthly wage of NT$19,045, the NT$1,000 nightly rate for hotel rooms is unaffordable. Official data puts the number of daily hotel users at about six, though the Kaohsiung Fishermen's Association said it is working to improve occupancy.
Distant-water fishing industry groups have urged the public to take a reasonable view of efforts to improve the human rights and working conditions of foreign fishing crews, per Liberty Times.
The new fish market has also faced criticism.
Fishmongers said traffic flow within the market is inconvenient, requiring more loading and unloading than at the old market, per UDN. They also cited cumbersome regulations and the lack of an announced rental rate as reasons for delaying their move to the new facility.
Access to the new market may also be an issue for buyers. Kaohsiung scrapped plans to extend its metro and light rail systems to the site, leaving bus services as the only form of public transportation, per UDN. Kaohsiung City Councilor Chen Li-na (陳麗娜) said visitors may need to make multiple transfers to reach the market and noted that a lack of sufficient parking space is another problem for people traveling from outside the city.
In addition to the newly built facilities, UDN reported that many mooring posts at the port's east-facing dock have suffered severe corrosion and appeared to have been excluded from the renovation project. The Fisheries Agency said Monday that those facilities were not covered by the renovation project and are instead handled through routine maintenance.
The agency also responded to concerns about the crew quarters, saying foreign crews who use the free amenities have spoken highly of them. It said descriptions such as "luxury bathhouse" do not benefit the workers.
Regarding the fish market, the agency said complaints about inconvenient operating rules stem from a misunderstanding of modern fish-market standards, per a FA statement. It emphasized that traditional retail practices no longer meet modern sanitation requirements or the demands of international markets.
The reports have also become part of the political debate ahead of the November local elections.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said KMT Kaohsiung City Councilor Hsu Tsai-chen (許采蓁) had warned in 2025 that charging for hotel rooms could result in low occupancy, per Tai Sounds. He called on the Kaohsiung city government and Kaohsiung mayoral candidate and lawmaker Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆), who represents the area, to explain their oversight and execution of the renovation project.
Chen also called on the National Audit Office to review the project.
KMT Legislator Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) said that during a December 2025 visit to the new fish market with the Fisheries Agency, she had already raised concerns about traffic flow and other problems at the facility, per China Times. She urged the administration to address the problems rather than tout the NT$8.1 billion in funding for the project.

Russia resumes mass launches of petrol-powered drones, threat of attack throughout the day
The Air Force is warning of a threat of a massive attack by Russian strike drones throughout Monday 14 September, as the Russians are once again launching large numbers of UAVs powered by internal combustion engines.
Source: Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "We are currently observing an attack by enemy strike UAVs on Odesa Oblast. The threat also remains, of course, for the northern regions. There is information that the enemy may attack today from both the north and the east. That is to say, a large quantity of enemy UAVs is available to be launched towards our country. Specifically, these are UAVs with internal combustion engines, non-jet-powered...
At present, the enemy has clearly expended large stockpiles of jet drones, having attempted to use them for strikes as much as possible in August. A certain number of conventional, classic Shaheds have evidently been accumulated... They have now been launched in several waves, primarily targeting western regions, likely because jet-powered ones lack the range to fly such long distances. A balance must be struck there between fuel capacity, warhead size, and so on. It is expected that these attacks may continue throughout the day."
Details: Ihnat added that defenders of Ukrainian airspace are doing everything possible to minimise Russian hits (which are currently around 10%, compared to an approximate 90% interception rate).
He emphasised that all available assets and personnel within the layered, integrated air defence system have been deployed to repel Russian air attacks.
Asked by a journalist about the reason for this shift in Russian tactics – deploying petrol-powered Shaheds again instead of jet-powered ones – the Air Force spokesperson noted: "Let's assume that the enemy is always planning an unexpected operation to catch our air defence off guard somewhere, utilising various types of munitions. This includes various types of missiles – ballistic, cruise and air-launched – as well as strike UAVs... The enemy is using all means available."

The pilot scheme, which the French call “one for one”, involves one asylum seeker who crosses the Channel in a small boat being returned to France in return for another in northern France being legally brought to the UK to claim asylum. The scheme is due to end on 1 October.
Samusocial de Paris (SSP) has been commissioned by Île-de-France’s regional health agency to provide healthcare for asylum seekers returned to France in the first eight days after their deportation from the UK, when they are accommodated in a shelter in Paris.

European leaders joined forces to highlight growing competition in the Arctic, where global warming is opening new shipping routes, governments are vying for vast natural resources and a Russian military buildup is heightening security concerns.

Finland joins France's nuclear deterrent initiative
Meanwhile, Sweden’s neighbour, Finland, has joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner European countries, Reuters reported.
In response to US president Donald Trump’s expressions of concern about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation,” Finland’s president Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland’s defence minister Antti Häkkänen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” after other Nordic countries, such as Norway, Sweden and Denmark, joined the initiative earlier in the year.

The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains - analysis
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable.
In 2022, they capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made their way into government.
A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment.
This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights.
Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions.
But Sunday’s results suggestthe march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now.
Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appear to have lost their route into government.
The Centre Party is expected to play an important role in any post-election talks.
Although aligned with the opposition, the party made clear this morning that potential coalition partners – including Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – “will need to see the big picture”and not let fringe powers dictate policy.
The party has long been critical of its potential future government partner in the Left Party, which feels emboldened by its strong election result and expected to demand a shift leftwards and its policies to be reflected by any future administration.
The projected result “shows the voters neither want to an economic turn leftwards, not a large role for the [far-right] Sweden Democrats,” party secretary Hannes Hervieu told SVT.
“There is no demand for fringe politics, but a desire for political stability,” he said, adding that the party would bring these points to the Social Democrats.
Curiously, prime minister Ulf Kristersson made similar noises last night about building an alternative majority around centre-right economic policies, but do not read too much into this: it’s still a very long way to go before that means anything more than just early post-election talk.
While the Social Democrats are understandably raring to take a crack at forming the next government, it’s easy to overlook that, despite coming out on top again, the party has actually lost ground since 2022 – recording its lowest vote share since universal suffrage was introduced in 1921.
With 95% of votes counted, the party sits at 28.1%, down more than two percentage points from 2022 (30.3%) and below its previous low of 28.3% in 2018.
Leader Magdalena Andersson was briefly asked about it last night, but waved these questions away, at least for now, as the focus is obviously elsewhere.
But leading Social Democrats are not exactly impressed by Kristersson’s chill approach.
The party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Morgan Johansson, accused him to trying to “cling on” to power, saying it was an “unsightly” behaviour, Expressen reported.
“If [the governing coalition] Tidö no longer has a majority, he will probably have to face the consequences of that.”
But in a stark warning highlighting just how tricky the government formation process is likely to be, Kristersson also said that if all parties stick to their red lines, “Sweden will not have a government.”
It’s clear he has some appetite for exploring a different majority to the red bloc.
PM Kristersson wants to 'take it easy' and wait until final results
Perhaps we should all just channel the Swedish PM, Ulf Kristersson, who essentially said this morning he was “going to take it pretty easy” until the final results are in.
He says there are some conversations scheduled in the meantime – including with fellow coalition leaders this evening – but he essentially wants to see the final results show first.
He also repeats his last night’s suggestion of exploring alternative majorities in the parliament.
One possible option could involve the Centre party switching sides, but it’s not immediately obvious how Kristersson would get them to accept a government with the far-right Sweden Democrats with it.
Social Democrat leadership meets for talks after election win
Senior figures in the Social Democratic party are meeting this morning with party leader Magdalena Andersson to discuss next steps.
The party topped the polls – that is certain – and is most likely to have a first go at forming the next government, but it will have to navigate the complex and often openly contradictory demands of the left-leaning bloc.
It remains to be seen whether they can get the Left Party to work with the Centre Party in particular, given rumbles on both sides about the feasibility of such an alliance.
But today’s doorstep comments suggest there is no rush just yet: all parties will want to wait for the final results on Wednesday or Thursday before committing to exploratory talks.
Party secretary Tobias Baudin confirmed, however, that he has exchanged texts with colleagues in other parties, SVT reported.
Asked about potential differences, he told P1 that he was “completely convinced” the parties would give it out with some “give and take” for all involved.
Hej from Stockholm as the dust settles (a bit) after a hectic election night.
With 95% of votes counted overnight, the left-leaning opposition bloc – led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – has widened its lead to three seats, leading 176 to 173 against the reigning centre-right coalition and their far-right partners in Sweden Democrats.
Formally, the result is not settled yet: there is only some 28,600 votes separating the two blocs, with 6% of the votes yet to be counted – and that includes some 200,000 votes expected to come and be counted only on Wednesday.
Still, the Swedish public broadcaster SVT said last night it was 90% confident that the opposition would clinch the victory, even accounting for all the votes yet to be counted.
There is plenty of time for early exploratory talks: the parliament won’t meet until 28 September, when its due to elect a new speaker, and any votes on who could be the next prime minister can only come after that.
But the process of forming the new government could take weeks if not months leaving Sweden in a state of political limbo at a time of unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty in Europe.
No doubt first text messages, frantic WhatsApp or Signals, and phone calls are already exchanged today.
I will be here to cover all this drama for you.
It’s Monday, 14 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

EU ambassadors fail to agree on extending sanctions against Russia
The Permanent Representatives Committee of EU member states (Coreper) in Brussels held an extraordinary meeting on the morning of Monday 14 September on extending the EU's individual sanctions against Russia over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity, but failed to reach an outcome – a further meeting will be held later the same day.
Source: a European Pravda correspondent in Brussels, citing three EU diplomats
Details: EU ambassadors failed to agree on extending sanctions against Russia on 14 September and agreed to try again later that day, since the deadline for extension expires on 15 September.
"Coreper met in Brussels at 9:00 on 14 September but failed to reach consensus – and agreed to hold another meeting later. The time of the meeting has not yet been set," one of the sources said.
The diplomat pointed out that the individual sanctions over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity need to be renewed before 15 September, otherwise they will automatically be lifted from more than 3,000 individuals and legal entities, mostly from Russia.
However, according to European Pravda, neither Slovakia nor France agreed by the morning of 14 September to change the demands without which they refuse to support extending the sanctions.
Slovakia is demanding that Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov be removed from the sanctions list, while France joined the demand to remove Usmanov as far back as 11 September.
Background:
- On 12 September, European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants sanctions lifted on Usmanov.
- It was also reported earlier that EU ambassadors once again were unable to agree on extending personal sanctions over Russian aggression on 11 September, due to demands from Slovakia and France as to changes to the lists of individuals under personal sanctions.
- The last extension of personal sanctions took place on 14 March. Then too, Slovakia pushed until the final hours on that occasion for Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the list.

Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy
September 14, 2026
European leaders gathered in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Monday to plan a path forward for the bloc's presence in the Arctic.
The talks focused on emerging shipping lanes, raw mineral deposits and security threats from the US, China and Russia.
They come as Arctic ice melts and northern waters become easier to navigate, and in the wake of US President Donald Trump's calls for the US to take control of Greenland which put severe strain on the NATO alliance.
Call for a 'more strategic and proactive' EU role in Arctic
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and 11 other EU leaders issued a joint statement amid Monday's meeting well to the north of Helsinki headed towards the Arctic coastline.
"We agree that the EU needs to step up its action to promote stability, sustainable development and prosperity while safeguarding its interests," the statement said.
"We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic," the declaration urged.
Besides Merz and Germany, the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden backed the statement.
They called for improved monitoring and information-sharing, increasing investment in transport links, digital networks military mobility and other infrastrure.
The statement also emphasized addressing hybrid threats and protecting critical infrastructure on land and sea.
Senior EU officials Kaja Kallas and Antonio Costa also attended the session.
EU using meeting to shape its new Arctic strategy
No formal decisions were expected on Monday, but the European Commission said the talks would help shape its new Arctic strategy, which will be unveiled over the next few weeks.
National leaders can still have a say impacting the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," said Tuomas Tikkanen — Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's senior adviser on European affairs.
The bloc's last strategy paper was released in 2021.
"The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably,"
Orpo, who initiated the summit, has emphasized that the Arctic is an, "increasingly important part of Europe's security environment."
The Arctic, which is warming nearly four times faster than other regions, has seen increased activity as receding ice opens potential transport routes as well as access to mineral resources.
The EU's foreign policy chief Kallas echoed sentiments of host Finland's government, saying that Brussels needed icebreaker vessels to boost its Arctic presence.
Kallas said that given "the situation we are in, and considering also climate change and the opening of maritime routes, we need icebreakers or ships that are able to navigate" in still-difficult conditions in the polar region.
The changing environment has spurred the US, China and Russia to increase energy, resource and military activity.
In August, China and South Korea both sent container ships through the region, testing the viability of the North Sea Route in Russian territorial waters.
As Arctic ice melts, desire for control of the Arctic has heated up
Although Canada, China, Russia and Scandinavian countries are all considered Arctic nations, the most concerning development of late for the EU and member state Denmark have come from an entirely unexpected corner — the United States.
US President Donald Trump has put severe strain on the NATO military alliance through his insistence that "the US must have Greenland" — a semi-autonomous island nation that is officially Danish territory — citing national security concerns.
Trump previously argued that Denmark cannot protect Greenland, which is not part of the EU, from China and Russia.
The US, Denmark and Greenland have set up a working group to discuss how to proceed, with Danish Prime Minsiter Mette Frederiksen expressing hope for the process on Monday.
"This working group is still working and therefore it's too early to draw any conclusions but I'm quite optimistic that we can find a way," she told reporters.
The US wants to increase its military presence on Greenland, something past treaties enable it to do, after decades of reducing its military footprint there since the end of the Cold War.
NATO has also launched a new security mission in the region in recent months.
Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, on a visit to Greenland, announced closer cooperation and an investment package of €200 million ($231 million) to be used in part to set up infrastructure to extract valuable raw materials.
During her visit, von der Leyen said that the EU would "be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic," saying the package would "create new opportunities and a strong and engaged EU in both Greenland and the Arctic."

Russia built five more halls for the drones it assembles using Chinese parts to hit Ukrainian cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:30:40 UTC
18:30:40 KST

Russia is building large new production halls at the Tatarstan site where it assembles the Shahed/Geran-type attack drones it fires at Ukrainian cities, the Ukrainian geospatial and satellite intelligence analyst Dnipro Osint reported, publishing satellite images of the work. At least five long buildings stand finished in the southern part of the Alabuga special economic zone, with internal roads and access ways laid around them and further construction under way. What the new halls are for is not known yet.
What the images show
Several of the large workshops in the zone's southern section are already complete, and several more sites are in active construction, the analyst said. Laid roadways, and the outlines of additional buildings appear beside the finished rows, and he published the coordinates of the site along with the images.
The plant behind the nightly waves
The zone lies near the city of Yelabuga, more than 1,000 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, and has been one of Russia's principal military plants since 2023. It assembles the Shahed-type strike drones Russia calls Gerans, along with the Gerbera decoys flown alongside them, built at a tenth of a Shahed's cost to make Ukrainian air defense spend interceptors on empty airframes.
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine’s interceptors cannot catch
Output has climbed with the attacks. Russia builds about 3,000 of the jet-powered version a month, by Ukrainian military intelligence's count, and has accumulated a reserve of more than 6,000 Gerans for large-scale attacks. The zone itself expanded by 340 hectares in a year, media reported in May.
Chinese firms supply the engines, navigation systems, and avionics, with Iran's role reduced to consultations and occasional deliveries, while Moscow claims the drones are fully localized. The workforce includes teenage students from the site's own Alabuga Polytech college and women recruited as labor migrants from African and Central Asian countries, some of whom were later sent to the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant.
Struck repeatedly, expanding anyway
Ukrainian long-range drones have hit the zone's workshops more than once, including a confirmed strike on Shahed storage there. None of them disabled the facility, since Ukrainian long-range drones carry too little explosive to wreck industrial buildings. Russia has also fortified the site, installing more than 20 towers with heavy machine guns on its territory and perimeter.

China sets up DNA, hotline mechanism for foreigners missing in Nepal-Tibet disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:30:22 UTC
18:30:22 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
China has informed foreign embassies about procedures for collecting DNA samples from relatives of foreign nationals missing after last month’s deadly floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, Beijing said Monday.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Chinese authorities were continuing search and identification operations in the Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
“China has informed the relevant foreign embassies in China of the procedures for collecting DNA samples from the families of the missing individuals,” Guo told reporters in Beijing.
If remains of foreign victims are recovered and their identities confirmed, the relevant embassies will be promptly notified about arrangements for handling the deceased, he added.
Authorities in Xizang have also set up a hotline to assist the families of missing foreign nationals.
On the Nepalese side, 1,385 people have been confirmed dead and 5,130 remain missing, according to the latest figures published by Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) on a government flood-update portal.
The authority said 13,676 people had been rescued, while 21,022 security personnel were mobilized for search, rescue and relief operations.
Among those missing in Nepal were 587 foreign tourists. Authorities said the missing-person count remains subject to verification and may include unidentified bodies and people who have already been rescued.
On the Chinese side, the death toll remains at 43, with 519 people missing, including 261 foreigners, in Xizang.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.
The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

Eesti 200: Herem brings data-driven approach to defense minister post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Eesti 200: Herem brings data-driven approach to defense minister post
Defense minister candidate Martin Herem can bring data-driven decision-making to a sector where things have been moving too slowly, an Eesti 200 MP said Monday.
Herem, a former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) is a Reform Party appointee and met with the Riigikogu faction of Reform's coalition partner, Eesti 200, on Monday morning, to outline his plans as minister.
"We wanted to understand what his plans are, what his strategy is, how he intends to achieve the maximum possible result during these six months, what he wants to get done, and so on. We received very good answers to our questions," MP and faction leader Toomas Uibo said after the meeting.
According to Uibo, Herem's experience and knowledge are extremely important for making the right decisions in the defense sector. "He can see areas where things have been moving very slowly but should be moving considerably faster. As he himself put it, the question was not really how many guns, rounds or shells we have, but how the entire system is structured – how we should be operating," Uibo went on.
"He is quite clearly guided by data. The gap today is largely that we lack data on how to do one thing or another. He also draws very effectively on Ukraine's experience, which we have so far been unable to fully adopt and learn from in the best possible way," Uibo added.
The MP said communicating the threat of war to the public in a more measured manner was also discussed.
"The defense minister candidate himself raised the issue and said that he has not actually engaged in that kind of warmongering and does not support it. We need to approach this very calmly, but we also need to clearly understand what both our intelligence services and those of our allies are saying, and take it very seriously. People must remain informed about the threats that actually exist; they must not be hidden from them. I think this is Herem's message," Uibo said.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) last week announced he would officially offer Herem the defense minister position, citing his experience and knowledge of needed improvements at the Ministry of Defense , and Herem accepted. As a precondition, he required that defense spending remain at 5 percent of GDP to address the threat from Russia. Herem had been on vacation and recently arrived back in Estonia.
His appointment has drawn concern from defense experts over his ties to defense industry private sector firms including Milrem Robotics and Frankenburg Technologies, and the associated risk of conflict of interest.
The vacancy arose after Hanno Pevkur tendered his resignation from the post on September 2, amid a defense procurement scandal. Herem has announced plans for a full audit of Estonia's defense readiness.
Herem also set as a precondition to taking the job, the removal from office of Kaimo Kuusk as Ministry of Defense permanent secretary. Kuusk had been in the job two years.
Herem: If president signs off on appointment, I could take oath of office Wednesday
Although under the Reform-Eesti 200 coalition agreement the defense minister's post is to be filled by the Reform Party, Herem felt that he also had the support of its partner. "Yes, firstly I feel that, and secondly, at the end of the meeting they also said that they support me," Herem, EDF commander 2018-2024, said.
Herem nevertheless had to answer several questions from Eesti 200 MPs. "We talked about what I have been doing over the past two years and my background, and whether I have ended my ties with private businesses. Yes, I have been an employee of companies, not a company executive or owner, so those employment relationships are over. We talked about the recent events concerning the procurement of shells and warehouse management, and what the problems are there. They mostly asked me how seriously I take all of this, and I take it seriously. And then we talked about comprehensive national defense and the defense minister's role in all of that," Herem went on.
Herem said that if President Alar Karis signs the government's decision to nominate him, he will take the oath of office before the Riigikogu on Wednesday.
As his first steps as minister, Herem said he would get an overview of the shortcomings in warehouse management and the plan for putting the situation in order.
"Then I can see whether I actually need to add very much to it at all or simply continue what Hanno Pevkur has already been doing. I definitely want to look at how our developments are progressing in three areas – the Baltic Sea, air defense and the Baltic Defense Line. These could be areas where we make significant progress over the next six months, or at least prepare decisions that would allow us to move forward very quickly in those areas," Herem said.
