Autumn session in Swiss parliament: EU treaties, army funding and Mercosur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Autumn session in Swiss parliament: EU treaties, army funding and Mercosur
Parts of the new package of agreements between Switzerland and the European Union are coming before parliament for the first time. With dual citizenship and referendum proposals, the autumn session also features other topics of interest to the Swiss Abroad. A preview.
The Senate will begin deliberations on the EU treaty package over three days during the autumn session. Key topics in the debates will be the dynamic adoption of EU law, wage protection and a safeguard clause in the event of excessive immigration into Switzerland.
From September 28, discussions will also focus on whether the EU treaties should be subject only to an optional referendum. This raises the question of whether a simple popular majority should suffice or whether, as several senators are demanding, a mandatory referendum – and thus the more difficult-to-achieve majority of the cantons – is required.
We have reported on this here:
More
Cantonal majority: an obstacle that could scupper the Swiss-EU deal
The Foreign Affairs Committee, as the lead committee, has clearly endorsed the package of agreements between Switzerland and the EU. The Economic Affairs Committee was more sceptical, and some members of the Senate appear to be determined to torpedo the new agreements with the EU anyway: a pinprick here, a hidden attack there, a deliberately placed insurmountable obstacle elsewhere.
For the Swiss Abroad, the new package of agreements with the EU is of considerable importance. A large proportion of them live within the EU and benefit directly from the free movement of people and the general legal certainty arising from the bilateral agreements between Bern and Brussels.
Supplementary benefits
Otherwise, the autumn session has few issues on the agenda that directly affect the Swiss Abroad.
A small number of emigrants, however, could be affected by another demand from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party that is due to be debated during the autumn session. It concerns the misuse of supplementary benefitsExternal link transferred abroad.
Such benefits are paid only to people resident in Switzerland. However, “it happens time and again that people stay abroad for longer than the permitted three months without good reason and without notifying the authorities”, says parliamentarian Thomas de Courten, who initiated the proposal.
Although the proposal targets foreign nationals rather than Swiss citizens, the Swiss Abroad who have retained an official residence in Switzerland in order to receive supplementary benefits would also be affected.
Dual citizenship in the spotlight
Another proposal from the People’s Party targets dual citizenship. Here too, the People’s Party explicitly targets only naturalised foreigners in Switzerland. “The Swiss Abroad who acquire another citizenship are not affected,” the motion states. However, the arguments put forward should also give the 840,000 Swiss Abroad cause for concern – at least the 630,000 among them who hold dual citizenship. For them, even the slightest changes in this area are significant.
Specifically, a parliamentary initiative by the People’s Party calls for foreign nationals to renounce their other citizenship upon naturalisation in Switzerland. The explanatory memorandum states: “The right to vote in two or more countries undermines the time-honoured democratic principle of ‘one person, one vote’. This creates the impression of a double right to participate in decision-making, which is unfair to those with single citizenship.”
Moves against dual citizenship crop up time and again in the federal parliament. So far, parliament has never seriously addressed the issue of dual citizenship for the Swiss Abroad, and even now the relevant committee is recommending rejection.
Farmers demand compensation for Mercosur deal
Domestically, the tug-of-war over the free trade agreement with the Mercosur states in South America is set to attract attention. The House of Representatives had surprisingly rejected the agreement negotiated by Switzerland, following opposition from an alliance of left-wing politicians and representatives of the agricultural sector. The matter now moves to the Senate, where the prospects for this free trade agreement are better.
If the powerful farmers’ lobby succeeds in its demand for compensation, it will drop its opposition. The relevant Senate committee is proposing accompanying measures for the agricultural sector worth CHF500 million ($612.5 million). If this agreement is approved, the House of Representatives would also have to reconsider the matter.
Army funding: Where will the money come from?
Finally, security policy is also set to spark heated debates. The Swiss Army is barely capable of defending the country and is in urgent need of funding. There is broad consensus on this. However, there is disagreement over how it should be financed.
The regular army budget, totalling CHF3.4 billion, is now before the House of Representatives. Also up for discussion is a special funding scheme devised by the government in August: surpluses from tax revenue are to be channelled not into debt reduction, as is customary, but into arms purchases. Finally, there is controversy over a planned defence fund intended to ensure the army’s long-term defence capability. Some CHF24 billion is to be set aside for this purpose.
Two proposals from the House of Representatives’ Security Policy Committee demonstrate that parliament is taking the heightened geopolitical situation seriously. On the one hand, it aims to prepare Switzerland for the possibility that, in the event of an armed conflict, railway stations, tunnels and underground car parksExternal link could be converted into shelters. On the other hand, it seeks to regulate the scenario in which hospitals, care homes and prisonsExternal link would need to be evacuated for security reasons – in other words, a state of war on Swiss soil.
Popular initiatives in both chambers
The Swiss Abroad who still vote in Switzerland are likely to be interested in the initiatives being prepared for votes during the autumn session. Below is an overview.
The democracy initiative calls for simplified naturalisation procedures and is due to be debated in the Senate. It proposes extending simplified naturalisation to second-generation foreign nationals and to those who have resided in Switzerland for decades. The relevant committee recommends a no vote.
The inclusion initiative aims to ensure that people with disabilities face fewer barriers in future. It is due to be debated in the House of Representatives. A counter-proposal is already on the table: the Inclusion Act. The relevant committee is now recommending that the House of Representatives further extend the scope of this Act. It is, however, recommending that the initiative itself be rejected.
The popular initiative ‘Yes to Security of Medical Supply’ addresses recurring shortages of medicines. As a direct counter-proposal, the government aims to ensure that Switzerland can take measures to tackle shortages. The matter is coming before the House of Representatives.
The force-fed liver initiative seeks to ban the import of products from force-fed animals, such as foie gras. The House of Representatives opposed the initiative and supported an indirect counter-proposal providing for a labelling requirement. The Senate will now consider the matter.
The fur initiative calls for a ban on the import and trade of fur produced through cruelty to animals and is also due to be debated in the Senate. The relevant committee supports amendments to the Animal Welfare Act as a counter-proposal. The committee is recommending that the initiative itself be rejected.

Piazzа praises Iran volleyball fighting spirit

Unknown Publisher

Piazzа praises Iran volleyball fighting spirit
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s national volleyball team finished runners-up at the 23rd AVC Men’s Volleyball Championship but Italian head coach Roberto Piazza praised his players for continuing to fight until the final point.
Iran lost to hosts Japan 3-0 (25–21, 26–24, 25–23) in the final match on Sunday and failed to book their place at the 2028 Olympic Games.
“I think the most important thing is that we never gave up,” Piazza said. “From the beginning, we were in the game. We lost the first set because of our own mistakes, not because Japan played an incredible volleyball. We also had an important role in the first set and contributed to the result ourselves.”
Piazza stressed that the defeat should be viewed as a team result rather than the responsibility of individual players.
“It doesn’t matter who made the mistake. I don’t want to blame anyone because we play as a team,” he added. “In the end, we were able to fight until the finish.”
“We were ahead in the second set, and in the third set we were leading 6-2,” Piazza explained. “But once again, at the crucial moment, when you need to find a special ball, Japan found it and we couldn’t.”
The Italian coach highlighted Japan’s ability to deliver in decisive moments, particularly when star player Yuki Ishikawa was serving.
“For me, this is the important conclusion,” Piazza said. “In the second set, when Yuki Ishikawa was in the service zone, they found a special ball. But the real question is whether only Ishikawa was special, or whether we could have done something better.”
The silver medal nevertheless marked a strong campaign for Iran, and Piazza said he was proud of the squad’s overall performance throughout the tournament.
“I am proud of my boys. I am really proud of all of them,” he said.
“In volleyball, you have to show your ability every day and on every ball,” he said. “That is why I am very proud of my players.”
The tournament also provided valuable lessons for Iran as the team continue to develop under Piazza. The coach believes his players are beginning to understand what is required tactically, even if they are not yet able to execute those plans consistently.
“This is part of the special conditions of volleyball, and it is something we have to learn,” Piazza said. “First of all, we have to focus on ourselves, not on the opponent.”
“Overall, we became more consistent, and my feeling is that the boys have started to understand what they need to do, even though they cannot always execute it. But the first step is knowing exactly what you have to do. Sooner or later, you will reach the goal. We came very close.”
Piazza nevertheless ended his message by thanking Iranian supporters for their backing throughout the competition.
“I want to thank the people of Iran for their support,” he said.

Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.
After the hottest summer on record for the US, the above average temperatures are expected to continue this week as a heatwave grips many central states. A persistent area of high pressure and a very warm surface after recent heat will help to drive the daytime temperatures widely into the high 30s celsius or up to 40C across Oklahoma, Kansas and nearby states. Models keep the heat locked in through much of the remainder of the month, increasing the risk of wildfires, with other parts of the country already under red flag warnings.

Alongside the competition, a panel highlighted women’s empowerment through the Run Like Her initiative, a female trail-running training camp held in the Kaçkar Mountains in July.
First of its kind at UTMB, the initiative was created as a movement to motivate and inspire women of different countries, cultures and backgrounds to take up trail running, whether as amateurs or elite athletes and regardless of distance. Organizers said the long-term goal is to achieve a 50-50 balance between women and men in trail races.
“This is a movement, an initiative to inspire women, to push them, to motivate them to come to trail running,” Carole Muller, a lead visionary behind the initiative, said. “It’s open to everyone, so come, run, no matter the distance.”
The panel also brought together Kaçkar by UTMB ambassador Beyza Güzel, Afghan-born, British-based ultra-runner Fatima Painda, elite runner Elena Polyakova and Turkish athlete Başak Ağdaş who spoke about their experiences.
Güzel, who had competed in the UTMB World Series finals in Chamonix shortly before the event, described her connection to the region as having grown since the project began. “Kaçkar by UTMB, for me, is not just a race,” she said. “The Kaçkars are special because even when you are struggling the most, when you lift your head, you see the view. It reminds you again why you are there.”
For Polyakova, the race carried an added significance as a new mother. “I’m a new mother, so during the difficult moments I’ll think about my baby waiting for me at the finish line, and I hope this will be a good example for our son.”
Painda, who grew up in the mountains of Afghanistan, trail running has also become a way to draw attention to women deprived of access to sport and public life under Taliban rule. “Every woman and girl in Afghanistan deserves to be out there at the start line of any race,” she said. “Mountain is medicine. Nature is medicine.”
Güzel went on to finish second in the women’s 100K, completing the race in 15 hours, 18 minutes, behind Germany’s Joanna Tallmann, who won in 15 hours, 13 minutes.
Türkiye’s Tuğçe Karakaya won the women’s 50K after returning to sport following a traffic accident that had threatened her athletic career. Spain’s Ainara Urrutia Yurreras was second and Türkiye’s Fatma Taş third.
Spain’s Sara Alonso won the women’s 20K, ahead of Ukraine’s Daria Boichuk and Türkiye’s Tuğba Akın. Nergis Durmuş, İrina Petrakova and Asya Esen took the top three places in the women’s 4K Ayder Run
Among the men, Russia’s Dmitry Mityaev won the inaugural 100K in 10 hours, 31 minutes, followed by Australia’s Michael Dimuantes and Ukraine’s Yevhenii Yermolenko.
Spain’s Antonio Martinez Perez won the 50K, while Iran’s Morteza Jafarzadeh topped the 20K. In the 4K, Ömer Asaf Durmuş won the men’s race. The 4K race also carried an environmental message, with participants wearing shirts reading “Running for Climate” to highlight climate change and nature conservation.

Sweden faces political uncertainty after knife-edge election
Unknown

2026-09-14

18:25:14 KST

Sweden faces political uncertainty after knife-edge election
Sweden was bracing for a protracted struggle to form a government on Monday after election results showed a thin and uncertain lead for the left-wing opposition, while the far-right Sweden Democrats lost ground for the first time since entering parliament 16 years ago.
Sweden faced political uncertainty on Monday, after an election thriller that saw the left-wing opposition holding a slim lead with votes still left to count.
Sunday's election also served up a surprise setback to the far-right Sweden Democrats, who lost ground for the first time since entering parliament 16 years ago.
The leader of the left-wing opposition, Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, and outgoing conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson have each said they want to explore coalition options to secure power, but both would have to make major concessions to obtain a majority.
Both the Social Democrats and Kristersson's Moderates held party meetings on Monday to hammer out their strategy.
While the left-wing held a slim lead, the bloc was expected to face thorny negotiations to form a government, with the talks expected to drag on for several weeks.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Parliament can vote on a new prime minister on September 29 at the earliest.
After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government, much shorter than the 134 days it took to do so in 2018.
Political analyst Mats Knutson told public broadcaster SVT that both blocs were likely to end up in a "stalemate that paves the way for a long and troublesome process of forming a government, which could end in a snap election".
"One or several parties may have to abandon their 'red lines'," he said, a point echoed by Kristersson on Monday.
"If all the 'red lines' remain, then Sweden will not get any government at all," he told reporters.
Read moreSwedes vote in close general election that could usher far right into government
With 95 percent of votes counted on Monday, the four opposition parties held a three-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Kristersson's right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration far right.
But those results could still change, with some votes only due to be counted as of Wednesday.
"The situation is really tight, and it's been more and more polarised in Sweden the last years," 48-year-old construction worker Mikko Duvaldt told AFP on Monday.
"It's going to be a tough situation for each side to form a government."
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Fractured
If the left-wing majority is confirmed, Andersson, a staunch defender of Sweden's welfare state, will attempt to form a government with the Greens, the Left and the Centre parties.
But the left-wing bloc is fractured by deep ideological differences.
The Centre has said it would refuse to support any government that includes the Left, while the Left has said it would not support any government of which it is not a member.
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson is meanwhile expected to court the Centre Party -- which until 2019 had been part of the right-wing bloc – to try to build a majority on his side.
"I will therefore, even if tonight's result stands, examine whether there are any possibilities within this non-socialist parliamentary majority to find some workable government constellation," Kristersson told his supporters on election night.
Annika Freden, associate professor in political science at Lund University, said Kristersson could expect to get the cold shoulder from the Centre.
"Kristersson reaching out to the Centre is expected, but the Centre is fundamentally opposed to entering into an alliance with the far right so nothing will come of it," she said.
She told AFP that she thought the parties would do everything in their power to avoid a new vote.
The negotiations on the left will be about "how much they can get through and will determine if and when the red lines are relaxed".
"In Sweden we have a culture of negotiation, and there is a strong reluctance to call a snap election."
Far right slips
The polls indicate that popularity for the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats party fell to 17.6 percent from more than 20 percent four years ago, relegating it to third place behind the Social Democrats and Kristersson's Moderates.
Observers attributed the drop to the fact that strict policies on migration and crime had now become part of mainstream politics.
"Migration issues were strongest in 2015-2016 and now many parties are in favour of a restrictive policy, and the Sweden Democrats haven't succeeded in being strong on other issues," Freden said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

EU rail freight transport volume falls by 1.8% in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:24:49 UTC
18:24:49 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Rail freight transport performance in the EU fell by 1.8% in 2025 to 368.2 billion ton-kilometers, marking the fourth consecutive year of decline, the bloc's statistical office announced on Monday.
The volume dropped from 375.1 billion ton-kilometers in 2024 to 368.2 billion ton-kilometers last year.
Germany remained the largest contributor to the union's rail freight transport performance with a 33.5% share, equal to 123.5 billion ton-kilometers.
Poland followed as the second-largest contributor with 54.3 billion ton-kilometers, while France ranked third with 34.4 billion ton-kilometers.
Eurostat data showed that rail freight transport performance decreased in 16 member states and increased in eight countries compared to 2024.
Ireland recorded the largest decrease at 35.2%, followed by Latvia at 18.8% and Estonia at 17.3%.
Greece posted the highest increase at 9.3%, while Portugal and France saw their figures rise by 8.4% and 6.6%, respectively.
Luxembourg registered the highest volume of rail freight transported per capita at 10.7 tons, followed by Austria at 10.5 tons and Lithuania at 8.5 tons.
Ireland recorded the lowest rate at 0.03 tons per capita, while Greece saw 0.06 tons and Spain posted 0.5 tons.

Yemen forces advance in Taiz; Houthis take key islands, attack Saudi Arabia
Yemeni government forces have advanced in western Taiz after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive.
Armed forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have retaken positions from the Houthis and are advancing in the southwestern Taiz province as clashes intensify.
Reporting from Taiz on Monday, Al Jazeera Arabic’s Yasser Hassan said forces loyal to the Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government advanced in western Taiz on Sunday after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies
- list 2 of 3The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop
- list 3 of 3Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
“This comes with the support of air strikes targeting Houthi gatherings. The air force continues to bomb the Houthis on the west coast in Mocha, Dhubab, and their surroundings,” Hassan said, citing a source in government forces.
In a statement on Monday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), said they launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
The group said the attacks targeted “military facilities and infrastructure, including aircraft hangars, radar installations, runways, ammunition depots and other targets at King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait”, Saudi Arabia.
It said the attacks were a response to a Saudi offensive, which involved more than 300 air strikes across Yemen over five days.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on the Houthi claims.
On Sunday, the Saudi civil defence agency sent alerts for the city of Abha and the region around Khamis Mushait, but they were quickly lifted shortly afterwards.
Fighting in Yemen’s more than 10-year civil war reignited in July, threatening a United Nations-brokered truce that halted large-scale violence in 2022, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
The fighting soon spilled over beyond the country’s borders, with the Houthis carrying out air attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities. Dozens of people were wounded in those attacks.
Clashes in Yemen intensified last week after the Houthis captured parts of the country’s Red Sea coast, fortifying their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a key waterway that normally handles about 12 percent of global trade, including 11 percent of maritime oil and 8 percent of liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The waterway has been an economic lifeline for Saudi Arabia and its oil exports, as the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively blocked by Iranian forces since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.
The Houthis captured more strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, The Associated Press news agency reported on Monday, citing Yemeni government and Houthi officials.
Houthi officials reported that the group’s troops had deployed on the islands of Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish, which sit about 86 nautical miles (160km) north of the Bab al-Mandeb.
Separately, repairs to a crucial Saudi oil pipeline, struck in an attack last week, could last three to five weeks, regional officials told AP, putting the route all but out of service.
Global oil prices gained more than 2 percent as the news increased concerns over the ability of the world’s biggest exporter to get its crude to market, potentially offering Iran additional leverage in its war with the US.
Meanwhile, the International Organization for Migration said on Sunday that the fighting in Yemen in recent weeks had displaced nearly 86,000 people.
It added that some of those displaced by the conflict were fleeing Yemen altogether, with more than 2,000 people reaching neighbouring country Djibouti.

18:21:45 KST

Mertkan Oruc and Emir Yildirim
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Türkiye’s civil aviation fleet grew to a total of 1,772 craft, including aircraft, helicopters and gliders, by the end of the first half of the year, according to the Transport and Infrastructure Ministry’s Civil Aviation General Directorate (SHGM).
Türkiye is increasing the number of aircraft in its civil aviation sector to meet demand at its major hubs, such as the airports in Istanbul, Ankara and Antalya, which make up some of Europe’s largest and busiest air hubs.
Türkiye’s number of airports rose to 60, while annual passenger capacity reached 400 million, propelling the country to the top ranks in global aviation.
The number of daily flights exceeded 6,800 in the country, accompanying the growth of the civil aviation fleet.
The number of aircraft, including hot air balloons due to their major contribution to Turkish tourism, reached 2,300 by the end of June this year, compared to 2,116 as of June 2025.
The data showed that airlines have the highest number of aircraft in Türkiye.
Flag carrier Turkish Airlines, AJet and Pegasus own a total of 846 aircraft this year, up from 751 in mid-2025.
The number of aircraft registered to air taxi operators rose from 235 to 259 over the same period.
Air taxi operators include firms providing commercial air transport using registered aircraft with a maximum capacity of 19 seats.
Meanwhile, the number of aircraft registered to general aviation operators, which operate passenger and cargo transport outside commercial air transport, rose from 595 in the first half of last year to 632 as of the end of this year’s first half.
The number of ultralight aircraft in general aviation operations fell from 36 to 35 as of the end of June.
Additionally, the number of hot air balloons rose from 499 at the end of the first half of last year to 528 as of the end of June 2026, the data showed.
The directorate categorizes hot air balloons as aircraft under its rules.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has launched the initial public offering (IPO) of his oil refinery, seeking to raise about 2.15 trillion naira ($1.62 billion) for a major expansion.
The company is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at 525 naira ($0.40) each, with the subscription period running from Sept. 14 to Oct. 13.
Retail investors can take part in the offering with a minimum purchase of 10 shares, according to the refinery’s official IPO platform.
The transaction is expected to become the largest public share sale ever carried out in Africa.

The Dangote refinery, which began operations in 2024, currently has a processing capacity of around 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
The company plans to double that capacity to about 1.4 million barrels per day as part of its next investment phase.
Since starting production, the refinery has reduced Nigeria’s dependence on imported petroleum products and significantly increased the country’s fuel exports.
It has also expanded jet fuel shipments to Europe and other African markets as Middle East supply disruptions reshaped global trade flows.
Proceeds from the IPO are expected to support capacity expansion and further strengthen Nigeria’s role as a regional refining and fuel-export hub.

Prosecutor General Kravchenko begins to release case materials on head of anti-corruption agency
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:20:00 EEST
18:20:00 KST

Prosecutor General Kravchenko begins to release case materials on head of anti-corruption agency
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has posted a video entitled "Episode 1. Part One", featuring case files which indicate that Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), is suspected of voter bribery and the fictitious adoption of a child to evade liability in court.
Source: a video on Kravchenko's social media accounts
Quote from the video: "According to judicial proceedings, in April 2008, the defendant, Semen Kryvonos, entered into a criminal conspiracy with other individuals to conduct illegal election campaigning by bribing students at Kyiv National Linguistic University and Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. According to the court materials, UAH 90,000 (about US$2,000) was provided to Semen Kryvonos and his accomplice to execute this criminal scheme, which was subsequently allocated towards bribing students."
Details: The video features an excerpt from Kryvonos's interview during the candidate selection process for the position of NABU director, in which a commission member mentions that between 2008 and 2009, Kryvonos was wanted in connection with the transfer of UAH 15,000 (US$330) for distribution to students in exchange for votes for the Yuliia Tymoshenko Bloc. However, the case was closed in 2010.
Kryvonos explained the incident as a trumped-up case stemming from an action he took in 2007, together with a group of like-minded students, against the administration of a university, allegedly over its attempts to pressure students into voting for specific candidates. He denied the allegation of voter bribery itself and said he was unaware he had been placed on a wanted list and had not been in hiding.
Kravchenko's video goes on to say: "However, according to investigators, Semen Kryvonos, the future head of NABU, intentionally misled the members of the selection commission, as he was not only well aware of the charges against him and the potential penalties, but also devised a criminal plan whose execution subsequently allowed him to be exempted from criminal liability."
The plan allegedly involved creating a contrived basis to qualify for amnesty. At that time, one such legal ground was having a minor child. Therefore, Kravchenko claims, Kryvonos and an accomplice persuaded a single mother (who appears in the materials under the pseudonym "Rhea", while Kryvonos himself is referred to as "Janus") to submit applications to registry offices to have Kryvonos recognised as the father of the child and a false birth certificate issued.
"Rhea" can be heard on the recording stating that Kryvonos wrote a letter of consent to adopt her child, after which amendments were allegedly made to the birth certificate.
However, according to the investigation, Kryvonos had no intention whatsoever of fulfilling parental duties.
The video states: "After obtaining the forged birth certificate in which he was named as the child's father from the registry office, Semen Kryvonos submitted an application, with the intention of misleading the court, to Kyiv's Holosiivskyi District Court requesting that an amnesty be applied to him, attaching the forged certificate... claiming that he had a minor child to support."
Kravchenko says this application led the judge to exempt Kryvonos from criminal liability without grounds in 2009, applying the amnesty law. The case concerning the bribery of students was also closed.
On the morning of 14 September, Kravchenko stated that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos, who is accused of forging documents to obtain an unlawful benefit on an especially large scale, as well as fictitious adoption. The prosecutor general also noted that he is prepared to publish all the materials related to the proceedings.
In a statement this morning, Kravchenko said: "As of today, the Office of the Prosecutor General is providing procedural oversight in dozens of criminal proceedings investigating grave and especially grave crimes committed by employees of NABU and SAPO [the Specialised Anti-Сorruption Prosecutor's Office]."

Succession row kicks off in Uganda after amateur goalkeeper says no to throne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:17:01 UTC
18:17:01 KST

The committee's first choice — a non-league goalkeeper from south-east London — declined, citing other responsibilities. His replacement was then rejected by the late king's own family, who produced a 2022 will that the committee ignored.
A non-league goalkeeper from south-east London turned down the throne of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom last week, setting off a succession battle that erupted into open confrontation prior to King Oyo's funeral on Saturday.
George Desmond Kamurasi, 36, captain and goalkeeper of SE Dons — a club competing at the ninth tier of English football in Crayford — had been selected by a 21-member royal succession committee as the preferred candidate to succeed his cousin, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.
Fifteen of the 18 members who took part in the vote backed him. He said no, citing other responsibilities, committee member Fr Charles Oyo told ESPN.
In Tooro tradition, refusing the throne after being formally selected is considered a disgrace. Kamurasi has not commented publicly on his decision.
Reports in Ugandan media said he was reluctant to leave London — he has family relations in England and was due to play an FA Vase qualifying round the same weekend as Oyo's funeral.
The committee then turned to Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at Uganda's public broadcaster UBC, who was announced as successor earlier this week. That decision has since been rejected by the late king's immediate family.
'Let us grieve'
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ascended to the throne at the age of three and reigned over the Tooro Kingdom for 31 years, died recently at the age of 34 while receiving cancer treatment in the US.
Guinness World Records had recognised him as the world's youngest reigning monarch.
Several thousand people gathered on Saturday in Uganda to pay final respects to the monarch, with President Yoweri Museveni urging unity.
"Once the matter of the new king of the Batoro is settled, we will be happy to work with him, just as we did with His Highness Oyo," he said in a statement read out during Saturday's ceremony at Saint John's Cathedral in the city of Fort Portal in western Uganda.
"I call on the Batoro to use peaceful and lawful means to resolve this issue and to favour unity over division."
The dispute fractured the royal family, with the late king's mother charging that she and other members of the royal family had been put under effective house arrest.
The king's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, accused "evil vultures" of conspiring against her and Queen Mother Best Kemigisa.
She produced a will, which she said the king drafted in 2022, designating "a biological son" as heir without naming him.
This came as a surprise to many in the Tooro elite, who had never heard of the son and did not include his name in the succession vote.
The Babiito royal committee, which traditionally presides over and determines matters relating to royal lineages, succession, and family affairs, defended its choice on Saturday.
"We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity," the head of the committee, Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, said.
The Queen Mother said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death.
“I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.”
'One of those deaths one never heals from'
Uganda is a republic but officially recognises four traditional kingdoms, banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country. They were restored in 1993.
The kingdoms serve mostly as cultural institutions with no formal political power, but the monarchs can command considerable support and loyalty.
King Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest monarch, a much-beloved figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela.
The late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi befriended the Tooro royals as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011.
“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X.
“Not Oyo, not that likeable young man, not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.”
"He had a gift to make people laugh," his sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said at the burial ceremony.
"He always knew how to brighten my day," she said.

The 'kooky' show that lured Celeste Barber back to the theatre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Celeste Barber returns to theatre for first time in 20 years in The Book of Liz
Comedian Celeste Barber is set to return to theatre for the first time in 20 years in "kooky" comedy play The Book of Liz.
While her last stage role was in 2006, the comedian and actor, known for Wellmania and Colin from Accounts, told ABC Arts in 2023 working at Sydney Theatre Company (STC) was "on the bucket list".
As the company launches its 2027 season, she says starring in The Book of Liz is "a dream come true".
It's a full-circle moment for Barber, who worked at the theatre's restaurant back in 2003, the year after she finished drama school.
She recalls her then-roommate landing a role alongside Hugo Weaving in Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing that year.
"I was cleaning cutlery at the end of the shift and looking down the corridor at them in the green room together running lines," she says.
"I remember thinking, as I scrubbed crusty pasta off a fork, 'One day that will be me'. And now it's happening."
Premiering Off-Broadway in 2001, The Book of Liz is a play by American siblings Amy and David Sedaris — Amy best known for Bojack Horseman and surreal sketch show At Home with Amy Sedaris, and David for his comic essays.
Barber will play the relentlessly positive Sister Elizabeth Donderstock, who decides to leave her cloistered community after she's forced to give up her treasured cheese ball recipe.
She soon finds a job as a waitress at a family-run restaurant, with help from a bizarrely Cockney-accented Ukrainian couple. They're just two of the eccentrics Liz encounters as she adjusts to life away from her community.
It was the opportunity to work on a play by the Sedaris siblings, who write together as "The Talent Family", that lured Barber back to the stage.
"I loved [The Book of Liz] as soon as I read it," Barber says. "It made me laugh.
"I feel like a Sedaris play about an Amish cheese ball maker who is on a quest to find herself is exactly what the world needs: something funny, with heart."
Stepping away from theatre for 20 years wasn't deliberate, the comedian adds, but a "pivot" because she "couldn't book a job or even get an audition".
To play Liz, Barber plans to draw on the skills in character comedy she's finessed over more than a decade as a stand-up, but is most excited by the chance to work collaboratively.
"My favourite part of performing is diving in and picking apart a character and finding out what makes them tick, what makes them laugh, cry, fart, scream," she says.
"That's where the juice is.
"I plan on approaching this play in the way I approach most things: panicked. Then as soon I step into the rehearsal room I'll take on the form of a human sponge.
"I love rehearsal rooms; I love working and performing with other people. I love actors and I love notes!"
The Book of Liz is one of 13 plays in STC's 2027 season, which also includes a Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries play, and an adaptation of Jenny Hocking's The Palace Letters, starring Georgie Parker (Dalliance), about efforts to unseal papers about Gough Whitlam's dismissal in 1975.
The season is artistic director Mitchell Butel's second, with his leadership steering the company to its first surplus — of $765,759 — since 2022.
That success is expected to continue, with ticket sales for 2026 already surpassing last year, thanks to new John Farnham musical Whispering Jack and An Iliad, starring David Wenham.
"There's always work to do and we have massive targets to keep the door open," Butel says.
"But hard as it is to produce theatre that's commercially successful, it's a great privilege and honour to do it, and we should celebrate it."
Companies working together
An Iliad will tour Melbourne in 2027, with more cities expected to be announced. It's just one example of STC collaborating with theatre companies, festivals and venues across Australia in 2027 to extend the life spans of local productions.
In another modern adaptation of an ancient Greek text, Oedipus becomes a political thriller set on election night. It will star Richard Roxburgh and Heather Mitchell and will head to Adelaide Festival.
Keeping with the theme of reinterpreting classic plays, STC also co-produces John Proctor Is the Villain, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC), which interrogates Arthur Miller's The Crucible through the eyes of high school students.
In one of the season's literary adaptations, STC and State Theatre Company South Australia (STCSA) will collaborate on The Bookbinder of Jericho, about twin sisters working in a bindery during WWI, from the same team behind the sell-out success of The Dictionary of Lost Words.
Logan St, about an unlikely friendship between an Aboriginal woman and an Afghan cameleer in Adelaide in the 1940s, transfers from STCSA.
Co-produced by STC, Queensland Theatre Company (QTC) and Jones Theatrical Group, Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is set on a boat and takes as its starting point one of the late Kerry Greenwood's novels not previously adapted for TV.
English writer Jack Thorne's reinterpretation of A Christmas Carol, which has played at Melbourne's Comedy Theatre every year since 2022, will come to Sydney for the first time, starring Tim Minchin in his first play since 2013.
Butel says collaborations across Australian theatre like these are "really important".
"Because you're sharing costs, there's suddenly an ability to up cast sizes," he says.
"Bookbinder's a cast of eight, John Proctor is a cast of nine. Oedipus is a cast of 11, A Christmas Carol is a cast of 18. They're pretty large-scale shows for us."
A theatre for actors
Cast size isn't the only thing determining the scale of a production: The now-international "cine-theatre" hit The Picture of Dorian Gray will return to Australia, with Nikki Shiels (Colin from Accounts) playing all 26 characters.
It's not Shiels's first time in the role, having been the alternate performer, or understudy, for the Australian tour since 2022. Next year she'll be taking over full-time from Eryn Jean Norvill, who originated the production.
Norvill will star in a one-woman show of her own as part of STC's 2027 season: Vanya, a new adaptation of Russian playwright Anton Chekhov's play, first brought to the stage by Andrew Scott (Fleabag).
Vanya is another example, along with The Book of Liz, of how Butel likes to program a season.
"I'm finding actors I love and want to be on our stage and asking 'What's going to float your boat?" Butel says.
That approach also led to Andrea Dimitriades (ABC TV's Return to Paradise) starring in the Australian premiere of Gina Gionfriddo's Becky Shaw, loosely based on William Thackeray's Victorian satire Vanity Fair.
Co-starring in Becky Shaw is Lincoln Younes (Last King of the Cross), in his first theatre role in a decade. He's just one screen star coming to STC, alongside Erik Thomson (Packed to the Rafters) in West End hit The Fifth Step and Gold Logie winner Lynne McGranger (Home and Away) and Annette Shun Wah in Disapol Savetsila's road trip comedy Amah and Nanna.
Developed by Bathurst's Arbour Theatre Company, co-founded by Savetsila in 2020, Amah and Nanna was the winner of this year's Patrick White Award. Earlier play readings were hosted at Bathurst Memorial Entertainment Centre.
"It actually shows the benefit of funding regional arts centres to do this kind of work, because they have the ability to workshop stories that are of the regions," Butel says.
STC's 2027 season feels notable for its sheer breadth, which might account for the company's success since Butel took the reins.
"We're often accused of being elitist … but it's not all high art," he says.
"For every Uncle Vanya, there's also this kooky, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt-like fall into the rabbit hole [like The Book of Liz].
"Some people like KFC; some people like caviar. We'll provide it all for you."

Kravchenko alleged that NABU Director Kryvonos had a sham paternity arrangement for the sake of an amnesty
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:12:13 EEST
18:12:13 KST

Kravchenko alleged that NABU Director Kryvonos had a sham paternity arrangement for the sake of an amnesty
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated that Semen Kryvonos established paternity over someone else’s child in order to obtain an amnesty in a 2009 case.
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has made public the first episode of the case underpinning the suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos. It concerns obtaining an amnesty in a 2009 criminal case by registering paternity of someone else’s child. He reported this on his Telegram channel, UNN reports.
The court established the fact of a crime in Semen Kryvonos’s actions. But no punishment followed: he fictitiously adopted a child and unlawfully obtained grounds for exemption from liability—amnesty. Later, with this past, he successfully passed a competition involving international experts and headed NABU. Integrity as it is
In particular, according to Kravchenko, in 2009 Semen Kryvonos was accused of a crime against citizens’ electoral rights.
In June 2009, the Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv was hearing criminal case No. 1-519/09 against Semen Yuriiovych Kryvonos, charged with committing a crime under Part 3 of Article 157 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. Semen Kryvonos was accused of intentionally committing a crime against citizens’ electoral rights while acting in prior collusion with a group of persons
In order to obtain grounds for amnesty, he allegedly organized a criminal scheme involving the registration of paternity of another woman’s child.
This concerned creating an artificial ground that would give him the right to qualify for amnesty. At that time, one such statutory ground was having a minor child. For this purpose, Semen Kryvonos involved an accomplice, who found him an unmarried woman with a child whose birth registration book listed the father’s details at the mother’s direction
According to the investigation, the suspect and his accomplice persuaded the woman to submit an application together with Kryvonos acknowledging him as the child’s father. After that, he received a certificate naming him as the father.
For this purpose, the perpetrators devised a cover story that Semen Kryvonos had allegedly worked abroad and that his immediate employer had asked him to provide documents confirming that he had a dependent child. The essence of the unlawful request was to submit to the civil registry offices a joint application by the woman (the child’s mother) and Semen Kryvonos recognizing Semen Kryvonos’s paternity of the child, followed by the issuance of a forged birth certificate naming Semen Kryvonos as the child’s father. The criminal plan was subsequently carried out
At the same time, the investigation established that after legally acquiring paternity of someone else’s child, Kryvonos had no intention whatsoever of performing parental duties.
Thus, according to the available data, after receiving the document, Kryvonos filed a motion with the court seeking amnesty, citing the fact that he had a minor child dependent on him.
Subsequently, on June 25, 2009, the presiding judge of the Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv, having been misled, based on the motion filed by Semen Kryvonos and following the court’s examination of the forged birth certificate attached to it, issued a ruling whereby Semen Kryvonos was groundlessly exempted from criminal liability due to the application of the Law of Ukraine "On Amnesty". The criminal case against Semen Kryvonos for bribing students was also closed
In addition, according to the available data, after carrying out the aforementioned criminal intent and avoiding criminal liability, in May 2018 Semen Kryvonos again applied to the Holosiivskyi District Court, this time with a claim to remove the information identifying him as the father.
The suspect in the criminal act attached to the statement of claim a DNA test report stating that the probability of Semen Kryvonos’s paternity was 0.00%
We remind you
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated that he had signed a notice of suspicion for NABU Director Semen Kryvonos, whom he suspects of forging official documents and other offenses. He also reported another notice of suspicion concerning a person close to the head of the SAPO.

France submits new proposal to ban social media for under-15s after failed attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:12:01 UTC
18:12:01 KST

France's Constitutional Council struck down the previous legislation in mid-August, finding that part of it constituted an unnecessary infringement on the freedom of expression of those affected.
The French government has submitted a reworked proposal to ban social media for children, after its previous ban was struck down by the country's top constitutional authority, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
France's Constitutional Council struck down the previous legislation in mid-August, finding that part of it constituted an unnecessary infringement on the freedom of expression of those affected.
"After rigorous technical work the government today is notifying" the European Commission of the new draft, Macron wrote on X.
The notification is a key step, as it ensures that the legislation is in line with European Union laws.
Macron has made banning social media use for children and teens one of his top priorities and hopes to see a working ban in force by the time he leaves office next year.
He has called for similar legislation to be adopted throughout the European Union.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen is due to address a possible bloc-wide social media ban for children in a speech in Brussels this week.
A growing number of countries are taking steps to restrict social media access amid multiplying warnings over its harmful effects on children.
According to a French government source, the new proposal lists around ten "features" that are harmful and/or "addictive" for younger users, such as the automatic launch of videos, notification feeds at night or communication with unknown accounts.
Emmanuel Macron hopes the text can become "the standard for all European children."

Finland has decided to join France’s nuclear deterrence initiative which is significant for security in Europe, the Nordic country's defense ministry said Monday.
"The initiative is a form of bilateral cooperation between Finland and France," the ministry said in a statement, mentioning that both countries have been discussing the initiative both at the highest political level and at the level of officials.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb also confirmed that the initiative does not replace NATO's deterrence, adding that Finland's primary starting point is to act as part of NATO and the EU.
"Finland does not intend to station nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime," he said.

Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli directors of citizenship over Venice-winning Gaza doc 'NAZA'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:11:30 UTC
18:11:30 KST

Israel’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of 'NAZA', Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be stripped of their citizenship. The documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza won Venice's Special Jury Prize.
One of the most talked-about and celebrated films at this year's Venice Film Festival is NAZA – the new film by Israeli No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and the only documentary selected for this year's main competition.
It shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
The 80-minute hot-button doc, shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They discuss how Palestinians are targeted – hence the title of the film, a military acronym used by Israeli Military Forces to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike in Gaza. It stands for "Nezek Agavi": collateral damage.
During Saturday's award ceremony, NAZA won the Special Jury Prize. Only a day later, Israel's Culture Minister Miki Zohar announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the directing duo, directly equating criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism.
According to a translation provided by X, Zohar called NAZA “vile” and the Venice Film Festival honour “shocking,” adding: “The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state.”
Here is a translation of Zohar’s statement: "The win of the vile film NZA [sic] at the Venice Festival is shocking. The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state. This is exactly the reason I led the important reform in cinema so that Israeli citizens will no longer have to pay out of their own pockets for the harm to IDF soldiers and the State of Israel. As Minister of Culture, I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for betraying the state."
“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right Minister of National Security of Israel, Itamar Ben-Gvir, added on X. “I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.”
NAZA received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation during its Venice premiere. Previously, the record was held by Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania’s Gaza-set The Voice of Hind Rajab, about the death of a 6-year-old girl killed by Israeli military fire while attempting to flee Gaza City with her family. The film, which premiered last year in Venice and was one of Euronews Culture's Best Movies of 2025, elicited a 22-minute standing ovation.
Unlike Zohar and Ben-Gvir, some have praised NAZA and its directors. The former lawmaker Yousef Jabareen, chair of the left-wing Hadash party, congratulated the directors on the award, thanking them for exposing “these horrific crimes and the brutal reality in Gaza”.
Additionally, the Haaretz newspaper wrote in an editorial: “By screening their film at the Venice Film Festival, Abraham and Szor are trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that there’s a black stain on the way Israel is conducting war in Gaza, to put it mildly."
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's previous film, No Other Land, was released in 2024 and followed Israeli settler violence against Palestinian communities in the West Bank. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide" - as well as a report published in June by a UN independent commission which found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank."
NAZA builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian. The documentary will screen in Spain at the San Sebastián International Film Festival on 23 September and then at the New York Film Festival on 26 September.
As of now, no official theatrical release date has been announced, but French distributor MK2 Films holds the world sales rights.

what we learned: modes of habitation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:10:18 UTC
18:10:18 KST

WHAT KIND OF WORLD DO WE REHEARSE AT HOME?
When Sofia Lekka Angelopoulou opened MODES OF HABITATION, she asked, ‘what if the home is where we first rehearse the world we want, in miniature, before we dare to build it?’ Over the weeks that followed, that question kept expanding. The home appeared less as a finished object than as a testing ground: for comfort and discomfort, solitude and community, permanence and change, efficiency and pleasure. Again and again, the spaces we inhabit revealed themselves as active participants in everyday life, shaping how we move, work, rest, meet others and understand what belongs to us.
As the chapter moved from kitchens and conversation pits to underground houses, residential towers and entire cities, another idea became increasingly difficult to ignore. Habitation is never only about the four walls around us. It extends into the landscape, the infrastructure outside the front door, the species sharing our buildings, and the economic forces determining who gets to stay in a place at all. Here is what this chapter taught us.
Site of Reversible Destiny, Critical Resemblance House, Yoro Park, Japan, 1993-95 | image via Reversible Destiny Foundation
COMFORT IS NOT ALWAYS THE GOAL
Few projects challenged our assumptions about domestic comfort as directly as the architecture of Shusaku Arakawa and Madeline Gins. Their Bioscleave House turns the floor into uneven terrain, lowers the kitchen into the center of the room and places poles throughout the interior to help occupants regain their balance. The pair believed that a home should prevent the body from slipping into habit, keeping its inhabitants alert through continuous physical negotiation with their surroundings. Their claim that such architecture might even extend life was intentionally extreme, but the question underneath it remains provocative: if comfort makes architecture disappear from our awareness, what happens when the home refuses to let us stop noticing it?
Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky approached the body from almost the opposite direction. Her Frankfurt Kitchen, developed for the Neues Frankfurt housing program in the 1920s, was designed to make domestic labor as efficient as possible. Every movement between stove, sink, cabinets and work surfaces was considered, turning the compact kitchen into something closer to a laboratory. Its rationalization would later attract criticism for reinforcing the idea of the woman in the kitchen, although Schütte-Lihotzky’s intention was precisely to reduce the time women spent on housework. A century later, the kitchen remains a reminder that even the smallest domestic plan can contain much larger assumptions about work, gender, time and freedom.
Kisho Kurokawa, Architect & Associates (Tokyo, est. 1962). Nakagin Capsule Tower, Tokyo. 1970–72. exterior view. 1972 | image by Tomio Ohashi
A HOME SHOULD BE ABLE TO CHANGE
Kisho Kurokawa imagined the Nakagin Capsule Tower as architecture capable of aging differently. Its 140 prefabricated capsules were attached to permanent concrete cores with the expectation that individual units could eventually be removed and replaced as technology and lifestyles changed. They never were. Ownership structures, maintenance, construction logistics and deteriorating infrastructure made a building conceived around transformation unexpectedly resistant to it, and the tower was dismantled in 2022. Nakagin’s story complicated one of architecture’s favorite promises: modularity does not automatically produce adaptability. A home can only change when the technical, economic and social systems around it are capable of changing too.
At the Jan Michalski Foundation in Switzerland, temporariness takes on a quieter form. Nine cabins by architects including Kengo Kuma & Associates, ELEMENTAL, Studio MK27 and Rintala Eggertsson offer writers and translators homes for residencies lasting from a few weeks to several months. Each responds differently to the relationship between living and working: some stack functions vertically, others separate concentration from everyday routines, while ELEMENTAL adds a communal space for cooking and gathering. Together, they form a small experimental neighborhood where retreat does not necessarily mean isolation. Perhaps temporary housing can be highly specific precisely because it does not need to anticipate an entire lifetime.
wood provides the starting point | image by Leo Fabrizio
LIVING TOGETHER NEEDS ROOM TO HAPPEN
Supaform’s Transit Encounters brought the conversation pit back without literally digging a hole in the floor. Maxim Shcherbakov’s large green seating landscape at Alcova extends the sofa beyond the limits of a conventional object, offering different heights and positions for sitting, lounging, listening and gathering around a central turntable. What became interesting was not simply its retro reference but how quickly people began negotiating the object together. At first visitors hesitated to enter; once one person did, others followed. The project reminded us that furniture can organize social behavior without prescribing it completely. Sometimes connection begins with something as simple as giving people a reason to sit differently.
That distinction between creating community and merely creating the conditions for it also runs through HOUSING — 33 Answers to the Housing Question. In conversation with designboom, editor Laura Traub described housing as something that must respond to lives increasingly defined by changing families, work patterns, care structures and stages of life. The projects gathered in the book reject the idea of a single housing solution, moving instead through cooperative models, shared spaces, adaptive reuse and renovation. Crucially, architecture cannot manufacture social relationships simply by inserting a communal room. It can, however, make different forms of everyday life easier to imagine — while still leaving room for privacy, retreat and change.
Supaform’s Maxim Shcherbakov discusses Transit Encounters and conversation pits | all images courtesy of Supaform
THE HOUSE HAS MORE THAN HUMAN RESIDENTS
Looking beyond human occupation widened the meaning of habitation considerably. At ChartierDalix’s School of Science and Biodiversity, cavities, ledges and irregularities were designed directly into the concrete envelope so vegetation, birds and insects could settle there; more than a decade later, hundreds of plant and animal species have been recorded around the building. Other projects extend the same idea through birdhouses, nesting cavities, reconstructed ecosystems and wildlife corridors. These are not simply green buildings. Their architecture physically changes because another species has been included in the brief. The wall stops being a boundary built exclusively to keep nature outside and becomes somewhere else to live.
Going underground, meanwhile, revealed how dependent the home remains on the world beyond it. From China’s centuries-old dikengyuan courtyard dwellings to contemporary houses buried into hillsides, subterranean architecture can use the earth itself as enclosure and thermal mass. Yet the most compelling examples repeatedly cut their way back toward daylight, air, landscape and the horizon. Courtyards bring pieces of sky below ground; glazed openings project views outward; buried gardens make orientation possible again. The contradiction is revealing. A home can disappear almost completely into the earth, but our sense of inhabiting it still depends on maintaining some relationship with what lies outside.
Reggio School Madrid, Andrés Jaque / Office for Political Innovation, Spain, 2022 | image © José Hevia
LANDSCAPE CAN BECOME PART OF THE PLAN
Javier Senosiain takes that relationship to its most fantastical conclusion at Quetzalcóatl Park outside Mexico City. Paths curl through grassy mounds, architecture takes the form of snakes and spirals, and a greenhouse filters daylight through stained glass onto plants below. Senosiain’s organic architecture deliberately weakens the familiar distinction between building and terrain: walls curve into ceilings, roofs become landscapes, and inhabitable spaces appear to have grown out of the ground rather than been placed onto it. The result suggests that domestic space does not always need to impose an ordering geometry on nature. It can begin by borrowing its forms.
BIG’s Park Rise in Athens translates that relationship between housing and landscape into vertical density. Rising within The Ellinikon development, the 88-home tower steps outward in a cascade of planted terraces, reinterpreting the familiar Athenian balcony as what Hanna Johansson describes as a three-dimensional landscape. Private gardens, communal amenities and pedestrian connections attempt to reconcile the intimacy of the individual home with the scale of a new urban district. Its proposition is a familiar but still difficult one: density does not necessarily have to mean giving something up. With enough attention to light, outdoor space and shared infrastructure, living closer together might also create more generous ways of inhabiting the city.
Quetzalcóatl Park, created by Javier Senosiain | image © Archivo Arquitectura Orgánica
THERE IS NO UNIVERSAL WAY TO BUILD A GOOD CITY
That skepticism toward universal solutions becomes even clearer at the scale of the city. OMA managing partner David Gianotten cautioned against treating ideas such as the fifteen-minute city as formulas that can simply be reproduced from one place to another. Accessibility, mobility and proximity matter, but so do existing buildings, cultural habits, land values and the people already occupying a neighborhood. In Rome, Taipei and Amsterdam, OMA’s work instead begins with what is already there and asks what should be retained as conditions change. Perhaps future cities require fewer masterplans pretending to predict the future and more frameworks capable of being negotiated, adapted and inhabited over time.
Digital nomadism showed what happens when those local conditions collide with an increasingly mobile global population. Across Lisbon, Mexico City, Athens and Bali, architecture is being reshaped around residents whose income and work may be disconnected from the places they temporarily inhabit. Apartments become short-term rentals, neighborhood businesses shift toward international clientele, interiors converge into a familiar global aesthetic, and in Bali even agricultural land and water infrastructure come under pressure. The question is not whether people should be free to move, but what happens when a city makes itself progressively easier to inhabit temporarily and harder to inhabit permanently. Habitation, we learned, is ultimately also a question of who is able to remain.
Roma Continua Mobility | image © IT’S, OMA, OKRA, NET Engineering, and LGSMA
THE PLAN IS NEVER REALLY FINISHED
MODES OF HABITATION began with the idea that the home might be where we first rehearse different ways of living. What emerged was something broader. A floor can alter how a body moves. A kitchen can redistribute time. A sofa can encourage strangers to gather. A wall can become habitat. An apartment can adapt — or fail to — as its occupants change. And beyond the front door, neighborhoods and cities continually reorganize who gets access to space, proximity and belonging. Perhaps the most useful lesson is therefore not that architecture determines how we live, but that habitation is always a negotiation between a plan and the lives that eventually occupy it. Those lives will change, ignore instructions, bring new needs, invite other inhabitants and sometimes make the original idea obsolete. The challenge is not to design a perfect answer, but to leave enough room for the answer to keep changing. We shape our homes, and then, slowly, they shape us back.
Twelve Ideal Cities – Twelve Cautionary Tales, 1971 | image via MAXXI
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

Pärnu's old dairy plant site set for major new development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

18:10:00 KST

Pärnu's old dairy plant site set for major new development
Pärnu's former dairy plant site is set for a €50–60 million redevelopment featuring business spaces, entertainment and a multipurpose arena.
Demolition of the old plant is already underway and expected to continue through next spring, with some of the existing buildings slated to be preserved.
The developer, Port Artur Max head Viljo Vetik, said construction of the new complex could begin within a few years and would proceed in stages. He says the 13-hectare site, located on the Tallinn side of the Pärnu River, would serve as a new gateway to the city.
"We're building a new city district here," Vetik said. "We call it the City Gate. Plans include various buildings, as well as stores, businesses and some light manufacturing — because demand for it exists and continues to grow."
Plans also call for a multipurpose arena capable of hosting various events and with seating for up to 3,000.
"The city has its own plan too, but we started working on our ideas before the city has unveiled its own plans, so we'll just keep moving ahead with our project," the developer added.
Other arena plans
Alongside Tallinn and Tartu, Pärnu was also one of three cities to submit bids by the deadline to host a major new arena planned by the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK).
The summer capital's proposed site is next to Papiniidu Bridge on the Pärnu riverfront, adjacent to the city's future Rail Baltica terminal.
Plans for the arena began to be pursued more seriously after Estonia secured the right to co-host the 2029 European Basketball Championship, or EuroBasket. Currently, the country's largest indoor arena is Tallinn's Unibet Arena, which can accommodate up to 7,000 spectators.
The Estonian government will make the final decision on which city the arena will ultimately be built in following the completion of an independent economic impact analysis and a recommendation by an expert committee formed in May.

Higher crude prices lift Swiss import costs
Higher global crude oil prices drove up Swiss production and import prices in August, with food products seeing a notable increase.
The Producer and Import Price Index (PPI) rose by 0.7% in August compared with the previous month to stand at 100.4 points, but fell by the same amount year-on-year, according to the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) on Monday.
As regards the producer price index, the 0.2% month-on-month increase “is primarily due to higher prices for petroleum products and pharmaceutical preparations”. Prices also rose for pigs for slaughter, pork, raw milk, rubber and plastic products, as well as basic plastics.
Basic pharmaceutical products, other chemical products and electricity (for large consumers), on the other hand, became cheaper. Compared with August 2025, this indicator fell by 1.3%.
More
Swiss inflation rate jumps to highest level in two years
For import prices, the FSO observed month-on-month price rises, particularly for petroleum products, organic chemical products and hydrocarbons.
Basic plastics, vegetables, melons and potatoes, rubber and plastic products, inorganic chemical products, other chemical products, paper and paper products, and green coffee also saw price rises. By contrast, the price of computers fell.
The index for imported goods thus rose by 1.9% month-on-month and by 0.8% year-on-year.

UK ministers urged to act after US flies out diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:06:53 UTC
18:06:53 KST

British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children.
US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police.
American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain, and there was no formal request for the man to be extradited.
UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which could further strain relations between London and Washington.
Elements of the case echo that of an American fighter pilot, first reported in the Guardian, who avoided being tried under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge while off-duty. Capt Jacob Wulfson was tried by court martial at a US airbase and jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation. He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact.
In a letter to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, his Conservative counterpart, Nick Timothy, said he was concerned US actions represented “a cover-up” and that the diplomat may have committed offences in the UK. “If this is the case, the diplomat should face trial in an English court.”
Timothy said the incident was part of a “concerning pattern” of US authorities prosecuting American service personnel accused of offences against British civilians while stationed in the UK.
Citing the Wulfson case, he wrote: “These cases should have been investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts. I ask you to urgently explain what action you are taking to address this, and what will be done to ensure the accused diplomat faces a proper investigation in this country.”
The diplomat’s case has also been likened to that of the US state department employee Anne Sacoolas, who caused the death of the teenager Harry Dunn in a car crash in 2019. Sacoolas was able to leave the country shortly after the fatal collision when the US asserted diplomatic immunity on her behalf.
She eventually pleaded guilty to causing death by careless driving at a virtual high-court hearing in December 2022, and was sentenced to eight months in prison, suspended for a year.
A UK government spokesperson declined to comment because of the ongoing US investigation but said Britain expects all foreign diplomats to obey the law while in the UK, “in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy said it was “aware of allegations” concerning one of its staff and expected “all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct”.
The spokesperson said: “We quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action, and we will continue to work closely with our law enforcement partners regarding these allegations.
“The individual in question has been reassigned to the United States in conjunction with an ongoing investigation. The embassy has informed British authorities of the case.”
A US state department spokesperson declined to discuss the specifics of the case, adding: “We take these allegations seriously.”
A Met police spokesperson said: “On Tuesday 25 August, US authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offences in London relating to indecent images of children. We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”

Ukraine May Get License for Older, Less Advanced Patriot Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:05:23 UTC
18:05:23 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday, Sept. 13, that Washington is discussing granting Ukraine a license to produce a less advanced version of Patriot interceptor missiles.
According to the White House, Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One en route to Joint Base Andrews.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We’re talking about it… a less sophisticated version,” Trump said when asked whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky would receive additional Patriot systems and production licenses.
Trump did not specify which Patriot interceptor model Washington might allow Ukraine to manufacture or whether the proposal had secured approval from US defense contractors.
The US president also said Washington was producing more Patriot missiles than ever before and rapidly replenishing stocks of advanced weapons previously supplied to Ukraine.
Has Washington agreed to the license?
Trump’s latest remarks stop short of confirming that a final agreement has been reached.
During a meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, Trump said the US would authorize Ukraine to manufacture Patriot air-defense systems.
“We’ll give them the right to make Patriots. We’ll show them how to do it,” Trump said at the time. “I think they can produce them pretty quickly.”
However, Trump later walked back the commitment. Speaking at a Cabinet meeting on July 31, he said the US had not agreed to transfer the technology and that discussions were continuing.
Trump Tells Zelensky to Stop ‘Knocking Out Diesel Fuel in Russia’
Trump argued that Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology because recipients could eventually use it against the US.
Ukraine has sought permission to produce Patriot interceptors domestically as Russian ballistic and cruise missile attacks strain its limited air-defense stocks and those of its partners. The Patriot system is Ukraine’s most important defense against ballistic missiles, which many other Western-supplied systems cannot reliably intercept.
Would domestic production solve Ukraine’s shortages?
Even if Washington grants the license, it is unlikely that establishing production in Ukraine would provide an immediate solution.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in early September that constructing factories, organizing supply chains and increasing production would take years. Sensitive components could also remain subject to US export restrictions.
Ukraine is working to secure approximately 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from its allies and an EU loan, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Sept. 8. Most of those interceptors, however, are expected to arrive over several years rather than immediately.
Kyiv has consequently urged its partners to release additional missiles from their existing stockpiles while negotiations over licensed production continue.
