Türkiye phases out 10 food additives in new health codex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:50:35 UTC
17:50:35 KST

(AA Photo)
The Agriculture and Forestry Ministry implemented a new food flavoring regulation on Sept. 14, restricting insect- and pork-derived additives while scheduling a phase-out for 10 specific substances by 2026.
The updated Turkish Food Codex prohibits products derived from pork and insects to align with broader public health guidelines. The directive bars 10 flavoring substances, including FL 04.029, FL 05.100, FL 05.175, FL 05.222, FL 15.029, FL 15.030, FL 15.060, FL 15.119, FL 15.130 and FL 15.131, from market circulation, food production and import effective Dec. 31, 2026.
Two other substances, FL 05.062 and FL 05.099, face usage restrictions limited to designated food categories starting on the same date. The regulation prevents any covered products from being marketed under alcoholic beverage names. Certain flavorings will now require explicit ministry approval to enter the permitted list.
To label a flavoring as natural alongside a specific food or biological source, at least 95 percent of the components by weight must originate from that referenced source. If the components consist entirely of natural substances, companies can use the natural flavoring substances label. Flavorings falling under genetically modified organism regulations require clearance before ministry approval.
Purely sweet, sour or salty substances and unprocessed foods remain exempt from the new rules. Flavorings not intended for the final consumer must now display detailed labels including purpose of use, storage conditions, batch numbers and manufacturer information.
Food businesses have until Dec. 31, 2026, to comply with the updated framework, which replaces the previous directive from 2011. Products containing the restricted additives placed on the market before the deadline will remain on shelves until their expiration dates.
Turkish authorities regularly update food safety guidelines to align with international health protocols. The revisions target clearer labeling practices and tighten administrative oversight on chemical additives entering the supply chain to prevent long-term public health risks.

Lee Hao-yu sets MLB RBI record for Taiwanese players
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:47:08 UTC
17:47:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Detroit Tigers infielder Lee Hao-yu (李灝宇) drove in his 41st run of the season with a sacrifice fly Sunday, setting a new single-season MLB record for a Taiwanese player.
Lee's sacrifice fly in the fourth inning helped the Tigers defeat the Colorado Rockies 8-1 at Comerica Park, completing a three-game sweep and extending Detroit's winning streak to four games, per UDN.
Lee, batting second and starting at second base, did not record a hit but contributed with the bases loaded in the fourth. Facing Rockies reliever Zach Agnos, he lifted a fly ball to right field to bring home the Tigers' sixth run.
He went 0-for-3 with one RBI, one walk, and one strikeout. He struck out against Rockies starter Gabriel Hughes in the first inning, grounded out in the second and sixth innings, and drew a walk in the eighth. His batting average slipped slightly to .259.
Lee's 41 RBIs surpassed the previous Taiwanese single-season record of 39 set by Yu Chang (張育成) in 2021. Lee had driven in three runs in Saturday's 11-7 comeback victory over Colorado, when he went 3-for-5 with two doubles, a triple, and three RBIs, per Reuters.
Lee has also set new Taiwanese MLB marks in several other categories this season. Through 102 games, he has recorded 72 hits, 15 doubles, 41 RBIs, and 35 runs, according to ESPN.
The 23-year-old is also one home run and one triple away from tying Chang's 2021 single-season records of nine home runs and three triples by a Taiwanese MLB player.
The Tigers improved to 70-79 with the victory, while the Rockies fell to 55-94. Detroit next faces the Toronto Blue Jays on Monday.

New Academia Historica head vows to deepen Taiwan democracy studies

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮), who took office as director of Academia Historica on Monday, pledged to deepen studies of Taiwan’s democratization history.
Chen said she would carefully examine authoritarian and dictatorial rule and how such systems harm society, per CNA. She emphasized that this work is about remembering Taiwan’s struggle for democracy and freedom and cherishing its hard-won democratic system.
Chen said she has observed increasingly serious conceptual distortion in news and political discourse in recent years. Elected governments that are subject to checks and balances are being maliciously labeled as authoritarian or dictatorial and described using terms associated with political terror, she said, according to CNA.
Chen argued that such political attacks could undermine public confidence in the nation’s democratic system and erode the core values of democracy and freedom, causing irreparable harm to society. Only continuous remembrance and clarification can defend the democratic system, she said.
Chen said it is also necessary to promote a shared understanding of Taiwan’s history and address difficult historical issues, CNA reported. With the increasing availability of political surveillance archives, society has gained a greater understanding of the past, but these documents also raise complex and challenging questions, she said.
She warned that if such archives are made public without careful analysis, research, and contextualization, they could allow the legacy of authoritarian-era intelligence agencies to continue dividing and harming society.
Chen said she hoped Academia Historica could become a platform for building a shared understanding of Taiwan’s history.

On Friday, Pashinyan said Armenia will move to diversify its energy sources.

Incoming defense minister: I will not interfere with the work of the EDF commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

Incoming defense minister: I will not interfere with the work of the EDF commander
Incoming Defense Minister Martin Herem tells ERR in an interview that he will lead the Ministry of Defense as a politician, not meddle in the work of the EDF commander and terminate any private sector contracts that could pose a conflict of interest.
Why did you ultimately decide to accept the prime minister's offer to become defense minister, even though you weren't entirely sure about it at first?
I wasn't sure and, even today, the position doesn't seem particularly pleasant or appealing to me. But I think someone has to do the job for about six months. I think I have certain qualities that would enable me to handle it. Perhaps someone like me would find it easier to do this job in the run-up to an election. Those six months definitely need to be put to good use rather than simply waiting and letting that time go to waste until the next election.
What do you think you can accomplish during those six months?
I've said this several times and it's been somewhat misunderstood. That's my fault. Our intelligence assessment today — although it's been said that this is something I've simply made up... If we look at it, Commander of the Estonian Defense Forces Gen. Merilo has said that 2027 is a critical year. Various intelligence agencies in Denmark and Lithuania have talked about a period of one to three years. Former Dutch chief of defense and NATO Military Committee Chair Adm. Bauer recently said that even while the war in Ukraine is ongoing, Russia could become strong enough within three years to test NATO.
What I would like to do is look at when that point could come. Not to say that war will begin at that moment, but to look at where our development will have taken us by then. And if our capabilities fall significantly short of the threat at that point, then we need to look at why they fall short and whether there is anything we can change.
We may not be able to change very many things in six months, but we can establish what needs to be changed and what it would cost. I don't think we're going to amend very many laws in six months or somehow start moving much faster. But some things do need to be reviewed. Perhaps the number one issue would be the Baltic Defense Line, because in my assessment, it is currently stalled. This isn't only about digging trenches or putting concrete positions in the ground; there are other activities involved as well. I don't want to say too much about it right now because I don't know how much has been done, but it seems to me that it has stalled.
Then there is air defense in the broadest sense — not just what kinds of weapons we procure, but what our surveillance system looks like, how the public is informed and how different government agencies would plan their operations and protection in general. In my assessment, we need to move faster on this, whether we do so through the Government Office or different ministries. But I quite literally need political backing and communication so that this doesn't look like fearmongering coming from the Ministry of Defense, but rather simply providing information. It's the same way medicine talks today about preventing serious illnesses, and that isn't fearmongering.
You already mentioned the intelligence assessment and the fact that some people say this threat assessment is essentially your own. So how will things work going forward? Are we going to make decisions based on Martin Herem's threat assessment or will we continue to rely on an intelligence assessment that has not been influenced by you?
I'm actually very surprised that the question is being framed this way — not here in the media specifically, but in general. Our intelligence services — both Estonian Defense Forces intelligence and the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service — are saying today that Russia is developing very rapidly. They have likewise said that within a few years after the end of the war in Ukraine, whenever that may be, Russia could test us militarily.
What I want is not to change the intelligence assessment, but to put it down on paper in a way that allows us to discuss it with government agencies and the country as a whole. We can then compare the appropriate trajectory of their preparations against that point in time and see whether we can do better.
I think this is also becoming very apparent today in the comments made by many people: We talk about this threat, but the next moment we say that we have six months, that we don't need to do things fast enough. A few years ago, those same people said that establishing the division was happening too quickly, that Ussisõnad [military exercise — ed.] was happening too quickly and that the procurement of ammunition, heavy weapons and armored vehicles was also happening too quickly — somehow, everything was too fast. I would say that even if Russia could become that strong within three years, we absolutely cannot allow these six months to go to waste.
Of course I'm not going to dictate anything to the intelligence services, but I would point this out: Look at the statements and annual reports of those agencies. Look at what the commander of the Estonian Defense Forces has said. He has said that 2027 is a critical year. So how is it that this has suddenly become something I've come up with?
Another point concerns Russia's growing strength: I don't know where critics get the idea that this has been pulled out of thin air. For the past two years, I've essentially been monitoring the development and strengthening of Russia's military power and advising both private companies and, to some extent, the Estonian Defense Forces on the subject. In my view, none of this has been pulled out of thin air. There are specific figures behind it and I'm always prepared to present them in terms of different capabilities.
Have you asked the prime minister for any special powers?
That's another very interesting point. I haven't asked for any special powers. Again: For me to be able to take this threat assessment to different agencies and ministries, discuss it calmly with them and have them consider how well prepared they are, I simply need political backing. If I start talking about these things now, for example as defense minister, people will say it's fearmongering. It isn't. This is deliberate action. It is the deliberate shaping of the state's activities, not fearmongering.
At the same time, you have presented the prime minister with certain conditions. So whose policies are you going to pursue? Are you going to pursue Martin Herem's policies? Is the government going to pursue Martin Herem's policies? Or are you going to pursue the government's policies? How exactly is this going to work?
I don't really understand the question. We will pursue defense policy. I can't demand anything from the state that the government doesn't approve. I can't say that certain laws must be changed overnight. That's not up to me. I'm still one part of the state: as a citizen, as a general in the reserve and perhaps, before long, as a minister as well. Whose policy is it? It's state policy, government policy and, then, defense policy.
But will you lead the Ministry of Defense as a military officer or as a politician?
As defense minister. If you want to call someone carrying out the duties of defense minister, someone who is the defense minister, a "politician," then yes, you can say I'll be doing so as a politician. But not as commander of the Estonian Defense Forces. That's Gen. Merilo's job and I have no intention of interfering in his work.
Let's also talk a little about your potential conflict of interest. Do you see a conflict yourself, given that you're currently involved with a defense industry company? How can we be sure that when you walk through the doors of the Ministry of Defense, you'll leave those business interests behind?
There are three safeguards, though people probably won't have much faith in them. First, I'm ending all of those working relationships. Most of them have already ended by now or I'll leave here and immediately sign the agreement terminating my contract with Frankenburg. Second, there is oversight. I'm a very open person; I don't hide anything and the relevant authorities can monitor me if I do anything wrong. Third, I'm also well aware of what the risks are. That's not my objective. Again, I could have had a fairly comfortable life outside of this challenge, so why would I need to get involved in some sort of scheme here?
I'll say it again: My concern was who would be handling national defense as defense minister for the next six months. What's more, when Äripäev asked me about this roughly two hours before Hanno Pevkur announced his resignation, I said that he shouldn't resign. I haven't sought this position in any way; rather, it was a politician who approached me.
The problems with the Estonian Defense Forces' inventories were already acute when you were commander of the Defense Forces and one of the decision-makers. How do you intend to solve those problems now if you weren't able to do so before?
To be very precise, and without blaming others, those problems existed before me and they still exist after me. You can take National Audit Office reports from before my tenure, during my tenure and after my tenure and compare them; they are somewhat different. Second, the Defense Forces and the Ministry of Defense have evolved and some additional responsibilities have been added. But there are also more resources available and Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has taken steps as well. Some things are already underway.
How exactly will I solve them? I'll give it everything I've got. But one thing is clear: Keeping track of inventories isn't actually just a peacetime issue. During wartime, the commander of the Defense Forces and the government need to know how many shells there are on the Narva front and how many there are on the Võru front so that additional resources can be sent to the right place at the right time or reallocated as necessary. That's why we need to think about how the information systems we use in peacetime today would also function during wartime. We tend to think that everything will somehow be simpler during wartime, but I don't think it will be. Perhaps we simply need to change how we keep track of things today, but this needs to be put in order. There's no question about that.
On Saturday, the prime minister mentioned bringing in an external partner to restore confidence in the defense sector. Do you know what that means? Do you have any idea what this external partner would do?
I've discussed with him the idea that perhaps we should adopt more of the accounting practices used in the civilian world. Within the Ministry of Defense's area of government, this information is often protected as a state secret. Because of confidentiality requirements, all of these information systems are expensive, cumbersome and difficult to build. That slows down the entire work process — I wouldn't say it obstructs it. Perhaps we should review those rules and see how we could operate more efficiently.
Because we ourselves — myself included — are very focused on protecting information, perhaps it would make sense to bring in someone from outside, from the private sector, who could look at it with a fresh perspective. That's what I've been talking about and that's what this external expertise means. It doesn't mean bringing someone in to handle communications.
But couldn't that mean that this same flow of information could somehow pose a security risk to us?
That's exactly what we're all afraid of — both the Defense Forces and the Ministry of Defense. But it does seem rather absurd that we publicly purchase 36 howitzers, everyone even knows how much they cost, but the moment they're entered into the Defense Forces' inventory system, they become classified, we stop talking about them and create problems for ourselves. Perhaps we should review rules like that when they don't make much sense.
But once again, that requires communication between government agencies and the political will to assess the risks involved in making changes, and then someone also has to be willing to accept those risks.
How extensive a shake-up are you planning at the Ministry of Defense?
I've said before that, as of today, I don't have the name of a single specific person I want to replace. I think some changes will take place simply because additional resources will need to be allocated somewhere. But I'm not fully up to speed on what changes Hanno Pevkur or the permanent secretary had already been planning. I need to review those things first.
If anyone thinks I'm going to come in with a broom and start sweeping people out, then no, because we have the people we have. Generally speaking, the Ministry of Defense's officials and Defense Forces personnel are all highly competent people.
Who will you bring with you to the ministry? Kusti Salm or Veiko-Vello Palm?
I'm fairly certain today that neither Salm nor Palm will be coming to the ministry with me. So if I do end up going there, I'll essentially be going alone.
But have you offered them positions?
I've talked and discussed these issues with them, but I have a feeling they wouldn't come.
Who will be the next permanent secretary?
I don't have a name. Several names have crossed my mind and come up in various conversations, but since I haven't spoken to those people, I'm not going to name them. That wouldn't be fair either.
Why was it necessary to get rid of Kaimo Kuusk?
You'll have to ask the prime minister that. He has stated very clearly that Kaimo Kuusk was dismissed from his position regardless of who the minister is.
But dismissing him was also one of your demands. What was your reasoning? Why did you think he needed to be dismissed?
I think it wouldn't be right for us to start discussing Kaimo Kuusk's actions here or those of anyone else. Kaimo Kuusk isn't a criminal or a villain and any further characterization beyond what has already happened would come across as criticism. I don't think either he or his loved ones deserve that, so I don't want to comment on the subject any further.
What are your plans for the election and afterward? Are you going into politics? Do you intend to run in the Riigikogu election?
Barely two weeks ago, I would have said that I would never become defense minister. I'm a little wiser now and won't say "never." But you'll find out fairly soon. The candidate lists should be finalized sometime in October or November, so you'll see then. I don't have any such plans at the moment.
Otherwise, I wouldn't have taken the position I did when I told the prime minister that becoming a member of a political party or running on its candidate list must not be a prerequisite for becoming defense minister. But today, I'm not going to say anything more. Let's keep things interesting for everyone. We'll see in October.
Have you had conversations with any political parties about possibly running?
Of the current parties that, according to opinion polls, would win seats in the Riigikogu, practically all but one have spoken to me over the past two years. And they all know that my answer so far has been no.
--

Researchers find rubber-related chemicals in Swiss milk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:43:18 UTC
17:43:18 KST

Researchers find rubber-related chemicals in Swiss milk
Swiss scientists have detected several rubber-related chemicals in Swiss raw milk. Their study suggests that dairy equipment may be an overlooked source of contamination.
For the study, a research team analysed milk samples from 17 Swiss farms, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL) said on Monday. At least one of the four rubber chemicals being tested for was detected in seven of the 17 samples. In three samples from Alpine farms located far away from busy roads, the researchers found none of the substances.
The effects of the substances found on human health are as yet unknown. Follow-up studies are planned. However, the concentrations measured in the raw milk were generally low. The results of the study were published in the journal Food Chemistry X.
Milking systems or tyres
The researchers considered one possible source of contamination to be particularly surprising: the milking systems themselves.
While examining hoses, seals and other rubber components used in milk production, they identified 14 different chemicals. According to study leader Florian Breider, it is astonishing that these compounds originated from materials that are legally approved for contact with food.
Among the materials from the milking systems examined, the researchers found, among other things, the compound 6PPD-quinone, which is known to be harmful to certain fish species. This substance is not intentionally added to rubber but is produced by oxidation as the material ages.
More
Polluting particles from car tyres – how worried should we be?
Another possible source of the contaminants is the abrasion of tyres and road surfaces. Worldwide, an estimated six million tonnes of rubber particles are released into the environment every year as a result. These particles can reach agricultural land and enter the food chain via the air, runoff water or fertilisers.
Further studies are now set to investigate how concentrations fluctuate across the seasons. In addition, the exact pathways by which the chemicals enter milk are to be investigated, in order to support the development of safer materials for contact with food.
The Federal Office for Food Safety and Veterinary Affairs and the Agroscope research institute also collaborated on the study.

150 civilians killed by Houthi fire since Sept. 3, Yemeni government says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:42:46 UTC
17:42:46 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Lina Altawell
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Yemen’s government said 150 civilians had been killed and more than 200 others injured by Houthi fire in the provinces of Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and Marib since Sept. 3.
The figures were announced in a statement by the Human Rights Ministry that was published late Sunday by the official Yemeni news agency Saba.
The ministry strongly condemned the “military escalation and widespread violations committed by the Houthi group” since Sept. 3 in several areas of Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and Marib.
The escalation included ballistic missiles and drone strikes, shelling with various types of weapons, as well as attacks on populated areas, displacement camps and convoys of civilians fleeing fighting zones, it said.
The ministry said 150 civilians were killed and more than 200 others were injured by Houthi fire, while around 85,000 people were displaced.
Property was destroyed and families were deprived of their homes, livelihoods and basic needs, it added.
Around 2,000 people had arrived in Djibouti because of the escalation, reflecting the spread of the humanitarian impact beyond Yemen, the ministry said.
It held the Houthi group responsible for the violations and called on the international community, the UN, the Human Rights Council and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to act urgently to stop attacks on civilians.
The ministry also called for the protection of displaced people, camps, evacuation convoys and medical facilities, as well as the release of abductees and arbitrarily detained people and information on the fate of the missing.
Territorial control in Yemen has changed significantly in recent days, with the Houthis announcing control of several districts on the western coast as well as islands in the Red Sea, including Mayyun Island, also known as Perim Island, in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemeni government forces announced advances in Al-Jawf province near the Saudi border and said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
In addition to repelling a major attack on Marib, they also reported airstrikes on Houthi targets in and around Mokha and in areas of Taiz, Lahij and Al-Dhale provinces, saying military vehicles and weapons were destroyed.
Confrontations between government forces and the Houthis have escalated since early July 2026, following years of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Turkish court jails 16 in Izmir after raids on LGBTQ+ groups
ANKARA, Sept 14 - A Turkish court ordered the detention of 16 people pending trial in the western province of Izmir as part of a government campaign that has included sweeping raids on LGBTQ+ associations, a prosecutor's office said on Monday.
The chief prosecutor's office in the western province of Izmir said 18 suspects had been detained under the "My Family is Safe" operation, with 16 of them ordered to be remanded in jail and the other two placed under judicial supervision.
A group protesting the raids and detentions scuffled with police in Izmir on Monday, and the police used pepper spray to disperse the crowd.
The group marched in downtown Izmir earlier, chanting slogans in support of LGBTQ+ individuals. They were later surrounded by police, who told the group to end their protest and disperse, leading to arguments and scuffles.
Police did not allow pro-LGBTQ+ signs and flags during the demonstration and some people were affected by pepper spray used by police to disperse the group.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on Sunday the investigations, coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin, involved 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.
The government says the operation is aimed at protecting children and family values. Authorities detained 26 people in Istanbul and 21 in Ankara over the weekend and raided the offices of several LGBTQ+ associations.
Rights groups accuse the government of increasingly targeting the LGBTQ+ community through rhetoric, restrictions and legal measures.
The Turkish Human Rights Association described the operation as "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society".
Nacho Sanchez Amor, the European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur, called the arrests "a shocking escalation" of repression.
Prosecutors have said the investigations cover alleged offences including prostitution and obscenity, and that children and minors were being inappropriately influenced on issues relating to sexual orientation and gender identity.
The operation comes as President Tayyip Erdogan promotes a "Decade of Family and Population" aimed at tackling falling birth rates and an ageing demographic.
In an official circular released on Monday, the Justice Ministry also instructed all prosecutors to promptly assess reports of obscene and criminal activities targeting children and young people, immediately secure digital evidence, and, where necessary, seek access blocks on online content.
Turkish authorities also banned access to websites and social media accounts of various LGBTQ+ associations, individuals and independent media outlets including the X account of Amnesty International's Turkey branch. REUTERS

Turkish Lira deposit rates hit lowest level since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:40:45 UTC
17:40:45 KST

(AA Photo)
The average interest rate on Turkish Lira deposits with maturities of one to three months fell to 37.3 percent as of Sept. 4, its lowest level since 2023, Central Bank data showed.
Personal loan rates rose to 49.8 percent after recently falling to 48.3 percent, while commercial loan rates increased to 40.8 percent from a recent low of 39.3 percent.
Deposit rates had already fallen below 40 percent in late July, before the Central Bank’s Aug. 23 decision to resume one-week repo auctions.
The auctions, suspended since March 1, allow banks to borrow at the 37 percent policy rate rather than the 40 percent overnight lending rate. The change lowered banks’ funding costs without a formal policy rate cut.
Analysts had warned that lending rules would limit the impact of cheaper funding on loan rates.
The Central Bank held its policy rate at 37 percent on Sept. 10. Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan have forecast cuts of 100 basis points at each of the year’s two remaining policy meetings, in October and December, taking the rate to 35 percent by year-end.
Bank of America expects a single 100-basis-point cut in October, leaving the rate at 36 percent at the end of the year.
Investors are also awaiting the U.S. Federal Reserve’s Sept. 15–16 meeting, with markets anticipating a 25-basis-point increase.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh signaled at Jackson Hole on Aug. 28 that further policy action could be needed if inflation failed to move toward the Fed’s target at a sufficient pace.

This happened in early July, when Iranian forces opened fire on three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s president, the General of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps and the Supreme National Security Council were all unaware of the strikes. The paper explains that the hard-liners succeeded because the man who has the power to resolve such disputes – the new supreme leader Khamenei – has been a ghost since taking office in March after his father was killed by joint US-Israeli strikes. According to three Iranian officials, even the president has questioned the authenticity of the statements attributed to the supreme leader.
Who orchestrated the strikes? Three anonymous Iranian officials interviewed by the paper point to one man whom the paper called the “influential spymaster”, cleric Hossein Taeb. He has opposed a peace deal with the United States from the very beginning. In a recent speech, he said he is not opposed to negotiations but is against the “excessive demands of the enemy” that have “no place in Iran’s politics”. The report also says that Taeb played a key role in selecting Khamenei junior after the death of his father.
Next, another type of crisis: artificial intelligence. US President Donald Trump is downplaying calls for an AI slowdown, reports the US’s NPR. There are concerns that AI could go rogue, and several tech leaders are saying we should hit the brakes. But for Trump, the warnings are “exaggerated” and come from “negative forces” making false claims.
But a couple of articles show a different reality: Wired Magazine interviewed the mathematician Steven Strogatz, who started to cry when he talked about the AI-driven breakthroughs in his field. He co-wrote a book about how math is moving beyond human understanding and why this is making him “really terrified”. A headline from The Atlantic reads, “It’s all fun and games until you give AI your credit card”. It’s an article about how AI personal assistants act on people’s behalf in the real world and all the strange things that could go – and already are going – wrong.
Finally, an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal says that "yes, children really are getting dumber". According to the author, COVID-19 and AI are among the factors degrading the quality of American education. Thau author says that “as machines get smarter, kids are getting dumber” and rapid advances in AI go hand in hand with “astonishing decline in student learning”. The article cites a study by the Programme for International Student Assessment – or PISA – that measures the skills of 15-year-olds across the world. The most troubling decline is in the skills that matter the most, according to the report: evaluating information, making connections and thinking critically about what we read. The conclusion: that “in a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise”.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:38:00 EEST

One day of war costs Ukraine US$190 million in 2026 – Budget Committee chief
One day of war in 2026 costs Ukraine's state budget US$190 million, excluding weapons provided by international partners.
Source: Roksolana Pidlasa, chair of the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee
Details: In 2024, one day of war cost Ukraine US$140 million.
Pidlasa said the main reason for the increase in the cost of the war is the expansion of the Armed Forces and, consequently, the greater number of military personnel and their families who receive state support.
Another reason is the need for more weapons, particularly medium- and long-range strike capabilities used to target Russian oil refineries.
Pidlasa said that national security and defence had cost almost US$42 billion over the first eight months of the year, excluding military assistance provided in kind. Meanwhile, Ukraine had raised only US$39 billion from its own resources, including revenues and domestic government bonds, meaning that the country was no longer able to cover even the share of expenditure that it had previously financed itself.
She added that the defence forces had also reported an additional funding requirement of US$27 billion by the end of the year.
Background: In early September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced that the government was introducing strict austerity measures for budget funds not earmarked for defence needs.

Auto output falls 7.3 pct in first eight months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:37:35 UTC
17:37:35 KST

Türkiye’s automotive production fell 7.3 percent year-on-year to 841,583 vehicles in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Automotive Manufacturers Association (OSD).
Passenger car output declined nearly 19 percent to 458,169, while commercial vehicle production rose 12 percent. Output increased 12 percent for light commercial vehicles and 7 percent for heavy commercial vehicles.
Including tractors, total production reached 854,860 units. The industry’s capacity utilization rate stood at 59 percent.
Vehicle exports fell 12 percent to 597,594 units in January-August. Passenger car shipments dropped 28 percent by volume, while commercial vehicle exports rose 9 percent.
Automotive export earnings increased 2.5 percent to $27.2 billion, according to Turkish Exporters Assembly data. The industry retained first place in the assembly’s sectoral export rankings.
Passenger car export revenue fell 9 percent to $6.8 billion, according to the Uludağ Automotive Industry Exporters’ Association. Exports by vehicle manufacturers rose 1 percent in dollar terms, while those by suppliers increased 4 percent.
Domestic vehicle sales declined 12 percent to 745,597 units. Passenger car sales fell 14 percent to 564,241, while the commercial vehicle market contracted 5 percent.
Locally produced vehicles accounted for 35 percent of passenger car sales and 23 percent of the light commercial vehicle market.

Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:31:19 UTC
17:31:19 KST

Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Government organisations have been working together to get the financial penalties they owe for missing their deadlines scrapped, an investigation by newspaper Trouw has found.
Officials at the immigration service IND, the benefits agency UWV and the tax office’s benefits arm have been in communication about whether they can push for a complete legal change, freeing them from any fines for failure to comply with their duties.
Internal emails and memos obtained via freedom of information requests show an IND adviser writing to a counterpart at the tax office last year saying they’re looking into abolishing penalties altogether and wants to “see whether abolition for the whole of administrative law is possible”.
Since 2009, anyone whose application for a permit, benefit or allowance is not decided within the legal deadline can be entitled to remedial payments.
The relevant agency is first put on notice, and then if it still fails to decide within two weeks, it owes a daily penalty, rising to a maximum of €1,442, and the applicant can go to court, where a judge can impose an even higher one.
The IND is by far the biggest payer. It paid out nearly €100 million in the first half of this year, almost all of it on asylum cases. Some individual claimants received over €100,000. The agencies say they cannot meet their deadlines because of staff shortages and rising caseloads.
Immigration applicants have already lost the right to automatic penalty payments under an earlier law. In March, MPs from the SGP, ChristenUnie, JA21 and VVD voted to scrap court-imposed ones too, for all immigration cases including residence permits.
The Senate is expected to debate it on September 22, broadcaster NOS reported. Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has said he wants the same for the UWV.
 Asked about the emails, an IND spokesperson told Trouw the service is in contact with agencies facing “the same problems” and that “experiences are exchanged”.

Turkey detains dozens in major anti-LGBTQ raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:31:17 UTC
17:31:17 KST

Breadcrumb
As part of 'Decade of the Family', Turkey detains dozens in major anti-LGBTQ raids
Turkish police on Sunday swooped on queer-friendly bars and the homes of LGBTQ activists, arresting at least 60 people in raids authorities said were aimed at "boosting traditional family values", officials and activists said.
Turkey's LGBTQ community has frequently been targeted by the government, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing it as a "deviant movement" of "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.
Sunday's raid came a day after the accounts of more than a dozen Turkish LGBTQ organisations were blocked on X at the request of the authorities, according to a watchdog.
"As part of the 'My Family is Safe' operations... carried out in collaboration with our police and gendarmerie forces, legal proceedings have been initiated against 162 suspects, 9 organisations and 13 companies in ... a total of 15 provinces," Justice Minister Akin Gurlek posted on X. Many were around Istanbul and Ankara.
Gurlek said the raids were part of the "Decade of the Family" proclaimed by Erdogan, aimed at "protecting our children, the institution of the family and social order".
According to prosecutors in Ankara, Istanbul and Izmir, quoted by the state news agency Anadolu, at least 63 people were detained.
LGBTQ and women's rights activists form one of the main centres of resistance to the conservative government in power since 2002.
In Istanbul, police raided several gay bars and a nightclub regarded as a haven for the LGBTQ community, according to video footage from pro-government media.
Also targeted was a men's hammam reputed to be a venue for prostitution.
LGBTQ rights organisation Kaos GL, whose offices were searched and whose leaders were taken into custody, earlier stated that "nearly 50 defenders of the rights of LGBTQ people (...) have been taken into custody or are subject to legal proceedings involving interrogations or detentions" across the country.
According to the group, judicial authorities in Ankara had alleged that Kaos GL made "posts containing obscenity" on its website and social media channels and that the content was accessible to children.
While same-sex relations are not a criminal offence in Turkey, homophobia is widespread.
Blatant violation
The European Union parliament's rapporteur on Turkey condemned the arrests as "a shocking escalation in the repression" in the country Turkey. Turkey's efforts to join the EU have been frozen in recent years, but it remains a key trade and political partner.
"This imposition of a moral agenda is a blatant violation of fundamental rights & Turkey's international commitments taking the country down a dark path," Nacho Sanchez Amor wrote on X.
"Existence cannot be banned or restricted. LGBTI+ rights are human rights!" Ozgul Saki, an MP from the pro-Kurdish left-wing DEM party in Istanbul, said on X.

Reform declines to say if £72m donors returned to UK within 12-month limit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:30:35 UTC
17:30:35 KST

Reform UK’s deputy leader has declined to say when two crypto billionaires who gave a combined £72m to the party returned to the UK, as the architect of a review into overseas donations said anyone here for less than 12 months would be subject to a limit on donations.
Richard Tice said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Ben Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Christopher Harborne spent in Britain.
“I’m not their executive assistant responsible for their day-to-day diary,” Tice told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme when asked about the details of their UK residencies.
He added: “Everything we’re doing is in accordance with the existing rules and the rules of the legislation that’s going through parliament as we speak.”
The legislation referred to, the representation of the people bill, does not currently contain any overall cap on individual donations, after lobbying from Labour-backing trade unions.
In response to the mega-donations by Harborne and Delo, trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at the bill. But in the wake of a report on overseas influence on UK politics by Sir Philip Rycroft, a former senior civil servant, Britons living overseas will be limited to giving a maximum of £100,000.
The bill, which goes further than some of Rycroft’s recommendations, sets out that the cap applies to anyone who was not UK-resident for electoral purposes for at least a year from March 2026, applying retrospectively once the bill becomes law.
Speaking to Today, Rycroft said that while he could not comment on the circumstances of Delo or Harborne, the residency rules would apply.
“What I do understand is that the way the law will work, it will implement my recommendation on a limit for Brits abroad, as it were. But there will also be rules on, if they return to the UK, how long they have to live in the UK before they can count as domestic donors.
“And my understanding is that they will have to be living in the UK for at least a full calendar year. Once they met that requirement, then they become essentially a domestic donor.”
Rycroft said his review concluded a cap on money from overseas-based British donors was important as it was harder to trace the origins of overseas money, and that it was “a question of fairness” in limiting the influence of “people who had chosen to take their wealth abroad and to be taxed abroad”.
The two separate donations of £36m by Harborne and Delo, announced within 24 hours, are unprecedented in UK political history and will give Reform enormously boosted resources before the next election.
Delo was based in Hong Kong but has returned to the UK. Asked when, Tice said this had happened “many, many months ago”. Harborne is registered to vote in the UK, but also lives in Thailand.
Asked how he could know the donations were permissible under the new rules, Tice said Reform’s compliance department had looked into it. But he condemned the retrospective plans of the bill, telling BBC One’s Breakfast that it was the action of “a socialist government that wants to retrospectively change the rules and regulations in order to protect themselves from a bit of competition”.
Speaking to Sky News, the schools minister Georgia Gould said the way the bill had been drafted was deliberate. Gould said: “The rules have been very clear, and the reason why it was applied retrospectively is because the risk is if you didn’t do that, then lots of donations would suddenly start flowing through before the legislation.
“The really important thing is this was an independent report that looked into these really serious issues that many people are concerned about, foreign interference in politics, and we made very clear at the time that it would be retrospective for good reason.”

At least 108 people have been rescued and six bodies recovered after the vessel overturned in the waters off Masalembo, about 148 km from Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province.
Survivors were taken to a temporary medical post at Trisakti Port in Banjarmasin. Some said passengers rushed to the upper deck and scrambled for life jackets as the ferry began to list.
According to its manifest, the ferry was carrying 243 people: 213 passengers and 30 crew, as well as 89 vehicles. The passenger breakdown included 59 adult passengers, one child, and 126 drivers and vehicle assistants, plus 27 ship‑related workers. The vessel lost contact at about 2 a.m. local time on Sunday after its captain reported waves of up to 3 metres and a heavy list to starboard; a passing helicopter later confirmed it had capsized. Authorities received a distress call around two hours after contact was lost.
By Monday, at least 622 personnel had been deployed on 17 vessels and five aircraft, including navy ships and helicopters, to search the area around the wreck. The national search and rescue agency (Basarnas) said divers and navy‑operated underwater drones would be used to look inside and around the overturned hull, but rough seas and strong currents were hampering efforts. Officials said the ferry was not overloaded and was carrying fewer than its maximum capacity of 500 people, though they noted that actual passenger numbers in Indonesia often differ from manifests.
The 119-metre roll-on/roll-off ferry was built in Japan in 1987 and sold to Indonesia last year. It left Surabaya in East Java on Saturday afternoon bound for Banjarmasin, but encountered severe weather overnight. The cause of the capsizing, whether weather-related, technical failure or human error, remains under investigation as families gathered at ports in Surabaya and Banjarmasin awaiting news of missing relatives.

Israeli experts are warning that AI is exponentially increasing cyber threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:28:13 UTC
17:28:13 KST

A global coalition of more than 150 cybersecurity companies has warned that artificial intelligence is rapidly increasing the speed and scale of cyberattacks, and called on governments and businesses to update their defenses before attackers gain a lasting advantage.
Among the signatories are major industry players, including Anthropic, OpenAI, KPMG, Visa, Oracle, Microsoft, and Palo Alto. They called on organizations to “raise the security bar” and for governments to immediately provide and coordinate defensive cyber technology at the local, national, and international levels.
The coalition’s statement said that AI systems now allow attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities far faster than human defenders can respond.
“In the coming months, AI-enabled cyberattacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable. The companies and public services our communities depend on - from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet - are at risk,” the letter said.
KPMG’s head of cybersecurity in Israel, Omer Or, told The Jerusalem Post that organizations are entering a period where traditional security models may no longer be sufficient. Or, who has spent more than two decades in senior government roles, described the current shift as unprecedented, with AI now boosting offensive cyber capabilities by all levels of threat actors.
“We are already in a rapid technological race, and AI is moving very quickly,” he said. “If we look at offensive cyber of all levels, from the individual hacker to criminal cartels and state actors, all are in the process of getting a boost to their offensive capabilities and have access to tools that were once only available to state actors. That creates a change in the equation.”
According to Or, one of the most significant shifts involves zero‑day vulnerabilities, which were previously the domain of highly resourced state actors.
“With these frontier models, we see the pace at which attackers can produce zero‑day vulnerabilities, 100 times more than humans can do on their own,” Or said, adding that AI is now finding weaknesses in legacy and operational‑technology systems that have historically been overlooked. “These areas received less attention and now it’s becoming identical.”
Old problems, new speed
While some imagine AI will introduce exotic new attack types, Ariel Litmanovich, founder and CTO of Aryon Security, told the Post that the opposite is true.
“Most people imagine that the main threat would be new futuristic attacks, but actually AI makes the weaknesses much easier to find and exploit. And that’s what the letter says.”
Litmanovich, who previously worked on the IDF’s transition to public cloud environments, said the vulnerabilities attackers are exploiting today, including misconfigurations, excessive permissions, and weak authentication, are the same ones that have plagued organizations for years. The only thing that has changed is the pace.
In the past, organizations could afford slow remediation cycles. A cloud resource might be deployed insecurely, detected later by a security tool, and fixed eventually. That model, Litmanovich said, no longer works.
“It’s the same problems; it’s just more dangerous because defenders don’t have the time to fix them. Time to exploit has gone down disproportionately because of AI,” he said. “Attackers can increasingly scan, analyze, adapt, and exploit the vulnerabilities or security issues at a speed and scale that humans cannot match manually. If defenders want to be ahead, they need to find a way to be faster than the attacker.”
To do so would require integrating AI into an organization’s internal defensive operations and quickly identifying anomalies. Otherwise, attackers will continue to exploit vulnerabilities and defenders won’t have enough time to remediate and fix the problems.
“Cybersecurity needs to move towards containment, resilience, and a quick incident response for business continuity,” he said. “Organizations have to be more proactive and preventative to stay ahead and break the status quo. You can’t fight machines and AI with humans. Humans can’t win against AI.”

After a decade of division: What the disarming of Yazidi forces means for their future - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:28:13 UTC
17:28:13 KST

The Yazidi militia, Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS), has agreed to hand over its arms and integrate into the Iraqi security forces. The Iraqi Prime Minister’s Office said on September 11 that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi “announced that the Sinjar Resistance Units will commence handing over their weapons to the state, and that Sinjar Mountain will be under the full authority of the federal government and its security and administrative institutions.”
The government emphasized that “confining weapons to the hands of the state and unifying security decision-making represent the foundation for protecting the people of the district, consolidating its stability, and ensuring its future.”
This is part of a broader push by Baghdad to get various armed groups in Iraq to hand over their weapons to the state. It has been an easier process with the YBS than with the more powerful Iranian-backed militias.
The deal with the YBS is important. It could pave the way for more peace and security in the Yazidi region in and around Mount Sinjar, also called Shingal. This area is populated by the Yazidi minority.
Massacre of Yazidis a major reason for intervention against ISIS
In 2014, ISIS, the Islamic State, attacked the Yazidis, massacring thousands and carrying out a genocide against the group. ISIS also kidnapped thousands of women and children, forcing them into slavery. The massacre of the Yazidis, along with the heart-wrenching scenes of hundreds of thousands fleeing the attacks, was among the reasons the United States and other countries intervened to help fight ISIS.
Many Yazidis were saved in 2014 in an operation by the People’s Protection Units (YPG) that crossed the border from Syria to help them flee. The YPG is linked to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). This led some Yazidis to choose to join a local Iraqi group called the YBS, which was linked to the PKK. This led to several overlapping controversies.
The PKK has been fighting Turkey for decades. Turkey has operated in Iraq against the PKK since the 1990s. The emergence of the YBS led to Turkey setting its sights on Sinjar, delivering several rounds of airstrikes over the years.
The Yazidis found themselves divided between those who were working with the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq and its Peshmerga, and those working with Baghdad, as well as those linked to the YBS. For a small and vulnerable minority, living in an economically deprived landscape that had just emerged from genocide and war, these divisions led to immense challenges.
For years, Sinjar has been largely ignored by Baghdad. However, changes in Ankara and Damascus may now have an effect.
Turkey is working on a peace deal with the PKK, hoping to see the group dissolved. The SDF in Syria has already been dissolved. The SDF was formed with the support of the YPG.
With the YBS now also moving toward laying down its arms, this basically means a swath of groups linked to the PKK are shifting back to civilian life. This could be good news for Sinjar because Turkey has objected to any real progress there as long as the YBS is active.
Iraqi parliamentarian Murad Ismail has played a key role. Iraq’s Prime Minister’s Office said that the recent meeting “came during his [the prime minister’s] reception today, Friday, of a delegation from the leadership of the Yazidi Cause Alliance and the head of its parliamentary bloc, MP Murad Ismail, along with the leadership of the Sinjar Resistance Units, to discuss the overall situation in Sinjar district and the files related to its stability, reconstruction, and the future of its people.”
Iraq’s prime minister said that “the state will guarantee the rights of members of the Sinjar Resistance Units and the Women’s Units and [respect] their sacrifices, by regulating their status and integrating the qualified among them into Iraqi security institutions in accordance with legal and official frameworks.”
Baghdad says it will focus on the Sinjar district and its “needs for infrastructure projects and reconstruction, the file of compensating those affected and preparing suitable conditions for the return of the displaced to their areas, in addition to addressing a number of administrative issues related to the management of the district and its institutions and government departments, as well as the management of the Sinjar Reconstruction Fund.”
This is important because Baghdad is now speaking of a project that may support one million “residential plots of land and [is] working to prepare the necessary conditions for the complete return of the displaced to their areas, and following up on the file of reconstructing Sinjar district and providing its service requirements, in a way that contributes to stabilizing the population and enhancing social and economic stability.”
Ismail posted on X/Twitter about the historic agreement “that resolves the integration of the Yazidi Resistance Forces – YBS – into the ranks of their brothers in the official security forces, the confinement of arms to the hands of the state, and the turning of an important page that preserves the rights of our people within the framework of the law and the constitution.”
Ismail, as head of the Yazidi Cause Alliance Bloc, said he was working with “various segments of our people, including the Sinjar Resistance Units.” He added: “For today we have succeeded in reaching a historic agreement that preserves the security and sovereignty of our beloved Iraq and grants our youth who bore arms the opportunity to integrate with their brothers in the other security forces, to protect their region and land and every inch of Iraqi soil wherever the national need calls for it.”
Extremist groups, al-Qaeda historically threaten Yazidis
It’s worth taking a step back to recall some of the complex and tragic history here.
The Yazidis suffered from the rise of the Iraqi insurgency and extremist groups that emerged after the US invasion in 2003. In 2007, four coordinated car bombings targeted Yazidi towns near Tel Ezer (known in Arabic as al-Qahtaniyah) in northern Iraq, near the Syrian border. Hundreds of people were killed. Gunmen also massacred Yazidis on a bus. Al Qaeda was suspected of being behind the attacks. Kurdish Peshmerga were deployed in some areas to help defend the towns. Reports indicated that they attempted a tactic they were using in other areas, digging ditches and trenches around towns to physically stop suicide car bombings.
This rudimentary type of defense continued until June 2014, when ISIS swept into Mosul, south of Sinjar. The Yazidis in Sinjar were left mostly defenseless, carrying only Kalashnikov rifles (AKs) and small arms. With the collapse of two Iraqi divisions, ISIS was far better armed than the Yazidis or the Peshmerga. Minorities, especially Christians, fled Mosul to safety in the Kurdistan Region. In August 2014, ISIS attacked Sinjar, rapidly taking over Yazidi villages and capturing thousands of people who were massacred and sold into slavery. People fled to Mount Sinjar, where they were dying of thirst in the hot summer.
After the YPG intervention, the Peshmerga launched an offensive that eventually helped push back ISIS. Yazidi resistance fighters also held out, such as Qasim Shesho, a well-known commander from the area.
Sinjar was liberated in November 2015. Dozens of mass graves were found containing the bodies of Yazidis murdered by ISIS. The result of the liberation battles was a patchwork of various armed groups, with Yazidis joining many of them.
In 2017, after a Kurdistan Regional Government referendum on independence, the Iraqi government and Shi’ite militias launched an offensive into Sinjar. The Kurdish Peshmerga were pushed back, but the YBS remained.
Airstrikes by Turkey followed, and the YBS also clashed with the Iraqi security forces. In March 2025, the YBS clashed with an Iraqi unit, leading to several Iraqi soldiers being wounded. The YBS was outraged after it emerged that the Iraqi soldiers had referred to them as “terrorists.” They said, “everyone knows that the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS) are the force that defended and liberated Sinjar from ISIS mercenaries, and it is the force that took over the protection of Sinjar’s security afterward.”
Now in 2026, all this complex and tragic history, going back to 2007, may be changing. If Sinjar can become a peaceful area, without various armed groups, and Iraq can invest in it, things may turn out better. The changes in Syria, stabilizing it as well, could help Iraq. It’s unclear at the moment whether these two trends, on both sides of the border, will progress.

====================================================================================================

Could AI threaten humanity? Here’s what’s behind the debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:27:03 UTC
17:27:03 KST

New warnings from within the artificial intelligence industry have revived a long-running debate over whether advanced AI could escape human control and ultimately threaten humanity’s survival, and whether the companies developing the technology are doing enough to prevent such a scenario.
The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning on Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place.
Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might pose to humanity were receiving too little attention.
Here’s what we know about the recent dire predictions and whether any brakes might be put on AI advancement:
AI models are becoming more powerful
Concerns over the potential risks of the technology are rising as new AI models become more powerful, heightening both the potential for misuse by people with criminal aims, such as creating and spreading a disease, and the risk of AI systems going rogue in a dangerous way.
Anthropic disclosed last week that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.
The company said it put stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could be used to make weapons but noted that “as models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer.”
Last year, Anthropic reported that hackers used the company’s AI in a cyberattack targeting about 30 companies and government agencies around the world.
Multiple AI models have acted on their own
When an AI agent “goes rogue,” it means the AI has taken action beyond the task it was asked to perform.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, said in July that their AI models had succeeded in acting on their own.
Anthropic disclosed that three AI models — Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model — hacked into three other organisations during testing just days after OpenAI revealed that its AI system hacked into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face.
OpenAI described the intrusion by a combination of models, including its newly released GPT‑5.6 Sol and an “even more capable” model that was still being tested internally, as a “significant security incident.”
Meta followed suit in early August with a similar case of an AI model finding ways around another company's digital security.
Although some observers noted that people had disabled some guardrails in the OpenAI and Anthropic cases, the episodes seemed to reflect one of the biggest fears around AI: that if models achieve artificial general intelligence, or AGI, a loosely defined term for AI that can match or surpass human abilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks, the technology could cause an irreversible catastrophic event or subjugate the human race.
How or when AI might cause a catastrophe is debated
Doomsday scenarios generally fall into two categories: An AI that achieves self-improving superintelligence controls people instead of vice versa, or AI used by a “rogue state” or “nefarious actors”.
Worries that artificial intelligence might overcome human limits on its reach or actions are not new.
Alan Turing, a British mathematician widely regarded as one of the earliest authorities on artificial intelligence, predicted in 1951 that AI would eventually take control from humans.
Less than a decade later, Norbert Wiener, another mathematician, warned that intelligent machines would seek to accomplish their own objectives and humans would not be able to stop them.
In 2026, how reasonable are fears that AI, either by escaping human control or through misuse by unscrupulous people, could cause a cataclysmic event or the downfall of civilisation?
No one knows.
Experts across computer science, philosophy and other fields have envisioned numerous routes by which a future AI system might cause a global catastrophe, either by escaping human control or in the hands of unscrupulous people.
They range from deploying weapons and identifying a lethal pathogen to manipulating governments into conflict or disrupting the food, energy and communications networks societies rely on to function.
There is no widely accepted estimate for how soon any of these scenarios might happen and no consensus on their likelihood.
In 2023, the nonprofit Center for AI Safety issued a statement cosigned by more than 350 researchers and technology executives, including Anthropic's Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, saying: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.”
The 2026 International AI Safety Report, written with guidance from more than 100 independent experts, says current systems show early signs of some relevant capabilities but not at levels that could enable a loss of control, and describes the risk’s likelihood, nature and timing as “unusually ambiguous.”
Some are stressing the need for AI safeguards before it's too late
An Anthropic researcher said last week he was resigning from the company over concerns that neither the company nor its competitors were acting responsibly in developing the technology.
In social media posts, Jacob Coxon estimated a 10 percent chance of AI causing human extinction within the next decade and said both Anthropic and OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Altman announced that OpenAI will not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render "unacceptable" even a 10 percent risk that AI could cause human extinction by decade's end.
Researchers have called for a slowdown of AI development and warned for years that the technology could pose existential risks to humanity.
Following the recent incidents, experts called for improved testing by AI companies and more dialogue between the US and China to come up with shared solutions.
But AI is growing so fast that government and evaluation systems are struggling to keep pace with the technology. Countries are cobbling together their own laws, some conflicting.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping warned at a conference in July of the need to keep AI from evading human control.
The Trump administration initially demonstrated reluctance to regulate AI but has become more keen to reduce cybersecurity risks.
On Sunday, President Trump downplayed the necessity for his administration to check AI development, but acknowledged the need for some regulation.

Gaza Health Ministry says WHO to stop diesel supplies to over 20 hospitals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:24:32 UTC
17:24:32 KST

Nour Mahd Ali Abuaisha and Lina Altawell
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Gaza Health Ministry Director-General Munir al-Bursh said Monday that the World Health Organization (WHO) has decided to stop supplying diesel to more than 20 hospitals and health centers in the besieged coastal enclave due to a funding shortfall.
“In light of the severe shortage of fuel and oils, and the failure to deliver the minimum needed to operate hospitals and health centers in the Gaza Strip, the WHO announced the suspension of diesel supplies to more than 20 hospitals and health centers, starting Sept. 19, due to a lack of funding,” Bursh said in a statement.
There was no immediate comment from the WHO on the decision cited by Gaza’s Health Ministry, although the organization has warned in recent months of declining funding for its activities and programs.
“The limited quantities of fuel reaching the enclave barely keep health facilities alive,” Bursh said.
“The halt in supplies does not only mean generators going dark, but the shutdown of operating rooms and intensive care units, the disruption of ventilators and oxygen stations, and threats to the lives of children in incubators, dialysis patients, the wounded and those with chronic diseases,” he added.
He said that the crisis would also paralyze ambulances and cold chains for medicines and vaccines.
“The fuel crisis is pushing hospitals toward complete shutdown and leaving patients facing preventable death,” Bursh said, describing the cutting of fuel from hospitals as “silent killing of patients in their beds.”
He called on the WHO, donors and the international community to assume their urgent responsibilities, ensure continued supplies of fuel and oils in sufficient quantities, and guarantee their safe and sustainable delivery to all health facilities.
 
Power generators stop working
The announcement coincides with a shortage of oil and spare parts for power generators operating in Gaza’s hospitals, which caused several of them to stop working, according to a Health Ministry statement Sunday.
“The past few days have seen several generators stop working due to the lack of oils, spare parts and sufficient fuel quantities,” the ministry said.
It added that the shortage of generator oil in Gaza hospitals is worsening the difficulty of keeping them running to meet daily electricity needs.
Power generators are the main source of electricity for hospitals to operate vital departments and medical equipment amid a complete power outage across Gaza for the third consecutive year since the start of Israel’s genocidal war in October 2023.
The generators also stop working because of fuel shortages, amid Israel’s closure of the Kerem Shalom crossing between Gaza and Israel since October 2023 and the Israeli army’s occupation and control of the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt since May 2024.
Since then, the two crossings have been opened only on a limited basis for the passage of dozens of patients, wounded people and returnees to Gaza, as well as the entry of limited humanitarian, relief and medical aid.
The Gaza government media office has repeatedly said Israel is evading its obligations under the ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025, including allowing the agreed quantities of aid and fuel needed for vital sectors to enter the enclave.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 injured, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

North Korea says recent drill shows 'huge destructive power'
September 14, 2026
North Korea said Monday that its recent "live-fire" drill demonstrated "huge destructive power."
During the test on Saturday, different types of weapons were fired simultaneously, with the aim of boosting the morale of North Korean troops and improving their capabilities to "completely collapse the enemy," according to the state news agency KCNA.
KCNA reported that the drill involved five army units and tested attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, tactical ballistic missiles, and other weapons systems.
Experts say North Korea is not slowing down its weapons activities, even after US President Donald Trump recently scaled back a military exercise with South Korea in an apparent effort to revive diplomacy with leader Kim Jong Un.
North Korea claims great military power
North Korean Marshal Pak Jong Chon was cited by KCNA as saying the drill intended to "improve the level of specialization to bring down the enemy's armed forces organizationally and structurally once an order is issued." He added that the mobilized weapons systems demonstrated "the huge destructive power of concentrated fire."
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said several missiles were fired on Saturday and traveled about 250 kilometers (155 miles) into North Korea's eastern waters.
The distances indicate that the weapons are designed to strike targets in South Korea, including US military bases.
North Korea's response to 'provocations'
The firing drill came a day after the United States, South Korea, and Japan concluded a trilateral military exercise that North Korea considers a provocation.
In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise conducted jointly with South Korea. According to the US president, the decision was due to his good relationship with Kim Jong Un.
North Korea rejected Trump's move, saying that shortening the exercise did not change its "provocative, aggressive nature."
The exercise ended six days earlier than originally scheduled.
Experts say Kim Jong Un likely believes his position in any potential diplomacy with the US has improved since his first meetings with Trump in 2018 and 2019. Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the US abandons its "hostile policy" toward his country and recognizes what he calls North Korea's status as a nuclear state.
